# THE HISTORY OF THE TWO WORLDS,
# NAMELY THE GREATER and THE LESSER,
# METAPHYSICAL, PHYSICAL, AND TECHNICAL.
## Divided into two Volumes according to the distinction of the COSMOS.
## BY THE AUTHOR ROBERT FLUDD, also known as "of the Floods," <note>original: "de Fluctibus"</note> Esquire and Doctor of Medicine of Oxford.
### Volume One
### Concerning the History of the Macrocosm <term>Macrocosm: From the Greek 'makros' (large) and 'kosmos' (world); the universe as a whole.</term> divided into two treatises.

**Of which**

*   **The First is about**
    *   The Metaphysical origin of the Macrocosm and its creatures.
    *   The Physical progress of the Macrocosm in generation and decay.

# TO GOD
## THE BEST AND GREATEST,
### TO MY INCOMPREHENSIBLE CREATOR,

->BE GLORY, PRAISE, HONOR, BLESSING<-
->AND TRIUMPHANT VICTORY,<-
->FOREVER AND EVER,<-
->AMEN.<-

It is yours, O **Nature naturing** <term>Natura naturans: A philosophical term referring to God as the active, creative force of the universe, rather than the physical world itself.</term>, infinite and glorious, to regenerate my soul—which is wasting away in ignorance—by the power of your splendor. It is yours, through the wonderful clarity of the Holy Spirit of discipline, to awaken, bring to life, and raise to the true summit or peak of knowledge those sparks of reason remaining after the fall of Adam <note>In early modern thought, the "fall of Adam" was believed to have physically and mentally dimmed human intellect; the author seeks to recover this lost "divine" light.</note>, which have been most miserably submerged for a long time in the abyss of bodily darkness. May your will be done in the celestial and immortal part of me, a man, just as it is in the earthly and mortal part, so that whatever is produced by and within them may all, through proper consideration, be a sharer in your goodness. Thus will this heartfelt offering, consecration, and, as it were, sacrifice of mine be pleasing to your most holy divinity. Thus the fruit of your goodness within me—receiving the rays of its own growth, which flow from your bright fountain of total and unique goodness—shall, with your divine Spirit leading the way, fly upward in a true resurrection with its whole self transfigured. Let it rejoice to visit its super-celestial homeland, in which you, **Highest Prince and greatest Emperor**, live and reign perpetually. Turn the hearts of malevolent readers toward better things, I pray; let them distinguish with open eyes your true light from the darkness of the Devil. Be favorable and gracious to me, O good God, who lives forever.

**Your Creature,**

->*the most unworthy of all.*<-

**I, A MAN.**

\* \*
\*

# TO THE MOST SERENE AND MIGHTY PRINCE
# JAMES
## OF THE EMPEROR
### OF THE HEAVENS AND THE EARTHS,
### THE THRICE GREATEST, AND OF HIS
### INCOMPREHENSIBLE CREATOR, IN THE KINGDOMS
### OF GREAT BRITAIN, FRANCE, AND IRELAND,
### THE IMMEDIATE MINISTER AND RULER, <insert>~~AND FAITHFUL DEFEND-~~</insert> <note>The struck-through text original: "FIDELIQUE PROPUGNA-". Combined with the next line, it forms "propugnatori" (defender). The strike-through suggests a contemporary correction or a deliberate omission of the King's title as "Defender of the Faith" in this specific context.</note>

->-er: Health of soul and body, joy in JESUS CHRIST, the abolition<-
->of darkness, and the enjoyment of super-celestial light through<-
->the illumination of the HOLY SPIRIT.<-

---

To whomever the secrets and sacred mysteries of Nature—everywhere revealed and offered to us by God, the best and greatest—are denied understanding; most powerful King and one most fortified in knowledge, for that person to know himself and to aspire to the true enjoyment of the Spirit of most holy understanding will be impossible. Therefore, with diligent contemplation leading the way, let the storehouse of nature be uncovered, so that we may finally arrive at the sanctuary of GOD and His wisdom. I speak now of great things (let it be said with Your Majesty’s kind permission) which cannot be acquired or compared to any royal power of the whole world, nor by violence, majesty, or any human art, but are drawn only from the spring of the good and sincere will of GOD, poured down from the holy heavens, and granted to those worthy according to the divine pleasure. 

May you be, O MOST SERENE KING, illuminated by a ray of divine light, purified from human mists and filth, adorned in mind with heavenly gifts, a scorner of earthly things, a contemplator of heavenly and divine things, immune to Diabolical arrogance, endowed with Christian humility, and full of Most Holy justice. May you possess, O MOST MERCIFUL KING JAMES, the true knowledge of Nature, the unique <term>ladder of Jacob<note>original: "Jacobi Patriarchæ scala". A biblical reference to the ladder reaching to heaven, used here as a Hermetic metaphor for the stages of knowledge that lead a philosopher from the material world to the divine.</note></term> directing the journey to heaven: for without this middle path, there is no passage from earth to heaven. Blessed be GOD, and blessed be He to you and your Empire, by which we, His creatures and your subjects under Him, may live happily with justice—not feigned, but sincere.

->To Your Majesty<-
->most devoted and most subject<-

R. FLUDD.

### OF THE MIRROR

# OF THIS MACROCOSMIC

## O B J E C T S .

In this emblematic mirror, therefore, it is demonstrated how:

**GOD**
*   In the beginning, He created all things metaphysically. <note>original: "metaphysicè"; here meaning in a spiritual or conceptual form prior to physical existence.</note>
*   From the beginning, He ordained whatever He willed.

**DAEMONS <note>original: "DÆMONES"; in this philosophical context, the term refers to intermediary spirits or "daemons" (including angels) that act as messengers between the divine and the earthly, rather than exclusively evil spirits.</note> metaphysically**
*   They carry out divine ordinations.
*   They announce the commands of God.

**NATURE Physically**
*   It fulfills the divine will.
*   It obeys the ordinance of the creator by generating physical things and, in turn, dissolving them. <note>original: "corrumpendo"; in Aristotelian philosophy, "generation and corruption" refers to the natural cycle of birth/growth and decay/death.</note>

**ART <note>original: "ARS"; refers to human skill, craft, and particularly alchemy or technology used to manipulate the natural world.</note> by divine permission, in its physical operations**
*   It imitates <gloss>Nature</gloss>.
*   It assists <gloss>Nature</gloss>.
*   It perfects <gloss>Nature</gloss>.

<term>Speculum</term> (Mirror): A common Renaissance metaphor for a book or system that reflects the truths of the universe.
<term>Macrocosmicus</term> (Macrocosmic): Relating to the "great world" or the entire universe as a whole, often contrasted with the "microcosm" of man.
<term>Physicè</term> (Physically): Relating to the laws of the material, tangible world.

# A MOST LUCID EXPLANATION
## AT THE BEGINNING OF THIS VOLUME
### REGARDING THE EMBLEM.

[Initial A] Before the creation of things, the incomprehensible and almighty Maker of the Macrocosm <term>Macrocosm: The "great world" or the universe as a whole, viewed as a complex, ordered system</term> divided the universal mass into three parts differing in their purity by his immense power. From the purest of these, he ordained that the Cherubim, Seraphim, Archangels, and all the orders of other Angels be created. From the less pure part, he ordained the heavens and the ethereal regions; and from the most impure, the elements and all sublunary <note>sublunary: literally "under the moon," referring to the earthly realm which is subject to change and decay, unlike the "perfect" heavens</note> things, by saying: *Let them be made, and they were made.* <note>original: "Fiant, & facta sunt"</note> However, because of the simple purity of its substance, he placed the first division of matter beyond the comprehension of natural things; for it is metaphysical and supernatural, which modern writers of philosophy confirm is bounded by the Empyrean heaven <term>Empyrean heaven: From the Greek for "fiery," this was considered the highest part of the universe, the abode of God and the angels, composed of pure light or fire</term>, that is, the glowing and fiery realm. 

But the remaining parts of the less pure mass—namely the ethereal and the elemental—because they are subject to Nature (the governess of the Microcosm <term>Microcosm: The "little world," usually referring to man as a reflection or miniature version of the entire universe</term> under God), are rightly called "natural" for that reason. Now, two efficient causes of these parts contained within the fabric of the Macrocosm are enumerated: namely Nature, and her "Ape," which we call Art <note>Art as the "Ape of Nature": A common Renaissance concept suggesting that human skill and technology (Art) can only imitate or mimic the creative power of Nature</note>. The Father and Lord of Nature is God, the Best and Greatest; to whom she is closest, and from whom we know all her virtues and effects are derived. She is, as it were, the knot and bond of the elements, and possesses the power to rightly temper the mixture of elements in their due proportions, to mingle them aptly in every composition, and to stamp upon each species its fitting form. 

Nature is also a certain infinite force procreating like from like, since she is the fertile mother of all qualities and things, which she increases and nourishes. And to describe her in a single phrase according to the opinions of Zoroaster <note>Zoroaster: An ancient Persian prophet often cited in Renaissance texts as a source of "Primal Magic" and deep wisdom</note> and Heraclitus <note>Heraclitus: A Greek philosopher known for the idea that "all things flow" and that fire is the fundamental substance of the universe</note>, she is the "invisible fire," which they call the Soul of the World <term>Soul of the World: Often called the "Anima Mundi," it is the animating spirit believed to permeate all of nature</term>. We, however, have depicted her visibly in almost the same way as several recent philosophers; we did this with the intention that her power might be better grasped by the reader's mind. And so, we have fashioned her as a naked virgin of tender and blooming age, with hair like the stars and most beautifully gilded, praiseworthy for the very clear sharpness of her eyes, and lovely for the blushing color of her cheeks. This virgin was so remarkable in the brightness of her whole body, and so sweetly adorned with all the gifts of the greatest Maker, that poets could not prefer Pallas <note>Pallas: Another name for Athena, goddess of wisdom and war</note>, nor Venus, nor Juno, nor any other goddess, however graceful, to her beauty. By her singular prudence the "first moveable" <term>Primum Mobile: In the old Earth-centered model of the universe, this was the outermost sphere that moved all the inner planetary spheres</term> is governed, and the eighth sphere...

*Adorned with stars, she holds and turns the celestial spheres with her hands, and the influences of those same spheres*
*are daily prepared and arranged by her fingers for the generation of elemental things. The bodies of the Planets also serve*
*as tools for the works of Nature; they are, as it were, the little hammers by which metals are produced in the terrestrial mines.*
*The region of this virgin’s heart and chest is the true seat and womb of the celestial Sun, and her belly is filled with the lunar body. From her breasts,*
*she perpetually instills innate heat and <note>original: "humidum radicale"</note> radical moisture—from which life and growth arise—into all creatures of the elements, and suckles them.*
*By a certain golden splendor of her heart, the stars—both fixed and wandering—are illuminated, and they borrow, as it were, their souls,*
*lives, and beauties from it. Their imperceptible influences, infused into her womb through the <term>Mercurial Spirit</term> <note>Which the Philosophers call the Spirit of the Moon</note>,*
*are carried downward to the earth, penetrating even to its center; through their impressions, diverse generations, differing in both place and species,*
*are constantly brought forth. By these actions of nature, the Planets come together, and by joining, they produce various things*
*differing in species in the animal, vegetable, and mineral kingdoms. Starting from the lower parts, from the loins, the four Elements are encompassed;*
*for the right foot occupies the earth, while the left occupies the water, signifying the conjunction of her sulfurous and mercurial nature:*
*by which it is argued that nothing can be generated or grow without the union of both. This, I say, is Nature—not a GODDESS, but God’s closest*
*minister—who has beneath her a handmaid or follower who, by imitating her mistress, impresses the likenesses of things produced by her into herself through consent,*
*and follows and imitates her tracks and outlines in a wondrous manner. And it is for this reason that we have depicted her in the form and habit of an Ape*
*beneath the feet of Nature; which we call by the more worthy name of <term>Art</term> <note>In this context, "Art" refers to human skill, technology, and specifically alchemy</note>.*
*This beast (I mean Art), born from human ingenuity, learns many secret, beautiful, and notable things from the diligent observation of her Mistress,*
*with which she is accustomed to enriching men in every kind of doctrine; so also, conversely, she brings no small utility and profit*
*to that same teacher and Mistress of hers. For unless Art, produced by human ingenuity, occasionally gives aid in certain matters,*
*Nature herself will soon fail in the perfection of her operation. For Art sometimes corrects and supplies Nature—indeed, in the discourse*
*on mineral things, Art even seems to surpass her, if only we give any credit to those Chemical Philosophers; especially since it is certain and proven by experience*
*that in the animal circle, eggs can be made to hatch more quickly, silkworms*
*multiplied, and by their growth transformed into diverse shapes in the manner of Proteus, and bees procreated from the head of an ox;*
*in the vegetable circle, crops grow and multiply by the skill of the plow, by which fields are cultivated and harrowed, trees by grafting, and herbs and other vegetables*
*by planting; and in the mineral circle, metallic bodies and lesser minerals are prepared both for medicine and other uses,*
*and cleansed of their dregs, and even the <term>Physical Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note>, whose praises the Philosophers so greatly proclaim, is forged.*
*It is our intention, therefore, in this volume, to discuss these two efficient causes of the <term>Macrocosm</term> both clearly and at length.*

# TO THE BENEVOLENT READER
## AND SINCERE SON OF PHILOSOPHY,
### FROM THE HOLY SPIRIT OF INTELLIGENCE,
->illumination.<-

To you, my friend, I most willingly offer these writings of mine to be read—not to Momus <note>The Greek personification of mockery and harsh criticism</note> or to anyone else overwhelmed by the darkness of ignorance or envy. Indeed, it is the nature of such people to defile with an impure mouth everything adorned in the garments of truth, and even to impiously profane, as they often do, the very rites of the uncreated Creator <note>original: "opificis increati"</note>. Furthermore, I do not believe this subject of ours should be submitted to the judgments of those who claim it is too deep and divine for the human grasp, and who for that reason decide that these sacred secrets <note>original: "arcana sacra"</note> are by no means to be searched out by us. They constantly drum in that old axiom: *What is above us is nothing to us* <note>original: "Quae supra nos, nihil ad nos"</note>. By trying to withdraw us entirely from the contemplation of divine things in this way, they seem to clearly imply that humans—though made in the image of the immense Creator—differ little or not at all from brute beasts devoid of all reason. 

But is it not found in the Holy Scriptures that the Wise man shall rule the stars, and that the very offspring of the uncreated Creator has promised us that the way will be opened to those who knock? To say nothing, meanwhile, of the fact that the immortal spirit breathed into man at the first creation by the divine mind made him closest to that same mind through this breath of life. It allowed him to look more deeply into the works of the mind, and to contemplate and investigate them with his soul. Indeed, this is what the most divine of all philosophers, and the one closest to Moses, Trismegistus <term>Hermes Trismegistus: a legendary Hellenistic figure and reputed author of the Hermetic Corpus, central to alchemy and Western esotericism</term>, confirms in the first discourse of his *Pimander* <term>The Poimandres: a foundational text of Hermeticism describing the creation of the world and the nature of humanity</term> with these words: *“Since man,”* he says, *“had power over all things within himself, he observed the handiwork of the seven governors <note>The celestial spirits associated with the seven planets who govern the material world</note>; these governors, rejoicing in the meditation of the human mind, each made man a sharer in his own order—”*

<summary>The author addresses the reader to defend the study of "sacred secrets," arguing against critics who believe divine mysteries are beyond human understanding. He asserts that humanity's divine origin and the teachings of figures like Hermes Trismegistus prove that we are meant to investigate the workings of the universe.</summary>

<keywords>Hermes Trismegistus, Poimandres, divine intelligence, creation, sacred secrets, seven governors, human reason, philosophy</keywords>

### LETTER TO THE READER.

It is therefore impossible to know yourself unless you also know <term>GOD</term> himself; for <margin>→</margin> he who knows himself, according to the testimony of the same <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the "Thrice-Great," a legendary sage to whom many foundational texts of alchemy and philosophy were attributed.</note>, passes over to <term>GOD</term>. This refers to the logical method of observing the physical world (the effects) to understand the nature of God (the cause).</note>. May the Almighty mercifully grant this to you, to me, and to all, through the merits of his only-begotten Son, Amen.*

# P R E F A C E,
## IN WHICH IT IS DEMONSTRATED,
### HOW CAUSES ARE TRACED THROUGH THEIR EFFECTS,
### THAT IS, BY DEMONSTRATION
### from what follows <note>original: *à posteriori*; reasoning from known effects back to unknown causes</note>.

---

*SINCE it is impossible for even the wisest or most ingenious person to demonstrate or know* **GOD** *himself—the author of the universe's structure <term>Macrocosm; the "great world" or the entire universe, viewed as a single organism</term>—through prior reasoning <note>original: *à priori*; reasoning from cause to effect, or from the nature of a thing to its consequences</note>, because it has never been granted to anyone to define Him in His essence, not even to the divine leader Moses himself, nor shall it be granted in any age (so omnipotent and incomprehensible is He in His very being!); therefore, it is necessary that He be sought from what follows <note>original: *à posteriori*</note>, so that our knowledge may approach Him through His more excellent effects. The Psalmist <note>Referring to King David, the traditional author of the biblical Psalms</note> in Psalm 19:4 teaches us to gaze upon His more noble effects in the heavens, and His glory in the firmament, as if in a most highly polished mirror, with universal eyes. To reach the knowledge of these things, because they are placed above us, it will be necessary to ascend through elementary steps—moving, as it were, from more complex things through analysis <note>original: *resolutionem*; the process of breaking a compound down into its simplest parts</note> toward the simpler; nor should any rest be taken in this ascent until those first principles are reached which, because of their simplicity, cannot undergo any further analysis. This journey is therefore immense, extremely thorny and dangerous; and truly, by what ladders we might reach the summit of this invisible height is not easy to discover without the help of divine light and the illumination of the Spirit. May it not, therefore, displease Your dignity, O most Merciful* **GOD**, *Creator of all things and my helper—I pray as a humble suppliant and implore Your mercy, I, an unworthy sinner; deign to illuminate me in the knowledge of created things, so that, since You are unknown through prior reasoning, You may at least be known from what follows, namely through Your glorious effects. For indeed, You promised to open the door to those who knock diligently, and You have forbidden no one from eagerly searching the fountain of Your goodness; especially since that Spirit of life, which You breathed into our father Adam, warns and urges us every moment to strive toward the clear fountain of blessedness and to struggle toward the ultimate goal of divine knowledge. This inner drive is no less than the heat from Your most noble creature, the Sun, which is seen to move a raw and unripe fruit constantly toward its mature perfection: indeed, by this very breath of Yours <note>original: *spiraculo*; the "breath of life" mentioned in Genesis</note>, adorned with a divine mind, the [minds] of men daily* <insert>are moved</insert>

<summary>In this preface, the author argues that God’s essence is unknowable to the human mind directly (a priori), so one must instead study the physical universe (the macrocosm) to understand the Creator through His works (a posteriori).</summary>

# PREFACE.

...contemplation is snatched up to that third heaven, the dwelling place of the blessed <note>In traditional cosmology, the "third heaven" was the highest realm, often identified as the residence of God and the angels.</note>, and is made happy by beholding your inexplicable glory, growing rich with spiritual wealth: Enlighten, I say, O good GOD, me your servant—though I am unworthy—with the splendor of your light, so that without the interruption of darkness or the Devil, I may rightly and effectively know you and your creatures, for the sake of the love and merits of our Lord JESUS CHRIST your son, who lives and reigns with you forever and ever.

*Since, therefore, one must arrive at the knowledge of causes through their effects, our inquiry must begin from the things better known to us, which are of two kinds: namely, matter and form <term>Matter and form: Aristotelian concepts where "matter" is the raw substance and "form" is the organizing principle or essence that makes a thing what it is.</term>. Moses and Saint Peter have left us the teaching that the matter of all things is water; which we perceive by our senses to be more subtle the higher it ascends, and thicker the closer it is to the center. For the earth, which is the dregs <note>original: "faex"</note> and the thicker, more shapeless part of the dark waters, has visible, sensible, and dense water falling back upon its surface. Similarly, that thick and visible water has a thinner and more invisible water floating above it; the more subtle part of which, overflowing even higher, forms the sphere of fire because of its heat and thinness—this is the portion of the waters of the lower region that is more subtle than all the rest. And so, without doubt, the watery mass ascends in the same proportion all the way to the summit of the upper heaven in the shape of a pyramid, always becoming sharper and thinner toward the top. From this it is certain that the water at the bottom is of the same substance as the water above, which is purely Spirit, but differs from it only in form—which we shall demonstrate below to be the light created on the first day. By the more abundant presence of this light, waters are made thinner; but with a smaller amount, they are rendered more thick and dense. Furthermore, the portion of light contained in the lowest heaven is of the same nature and essence as that of the upper heavens, but differs only because of its composition; for the density of matter hinders the active disposition of the lower light, and so constricts its rays that it renders them destructive and burning, just as is seen in artificial fire. Having learned these things, then, will it be impossible—through experiments and conclusions made in water, both visible and invisible, and in the fiery light of the lower region of the world—to also investigate the natures of those subtle waters and the most thin light of the upper heavens, since there is no difference between them except in the proportion of their thickness? For we see that a smaller machine performs the same work as a large one, though not in the same proportion. Our thick fire makes images painted on paper move by its power; and in this same way, the lucid nature of the sun moves its light and ethereal body from the west to the east. Similarly, a spindle <note>original: "fusum"</note> is driven upward and tossed here and there by the power of artificial fire; so that fire sent from heaven into animate bodies drives them here and there and makes them move. Finally, we perceive the sun itself, by the effect of its light, thinning out denser things; will the faculty of elemental and artificial fire not also perform this same task? Therefore, through experiments of this kind, and from the action of the heat of the lower, thick light in that same region...*

# CHAPTER I.

### *On the infinite nature and the maker of all things.*

**I**NFINITE nature, which is the immense Spirit, ineffable, beyond understanding, outside all imagination, above all essence, unnamable, to be proclaimed only by the heart, most wise, most merciful, FATHER, WORD, holy SPIRIT, the highest and only good, incomprehensible depth, the unity of all creatures, which is stronger than all power, greater than all excellence, worthier than all praise, indivisible TRINITY, most splendid and unspeakable light, *finally the divine mind*, free and separated from all mortal composition, the glory of all, divine nature, necessity, end, and renewal; <margin>Hermes, Sacred Discourse</margin> *This, I say, GOD, the highest and greatest of all, whose name be blessed forever, most skillfully established the wonderful machine of the whole Macrocosm <note>The 'Macrocosm' refers to the universe as a whole, viewed as a large-scale reflection of the human 'microcosm'.</note>, and most beautifully adorned its structure:* This is also what almost all philosophers, both ancient and modern—except for the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle who believed the universe had no beginning and would have no end.</note>, who argue the world has existed from eternity—assert with almost unanimous consent, naming this most divine founder of the universe with many titles fitting to every property of his action. Among these, *Hermes calls him the eternal*, *Thales the most ancient*, *Plato the unbegotten principle of the world*, *others the infinite cause, existing as if outside all things and yet within all things and everywhere*, *others the Being of beings, the first cause*, insofar as other causes and effects depend on him, *the maker, the author, and according to Plato, the building intellect*. Whence some others have called him the Prince of worldly things, the governor, the orderer, the first motor and the first mover, and the immobile principle; since all things are moved by him while he remains immobile and subject to no passion, being always stable, fixed, and permanent; *Trismegistus calls him the principle of the universes*, by which he seems to understand the sole maker of the work; finally, *Plato and Hermes Trismegistus* call him the Father, insofar as he is the author of all fertility and the parent of all things; finally, the great chorus of Philosophers concludes (among whom I name *Orpheus and Democritus*) *that GOD has every name, since all things are in him and he himself is in all things*; not otherwise than how all straight lines drawn from the center to the circumference are said to be in the center, or as a number is said to be in unity, which is the common measure, source, and origin of all numbers, and contains every number uniquely joined within itself; Whence the Pythagoreans and those most skilled in numerical science, *assigned the monad or unity to GOD* the maker <term>Monad: In Pythagorean philosophy, the 'One' or the indivisible source from which all other numbers and the universe itself arise.</term>; both because before all things he was alone and unique, and also because he stood as the first actor and sole mover to complete the vast structure of the work; however, to his matter or subject, which was the second Being, upon which the maker acted for the perfection of the world, they attributed the *Dyad or duality* <term>Dyad: Representing the number 'Two', signifying the first step from unity into the multiplicity of the physical world.</term>; and finally, to his spiritual power, or fiery and radiant form, through whose presence the said matter or subject of the world was led from potentiality into act, and all the machines...

Although the triangular figure is the least spacious of all shapes in the nature of things, yet this triple essence—on account of the Trinity of Persons and their equality in the divinity—when compared to an equilateral triangle, is extended beyond all nature and is so spacious in its own nature that it even encompasses with its infinity the most spacious figure in the entire universe of things: namely, the circular one. We have described **GOD** in this place, therefore, insofar as He is said to be within all things—that is, insofar as He is said to be present everywhere. But indeed, insofar as *Trismegistus* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the "Hermetic" wisdom that influenced alchemy and Renaissance philosophy.</note> called the *world the image of* **GOD** *himself*, to that extent we say the image and likeness of **GOD** Himself is seen in the Spirit of the world, just as a human likeness is perceived in a mirror. For nothing could be seen in the mirror of the world before **GOD** shone upon it; no more than a man’s likeness can be perceived in a mirror without the light of a fire or the Sun. **God**, however, before the creation of the world, shone only upon Himself, and reflected His own heat into Himself, as *Trismegistus* testifies. But when He wished to create the world, He changed His form and all things were suddenly revealed, and all were turned into light, as is held in the *1st Pymander* <note>The "Pymander" (or Poimandres) is the first book of the Corpus Hermeticum, a collection of texts on philosophy and spirituality.</note>. Thus the hidden **GOD** has now manifested His own splendid face in the worldly mirror, His light having been set into action; and He constantly communicates His idea to us and to His creatures through that most holy gift, because the Sages have said that this visible and external world was formed according to the example of its Maker. Therefore, just as the face of a man is seen in a mirror through reflection, so the triple distinction of the one essence is reflected everywhere into the universal spirit of the world. The demonstration of this matter is clear to the eye in the following example.

->*In how many ways God is said to be in a place, how He is present everywhere*<-
->*and fills all things? And concerning His principal seat*<-
->*in this world?*<-

**B**EFORE we treat of the proper seat or dwelling of creative Nature <term>Natura naturans</term> <note>A Scholastic term referring to God as the active, creative force that gives birth to all things in the universe.</note>, it must be asked: is it possible for Him to be in any specific place, since He is infinite in His essence? To this doubt, the entire School of Theologians responds by making a distinction: that He is in a place *not definitively* <note>original: "non definitive"—referring to being limited by spatial boundaries, like a soul within a specific body</note>, as spiritual intelligences or creatures are; nor *circumscriptively* <note>original: "circumscriptive"—occupying space with physical dimensions</note>, as corporeal things are; *but only by presence*. Nevertheless, <margin>according to Gregory</margin> <note>Likely Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD).</note> **G**OD is said to be in all things in a *threefold* way: namely, either *by presence*, as He manifests good to them; or *by power*, namely through His influence; or *by essence*, that is, through the intimacy of His very being. **G**OD is said to be everywhere insofar as His divine power permeates all beings, through which He defines the relationship of the entire universe's potentiality to Himself: thus He is also said to fill all things, not so that He is contained by them, but rather that they are contained by Him. *For it is*, says Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose of Milan (c. 339–397 AD), an influential Bishop and theologian.</note>, *a property of the Deity to be everywhere and in all things*. It is manifest, therefore, that **G**OD is not in all things in such a way that any thing could grasp Him according to the measure of its own portion—as larger things grasp smaller ones; rather, He is said to fill all things so that there is nothing where He is not. Thus we understand that **G**OD is within all things, but not enclosed, because He is infinite and immeasurable; and outside all things, yet not excluded, insofar as He encompasses all created things with His uncircumscribed greatness. And from this, it is said that all things created by **G**OD are good because of Him, by participation—that is, through His presence, or according to the degrees of essence by which angels are preferred to souls, and souls to animals. And yet, as each creature has obtained more or less dignity according to the beauty of its form proceeding from the first Nature or Being, to that extent—as **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who explored how the divine "One" interacts with the material world.</note> testifies—it will possess a higher or lower seat in goodness acquired through participation. But truly, as "Good" is accepted absolutely, simply, and—to use the words of **Iamblichus**—above essence <note>original: "super essentiam"</note>, to that extent it is taken for the cause of good, that is, for the principle of essential good. <margin>Hermes Trismegistus</margin> **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>The legendary author of the Hermetic Corpus, which combined Greek and Egyptian wisdom.</note> treats of this in that place where he warns us to beware of calling anything "good" except **G**OD alone. Therefore, all the Creator's works are found to be participants in goodness—not that goodness which is "above essence" and proper to **G**OD alone, but according to essence; that is, insofar as they receive essence, form, and substantial light from the fiery benevolence of the Creator, by whose gifts they are illuminated, shaped, and led from potentiality into act, and consequently are called "good by participation." And indeed, the world and the creatures of the world received this essence-making goodness <note>original: "bonitatem essentificam"</note> from the Creator Himself, not compelled by necessity (as some Philosophical traditions hold), but from His free and most abundant will, wishing to perfect all His creatures, according to the mind of the Royal Psalmist: *Whatever the Lord willed, He did in heaven and on earth* <note>original: "Quaecunque voluit Dominus fecit in caelo et in terra." Psalm 135:6</note>. Finally, the ancient Philosophers placed the habitation of this creative nature in heaven, because of the beauty and clarity of that place. Hence **Plato** *asserted that God dwells in a fiery substance*, that is, in the ether. In this, more recent Philosophers also seem to agree (among whom I name **Isidore**, **Bede**, and **Basil** <note>Isidore of Seville, the Venerable Bede, and Basil the Great: significant medieval and late-antique scholars.</note>, true cultivators of this Nature), calling the **Empyrean Heaven** <term>Empyrean Heaven</term> <note>The highest, most spiritual part of the heavens, associated with pure light and fire.</note> the *dwelling of **G**OD*. For although **G**OD is said to be everywhere (as stated above), yet properly and principally, that is,

For **GOD** is not said to be above all things and outside all things by a distance of place, but by the excellence of His nature, as is held in the *Theological Resolutions, tractate 1, part 1, question 4.* And for this reason, this heaven is called *intellectual*, because **GOD**, whose seat it is, is called the Intellectual Spirit. Some others have attributed this super-celestial region to the angels and blessed souls, and therefore established another dwelling place outside of this one, which they called the *Heaven of the Trinity*, suitable for the Trinity alone—namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. They say that this is **GOD** Himself in reality, though it differs in our reasoning. For according to *Albertus* <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a prolific medieval scholar and teacher of Thomas Aquinas.</note>, this heaven is the excellence of divine power, which contains and circumscribes all created things. Hence, *to be in this heaven is to be in the equality of the power of* **GOD** *who creates, contains, and saves all things*. Through the vision of *Ezekiel*, all these things are clearly explained; although these two regions—namely, that of the Intelligences and that of the Trinity—seem to differ only in the purity and exaltation of their essence, the Prophet denotes that they are contained within one <term>Empyrean heaven</term> <note>Derived from the Greek word for "fire," the Empyrean was considered the highest, most brilliant part of the universe, composed of pure light or fire.</note> (so called from its perfect illumination), not otherwise than air and fire are contained in the ethereal heaven. For the single heaven, encircling the curvature of the firmament, bore a likeness to a man, whose upper part from the loins upward shone with a fire of an amber-like form <note>original: "ignis carabeæ formæ." This refers to the "shining metal" or "amber" described in Ezekiel 1:27.</note>—that is, a fire most thin and spiritual; but the lower part from the loins downward sparkled with a fire somewhat denser and thicker. Through this partitioning of the place, he seems to indicate two regions differing in dignity: namely, the pre-celestial heaven proper to spiritual creatures, and that super-celestial heaven.

### CHAPTER III.

->*Concerning the origin of first matter: is it created or <unclear>uncreated</unclear>?*<-

**A** HUGE disagreement arises among recent philosophers concerning the origin of the <term>first matter</term> <note>original: "materiæ primæ." In Aristotelian and alchemical philosophy, this is the formless "stuff" from which all physical things are made.</note> of creation. The majority chorus asserts that it was created; among whom *Artephius* <note>An Alchemist to whom many medieval and Renaissance texts were attributed.</note> uses nearly these words: *The Creator of all in the beginning, without the utterance of speech, said: "Let such a creature be," and afterwards nature itself, or the first matter, was created by* **GOD**. But another, smaller chorus, in which *Paracelsus* <note>The famous 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist who challenged traditional medical and philosophical views.</note> participates with the rest of his school, calls this matter the *Great Mystery* <note>original: "mysterium magnum."</note>, which had no likeness to anything created, nor was it even created, but was only prepared by the highest craftsman, **GOD**. Both of these schools attempt to prove their reasons from the Holy Scripture brought forth by *Moses*, interpreting the nature and sense of the word *Beginning* in various ways. For *Artephius*, with the others of his opinion, explains the start of the narrative of Genesis delivered to us by *Moses*—namely, *In the beginning* **GOD** *created the heaven and the earth*, etc.—in this way: *In the first place, or firstly,* **GOD** *created the heaven and the earth*. Endeavoring to refute this exposition of the word *Beginning*, the followers of *Paracelsus* propose these three doubts to us: namely, whether the interpreter intended to refer the name *Beginning* to *some time, or to order and time together, or whether he intended to designate a first place by it*. To which questions they respond by absolutely and confidently denying them. To the *first*, because time did not yet exist, as it only had its origin from the evening and the morning; hence they in no way admit that interpretation of *beginning*. To the *second*, because it is absurd to place the world before its matter in time and order...

The major premise is clearly demonstrated by the fact that *creation is the bringing into actuality, and making something out of nothing: But hyle in its nature is nothing in actuality, wherefore it is certain that it lacks all form*. However, leaving all these ambiguous and controversial disputes of those philosophers to my superiors in Philosophy and those far more learned than me in these matters, I shall at least descend to the description of that matter.

## CHAPTER IV.

### Description of primary matter, or the subject of the universal workmanship.

**M**ATTER, or the subject in whose womb that greatest creator of our Macrocosm <note>The "Great World," referring to the universe as a whole.</note> arranged his structure, is that Philosophical <term>hyle <note>original: ὕλη</note></term>; which the Physicists <note>In this context, natural philosophers who study the physical world.</note> have called absolutely primary matter: because, just as nothing is more common, so also nothing is found to be more unknown than it. Regarding its investigation, two among the other older philosophers especially devoted diligent effort: the first of whom, namely *Thales* (with whom *Heraclitus* and *Hesiod* agreed), after long study and many sleepless nights, *constantly affirmed that water is the first matter of things*, and he confirms the reason for his opinion, *because, he says, the seed and nourishment of all things is moisture*. Both the *Pagans* and the *sacred writers* seem to approve of this sentiment. For the former consecrated *Neptune, Oceanus, and Thetis* <note>Deities associated with water and the sea.</note> for this reason; the latter—among whom I name that divine High Priest of Philosophy, *Moses*—called that matter the *abyss and water*; and *St. Peter* in his *second epistle, chapter 3*, indicated to us that *the heaven and earth were out of water and through water*. Another diligent searcher of this matter was *Anaxagoras*, who after many labors exhausted in this study, believed *the first matter of things to be a rude and indigested mass, called Chaos*, with which the *Poet in the Metamorphoses* <note>The Roman poet Ovid.</note> also seems to agree. Other philosophers wrote differently about this matter: For *Anaximander* established infinite principles as the material origin, *Anaximenes* infinite air, *Diogenes* air endowed with divine reason, *Plato* an invisible and unformed species, *Zeno the Stoic* the substance of fire converted through air into water, the *Epicureans* atoms, *Empedocles* the four elements; almost all of whom, on account of the hidden and concealed arrangement of this mystery—which without doubt is truly and essentially known only to **GOD** alone—wrote uncertainly and indeterminately, contradicting one another, and

# ON THE PRINCIPLES OF THE MACROCOSM.
<sig>D</sig>
<meta>The previous page discussed the origins of the universe and the diverse opinions of ancient philosophers. This page continues by exploring the nature of "Prime Matter," the raw material of creation.</meta>

Whatever the philosophers vigorously and plausibly conceived in their minds, they immediately set forth in their books. **Plato** seems to confirm this sufficiently in his *Timaeus* <note>A famous Socratic dialogue regarding the nature of the physical world and human beings.</note> when he describes this matter as a thing perceptible without the senses and scarcely believable by a kind of "bastard reasoning." From these words, it is clear that his knowledge of this matter was like a dream or mere imagination. **Augustine** also seems to agree with him in this regard, as is clear from the following discourse:
> When I conceive of something unformed, says he, I understand nothing sooner than I understood; just as by seeing nothing, darkness is seen, and by hearing nothing, silence is heard. <note>original: "Cum, inquit ille, aliquid informe concipio, prius nihil intelligo, quàm intelligebam; quemadmodum nihil videndo videntur tenebrae, nihil audiendo auditur silentium."</note>

**Aristotle** himself admits the difficulty of understanding this thing, asserting that this matter can neither be known nor described in itself, except through analogy—that is, through examples taken from external characteristics. For this reason, he and other Greek philosophers likened it to *hyle* <note>original: $\tilde{\upsilon}\lambda\eta\nu$; This Greek word originally meant "wood" or "timber," suggesting a raw material ready to be shaped.</note>, which is like an immense forest where the wood is fit for building any house, machine, or other object. Hence, the divine **Moses** compared it at times to an empty and void earth, and at other times to waters and the abyss. **Hermes Trismegistus**, in his *Poimandres* <note>A foundational text of Hermeticism, often presented as a revelation from the "Shepherd of Men."</note>, compared it to a horrendous shadow migrating into a moist nature. **Plato** called it the mother, nurse, and seat of generated things, because it contains and nourishes everything. **Augustine** compared it to darkness and silence, as has been said. **Pythagoras** likened it to duality. *Some* compare it to a mirror in which the Soul of the World is seen; *others* to wax or clay, which are fit for receiving any impression. *There are also those* who wish to compare it to an ointment, which is ready to receive and retain any scent. And for this reason, **Plato** called it infinite, specifically because of its inclination toward infinite forms—though this matter could also be called infinite in relation to us, for only GOD knows how far this potential extends beyond the curvature of the world. **Aristotle** seems to mean the same thing in his book *On the Heavens and the World*, where he says that outside of heaven there is neither place, nor body, nor dimension, nor fullness, nor time, nor number, nor measure of movement; consequently, nothing exists outside of heaven except this unformed matter, to which alone the aforementioned properties belong. Hence, **Hermes Trismegistus** speaks such words in his sacred discourse:
> Infinite shadow, he says, in the abyss, etc. <note>original: "Umbra, inquit ille, infinita in abysso &c."</note>

We conclude, therefore, from all the writings of both ancient and more recent philosophers, that this first matter is the <term>Ens primordiale</term> <note>Translated as "Primordial Being," referring to the very first state of existence before things took specific shapes.</note>: infinite, unformed, with the potential to be either something or nothing. It has no quantity or dimension, as it can be called neither small nor large; it has no quality, as it is neither subtle nor thick, nor perceptible. It has no property or inclination; it is neither moving nor resting, and lacks any color or elemental quality. Yet, it is the first "passive recipient" of all actions and is capable of containing all things. For this reason, it is called the "Mother of the World," in whose womb the ethereal spheres—decorated with glowing fires—and the four elements suspended below near the center are gathered as if in a mother's uterus.
Furthermore, by imitating the descriptions of **Hermes Trismegistus** and the truth-telling **Moses**, we have depicted in this place an imaginary image of this unformed matter in the form of a black smoke or vapor, or a horrendous shadow, or a dark abyss, or finally, as a kind of rude, undigested, and imperceptible mass.

## CHAPTER V.
### *Concerning darkness and privation.*

**A**ugustine, <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a central figure in Western Christian philosophy.</note> in his arguments against the *Manichaeans*, <note>A religious sect that believed in a cosmic struggle between equal powers of Light and Darkness.</note> asserts that privation <term>privatio: the lack or absence of a quality that should naturally be present, like blindness is the privation of sight</term> is nothing other than darkness, which is defined by the absence of light. But if the meaning of "darkness" is correctly considered, we will perceive that it extends much further than the term "privation." For, according to the testimony of *Moses*, <note>Referring to the Book of Genesis in the Bible.</note> *darkness was upon the face of the deep* <note>original: "tenebrae super faciem abyssi fuerunt"</note> before light or form was created; however, "privation" cannot be named except in relation to some positive state—that is, where there is an absence of some form that existed previously. Therefore, to agree with *Augustine*, *every privation is darkness*, that is, [the absence] of form...

...the removal of light; *but not the other way around*: From this it is clear that darkness, or "privation," only happens to those things subject to decay from the time of the world's creation, such as the elements and the "elementated" <term>elementata|Objects or beings composed of the four basic elements—earth, air, fire, and water.</term> things of the lower heavens. Since the form of the elements is not enough to satisfy the "hunger" of matter (which explains their volatility and imperfection), it is necessary that this same matter always hungers for a new form. Because it cannot satisfy this hunger without the absence of the previous form, it is necessary that decay or "putrefaction" <note>original: "corruptio seu putrefactio"</note> must precede that new form, once the old form has been extinguished and cast off. The signs of this are darkness, which is nothing other than blackness and obscurity, signifying the absence of light and form—from which the beauty and essence of the decayed thing was previously derived and understood. 

The Chemical Philosophers <note>A term for alchemists who studied the transformation of matter as a philosophical and spiritual pursuit.</note> have called this blackness by many names; among these, they most often called this sign of decay the *crow's head* <note>original: "caput corvi" – in alchemy, this refers to the 'Nigredo' or blackening stage, the first step toward the Great Work.</note>. By this, they understood a purely accidental principle and a middle ground that links matter and form, joining the "groom with the bride" <note>A common alchemical metaphor for the union of opposing principles, such as spirit and matter.</note>; indeed, this dark color perishes immediately after the process of generation. 

Here, then, it must be considered that the matter of a thing, while it is submerged in darkness, exists in a state deprived of form, much like the "first matter" of the <term>macrocosm|The universe as a whole, often seen as a large-scale reflection of the human being (the microcosm).</term> before the production of light; for it possesses the potential for the presence and beauty of a certain light, without which it can never be brought into actual existence. It must be understood, however, that the word *darkness* has a double meaning among the Philosophers. *Sometimes* it is taken to mean a certain dark substance—namely, as dark and black air, or as the shadow of some opaque body—and *sometimes* it is taken as a mere "accident" <note>In classical philosophy, an 'accident' is a property that can change (like color or size) without changing the essential nature of the thing itself.</note>, specifically for the color of blackness. 

In the first meaning, it is said by *Moses* to be "over the face of the abyss"; in the second, it is held to be the "deprivation of light." Regardless of how it is understood, *darkness is always entirely opposed to light*. For darkness makes a thing hidden and concealed; it brings about fear and sadness; it removes shame, invites sleep, and is a great friend to rest; thus, it is the companion of matter. Light, however, makes a thing known and manifest; it takes away dread; it brings confidence, courage, and joy; it makes one feel shame; it drives away numbness and laziness, and does not allow an animal to rest, since it excites life and movement in its blood. For light is, as was said above, the origin of all forms and actions.

# CHAPTER VI.
### *On the universal essence, by which the Craftsman informed the matter of the universal workmanship.*

THE MOST WISE Craftsman of the world, who said, *I am the light of the world, the true fire, and the father of lights*, decreed that this unformed matter—this foundation of nature or the subject of the universal machine—should be made a *habitation of forms* and, to use Plato's words, their "nurse." He did this so that by their presence, the mass of the whole abyss, which was buried in darkness, might be made visible and perceptible, and be brought into actual being. To accomplish this with ease, He first communicated the clarity of His fire to the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest, most spiritual part of the heavens, believed to be composed of pure light.</note> (for *his breath* <note>original: "spiritus ejus oris"</note>, which *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>original: "Mercurius Trismegistus"</note> calls the GOD of fire and the divinity of spirit, *was carried over the waters*). Secondly, He communicated it most freely to the ethereal heaven, the sun, and the rest of His spherical creatures, so that through their power—acting as His instruments—the ethereal heaven might be decorated, and form and life might be planted into the lower creatures. 

Moses called this fiery creature, created on the first day in the likeness of the Divine Idea and given by GOD as the first and most excellent gift for the perfection of the rest of His structure, LIGHT. *Artephius* called it clarity; *Plato* called it the "Idea"; and *Aristotle* called it the divine and best principle. For Aristotle himself, in his book *On the Five Substances*, acknowledges that light gives form, beauty, and being to all things; indeed, without it, no matter can be manifested or known, but remains hidden and, as it were, only a potentiality. <note>Hermes Tris-</note>gistus, in his sacred discourse, called it **holy splendor**, asserting that it flourished in the beginning and led the elements out from beneath their dry and moist natures; by this holy splendor, **Marsilio Ficino**, in his commentary on that discourse, maintained that the formless womb of matter was intended to be enlightened by forms. Finally, almost everyone, by unanimous consent, is accustomed to calling it the *first act, form, species, and essence.* Therefore, this light is a unique substance, and a bodily one at that, existing simply in itself, the simplest of all things, the most worthy and most noble. Indeed, it is of such great nobility, according to **Augustine** in his work *On Genesis*, that even physical bodies are judged more perfect and noble the more they participate in light; hence, he asserts that light holds the primary place among bodies. 

And this **Substance of Light**, the same **Augustine and Dionysius** <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist.</note> define—on account of its sweet warmth—as *a pure fire, uncombustible, immeasurable, and indivisible, increasing and multiplying itself into infinity, extending itself everywhere, and present to all things in a single moment, grasping all things yet not to be grasped itself, always shining in itself, but invisible and unknown to others by its own nature:* for it never illuminates visibly unless some body intervenes whose matter is fit to be illuminated. And it is for this reason that the substance of the middle heaven, although it is very bright in itself and holds the first place among composite bodies due to the abundance of its light, nevertheless does not illuminate during the night. 

From the source of this super-celestial light is undoubtedly derived that **invisible fire of Zoroaster and Heraclitus** <note>Heraclitus was a Greek philosopher who taught that the world arose from an ever-living fire.</note>, from which they teach all things were born; whose power, though invisible, all animals and all other sublunary creatures—and indeed even the sea itself in its ebb and flow—seem to recognize and feel deeply by day and night. Finally, the Philosophers, because of its vitality, call this fire a **simple act**; than which nothing is more mobile, or swifter and more powerful in its motion, nothing more subtle, and by its subtility more penetrating, nothing more useful or fuller of virtue, nothing more beautiful, or more uniform in its essence, nothing more capable of perfecting and exalting Beings according to their degree, and nothing swifter at dissolving them and easily undoing their bonds, as **Chalcidius** <note>A 4th-century philosopher known for his commentary on Plato's *Timaeus*.</note> testifies in his work *On the Timaeus*.

From these points it is manifest that—contrary to **Damascene** <note>St. John of Damascus.</note> and **Aristotle**, who in this way somewhat contradicts himself—light is not an **accident** <note>In traditional philosophy, an "accident" is a property (like color) that cannot exist on its own, whereas a "substance" can. The author argues light is an essential substance, not just a property.</note>, which is nothing in itself; for it does not seem likely that an accident could make the substance in which it inheres more noble, since that is the function of an **essential form**, from which both the name and the being of any body are derived.

We conclude, therefore, that **light is either uncreated**, namely GOD who gives nature to all things; (for in GOD the Father is the true light; then in His Son is the illuminating and nourishing splendor, and in the Holy Spirit is the burning radiance surpassing all understanding) **or it is created by that uncreated light**, which is either the simplest soul and true essential form of each of the three heavens, informing the clearest spirit as its bond and vehicle. Hence **Iamblichus**, because of the brightness of the ether, thought that it was nothing other than light itself, even within any of their composite creatures. For in the angels, it is a certain infused, shining intelligence, poured over all limits of reason, yet received in different degrees according to the nature of the recipient. It descends next to the heavenly bodies, where it produces in them a life-giving power, from which life and effective propagation, along with a life-giving splendor, are bestowed upon the lower things. In humans, it is the bright discourse of reason; in other animals, it is a hidden fire clearly governing the actions of life and sense; in vegetables, it is a certain bright soul hiding around their centers, causing growth and multiplication into infinity; in minerals, it is even a spark of splendor driving them toward the goal of perfection. 

From this supernatural light, created on the first day, arise the differences of the macrocosmic heavens and of the bodies existing within them (for they are distinguished by purity, simplicity, and nobility). For according to the degrees of excess or lack of this essence, the highest heaven differs from the lowest, and the lowest from the middle...

...and every element of each heaven is found to be either lowered or exalted by the presence or absence of this [light/form]: for the more distant matter is from the nobility of form, the coarser, more impure, darker, and more unworthy it is. Hence also arises the diversity of created things and substances; hence their perfection and imperfection, their rawness and maturity, their volatility and fixation, their density and subtlety, their darkness and splendor, their heaviness and lightness, and every proportion of things that distinguishes one from another. This is according to *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>original Latin: *Mercurium Trismegistum*; Hermes Trismegistus was the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational texts of alchemy and philosophy were attributed</note>, who asserts in his Sacred Sermon that distinct things are held in balance by the *fiery spirit that carries them*. 

For prime matter <term>materia prima: the formless, chaotic "first stuff" of the universe before God gave it shape</term> was not capable of possessing the aforementioned qualities before the production of this light; because it was equally dark and void, it always retained the same state of imperfection, as if it were entirely devoid of any action by which it might move from one state to another. From these facts it is manifest that, should brightness and light be withdrawn from the world, it must be believed that the matter of the world would return to its first state and disposition. No particle of it would then be superior to any other in dignity, location, or any other quality or quantity. 

We shall explain that all these things are possible through the following demonstration from experience <term>a posteriori: reasoning based on observed effects and physical evidence rather than theory alone</term>, making it clear even to the senses, since the fiery nature comes from light, and the airy body draws its first origin from water. ### TREATISE I. BOOK I.

In this stage, the **luminous form**, beginning to appear and shine in a circular fashion within the womb of the **abyss of matter** <note>original: *hylæ abyfsi*</note> or darkness, drives the specific darkness and the thicker parts of matter—contained within the circle of light—toward the center by its own power. At this moment, the watery spirits begin to reveal themselves; they are finer the closer they are to the seat of light, and thicker the further away they remain.

->*Demonstrations making it clear that if the action of the luminous form were to cease, and if it were entirely absent, the world and its matter would necessarily return to the first abyss and*<-
->*dark matter, according to the reasons*<-
->*we have expressed above.*<-

Because the presence of solar light is the closest and most similar thing to the **luminous creature** created on the first day—since, according to the Fathers of Theology, the solar body was made on the fourth day as a vessel for all those same rays—we shall therefore begin our demonstration with its power and effect. By this, we will prove that the presence of light itself caused this formal change in <term>hyle</term> <note>The Greek term used by Robert Fludd and others for the unformed "prime matter" of the universe</note>, and that in light's absence, that same matter, once formed, would return to its former, shapeless state.

Let a sphere <note>original: *pila*</note> be made of lead, of a large enough capacity, so that the thickness of its material is neither too thin (lest it break easily) nor too porous (lest air penetrate through it). In the top of this, let a hole be made, into which a certain curved tube, descending almost to its bottom, is fixed. It should be made of the same material and in such a way that no air can enter or exit except through the hollow of that pipe. The other end of the same curved tube or pipe should extend almost to the bottom of another vessel filled with water. Let the sphere be **A**, the pipe or tube **B**, and the vessel filled with water **C**.

We conclude, therefore, that the sun's rays, by heating sphere **A**, will expel the thick and smoky air contained within it through pipe **B** into vessel **C**, down to the bottom of the water contained in that vessel **C**. This thick air, driven out by the force of heat, will mix with the water in vessel **C** and produce many bubbles, one after another. However, as soon as the sun has withdrawn, or some other object is placed between the sun and the sphere, or even if the sphere itself is placed in the shade, the absence of the sun and the cooling of the sphere will cause the previous state to return to the sphere’s cavity—namely, the same portion of thick and dark air that was there before.

The proof is as follows: since the sphere cannot find air of the same nature within the water-filled vessel, it draws the water itself (which is even thicker) into the place of the air. Necessity forces as much water to descend into the sphere as the solar rays originally expelled through the refinement and purification of the air. By this experiment, it is demonstrated as if by a pointing finger that every purification in this world, and every inequality or diversity in thickness or thinness, arises from the act of the **essential light** itself. Its presence maintains this difference in state until the end of the world. By this very experiment, it is infallibly proven that if light should fail, all things would return to their original state. The two experiments written below, which derive their effects from elementary fire, declare this truth even to ordinary eyes. We have illustrated the demonstration of this first experiment as follows:

# CHAPTER VII.

->*Concerning the two simple and primary qualities derived from the two first*<-

**F**rom each of the two aforementioned parts of the constitution of the world arises a certain simple nature, which carries with it the character of its source. For when the fiery spirit was carried over the waters (which we called above the fountain of light and the origin of forms), it produced a certain essential quality accompanying its actions. Hence the Philosophers have called it an "active" quality, as if it were the effect of form or of the most lively light, which they also named <term>heat</term> <note>original: "caliditas"</note>. The nature of this heat is to penetrate to the very center of thickness; by penetrating, it opens dense and solid things, and by expanding them, it dissolves them and makes them loose. After this dissolution, it dissipates and separates the coarse from the subtle, cleansing them by rarefaction <note>the process of making something less dense</note> or thinning, making them volatile and light; thus they are raised by nature and carried upwards. Finally, it gathers like things together, digests, matures, fixes, and perfects them; but it cuts through, breaks apart, expels, and reflects unlike things. It completes all these actions insofar as it is immediately derived from the most noble and subtle body of all, and accompanies its thinnest and most noble substance. Having thus declared the origin of this active nature, it remains for the quality or simple nature of the other constitutive part—namely the passive one—to be revealed, since no action can occur without a corresponding <term>passion</term> <note>In this context, "passion" refers to the capacity to be acted upon or to receive an impression, rather than an emotion.</note> or receptive state. ### TREATISE I. BOOK I.

...the matter of the cosmos, buried in darkness before the rising of heat, is derived. For at the first appearance of light, the shadows began to move; and just as heat was brought in by the motion of light, so also by the motion of the substance of the abyss, another quality is produced—one that endures the actions of heat, and is therefore called "passive" (insofar as it suffers more than it acts). <note>The author uses the Aristotelian distinction between active qualities (like heat) and passive qualities (like cold or moisture) that receive the action of the former.</note> This quality accompanies the thicker substance of matter in no different a way, and is intensified or lessened according to its thickness, just as heat is perceived as more intense or more relaxed according to the abundance or scarcity of that essence of light. Therefore, the nature of Coldness, revealed by the rising of heat, is entirely opposed and adverse to Heat. Because of heat's subtle penetration, Coldness stands firm against it as it pursues her, and by resisting, it contracts the more impure, thicker, and darker parts of the substance of the abyss toward the center of the cosmos—gathering, restricting, and condensing them together. 
<margin>→</margin> 
Indeed, coldness naturally flees there, as if to a place more remote from the world's periphery, in which a greater and purer essence of the radiant Spirit <note>original: "Spiritus"</note> exists, having been included within it from the beginning. 
<margin>→</margin> 
And from this comes the thickness of the elements of the lower heaven; from this comes the density, opacity, and darkness of the earth. From this it also follows that no heavy object could pass beyond the point of the center, even if a hole were bored directly through the entire mass of the earth; specifically, because the central point of the earth itself is the part most remote from the world’s circumference, and consequently, it is the seat in which coldness 
<margin>←</margin> <margin>→</margin> 
naturally desires to rest, as if free and immune from the enmity of heat and its contrary action. We conclude, therefore, that Heat more readily embraces forms <note>Heat is seen as the formative force that gives shape and life to matter.</note> and provides the functions of life to each thing, being the companion of its soul; cold, however, possesses material bodies, loves them, and naturally inheres in them. Therefore, from the mutual action and "passion" <note>The state of being acted upon.</note> of these two, certain parts of the macrocosm <term>macrocosm: the universe viewed as a large-scale reflection of the human being or "microcosm"</term> are refined more or less according to the retreat of coldness and the approach of heat—namely the upper regions—and certain parts are thickened according to the absence of heat and the presence of coldness—namely the lower regions. Thus was the world made and its regions distinguished; if these natures were to fail, it is necessary that all things should return to their former state, and be reduced from something *in act* to something *in potency*. <note>Aristotelian terms: "in act" means currently existing/manifested, while "in potency" means returning to a state of mere possibility or raw matter.</note> From these natures or simple qualities, however, arise two other dispositions, which *Artephius* <note>A famous, possibly legendary, medieval alchemist often cited in Hermetic texts.</note> called "simples from simples": namely, moisture and dryness. The first of these arises from the mixing and tempering of the two simples: for if heat is joined with an equal part of coldness, the nature of moisture is created. But we call dryness that quality joined with heat or cold where moisture is entirely absent. It is certain, therefore, that dryness is nothing other than the absence of moisture, and hence these two qualities are called contraries to one another; yet they are passive in respect to the primary simples, as we shall declare below in its proper place.

## CHAPTER VIII.

->*That two things concur for the existence of prime matter: under what form*<-
->*prime matter appears when reduced into act? and what is*<-
->*gross and subtle water.*<-

---

For the existence of **prime matter** <term>materia prima: the fundamental, formless substance from which all physical things are created</term>, two things are required. The first is a certain **Being in potential**, which is the subject of that hidden matter; the other is like a misty veil of the same, which removes the impression of any specific thing from it as long as it is present. This veil is called **Darkness** by **Moses**; by its presence, beings are said to exist in potential, but by its absence, they are said to be "reduced from potentiality into act" <note>This is Aristotelian terminology: 'potential' is what could be, 'act' is what actually exists.</note>. 

This matter, while still unformed, **Moses** called the **abyss**, reporting that *darkness was upon the abyss* <note>original Latin: "tenebrae fuerint super abyssum"; see Genesis 1:2</note>. As soon as the **Spirit of the Lord** was said to be borne over the waters, providing them with a fiery vigor, the darkness gradually departed. That which was previously called the "abyss" because of its gloom, now beginning to take form, claimed for itself the name of **waters**; for it was seen to represent the appearance of water before it was reduced into a spirit through the process of thinning. 

The divine **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and scientific texts were attributed</note> in his *Poimandres* <note>The first tractate of the Corpus Hermeticum</note> seems to assert this, saying that *a horrendous shadow sliding around in an oblique revolution migrated into a moist nature, that is, it was turned into water* <note>original: "umbram horrendam obliqua revolutione circumlabentem in humidam migrasse naturam"</note>. Moreover, in his sacred discourse, he says that *an infinite shadow, water besides, and a thin intellectual spirit were in chaos through divine power*. 

Those shadows, namely the darkness, are scattered by the presence of a specific light; but this—namely the matter of that light—is purified from its dark mist by the clarity of light. It is then called a **thin spirit**; and from a thing deeply hidden and once covered by the sooty face of dire gloom, it is now rendered visible, pleasant, very transparent, and indeed most clear. However, it remains more clear in one part than another, depending on its position nearer or farther from the source of light. 

The lower part of it is turbulent, becoming gross and thick because it is compacted and defiled by moist vapors and earthy exhalations, which the dark abyss vomited and exhaled from its gulf. From the forceful agitation of this matter, the winds, as well as clouds, thunder, hail, and snow, are stirred up. Therefore, this part of the waters is called **corporeal and corpulent**. 

The middle part, however, is not entirely bodily, nor plainly spiritual; but according to the **Philosophers**, it is as if it were not a body, but as if already a soul—or as if not a soul, but as if already a body. That is, it participates in both extremes. Because the luminous soul, possessing the upper part and making it entirely formal, degenerates from its opposite—yet without it, corporeal creatures cannot live—the Creator ordained this **middle spirit** (beyond its use in the separation of the waters from the waters) to be a **receptacle and vehicle for the soul**. Through this vehicle, the soul may move toward the lower regions, through which it is further introduced into bodies, and thus exhibits its powers to their members by means of this vehicle. 

And hence it is that the **Philosophers** call it the **spirit of the world** <term>spiritus mundi: a vital, celestial substance that acts as a bridge between the spiritual soul and the physical body</term>, and **Albertus** <note>likely Albertus Magnus, the 13th-century philosopher and alchemist</note> calls it the **Mercurial spirit**, because it has the power of penetrating and altering bodies. Likewise, the **Greeks** name it **air and ether**, as if a burning spirit, as if they were saying...

...a spiritual receptacle and container of the <term>fiery soul<note>original: "anima ignea"</note></term>, bright and shining, descending from the <term>Empyrean Heaven<note>The highest part of the universe in ancient and medieval cosmology, believed to be the realm of pure light and fire.</note></term>: wherefore in this spirit or <term>quintessence<note>The "fifth element" or pure essence that permeates all nature.</note></term> all generative and seminal power resides. Finally, the highest part of this spiritual matter was so purified by the newly created light, and made spiritual by its inexplicable splendor—as if intoxicated by that same bright and illuminated nectar—that almost its entire substance is nothing other than pure <term>essential form<note>The fundamental nature or "soul" of a thing that gives it its specific identity.</note></term> (especially when considered in relation to the lower realms), by which the other dark parts of the <term>hyle<note>A Greek term for "prime matter," the raw, unformed substance of the universe.</note></term> are brought from <term>potentiality into act<note>A concept from Aristotelian philosophy where a thing moves from a state of "could be" (potential) to "actually is" (act).</note></term>. If any spark of this formal mass should descend into its middle region, it is immediately received by the middle spirit—namely, the <term>ethereal<note>Pertaining to the ether, the rarified atmosphere of the heavens.</term></ spirit—and is wrapped in its thin little body; then both, namely the vehicle and that which is carried, descending downwards, are enclosed in the body of the lower region, just as the soul itself descended in the middle spirit, as will be more fully explained at the end of the second book of this treatise. 

From these things it is manifest that darkness relates to matter in potentiality just as light relates to matter in act; and that matter not yet brought into act is like a certain substance overshadowed and hidden by the gloom of darkness. That is, it exists between "something" and "nothing," a thing scarcely imaginable because it is formless and unknown *a priori* <note>Known beforehand or by its own nature.</note>, which indeed is clarified, informed, and manifested by the presence of light. It is known *a posteriori* <note>Known after the fact or by its effects.</note> in the form of thin waters, as noted by Thales, Hesiod, Moses, and Peter the Apostle. Of these, the lower region is called <term>air</term>, which contains water—called <term>thick air<note>original: "aër spissus"</note></term>—and the spheres of the upper <term>sublunary<note>Everything below the orbit of the Moon, traditionally composed of the four changing elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note></term> elements; the middle region is called <term>ether</term> and the middle spirit; and the highest is called the dwelling place of light and fiery love, as we will demonstrate more extensively below in its proper place.
