Therefore, no one can deny that the elements are found everywhere and in all regions of the world, but in different proportions according to the lack or abundance of the universal form; namely, in the lower region they are dreg-like and thick, in the middle part purer and cleaner, and in the summit or super-celestial part most spiritual and in every way blessed. One of these partakes more of earth, namely **water**, since both are cold, because they have less form and more matter; the other partakes more of fire, namely **air**, since both are hot; and accordingly they have more form and less matter. From this it is manifest that the elements are made from the various actions and passions of the simple natures, since every portion of matter called an "element" is derived and distinguished from them.

### CHAPTER X.

#### *On Chaos, and the principles of the creatures of the lowest heaven.*

<margin>*Chaos, or matter as a confused and undigested mass, in which all things—namely, the four elements—were confused and mixed together; because of this, earth and water, which are heavier than the rest, rose up as far as the sphere of the moon, while fire and air, being lighter, descended as far as the center of the earth.*</margin>
M<gloss>ultifold</gloss> is the prime matter of things, as is manifest both from what precedes and what follows; of these, that which we called *Hyle* <term>from the Greek word for "wood" or "matter," used here for the most primordial, unmanifested substance</term> above is the most remote from composition. *The second is the matter of the elements*, distinguished by its own nature according to the predominance of cold or heat, and called by various names because of its various locations and operations. *The third is*—and this, according to some, was that formless mass of the matter of heaven and earth, gaping from the beginning, from which all things afterward came forth one by one through various species and their own proper forms. For without a doubt this formless mass was present on the first day of creation in both lower heavens, under a veil of blackness, reverberated by the light acting within it; and on the second day it was compressed into the lowest heaven. We can more rightly define this as a formless mass of darkness, or of waters lurking in the darkness, supplying the material for the entire Work <note>original: "opificio," referring to the divine act of creation</note>, with a small portion of the radiant rays of each heaven retained in a dark prison by the stickiness <note>original: "visciditatem"</note> of the said waters. Yet these portions of light could form nothing without the aid of the perennial fountain of light (which they received gradually on the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth days—that is, more and more according to the divine will of the Creator); for as yet nothing held its proper place. For that portion of light belonging to the Empyrean heaven <term>the highest heaven of pure fire and light</term> occupied the center of the dark mass against its own nature, and that other portion, which was proper to the middle heaven, was further up—that is, above the imprisoned light of the Empyrean heaven toward the concave...

# TREATISE I. BOOK I.

Although we are ourselves eyewitnesses <note original: "oculati testes">to these things</note>, because in the dissection <term>anatomisatione; the author uses the language of anatomy to describe the chemical or spiritual separation of a substance</term> of any part of that mass—for according to *Giles de Vadis* <note>Giles de Vadis (Ægidius de Vadis) was a 16th-century alchemist known for his work "Dialogue between Nature and the Son of Philosophy."</note> a certain part of that material, well enough known to all, remained in the world <margin>Handwritten arrow pointing left</margin>—we are able to sketch a better demonstration of this matter. For in the outer part of that same mass, I clearly perceived at first glance at the house of a certain friend of mine a foul, very black, and heavy substance of earth. By its blackness and dreadful veil, all the remaining elements—indeed, even the substance of the Sun and the heavens—were so covered over that no natural order could be found within them. For I discovered everything therein <margin>Handwritten arrow pointing right from the left margin</margin> positioned against the laws of nature; namely, I perceived those things which were light to be pressed down toward the center, while those which were heavy dwelt around the outer edge <note original: "peripheriam">of the mass</note>. For by dissecting this deformed body with the most burning <margin>Handwritten double arrow pointing right</margin> knife of nature, namely fire, I saw fluid water to be touching this deformed, most black, and earthy crust appearing in the outer part of the mass. Thus, that middle part of the water, being more involved and joined with this earthy nature, flowed out first of all according to that earthy coldness which it held within itself, clear and raw. But I perceived another part of that element, closer to the fire and the center of the mass, and tinted and mixed on every side with the airy spirit, to distill after that raw nature. Thus, I observed the air to be equally mixed with the water in the lower part of the watery sphere—that is, tending more toward the center of the mass. Yet, the moisture of this kind of air was not free from the rebellious dryness of the black earth; for indeed, this earth had not only occupied its principal and more royal seat in the confusion at the edge of the mass, but had also diffused its power through the whole mass and dispersed the vapors of its nature through it, so that no part of the whole mass existed pure and free from that darkest pollution. After the airy [part], the fire rose out of the abyss of that chaos, foul and evil-smelling on account of the earthly pollution.

From these things it is certain that this fire held a continuous war and conflict with that part of the watery substance which was imbued with air; for while that fire naturally sought and attempted to be refreshed by its airy fuel, it repeatedly experienced the constant injuries of that hostile water mixed with the said air.

<margin>Handwritten double arrow pointing right</margin> Moreover, from the middle and most inward center of the entire formless mass, as if from the very <margin>Handwritten vertical bracket on the right margin</margin> point of the whole abyss, I beheld the solar substance of the mass rise—wretchedly and as if from purgatory, or as if rising from the dead—appearing still struggling with the impurity of the mass and as if sickly. I saw it be refined <term>sublimari; to be raised or purified through alchemical sublimation</term> by a marvelous operation of wit and philosophical industry. And indeed, some Philosophers have called this dark part of the mass the "Central Sun." By its operation we are truly taught in what manner at the beginning of the world this celestial Sun of ours—after a purification was first made in this lower place—was exalted into its incorruptible place, that is, into the heart of the ethereal heaven, just as we shall demonstrate more clearly in *the fourth book of this treatise, in the chapter on the rising of the Sun*.

When these precious gems had been extracted from that blackest mass and seized as if by violence, I found a certain dreg-like and very black material <margin>Handwritten double arrow pointing right</margin> left at the bottom, whose blackness was manifest, **but whose redness was hidden, having as it were a metallic nature; this, like Lucifer, having fallen from heaven, was cast down to the lowest abyss**, <margin>Handwritten arrow pointing left</margin> because it had even striven to preside over and predominate against the celestial material.

The process leaves behind a foul, metallic residue compared to the fallen angel Lucifer, symbolizing the separation of the divine from the dregs of matter.</summary>

# CHAPTER I.

### *On the world and its division.*

**M**ARTIANUS takes the word "world" in three ways: namely, for that which is called the <term>Archetype<note>original: "Archetypus"; the original model or divine blueprint of the universe existing in the mind of God</note></term>, whose substance is incorporeal, invisible, intellectual, and eternal. It was according to the example and divine image of this archetype that the beauty and likeness of the physical world were crafted, as **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century Christian philosopher and author of "The Consolation of Philosophy."</note> testifies; and this world remains permanent within the divine mind. Or, he takes it for the corporeal heaven, which is the <term>Greater World<note>original: "mundus ille major"; also known as the Macrocosm</note></term>, which is bounded and contained by the concave surface of the <term>First Mover<note>original: "primi mobilis"; in ancient astronomy, the outermost sphere that gives motion to all the inner celestial spheres</note></term>; and this world is also eternal by the will of GOD. Or finally, he takes it for man, who is called the <term>Lesser World<note>original: "mundus minor"; also known as the Microcosm</note></term>, and with respect to his form he is called perpetual, but with respect to his matter, he is corruptible.

We, however, not differing much from the opinion of **Martianus** <note>Martianus Capella, a 5th-century writer whose work on the Seven Liberal Arts was a foundation of medieval education.</note>, shall treat of a twofold world; namely, of the **Macrocosm** and the **Microcosm**. We distinguish the former from man (or the Microcosm) by regarding the whole space of primary matter as the World, <term>Cosmos<note>original: "Cosmo"; from the Greek word for order or the universe</note></term>, or Macrocosm—that which the spiritual light or Spirit of the Lord, encircling the waters, encompasses in its circular embrace. Indeed, this circular portion of the abyss—consisting of a substance formed from various concurrences of light and darkness through a specific arrangement (that is, distinguished into degrees of purity and impurity)—is distributed into three parts differing in their formal nature.

The upper part is that space of the world in which the fiery spirit was carried, and where the primary substance of light is contained, extending itself from the concave edge of the <term>Sphere of the Trinity<note>original: "sphaerae Trinitatis"</note></term> down to the outer surface of the starry heaven. Indeed, the substance of this part of the world, because of the abundance of its form, is so subtle and pure that in relation to us it is considered insensible and entirely imperceptible. Hence, the Philosophers have called it intellectual and spiritual in the highest degree.

The middle part is adorned with fixed and wandering stars; indeed, it occupies that entire concavity of the universe which is contained between the outer surface of the moon's sphere and the inner surface of the First Mover; and the substance of this region is corporeal in comparison to the upper region.

Finally, the lower part of the world is all that space which the inner surface of the moon's sphere embraces. From this it becomes clear that the mass of the world is distinguished into two principal parts: one of which is incorporeal, spiritual, most pure, and most subtle—namely, the upper part; while the other is corporeal. And this corporeal part is again subdivided into two parts: one of which is subtle, thin, and incorruptible—namely, the middle part; the other is impure, gross, and subject to corruption; and this is the lowest portion of the world, which we shall hereafter call the sublunary and elemental region. Both the ancient Philosophers and the sacred Writers called these regions of the Macrocosm "Heavens." For they named the upper part the **Empyrean Heaven** <note>original: "coelum Empyreum"; from the Greek word for "fire," traditionally the highest part of heaven inhabited by God and the angels</note>, and spoke of it as fire, because it is filled on all sides by the spiritual fire or substance of light. And this was that "third heaven" into which **Saint Paul** confessed he was snatched in spirit, and which he himself called **Paradise**.

<summary>This page defines the tripartite division of the universe into the Archetypal, Macrocosmic, and Microcosmic worlds, focusing specifically on the three regions of the Macrocosm: the spiritual Empyrean, the starry middle heaven, and the corruptible sublunary realm.</summary>

From these things, therefore, it clearly appears that the entire substance of the world is nothing other than these three heavens, differing in their subtlety and density—that is, in their purity and impurity.

## CHAPTER II.

<margin>He made darkness His secret place, and made His tabernacle in dark waters, and veiled it with thick clouds. By this, the portion of *hyle* <note>The Greek term for primordial, unformed matter.</note> outside the world is signified: "Clouds and darkness are round about Him" (Psalm 97, verse 2).</margin>
**M**ONAD <note>The Monad refers to the concept of the "One" or the single, indivisible source of all existence.</note> according to Hermes Trismegistus (who is the light of the world) brought forth a monad—that is, the GOD of fire—before the ages, and reflected His own heat back into Himself. For this Father of Lights, before the creation of the world, shone only within Himself, nor did He wish to reveal His brightness before He conceived of the world's creation. (Psalm 18, verse 11.) For then, says *Mercury Trismegistus* <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure often equated with the Egyptian god Thoth, credited with ancient wisdom.</note>, He changed His form—that is, He manifested His hidden essence, through which He suddenly revealed all things. (Psalm 18, verse 12: "at His brightness, the clouds and dark water fled away.") Therefore, this Almighty GOD, freely and not by compulsion, determined in His ineffable wisdom to build the Macrocosm <note>The "Great World" or the entire universe, as opposed to the Microcosm, or man.</note>, and before its construction, to mystically decide upon its matter, essence, shape, dimension, and the connection of its parts. 

He chose the matter for this structure from the womb of infinite <term>hyle</term> <note>original: ὕλης (*hylēs*); primordial matter that exists before form is applied.</note>, suitable to be adorned with various virtues and essential forms. He wished to freely impart to it a holy gift of love, proceeding immediately from Himself. For GOD was actually breathing before the creation, and the "Spirit of His mouth"—that is, the passive breathing proceeding from Him by way of a bestowable love—was carried over the waters. This means over the watery sphere, or rather, it moved around and over the whole material of the corporeal world—namely, over the two lower heavens as yet unformed, whose primordial matter was water, as *Saint Peter* testifies (2 Peter 3). 

It was carried, I say, undoubtedly in a circular motion in the world, made present by the spiritual presence of that same Spirit, over the convex surface of the material world. This motion is the most noble of all, by which the matter of the corporeal world and its simplest spiritual substance are distinguished from that mass of infinite *hyle* or unformed heap thrust outside both worlds. Thus, the corporeal world received its convex limits or margins and the most capacious and noble of all shapes: the sphere. 

Indeed, this is that exalted gift of the divine essence which GOD gave to it, having an aptitude most full of the power of its own proceeding, to be given and proceeding only by way of a bestowable love in which all other things are given. For all gifts are called "common" by reason of the love of this Holy Spirit, who is the infinite love proceeding from the Father and the Word. Therefore, from His simple act, all virtues and essences are distributed like gifts to every part of the world by the command of the divine will, according to the sentiment of the royal *Psalmist*: "By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the Spirit of His mouth." 

*Saint Paul* also seems to confirm this same thing: "Through the Holy Spirit," he says, "all things are searched out and each is distinguished by its own degree." Therefore, this Spirit of the Lord, which is a fiery love, was carried over the waters, imparting to them a fiery vigor as the divine will commanded. Whence the first creature of the world, the most subtle, simple, noble, and active of all, first shone upon the world. <margin>☩ Some more recent philosophers wish to claim for each thing as much of Divinity as it is capable of holding light.</margin> 

Indeed, it is no wonder, since GOD Himself, as is handed down in the Sacred Scriptures, calls Himself the light of the world and the Father of lights. By His holy gift or fiery spirit—which appeared to the Apostles in the form of fire—the worldly light (that is, the fiery vigor of the waters) was honored on the first day of creation. From His essential substance, the heaven in which the spirit moved, as well as both lower heavens and their creatures, received their beauties divinely and metaphysically. 

And it was from this that *Democritus*, *Orpheus*, and many of the *Pythagoreans*—since they perceived the power of this divine nature to be present in all lower creatures to a greater or lesser degree—were of the opinion that "all things are full of Gods." They established divine honors for these, dedicating prayers and sacrifices to them, and venerating them with divine worship. 

<margin>☩ Furthermore, they reduced all these Gods to one, JOVE;</margin> 

By this, they most clearly signified that all streams of heat, clarity, life, and essential forms flow from a single, supernatural, lucid fountain, and from His perennial and spiritual water they attain their growth and multiplication.

### CHAPTER III.

#### *Concerning the first three days of creation.*

**I**t seems a difficult task to understand the arrangement of the days that occurred before the creation of the Sun, especially since no small difference of opinion arises among the holy Church Fathers themselves concerning the nature of those days. For *Basil*, *Damascene*, and other *Greek* authors <note>original: "Græci"; referring to the Eastern Church Fathers such as St. Basil the Great and St. John of Damascus, who were influential in early Christian cosmology</note> contend that the light created on the first day produced "day" through the emission of light, and "night" through its withdrawal, performed by the divine will. But the *Doctors* <note>The "Doctors" usually refers to the authoritative theologians of the Western or Latin Church</note>

<sig>G</sig>
<meta>catchword: Latini (Latin)</meta>

<summary>This page explores the theological debate regarding how day and night existed during the first three days of Creation, before the Sun was made, focusing on the theories of the Greek Church Fathers.</summary>
<keywords>Cosmology, Macrocosm, Creation, Genesis, Robert Fludd, Divine Light, St. Basil, St. John of Damascus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the origins of the universe, focusing on the nature of the first three days of Creation before the sun was formed. It follows the discussion of the "unformed matter" and the initial separation of light from darkness.</meta>

# TREATISE I. BOOK II.

<meta>catchword: but (original: "quin")</meta>

The Latin theologians probably say that the light made a circulation, similar to that which is now performed by the Sun, and that it illuminated the hemisphere in which it was present. Thus, they argue, darkness was introduced into the opposite hemisphere because of the obstruction of the thicker, denser, and blacker matter which existed in the middle of all that unformed matter. 

We, however, will put forward a twofold interpretation of those days; perhaps neither of these, when considered somewhat more exactly, will seem to wander far from the boundary of truth. The first interpretation is that the "day" before the creation of the Sun can be regarded as a primary, secondary, or tertiary light extending itself through the transparent universe. In this view, night is understood as the dominion of darkness in that part where no light had yet shone. Thus, the first day is taken to be the clarity generally dispersed through the entire **Empyrean** <term>Empyreum: The highest part of the heavens, thought by ancient scholars to be composed of pure fire or light and to be the dwelling place of God.</term> heaven, specifically after that light had driven the darkness downward from its region and had purified and refined the spiritual matter of its own heaven according to the strength of its action. 

The "morning" of this day was the first penetration of divine light into the darkness, and the beginning of the action of light in the upper darkness—not unlike how we use the word "morning" for the time when the Sun’s rays begin to penetrate the obscure and gloomy mass of the night. Similarly, "evening" is the lowest surface of this heaven, where dark vapors still exist (as if on the surface of a middle region) and there they still revolve in an oblique circuit, marking the end of the first day’s action; and so it continues for the others. Certainly, this explanation is not to be entirely rejected, since both day and night must be considered in relation to the subject matter upon which these two temporal states act. Yet, the **Empyrean** heaven was entirely bright and clear after its creation; indeed, it received its name from fire <note>original: "ab igne nomen ſuum accepit"; the Greek word 'empyros' means 'in fire'.</note>, and for that reason, neither night nor darkness was tolerated within it in any way immediately after its creation. The same can be said of the substance of the ethereal heaven.

Our second interpretation, however, is closer to the truth in our view, as it agrees directly with the Latin theologians and will clarify itself through the following declaration. For it is probable that the divine Spirit, sent forth and carried over the waters before any creation occurred, encircled them with a triple revolution. Each of its circuits produced a spiritual or supernatural day. Thus, by the first circuit, it established the first day, in which it perfected the **Empyrean** heaven and pushed the darkness down by one degree. By the second revolution, it brought forth the second day, in which—through a double presence of divine power—the darkness was pushed down a second degree; in this way, the divine light and power shone in the middle and ethereal region of the world. Finally, by its third and last revolution, the darkness was dispersed by the power of the third divine impression through a third degree and to the ultimate boundary from the circumference. 

In this way, the tabernacle of the entire world was completed, and all the powers and essences of its regions were produced by the power of the divine Spirit. Here, therefore, those three spiritual days were finished, measured by nothing other than the act of the divine Spirit, and related to the number of persons in the **Trinity** <term>Trinitas: The Christian doctrine of God as three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</term>, all of whom acted toward the creation of the world.

->For GOD the Father spoke; and by His Word the heavens were established; and by the Spirit from His mouth all their power was made.<- <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 33:6.</note>

Therefore, within the span of these days, and after their completion, the heavens were produced and given essence by divine operation; in them, the entire spirit of the **macrocosm** <term>Macrocosmus: The "great world," referring to the entire universe as a single, integrated structure.</term> received its form and being. Soon after, the solar days—which are concerned with the more physical things of the world—attained their origin. To produce these types of creatures, the first three of these solar days came forth, just as the three spiritual days first shone out to build the dwellings of the three heavens. For on the first solar day (which is the fourth from the beginning of creation), the stars or wandering planets and the creatures of heaven were made; on the second, all irrational animals; and on the last day, the "lesser world" or **Microcosm** <term>Microcosmus: The "little world," a term for a human being, viewed as a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</term> was created and completed. This mirrors how the **Macrocosm** was brought to its perfection on the last spiritual day. Who, therefore, can hardly doubt...

It establishes a parallel between the three spiritual days that formed the celestial Macrocosm and the three solar days that formed the physical world and the Microcosm (humanity).</summary>

Why would the motion of the Sun after the world was completed not be like the motion of the Spirit before its perfection, since God, after the limit of the three spiritual days, placed his tabernacle in the Sun itself? Therefore, through the Sun itself—as if by the only demonstration <term>a posteriori</term><note>A logical term meaning "from the effect to the cause." Here, the author argues we can understand God's invisible actions by observing the visible Sun.</note>—we can arrive at the true motion of that divine Spirit, by which it moved on any given day toward the composition of the world. For no one will doubt that the subsequent days in creation were equal in duration to the preceding ones, and consequently, that the divine Spirit moved in its revolution in the same amount of time that the Sun moves in its own. Indeed, the solar body itself seems to be like a mirror and the heart of the world, into which the supernatural rays of the Spirit shining from the Trinity are poured. By its radiant power, that solar body is made visible beyond all human reason, and it always maintains a constant and immutable motion by the divine will, producing days of the same length at all times as those in which creation was completed. It seems, therefore, that the Holy Spirit, who appeared to the apostles in the form of a radiant and shining dove, circumambulated the waters in a spiritual form, illuminating their darkness by its motion and pouring its rays into them. By leaving these rays behind after its departure so that the waters might be shaped by them, the Spirit clarified and illustrated all things spiritually in an ineffable way by its presence, no differently than the Sun does physically by its presence. And (to pass to the opinion of the Latin theologians) that uncreated light, by pouring light into created things, made the same circulation during the first three days of creation which the Sun thereafter completed each day by its own motion. It illuminated its own sphere in which it resided just as the Sun illuminates its own; and likewise, darkness was created in the opposite hemisphere due to the interposition of grosser, thicker, and more opaque matter in the middle of the whole formless mass or "horrendous shadow" <note>original Latin: "umbræ horrendæ"</note>. We spoke of the motion of the divine Spirit over the waters in the preceding chapter, at the end of which we also depicted its motion made on the first day of creation according to human understanding; we have explained the reasoning for that emblem near the end of this fifth chapter.

## CHAPTER IV.

->*On the creation and nature of light, and on its operation, and the constitution*<-

THE LORD SAID: "Let there be Light," and on the first day the highest heaven was made, filled with light. For the content of this heaven is nothing other than the most essential and spiritual substance of light, composed of a great portion of the soul and a small amount of the thinnest Spirit; it is therefore called the "fiery Spirit" and the "Empyrean heaven"—that is, fiery and burning—as *Isidore* <note>Referring to Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), a scholar and archbishop whose "Etymologies" was a standard reference for the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> says. This is not because it burns like elemental fire, but because it is suffused everywhere with the splendor and clarity of light. Hence I do not agree with the opinions of those who thought this heaven to be immobile and at rest; for these properties are entirely contrary to the substance of light from which this heaven is fashioned, since light is the "first and simple act," than which nothing is faster in its motion. (*His lightning illuminated the world, and the earth—that is, the darkness—seeing him, was afraid and fled:* <note>original: "Fulgur ejus eluminabat mundum..."</note> Psalm 97, v. 4). Therefore, by the presence of this creature or fiery vigor, the darkness and gloom of that still formless and dark upper part are driven downward through an oblique revolution. This happens for two reasons: first, because the hidden and potential quality of the shadow is now revealed by the fiery activity of light and takes the name of "coldness"; since its disposition is in every way contrary to the quality of lucid heat, its tendency is to flee and turn away from the operations and the object of light. ...the coldness predominating in it retreated more and more toward the center of the universal globe, which is more distant from the dwelling of the primary light. The second reason is that the relationship between light and darkness is the same as that between form and privation; therefore, darkness, avoiding the sight of light like a "terrible shadow" <margin>as *Hermes Trismegistus* says</margin>—to use his words—slipped away in a slanted revolution and sought the center of the circumference. And from this it follows that this heaven is purified and cleansed to the highest degree, separating the subtle from the dense, and is illuminated and made to shine beyond measure, driving all darkness from its edge toward the center. 

Therefore, this heaven, or the supreme and supernatural region of the world, is the dwelling of the fountain of light, and as it were the homeland and native soil in which light, the first-created principle of things, was first placed. From this, it is called the "foundation of the world," by whose formal presence the appetite of the matter of this entire heaven is fulfilled in the highest degree. For it is certain that the matter of this heaven is exceedingly thin and subtle, since its entire substance is formal <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "formal" refers to the essence or "form" of a thing that gives it identity, as opposed to its physical "matter."</note>. For according to *Aristotle* in the 4th book of his *Metaphysics* <margin>*Aristotle* 4. *metaphysics*</margin>, where there is more form, there is less matter, and consequently, the thickness of matter argues for a scarcity of form. 

For the multitude of luminous form, through its actions, constantly rarefies <note>To rarefy is to make something less dense; the author suggests light "thins out" the substance of heaven.</note> the purer part of the matter of the abyss, retained in this heaven by divine will, and extends its mass more widely through rarefaction, just as is perceived in the chemical art. There, if a thick substance in a sufficiently large glass flask, <margin>Hermetically sealed <note>An airtight seal used in alchemy, named after Hermes Trismegistus.</note></margin> is made subtle by a more vehement fire, its rarefied parts naturally seek a larger place; hence the glass breaks so that the thinned vapors may find space more freely. So also the clear matter of this heaven extends itself very widely, rarefied by the lovely heat of this heaven. And from this it follows that this heaven, according to *Basil* in the 2nd book of his *Hexaëmeron* <note>original: *Hexaëmeron* — a treatise on the six days of creation</note> <margin>*Basil* book 2. Hexaëmeron</margin>, extends itself more widely than all the other heavens. 

We conclude, therefore, that this heaven is the most noble form of all, spiritual and simple beyond all imagination, the greatest of all in quantity because of the thinning of matter, the most luminous in quality, and most full of fiery vigor, most active in action, and swiftest in the motion of its luminous substance. It is most sweet in the heat derived from its motion, most temperate, lovely, not burning or destroying, but connecting all lower things in harmonious peace with proportional bonds. It preserves them in its own spirit—which can hardly be perceived by the imagination due to its subtlety—self-moving and living, and existing in its natural seat without the contact of any heterogeneous thing or the hindrance of any coldness. In shape it is spherical, which it received from the motion of the Spirit that "was carried over the waters" and from the luminous power proceeding from it by divine will. It is called by the name <term>Empyrean</term> <note>From the Greek 'empyros,' meaning fiery; the highest, most spiritual part of heaven.</note>, as if fiery, as stated above. It is also called <term>Olympus</term> because of its clarity. It is also called supernatural, because it is spiritual beyond the laws of nature as opposed to corporeality; and intellectual, because it is not visible to us but only intelligible, and perceivable only by demonstration "from the later" <note>original: *a posteriori* — reasoning from observed effects back to their causes</note>, or because it is most full of angels and divine intelligences.

For this sphere is of the most noble condition in its kind, because it participates in the nature of the clarity and thinness of the Empyrean heaven, of which it is the base; for this reason, it is introduced by both the Prophet and the Evangelist in their spiritual visions when explaining the **GLORY OF GOD**, and it is placed under the likeness of a throne or seat, existing as a medium between the nature of spirituality and corporeality. Indeed, around its convex surface, it participates more in the nature of the spiritual heaven, yet in its hollow surface, it is more corporeal in its intervals, as will be explained in its simple composition, or rather in the positioning and assimilation of its parts. For just as the thicker part of the elements of the lowest heaven resides sensibly in an earthy disposition, so also it must be intellectually conceived that the denser part of the most limpid material of the spiritual heaven—already purged of impurity and darkness by the presence of light—is imbued with an insensible and scarcely credible coldness due to its density, and is driven toward the base of this heaven by the action of benevolent heat. For in a certain way, though lightly and gently because of its smallness, this coldness suffers the actions of light, since it is a quality of matter and a friend to darkness; hence it is clear that the greater portion of its substance is more spiritual than corporeal. Similarly, it is to be understood that the rays of the primary light (whose nature it is to penetrate the dense), quickly pursuing the "dreadful shadow" in the beginning, penetrated downward beyond the limits of the Empyrean heaven; and because of the vehement resistance of the dense and dark matter tending slowly downward, they leaped back and were reflected. By these reflections, vapors are refined and, by the motion of the leaping rays, are raised as cloudy exhalations to the concave surface of the watery sphere, and are there constricted and congealed in a glandular manner by dry coldness. For the reflected light rays, exciting an accidental heat by their motion, preserve and increase the benevolent coldness enclosed in the <term>glacial matter<note>original: "materia glacialis"; referring to the icy or crystalline substance believed to form the outer layers of the universe.</note></term> in the concave part of the sphere through <term>antiperistasis</term>; <note>Antiperistasis is a philosophical and early scientific concept where a quality is intensified when surrounded by its opposite, such as cold becoming colder when surrounded by heat.</note> not otherwise than the solar rays, reverberated from the earth of the lowest heaven, strengthen the cold of the middle region of the air. In the convex part of that same crystalline sphere, the heat derived essentially from the action of the first light performs the same office, just as the coldness of the middle region of the air [is strengthened] by the power of the sphere of fire in the lowest heaven. This sphere, therefore, because of the constant action of forms, is as if "fixed" and sublimated to the ultimate peak of its perfection into a **crystalline or adamantine form**, <note>original: "adamantinam"; meaning diamond-like or unbreakable.</note> embracing cloudy and dark globules. These globules have a magnetic power to attract invisible rays passing by and to ejaculate them into the middle world; for their matter desires form no differently than a female desires a male. They are, however, never subject to corruption, because there is such an abundance of form in them that the appetite of their matter is entirely satisfied; nor can the presence of coldness find any putrefaction in that place, because it is "terrestrial"—that is, joined with the essential nature or quality of the earth, namely dryness, which is most friendly to the fiery nature. Not in vain, by the ordination of the Divine Will, was this crystalline and dry mass of waters placed in this region, since its position brings great advantages and no small utility both to the spiritual heaven and the corporeal medium. For it is not only held to be the medium by which spiritual and supernatural things are distinguished and separated from corporeal and natural things, but it is also like a rare **sieve**, through whose diaphragm the rays of spiritual light pass in divine proportion, are sifted, and are as if poured into these lower things. # CHAPTER VI.

## *Concerning the middle heaven and its various names, and the reasons for them.*

The middle region of the world, completed on the second day of creation, has various names because of the downward-tending operations of the matter of light. For when considered by itself—that is, in respect to its own proper matter—it is called the **middle spirit** after the dispersing of the darkness. However, in respect to the higher heaven—that is, the shining substance and its mixture with this spirit—it is called **ether**. Furthermore, insofar as it refers to the four lower elements which appeared and became distinct on the third day, it is called the **Fifth Essence** <note>Also known as the Quintessence, this was believed to be a pure, incorruptible substance superior to earth, water, air, and fire.</note>. 

Therefore, in itself—that is, revealed in its own substance on the second day and purified of its darkness—it displays the form of the subtlest waters, and of a certain vaporous and never-resting smoke. Wherefore among the *Platonists* it is called the "middle spirit of the world," which we called the receptacle, bond, and vehicle of essential light and of the Soul of the World above in chapter 5 of book 1; there we also demonstrated the reason for that name. 

But insofar as this spirit is the bond of light descending from the spiritual source, by whose action a life-giving and natural heat is excited, it is to that extent called **ether**—that is, "shining," according to *Isidore* <note>Saint Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), an influential scholar whose encyclopedic works preserved much classical knowledge for the Middle Ages.</note>, because there is perpetual clarity and brightness there. Or it is called "fiery" according to *Anaxagoras* <note>A Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who proposed that the sun was a red-hot stone and the heavens were made of ether.</note>, who asserts that everything that burns is called ether, since ether is nothing other than inflamed air. Hence, according to Greek grammar, it is derived from <term>aithō</term> <note>original: αἴθω</note> which signifies "I burn"; air spirit, as if *aeth-aer*, that is, "burning spirit." 

For this reason, *Orpheus* calls it *Pyripnon* <note>original: Πυρίπνουν</note>, that is, "fiery breath," and *Porphyry* <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who was a student of Plotinus.</note> with the rest of the Platonists calls it the "spirit," in the middle of which they placed the Soul of the World. And hence it is that, according to *Marianus* <note>Likely Martianus Capella, a late Roman author whose work on the liberal arts was a foundation of medieval education.</note>, there is perpetual day in the ether, because darkness never approaches there; although its simple substance, separate from the stellar bodies, is invisible—that is, not perceptible to mortal eyes—as we shall declare more broadly in the following chapter. 

Finally, it is held to be a single element, just as *Aristotle* maintains in his book *On Meteorology*, where he asserts that the ether is nothing else but a unique element. Hence it is necessary that this unique element be outside the count of the four inferior essences <note>Earth, water, air, and fire.</note> to be produced soon in the lowest region; and for this reason it is also called the **Fifth Essence** by the Philosophers, in which nothing of corruption is found, since two contraries inducing putrefaction are not found in the same element. 

From the reasons for these names, therefore, it is manifest that the matter of this region—formerly primary <note>In its chaotic, unformed state.</note>, but now made secondary through being brought into active form—is nothing other than a most pure vapor, or a certain most subtle mist, generally called **spirit**. Its form, by whose presence it is brought into action, is that light or clarity essentially gushing forth from the perennial fountain of the divine and super-celestial spirit, totally fulfilling the appetite <note>In the philosophical sense, "appetite" refers to the natural tendency of matter to seek a form.</note> of this spiritual middle matter, as will be declared below.

# CHAPTER VII.

### *The composition of the middle heaven: why is it called the sphere of equality? And why is this region called the corporeal heaven with respect to the one above?*

---

**J**ust as the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest, most spiritual part of the universe, often associated with pure light and the residence of the divine.</note> was created on the first day from a single thing—namely, from the substance of light—and was composed of three parts of the thinnest fire and one part of the most subtle spirit; and whereas it is entirely "formal" <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "formal" refers to the active, spiritual essence or "form" of a thing, while "material" refers to its physical weight and passivity.</note> with respect to the lower realms, and is named "fiery" because of the predominance of fire within it: so too the matter of this second heaven, since it is more corporeal than that of the first and higher heaven, corresponds to its own luminous form in that due proportion by which matter is usually weighed against its form on equal scales. Thus, it is composed of one part of fiery and most thin light—which descends from the source of the Empyrean heaven through the diaphragm of the crystalline sphere—and an equal quantity of primary matter, which by then was already shaped and had <margin>1</margin> obtained the name of "spirit." This is also what Pythagoras <note>The ancient Greek philosopher who viewed the universe as a harmonic and mathematical construction.</note> seems to assert when he writes that the sun, moon, and other stars are composed of fire and air. For this reason, Artephius <note>A legendary medieval alchemist whose writings were highly influential in the occult sciences of the 17th century.</note>, with the consensus of the ancient philosophers, called this region the "heaven of equality," in the center of which the wise placed the sphere of the soul. From these principles, it seems likely that the constitution of this heaven consists of two parts of middle spirit and an equal amount of that most beautiful substance, the luminous soul, which is perfectly suited to satisfy the appetite of that same spiritual matter and to preserve it from corruptible changes.

That this region is more corporeal than the highest one can be proven by many reasons. One of these is that where there is less form, there is more matter; but in this second heaven there is less form than in the Empyrean heaven, whose entire substance is completely formal; therefore, in this heaven there is more matter than in the Empyrean heaven. This major premise is taken from the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Referring to Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, the foundational text for understanding the nature of existence and reality.</note>. Another reason is that the mass of primary matter <term>materia prima<gloss>The formless, raw substance that existed at the beginning of creation before it was given specific shapes or properties.</gloss></term> always maintained one and the same state before the appearance of light; for it lacked an agent whose actions could lead it from one disposition into another. Hence, it could be called neither thinner nor thicker, since all its potential and imaginable parts must be considered to be of the same condition in one potential region of the world as in another. 

However, since the disposition of light is such that nothing exists more subtle than it, nor more capable of penetrating and opening bodies, it must be that light always desires to thin the parts of thicker matter, so that it may act and move more readily within them without hindrance. Hence, the more "formal" a thing is, the more subtle its substance must be. The reason for this is purely philosophical: because "formal" light is moved by its own act, and by its motion it excites heat, the nature of which is to thin, dilate, and dissipate. Therefore, that perennial spring of light created on the first day in the upper region of the world, immediately revealing the hidden matter of that region and bringing it into action, shaped a thin and most subtle part according to its own nature. It pushed the thicker portion of that matter downward toward the center into the middle region, so that it might govern the simplest substance of spirit (which it reduced, as it were, into a universal form) without any hindrance, and carry it with itself through all the hiding places of the world. And from this it follows that half of the corporeal nature of this "informed" region, having been reflected into the middle, [makes] the middle more corpo-

### CHAPTER VIII.

*Concerning the reflection of the double darkness of the middle heaven into the lowest region of the world, and concerning the arrangement and effect of its light—that is, the heat proceeding from it—and how light shines invisibly through itself and in itself.*

**T**HE virtue or supernatural brightness of the heaven, descending by the ordinance of the Creator through the openings—or rather the breasts—of the watery sieve <note>original: "cribri aquei foramina vel potiùs ubera"; Fludd uses the "watery sieve" as a metaphor for the boundary of the Empyrean heaven which filters divine influence</note>, and pouring itself downward as if from its own perennial fountain into the middle heaven (which was still potential and unformed), dispelled the gloom and darkness of this part of matter by its presence. It drove those darknesses toward the lowest region, which was still invisible and hidden, and by this means made its substance visible and formed, pure, subtle, thin, and far more excellent in perfection and beauty than the mass of the lower heaven. Indeed, this is that luminous essence springing from the first super-celestial source through infinite rivulets into every part of the celestial sea, which the ancients called *ether*; we, however, call it *Secondary Light*, because it is derived immediately from the first root. So also we shall call the rays of the Sun and stars that penetrate into the lowest region of the world *tertiary light*.

Therefore this light, although secondary, is filled with such active and most vivid power that it frees this entire heaven from its original impurity, drives away its obscurity, and causes it to glide away like a dreadful shadow into the lowest part of the world by a slanted revolution. It thrusts the more imperfect and thicker parts down to the lower depths along with the darkness, separating the subtle from the dense <note>A classic alchemical and Hermetic principle of refinement</note>. It illuminates its substance and makes it ethereal; it fills its material spirit with its own perfection and satisfies the entire "appetite" of matter <note>In Aristotelian terms, matter has an "appetite" or "desire" for form and perfection</note>, so that it is not subject to corruption or putrefaction and is very little afflicted by contraries, because all its parts are uniform. Finally, this was that secondary essence which, acting in place of the Sun for three days from the creation of the world, passed into the substance of the Sun on the fourth day—as <margin>Dionysius</margin> <note>Likely referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist theologian</note> maintains. Indeed, this is that simple act by whose operation this ethereal heaven is most skillfully adorned with glowing fires. From this arise its motions, differing in various ways—namely, the Eastern, Western, and those according to latitude, which they call *trepidation* <note>An astronomical theory describing the oscillation of the equinoxes</note>. Finally, a kindly heat, most friendly and thoroughly necessary to the life of creatures, is kindled; this heat is more intense and sensible in this place than in the higher region because of the thicker substance of this heaven. For the denser the matter, the more vehemently it resists the agent, and consequently, the agent acts more strongly upon the subject <term>patientem</term><note>The "patient" is the philosophical term for the thing being acted upon by an "agent"</note>. But the matter of this heaven, as has been said, is thicker than that of the Empyrean heaven. Therefore, the light acts more strongly upon it, and the matter likewise resists it, and consequently produces hotter effects to repel the injuries of the cold—which was once hidden, but is now made manifest by the presence of heat—whose nature it is to always accompany thicker matter. Thus, just as this heat is more intense than the supreme heat, so it is far more tempered, subtle, and simple with respect to the lower regions, because it follows the disposition of the form from whose action it immediately proceeds. We conclude, therefore, that just as the substance of the form of this heaven was born from an immortal parent and is in no way to be corrupted, being exalted and most noble in dignity because of its origin, breathing life and soul into mundane creatures and nourishing them with its light; so also its heat from...

The reason is ready at hand why the light of this region—although constantly clear, bright, and transparent regarding the substance of that place—nevertheless sometimes exists invisibly when compared to lower things; for, according to *Dionysius* <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a philosopher whose "metaphysics of light" heavily influenced medieval and Renaissance thought.</note> light is a substance existing in itself, and from which the clarity, splendor, and brilliance of bodies proceed: Therefore, light shines through itself only in itself, but to others by accident <note>original: "per accidens." For according to the teaching of *Hippocrates* <note>The famous Greek physician; the author likely refers to the idea that celestial "breaths" or influences temper the atmosphere.</note>, if the life of the stars did not temper the thickness of the air in the nighttime, their bodies and spirits would be suffocated, and yet this impression of the stars is not perceived at night; indeed, their splendor, dispersed everywhere, is distinguished only with difficulty, except in the luminaries themselves.

### CHAPTER IX.

->*That the poles and circles of this heaven are merely imaginary, artificial,*<-
->*and in no way naturally suited*<-
->*to it.*<-

MANY things have the experts in Astronomy found that are more useful to the art of cosmography <term>Cosmography: the science of mapping the general features of the universe, encompassing both geography and astronomy.</term> than they are true; which, although they are fictional and artificial, nevertheless, because they more readily guide students in the art, are to be esteemed as true and natural; among which, on the periphery of this heaven, they have placed two poles, opposite to each other, which they have called the ends of a certain imaginary axis or diameter passing through the center of the world, and the vertices of the world; upon which they imagined its globe to be turned; they also described *circles* in these, *greater* and *lesser*; of which they made the *greater* partly *immobile* and partly *mobile*: they established only two *immobile* circles, which they called *external*, one of which they called the *Meridian*, drawn through the poles of the world and the *Horizon*, and the other the *Horizon*, dividing the upper hemisphere from the lower and bounding our sight; and they made this more direct or more oblique according to the depression or elevation of the pole. Moreover, the *mobile circles*, which they imagined to be *internal*, they called either *greater* or *lesser*. All the *greater* ones, except one, lack width, and they distinguished them into *parallel* or *non-parallel*; the greater parallel they called the *Equinoctial* <note>The celestial equator.</note>, because of its division of the world into two parts (for equally...

All of these things, because they pertain more to technical history than to physical history, we shall reserve for the treatise on Astronomy.*

### CHAPTER X.

->*Of the third heaven, and its various names; Why this lowest region is called heaven?*<-

Before the action of light upon the third and lowest region of the world, its container was like a shadow or a most foul and thick smoke, endowed with no visible form, but in a way distinct by the density of its substance: For it was thicker below on account of the presence of light and heat <note>The author suggests that the action of light and heat from above compressed or "thickened" the lower elemental matter</note>. But afterward, on the third day, when the operation of light—tending downward toward the earth to create the mathematical center—was completed, I say, this heaven being finished, as will be said below, philosophers both recent and ancient attributed various names to it. For some, wishing to signify its dimension, called it the *sublunary region of the world*, denoting all that space which is measured between the concave surface of the middle heaven (or the sphere of the Moon) and the convexity of the physical center (or the Earth). Others, considering its elementary spheres, with whose bodies the capacity of this heaven is filled, called it the *elementary region*; although we have declared above that the higher elements also fill the heavens in a certain way.

## CHAPTER XI.

->*On the element of fire.*<-

SOOTY matter, covered in darkness, was thrust down from the supreme heaven on the first day of creation by the power of the primary light into the region of the middle heaven; and thereafter from the middle heaven, by the power of the secondary light on the second day, with all the darkness of that region, it was driven down and contracted into the third and lowest heaven. It is now rendered very thick, dark, and rebellious in this lower region, so much so that the power of the natural light of the third order (which is merely an offspring of the second heaven) is not sufficient to propel and depress that foul, formless, and black matter into the center of the universe, on account of the multitude of cold lurking within it. From this, therefore, that greatest Architect <note>original: *opifex*; the Creator</note> ordained that the natural faculties of the hot light of the third order should be strengthened by accidental means; for He willed that a certain adventitious heat should arise, not proceeding immediately from light, but from the violent agitation or motion of matter. For by the circular and hurried vibration and rotation of the middle heaven from the east to its opposite part—proceeding immediately from the action of the primary light—and because of the fitness of the lower heaven's matter to receive any form, whether accidental or essential; and also because of the resistance of the cold of the thick matter, which preserves and strengthens that adventitious heat through <term>antiperistasis <note>A philosophical term for the intensification of a quality when surrounded by its opposite, such as heat becoming more intense when compressed by surrounding cold.</note></term> on the convex surface of the lowest heaven; and finally because of the density of the matter, a certain collision occurs between the convexity of one and the concavity of the other. Thus, through the reflection of the shining rays emerging from the middle heaven, a burning heat—adventitious and accidental nonetheless—is excited in the upper part of the lowest heaven, the

In its current state, its convex surface and the entire substance surrounding it are ignited by an invisible flame. Because of this, the power of cold is utterly expelled from that sphere, and consequently, it is not impregnated by any portion of moisture. Instead, "by accident"—that is, through the total absence of moisture which usually occurs when cold and heat join—it must necessarily be extremely dry. 

This heat, although it naturally exists in this region, is not part of the true essence of light. Rather, it is the final effect of light's action, flowing immediately from the movement of matter. Therefore, it contributes nothing to the functions of life, except insofar as it relates to the physical makeup of the body, which serves as the seat of life. This is not that "invisible fire of the Philosophers" <note>original: "ignis Philosophorum"; likely referring to the spiritual or alchemical fire that creates and sustains life</note> from which they say all created things are born. Instead, it is merely that heat whose unnatural dominance leads all things toward putrefaction. Under its influence, the **radical moisture** <note>original: "humidum radicale"; in medieval medicine, this was the vital fluid or "lamp oil" of life within an organism</note>—or the spirit of moisture—is consumed by an unnatural blaze. The viscous and watery fluids are turned into poison, and the substance of the universal composite is ignited and dried out by a feverish heat.

However, as long as a proper proportion of natural moisture remains to balance the **innate heat** <note>original: "calidum innato"; the internal heat that maintains life</note> (which we call "vital"), the forces of that external, intrusive quality are suppressed. Thus, they are prevented from crossing into the physical body against the laws of nature. This intense heat and its entire substance—which is to say, the "disturbed spirit"—the Philosophers have called the <term>element of fire</term>. It occupies the highest seat of the lowest heaven. By unanimous consent, they have defined its nature as hot and dry for the reasons stated above. Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that celestial light exists within this element, since light cannot descend into the lower realms unless it first penetrates the sphere of fire. # CHAPTER XII.

## *Concerning the element of earth.*

**W**ith two powers therefore united—namely, the natural and the adventitious—the matter, which is rebellious on account of its own coldness, is strongly beaten back by them. That matter, following its own natural instinct, flees from those powers sent out from the periphery. Pursuing its own cold nature and fleeing both the primary and secondary effects of light as far as the seat of the place most remote from the circumference of that same light, it restricted itself into the form of a horrific shadow, gliding beneath in an oblique revolution. Around the center or middle point of the spherical machine <note>The "machine of the world" was a common early modern term for the physical structure of the cosmos</note> of the universe, it formed itself into a hard, solid, and opaque globe. For in this place, it is much more secure from the actions of its adversary, namely heat, and far more remote from the dwelling place of light, since it is from the action of light that this enemy heat arises. Indeed, this motion of matter was stirred up not by itself, but by that aforementioned double action of light. For just as without the manifestation of light the matter of darkness was only something potential; so also without the presence of heat, which is an essential quality of light, that natural disposition of matter—namely coldness—produces nothing in actuality and consequently produces no changes through itself. Therefore, the coldness of matter is driven downward by the active power of both the primary light and the element of fire produced by the motion of matters; for without these, nothing whatever is done. Moreover, that coldness, by suffering the repercussions of heat, seems in a certain way to resist, and by resisting, it appears to react. By these actions and passions, other grades are produced in this lowest heaven, and intermediate regions differing in disposition are established, which the Philosophers call the lower elements. From these things, therefore, 
<margin>/</margin>that principal reasoning is explained as to why heavy things cannot fall beyond the center of the world, and why they rest there perpetually; namely, because gravity exists as a companion to denser and more compact matter. The cause of this thickness was coldness, which contracted the scattered and thin matter toward the center of the world to escape the fury of the penetrating heat, constraining it there and defending it against the invasions of the rays of light. However, since the action of heat pursues the cold dispersed in every part of a thick object, and especially around the center, throughout the whole mass of its body, and since the rays of light (whose nature it is to penetrate bodies most easily) as if besiege and surround it everywhere, it happens that heavy things can in no way proceed beyond that center toward the natural habitat of light, unless that cold, enclosed by nature within heavy things, is overwhelmed and violated by the violence of heat. And from this it follows that any heavy thing violently thrown upward returns naturally and of its own accord downward to the center or the seat of coldness. It is manifest, therefore, that the entire substance of darkness—by whose presence the spiritual matter of the whole world was hidden and unformed—is now finally, by the power of light, reduced and gathered into a dense and opaque mass around the center of the world, which is indeed called the element of earth. The remaining spiritual mass of the now-formed matter is pellucid and wonderfully transparent; extending from the margins of the earth even to the convex surface of the world, it is known by the general name of "heaven." Among the sacred writers, the most divine *Moses* confirms this at the very threshold of *Genesis*: *In the beginning*, he says, *God created heaven and earth* <note>original: "In principio... creavit DEUS cælum & terram"</note>, which is to say, He separated light from darkness; for He made the heaven clear and luminous, but the earth opaque—that is, He immersed the center of the world in darkness. The Creator established the origin and designated the privative part <note>original: "partem privativam"; in Aristotelian philosophy, "privation" is the absence of a quality that should naturally be present, such as darkness being the absence of light</note> as the cause of nights. For if the Craftsman had not placed the earth in the center of the world, the world would not be defiled by any filth or impurity; everything would be radiant, and perpetual day would shine forth. It is, therefore, not at all surprising that so many and such great corruptions and transformations of things occur in this lower world. Indeed, in its center or heart lies hidden that most corrupt mother of ruin and privation—that mournful and dark seal of the separation of forms and essences from composite creatures. There, the true witness and messenger of the supernatural tyranny of the elements is perpetually stationed within physical things as they were once formed. Hence the most holy **Job** says: *And the dark land is covered with the shadow of Death*; <note>original: "Et terra tenebrosa cooperitur cum obscuritate Mortis"; a reference to Job 10:21-22</note> and elsewhere, the earth is said to be *a land of misery and darkness*. Indeed, this is, as it were, the place of perdition, in which Adam, along with Eve, having been banished from the joys of Paradise, received for himself and left to his heirs the sign of inevitable death. 

The element of fire is like the fiery sword of the **Cherubim**, wielded by a celestial spirit to block the way to the tree of life—that is, to that divine and immortal nectar—and to bring either sudden or unexpected death to all who thirst too greatly for immortality. Finally, this central mass is a dire companion of sadness and error because of its blind and stealthy condition; it is an enemy not only of men but of **GOD**, the Best and Greatest, and of the celestial intelligences, because its horrendous rebellion is enclosed in the very middle of its belly. Therefore, woe to us miserable creatures on earth, for whom such a crowd of miseries lies in wait every day, and such great danger to both body and soul is always imminent! But you, O celestial creatures and true inhabitants of the sweetest Paradise—you, I say, who are more than thrice happy and blessed beyond human understanding—you are free and immune from such wretched chains of distress through the ineffable power of light!

As for the arrangement of this central mass, although nearly all philosophers assert its natural quality to be dryness, and wish for dryness to predominate in it—viewing its coldness as clearly accidental and acquired, derived from the nature of water—nevertheless, if we consider our preceding argument and the possibilities of nature itself more accurately, we will see that nothing wanders further from the goal of truth than that fantasy of theirs. Since the essential seat of natural light exists at the periphery of the world, and the origin of heat depends on that same source of light, it is necessary that darkness (which is the contrary of light) and coldness (which is the opposite of heat) should be located at the furthest distance from each other. 

Consequently, just as the seat of original heat is in the highest heaven, so the primordial dwelling of cold is in the physical center of the world, as the most remote place. From this, it follows that coldness predominates in the center more naturally, while dryness is more adventitious <note>meaning "added from outside" or secondary</note> there. That is to say, because of the absence of natural moisture in that place, the parts of the earth are said to be dry; for moisture is created from the tempering of coldness with a portion of heat, and that heat (for the reasons stated above) has no power or possession in that central place. Furthermore, I think no one would be so foolish as to not call that body "colder" which has no portion of heat reaching it at all. It is certain that some portion of airy heat exists in the element of water, since it derives its fluidity (its moisture) from the air itself, which is most certainly moist and hot. But it is certain that the earth does not participate in the nature of air, because it has no fluidity in itself; nor does it have any commerce with fire, both because it is most distantly removed from fire's sphere, and because water—which is the contrary of fire—is placed between the earth and fire. Finally, since the earth is by far thicker than the other elements, and it is the nature of coldness to condense both unlike and like things, it is infallibly proven by the effect that coldness abounds more in the earth. We have delineated the region of earth and fire in this manner.

<vocab>Macrocosm: the universe; central mass: the Earth; privation: the lack of light/life; Cherubim: angelic guardians; adventitious: not inherent, coming from outside.</vocab>

## CHAPTER XIII.

->*Concerning the middle sphere, which is called the sphere of humidity, and concerning the elements of water and air.*<-

**T**HE sphere of humidity, situated in the middle between the center of the earth and the outer curved surface of fire, is called the *sphere of equality* <note>original: "sphæra æqualitatis"</note>, because it is forged from an equal portion of each extreme element. For neither the coldness of the earth by itself, nor indeed the heat of fire alone, is able to produce humidity; rather, the conjunction of both—and, as it were, the union of the male with the female—establishes it. For just as terrestrial coldness alone constricts the <term>middle spirit<note>In this context, "spirit" refers to the subtle, fluid substance that fills the universe, acting as a medium for elemental qualities.</note></term> where it is present, so it is the role of the heat falling upon it to dissolve that icy spirit, liquefy it, and render it fluid. Similarly, heat by itself—that is, when joined to its own dryness—[absorbs] <note>The catchword "abfor-" at the bottom suggests the word "absorbere," meaning to swallow up or dry out.</note> the juice of that spirit...

...absorbs [it], or certainly dissipates it by its own quality into insensible parts; for this reason, it deserves to be called a separator of moisture rather than a producer of it. Therefore, the violence of <term>heat|caliditas</term> is blunted by the greater or lesser meeting of <term>cold|frigiditas</term>. Thus, the intense operations of both are hindered, and the <term>spirit|spiritus</term> <note>In this context, "spirit" refers to the subtle, vaporous substance that fills the universe</note> is not permitted to be coagulated by the cold because of the presence of heat. Nor is it possible for heat, according to the property of its nature, to dissipate and scatter the parts of the moistening spirit, which happens because of the resistance of the present cold. Thus, the spirit is dissolved by the assistance of heat; but once dissolved, it is not dispersed, nor is it thinned down almost to nothing—which would be fully accomplished by the presence of cold—but rather it remains in the middle, naturally flowing. Through its fluid nature and liquidity, it moistens all intermediate things, either more bodily and visibly—that is, if it adheres to a larger portion of cold—or more spiritually and insensibly—namely, if it embraces a more ample part of heat. And it is from this disposition of the <term>moist|humidi</term> that the two intermediate elements are derived, as we shall immediately demonstrate.

Therefore, the thick matter, as was said before, having been driven down from on high to the center, and retained there because of the immense cold with which it is endowed, desires to rest there. But truly, because it is the nature of heat to always attack cold as an enemy and to pursue it with a certain natural antipathy; and likewise, because it is the nature of any subtle thing to penetrate, therefore this active quality, pushing that passive quality downward, pursues it there and continually tries to penetrate its mass. And because the end of any thing is its opposite, and not only rest, but even motion is opposed to motion; therefore, to that motion intended downward toward the center or the middle, another motion succeeded from below upwards toward the element of fire, stirred up by the resistance of the cold opposing the injuries of the heat, and by the reverberation of the rays of light fighting against it. 

Whence two parts of the earthly cold, ascending upward to repel the injuries of the heat, met just as many parts of heat in the middle way between the center and the sphere of fire, which were descending to fulfill that coldness. And by the union of these parts, the **sphere of moisture** is established, the middle part of which exists as simply and equally moist. For the forces of heat in its middle are proportional to those of cold, so that they are weighed as if on an equal scale, leaning to neither side, and they possess the same strength and power of acting on both sides; that is, they tend no more downward than they do to the side, and consequently, while they are moved, it is necessary that they be carried ->**circularly**<-. 

The dimension of this middle sphere, however, tending downward toward its concavity, is called the element of **water**, which—because of its proximity to the element of **earth** and its greater distance from the sphere of **fire**—appears more earthly, thick, visible, and sensibly moistening. For its temperament is fashioned from three-quarters of earthly cold (for it is much more contiguous to the earth) and one-quarter of the heat of fire; in which temperament, although the smallest portion of heat is present, it is nevertheless sufficient to hinder the freezing disposition of the cold and to preserve this part of the sphere of moisture in its fluid quality. 

And this is the same reasoning that we brought forth above; that it may appear most clearly that cold exists much more intensely in earth than in water, since water, through the absence or reduction of that fourth part of heat, is frozen and reduced into ice—that is, a more earthly and non-fluid substance. The other half of the aforementioned sphere, protruding upward toward the concave surface of fire, because it is further distant from the earth and because of its vicinity to the element of fire, is a great participant in heat and contains very little cold in itself by which its fiery heat might be tempered. For that reason, it is much subtler, more spiritual, and more invisible than its lower part, and because of its subtlety, it penetrates more and moistens more deeply. From which it is gathered...

### CHAPTER XIV.

#### *On the form of the elements.*

**T**HE FORM of this heaven <note>referring to the lower or sublunary "heaven" or atmosphere</note> is weaker than that of the higher ones, because of its distance from its origin; this indeed is very easily proven by its effect. For indeed, our terrestrial fire, receiving its power of heating from the action of light, the further it is distant from its subject <note>literally "passive," referring to the object being acted upon</note>, the more weakly it is accustomed to heat; and consequently it is certain that the matter of this heaven, the more it approaches the center <note>the Earth, considered the center of the universe in this system</note>, the grosser, more impure, and less worthy <note>indignior: in a Neoplatonic sense, further from the perfection of the Divine source</note> it is; according to that saying of *Aristotle* in his <term>Metaphysics</term> <note>Aristotle’s foundational work on the nature of existence and reality</note>, *where there is more matter, there is less form, and vice versa.* <note>original: "ubi plus est materia, ibi minus est forma, & è converso."</note> From this it clearly stands that the matter of this heaven predominates because of the weakening of its form, and consequently it constantly seeks a new form daily; for there is not enough form supplied to this region so that the appetite of its matter can be filled and satisfied. Hence, therefore, constant changes of things arise within it; hence the corruptions where—

### *An experiment with wine, from which the nature of each of the elements*
### *can be gathered.*

## CHAPTER XVI.

-> **Concerning certain experiments with waters which, through the action of light, demonstrate various arrangements in the constitution of the aforementioned heavens.** <-

**IT IS CERTAIN** that fire is understood under the name of light and originated from light itself; since nowhere in the universal description of creation did our divine leader <note>original: "Antistes," usually meaning a high priest or prelate, here referring to Moses as the divinely-inspired author of Genesis</note> **Moses** mention that most noble creature, fire, except when speaking of light: This is also more clearly declared in Book VI, Chapter 8. No one will doubt that air and water were also from the substance of that mass—namely, the universal waters—since the sacred Scriptures testify that all things were forged from it. Now truly, because these operations are undoubtedly viewed with suspicion by some who rely more on their physical senses than on reason, it remains to represent these operations to their eyes through the effects derived from those two primary causes—namely water and light. They will perceive these visibly and quite easily if they diligently observe the following experiments.

-> *First experiment concerning fire and air, or subtle water.* <-

With a fire lit in the upper part of a concave and perfectly sealed instrument, in the bottom of which (opposite the fire) a hole or a very small tube is placed, the air inside becomes more <term>attenuated</term> <note>thinned or rarefied through heating</note> the closer it approaches the location of the fire. The thicker part of this thinned air, which is colder, moves away from the active fire toward the lowest part of the vessel, as if fleeing from its enemy. This is visibly evident because it is perceived to exit gradually in the form of a moist vapor through the tube or hole of that region.
