From this, therefore, we conclude that thick air—fleeing from fire because of the coldness contained within it—tends toward a region more remote from the fire's presence. But the center is the place most remote from the circumference. Accordingly, when the fiery virtue <term>virtus ignea: the active power or essential energy of fire</term> occupies the surface of any concave globe, the air or thin water held and enclosed within it will send its thicker parts toward the center. Indeed, all parts of the air contained within the concave globe are gradually thicker the more remote they are from the vigor of the fire, as is explained by the following experiment.

### *Experiment II.*

Let there be made, therefore, a certain globe of glass or copper, with three distinct regions, such that one encompasses the entire concavity of the other. And let these regions have certain openings or tubes protruding in the manner depicted below, and let the outermost surface of the globe be surrounded on all sides by a most lively fire. 

When this is done, it will be visible to the eye that the external fire imparts its more lively vigor to the upper <note>In the context of these concentric spheres, 'upper' often refers to the outermost layer closest to the heat source.</note> region, and the air contained within it is wonderfully thinned <term>attenuari: the process of making a substance less dense or more subtle</term> due to its proximity to the living fire. Furthermore, the second or middle region receives the fiery vigor from the first; but nevertheless, because that vigor is milder there than in the upper region, the air existing in it is consequently less subtle and thin, as the fiery force is certainly not strong enough to rarefy it further. 

Finally, the fiery virtue hiding in the middle region will also infuse some force, albeit a small one, into the lowest region. Whence the preceding proposition—as well as that expressed after the end of the seventh chapter—demonstrates that the thick air of the upper region (which is greater in quantity), that of the middle region (which is smaller in proportion), and finally that of the lowest region (which is the least of all), tends toward the center and clusters there into drops. The demonstration follows.

## THE EXPERIMENT IS AS FOLLOWS.

In the beginning, the potential substance of the waters in the world was no different than if a portion of an artificial globe—divided into various hollows with specific intervals passing from the circumference to the center—were filled with clear water or air (as seen in the arc *a-c-b* in the previous demonstration), where all parts of the water are of the same density and arrangement. But if fire <note>In Fludd's cosmology, fire represents the divine light or active heat that causes expansion and contraction</note> touches the outer surface of that arc, the thicker air of the upper region (denoted by *I*), which is found to be much larger in relation to that center, and similarly the air of the second and third regions, will become extremely thick and compact when it is reflected back toward the center. Indeed, it could not be contained otherwise in such a narrow place as that of the center; for the air, which was previously contained in the spaces *A. C. D. E.* and *D. E. F. G.* and *F. G. H. I.*, is compressed and squeezed into that tiny angle of the arc and reduced into a thick and vaporous mass. From this, therefore, depends that great mystery of the ancient Philosophers: finding the weights and proportions of the elements <note>original: "pondera atque proportiones elementorum"</note>.

<margin>/</margin> And indeed, for this reason, the whole world was reduced into a spherical form, and the Archetype <term>Archetype (Archetypus): The divine blueprint or the Creator's mind upon which the physical world is modeled</term> arranged the thicker bodies toward the center of the world-machine <note>original: "machinæ centrum"</note>, so that those substances made finer through <term>rarefaction: The process of a substance becoming less dense, the opposite of condensation</term> and thinning could, by always ascending, choose a more spacious place for themselves. For thick things require less space before they are dissolved than after they are refined, as was stated above. With the completion of this knowledge, it will not be difficult to measure the capacity of the heavens, provided the size of the earth is known first; nor will it be difficult to determine the proportions of the elements to one another...

# BOOK THREE.

**Concordances; From which its Music arises.**

    *   General, pertaining to the harmonies of the whole heaven, discussed in chapters 1, 2, and 3.

    *   From these proportions, the harmonies of the same, discussed in chapter 3.
    *   Finally, from these harmonies, its Music.
*   **Practice,** discussed in chapters 7 and 8.

**Discordances, discussed in chapter 9.**

# CHAPTER I.

## *Concerning the account of worldly proportions.*

---

**F**rom what has preceded, it is clear that just as the Empyrean Heaven <note>The "Empyrean" was considered the highest, most spiritual part of the universe, composed of pure light and fire.</note> is the home and seat of supernatural fire and light—from which natural fire proceeds directly, and that other, more accidental fire proceeds indirectly—so also its opposite place, which terminates and ends the movement of its rays, is the receptacle of matter and darkness. Since the relationship between opposites is the same, it is necessary for the sake of the world's continuity that the disposition of the moist nature of darkness stands in the same degree and proportion to that fiery nature of light. Hence, as we have declared above that the physical center <note>The Earth.</note> is naturally cold in the fourth degree <note>In ancient and medieval science, qualities like heat and cold were measured in four "degrees" of intensity.</note>, being most dense, most opaque, and heaviest, and naturally seeking rest by its own nature; so also the outermost region of the world-machine is undoubtedly opposed to it in all things, not only in location but also in condition. Thus, by the equal action of the one and the proportional reception <margin>/</margin> of the other, all intermediate bodies are established; according to the nature of the subject—that is, by the abundance or lack of the light predominating within it—they either resist privation <note>The absence of form or light.</note> for a long time or more quickly yield and are subjected to it.

Who then will doubt that the highest region of the Empyrean heaven is free and immune from every invasion of coldness, whose property it is to thicken or condense? For it is most subtle, purest, lightest, transparent in the highest degree of clarity, and is almost nothing other than fire sublimated to the ultimate <margin>/</margin> peak of the sweetest and most loving warmth. Without doubt, therefore, those proportions of things introduce a truly noble worldly harmony; through these proportions, as the power of the primary light works upon the intermediate matter, an indissoluble concord of things is settled, and the ears of the intellect are soothed by a certain inexplicable music. For the instrument of this melody—namely, the machine of the world—is like a monochord <note>A one-stringed musical instrument used to demonstrate the mathematical ratios of musical intervals.</note>, whose string, through which the consensus of parts is introduced, is the intermediate matter of the whole world. The composer in this music <margin>/</margin> is the World Soul, or the essence-making light <note>original: "lux essentifica"</note>; just as in the instrumental music of man, in which **Γ** (that is, Gamma) <note>Gamma-ut was the lowest note in the medieval musical scale.</note> takes its beginning from the lower part of the system, ascending with low, high, and superlative voices. Such a progression also occurs in the worldly monochord, namely ascending proportionally from the Earth to its "ee la" <note>The highest note in the standard Renaissance musical scale (Guidonian Hand).</note>, which is the boundary of the outermost periphery. And as in the Gamma the sound is lower and deeper because of the extreme distance from "ee la," from which the striking of the voice becomes more intense by ascending; so also the higher one ascends from the Earth toward the Empyrean heaven, the stronger the effect of light and heat is found to be, and the world-spirit <note>original: "spiritus mundanus"; the subtle medium connecting soul and body/matter.</note> is rendered thinner by its power. Just as a greater force, and therefore a greater power of the shining soul <margin>/</margin>, is required for the raising of the human voice, while in its lowering, altogether less is desired;

For each of these has a pyramidal dimension in this <term>Macrocosm</term><note>The "Great World" or the universe, which Fludd believed mirrored the structure of the human being (the Microcosm).</note>, by which it is accustomed to operate (more in one place and less in another) in no other way than how one portion of a physical pyramid gradually requires a wider cavity in which the other may be contained.

We have delineated these formal dimensions of the world at the end of the fifth book, where that pyramidal dimension is to be understood in physical things. Here, however, we have briefly sketched the proportional embrace of one pyramid by the other, so that we may better lead students to the perfection of our explanation of this **world-music** by a more sensible demonstration of proportions. In this light, it is more manifest that three parts of the material pyramid occupy the lowest region of the world, with which one part of the formal pyramid mixes (namely, the part near the point); it is this which gave essential form to that entire mass of matter. Two parts of the same [material pyramid] fill the middle region, which are there informed by just as many portions of the formal pyramid. Finally, a single portion of it gives substance to the Empyrean heaven, which three portions of the formal pyramid inform supernaturally. 

From these things it clearly appears that the material pyramid grants substance to every part of the world, and that the reciprocal reception of the **shining pyramid** transforms it from primary matter into secondary and formed matter. Consequently, everything between the borders of the earth and the highest boundary of the Empyrean heaven has received its proportions from the action and passion of these two pyramids; from these are also derived all the proportions and consonances of the Macrocosm that constitute the **universal harmony**. <margin>-</margin> SINCE in every part of the **hyle** <term>hyle: the primal, unformed matter of the universe</term>, and similarly in every portion of the most beautiful light, there was no difference at all but rather the highest equality before their mixing took place, it follows necessarily from this that the alteration, both in the already informed matter of the hyle and in the already created form itself, consists in the greater or lesser action and passion of these principles. But because the rays of natural light tending downward with the tip of their pyramid have not yet penetrated to the bowels of the earth itself, it is therefore necessary that the inner parts of the earth—since any thing is composed of four quarters—should retain and possess four testimonies of coldness due to the complete absence of light. But truly the transparent region born above it, since it is clear, see-through, and bright, denotes by this very fact that a single portion of light has been granted to it, by which it obtains its transparent and mobile nature of this kind. From this it appears that the proportion between the earth and that lowest region is clear, since the earth has four testimonies of thickness <note>or density</note>, while the transparent elementary region has only three; so indeed, they stand in a **sesquitertia** <term>sesquitertia: a 4:3 ratio, corresponding to the musical interval of a fourth</term> proportion, seeing as the earth relates to that transparent elementary region as 4 does to 3. ## C H A P T E R III.

->*Concerning the world monochord, and the discovery of its consonances, both simple and compound, from which world harmony is forged.*<-

**SINCE** all those proportions in each aforementioned pyramid <note>Fludd previously established two overlapping pyramids: one of Light (form) descending from God, and one of Darkness (matter) ascending from the Earth.</note> are of no value by themselves for producing musical consonances without a mixture of both—for neither the lute <note>original: "barbiton," an ancient stringed instrument similar to a lyre or lute.</note> without the musician, nor the musician without the lute is sufficient for making musical consonances—it is therefore necessary that both pyramids concur to constitute the world harmony. Specifically, the material pyramid serves in the place of the musical instrument, or the string of the monochord, or the instrument and the breath of the singer; the formal pyramid, meanwhile, performs the office of the soul striking or singing and producing the voice. Therefore, an increase in the formal substance produces a sharper and more subtle air, and consequently brings forth more rare and excellent world symphonies; <margin>$\rightarrow$</margin> in no other way than how a more intense human spirit or a tighter instrument string will give sharper voices and more subtle air through more violent vibrations. Conversely, its decrease makes a thicker air, and consequently a deeper world harmony, not otherwise than how a relaxed human voice or a loosened monochord string renders softer sounds; and this happens because of the excessive thickness of the air. <margin>$\rightarrow$</margin> Light, therefore, acts upon the world matter by the same means as the human spirit acts upon the air. From these things it is manifest that one nature, whether material or formal, is worth nothing without the other, and hence World Music arises from both pyramids mixed at the most minute level. For without the presence of light, moist matter would have no pyramidal form, nor would the created form have its own without moist matter. Whence it is certain that they are mixed with one another according to "more or less," following the nature of the portions of each pyramid moving oppositely in the <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>The "Great World" or the universe as a whole, which Fludd believes mirrors the "Microcosm" of the human being.</note> and concurring with each other. These things being known, let us take our beginning from the world matter, <margin>$\rightarrow$</margin> which we have likened to the string of a monochord (whose great instrument is the <term>Macrocosm</term> itself), so that we may aptly compare every degree by which any difference of places is discerned between the center of the world instrument and its periphery to musical intervals, both simple and compound. Therefore, it should be known that just as the string of an instrument is usually divided by metric proportions starting from Gamma <note>original: "Γ," the lowest note in the medieval musical scale, known as the Gamut.</note> by way of ascent through intervals, so also both matter and its form are distributed by quantitative degrees, and distinguished by similar proportions that constitute musical consonances. For if a monochord <note>A scientific and musical instrument with a single string, used to demonstrate the mathematical relationships of intervals.</note> were imaginatively extended from the summit of the Empyrean heaven to the base of the earth itself, constituting the radius of each pyramid, we would perceive that it is divided into parts constituting consonances; if half of this part were pressed, it would produce the <term>Diapason</term> <note>The musical interval of an octave.</note> consonance, just as experience teaches that same thing happens on an instrumental monochord.

It must be considered, moreover, that in a world monochord of this kind, consonances both simple and compound, and similarly the proper intervals measuring them, can be outlined in no other way than when we divide an instrumental monochord into proportional parts. For the effect of coldness in the earth, and consequently the matter of the earth itself, in its thickness and weight, stands naturally in such a relation to the coldness and matter of the lowest region, in which there is only a single...

For the earth, in the music of the world, holds itself as the number 1 does in music, the unit in Arithmetic, and the point in Geometry. It is, as it were, the boundary from which the ratio of proportional matter must be calculated, since it is the base and foundation of the material <term>pyramid<gloss>Fludd uses the "pyramid" as a visual metaphor: a pyramid of darkness/matter rising from the earth, and a pyramid of light/spirit descending from God.</gloss></term>. 

Water, therefore, will occupy the place of one whole tone, and air also the place of one further interval. The sphere of fire, however—since it is nothing other than the ignited summit of the region of air—holds the place of a minor semitone. 

But insofar as two portions of this matter are elevated pyramidally upward to the point of the <term>middle heaven<gloss>The "medium coeli," the central part of the universe where the Sun resides.</gloss></term> to resist the actions of the supernatural heat, and just as many parts of light also act pyramidally downward upon those two portions of matter, they create the composition of the Sun's sphere. To this, they naturally attribute the name of "equality." In that place, the <term>sesquialter proportion<gloss>A 3:2 ratio, which creates a Perfect Fifth.</gloss></term> is produced, specifically because the three parts of the spirit (or the lower matter of the middle heaven) are related to those two parts of the solar sphere, and consequently they produce the harmony of the <term>Diapente<gloss>The musical interval of a Perfect Fifth.</gloss></term>. 

Such is the difference between the moon and the sun: since between the curve of this heaven and the middle of the solar sphere there are four intervals—namely, the spheres of the Moon, Mercury, and Venus (compared to whole tones), and the half of the solar sphere, which we have composed as a semitone. 

Now, since the harmony of the <term>Diapason<gloss>The musical interval of an Octave.</gloss></term> is constituted from the *Diatessaron* and the *Diapente*, it is necessary that this *Diapason* harmony be produced there. And this is the more perfect harmony of matter, which can in no way acquire its perfection unless it has satisfied its longing through the solar form. 

Furthermore, although this middle heaven ends in a more perfect harmony of matter within its very heart—namely, in the Sun—and begins a motion toward the "formal" <note>In this context, "formal" refers to "Form" (Spirit/Light) as opposed to "Matter."</note> *Diapason*, nevertheless, in its concavity, both above the sphere of equality and below it, it sounds nothing but the harmony of the *Diapente*. Therefore, among other harmonies, this one is most suited to this place, because just as it is less than perfect and situated in the middle between the perfect and the imperfect, so too is this heaven: although it is perfect and free from corruption, it is nonetheless called "less perfect" in respect to the higher heaven, and it occupies a middle position between both heavens—the perfect and the imperfect. 

Moreover, the point of exact equality—which is the exact intersection of the two pyramids, labeled **N. H.**—is the true boundary of the more perfect harmony. There, such is the union and embrace of matter with form that a separation and division can never occur. 

But in truth, because the parts of the pyramids in the ethereal region—both above the sphere of intersection (namely, **S. Q. O. P.** and **N. H.**) and below it (namely, **R. M. Q. G.** and **N. H.**)—are equal enough for perfection, the ethereal matter outside the sphere of the soul has enough "form" to fulfill its appetite, though not to the perfection of the solar sphere. Therefore, the proportion joining the intervals is called a perfect harmony, but it is less complete than that of the sun, which the more excellent Musicians have called the *Diapente*. 

And this was the sole reason why some of the Philosophers distinguished its substance by the name of the <term>Fifth Essence<gloss>The Quintessence; the pure, incorruptible element that makes up the heavens.</gloss></term>, since its composition, in respect to both extreme heavens, participated more in the harmony of the *Diapente*. For in descending from the sphere of the sun, it stands in a *sesquialter* (3:2) proportion to the lowest heaven; and in ascending to the borders of the spiritual heaven, it is found under the same proportion. 

However, the upper harmony differs from the lower because the former refers to Form, while the latter refers to Matter. Therefore, just as Form is more excellent than Matter, so the natures of its harmonies are more eminent than those of matter. Just as the *Diapason* (Octave) from the center to the sphere of the sun was produced from what was material, so also another *Diapason* is raised upward from the head of the material pyramid to the highest peak of the <term>Empyrean heaven<gloss>The highest, spiritual heaven, composed of pure light and fire.</gloss></term>, which exists as a spiritual Octave. ## ON THE MUSIC OF THE WORLD.

The higher <term>Fourth<note>original: Diatessaron; a musical interval spanning four notes of a scale.</note></term> agrees with the material Fourth in this regard: just as the lower Fourth—though it is more perfect relative to the earth positioned beneath it, because it possesses more of the "form" that gives it shape than the earth does—is nonetheless found to be imperfect when compared to higher things (that is, when related to the <term>Fifth<note>original: Diapente; a musical interval spanning five notes, considered more harmonious than the Fourth.</note></term> of its own nature), and can in no way be compared to the matter of the ethereal heaven, any more than the consonance of a Fourth can be compared with that of a Fifth; so too does the formal Fourth behave in every respect. For if it is compared to the nature of the ethereal heaven, it is more perfect than that heaven; indeed, it is even more perfect than its own formal consonance, the Fifth, insofar as the intervals of the Fifth are more material, while those of the Fourth are more spiritual. But if it is compared to the pure "form" that exists above itself, the intervals of this consonance are still imperfect. Thus, this consonance is found there so that our intellect may see that this very region—even if it is the purest and most perfect of all the world's regions in relation to us—is nevertheless removed by an immense distance from the perfection of the heaven of the Trinity.

The logic of this <term>mundane monochord<note>The "monochord of the world" is a symbolic musical instrument used to explain the mathematical and harmonic proportions of the universe.</note></term> is proven by its effect, which aptly explains to us that pyramidal proportion and quality of the world's matter. Therefore, let a musical instrument be constructed in a pyramidal shape, and from one point on one side of it, let a brass string be stretched to a point on the other side diametrically opposite to it. Then, let a second string also be stretched from another point to its opposite, and then a third and fourth, proceeding through the rest in the same way, until the thickness of the entire pyramidal instrument is filled with strings that differ proportionally among themselves. We say, therefore, that these same strings, when stretched with equal force, maintain the intervals of <term>Whole Tones<note>original: Tonorum</note></term> and <term>Semitones<note>original: Semitoniorum</note></term>, so that from the base of the pyramid toward its apex, through those musical scales (which we more rightly call intervals), we shall always ascend from deeper sounds to sharper ones, until the apex is reached. Beyond this, it will be no less impossible to ascend higher than it is to progress further by going beyond an Arithmetic unit or a Geometric point. # ON COSMIC MUSIC.

We can also draw out many hidden truths from the nature of this instrument by carefully considering the principles of its low and high sounds. For a string A. B. of the same dimension and length would sound in the extremely thin spirit of the upper heavens just as string C. D. sounds in the airy medium of the lower region; that is to say, string A. B. would yield a sound just as high-pitched and excellent as string C. D. However, the reason why string A. B. sounds so low in this airy medium is because the medium is too dense <note>original: *spissum*; thick or crowded</note> and drowns out the clarity of the sound, and the moving soul <note>original: *anima movens*; the vital force that initiates motion</note> is found to be too weak to refine that dense matter. Note, therefore, that the soul of sounds in a string proceeds from the action of the agent; the medium, however, through whose dimensions the sound is produced, is the substance of the air itself, which receives the modulations of the soul through vibration. For the same string, when tightened or loosened, produces various voices, not unlike what is seen in the human voice, which produces various tones through the same windpipe <term>trachea arteria|The historical anatomical term for the trachea or windpipe</term>.

Air is therefore the medium, and as it were the instrument, in which music is made; hence, just as a small instrument usually produces higher voices and a large one lower ones, so too thinned and subtle air produces more refined sounds, and conversely, thick air produces lower ones: <insert>It is not the string, therefore, but its soul—sent into the medium or instrument by the vibration of the string—which produces the sounds; nor does the principal power of sounds reside in the windpipe, but in the vital soul <note>original: *anima vitalis*</note> pushing against the surrounding air.</insert> For just as a thicker medium refracts and hinders the rays of sight the denser it is—as can be seen in foggy and cloudy air—while in a clearer and thinner medium the effects of sight are sharper and more certain, so too a dense medium offers lower sounds to the sense of hearing, and more rarely high ones; indeed, the thinner the medium, the more excellent the sounds produced.

Furthermore, we see that when the soul of the player mingles with the string through vigorous striking, the string itself produces harsher and more intense sounds by a stronger vibration; but where that soul presses the string more weakly, it forces the string to emit a lower voice with a more relaxed vibration. This is also seen in the human voice, where more intense and clearer sounds are produced by a stronger impulse of the moving soul, while weaker ones are more relaxed and obscure. We also see wind forcefully penetrating a crack in a house, yielding a higher and sharper voice, whereas that same wind blowing weakly always stirs a lower sound through that same crack; this is also clearly demonstrated in the way a trumpet is sounded: <insert>The reason for this lies in the more relaxed or more intense powers of the moving soul, and consequently in the medium into which the soul enters by the vibration of the string or voice;</insert> for a weaker moving soul does not have enough power to refine the air <term>subtiliatio|The process of "thinning" or refining matter to make it more spiritual or active</term> so that it produces sharper sounds. Conversely, a moving soul acting powerfully produces sharper and more sublime voices in the air because of its great force and virtue in refining the air, whence the sounding soul dilates itself more easily and acts more sharply within it.

The demonstration of this matter is seen in the stronger and weaker plucking of a string and its vibration, and especially in the raising or lowering of the human voice. Similarly, a string achieves the same through its tension and relaxation in another way; namely, when the moving soul contracts the string with greater force, it sounds higher because, according to the greater force and proportion of the contracting soul, it vibrates with greater violence and refines the medium with its vibrations so that higher and sharper voices are produced. In like manner, a string of less thickness <note>literally "lesser corpulence"</note> requires less power from the moving soul to produce high and elevated sounds than a larger string does, because it makes its way into the air with an easier motion and lighter vibration due to the slenderness of its body. Hence it fills a smaller space in the air, and yet its power extends widely and sharply. This is something a string of greater thickness cannot do; thus it requires a stronger contraction of the soul. Is it not also the case with an instru...

# ON THE MUSIC OF THE WORLD.

<margin> → </margin> Indeed, from this musical instrument, called a <term>pipe<note>original: "fistula"; likely referring to a flute or panpipe used as a model for the universe's proportions.</note></term>, the true proportion of the whole world is gathered. It is divided into three regions; the two lower ones have three holes each, denoting the beginning, middle, and end of each respective region. The highest region, however, consisting of only a single large hole, designates the nature of the super-celestial heaven, of which every part is of the same condition, as if filled most completely by divine unity. But truly, just as this instrument in its own nature and by itself does not sound, move, or have any power without a soul moving it; so also neither the world nor the parts of the world can move or act by themselves without the excitation of the infinite mind. Therefore, as the supreme mind, GOD, at the summit of the whole machine, and as if outside the outermost surface of the world, causes the joints of the world to exhibit their music—deeper in the lower part, and sharper and clearer the more nearly they approach that very summit—so also, with the musician blowing life and motion from outside the enclosure of the pipe and at its summit, the further the holes are distant from his underlying breath, the deeper the voices they emit; but the higher one ascends toward the bellows of his spirit, the more excellent the sounds produced. And just as that single hole, **A**, gives as if life and soul to the others below it (since without it they return no voices), so also the Empyrean heaven <margin> → </margin> [gives life] to all the lower spheres. Oh, how great and how heavenly would this contemplation be in so trivial a matter, if it were considered diligently and somewhat more deeply by an intelligent mind!

### CHAPTER V.

->*On elementary music.*<-

**I**t is established that there is also a certain harmony in the elementary part of the world. Its <term>consonances<note>In this context, harmonious sounds or musical intervals.</note></term> proceed from proportions governed more by the heat of the celestial fire—which is not of the true essence of light, but rather forced and external—than from that essential Light. For this reason, they produce symphonic compositions whose harmony, due to the scantiness of the true luminous form within them, is not permanent, but rather transitory and vanishes with a sudden speed. Furthermore, we shall perceive that every element is disposed by natural consent through musical proportions, both in its own "heaven" and in any composite of heaven, clearer than light itself, if we look more exactly and deeply into their natures and positions. For it is certain that their matter, or substance, is either thicker (and consequently heavier and harder) or thinner (and therefore lighter and softer). This occurs according to the greater predominance of the coldness of the earth or the heat of fire within it. Since coldness has dominion in the earth alone (wherefore, due to the absolute absence of fiery heat, those four quarters of coldness are present in it, which is the complete nature of earth); but the element of water possesses no more than three quarters of coldness joined with one of fire (which happens to it because of its participation with the middle sphere of moisture); similarly, the middle sphere of moisture contains only two portions of coldness and as many of heat; and finally, the element of air has acquired only one portion of moisture, since it embraces three quarters of the quality of fire from the neighboring element. It is necessary, then, that the earth be denser, heavier, and harder than water; and water more so than the "spurious sphere of equality"; and that, finally, more than the air, which is the upper part of that moist sphere.

For water in the center, thinned by the force of heat, seeks a wider place to contain its body, since it cannot remain in its former seat due to the expansion of its substance. Therefore, partly because of the expulsive nature of fire, and partly because of its own thinned substance, it very easily bursts forth into the region of the air. It stirs the air here and there by its presence and motion, and by reason of the sulfurous spirits retained within its vapor, it generates thunder, lightning, flashes, and other such <term>meteors<note>In the early modern period, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just space rocks.</note></term>. From this kind of hot vapor, therefore, that wind is derived which they call a **Typhoon** <note>original: "Typhonem"</note> because of its fiery nature. We can prove that these causes of the winds are certain and infallible, not only by the artificial examples described above, but also by natural experience. For in **Dalmatia**, as **Pliny** and **Pomponius Mela** <note>Roman natural historians and geographers.</note> relate, they write that there is a lake in a certain very deep cave with a vast, steep opening; if even the lightest stone is thrown into it, even on a calm day, winds are suddenly stirred up and storms similar to whirlwinds arise. Here, without a doubt, a vast quantity of air is trapped at the base of the hollow, which the multitude of waters blocking the mouth of the cave prevented from escaping. When the stone is thrown down, a penetration is made, and a large part of the air is pushed out and escapes as some parts of the water enter. Furthermore, in the **province of Cyrenaica** <note>A region in modern-day Libya.</note>, a certain rock is said to be sacred to the **South Wind** <note>original: "Austro"</note>; and from the **Aeolian** region, because of the multitude of infinite caverns and caves contained within it, winds are observed to blow constantly. For this reason, the Poets imagined its first king, named **Aeolus**, to be the GOD of the winds; for through such caves the earth more easily emits the smoky matter of the winds. Indeed, some inhabitants of the **Promontory of Puteoli** <note>Modern-day Pozzuoli, near Naples, Italy.</note>, even those still living in this latest age, have said they remember a horrific earthquake happening on their promontory. They testified that winds and sulfur with stupendous thunder were stirred up for the space of 48 hours, and the earth moved from one place to another, and a mountain was raised up in one spot which they called the **Ashy Mountain** <note>original: "Cineritium"; this refers to Monte Nuovo, formed in 1538.</note>. In the part nearest to it, a significant portion of land—indeed, the greater part of the city of **Cuma**—was submerged by sea waters (*a wondrous spectacle of this time*). All these things I have seen myself, and I posit the reason for this matter to be the immense quantity of sulfur burning under the earth. By its destructive power, the greater part of the sulfurous earth in that region was turned into ashes and gave way to the weight of the earth hanging above it. This earth, precipitated into the bowels of the earth down to the burnt ashes, forced the trapped hot air to burst out. By the violence of this air, the aforementioned earthquake, flaming winds, lightning, thunder, and other mournful accidents were undoubtedly brought about. Therefore, such sulfurous vapors are for the most part the authors of fire-vomiting winds. Hence, in those regions where the bowels of the earth are either visibly inflamed or where the air is customarily polluted by such vapors through insensible breathings, flashes and thunder happen very frequently.

->We conclude, therefore, that winds are customarily excited<- either by the expulsion of air trapped in the bowels of the earth, or by its thinning (and then it stirs the weak wind called the **Zephyr**), or while its entire substance bursts from the womb of the earth, both because of the violent entry of waters occupying its seat and because of an immense portion of earth falling downward toward the center (by whose fall and presence the air retained there is suddenly thrust out, inducing a vehement agitation of both the earth and the air). Or, winds are caused by the thinning of waters in the womb of the earth, arising from sulfurous heat; such a wind is more often perceived to blow from the Southern part because of the Sun's constant familiarity with it. Its fiery faculties are removed in the winter time because of the vehement resistance of the northern blast, which is why thunder and lightning are not produced as frequently in winter as in summer. Winds arising from thinned air shaken out of the belly of the earth are also more frequent in summer; but those arising from air disturbed from the earth in its entire nature remain more common in the spring time...

# C H A P T E R VI.
### Concerning lightning and thunder.

THE PERIPATETICS <note>followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy</note> write that thunder and lightning occur when a hot and dry exhalation is raised by the heat of the Sun along with a moist and watery vapor into the upper part of the middle region of the air. There, they claim that exhalation is surrounded and enclosed on all sides by the vapor, and condensed into a cold and thick cloud. Being poorly able to endure the injuries of that intense cold, that enclosed exhalation is driven here and there as if indignant, seeking an exit. Finally, by this agitation and *antiperistasis* <note>original: "antiperistasi" — a philosophical concept where a quality is intensified when surrounded by its opposite, such as heat becoming more concentrated when trapped by cold</note>, it catches fire like tow <note>coarse flax or hemp fibers</note> and bursts through the sides of the cloud by its fiery force. As the cloud is shattered and disrupted, it gives out a huge crash, which they call **thunder**, while simultaneously calling the light of the ignited exhalation a **lightning-bolt**, **lightning-flash**, and **glimmering** <note>original: "fulmen, fulgur & coruscationem"</note>.

We cannot entirely disapprove of their opinions in all respects; for we say that the "passive matter" which gives out the crackling sound is air reduced to the substance of a cloud; but the "active form" which brings about the crash is that sulfurous and windy matter, ignited by the force of both cold and moisture. This matter, illuminated according to the nature of the enclosed fire, seeks the open air, and to satisfy its desire, it bursts its prisons and flies away and vanishes into a wider and thinner place where it can live more freely. Thus we also see that the substance of **saltpeter** <note>original: "Salis Petræ" — potassium nitrate, a key ingredient in gunpowder</note> is nothing other than air congealed by cold, to which, if some portion of sulfur is added—even a very small amount—it gives out a huge noise and emits artificial lightning, as is demonstrated by the following experiment.

> *Upon saltpeter <note>original: "salem nitri"</note> [D] melted in a pot [A, B, C] by a charcoal fire and sprinkled with sulfur, I threw a piece of live charcoal [E]. Having observed these things, I judged more precisely the arrangement of thunders.*

Indeed, this very phenomenon is sufficiently demonstrated in the discharge of gunpowder <note>original: "pulveris bombardici"</note>. From these observations it is clear: thick air, containing within itself a nitrous disposition, is the material cause of lightning and thunder; and a sulfurous exhalation is their formal cause. How this condensation of the air occurs, we have explained clearly enough in the section on the generation of clouds, where we dealt with the matter contrary to the opinion of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy, whose physical theories the author is challenging here</note>. For when the south wind blows—whose vaporous matter we have said is mostly drier and more sulfurous because of the sun’s proximity to that part of the world—especially in the summer time, sulfurous vapors are often and more strongly (though invisibly) raised upward by the perpendicular attractive power of the sun. These vapors, moved toward the North while the North wind is also blowing at that time, are swirled and gathered into a cloud formed by the opposition of the aforementioned winds. All its previously scattered parts are reduced into one dense mass, whereby strength is joined to strength and sulfurous atoms to atoms. Finally, due to the resistance of the freezing nitrous nature, both by the percussion shaking the sulfurous mass and by the active power of the fiery mass itself, they are ignited, strengthened by <term>antiperistasis<gloss>The intensification of a quality when surrounded by its opposite, such as heat becoming more intense when compressed by cold</gloss></term>. The sulfurous parts, which previously operated only in potential, are now brought into action and refined by the lighting, so that they vigorously penetrate downward through the outer parts of the cloud seeking a larger and more spacious place because of the refinement of their parts. They violently burst through its sides and are perceived to emit a huge crash, which we also call <term>thunder<gloss>original: "tonitru"</gloss></term>. That a sulfurous mixture can be ignited and lit through antiperistasis—that is, because of the resisting cold—the following experiment confirms.

Let this egg [A], thus artificially composed, be thrown into a stream [B], and suddenly a flame will emerge from the water itself.*

Finally, we do not say that only the blowing and nature of the South wind <note>original: "venti Australis"</note> produce sulfurous and drier vapors of this kind, but also the other winds blowing from any part of the world, provided they partake in sulfurous spirits. And these things will be perceived more clearly if we carefully observe the movement of a thundering cloud that vomits forth lightning. For a cloud emitting flashes is noticed to be driven against the motion of clouds that lack sulfur. A cracking sound is most often produced when both clouds have come together into one mass and have firmly and powerfully enclosed the sulfurous vapor accompanying the opposing wind.

It must also be observed here that in the opposing clash of clouds, the cloud burdened with sulfurous spirit even moves the contrary cloud against its own motion. This is due to the multitude of living fire, in the manner of a most powerful soul moving its own body. By its vigor, the power of the other contrary cloud is repelled, no differently than when a stronger man carries away a weaker one against his will and desire, despite his struggles. From this, therefore, comes the origin of the contention. Since the disposition of the sulfurous cloud is fiery and sulfurous, while the constitution of the cloud moving against it is extremely cold, the sulfurous nature is ignited for the reasons shown in the previous demonstration regarding artificial fire in water <note>The author likely refers to a chemical experiment, perhaps involving quicklime or phosphorus, where heat is generated by contact with water</note>.

We conclude, therefore, that common experience has sufficiently and clearly demonstrated that the formal origin of thunder and lightning is certain sulfurous vapors dispersed invisibly in the air. When gathered together, these are brought into action—that is, they are ignited. For while lightning and flashes are scattered through the air, very sulfurous odors are perceived. Indeed, the true nature of sulfur is discerned even by common eyes, both in the color of its flame and in the condition of its execution. Furthermore, we have seen in foreign regions that thunder is more frequent near those places where sulfur mines or sulfurous mountains are found ignited by some accident, as in Sicily and around Naples; similarly in rocky regions, where the solar rays are strenuously concentrated against the peaks of mountains. Finally, what could more clearly show the origin of thunder than that horrendous production of the Cinder Mountain of Puteoli <note>original: "montis Cineritii Puteolorum." This refers to Monte Nuovo near Pozzuoli, Italy, which formed during a volcanic eruption in 1538</note>, of which we spoke in the preceding chapter.

### C H A P T E R VII.

->*How the heavens act in the production of such meteors?*<-

In the preceding sections, we made mention only of the more immediate causes of <term>meteors</term> <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars</note>. Here, however, we shall briefly explain in what manner the stars and planets produce these imperfect mixtures. Since it has been determined among all philosophers that the higher things continually act upon these lower things to produce new things, it is certain that these celestial bodies are the primary causes of the production of any meteor and of the positioning of its substance in its proper place. But we will here review in passing what <term>astrologers</term> <note>scholars who studied the influence of stars on earthly events</note> think and strenuously affirm in this matter; then we shall conclude with our own opinion.

Some astrologers teach that comets for the most part imitate the nature of <term>Mars</term> <note>the planet associated with heat, fire, and war</note> and <term>Venus</term> <note>the planet associated with moisture and air</note>, and for this reason they maintain that comets portend wars, heat, and tumults. Others say that they have their origin from some unlucky position of the stars, such as the conjunction of the superior planets and an eclipse—especially when <term>Saturn</term>, <term>Mars</term>, and <term>Mercury</term> look upon the Sun or Moon with unlucky aspects during an eclipse, and most especially if some other event has also preceded...

From these assertions of the astrologers, we conclude that our aforementioned opinions on the origin of <term>Meteors</term> <note>In this period, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and comets.</note> are not fictions, but very close to the truth itself. For in the composition of a *Comet*, they say the natures of *Mars* and *Mercury* converge; and they have spoken truly: for a spark of *Martial* substance flowing down from on high is like the soul and life of the *Comet* itself. Its body and substance, however, is entirely *Mercurial*—that is, gathered from the inconsistent substance of the most subtle air—having the aptitude, in the manner of *Mercury*, to take on any form or impression. What better evidence can there be for the generation of *clouds* (namely, when the air is thickened by the blowing of opposing winds, which condensed state we have called a *cloud*) than that they are primarily generated by the aspect and opposition of different planets, which stir up distinct winds in these lower regions according to their various influences? For in the aspect of the *Moon* with a predominant *Saturn*, the humidity of the one is repugnant to the dryness of the other. Thus, from such a conflict, a contrary motion arises in the air, compressing it so that a cloud is generated therefrom. Similarly, two *winds* of contrary condition are produced in the summer time from the opposition, conjunction, or other malevolent aspect between a predominant *Saturn* and *Mars*. For *Mars*, because of his familiarity with fire, gathers sulfurous vapors and moves them by his power in the form of a wind against the breath produced by *Saturn*, just as his own body moves against that of *Saturn* in the ethereal heavens. *Saturn*, however, since he is cold not only in motion but also in quality, is opposed to *Mars*. Thus, the coldness of *Saturn* ignites the sulfurous matter gathered by *Mars* in no different a way than the spring water ignited the other mass described *in experiment 2 of the preceding chapter*; from this, thunder exists; but because *Saturn* is stronger, *hail* also falls. Similarly, if *Jupiter* should have dominion in the heavens and look upon *Mars* in the summer with some malevolent aspect, he induces various and opposing motions in the air, since the humidity of *Jupiter* is contrary to the dryness of *Mars*. Therefore, that humidity of *Jupiter*, although warm, ignites the inflammable matter gathered by *Mars* in no different a way than the humidity of spit ignited that mass *described in experiment 3 in the preceding chapter*, in which the humidity of the spit, penetrating and submerging itself into that fire-bearing body, brings back that fiery force (which was hidden and existing only in potential) into an inflammable act; the composition of which is this:

### C H A P T E R VII.

->*Concerning the practice and application of cosmic music and its harmonies, infused from the ethereal celestial spheres into these elementary regions.*<-

**JUST AS** in vocal or instrumental music, theoretical contemplation is not enough unless it is put into practice and its use is recognized through practical experience; so too in this cosmic harmony, our present discourse might perhaps be thought a fiction, unless we extend it to a practice familiar not only to the intellect, but to the very senses themselves, according to our strength. We shall therefore first explain by what proportions and harmonies <note>original: "consonantiis"</note> each sphere of the world pours its own harmony into another, and then, in the second place, we shall declare the nature of cosmic discords.

Since, therefore, the space of the transparent lower region is related to the earth in a <term>sesquitertia ratio</term> <note>original: "proportione sesquitertia"; a 4:3 ratio, which in music creates the interval of a Perfect Fourth</note>, it follows that "accidental fire" <note>Fire as a quality or property rather than the pure element</note> corresponds to it, but with an imperfect harmony; for in respect to dryness alone, which is an accidental quality proper to both fire and earth, it exists in such a concord with the earth. But the reason why this region generally agrees with the earth lies in the abundance of bodily substance which it originally received from the earth. Thus, the intervals of the transparent region serve to connect this more material region to its foundation with an imperfect harmony (suitable to the nature of the place) so that a symphony may arise from the fit chaining together of its spheres.

But truly, if we ascend to the first level of the ethereal region, we shall find that the **sphere of the Moon** has a relationship to the earth in a <term>sesquialtera ratio</term> <note>original: "sesquialtera proportione"; a 3:2 ratio, creating the interval of a Perfect Fifth</note>. By virtue of this proportion, the earth tastes of the <term>Quintessence</term> <note>original: "Quinta essentia"; the "fifth element" or pure celestial ether, distinct from the four earthly elements</note>, and cosmic melody is infused into the earth by this same proportion, joined with it in a less-than-perfect harmony. For insofar as four intervals are found between the earth and the *sphere of the Moon*—namely water, air, and the sphere of the Moon itself, which carry the weight of a **Whole Tone**, and the sphere of fire, which takes the place of a **Semitone**—to that extent a <term>Diapente</term> <note>A Perfect Fifth</note> will harmonize with the earth, and a <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>A Perfect Fourth</note> with the water. This consists, as was said, of two tones (namely air and the sphere of the Moon) and one semitone (namely fire). And this is the reason why the Moon continually acts so strongly and vigorously upon these lower parts, and especially upon the earth, through its influences. Similarly, the *sphere of Mercury* will resonate a **Diapente** into the sphere of water: hence come the floods of waters and the disturbances of the seas, on account of the thin and windy <term>Mercurial spirit</term> hidden within them; and likewise by this means, with the help of the Moon, the ebb and flow of the sea occurs. Furthermore, by a similar harmony <margin>←</margin> *Venus* is related to the sphere of air, possessing a mild and sweet symphony in the air because of the exact concord of her proportions. Hence the air retains within itself the same qualities that Venus has—namely heat and moisture—which are always favorable to animal life; indeed, they even serve the plants themselves in place of a "radical moisture" along with their own proper spirit. Finally, the lowest part of the **sphere of the Sun** scatters its influences into the sphere of fire, which are carried down together into these lower regions, and contribute to the multiplication and perfection of the planets by the power of the **Diapente** harmony. But, to come to the powers and faculties of a more perfect harmony <margin>→</margin> which is found between the earth and the "sphere of equality," it is certain <margin>→</margin> that all the perfections of the life of every terrestrial animal <margin>→</margin> proceed from the intervals of this harmony: namely the growth of bodily matter, and that of the living form...

For when the cold nature of *Saturn* terminates in that heat of fire, the quality of heat is repugnant to coldness; and so, even though that quantitative proportion is consonant on the "Mundane Monochord" <note>A symbolic single-stringed instrument representing the harmony of the universe.</note>, the contrary qualities of the giver and receiver produce a significant <term>dyscrasia<note>A medical or philosophical term for a harmful imbalance of qualities or humors.</note></term> in that concord, which living beings, due to the weakness of their forms, very easily sense and perceive. Those that flow favorably do so clearly, purely, and simply; but those that flow unfavorably transmit their natures into these lower regions through the intervals of the <term>Octave<note>original: *Diapason*</note></term> in an interrupted manner, which acts very disruptively upon all bodies unless they are very well disposed.

Finally, the natures of the stars also concur with the natures of the Planets themselves through a certain harmonic consensus. Thus, *Leo*, because of the singular vitality of its life, receives the *Sun* as its Lord; hence *Leo* is, as it were, in unison with the nature of the *Sun*. So too is *Cancer* with the *Moon*, *Aries* with *Mars*, and so on for the others. For every house of the Planets must be conformable with the nature of its Lord, and be like a unison—that is, it must resonate with its Lord in the same sound. From this, they flow with their Lords in the same way and with the same harmonies.

Finally, as far as the <term>Fourth<note>original: *Diatesfaron*; a musical interval representing a 4:3 ratio.</note></term> of the upper region is concerned, it must be understood that the higher Hierarchy pours its virtues into the middle one, and the middle into the lowest. This lowest hierarchy communicates with the ethereal heaven, which expects and receives not only its splendor from that fiery heaven, but also the messages and commands of GOD from its creatures <margin>-></margin>, and executes them once received. By the harmonies of this love, all rational spiritual beings descend into well-disposed bodies by means of that ethereal vehicle. Since we shall discourse more extensively on these matters in our books on the **Macrocosm**, we shall omit them here, so that we may more rightly move on to more natural subjects.

# CHAPTER VIII.

### *On the practice of elemental melody, and its effect, both in simple and composite bodies, and on its discordance and strife.*

---

<margin>--></margin>JUST as the more subtle dispositions and natures of the higher realms are infused into lower bodies; so also is it necessary for bodies to be aptly composed from the region of the "material pyramid" of substance—which is divided into the elements—in order to properly receive such influences. And indeed, this material composition receives its essential form not from the elements themselves, but from heaven itself; <margin><--</margin> just as I myself have experienced by seeing such things with my own eyes. For I have separated the four distinct elements from a living thing; then I perceived in the final stage, and saw with the clearest eyes, the life of the thing, which I recognized to be from heaven, the <term>Quintessence<note>The "fifth essence," a celestial substance distinct from the four earthly elements, thought to be the matter of the stars and the spirit of life.</note></term>, and the solar nature, once I had separated the four lower elements aside.

Our intention here, therefore, is to treat of proportions, and of those consonances by which an apt connection of one element with another occurs in the mixture and composition of worldly bodies. Thus, in elemental Music, Earth stands to the sphere of Water in a ratio of 4 to 3, since there exist in Earth four units of the "fourth degree" of coldness, related to those three units found in Water. For that single part of the element of Fire, together with the tip of the "pyramid of light," exists within the sphere of Water; indeed, if more parts of heat existed in it, it would be of a thinner substance, and thus even converted into Air. For that reason, its sphere would neither remain closest to Earth, nor be burdened with such great heaviness or weight.

Moreover, that it has something of heat—that is, of a fiery form—within it, is attested by its transparency and fluidity, as was said before in its proper place. Therefore, because of this <term>sesquitertial proportion<note>original: "proportio sesquitertia"; a 4:3 ratio, which in music corresponds to the interval of a perfect fourth.</note></term>, Earth accords with Water; but this combination of the said elements is imperfect and less than absolute, because the moist parts of one are contrary to the dry parts of the other. Yet they harmonize with each other through the consonance of the <term>Diatessaron<note>A musical interval of a perfect fourth.</note></term>, because they agree in the active qualities that predominate within them. 

Thus also toward the "sphere of false equality" <note>A point in Fludd's elemental diagram where the material and formal qualities appear balanced, though not perfectly.</note>, in which there are two material parts and just as many of fire, Earth stands in a double proportion—namely, as the 4 parts of Earth to the 2 of that same sphere; for the terrestrial nature produced these moist parts, being dissolved and refined by the power of the light joined with it. Similarly, Water stands to that sphere of equality as 3 to 2, whence the <term>sesquialter proportion<note>original: "proportio sesquialtera"; a 3:2 ratio, which in music corresponds to a perfect fifth.</note></term> arises. And thus we have obtained the Diatessaron, <term>Diapente<note>A musical interval of a perfect fifth.</note></term>, and <term>Diapason<note>A musical interval of an octave, representing a 2:1 ratio.</note></term> of the terrestrial pyramid. 

Likewise, the sphere of equality stands to that of Air by comparing the two fiery parts of the sphere of equality to those three portions of Air, from which the "fiery Diapente" arises; and the three fiery parts of Air to those four of the sphere of Fire produce the consonance of the Diapason. Earth, therefore, accords with Water in a Diatessaron, and with the sphere of equality in a Diapason; and Water accords with the sphere of false equality in a Diapente, and the sphere of false equality with Air in a Diapason—namely, because they are held in a double proportion. 

Thus also Fire accords with Air in a Diatessaron, and with the sphere of equality in a Diapason; and Air accords with the sphere of equality in a Diapente, and the sphere of equality with Water in a double proportion or Diapason. Therefore, the two visible elements [Earth and Water] concur best for composition through the bond of the Diatessaron consonance, and the two invisible elements [Air and Fire] mix themselves with them by virtue of the embrace they have with the corporeal proportions. ### TREATISE I. BOOK III.

<margin>The author uses hand-drawn arrows here to emphasize the delicate balance between elemental harmony and the "strife" that leads to decay.</margin>

...air through the <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>original: "consonantiam Diatessaron"; a musical interval of a perfect fourth, represented by the ratio 4:3</note> harmony, and air to the sphere of equality through the <term>Diapente</term> <note>original: "Diapente"; a musical interval of a perfect fifth, represented by the ratio 3:2</note>, and both fire and air are joined in the sphere of equality in the proportion of a <term>Diapason</term> <note>original: "Diapason"; a musical interval of an octave, represented by the ratio 2:1</note>. This sphere of equality connects those invisible elements, which are linked together by formal harmonies, to the visible elements through bodily bonds or musical consonances. Similarly, air is joined to the earth in a quadruple proportion, and consequently fire—already glued to the air by the bond of the Diatessaron—is accustomed to being united with water and earth. However, they are joined to one another in such a way that the proper seat of the harmonies and the legitimate order are observed, lest discord and strife arise between them. For this reason, the bodily harmonies ought to regard the more physical elements, and the fiery harmonies the fiery ones.

The reason for this is that the region which is more terrestrial and visible, as well as the fiery and invisible region, is bounded and perfected by the most perfect harmony. Thus, the limit of the physical or visible pyramid <note>In the author's cosmology, the "pyramid" represents the waning of formal/spiritual power as it descends into matter.</note> lies within a physical Diapason; likewise, that fiery region lies within its own less physical Diapason. But truly, insofar as both octaves are joined by the power of the "spurious" sphere of equality, the physical elements are joined and linked to those invisible ones. Therefore, a single proportion should not look toward another outside its own region; for otherwise, discord would arise instead of concord. 

For example, fire consists of 4 parts of heat, and water of three parts of coldness; although there is a <term>sesquitertia</term> <note>A ratio of 4:3, which corresponds to the Diatessaron (a musical fourth).</note> proportion here, it sits poorly between bodies because of their qualities, being ill-disposed; a progression occurs from the fiery kingdom to the physical one, whose natures are entirely opposite. Similarly, earth relates to air as 4 to 3; but for the same reason, they can in no way agree. Thus, fire is enclosed by air, through which air passes by means of the sphere of equality—which is to be regarded as a medium for joining fiery and airy forms with watery and terrestrial bodies, just as the ethereal spirit is regarded in the joining of the soul with the lower body. And so, air is grasped with its fiery soul and with water, which water is most easily and naturally joined with the earth by the power of the Diatessaron harmony. And this is that harmony by which the composition of mixed sublunary bodies <note>Refers to everything below the moon, i.e., the terrestrial world subject to change and decay.</note> is made.

However, these types of bonds are dissolved by strife and discord. For when the proportion of <term>Martial fire</term> <note>Fire associated with the planet Mars, signifying excessive, aggressive heat.</note> is increased beyond the proper nature of its harmony, it very quickly consumes the moisture of its airy vehicle. Having violated the harmony of the fiery Diatessaron, it breaks out of its prison into the watery region and causes war instead of peace within the compound body. From this, desperate and incurable diseases arise. That fiery nature, violently penetrating through the water and earth and breaking out from them, snatches away the celestial soul—to whom it is closest in composition due to the familiarity and kinship between the ethereal heaven and the sphere of fire—and by this path the compound is dissolved, suffers corruption, and is gradually reduced back into its primary matter. The same thing happens when earth, with its <term>Saturnine</term> <note>Associated with the planet Saturn; cold, dry, and heavy.</note> coldness and dryness, destroys the airy heat and moisture,

->so that it may find a way with the water by which to extinguish the fire<-
->and choke the life of the thing. But of this worldly strife we shall say<-
->more in the following chapter.<-

*With vessel A.B.C.D. filled with water, the water itself, rising above hole H of tube G. H., will exit from the vessel through that same tube: nor will it stop ascending through the larger tube E. F. until the entire water of the vessel has been evacuated through tube H. G.*

*The following experiment demonstrates that air, when thinned by heat <note>original: "calore subtiliatus"</note>, can expel water from the bowels of the earth to its surface:*

---

*Let water be poured into sphere A so that half of it is filled; and let hole B be plugged. By the presence of fire lit upon the brazier <term>brazier (arula)<gloss>A small portable stove or altar used here as a heat source for the pneumatic experiment</gloss></term> C. D. E. F., the thicker air existing within it is expelled through <term>thinning (subtiliatione)<gloss>The process of making air less dense through heating, causing it to expand and create pressure</gloss></term> into sphere A by way of tube G. A. This air then further pushes down the liquid contained within it into vessel N. L. P. O. through tube H. I. L. M.*

*For the reasoning behind this experiment, see Hero’s 37th experiment.*

*Finally, there is a unique experiment, which we expressed at the beginning of this treatise, in the observation of which a wonderful secret concerning the flowing of springs from the earth will be perceived. For air trapped in the earth through <term>rarefaction<gloss>The expansion of air as it warms</gloss></term>, and similarly water fleeing the solar force, tends toward the vacuum of the earth's center through thinning. While the Sun remains perpendicular over the earth, bringing the season of summer, that denser air and the water hide in the bowels of the earth around that center; but indeed, as the Sun recedes from that summer region and winter approaches, the thick air and water return once again from the center to their previous location—that is, to the surface of the earth—and flow as they did before.*

### TREATISE I. BOOK III.

which had reached this point from the heavens; the reasoning of which is confirmed by the effects of our philosophy. For first, speaking universally, the sphere of water receives the influences of **Mars** through the harmony of the <term>Diapason</term> <note>The Diapason is the musical interval of an Octave, which the author views as a fundamental ratio of the universe.</note>, but it receives them as things contrary to the nature of that sphere. Hence, fire invisibly battles with water, and the water, in resisting, is unnaturally disturbed. Likewise, **Saturn** emits its influences in the same proportion into fire, which, in receiving them, similarly acts and suffers in more specific ways. 

<margin>[</margin> We see that the power of **Saturn** is restrictive, and by accident it frequently causes harm, namely when it is received by colder matter; for then it hurts because it is received, for the most part, by way of freezing. Similarly, we know the power of **Mars** to be motive, and we see its influences cause harm when they are received by more fervent matter; and then it hurts because it is received through heat. These harms do not occur because of a wicked operation of the influences themselves, but because of a <term>poor disposition of matter</term> <note>original: *malam materiæ dispositionem*; the idea that the stars are perfect, but the "soil" they land on—the physical body or element—may be too weak or ill-suited to handle the energy.</note>. 

In the same way, the density or rarity of matter can be at fault. We also sometimes find the weakness of the subject to be the cause, so that good rays and influences produce bad effects within it; for it happens at times that the light of the **Sun** offends the eyes of the weak, and its heat and summer rays hurt even the strong and those of a "bilious" temperament. Thus we also find that the influx of **Mercury** and **Venus** sometimes stirs up blasts and winds in the air. 

Experience also teaches that in a bilious nature, mixed with superfluous phlegmatic humor, foul ulcers are birthed through the influences of **Mars** and the **Moon** when they are in a "bad aspect"—such as a square, a conjunction, or in opposition to one another. This happens because the fiery nature of **Mars** acts persistently toward corruption alongside the watery nature of the **Moon**, until purulent matter is produced. Similarly, when **Mars** and **Saturn** themselves find contrary subjects in a single human or animal, they affect it, most often with plague, putrid fever, or similar diseases; while in the meantime, other animals of the same species—due to a lack of matter contrary to the **Martial** or **Saturnine** natures—freely receive the influx of these planets without danger and without any manifest alteration. 

From these examples it is clear that, although all celestial influxes are healthy in themselves, the perversity or weakness of the subject is sometimes unable to tolerate the natures of the higher powers. By the same logic, in the Elementary region, after every indistinct and once-disturbed nature was reduced to consonant proportions by the rules of harmony, the Earth obtained a place furthest from Fire, its contrary. Similarly, Water was placed between Air and Earth so they would not contend again; indeed, a "spurious sphere of equality" <note>An intermediate zone or buffer where the qualities of two elements balance out.</note> interposed itself between the coldness of Water and the heat of Air. Thus, by means of this middle sphere participating equally in both, peace is maintained between these opposing elementary spheres, as was said above. 

Therefore, wherever the bonds of this kind of peace are broken in simpler bodies, we see the effects of strife and discord in the elements. For example, if fire is mixed with water, thunder and lightning are caused; if fire is mixed with air in too great a proportion, flashes, comets, and other fiery <term>meteors</term> <note>original: *meteora*; in this period, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rainbows and lightning, not just falling stars.</note> arise. If the coldness of the earth meets the air, snow and hail are driven together and collected in the air; if water meets the air, mists and clouds appear. And so, a confusion of harmonies and even of the musical tones themselves sometimes occurs; all of which accidents produce "diseases" in the lower region of the world within simple bodies or elements. 

Furthermore, even in composite bodies, a great strife sometimes arises that is fatal to the body, occurring either because of a violation of the elementary ligaments contained within the compound, or because of an inequality in the proportion of one element to another. To discuss these things more broadly in this place is not our purpose, since that would be more tedious due to the vast field of that subject than it would be suitable for our musical discourse. We conclude, therefore, this <term>World Music</term> <note>original: *Musica mundana*; the ancient theory that the universe functions like a giant musical instrument.</note> of ours with this axiom:

<margin>☛ 2</margin>
->*The Sun thunders its Octave toward generation, and the earth thunders its own toward corruption.*<-

## CHAPTER X.

->*A brief reduction of the whole treatise into one.*<-

**H**ow much divine admiration and speculation—following a pious contemplation of the entire Archetype <note>The divine "Archetype" refers to the original pattern or "Idea" of the universe as it exists in the mind of God before creation.</note>—should be accorded to those two principles of created things: namely, the dark mass of matter, and that Substantial Light granted on the first day by the inexplicable and divine will of the Architect Himself to the world, its parts, and to living things yet to be created. This must appear clearer than the midday sun to all of you endowed with a more sagacious mind, and who look somewhat more deeply into the hidden causes of things with your Lyncean eyes <note>original: "lynceis vestris oculis"; a reference to Lynceus, the Argonaut famed for his keen sight that could pierce through wood or stone. It was a common metaphor for scientific or philosophical penetration.</note>. For it is beyond doubt that we can find nothing at all in this entire universe that does not participate in one or the other of the aforementioned principles. Indeed, just as those two primary substances are contrary to each other in nature and disposition, so too whatever is detected in this world adheres more to one of them, and is therefore entirely opposed both to the opposite principle and to whatever is ruled by it. There is, therefore, Light, to which Darkness is opposed: we have GOD, the Father of Light, and we have the Devil, the Prince of Darkness. The day shines upon us and the world, against which we find the night as a veil of shadows. Light produced the heavens for us, converting the purer part of the dark mass into its own substance; and <margin>→</margin> darkness left for us and for the Macrocosm <note>The "Macrocosm" refers to the universe as a whole, viewed as a large-scale reflection of the "Microcosm" or human being.</note> the earth, burdened with the depth of blackness and obscurity. The essence of Light infused us with the sparks of life, but the body of darkness maliciously encloses, retains, and imprisons that same substance. It compels the splendor of the mind to suffer and endure the most miserable tortures of the flesh, and, seduced by the body's various deceptions and snares, causes the mind to deviate and wander from the truth and the right path, as if blinded by ignorance. Finally, from Light we have fire, form, essence, perfection, life, generation, motion or action, and beauty; but from darkness we receive water, matter, privation, imperfection, death, corruption, rest, and ugliness. Similarly, who can doubt that whiteness, exaltation, love, virtue, good, truth, knowledge, wealth, and other things of that kind proceed from the messenger of the Supreme Architect, since it is manifest and certain beyond any controversy that blackness, depression, hatred, vice, evil, falsehood, ignorance, poverty, and similar opposites proceed from darkness by the messenger of the Devil? O how great and how deep is the dimension of these principles, and how inscrutable are their secrets! Though they can in no way be investigated through *a priori* demonstration <note>An "a priori" argument moves from causes to effects; the author argues we cannot know God's primary reasons directly.</note>, GOD has nevertheless granted us permission to contemplate them *a posteriori* <note>An "a posteriori" argument moves from observed effects back to their causes.</note>. Indeed, happy is he who can rightly know their mysteries, upon which the most profound of the Pagan Philosophers were accustomed to spend not just a year or years, but the entire span of their lives; for they were driven by a greater wonder and more vehement study to inquire deeper into these mysteries, the more they found something of probability within them.

<margin>→</margin> We conclude, therefore, that if anyone wishes to judge our preceding subject rightly and not rashly, they will perceive this opinion of ours to be not only probable but also (unless I am mistaken) not far removed from the truth itself. In the meantime, however, I will most gladly accommodate and submit myself to the judgments of all those better versed in this divine Philosophy, asking them again and again that...
