## CHAPTER VI.

### *Concerning the differences of Daemons, and their duties, according to the tradition of both the ancient and more recent Magi.*

**T**HE MAGI, establishing three kinds of Daemons <note>original: "Dæmonum"; in this context, "daemons" refers to mediating spirits or intelligences, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense of evil spirits.</note> and intelligences (for some according to them are *pre-celestial*, others *celestial*, and the rest *ministers of lower things*) called the pre-celestial ones "minds," completely separated from the body, and as if intellectual spheres, worshiping the one **GOD**, as their most stable point and center; indeed they assert them to be full of **GOD**, and as if intoxicated with divine nectar, and believe they turn about **GOD** alone, nor do they think they take any care at all of mundane bodies, nor do they judge them to serve the administration of lower things by any means; They conclude, however, that it is their duty to pour the light received from **GOD** soon into the lower orders, and to distribute individual duties to each. And this species of Daemons is undoubtedly that which *Iamblichus* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on theurgy and the divine hierarchy.</note> calls, **GODS**, *following the first* **GOD** *who gives all things to all, who bestow some things upon all*. This is also the first and superior Hierarchy of Angels, comprising the orders of *Cherubim*, *Seraphim*, and *Thrones*, whose duty is to contemplate the order of divine providence; For the Angels of the first order look into the goodness of **GOD**, those of the second into the essence of **GOD** as a form, and those of the third into his wisdom. Finally, these are the Angels closest to **GOD**, whom they magnify with continuous hymns and eternal praise <margin>→</margin> and *they pray to* **GOD** *for our salvation, as Athanasius says*. <margin>←</margin> *The Sages call the celestial intelligences "mundane Daemons"*; because beyond divine worship they are adapted to the spheres of the world, and preside over each of the heavens and stars; Whence it happens, that they are distributed into as many orders as there are orbs in the world, and as many stars are counted in the orbs: And from this it is, that some are called *Jovial* <note>Associated with the planet Jupiter.</note>, others *Saturnial* <note>Associated with the planet Saturn.</note>, etc. Daemons of this kind *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>original: "Mercurius Trismegistus"; the legendary figure to whom the Hermetic writings are attributed.</note> in his sacred sermon calls **GODS**, who, after the heaven had shone out in seven circles, were seen in the ideas of the stars with their signs, and it is said that the stars were numbered according to those **GODS** who inhabit them. These are undoubtedly those Daemons of *Iamblichus*, whom he calls ministers of the Gods, like architects in the mundane workshop, who express those things which are ineffable and hidden in the Gods. These also are those Angels who are placed in the middle hierarchy, as having command over the middle region of the world; They are called moreover by *Abbot Trithemius* <note>Johannes Trithemius, a famous Renaissance polymath, cryptographer, and occultist.</note>, secondary intelligences, who by the ordering of the first intellect, that is **GOD**, are said to govern the aethers and orbs <margin>→</margin> of the Planets. The Magi call Daemons of the lower order "ministers," who are referred to those things which are to be disposed in the lower parts: These *Origen* <note>An early Christian theologian.</note> calls certain invisible virtues, through which any earthly things <margin>→</margin> are disposed, and he asserts them to be visible to no one and to complete our business, and direct our journeys, and being present, to turn away the dangers of battles, and to prevent the outcomes of secret ambushes,

...a certain spark; *Posidonius* <note>A Stoic philosopher and polymath from the 1st century BCE.</note> calls it an "idea," insofar as it is the form of a living species; *Asclepiades* <note>Likely Asclepiades of Bithynia, a Greek physician who worked in Rome.</note> imagines it as a kind of chord <note>original: "chordam", referring to a stringed instrument, suggesting the soul "tunes" the body</note> that grants the five senses the faculty to carry out their functions; *Hippocrates* <note>The famous Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> considers it a subtle spirit dispersed through all the passages of the body; *Democritus* <note>The philosopher who first proposed that the universe is made of "atoms."</note> thinks it is an uncertain subtle spirit made of the smallest and indivisible particles, which he calls atoms, colliding and clinging together; *Tertullian* <note>An early Christian author from Carthage.</note> and *Avicenna* <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians/philosophers of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> claim that the soul is born from a soul just as the body is procreated from seed, and that it multiplies in the same way that the light of many candles is lit from a single flame; *Thales of Miletus* <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece, often called the first philosopher.</note> calls it the "motive power" of every thing; and from this is derived his opinion that a magnet is alive because it draws iron plates to itself; *Alcmaeon* <note>An early Greek medical theorist.</note> compared it to the celestial bodies because it is a most mobile thing—indeed, always in motion—and from this disposition, he says, its eternity can most easily be perceived; *Parmenides* <note>A Pre-Socratic philosopher.</note> wants it to be made of earth and fire; *Epicurus* <note>The philosopher who taught that pleasure and freedom from fear were the highest goals.</note> from fire and air; *Empedocles* and *Ericrates* say it is the strongest thing in the body; finally, others feel it is the brain, *others* the blood (as *Critias* <note>An Athenian political figure and author.</note> does); *others* believe it to be vapor and moisture; *some* entirely deny that it is a substance at all. However, although the assertions of these ancient philosophers seem to differ most severely among themselves for the most part, we shall clearly demonstrate from the writings below that some approach closer to the truth than others, and indeed some even agree with the truth itself.

# CHAPTER IX.

## What is the Soul? And about its properties.

<margin>Agrippa book 3, ch. 37</margin> <note>Referring to Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa’s *Three Books of Occult Philosophy*, a standard text on Renaissance magic and philosophy.</note>
According to the opinions of *Augustine, Damascene, Isidore, Bernard, Remigius, Chalcidius*, and almost all the *Philosophers*, both Pagan and Christian, we gather that the nature and disposition of the soul can be explained in two ways: either it is considered by itself—that is, separate from the body—or insofar as it is joined to the body and gives it form <note>original: "informat", a technical term meaning to give essence or structure to matter.</note>. Therefore, as it is understood in its own proper and free state, it is described as: I. Being a certain divine light, created in the image of the first pattern—that is, of the uncreated light—and adorned with a beauty that is almost angelic. <margin>Damascene's homilies and Bernard. Damascene ibid. Seneca. Augustine.</margin> II. A spiritual substance, flowing from divine springs: simple, indissoluble, immortal, free, incorporeal, and invisible, lacking size, shape, weight, or color. III. *Rational intellect.* IV. *An intellectual spirit, participating in reason, always moving, and tending toward blessedness by its own nature.* V. *Finally, a divine mind, understanding all things and making itself like all things.* And indeed, in this description, its properties are precisely outlined. *One* of these is to illuminate knowledge: Hence, *in the Resolution of Theology, tract 2, part 2, portion 3, question 2*, the *intellect* is called the *light and reason* of knowing, because it is the *active* principle of knowledge. *Another* is to lead the Microcosm <note>The "Little World," a Renaissance term for a human being viewed as a reflection of the entire Universe.</note> back to GOD by its presence, as is found in the first [chapter] of *Genesis*; hence we defined the soul as light created in the image of uncreated light. Its *third* property is that, since it is a most pure, simple, spiritual, invisible, and incorporeal substance, it has communication with the intelligences <note>Angels or higher spiritual beings.</note> and—to speak with *Iamblichus* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>—sometimes unites itself with the divine through the harmonies of its essence and actions. The *fourth* is that, while it is enclosed in the body, it never permits it to die, because it is life itself, nor is it ever destroyed by the violence of death (as *Porphyry* <note>A student of Plotinus and a major figure in Neoplatonism.</note> speaks excellently). Hence, with the Sages, we call it immortal and indissoluble. But it is marked by another property besides,

<insert>←</insert> [the soul is moved] so that it may indeed always remember itself, and never fail to understand itself. For it knows nothing so well as that which is present to it, and nothing is more present to the mind than the mind itself; as **Aurelius Augustine** testifies in *Books 10 and 14, chapter 10*. And it is from this that we have defined it as a rational intellect and an intellectual spirit, because all things are understood by the mind. Because the mind assimilates itself to all things, it is called by **Augustine** "the likeness of all things" <note>original: "similitudo omnium"</note> in his *Book on the Spirit and the Soul*, or because it retains within itself the likenesses of all things which it intends to understand; for all knowledge comes by way of <term>assimilation</term> <note>The philosophical idea that to know something, the mind must become "like" the object it perceives.</note>. Thus, through its essence, it is assimilated to the earth; through imagination, to water; through reason, to the air; and through the intellect, it is assimilated to the firmament. The **sixth** property follows, which is, according to **Bernard**, that it be a "Companion of Reason." The **seventh** is that it tends by its own nature toward <term>beatitude</term> <note>Supreme blessedness or happiness.</note>, which **Porphyry** calls the "divine life" itself. The contemplation of this state fuses the contemplator into one with that which is contemplated, as can be seen in the aforementioned author; hence it is that **Bernard** called the human soul a participant in bliss and an heir to salvation. <insert>←</insert> The **ninth and last** of its properties, which we have observed from the aforesaid definition, is that it is always and unceasingly moved. Therefore, it is certain that the soul is a most vital form and a primary act. Hence, by **Plato** in the *Phaedrus*, it is called a "self-moving number," and by **Xenocrates**, a "number acting in itself"; for the soul is moved within its own spirit. From these points, therefore, it clearly appears that the first of the aforementioned properties concurs with the opinions of **Hipparchus**, both **Heraclituses**, and **Epicurus**. Through the third property, the wisdom of **Plato** and the depth of **Alcmaeon** shine most clearly. Finally, the sentiments of **Thales of Miletus**, **Aristoxenus**, and **Xenocrates** agree with the ninth.

Furthermore, insofar as the soul is joined to the body, we have described it in two ways: either in respect to the **Microcosm** <note>The human being viewed as a miniature replica of the entire universe.</note> alone, or insofar as it relates to animals and plants. However, as it is joined with the body of the Microcosm alone, the Soul is defined with its "vehicle" as an incorporeal principle, a proportional number, and a primary act adapted to our bodies, by whose presence we live, feel, move according to place, are endowed with reason, understand the "First Cause," and are capable of good or evil will. From this description, we have observed certain properties of the soul regarding the disposition of the human body: the **first** of which is that it is a principle connecting the four elements in a composition so aptly and agreeably that it imparts to them a most beautiful temperament and a sweet harmony. The **second** is that, insofar as it is a "proportional number," it has the power to rightly dispose the parts of the body toward the functions of life, sense, motion, and action through a certain harmonic consensus. This kind of proportion in the human body produces "Human Music" <note>original: "humanam Musicam"; the concept that the human body and soul are tuned like a musical instrument.</note>, which is nothing other than concord, through which the soul loves the body and the body's parts. Hence, the opinion of **Pythagoras**—who thought the Soul was a concordance of melody—was not unwise. The **third** property is that it is necessary for the body where this soul is found to live, feel, move, and reason. The **fourth** is that in its motion, it is always capable of good or evil will. For, although when free and separate from the body it never ceases to remember and understand itself (as has been said), yet insofar as it is involved in earthly things which it drinks in through the senses, it is never accustomed to perform those functions quite so perfectly. And here, we think the opinion of **Iamblichus** should by no means be rejected, by which we are taught that whatever passions animals have do not truly reside in their souls, but in the body, which possesses a certain quality under the soul by which it acts and suffers. <insert>→</insert> The **last** property is that it universally rules and governs the body according to the opinion of **Remigius**, not otherwise than a sailor governs a ship; or according to **Chalcidius**, just as a spider remaining in the center of its web is perceived to move the entire web by its own motion, so also the soul, hiding itself in the heart, which is the center of the body, is accustomed to move the entire mass of the body. # TO THE KIND READER.

<insert>
Decorative woodcut headpiece featuring a central mask or face surrounded by symmetrical foliage and scrolling flourishes.
</insert>

**W**HEN, in foreign and overseas regions—having previously attained the rank of Master of Arts—I traveled through France, Spain, Italy, and Germany for nearly six whole years, I applied my primary efforts to the more liberal arts. This was because I was urged by several princes and noble friends of mine, and especially by the French, to instruct them in some manner in those sciences.

First of all, therefore, I composed a compendium of <term>Arithmetic</term> <note>The science of numbers and calculation.</note> described in this treatise for <term>Charles of Lorraine</term>, Duke of Guise, and dedicated it to him, and I also privately instructed him in the knowledge of it.

Moreover, I compiled <term>Geometry</term>, <term>Perspective</term> <note>The art of representing three-dimensional objects on a two-dimensional surface; often linked to optics.</note> and the secrets of the <term>military art</term> for a most noble youth of the greatest promise and a magnanimous Prince, <term>Francis of Lorraine</term>, Knight of Guise. Sadly, he was violently snatched from human society by an untimely death—alas!—having been unhappily torn apart by an ill-fated engine of war <note>original: "per infaustum tormenti infeliciter dispersictum"; referring to a fatal accident involving artillery or a cannon.</note>. Indeed, with me as his teacher, he not only grasped these sciences with wonderful speed, but also practiced them with such delight of mind that he even strove to surpass me, his own teacher, in their application. Furthermore, I dedicated <term>Music</term> and the <term>art of memory</term> <note>A system of mnemonic techniques used to recall large amounts of information, often involving mental "palaces."</note>—of which a sufficiently full mention will be made in the second volume—to the <term>Marquis of Orizon</term> and the <term>Viscount of Cadenet</term>, as he was kindled with a wonderful love for learning those sciences. Indeed, I presented my <term>Cosmography</term> <note>The study of the general features of the universe, including both geography and astronomy.</note> to my father, who was at that time the Treasurer for military affairs throughout France and the Lower <term>Belgium</term> <note>referring to the Low Countries or the Netherlands.</note> under <term>Elizabeth</term>, Queen of England—of pious and never sufficiently praised memory. May his soul be blessed. I presented it to him as the one from whom I drew the origin of my life and from whom I had the necessary support to taste the honey-sweet nectar of the Muses, so that I might be lifted by a most sweet and delightful breeze on feathered wings to the periphery of the upper heaven. I did this, however, with the intention that he might the more easily and better [understand] those regions—

If any error should occur in them—as will undoubtedly happen in so great a work—do not ascribe it entirely to our lack of skill or ignorance. Rather, attribute it partly to the weakness of our body, which is nearly exhausted by unceasing labor and thus unable to examine everything with such an exact balance <note>original: "exacta trutina"</note>, and partly to our other occupations, which call us away to various matters. 

<margin>-</margin> Guided by a fiery love, restrain yourself from the "viper’s tongue" <note>A common rhetorical warning against malicious critics who "poison" a book's reputation.</note> which serves as a minister of darkness, malice, and indeed the Devil himself. Approve and praise those things you find well and correctly written, but correct all errors (which I know are not few) with a calm face and a judgment removed from all envy. In this matter, do not act toward me differently than you would wish others to act toward you in a similar case. Indeed, if you do this, you will deserve to be called a "son of light," and this book of ours will emerge more blessed through your kindness. Farewell.

# BOOK ONE.
## On number & numeration.
### CHAPTER I.
#### On Physical & Mathematical number.

**Number is twofold:**

*   **Physical**, which is likewise twofold:
    *   *Enumerated or material.* <note>The objects being counted.</note>
    *   *Numbering, or formal, and is twofold:*
        *   Principal, such as the numbering soul itself. <note>In traditional philosophy, the "numbering soul" (anima numerans) refers to the human mind's innate ability to perceive and organize quantity.</note>
        *   Intermediate, which the soul uses as a kind of instrument for counting: This is understood in three ways, either
            *   For the act or operation of the numbering soul.
            *   For the concept of that act's distinction; thus time is called a number—that is, the distinction of the space before and after.
            *   For the sign and the numeral word, such as one, duo, tria; and this indeed is called **Mathematical number**.
*   **Mathematical**, in which two things are observed:
    *   *Unity, which is the beginning of numbers.*
    *   *Subject, of which there are two parts:*
        *   The collection of units, from which is made a number that is
            *   Abstract, and this is:
                *   Absolute, and it is:
                    *   Even
                        *   Simple,
                        *   Composite.
                        *   Of which each is either:
                            *   Evenly even. <note>A number that can be halved repeatedly until reaching 1, like 8 or 16.</note>
                            *   Evenly odd. <note>An even number whose half is an odd number, like 6 or 10.</note>
                            *   Oddly even and odd.
                    *   Odd,
                        *   Simple.
                        *   Composite.
                *   Relative, which is:
                    *   Commensurable.
                    *   Incommensurable.
                *   Figural or Geometric.
                    *   Linear,
                    *   Plane,
                    *   Solid, } from which come <term>Cossic</term> numbers. <note>Cossic: From the Italian 'cosa' (the thing), an early term for Algebra where the unknown variable was called 'the thing'.</note>
            *   Applied, which is taken <note>The Latin 'contractus' here refers to 'concrete' numbers—numbers applied to specific objects or measures.</note>
        *   Arithmetic, which observes the subject of numbers, and is:
            *   Proper.
            *   Improper.
            *   Common.
            *   Cossic or Algebraic.
            *   Geometric.
            *   Military.
            *   Musical.
            *   Astronomical & Astrological.
            *   Geomantic; Pythagorean, and jocular. <note>Recreational or puzzle-based mathematics.</note>

### TREATISE II. PART I. BOOK I.

**P**hysical Number is a measure by which we judge the difference in quantity—whether smaller or larger—of any substance. We call that the numbered or material number which is a physical thing or a specific numbered multitude, such as a pile of bricks, a handful of barley, etc.

However, we call the rational soul itself the primary **numbering number**, because it distinguishes species and individuals from one another; from which it is manifest that the souls of brutes <note>original: "brutorum"; refers to non-human animals, which the author believes lack rational discernment</note> are able to number or discern nothing at all.

Moreover, that the soul is a number is confirmed by **Plato** in his *Timaeus*, where he calls it a harmonic number for the reason that it is constituted from the <term>Monad<note>The 'Monad' or unity represents the number one as the indivisible source of all other numbers.</note></term> or unity, and from the numbers two, three, and four. Nor indeed does **Pythagoras** dissent from **Plato's** opinion, for he asserts that the soul is composed of single, double, triple, and quadruple proportions, and as if from a point, a line, a surface, and a cube; by which Pythagorean symbol the intellect of the soul and its powers seem to be signified. For the Monad signifies the intellect, which is most simple and unique. The Binary <note>The number two</note> signifies knowledge discerning two things, namely truth and falsehood. The Ternary <note>The number three</note> signifies doubtful opinion judging between three things, namely truth, falsehood, and probability. However, the Quaternary <note>The number four</note> expresses sense; for this perceives only corporeal <note>Physical or bodily</note> things, since incorporeal things are by no means presented to the senses. Finally, through numbers are denoted the elements of species, which the soul, conceiving them as known, numbers and discerns either through principles or through the effects of principles.

**Mathematical number** is <term>discrete quantity<note>Quantities that are distinct and countable, as opposed to 'continuous' quantities like a line or time.</note></term>, collected from two or more. Therefore, no number is unity, because the smallest number is greater than unity.

Unity is the limit from which every number is derived and into which it ends; just as in Geometry the limits of lines are points. For as a line is formed from the flow and series of points, so also number is compounded from the gathering of unities.

Unity in Arithmetic and the point in Geometry are indivisible. For unity multiplied by itself produces nothing new; and that which cannot be multiplied can in no way be divided.

*Abstract number is* that which has no denomination annexed to it, such as 5 or 10 without another thing joined to them.

*Contracted number is* <note>Also known as 'concrete' number</note> that which has some denomination coupled to it, such as 5 lines or 10 degrees.

*Proper contracted number* is a whole number, such as 6 or 10. *Improperly called contracted number* is a fractional number, which is less than a whole unit, such as 2/3 or 7/9.

*Absolute abstract number* is that which has no respect or relation to another, but is considered through itself alone and absolutely.

*Absolute even number* is that which can be distributed into two equal parts, such as 4, 6, 12, 20, etc.

*Even-times even number* is that which can be divided into equal parts all the way down to unity, such as 16 into 8, 8 into 4, 4 into 2, and 2 into 1.

*Even-times odd number* is that which cannot be pulled apart by equal division all the way to unity, such as 18 into 9 (and no further), or 10 into 5, etc.

*Even-times even and odd number* is that which, when divided, gives even numbers, but those subdivided parts eventually produce odd numbers, such as 60 into 30 (which are even) and 30 into 15 (which is odd).

*Odd number* is that which cannot be led into equal parts without the breaking of unity: thus 9 divided equally will produce 4 and 1/2. And fifteen will give 7 and 1/2 in the quotient.

<margin>Two things concur for the numeration of abstract numbers</margin>

                    *   20.
                    *   30.
                    *   40.

    *   **Certain, which is found in digits alone.**
    *   **Uncertain <note>Referring to place value, where the "uncertainty" lies in the fact that a '5' can mean 5, 50, or 500 depending on its position.</note>, in which two things are to be noted, namely**
        *   **Place, and in this two things occur to be observed:**
            *   **<term>Numerator</term>** <note>In this context, the specific digit being counted.</note>
            *   **<term>Denominator</term>** <note>In this context, the power of ten or the specific column (units, tens, etc.) assigned to the digit.</note>
        *   **Order of places, counting from the right, of which**
            *   **The first is of units**
            *   **The second of tens** <note>original: "denariorum"</note>
            *   **The third of hundreds**
            *   **The fourth of thousands**
            *   **The fifth of ten thousands**
            *   **The sixth of hundred thousands**
            *   **The seventh of millions.** <note>original: "millies millium," literally a thousand thousands.</note>

---

**N**umeration is the method by which the proper value of each number is estimated, and by suitable figures and their proper places, it is either increased or decreased.
A *significative figure* is one by whose value a unit or a digit is signified.
A *non-significative figure* signifies nothing by itself, such as a cipher. What a *unit* is, and what a number is, has been stated above.
A *digit* is each simple number that is contained between a unit and the first simple article, such as 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9.
An *article* is every number which is divided into ten equal parts without a remainder, such as 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 100, 1000.

# CHAPTER III.

## *That it is likely the fixed stars were made on the second day of creation; Of their origin, place, and diversity, both in size and in brightness.*

I n the preceding sections, it was demonstrated that light was created on the first day, and that it filled the entire concave surface of the highest heaven. In this way, the light inhabiting the supreme region—which we have called primary light—was separated from the darkness. That light thickened the darkness in the lower parts by thrusting it away from its presence and action toward the bottom and the center of the whole universe. Thus, the first day (that is, the first light) occupied the Empyrean heaven <note>The Empyrean was considered the highest, most spiritual part of the universe in medieval and early modern cosmology, often thought to be the dwelling place of God.</note>, while night (that is, darkness) occupied all that space interposed between the base of this heaven and the center of the whole. 

Then, when the light in its spiritual heaven was established and most active, never resting, it acted most sharply on the second day with its force against the opposite—namely, the dark matter thrust below the base of the supreme heaven—hostilely driving it downward from its boundaries as if it were a great adversary. Therefore, innumerable parts of this primary light penetrated the diaphragm of the crystalline heaven <note>The "crystalline heaven" was a layer of the cosmos often described by ancient astronomers as a clear, watery sphere above the stars.</note>, disturbing the quiet of the middle region’s darkness. Although this darkness resisted the invasions of the light rays strongly enough, it was nevertheless compelled to descend gradually by a slanted revolution toward the concavity of the lower heaven, where it joined with its own darkness. Thus, the mass of darkness in the lowest region was made extremely thick, dense, and opaque, because the darkness from the other heavens was mixed with it. 

And so on the second day, there was day in both upper regions, which are now called the heavens; but night possessed the lowest region, while that light which we have called secondary (being immediately derived from the primary) filled the entire concavity of the middle heaven. For this reason, the substance of that region is called ether <note>In traditional physics, ether was the "fifth element," a pure and unchanging substance that made up the celestial spheres.</note>. Finally, when the secondary light had illuminated this region, some of its rays—specifically a third part of it—penetrated into the lowest region (which was still unformed) on the third day. These rays reverberated all its smoky, and indeed blackest, vapors around the center of the universal machine. This happened with the assistance of the element of fire, which resulted accidentally from the motion of the heavens and the bending of the rays. There, by the power of the cold contained within the matter, they were constricted into a hard mass.

Now, therefore, a great doubt may arise: by what means was that ethereal heaven illuminated on the second day, and the lowest heaven on the third, since we have stated above that light is invisible by itself? We also declared elsewhere that light is present abundantly in every part of this heaven and the middle heaven, even at night, and yet it is in no way visible to the eyes. Therefore, so that a distinction may be made between darkness and light, it is necessary to have an object of sight that is both privative <note>A "privative" object is the absence of something (like darkness being the absence of light), while a "positive" object is the presence of something tangible.</note> and positive; this cannot be had in invisible things. Wherefore, it is necessary that this invisible light be produced visibly. For this to happen, certain bodies are required, acting as organs and polished mirrors, to manifest the form lying hidden invisibly in the medium or "common spirit." The substance of these bodies must be fit and naturally disposed to gather and multiply the multitude of light rays lying secretly hidden. Such are the bodies of the constellations and the stars, as we explained in the first chapter of this book. Since, however, in the middle heaven

# OF THE CREATURES OF THE ETHEREAL HEAVEN.

After the purification of that region from its dark filth, no such bodies—except for those of the stars—are found there due to the thinness of the other parts. It is therefore necessary that certain stellar bodies act as the organs and instruments through which that secondary light (which is otherwise only bright to itself) may visibly show itself to illuminate the other substances of the world. For this reason, it does not seem far from the truth that the **fixed stars** were made on the second day, before the creation of the ethereal heaven was completed, since it does not seem consistent with reason that a visible day could appear in this heaven without them. For they are like breasts through which <term>divine Nectar</term><note>original: "Nectar divinum"</note>, <term>super-celestial Ambrosia</term><note>original: "Ambroſia ſupercœleſtis"</note>, or a luminous milk, are poured into the lower regions as if from a nipple filled with light. By this, the "Son of the World"—whom they call the **Sun** or **Phoebus**—is nourished and suckled after his birth. For this kind of celestial milk is prepared in the breasts of the upper heaven, and its breasts swell before the birth of the Sun, just as a woman's breasts do before they give birth.

*But here someone will object: was it not unnecessary for light to appear visibly on the second and third days, since sensible beings <note>Beings with physical senses, like animals or humans.</note> had not yet been created?* We can answer this in three ways; *First*, because day could not be distinguished from night, nor light from darkness, without a visible manifestation of light; *Secondly*, because the celestial light descended visibly and sensibly toward the center to expel the darkness and to provide for the growth of plants rising from the earth, since three things are required for their essence: light, heat, and influence; *Thirdly and lastly*, because the Sun appeared visibly in the heaven even before the production of animals, and consequently, it is not necessary to require a specific sense <note>i.e., an eye to see it</note> for a thing to be visible. From these points, it is manifest that light was manifest and visible before the creation of seeing animals. Nor will it suffice for such doubters to assert that the sacred Scriptures of **Moses** are contrary to this opinion—where it is found that GOD *made two great lights on the fourth day, and that the other stars were also made on the same day.* For here it is likely that the Holy Leader <note>Moses</note> meant the other **Planets** or "wandering stars," since he had mentioned the two principal ones immediately before. Even **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with hermetic philosophy.</note> seems to verify this in his sacred discourse, where he says *that when all things were in confusion, the light things were carried to the higher regions by a fiery spirit, and immediately the heaven shone forth in seven circles;* from which it was manifest that the seven Planets were made immediately after the ascent of fire into the highest region; however, he makes no mention of the other stars. Furthermore, it would be an irregular order if the creatures of the <term>Empyrean heaven</term> were created on the very day that heaven was established, and similarly, if some creatures of the earth came forth during its creation, yet no creatures were granted to inhabit the middle heaven on the day of its creation.

But perhaps someone might doubt the manner in which such a mass of stars was forged; *namely, by what path or from what subject could their bodies be produced, and raised on the second day into that place called the firmament, to remain fixed there as if clinging to it?* Similarly, *by what reason are they distinguished by such diversity of light and size of body?* To answer this person in a probable and philosophical way, it must be known that immediately after the penetration of light through the diaphragm of the <term>crystalline sphere</term> <note>The crystalline sphere was thought in pre-modern astronomy to be a clear, solid shell surrounding the Earth.</note> as if through a sieve, a great conflict arose between the rays of light and the matter of dark shadow found there. This was due both to the actions of the one substance and the dullness and forced motion of the other, as well as their contrary qualities. For the rays of light acted vigorously upon the passive substance of the darkness, pushing it downward and pursuing it so greedily and livelily that sometimes a part of them was submerged in the bowels of the shadow. There, they were imprisoned as if in the snares of a certain <term>viscous Spirit</term>, which is the true matter of shadow. When the neighboring rays tried to redeem and free their "brother" from prison, they lifted him upward by the power of this aid, as well as through the jumping back and reverberation of the invading rays...

...the reason from resisting matter, as well as by the attractive faculty of its heat; which part of the **imprisoned light**, although it may be liberated from the entire mass of darkness by the **magnetic virtue of light**, was nevertheless so imbued with that **thick and viscous spirit** that it can never be freed from it; since matter naturally desires its own form and retains it once attracted. But here, with the very part of the light which it contains—acting like a body moved by the motion of its own animating soul—it is carried upward, like the **substance of a comet**, to the concave surface of the **crystalline sphere**. There, by the congealing power of that sphere, it is coagulated and hardened into the form of a dark crystal, or perhaps into darker spots of darkness verging toward opacity (as we find in the matter of a **falling star** <note>original: *stellae cadētis*</note>), and it adheres to the substance of that sphere in the manner of ice. Because of its dark thickness, the rays of light passing through the **sieve** of that sphere strike against these icy and crystalline globules in their transit, and are presented to the **power of sight** <note>original: *potentiae visivae*; the faculty or ability of the eyes to perceive.</note> as if in a mirror. 

Simply put, <term>formal light <note>original: *lux formalis*; the essential, structural light that gives "form" or life to a substance.</note></term> is attracted from every part of the middle heaven to satisfy its appetite. Thus, whatever the nature of the middle heaven is, such also is its luminous form, since the composition of this heaven is forged from an equal proportion of the **material heaven** and the **spiritual heaven**. Therefore, if the matter of the heaven is invisible, it is necessary that its light also be invisible; since being visible proceeds from the visibility and appearance of light, and the visibility of light arises from the colored object of matter. 

However, because every part of the middle heaven is forged from an equal substance of matter and light, it is necessary that where the matter is invisible due to its thinness, the light also shines invisibly and secretly; since such matter is too **diaphanous** <note>transparent or translucent</note> and bright, and consequently not "colored." But the thicker the matter is, the more visible its light will be. For any dimension of this heaven never ceases to hunger until its appetite is filled by an equal part of light. Therefore, every part of it, even the thicker parts, has a portion of light similar to itself, by which it may be led to the **goal of perfection** and liberated from the **door of corruption**. If, therefore, the matter is visible because of its dimension, it is necessary, I say, that its formal light also appears to the eyes. And this is why those **stellar bodies**, because of their greater or lesser thickness, are more or less luminous, and by their clarity are more subject to the power of sight than the other parts of the ethereal heaven. 

The probability of this matter is shown by common demonstration. For **thin air** <note>original: *aër tenuis*</note> is invisible by itself because of its subtlety; but if it is condensed into a cloud or mist by the force of cold, it takes on a visible form—sometimes bright and flashing with splendor, sometimes whiter, and sometimes fiery, or verging toward blackness or a leaden hue, according to the greater or lesser predominance of light within it. That the body of one star is larger and denser than another occurs according to the quantity of the **viscous matter** enclosing the light; just as we see in this lower heaven larger or smaller vapors or exhalations rise up, according to the more effective power of the light or soul included within them, which is fit to sublimate a greater or lesser dimension of weight upward. Why, however, the substance of one star is less bright than another, we explained the reason above: for because of its greater or lesser opacity, according to the nature and disposition of the celestial matter, we have said it is either brighter or darker. ->*Concerning the bodies of the Planets, their positions, and how they are always sustained in the same place—that is, why they do not tend further downward at any time, even though they are somewhat heavy due to the density of their matter?*<-

<meta>This page outlines fundamental rules for calculating mathematical proportions, continuing the author's exploration of numerical harmony and its infinite applications.</meta>

<page-num>14</page-num>
<header>TREATISE II. PART I. BOOK I.</header>

# TREATISE II. PART I. BOOK I.

->*That every species of proportion can be extended to infinity according to the order of this mirror.*<-
<note>The "mirror" likely refers to the "Speculum" or the systematic framework the author is using to demonstrate these mathematical truths.</note>

### Rule I.

In a **multiple proportion**, an even number, multiplying either itself or any odd number, will produce infinite **double proportions** <note>original: "proportiones duplas"; a 2:1 ratio</note>, where the number to be multiplied is considered the smaller, and the product is considered the larger proportional number. Thus, 2 multiplied by 2 makes 4 to 2; and 4 multiplied by 2 will produce 8 to 4; and 8 by 2 will give 16 to 8. Similarly, 3 multiplied by 2 will produce 6, and 6 to 3 is a double proportion; as are 12 to 6, and 24 to 12.

A **triple proportion** <note>a 3:1 ratio</note> is also produced to infinity by multiplying any digit in the preceding manner by 3. Therefore, multiply 2 by 3, and it will give 6; and 6 to 2 is a triple proportion. And 6 multiplied by 3 will make 18, which is also a triple proportion to 6. Likewise, 3 multiplied by 3 makes 9 to 3, and 9 by 3 makes 27 to 9.

The same reasoning must also be observed in a **quadruple proportion** <note>4:1 ratio</note> by multiplying any digit by 4; in a **quintuple** by 5; in a **sextuple** by 6; and so on for the rest.

### Rule II.

*If two even numbers are compared in an equal proportion, such as 4 to 4, 6 to 6, 8 to 8, etc., and half of the first part is added, then between those related numbers there will be a <term>sesquialtera</term> proportion;* <note>A ratio of 3:2, where the larger number contains the smaller once, plus half of it.</note> thus, the half part of 4 is 2, which numbers joined together make 6, and 6 to 4 will give the aforementioned proportion. Also, 4 added to 8 makes 12, which is related to 8 by the preceding proportion.

Similarly, where 3 is compared to 3, or where two equal numbers composed of 3 are related—such as 6 to 6 and 9 to 9—if a third part of one is added to the first, it will give a <term>sesquitertia</term> proportion <note>A ratio of 4:3, where the larger number contains the smaller once, plus a third of it.</note>, such as 4 to 3, 8 to 6, and 12 to 9.

The same applies to the <term>sesquiquarta</term> <note>5:4 ratio</note>, where a fourth part is always added; the <term>sesquiquinta</term> <note>6:5 ratio</note>, where a fifth; and the <term>sesquisexta</term> <note>7:6 ratio</note>, where a sixth part of one is added to the other.

### Rule III.

*Every <term>superpartient</term> proportion* <note>A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller once, plus several fractional parts of it.</note> *has respect to the parts of the smaller number: such as the <term>superbipartiens</term>, that is, the smaller and two of its parts. The <term>supertripartiens</term>, that is, the smaller and three of its parts. The <term>superquadrupartiens</term>, that is, the smaller and four of its parts; and so on for the rest.*

Similarly, the naming of these kinds of proportions is done by the smaller number; for instance, the **superbipartiens thirds** proportion <note>A 5:3 ratio (1 + 2/3)</note> signifies the smaller number and two-thirds of it; and the **superbipartiens fourths** proportion requires the smaller and two-fourths of it <note>A 6:4 or 3:2 ratio</note>, and so on for the rest.

In the same way, the **supertripartiens fourths** denotes the smaller and its three-fourths <note>A 7:4 ratio</note>; the **superbipartiens fifths** <note>The text likely means supertripartiens here based on the logic of "three fifths," or 8:5</note> the smaller with three of its fifths, etc.

### Rule IV.

*A **double sesquialtera** proportion* <note>A ratio of 2.5:1 or 5:2</note> *can be expressed in a threefold way, namely as 5 to 2, or 5/2, or 2 1/2.*

Similarly, a **triple sesquiquinta** proportion <note>A ratio of 3.2:1 or 16:5</note> can be expressed under these formulas: 16 to 5, or 16/5, or 3 1/5. We can observe this kind of order in every other proportion.

### CHAPTER V.

*That every Spirit of Darkness carries away a small portion of the luminous essence of its region. Concerning the generation of minerals and plants. That the work of the third day is a kind of prelude to that of the following day.*

**O**n the FIRST day of creation, immediately after the production of the essential light in the higher heaven, it was necessary that the darkness of that same region should yield its place to the substance of that light (which is contrary to it), and be thrust downward by its life-giving activity into the depths of the second and third regions; yet in such a way that some part of the aforementioned light, because of its very deep penetration into the spiritual matter of that darkness, was held captive in its womb. So too, on the second day of creation, the darkness of the middle region is driven down into the lowest region by the active power of the luminous rays penetrating them—which we called "secondary light" above—and for the reasons mentioned before, they also hold a portion of those rays imprisoned in the heart of their spiritual matter. Finally, on the third day, the three kinds of darkness, joined and gathered together in the lower place, constituting the <term>Philosophers' Chaos<note>original: "Chaos Philosophorum". A term used by alchemists and natural philosophers to describe the raw, unorganized matter of the universe at the beginning of creation.</note></term>, crude and undigested, were driven back toward the mathematical center of the cosmic machine by the power of the third light with the help of the <term>sphere of fire<note>original: "sphaera ignis". In the traditional geocentric model, a layer of elemental fire was believed to exist just below the orbit of the moon.</note></term>, and were compressed into a heavy, dense, and opaque mass called the <term>physical center of the world<note>original: "centrum mundi physicum". Here referring to the Earth itself.</note></term>. Moreover, the clearing out of not only the darkness but also the matter enclosed within it from the aforementioned heavens was very necessary, since without it, the operations of light—which are to purify, illuminate, and refine—could in no way have been completed in those regions of the world. Therefore, from the retention of light in the spiritual matter of the lowest darkness (which is the thickest matter of all), the metals and minerals of every kind are procreated; just as from greater or smaller sparks of that same light in the spiritual matter of the darkness of the middle region, various species of vegetables arise, and growing plants spring up from the earth. For because the light of the middle heaven was not as effective as that primary light which is enclosed in the spirit of darkness of the first region, it consequently does not have the same benefit for heating, refining, and dispersing; therefore, the thickness of the earth and the moisture of the water resist it more. But since it is the nature of every luminous thing to strive upward as if toward its natural homeland, and because the rays of every heaven (both visibly and invisibly) join themselves through penetration with the imprisoned rays (by whose union the strength of both is made stronger), it follows that a <term>luminous soul<note>original: "anima lucida". A spark of divine or celestial light that provides life and growth to material things.</note></term> of this kind, enclosed in the spirit of the middle darkness, gradually strives upward and raises itself from the womb of the earth. But since this light is most familiar to the element of fire, and is bound by a certain closeness as if to its own illegitimate brother, it is necessary in its ascent that a portion of the element of fire should accompany it; and also, because the sphere of fire is touching the middle spirit which is the vehicle of the aforementioned light, the element of fire clings to it by the bonds of nature and is raised above the earth with it. And because the element of air is touching and joined to the sphere of fire, therefore no [ascent] can take...

# CHAPTER V.
## On Cossic numbers. <note>original: "numeris Cossicis". The term 'Cossic' comes from the Italian 'cosa', meaning 'the thing,' which was the standard term for the unknown variable (our modern 'x') in early algebra.</note>

<margin>
In Cossic numbers, because they are contracted <note>meaning expressed in shorthand symbols</note>, two things are considered.
</margin>

*   **The Numerator** <note>In this context, the 'numerator' refers to the coefficient or the ordinary number that precedes the algebraic symbol.</note>, which is either:
    *   A **Digit** such as
        *   1.
        *   2.
        *   3. etc.
    *   An **Article** <note>An 'article' or 'joint' refers to multiples of ten.</note> such as
        *   10.
        *   100.
        *   1000.
    *   A **Composite** such as
        *   **From digits** such as
            *   24.
            *   642.
            *   244325.
        *   **From articles and digits** such as
            *   240.
            *   3040.
            *   30043.
    <insert>Which were discussed extensively in chapter 3 of this book.</insert>

*   **The Denominator** <note>In early algebra, the 'denominator' was the name or symbol assigned to the power of the unknown variable (e.g., the symbol for a square or cube).</note>, in which two things are especially to be observed, namely its:
    *   **Value**, which is either:
        *   **Simple**, such as:
            *   Linear, like the root. <note>original: "radix". The 'root' is the first power of the unknown, or $x$.</note>
            *   Superficial <note>referring to a surface or area</note>, like the Square ($x^2$).
            *   Solid, like the Cube ($x^3$).
        *   **Composite**, such as:
            *   The square of squares ($x^4$).
            *   The first sursolid ($x^5$). <note>A 'sursolid' was a term for powers that could not be described as simple squares or cubes.</note>
            *   The square of cubes ($x^6$).
            *   The second sursolid ($x^7$).
            *   The square of squares squared ($x^8$).
            *   The cube of cubes ($x^9$), etc.
    *   **Signs or characters.**
        *   **Of simple value**, namely:
            *   Of Unity. ⊕. <note>The symbol for a constant number without a variable.</note>
            *   Of the Root. ℞ ℞. <note>The symbol for $x$.</note>
            *   Of the Square. 𝓆 q. <note>The symbol for $x^2$.</note>
            *   Of the Cube. 𝒞. <note>The symbol for $x^3$.</note>
        *   **Of composite value**, specifically:
            *   Of the square of squares. 𝓆𝓆 Q. or qq.
            *   Of the first sursolid. S. q.
            *   Of the square of cubes. qc.
            *   Of the second sursolid. b s q.
            *   Of the square of squares squared. qqq.
            *   Of the cube of cubes. CC.

For this mass, reigning at the heart of the middle heaven, possesses a pure substance and a simple nature. Because it shares the same essence as the spirit of the radiant source <note>original: "spiritus fontis lucidi"</note>, it greedily draws to itself those rays which distill from the radiant source through the portals of its "diaphragm" <note>The author uses anatomical metaphors to describe the boundaries between celestial spheres</note> and are scattered throughout the middle heaven. It does this by that magnetic power <note>original: "magnetica illa virtute"</note> through which matter naturally seeks out form to reach its own perfection. In fact, these rays of primary light are pulled toward the center of this spiritual mass, where their "brother" <note>The divine spark or "World Soul" trapped within the material world</note> dwells. Since like things naturally delight in their own kind, they celebrate their brotherly freedom and the light's return from the lower, hellish realms <note>original: "regnis Tartareis," referring to the dark, chaotic depths of unformed matter</note> with a passionate, fiery love.

Therefore, once such an abundance of light from the highest heaven is gathered into the center of this matter (which is similar in substance to the heavens), a perfect balance is struck: the portion of light is weighed in equal <gloss>paribus</gloss> scales against the other <gloss>alteram</gloss> portion of spirit. Consequently, this mass—now fully illuminated and gazing upon the world with a calm, daylight face—must be in constant motion, driven by the active quality of its "form" <note>the soul or light</note> and the passive nature of its matter. Because the resistance of the matter being pushed upward from the center is equal to the force of the "form" penetrating downward, the mass does not move down. Likewise, it does not move upward, because the action of the descending rays prevents it from rising toward the central point of the vaporous matter. From this balance of forces, it follows that its motion must be circular <note>original: "motus circularis"</note>, as we shall explain further on.

Yet many objections could indeed be brought forward against this opinion of ours: among which someone might start by asking, if the substance of this spiritual mass were *originally* from the highest heaven, why does it not return again to that heaven, since it is of the same *nature* and *condition*? But a response will be very easily fitted to this, namely: partly because the substance of the upper heaven cannot become thicker, due to the immense predominance of light within it; and partly because the cluster of the aforementioned spiritual matter is too dense to ascend higher, but too thin and spiritual to descend lower. For this solar mass is sustained in the middle of heaven, both regarding its matter, which it received from the earth, and principally by its formation; for the spiritual matter of each heaven, which we mentioned before, ascends from the earth into the heaven in a pyramid-like shape; *(we are not speaking of a mathematical pyramid having a thin base, but we understand a certain physical body ascending circularly from a thick central base, always more sharply and thinly toward the circumference)* it ascends, I say, in a physical way like a pyramid, after the manner of a tree, from whose root its size always decreases as it ascends upward, since the lower part of the trunk is thicker than the upper, and the branches, the higher they are, the smaller they become; finally, the leaves and flowers are the thinnest of all its parts. And so also the spiritual tree of the heavens is situated; for the earth is the thickest of all, followed by water, then air, and fire, which are compared to twigs and foliage; the Planets surrounding the Sun correspond to the flowers, and in the solar body the true seeds of this tree are gathered, through which all natural things flourish and multiply. 

And certainly, if we look more closely at the anatomy of a tree, we find that a certain earthy disposition is the only impediment standing in the way of its other parts, preventing them from returning to their own proper places; for all the elements are found distinctly within the tree; indeed, we shall even find a portion of the <term>Quintessence</term> <note>original: Quintæ essentiæ. In alchemy and ancient philosophy, the "fifth essence" or ether, a substance purer than the four earthly elements.</note> there with its soul, since it is by its motion that the plant is raised upward. For if a large mass of some tree were thrown into a fire and turned to ashes, we would find a very small quantity of earth within it; from which it certainly seems quite probable that a certain spiritual tree, rising from the earth, is liberated from its earthly bonds by the power of the rays of natural light—just like a burned tree, in which the spiritual parts of whatever thickness are liberated by the power of elementary or spiritual fire. By the support of this spiritual tree, the solar seed is retained in the heart of the middle heaven, partly in the manner of plant seeds, and partly by the restraint of the permanent light of its body (whose nature it is to always remain the same, and therefore to hold its body in the same place by that same durable virtue), because it cannot ascend higher due to its thickness. 

That such is the power of this essential light, we are taught both by natural and artificial effects: for animals are moved to the operations of their souls; similarly, by the activity of artificial fire, heavy things are known to be carried upward and held there for the duration of that fire's vigor, and by its failure, they are known to descend again downward to the natural place of heavy things. We conclude, therefore, that the Sun received its matter from the earth or from condensed and coagulated chaos, but derived its form from heaven, according to the doctrine of <term>Hermes</term> <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure associated with the "Hermetic" wisdom that combined philosophy, alchemy, and astronomy.</note> which flows through the mass of the Sun.

# A MIRROR OF COSSIC NUMBERS,
### in which their value is perceived by those who regard the nature of their roots more than their forms.

## Rule I.

->One must proceed in the same way with mixed roots as with digits or simple roots.<-

## Rule II.

->By what method may we find the root of any number?<-

You must examine the nature of the number, specifically what its denomination <note>In this context, denomination refers to its power, such as square, cube, etc.</note> is, and the given number is to be sought within the arc of that quantity. Once found, the root of that sphere <note>The author uses "sphere" to refer to the concentric rings or rows in the accompanying diagram</note> in which the said number is located must also be sought. For in the arc of roots, and within that same sphere, you will find the radical number of the same given number. 

For example: let the given number be 7776, which will be the numerator, and its denominator will be the <term>Sursolid</term> <note>original: "Sursolidus"; in early modern algebra, this refers to the fifth power ($x^5$)</note>. Therefore, the said denominator is to be examined in the arc of Sursolids—specifically 7776—and then one must proceed through the same sphere toward the left; for the root found there will be the radical number of the given number 7776: namely, 6.

# CHAPTER VII.

## *Physical and Chemical, as well as Theological reasons defending the probability of the preceding opinion.*

**A**LTHOUGH this opinion of ours regarding the origin of the solar body will perhaps seem new and unheard of to the Philosophers of this age, we shall nevertheless attempt to demonstrate that it rests upon probable arguments and reasons—not only Philosophical and Chemical <note>In this context, "Chemical" refers to Alchemy, the study of the transformation of matter.</note> but indeed Theological as well. For what should be thought concerning the density of the body of the Planets, since, because of the placement of many spirits, it possesses a dark and in some way opaque shape, so that it might be more capable of receiving visible light? This is not unlike how invisible air, when condensed, produces a visible, shining cloud. Since, therefore, according to the said *Philosophers*, the matter of a hail-cloud evaporates from the bosom of the earth, and in its density is made altogether like a subtle earthy substance, why then should that solar body not be fashioned from the most subtle matter of the earth's belly, since the earth is called the <term>parent of all things</term> <note>original: "rerum omnium parens"</note> which are created after her? Do not meteors, or "corruptible suns," appear in the upper region of the air, arising from the earth's exhalations? These are not much different from the form of the incorruptible Sun, though their bodies could not ascend higher into the ethereal region because of their false impurity. <margin>Handwritten bracket and symbol</margin> Is it not also by the authority of almost all the aforementioned Philosophers that fire is converted into air, air into water, and water into earth through a certain thickening? By this, it is also very easily seen that earth, conversely, is transmuted into water, water into air, and air into fire through refinement! And thus, fire has something in common with the ether. Furthermore, since all things are from water, what is the difference between thick water and that which is subtle, except that the latter is on the side of the most subtle spirit, while the former is on the side of the earth? <margin>Handwritten arrow pointing to this sentence</margin> From this, it is certain that the thickness of the Sun is on the side of the earth. Indeed, this assertion of ours rests upon and is supported by the very words of certain Philosophers; for it is found in *Hippocrates* <note>The famous Greek physician, here cited as a natural philosopher.</note> that *a part of that immortal element, which he called "Heat," when all things were confused, departed into the highest periphery, which the ancients called the ether.* That is to say, when the triple portion of the darkness of the triple heaven—enclosing the bright rays and constituting a crude and undigested chaos—had been gathered into the lowest heaven, the light, which they call the *Immortal Heat*, ascended, and so on. Certainly *Mercurius Trismegistus* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the Hermetic texts which blended Egyptian and Greek wisdom.</note> seems to confirm this in his sacred discourse, where he speaks thus: *There was an infinite shadow in the abyss; moreover, water and a thin intellectual spirit existed in the chaos through divine power; and when all things had been indistinct, the light elements soon flew forth into the high region, while the heavy ones settled under the moist sand; when things were distinguished and balanced, which were carried by a fiery spirit, the heaven shone forth in seven circles.* For what else would that Wise Man mean by these words, other than that the essential light and spirit, through the word of God, were in the chaos of the lowest heaven, and that then the light things—that is, the spiritual things enclosed in the chaos—were carried up into the celestial region by a fiery spirit, which is to say, by the bright rays enclosed in the chaos? Once this was done, the Sun and the other Planets shone forth. From those words of *Trismegistus*, it also evidently appears that Chaos is a heap of the darkness of all the heavens compressed into the lowest part along with captive rays. For he says: *light things are carried by a fiery spirit into the high region, that is, into heaven.* He himself emphasizes this in almost the same sense—

### TREATISE I. BOOK V.

<margin>☞</margin>But setting those things aside, what should we think of the constant communication of the Sun with the Earth? Since the Sun daily copulates with the Earth as if with his own wife, or at least with some moist spirit retained in the earth, like a receptive patient disposed to play the role of the woman or of the womb itself; by whose annual coupling or coitus, infinite things differing in species are produced, and each species is multiplied within itself. This truly could not be accomplished unless there were a great affinity between the spirit of the terrestrial <margin>←</margin> and solar body. This affinity is undoubtedly on the side of matter, of which the earth is the source, and not from the form, since the spring of form is found in the opposite part—namely, in the <term>Empyrean heaven: In ancient and medieval cosmology, the highest part of the heavens, believed to be filled with pure light or fire and the dwelling place of the Divine</term>. Finally, since the solar body is visible, and therefore partially material, it is necessary that its more corporeal part be derived from the source of matter, which we have demonstrated above to be the earth. What else did the <term>Philosophi Chymici: Alchemists or 'Chemical Philosophers,' who studied the transformations of matter and the spiritual forces within nature</term> intend, who almost with one consent said that that most noble progeny of the Sun, which they called **the son of the sun and the terrestrial Sun, received its substance from the earth and the other elements, but its form from heaven?** <margin>←</margin> Did not <note>original: 'Behemius'. Likely referring to a mystical philosopher or author such as Jacob Böhme, though the spelling varies in Latin texts of this period.</note> also call the Earth, in the Lamentation of Nature, the mother and nurse of all things, who conceived in her womb from fire—that is, from light? Finally, to approach the reasons of Holy Scripture, if we consider more diligently the time of the creation of the earth and the solar body, we shall perceive a great mystery in the <term>creationis ordo: The order of creation as described in the Book of Genesis</term>.

<margin>«««</margin> For on the third day of creation the earth was made, and its creatures were purely vegetable; and after the creation of the earth, on the fourth day, the spherical body of the Sun was produced, in whose dimension the rays dispersed everywhere in the sky were gathered on the same day. Since, therefore, the Sun is a body to be placed many infinite degrees above the earth, why would nature not have made it infinitely before the fabrication of the earth, since it had begun its creation from the most perfect creature—namely, light—and since it had perfected the ethereal heaven before the creation of the earth, of which the Sun is a far more excellent creature? Why, unless because nature preferred to choose the mass of its body from the earth to receive such a noble form, and to make the invisible and hidden rays of the middle heaven manifest and visible? Indeed, this creation of the Sun is deeply mystical, and an evident sign of the future uncreated Good that was to come to men. <margin>←</margin> For just as the created super-celestial light descended from heaven into the earth—that is, into the shadow by means of the spirit—and was buried there for three days in the abyss of darkness and earth after the creation of the Empyrean heaven (just like a vegetable body), and then, with the assistance of the higher rays, stripping off the corruptible filth of the earth, it was itself glorified with its body, and as if regenerated, it ascended into the ethereal heaven on the third day after its inclusion in the shadow; from which place, being gifted every year with a shining scepter and diadem, it rains down life, form, and the power of growth upon all vegetable bodies: **So too that Uncreated Light, the true and only offspring of the uncreated Father, descended to earth by divine will, took on the nature of a human body, and died according to the corruptible flesh; but by His divine and uncreated essence He rose again on the third day after death, with His body now purified from all mortal corruption and glorified beyond human intelligence; whence He ascended into the Empyrean heaven with inexpressible splendor, where, exalted at the right hand of His Father and brighter than all clarity, He daily and liberally pours out spiritual gifts upon human souls, illuminating them with His divine light and defending them from the rage of evil demons; indeed, washing away the perishing men with the water from the fountain of life, and regenerating them by spiritual washing, and redeeming and saving them from the corruption of sin. Therefore, no one should consider it impossible that this created solar essence descended to the earth so that it might there lay aside the opacity and filth of its vehicle or body into which it descended.** <margin>»»»</margin>

That bright globe, which we call the planet *Mercury*, is a body in which solar light is visibly collected by a certain magnetic force, and it is by the presence of this light that its body appears to our eyes. In a similar way, through the constant rebounding of rays from this spherical Mercurial body, certain thinner vapors are stirred up and driven upward from its body to a point midway between the solar body and the Mercurial one. At that same point, another movement occurs to prevent the further ascent of the aforementioned vaporous Spirit—namely, the movement of rays descending from the solar body. Therefore, the equality of the nature of the *Sun* with the equality of the nature of *Mercury* generates a middle orb between them. By the dual circular motion of this orb, its thicker matter is gathered into one spherical mass, which Astrologers have called *Venus*. And this is the reason (namely, the closeness of the nature of the matter of these two planets to the essence of the Sun) why their natural motion differs less from the solar motion than those of the other planets, as we shall declare more fully below.

There is also another motion from that lowest sphere upward toward the globe of *Mercury*, and another from the body of *Mercury* downward toward that sphere, such that in the middle path, the motion of one is opposed to the motion of the other. By the equal struggle of these two, a double motion is stirred up in that middle orb; by its positioning, that spherical mass is gathered together from the equal nature of the Mercurial body and the moist disposition of the lower sphere, which is called the *Lunar Body*, or the *Moon, Phoebe, Diana, Cynthia, Lucina*, etc. <note>These are various classical names for the Moon goddess used in poetic and astrological texts.</note> Because of its proximity to that region of corruption <note>The "sublunary" world—the Earth and its atmosphere—where things are subject to change and decay.</note>, and also because it receives only a tiny amount of lucid form from its neighbor *Mercury*, its body hungers more and more for the solar form. Although it is adorned by this solar form equally—that is, in the same proportion—nonetheless, according to its distance from or proximity to the solar body, the illumination of its body appears more or less visible to us. From this, it is manifest that the greater part of it is in some way opaque, and consequently, a certain opacity is required for the visibility of the bodies of the stars. Similarly, it is certain that this body is fashioned from the denser substance of this heaven, since it cannot be totally penetrated by solar rays. And in this way, we have three planets moving in their own proper orbs, arranged at a proportional distance and order from one another within the convex surface of the lowest heaven; their bodies are to be considered thicker and denser the further they exist from the solar body.

Since just as many planets are also found above the solar body (namely, between the place of the fixed stars and the orb of the Sun), we must diligently investigate how and by what reasoning they could be produced there in their distinct orbs. We have said, therefore, that one part of this heaven, thicker and moister, is driven downward from its heart by the presence of the *Sun*, and the other part, which is drier, is driven upward toward the concave surface of the watery or crystalline sphere, in which we declared above that the fixed stars are congealed. At these limits, coldness also abounds through <term>antiperistasis: a philosophical concept where a quality is intensified by being surrounded by its opposite, such as cold becoming more intense when compressed by heat.</term>, just as it does in the opposite location. This happens because of the gentle warmth of the most spiritual heaven hovering above, which is contiguous with the crystalline sphere, and the lively heating of the solar body. By the Sun's operation, dryness is shaken out from the solar orb toward those margins, and its dryness comes from the congealing disposition of the crystalline sphere—which, for this reason, everyone has called the "icy heaven" <note>original: "cœlum glaciale"</note> and "crystalline" because of the multitude of dry waters. Therefore, the action of solar rays upon this overarching subject is the sole reason and origin of the planets suspended step-by-step above the Sun. For, just as we demonstrated in the birth of the elements regarding the production of the sphere of moisture in the lowest heaven, the constrictive nature of the earth and the nature of fire meet and concur in equal proportion in the middle way; so also, by the upward motion of the solar rays and the downward movement of the dry coldness driven to repel the attacks of said rays, in the middle way between the solar body and the convex of this...

## CHAPTER X.

### *On the natures of the Planets, and their dispositions, by which they act upon these lower regions.*

---

ALTHOUGH it is clear enough from what has preceded that the bodies of the three lower planets <note>The "lower" planets in the traditional geocentric model are the Moon, Mercury, and Venus.</note> and the three upper planets <note>The "upper" planets are Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> proceeded from the power of the Sun, we shall here provide another reason. By this, we shall declare both that the creation of the solar body was prior in order to the bodies of the other wandering stars <note>term: wandering stars (original: *stellæ erraticæ*), the literal meaning of the Greek word *planētai* or planets.</note>, and that it received the formal arrangement of light earlier. For almost all Philosophers have agreed on this: that light exists in the **Sun** as if in a thing luminous in itself, but <margin>→</margin> in the other planets by participation <note>original: *participativè*; meaning they share in the Sun's light rather than producing their own.</note>. Since, however, the light of a star is its "essence-making" form <note>original: *forma essentifica*</note>, without which the stars cannot exist or even be named, and since the remaining planets received this from the Sun itself as if from their own informer, it is necessary that the **Sun** precedes the other planets in the order of creation, just as a principle precedes that which is derived from it. Therefore, light emitted from the highest heaven downward through its common partition <margin>←</margin> was received into the Solar body on the fourth day and is guarded there, as **Basil** <note>St. Basil the Great, a 4th-century Church Father who wrote on the six days of creation.</note> testifies. The **Sun** imparted a certain portion of this light to every planet, both above and below it, granting more or less according to the proximity or distance of that planet's body from its seat, and also according to the disposition of the planetary body to which it gives. And it is from this that, according to **Iamblichus**, all celestial virtues are present in the Sun; and, as **Proclus** testifies, at the Sun's aspect, the powers of all celestial things are gathered into one, which we believe are finally scattered into this lower world through its fiery vents. Hence the **Platonists** believed the "World Soul" <note>original: *anima mundi*</note> to be enclosed within the Sun. Therefore **Phoebus** <note>A poetic name for the Sun or Apollo.</note> sits in the center, shining with golden hair, holding a scepter and a helm like a King and Emperor, most full of the light of all the stars. He received this from the "intelligible world" <note>In Neoplatonism, the realm of pure ideas or forms.</note> above all other stars because his soul exists as more capable of intelligible splendor, as some of the **Platonists** maintain. Moreover, the primary royal disposition clearly reveals itself, both by reason of its composition and by its effect. For it is composed of an equal part of spiritual matter ascending from the earth and of the essential luminous form descending from the Empyrean heaven. Hence, its orb is called by **Artephius** the *sphere of the soul and of equality*. From these things it is clear that its temperament is warm in the most pleasant degree—which it received from the arrangement of secondary light—and imperceptibly moist, this coming from the nature of its spiritual body. But because the abundance of its form satisfied the appetite of its matter in every way, heat certainly predominates in its body; by the benefit of this heat, not only did the planets receive their natural dispositions, but so did every lower thing. It is for this reason, then, that **Mercury**, receiving one part of its nature from the Sun but another from the moist and cold mass scattered spherically below, has three parts of coldness and moisture and as many from the temperament of the Sun. Thus, **Mercury** is much more moist and cold than it is warm, because in the arrangement of the Solar body, we said that one part of the body concurs with one part of the luminous soul. And it is for this reason that **Mercury** is so variable in its nature, and so inconstant, that it sometimes joins itself to good planets and sometimes to evil ones, [assuming] their natures...
