### Rule.

Among the common people, this figure is called the **Cube of cubes** <note>original: *Cubes de cubis*. In Renaissance mathematics, this usually refers to the sixth power ($x^6$), created by cubing a square or squaring a cube.</note>; because when a cube is multiplied by itself and the result is extended, the final product will again produce a cube from cubic cubes.

### Rule.

Just as the progression of numbers is entirely infinite, so also the proportional series of these geometric figures is altogether immeasurable, proceeding always from multiplied cubes to larger cubes. If we wish to proceed further, let us double the **cube of cubic cubes**; and from there, a **long cube of cubic cubes** is composed, or a **square of Sursolids** <note>original: *quadratum de Surfolidis*. The term "Sursolid" was used by early mathematicians like Robert Recorde to describe prime powers beyond the cube, specifically the fifth power ($x^5$).</note> is formed. By doubling this figure, we shall shape a square of the cubes of cubic cubes, and so on for those that follow.

### Rule.

The operation will always be the same as above, where the root <term>Radix: the base number (root) from which a square or higher power is calculated.</term> consists of several units, by multiplying the preceding figure by the simple root; for the product will be the value of the figure immediately following, as seen below.

### CHAPTER VI.

#### ->Concerning metric numbers.<- <note>original: "De numeris metricis." In this context, "metric" refers to the general science of measurement (metrology) rather than the modern Metric System.</note>

Metric numbers are either:

*   **Of Distances**
    *   Of places or of particular surfaces, which are made:
        *   By the union of many grains. For
            *   From the width of one grain of barley:
                *   <gloss>Is formed from</gloss>
                *   A Finger [Digit] (from 4 grains.)
                *   A Palm (from 4 fingers.)
                *   A Foot (from 4 palms)
                *   A Cubit (from 1 ½ feet.)
                *   A Step [Grade] (from 2 feet)
                *   A Pace (from 2 ½ feet.)
                *   A Rod, which the French call *la Perche.* (from 10 feet.)
                *   A Stadium (An eighth part of a mile, namely 125 paces)
                *   A Mile (from 1,000 paces)
                *   A French League (from 1,500 paces)
    *   Of regions or universal lands, for some count distances by:
        *   **Miles, such as**
            *   The Russians.
            *   The Italians.
            *   The English.
            *   The Scots.
            *   The Germans, etc.

            *   The French,
            *   The "Hour-leaguers," <note>original: "Horarij," referring to distances measured by the amount of ground covered in one hour's walk.</note>
            *   The Spanish.
            *   The Gascons.
            *   The Swedes.
        *   **Signs, as the Egyptians do**
        *   **Parasangs, as the Persians do**

*   Of lines, which in the measurement of heights and the measurement of surfaces (lines) }
*   Of surfaces, which in the measurement of surfaces (planes) } <gloss>are dealt with</gloss>
*   Of bodies, which in the measurement of volumes [polymetry]. }

*   **Of Weights, for weight is made either from**
    *   A grain of barley
    *   A multitude of grains, in which there are two things:
        *   **The Value, for it is established from:**
            *   20 grains make a <term>scruple</term> <note>A small unit of weight in the apothecaries' system.</note>
            *   60 grains make a <term>dram</term> [drachma]
            *   8 drams make an <term>ounce</term>
            *   16 or 12 ounces make a <term>pound</term>.
        *   **The Symbols, such as:**
            *   <term>Grain</term>. g.
            *   <term>Scruple</term> ℈ j.
            *   <term>Dram</term> ʒ j.
            *   <term>Ounce</term> ℥ j.
            *   <term>Pound</term> ℔.

### ->The Rule.<-

Although the same object [the barley grain] is the starting point from which the count of distances and weights originates, it is nevertheless considered in different respects. For in the measurement of distances and dimensions, the width of the grains is required, while in weights, their heaviness is considered.

# ON THE CREATURES OF THE EMPYREAN HEAVEN.
<meta>catchword: dam (likely part of the word 'quandam' on the following page)</meta>

<margin>chapter 4.</margin> ...the tradition of the <term>Magi</term><note>The author refers here to the legendary "wise men" or practitioners of ancient wisdom, likely referencing Hermetic or Zoroastrian traditions popular in the Renaissance.</note> called them celestial and worldly, we do not exclude them from the bodies of the stars as if they held no office or dominion over them. For we confess, according to the opinion of the ancients, that beyond divine worship, they are assigned to the spheres of the world and preside over each of the heavens and stars. They are distributed into as many orders as there are heavens in the world and stars in the heavens. For this reason, the wiser *Magi* classified some as *Saturnine* <note>original: "Saturninos"; spirits associated with the planet Saturn.</note>; others as *Jovial* <note>original: "Joviales"; spirits associated with Jupiter</note>, and so on. Nor indeed was that opinion of the *Platonists* far from reason, which affirmed that *infinite spirits <note>original: "Dæmones"; in this context, "daimons" refers to intermediary spirits or intelligences, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense of evil beings.</note> inhabit the spherical substances of the stars, no differently than animals inhabit the earth*. They divide these into legions, over which they say kings, princes, or governors are placed. And this is the very same thing that the Abbot <term>Trithemius</term><note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516) was a famous German abbot and polymath known for his writings on cryptography and angelology.</note> seems to confirm, saying: *seven spirits have been set over the seven Planets from the beginning of heaven and earth*. From among these, the governor of the kingdom of *Saturn* is called *Orifiel*; of *Jupiter*, *Zachariel*; of *Mars*, *Samaël*; of the *Sun*, *Michael*; of *Venus*, *Anaël*; of *Mercury*, *Raphael*; and of the *Moon*, *Gabriel*. We conclude, therefore, that the motion of the planetary bodies no more consists in the power of the spirits inhabiting and occupying them, than the spherical motion of the terrestrial body consists in man—who stands as the most noble among all its inhabitants and Lord over all earthly things. Rather, we affirm more confidently that it derives all the power of its motion from its own soul and essential form. This is because in the works of *Augustine* and the *Resolutions of Theology (tract 2, part 3, question 1)*, we find that GOD administered the things *which He created in such a way that He allows them to be driven by their own motion*. But GOD gave to the stars and His other creatures those things which suffice for their operation; therefore, they can have their own operations without special illumination or the assistance of [external] intelligences. For the soul of any mobile body is the "first mobile"—that is, it is movable spontaneously and by itself—since its matter is quite ineffective on its own and far degenerate from the soul itself.

### CHAPTER XIV.

->*Why the heavens are moved in a circle, and concerning the duration of the daily motion—that is, the revolution of the heaven within the space of twenty-four hours.*<-

I fall into a great error, if I am not mistaken, if I agree with those who say that *the substance of the Empyrean Heaven is immobile*. Indeed, we said in *Chapter 2, Book 2*, that the Spirit of the Lord moved first of all in that place; by whose motion it is certain that the simplest Spirit of that place is further moved, no differently than we perceive the air to move at the motion of a lower fire. By the presence and ineffable power of that uncreated moving Spirit, the sacred Scriptures also report that this first creature—the swiftest, most lively of all, and the opposite of rest—was produced by the brightness of that same Spirit. For as the *Royal Psalmist* says: *By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their power by the Spirit of his mouth* <note>A translation of Psalm 33:6.</note>. Since, therefore, light is the first and primary power of the heavens and the universal world, it is necessary that it proceed immediately from 그 divine and inexplicable Spirit. *The Spirit of the Lord was moved* in the spiritual Heaven above the waters or the corporeal heaven, bounding them and attributing a spherical shape to them by its motion, as is evidently demonstrated to rational eyes by the effect. From this, it is manifest that the motion of the same divine Spirit was not straight, but circular, so that by its motion it might make that mass of <term>hyle</term><note>A Greek term (ὕλη) referring to primordial, unformed matter.</note>—which it was surrounding and separating from the other parts of matter excluded from the world—round and spherical. This was done because such a spherical shape, insofar as it has neither beginning nor end, is in some way likened to the creator, since every effect necessarily [possesses] some... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "quandam" (some/a certain), continued on the next page.</note>

<summary>This page discusses the hierarchy of planetary spirits (archangels) and argues that celestial motion stems from an internal "soul" or form granted by God, rather than constant external pushing. It further explains that the universe is spherical and moves circularly to mirror the eternal nature of the Creator.</summary>

# TREATISE I. BOOK V.
<page-num>132</page-num>

...usually has a likeness to its cause; also because such a shape [the circle], the most noble, useful, perfect, and convenient of all others, is far more capacious than the rest. Immediately, therefore, following the action of this Spirit, that first creature <note>Likely referring to the first manifestation of created light</note> shone forth, arising from the motion and brilliance of the **uncreated light** <note>original: *lucis increatæ*</note>. It is probable that it moved by the same path and by the same logic of motion, imitating the actions of its primary cause. Furthermore, the effect seems to reveal to us the path of this circular motion—that is, the boundary from which and to which it moves—namely that it was from the east <margin>/</margin> to the west, or rather from the right hand toward the left, when looking toward the northern pole. (For ***East and West*** <note>original: *Oriens & Occidens*</note> received their names from the creation of the Sun).

This is for two primary reasons. The *first* is because human nature, in which that divine light dominates above all other animals, usually moves the right hand—due to a divine appetite for its own light—and employs it in every manual task as the more excellent and noble side. From this, it is clear that the natural appetites of the primary light are moved from the right side of the heavens. The *second reason*, which indeed seems infallible, is because the rapid and most swift motion of the heavens is perceived to tend from that side toward the west. 

But since the created essential light proceeding from that uncreated light is called the most noble—according to most philosophers and even those most skilled in Theology, among whom I name *Augustine in his Literal Commentary on Genesis*—because nothing is more mobile or subtle, and is even called by him in that same place the *foundation and principle of the highest natural motion*, it is necessary that the more grasping and swift motion of the entire heaven be derived from its source. Consequently, the **diurnal motion** <term>The apparent daily rotation of the celestial sphere from east to west</term> by which the entire material world is revolved from the ***East*** (contrary to the *opinion of Copernicus*) to the ***West*** in the space of twenty-four hours, flows from that same source by the power of that luminous spiritual fountain. 

This *Trismegistus* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus</note> also seems to confirm in his *first discourse* with these words: "The creator Mind, together with the Word, containing the circles and turning them with swift speed, turned his machine toward himself, and commanded it to be rolled from the beginning to the end without end." By "the beginning," he seems to mean the east, and by "the end," the west. Do we not also see that Holy Scripture almost everywhere always places the name of the ***East*** before the ***West***, as in *Genesis 13:14, Psalm 50*, and countless other places? Furthermore, in all adoration, the worshippers turn themselves toward the ***East***, as in *Ezekiel 8:16, Matthew 11, Luke 13:29*, and many other places. Similarly, *that star declaring the coming of Christ* appeared in the ***East***, <margin>/</margin> and so also the coming of the Lord will be from the east toward the west (*Matthew 24:27*). By these things, it is sufficiently demonstrated that the uncreated Light moved from the ***East*** toward the ***West***. 

For what could be clearer than this? Especially since the effect of that matter falls under the senses. Are we not certain that a soul exists in a human or any other animal, although invisible, while we perceive its body moving itself here and there? Do we not recognize a visible act included in a plant when we see it flourish and sprout? Are we not also certain that an **intellectual soul** <note>original: *animam intellectualem*</note> exists above the surface of the corporeal world, while experience testifies that it gathers itself together and revolves in a natural day? Indeed, the matter of this world—since it is by itself ineffective for motion—could in no way accomplish this movement except through the motion of the luminous fountain, which is the foundation, source, and origin of any natural motion. And consequently, it is certain that the motion of that first luminous creature was circular, and from east to west; this motion was the primary one of all, and faster, nobler, and more powerful than the rest, since it arose from the source of universal action. 

However, how that spherical matter—unfit for motion by itself—is moved by that fiery soul placed above <margin>-></margin> the surface of its periphery, is declared by the following experiment: <margin>->></note> where B. C. A. is a wheel, on whose circumference that artificial fire, called A. ***the Fuse*** <note>original: *Fusum*</note>, is tied. By the power of this ignited fuse, therefore, the whole wheel is violently snatched away, completing its circular motion as swiftly as possible.

He uses the analogy of a firework fuse attached to a wheel to illustrate how spiritual energy drives material rotation.</summary>

<page-num>153</page-num>
# CONCERNING THE CREATURES OF THE ETHEREAL HEAVEN.

We conclude therefore with the opinion of *Trismegistus* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure to whom various mystical and philosophical texts were attributed.</note> expressed in his *third discourse*, that a wider circuit in the aerial circle has been carried along by the breathing of the divine Spirit; and indeed from the beginning toward the end, and by the action of its brilliance and the resistance of moist matter, a threefold circular motion is created in the heavens. Of these, <margin>1</margin> the *first* is this motion from East to West, or from right to left, which we have already said is driven according to the arrangement of the first heaven’s source of light. <margin>2</margin> The *second* has its cause in the matter of the stellar body and the heavens, as we shall declare below; that is, the one which occurs from West to East, or from the left part of the heaven to the right. <margin>3</margin> The *third* takes its origin from the mutual action and passion <note>In traditional natural philosophy, "action and passion" refers to the relationship between an active force (form) and the thing it acts upon (matter).</note> of form and matter, which we call the motion of trepidation <note>A historical astronomical theory used to explain the variation in the precession of the equinoxes.</note>. <margin>4</margin> There are also circular motions proper to the creatures of heaven <note>Referring to the stars and planets themselves.</note>, which are stirred up by the action and passion between the matter of the star's substance tending upward, and its form seeking downward; of this kind are their motions in their Epicycles <note>A term from Ptolemaic astronomy describing a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger circle.</note>; concerning which we shall also treat more extensively below.

### CHAPTER XV.

<margin>❦</margin>#### *Concerning the error of Copernicus and Gilbert, who assert the daily revolution of the earth.*

**C**oncerning the daily revolution, various disputes arise among philosophers, and it is a controversy not quickly determined; while some wish the entire machine of the universe to be revolved in the space of twenty-four hours by the seized motion of the prime mover <note>original: *primi mobilis*; the outermost sphere in the traditional geocentric model which was thought to drive the rotation of all other spheres.</note>, and they think that this motion occurs from East to West; of this opinion are the *Peripatetics* <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note>, and almost everyone of our age, with only a few of the contrary opinion excepted. In the rank of those ancients, we find enumerated and named *Heraclides Ponticus* and *Ecphantus*, both *Pythagoreans*, *Nicetas of Syracuse*, and *Aristarchus of Samos*, and several others of the same kind; but among the moderns, *Copernicus*, that most skilled Astronomer, and *William Gilbert* our colleague <note>Gilbert was a prominent English physician and scientist known for his work on magnetism; the author calls him "colleague" likely as a fellow physician or member of a learned society.</note>, for many years a studious investigator of magnetic power; their opinion is that the daily revolution occurs in no way because of a prime mover, or from East to West; but that the globe of the earth itself [rotates] from West to East according to...

...while they constantly assert that the natural progression of the Planets naturally revolves within a 24-hour period. And certainly, although their arguments may seem probable and plausible at first glance, if they are inspected more precisely and considered diligently, we shall very easily discover them to be entirely trifling and frivolous. We shall attempt to prove this with reasons relying both on philosophical speculation and common practice, as well as those drawn from <term>Holy Scripture<note>Referring to Biblical passages often cited at the time to support a stationary Earth, such as Joshua 10:12-13 where the sun stands still.</note></term>. **First**, <margin>1</margin> it would therefore be miraculous if all the Planets of heaven moved according to the breadth of the world, while the terrestrial sphere—far viler and more ignoble than them—constantly completed its own natural course every natural day under the same <term>elevations of the pole<note>A reference to latitude; the author argues that if the Earth moved, our orientation to the North/South poles would not remain so stable.</note></term>, and consequently was irregular in its motion compared to all other globes; for it is certain that no place on earth is raised higher nor depressed lower, but always occupies the same position of latitude. <margin>2</margin> **Second**, if the circular motion of the earth were completed in a space of 24 hours, the earth would move infinitely many times faster than the swiftest horse at full gallop, a stick violently struck, or a <term>cannonball<note>original: "globo tormentario"</note></term> emerging from the fiery mouth of a <term>cannon<note>original: "bombardæ"</note></term>. Now, a horse’s violent run is seen to somewhat hinder the rider’s breathing through the compression of the air and its resistance; a stick swung by a strong arm through the air is perceived to give off a sound and stir up no small noise; and a cannonball ejected from a cannon by the power of fire is proven by experience to create an even greater noise flying through the midst of the air. Yet the motion of all these things could in no way be compared with that which the earth would stir up by its daily revolution (if it were ever moved by such a motion). Consequently, from that swifter motion of the earth by which it would complete its daily revolution, <margin>1</margin> men standing perpendicularly upon the earth's surface, great crags and those protruding highest from its surface, <margin>r</margin> trees stretching upward, and proud palaces and towers reaching even to the clouds, would produce a far more violent noise and <term>clangor<note>A loud, resonant metallic sound; here used to describe the imagined roar of the atmosphere against a moving Earth.</note></term> through the striking and resistance of the air. <margin>*</margin> Since none of these things can be perceived by any sense, we judge that the earth is in no way moved by such a rapid motion. <margin>.</margin> For it is not a sufficient answer to say that the air itself is also moved with the motion of the earth and gives way to it in its movement; for we perceive that winds sometimes blow violently from east to west, and the blast of these winds sent against the earth's motion would likely cause horrendous whirlwinds and storms because of the opposing motion of the earth. Since all these things do not happen, they evidently demonstrate that the earth does not move by itself in a daily revolution. <margin>3</margin> **Third**, we shall prove by these experiments drawn from nature itself that the natural motion of the earth itself is in no way to be compared in speed to the motion of the heavens.

...and that a great weight be raised by many hands, which because of its heaviness cannot be sustained by the strength of a single living soul. But, if any part of the earth is dissolved into water, ten parts of that water will equal that single portion of earth in its weight. Similarly, one part of water corresponds in its weight to ten parts of air made through the thinning <note>The author is describing "rarefaction," the process by which a substance becomes less dense, such as water turning to steam.</note> of water; and the same proportion will exist between the substances of air and fire, and between those of fire and the <term>Fifth Essence</term> <note>original: "Quintæ essentiæ"; the Quintessence or Aether, the pure, incorruptible material that ancient and medieval philosophers believed filled the universe beyond the sphere of the moon.</note>. From these facts it is manifest that earth dissolved into water requires a space ten times larger than it occupied before its dissolution and thinning; just as it appears in the thinning of any crumbly mineral caused by a sudden fire. For by violent heat, vitriol or antimony is suddenly dissolved into so many airy and watery spirits that the body of the <term>Retort</term> <note>original: "Retortæ"; a glass vessel with a long, curved neck used in chemistry and alchemy for distilling substances.</note>, which previously held the mass calmly, can no longer contain that rarefied matter; instead, it bursts with a great crash as those spirits seek a wider space. 

We say, therefore, that the proportion of the heaven in weight is equal to the proportion of the earth, and its body is well-disposed toward motion because it is subtle, thin, and easily moved; whereas the body of the earth is ill-disposed toward motion because it is thick, heavy, and very near to rest—a receptacle of darkness, which is the opposite of motion. For we see that the Sun, by the action of its light, daily lifts up the thinner parts of the earth; but against the denser parts, namely rocks and other things of that kind, it strikes in vain and without any sensible motion or thinning of the parts. 

Finally, what is to be thought of the nature of the earth, which all philosophers have maintained to be cold? Did not *Gilbert* <note>William Gilbert (1544–1603), an English physician and scientist who argued that the Earth was a giant magnet and that it rotated on its axis.</note> himself confess, insofar as he was well-versed in medicine, that coldness is the cause of numbness, rest, and stupidity; whereas heat—which has no dominion in the earth—bestows motion, sense, and action upon all things? And yet, he was so carried away by his magnetic virtue that he dared to call the entire body of the earth a <term>magnet</term> or <term>magnetic</term>; because he observed that some mineral of it, namely the loadstone, attracts iron to itself, turns toward the poles of the world, and marks the variations of the poles; and so he seems to take the whole for its smallest part. In such a way we might also call the Sun a <term>Carbuncle</term> <note>original: "Carbunculum"; a gemstone, usually a deep red garnet or ruby, which was anciently believed to glow in the dark with its own light.</note>, because we see it shine at night.

We conclude, therefore, that the heaven, with respect to its matter and its weight, can be moved around in the space of twenty-four hours just as easily as the earth; since it is proportional in its weight to the earth. But with respect to its preparation, it has been demonstrated above that it is moved better and more easily than the earth. 

But if all these things are not enough for the reader, we finally call upon Holy Scripture as the witness of truth in this matter, which Christians acknowledge would be most impious and wicked to call false. It is found, therefore, in the book of *Joshua, chapter 10: The Sun and the Moon stood still in the midst of heaven, and did not hasten to go down for the space of a single day*. For it is not permitted to answer there that this passage of *Joshua* should be understood as the "natural" motion of the Sun: for he speaks of the day and the <term>diurnal motion</term> <note>The daily rotation of the heavens around the Earth.</note>, of which he confesses the Sun to be the author, since without its standing or staying, the day could not be continued. But if we desire an even more manifest testimony, it is recorded in *2 Kings 20* that God *made the Sun go backward*; for the shadow of the dial was moved back by ten degrees. Similarly, this diurnal motion is best declared by the Psalmist in *Psalm 19:5*, where he clearly expressed that *the Sun, coming out of his tabernacle, moves from the rising to the setting*. Does this not also agree with the intention of *Saint Matthew, chapter 24:27*, saying that *the lightning comes from the East to the West, and that in the same manner, from that part to the setting, the Lord himself shall come on the last day*? In these passages it is taught clearly enough that the motion of the uncreated essence—such as the Son who is to come on the last day from East to West, and the Holy Spirit of the Lord moving in the same way over the waters on the first day. And hence also the name of the East, as the starting point, is always placed before the West in the sacred letters, as we said before, just as adoration is made toward that part, and the tem-

### CHAPTER XVI.

->*On the nature of the natural motion of the Planets, that is, from west to east, and against those who argue that stars move according to the motion of their spheres, from which arises the astronomers' observation regarding the motion of the Epicycle.*<-

**T**HE MOTION of the heavens of the middle region from East to West is not called their natural motion, but rather "violent and rapt" <term>raptus: the "dragging" or "carrying" motion of the outer heavens that sweeps lower spheres along with it</term> (although in its own nature—that is, in respect to the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest, most spiritual part of the heavens, often associated with light and the divine</note> from whose lucid fountain it is derived—it also occurs naturally). For the natural motion of bodies is not to follow their source, but rather the motion of that mass in which the movement occurs. And here indeed a great mystery must be observed; specifically in this: that just as celestial motion is distinguished from lower things because of the excellence and perfection of its essence, it also possesses a motion contrary to them in every way—namely, a circular one, which befits the perfections of all parts of the world. Thus also, a great contrariety of motion arises between the heavens of the more perfect part of the world. For although there is no difference in the order and figure of their motion between the two superior heavens—the spiritual as well as the physical—yet in their "starting points" <term>terminis à quo: the point from which a motion begins</term> there is the greatest contrariety. Since the former (the spiritual) is carried from the sunrise, and the latter (the material) from the opposite point of the same hemisphere—namely, the sunset. This opposition of circular motion is derived from that difference which exists between matter and form; it is natural for each of these, because of the separation of one from the other, to produce contrary motions. Hence heavy things, on the side of matter, tend to move downward (as was said regarding the heap of darkness), while light things move upward toward the natural seat of light (as we have sufficiently declared in the discussion of the fiery disposition and the production of the Sun). But truly, where the proportion is best—in the embrace of the agitated and ascending matter and the descending form—there the radiant form is not sufficient to propel the vaporous ascents of matter further down, nor is the ascending matter able to rise higher, since it is hindered by the proportionally descending rays. From this it happens that a dual circular motion is induced in the same body, due to the diverse dispositions of the things concurring in its composition—namely, matter and form. For it is necessary that ethereal bodies move circularly, because of the equal proportion of their parts, which prevents universal motion upward or downward. We have described above the manner in which the prior motion, which we called "rapt," is induced. Here, however, we shall say a few things about the motion opposite to it—namely, from west to east—which we have called the *proper motion of the stellar bodies*. Although it is the office of the "form" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the essential nature or "soul" of a thing, while "matter" is the physical substance.</note> to provide the name and being to the body in which it exists, we nevertheless call the whole thing that moves the "body" and the "mobile." If it moves by itself, it is moved by that intrinsic active principle which we have called "natural motion"—that is, the motion by which any body moves according to the appetite of its own nature. But if it receives motion from an external principle (such as that "rapt" motion), in that case it is not a natural motion, but a motion by accident...

It is certain and proven that in every movable body there is action and resistance; action from the intrinsic moving principle, but passion and resistance from the movable subject. Thus, that body of the Planets, agitated by the rapid motion of the heavens, seems to move backward by resisting; not unlike how, in the discharge of a <term>bombard</term> <note>an early type of cannon</note> loaded with gunpowder, a great weight of matter is seen to move against the motion of the **ignited Spirit**, and due to its resistance against the fiery nature of the powder, it is perceived to move backward; and similarly balls thrown against a wall are known to recoil and move in the opposite direction; through which a great discrepancy between the motion of matter and form is clearly seen. In wheel B. C. D., let there be a wooden ball running here and there upon the circumference of the wheel, moved by the power of small wheels moving on two sides. Similarly, let **A.** in wheel B. C. Thus we see an animal move here and there according to the appetite of its own body by the power of its <term>central essence<note>original: "essentiâ centralis"; the vital or spiritual spark located at the center of a living being that governs its movement and life.</note></term>. And this natural motion of the planet is what <term>Trismegistus<note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure believed to be the author of the Hermetic Corpus, which combined philosophy, alchemy, and magic.</note></term> calls "natural" in his fruitful discourse; but that other motion, by which the stars are rotated from the east, he properly calls not motion but "resistance." For he says that opposition contains the reverberation of motion, and he intended the percussion of a stationary state to be agitation.

From these points, therefore, it can be gathered that it is not difficult for planetary bodies to move against the motion of the first heaven. For insofar as they are physical, they resist contrary actions; and through this resistance of theirs, they are able to produce a contrary motion, even if it is a slower one. Furthermore, the light enclosed within the planets—whose nature is to seek its own natural place—is held back by matter which, because of its own appetite, does not permit that light to ascend higher...

# C H A P T E R XVII.

## *Concerning the opposition of the universal motions of form and matter, and the proportion of these in each heaven, and a most effective demonstration of the position of the true Sun in the middle heaven.*

---

**C**INCE in the previous discourse we demonstrated that formal light, the more it tends downward, the smaller and weaker it becomes, while matter, the more it ascends upward, becomes thinner, more spiritual, and smaller in its proportion; it is certain from this that the formal splendor descends from its source—that is, from the summit of the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest, most spiritual part of the universe, often associated with the presence of God</note>—in the manner of a pyramid or cone from its base, down to the earth, so that its base is contiguous with the concave surface of the Empyrean heaven, while its point (the cone's apex) reaches the earth. For GOD is its root, source, origin, and father. On the other hand, because matter arose from the abyss of darkness, and all darkness is gathered into the terrestrial mass, of which the Devil is the prince, it follows that its motion is contrary to the motion of light. For the base of its pyramid is pressed into the center of the earth, while its point is raised even to the concave surface of the Empyrean heaven.

From this, therefore, arises the composition of each heaven from matter and form; hence the heavens are more formal <note>Possessing more "form" or spiritual essence</note> the more sublime they are, and more subject to matter the lower and closer to the center they are. From this comes the most luminous description of the soul, which is of a middle nature, and an excellent demonstration of its reasoning and composition. From this also follows the position and arrangement of the Sun in the middle of that middle nature; hence its nature is exactly tempered and life-giving, infusing natural heat <term>calidum naturale: the vital heat thought to animate living things</term> and radical moisture <term>humidum radicale: the essential life-sustaining fluid of an organism</term> into the lower things. From this arises the harmonic proportion of the world and the heavens, and indeed the various arrangements of the elements themselves; hence the lives of creatures and the receptacles of those lives—in short, everything brought into action—proceed from this kind of mixture. Even the infinite differences between species arise from the infinity of points emanating from the rays or diameters of these two pyramids.

From this, too, come the orders of angels, in which some are more eminent than others in their administration and rank, and closer to GOD. From this come the various temperaments of the ethereal bodies, and the distinction of the sublunary elements <note>The four elements beneath the moon: earth, water, air, and fire</note>, from whose diverse natures diverse creatures are born, some hotter or colder, others more humid or dry. But in this place, as if in a mirror, an admirable mystery shines forth, which makes it clear that all these things flow from the one and only GOD. For beyond the convexity of the final heaven <note>The outer boundary of the universe</note>, no angle is found except for that one and only one, who is altogether incomprehensible. And because the inner side of the Incomprehensible Triangle has its seat within the convexity of the Empyrean heaven, it is declared by this very fact that GOD communicates Himself to the world, since by His verbal and spiritual essence the heavens were established, along with all their power. And hence two angles of the one triangle are contiguous and, as it were, continuous with the convex surface of the Empyrean heaven; from their rays the light of the world is derived, and by their presence (as uncreated things) its most spiritual matter is already informed and created out of nothing. Thus we say that GOD is present everywhere, that is, His rays are seen as if in a mirror within the Universal Spirit. From this it is clear and manifest that GOD Himself—both beyond the world and insofar as He exists present within the world—is one and three, whose Monad <note>Unity or the Divine One</note> or the head of the triangle descends even to the earth, so that by its presence it might restrain all darkness within the bosom of the earth. And thus, since His triangular form is dispersed through the capacity of the entire machine <note>The "world machine," a common term for the structured cosmos</note>, God is said to be present everywhere—not indeed that He is contained by any place, since He Himself...

# BOOK SEVEN.

## Concerning our Great Instrument.

---

### CHAPTER I.

->*Concerning our instrument and its general construction.*<-

**T**his instrument, recently invented by us, will certainly, if inspected with curious eyes, not only bring utility to listeners but also affect their senses with the greatest delight. I say delight, because we shall demonstrate below that with its help, Music and the symphonic harmony of various parts can be produced without a Musician; so that one may have Music without a musician, or the action of any living creature <note>original: "animalis" - here referring to any biological being, human or otherwise</note>, and therefore without cost and according to the owner's pleasure—which indeed, as it seems to me, is no ordinary thing. It will therefore seem elegant and quite pleasing and wonderful to those feasting, or present at a banquet, to hear unexpected Music in some corner of the dining room <note>original: "triclinii" - the Roman-style dining room</note> without the presence of any moving creature, and to perceive for the greater part of the dinner or lunch a song composed of many symphonic parts, sounding indeed according to the Master's will. So that this may be more easily accomplished, it must be known that three things converge for the structure of such a musical machine: namely, the body of the sounding musical instrument with its necessary ornaments; a moving framework <note>original: "fabrica cursoria" - a sliding or running carriage</note> arranged for striking the strings of the instrument; and a machine constructed of wheels, by whose proportional motion that framework gradually and proportionally descends downward. By its descent, it strikes the strings of the instrument to provoke harmonic sounds by means of quills <note>original: "pennis" - the same term used for the plectra in a harpsichord</note> inserted in its lateral parts, or rails, or ribs; and consequently it produces Music consisting of many parts for as long as that framework moves toward the base of the dining room.

---

### CHAPTER II.

->*Concerning the structure of the sounding body.*<-

**F**or the constitution of such a body, two things are required: namely, its shape and the arrangement of that shape, and the suitable placement of the strings upon it. Regarding the shape of this instrument, it is necessary that it be more conveniently formed from that Geometric figure which they call Triangular, of which all sides must be equal. For descending from the cone <note>the apex</note> of such a figure to the base, as its whole capacity is seen to be fuller and wider until it reaches the base, so also all its strings—extending from a point on one side to another point on the opposite side—the further they are extended from the point of the cone toward the base, it is certain they yield a deeper <note>original: "graviorem"</note> sound; however, the closer they are to the cone, the higher <note>original: "acutiorem"</note> and more excellent the sound. Let this triangular body therefore be skillfully made in such a way that its whole belly is hollow; however, the margins are triangularly formed from boards—

...with iron fittings in a square fashion, yet in such a way that the board to which the strings are fixed is made of fir, so that it yields sweeter and more pleasant sounds. For woodworkers, whose duty it is to make musical instruments, use wood of this kind. Next, from the apex <note>original: "cono" (cone/point)</note> toward the base, let the two opposite sides be divided into 40 or more parts, in such a way that any part of one side, at a proportional distance from the apex, corresponds to the part on the opposite side at an equal proportional distance from the apex. 

Afterward, let brass strings of one and the same dimension be fastened upon the point of division of each side; these must be stretched to the points on the opposite side and there fixed with some iron peg <note>original: "clave" (key/peg)</note> in such a way that they can be tightened or loosened to the true pitch <note>original: "altitudinem vel depressionem" (height or depth)</note> of the <term>monochord|A single-stringed instrument used to measure musical intervals, here used as a reference for tuning</term>, according to the proportions of the musical system. 

Then, next to each iron peg, the <term>keys of the system|The letters representing musical notes in the hexachord system</term> are to be marked, beginning from *Γ* <note>The Greek letter Gamma, representing the lowest note of the medieval/Renaissance scale</note>, which will be the name of the lower string toward the base. Or, if you wish to use the *Diapason* <note>original: "Diapason" (the octave scale)</note>, as is customary nowadays, you may go up to *C. fa*; then *C. fa* will be the first string, *D. la* the second, *E. mi* the third, *F. fa, ut* the fourth, *Γ. ut* the fifth, *A. re* the sixth, *B. mi* the seventh, and so on for the rest, up to *ggg*. 

And because both <term>B-flat|b moll</term> as well as <term>B-natural|♮ quadratum (square B)</term> occur very frequently in many musical compositions, strings must also be provided for them in the proper places on the monochord. Thus, in *A re* a B-flat sometimes occurs; in *B. mi* it occurs frequently; in *D. sol, re* sometimes; and often even in *E la, mi*. Similarly, the "square" B-natural is sometimes found in *F. fa, ut*, and likewise in the rest of the higher registers—namely the high and ultra-high <note>original: "acutorum & peracutorum"</note>—to which these low keys correspond in the octave. 

In this way, you will have the brass and copper strings stretched over this instrument of ours, corresponding to each key of the system, whether in the "soft" or "hard" <note>Referring to the 'mollis' (flat) and 'durus' (natural/sharp) hexachords of traditional music theory</note> positions. It still remains for us to manufacture the locations, or slotted holes, in whose joints two manufactured sliding belts <note>original: "cursoriæ Zonæ"</note> can be inserted, so that they may move evenly and steadily. Therefore, let a radius or diameter be drawn from the apex of the triangle to the middle of the base. Where the ends of the radii touch, oblong holes are to be manufactured there, which we have designated by the two large letters A and B.

This body of the instrument, now sufficiently well prepared and arranged for emitting harmonious sounds, must be positioned in the manner of a horizontal sundial <note>original: "horologii Horizontalis"</note>, so that no part of the triangle inclines more upward or downward; rather, according to the flatness of its base, it must be firmly attached to the wall of the hall <note>original: "triclinii" (dining room or formal hall)</note>, namely in such a way that it stands at exactly half the height of the hall. 

For in this way, the sliding mechanism constructed at half the height of the hall will have a sufficiently suitable proportion and target so that it may descend beneath the machine along its entire length; thus, it may perform its full duty in its descent, as we shall declare more broadly below. We have attached here the figure of this body or instrument with all its necessary ornaments.

## CHAPTER III.

### *On the construction of the sliding mechanism.*

**I**n order to bring this musical arrangement, described in the aforementioned Triangle <note>The "Triangle" refers to the geometric diagram used to calculate string lengths and musical proportions.</note>, into harmonic action, it is necessary to also devise some instrument by whose motion these strings—ordered according to the proportions of the musical system—may produce perceptible and concordant sounds. To do this more conveniently, a certain parallelogram-shaped surface should be formed from a solid wood; that is, it should have shorter ends and sides that extend to an equal, but much greater, length. Let the ends be of the exact size as the radius or diameter of the triangular instrument, so that they extend along their length from the end of the joint or slit <term>A</term> <note>original: "fissuræ"</note> of the same, to the end of the slit of the long aperture opposite to it <term>B</term>, so that the radius of the Triangle <term>A. ### TREATISE II. PART II. BOOK VII.

...[the width] of the structure itself; but the length of its longer sides will be half the width of the chamber <note>original: "triclinij"; referring here to the frame or "bed" of the instrument where the mechanism sits</note>. They shall be crafted in such a way that they can be very easily inserted into cracks or oblong holes, so that they can slide up and down through those narrow spaces regularly and without any tilting to one side. Let the thickness of these sides, or rather the width, be three or four inches, so that it has a hollow center within. Next, let the outer sides be divided from that point where they join the end of the longer sides into as many equal parts as half the number of strings; and at the point of each division on both opposite sides, let a small slit or oblong hole be made, so that the thickness of some sufficiently thin wooden rule <term>rule: a flat strip of wood used as a slide to trigger notes</term> can enter and exit as the craftsman pleases.

Then, wooden rules are to be prepared, equal in their length to the whole machine, in thickness to one quarter of an inch, and in width to nearly one inch; and let their material be well-dried and not green, lest they later warp in drier air; for they must be very straight, equal in length, and polished. Their number shall be according to half the number of strings, as has been said, and their length must be exactly equal.

Afterwards, let them be prepared in this way: First, let them be divided into 40 equal parts, and let each of those parts represent that musical proportion of time which they call a **Breve** <note>a note value in early music, usually the longest standard duration</note>. Next, let each part be subdivided into two equal parts, and let each of them represent a musical **semibreve**. And again, let each portion of those subdivided parts be subdivided, and let these subdivided parts represent a **Minim**—that is, half the quantity of a Semibreve—which, if subdivided again, will produce a **Semiminim** or "black" note. And any of these parts, subdivided again, will produce two **Fusas** <note>equivalent to an eighth note</note>; and finally, each of those subdivided will constitute **Semifusas** <note>equivalent to a sixteenth note</note>.

But these rules are not yet sufficiently prepared to produce the desired effects; wherefore in the center of each division, very small cavities or slits must be carved out, into which small plectra <term>plectra: small plucking mechanisms, similar to those found in a harpsichord</term> can be inserted and pushed, and held there quite firmly; which plectra can be most suitably made from quills, because these are more fit to be bent, to give way to the resisting strings, and afterwards to return to their original straightness. Therefore, let quills of this kind be cut and formed in the shape of a small Triangle, so that the part of each converging more toward the point of the Triangle may pluck more easily, give way to the string, and in its retreat lightly strike the strings, and having done so, return to the original form of a single beat. The length of the Triangle should be about one-quarter of an inch; in its tail or base, a small quadrangle is to be left of the same size as that part of the Triangle which must be inserted into the slit. And here it must also be observed that the dimension of almost every Triangle must always be the same; that is, so that one in no way exceeds another, lest the plucking be stronger on one string and weaker on another; for the same form of plucking must always be maintained.

The triangular shapes of the quills, which we call striking plectra <term>plectra: the plucking mechanisms of a stringed instrument, similar to the jacks in a harpsichord</term>, have been explained by us in this manner:

---

<note>Illustration: Six triangular quills arranged in two rows, used for plucking strings in a mechanical musical instrument.</note>

There are also certain plectra to be prepared which must have a woolen cloth at the end, by which the strings may be hindered <note>original: impediantur; meaning the strings are dampened to prevent unwanted vibration</note> so that they do not sound beyond the established limit; for otherwise it would happen that discordant sounds would be heard along with the concordant ones, and in that way the entire harmony would be defiled. For this reason, we call these *plectra of silence and mute voices*; their shape, indeed, is as follows:

---

<note>Illustration: Four plectra equipped with wool or cloth pads at the tips, designed to dampen the strings.</note>

---

Therefore, from the arrangement of the aforementioned ribs or rules <note>original: costarum seu regularum; these are the mechanical bars or levers that hold the quills</note> contained within the belly of the parallelogram <note>the rectangular soundbox or frame of the device</note>, it is clear that only one of those rules will correspond to two of the instrument's strings. This is so that the aforementioned temporal divisions <note>the rhythmic markings on the mechanism</note> must be expressed across the width of both, and consequently those quilled plectra, following the division of the side of that same rule, will strike the string closest to them on either side. By this method, the same rule can produce a double sound at the same moment. From this, it is manifest that ribs or rules of this kind ought to be enclosed and inserted into the said triangular slits according to their thickness, and not according to their width; specifically, so that the width of that rib or rule faces the larger sides of the parallelogram on both the right and the left.

It must also be observed here that the same rule or rib usually denotes a double key of the system <note>original: systematis clavem; referring to the musical scale or gamut</note>; so that Gamma-ut and A-re <note>the two lowest notes of the traditional musical scale used in the 17th century</note> can resonate with its help through movement; and likewise for the rest, just as is shown in the preceding drawing of the structure.

Regarding the simple bodies of the elements, we have dealt with them quite abundantly in the preceding sections. And this is what the Philosophers seem to suggest when they assert that in intellectual beings, **fire** predominates; in sensitive beings, fire is equal to **air**; in vegetative beings, **water** is weighed in equal scales with air—though in these, the dignity of the air is diminished because of the cold disposition of the water. Finally, they maintain that minerals are composed mostly of **earth and water**. From this, it is manifest that in humans, that celestial fire prevails more insofar as they are intellectual; next in other sensitive beings, insofar as air and fire predominate in them; then, at a still lower degree, in vegetative things, insofar as their airy parts are tempered by the coldness of water; and finally, the smallest portion of the "lucid form" <note>the spark of divine or celestial light</note> is found in minerals, because earth and water hold dominion in them, and consequently, they admit a smaller portion of fire into their composition.

### CHAPTER VI.

->*On the manner of arranging the Bass melody of any Symphony for this instrument.*<-

**I**t should be understood that those ribs or rules of the sliding mechanism <note>the *fabrica cursoria*, a device for mechanical music composition or performance</note> are to be removed and pulled out from the slots at its ends at the Artist's pleasure. Therefore, when you wish to arrange a Bass melody according to this order, pull out five of its sides from that machine starting from Gamma [Γ] <note>Gamma refers to the lowest note of the traditional musical scale, the G at the bottom of the bass clef</note>. Or, if any note of the Bass falls below Gamma, a sixth rule should also be taken, namely F, *fa ut*. Then, the first note must be sought in the Bass melody, observing specifically in which space or on which line it is placed. On the rule corresponding to that place, toward its lowest end—which is the starting point <note>original: *terminus a quo*</note>—one must insert a triangular plectrum <term>plectrum: a small peg or pick used here to trigger a sound</term> at the first point of the starting end, according to the division or proportion that matches the duration of the note. And where the duration <note>original: *quantitas*</note> of that note ends on the rule, a "plectrum of silence" <note>original: *plectrum taciturnitatis*</note> made of woolen cloth must be fixed there, so that the string does not sound longer than is proper or beyond the duration of its note—unless two or three notes follow consecutively in the same place on the system (that is, in the same space or on the same line), in which case the "silent" or "mute" plectrum must be inserted at the end of the duration of the last note. Afterward, the second note of the same melody should be sought, and its place among the five rules and their positions should be carefully searched out. Once found, count a length on the rule from its lower end such that the space of the first note is omitted; at the end of the previous space, the second sounding plectrum should be applied to play the duration of the second note. At the end of this duration, a plectrum of silence must also be applied for the reason stated before, unless other Bass notes immediately follow in the same place. From here, one must proceed to the third note and also seek its key <term>clavis: here referring to the pitch or "clef" position</term> among the aforementioned rules. Once found, at the end of the boundaries of the durations of the two preceding notes, a third sounding plectrum expressing the note's duration should be fixed, and again, at the end of its time, a plectrum of silence should be deployed. And in this manner, one must proceed with all the other notes of the Bass melody until you have adapted the entire Bass song through the plectra of that rule.

For example, in the demonstration below, I find that the first Bass note is placed on the first line, where the key Gamma [Γ] holds its place. I see also that this note is a Semibreve <term>Semibreve: a musical note value, roughly equivalent to a whole note</term>. I therefore look for that rule among the five extracted from the machine, on one side of which Gamma [Γ] is expressed, and on the other, A *re* <note>Kircher uses the Guidonian solfège syllables to identify pitches; A *re* is the pitch A</note>. At the beginning of this, starting from the lower end toward the upper, I fix a triangular plectrum. Since I perceive the note to have the value of a Semibreve, I measure from the position of the plectrum to half of a Breve <term>Breve: a long note value; a semibreve is half of its length</term>. For the duration of a Semibreve extends from that starting point to the division made at the midpoint of the first Breve. Therefore, at that midpoint, a plectrum of silence must be inserted so that the sound of the string Gamma *ut* is blocked from sounding further. Next, we find the second note of the Bass is placed on that Bass line which D *sol re* <note>the pitch D</note> claims for itself. Therefore, the rule must be sought among those five pulled out, on one side of which D *sol re* is found, and on the other, E *la mi*. And since the space of one semibreve, counting from the beginning, was previously assigned to the first note, I therefore omit the first space signifying a Semibreve, and at its end, I apply a sounding plectrum. # CONCERNING OUR GREAT INSTRUMENT.

Since this second part is only half of a <term>Semibreve<note>A musical note value; in the hierarchy of this period, it is half of a Breve.</note></term>, namely a <term>minim<note>A shorter note value, half the duration of a Semibreve.</note></term>, therefore only half of the space between the end of the <term>Breve<note>The "Brevis" was the primary unit of time measurement in early music notation.</note></term> and that of the preceding Semibreve is to be taken; it will thus occupy a fourth part of the space of one Breve. In this manner, three quarters of the first Breve are completed and occupied. Therefore, at the end of that fourth part of the Breve, which is the limit of the Minim, the <term>pin of silence<note>original: "plectrum taciturnitatis." This likely refers to a mechanical component or dampener that stops the note from sounding.</note></term> must be placed.

I find the third note of the Bass on the second line of its <term>staff<note>original: "systematis."</note></term>, where <term>B natural<note>original: "B. mi." In the hexachord system, "mi" indicates a natural note.</note></term> is found. I therefore seek the slider in which B natural is marked; and in its space, after the Semibreve and Minim, I fix a pin on that side where B natural is found. And because this note is also a Minim, its quantity completes the last quarter of the Breve and runs through it; wherefore, at the final point of that fourth part of the Breve, or at the end of that Minim (which is the third note of the Bass), a pin of silence or a <term>mute pin<note>original: "plectrum mutum."</note></term> is to be fixed. Afterward, I find the fourth note of the Bass on that line of the Bass staff where the <term>F clef<note>original: "clavis F. faut."</note></term> is expressed. I therefore seek the F slider and set aside the space of one Breve, which was given to the preceding notes. At the end of the previous Breve, I place a <term>striking pin<note>original: "plectrum pulsans." The component that actually triggers the sound.</note></term>. And, because the quantity of that note is half of the second Breve, if another note did not immediately follow on the same line, a mute pin or pin of silence would be inserted there. But a minim is found on the same line very close to it; therefore, where the mute pin should have been expressed, a striking pin must be placed. And because its quantity is only a minim, it extends itself from the midpoint of the second [part] to the end of its third part; and, because another quantitative note does not follow immediately on the same line, therefore at the end of that third part, the pin of silence must be applied. And in this way, one must proceed with all the following notes expressed in the Bass part written below.

# ON OUR GREAT INSTRUMENT

## C H A P. IX.

### *Regarding the translation of the upper song, or Treble <note>original: "Discanti"</note>, for the use of our moving mechanism.*

**F**ive rules must also be drawn from the mechanism to transfer the sounds of this part of the melody to the harmony of the machine; namely: E <note>E-la-mi</note> with F <note>F-fa-ut</note>; G <note>G-sol-re-ut</note> with double-a <note>aa-la-mi-re</note>; b-flat <note>bb-fa</note> and b-natural <note>♮-mi</note> with double-c <note>cc-sol-fa-ut</note>; d <note>la-sol-re</note> with double-e <note>ee-la-mi-re</note>; and f <note>f-fa-ut</note> with double-g <note>gg-sol-re-ut</note>. Regarding the use of the pins <note>original: "plectrorum" - the pegs or strikers on a mechanical cylinder</note>, whether they are sounding or silent, it must be understood that the same logic applies to them as to the Bass and Tenor parts of the song. Consequently, we shall not provide a more lengthy discourse on adapting any particular melody to the mechanism and our instrument, since all of this can be very easily understood and observed through diligent and studious investigation.

---

## C H A P. X.

### *That many other musical instruments can sound according to the movement of this great instrument.*

**W**e can also adapt other wind instruments—those that create musical harmony through airflow—to this great instrument of ours in such a way that the dimensions of the mechanism itself become the moving cause of their sounds. The cause of the airflow can be the descent of the mechanism itself, whereby some protrusion or attachment sticking out from its solid side can depress the upper part of a well-fitted bellows <note>original: "follis"</note>; this part of the bellows can then be raised back up by the power of a counterweight after the protrusion has passed. When a second bump on the side arrives, it is depressed again. In this manner, through the entire passage of the mechanism, those artificial bellows will be seen to emit their breaths. Consequently, by the power of the pins <note>original: "plectrorum"</note> fitted into the thickness of the ribs or rules, the keys <note>valves</note> that block the openings of the pipes <note>original: "fistularum"</note> can be lifted away from the pipe orifices. This allows the breath of the bellows to penetrate into their throats, pouring forth or exciting various symphonic sounds that harmonize with the song of the larger instrument. Similarly, small bells <note>original: "tintinnabula"</note> can resonate harmonically with the song of this instrument by means of pins attached to the outer side of the mechanism, both those that strike and those that remain silent. 

Studious people and those eager for new inventions will easily be able to add infinite other things to this invention of ours. Indeed, I would even dare to assert that I could accommodate to this instrument's movement not only the music of the Lute <note>original: "Barbiti"</note> itself, but also the parts for the Viol, Cittern <note>original: "Sistrenæ"</note>, Pandora <note>a wire-stringed bass instrument</note>, and other instruments of this kind, so that they might sound in symphony with this device of ours. However, since explaining all these things in this place would go against our purpose and plan, we shall intentionally omit them and restrict ourselves to the simple

->quality of this, our<-
->instrument.<-

...from this smallness, perhaps, sickness and a disturbance of the body occurs. So that a proportion of each of the aforementioned qualities may be maintained in weight, or at least in justice, a double **nourishment** <term>nutrimentum; the substance required to sustain a living being</term> is required for the preservation of the whole composition: namely, *spiritual or ethereal, and corporeal or elementary.* That *spiritual* food enters the body either by means of a thin and invisible body—namely, the air—or by means of a thick and visible body, such as that common nourishment of animals and vegetables. This invisible food keeps within itself a certain portion of solar light and ethereal spirit, by which the vital spirits lurking in the animal’s arterial veins are wonderfully and at every moment refreshed. Therefore, this kind of food—the air—is drawn during respiration into the innermost chamber of the heart; its more essential parts are received for the refreshing of the vital spirits, while the rest, being as it were waste and superfluous—namely, the more watery substance of the air—is exhaled. 

In its visible and corporeal food as well, which is usually either animal or vegetable, two subjects are found, each fit to feed one of the two balances [spiritual or physical]. One of these is of the nature of the heavens, which is called the essential or ethereal part of the nourishing thing—namely, the **radical moisture** <note>The "humidum radicale," or the vital fluid believed to sustain life and host the "innate heat."</note> with its **innate heat**. The other is of the nature of the elements, namely its more corporeal part, from which a portion of the element of fire is drawn and separated for the proper nourishment of the **choleric humor** <note>One of the four bodily fluids or "humors" in ancient medicine, associated with fire and a hot, dry temperament.</note> in the thing being fed. Similarly, the substance of the element of air feeds the animal’s blood; the element of water, by its addition, preserves the substance of the **natural phlegm**; and finally, the coarser parts of the food strengthen the **melancholy**. 

Since the composition of the whole animal body is made from these elements, it is necessary that its more solid parts be extracted from the more subtle parts of the body's nourishment to preserve it in the state and vigor of a natural and well-disposed body. Meanwhile, the coarser and more dreg-like portion, being useless, is expelled either through the bowels or through the urine. Hence it is that from a lack of this elemental food, the animal body withers; indeed, it is rendered weak and, with its strength utterly cast down, falls into **wasting** <note>original: *tabes*; a general term for a consumption or localized decay of the body.</note>, just as happens to those who are pressed by the sharpest hunger. 

From these things, therefore, it becomes clear that the old axiom of the Philosophers is most true: *Namely, that like rejoices in like, and that nature is not improved except in its own proper nature.* <note>original: "Similia nempe similibus gaudere & naturā non emendari, niſi in natura ſua propria."</note> Finally, we conclude that if the matter of a creature is purer and more subtle than that of vegetables, and the essential light more powerful, a work is produced that is far more beautiful and noble than the vegetable—one which is called an "animal," in which air and fire work wonderfully. We shall treat the virtues of specific animals, both hidden and manifest, in Volume 2, Treatise 4.

***

# C H A P T E R VII.
## From where does the difference of species arise, and why are some hotter, colder, wetter, or drier than others?

It is certain that the universal difference of all things flows, without a doubt, from their souls or essential forms, which we have called above "substantial sparks of light" enclosed within the spirit. This is because matter, by itself, is only in a state of potentiality; it is not brought into actual being unless it is informed by light. Some Philosophers call these forms **Influences** <term>Influentias; the celestial forces or "flowings" believed to shape terrestrial matter</term>, which descend through the element of earth even to its center in such varied ways and for such diverse reasons that they produce different generations in the bowels of the earth through different impressions. 

This luminous soul, I say, does everything; without it, no action is found in the body. It draws fire out of the creature’s earth, and out of the water it draws that light and windy spirit which we call air. Thus, if there is a great quantity of earth in a creature and very little water, mixed with a strong portion of essential heat, then the element of fire will show itself in that composition and will have dominion. But if the heat in the aforementioned measure of earth is small, and there is little water, the earth will have...

dominion: on the contrary also, if a sufficiently powerful operating heat is found acting upon a small quantity of earth and a larger quantity of water, the composition will be raw and watery; but if in that same composition the heat is found to be even stronger and more powerful, the compound will be drier, and a <term>fatty body</term><note>Latin: "corpus pingue." In 17th-century science, this refers to oily, flammable, or sulfurous substances.</note> will arise from such a mixture. Wherefore, when the **soul** descends upon such matter, clothed in a **spiritual garment** most familiar to the ether—without whose dryness that soul and the composite body would never agree, be familiar, or be joined to one another—it moves that matter by its own most tempered heat. It alters it in various and diverse ways, producing the various habits and species of things according to the greater or lesser proportion of that same light, differing according to the **obedience** of the material subject into which it enters.

For a multitude of <term>Form</term><note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "Form" is the organizing principle that makes a thing what it is (e.g., the "soul" of a plant).</note> brings greater perfection, activity, subtlety, and purity to the body, provided the matter is well-prepared to receive it; and in this manner, **vegetables and animals** are born. But if the body be rebellious, coarse, and disobedient to the quantity of its form, in that case the vigor of the soul is hindered in its actions, and it produces a **mineral species**. 

Furthermore, where any individual species has its own distinction within the three-fold division of things mentioned above—as in the animal kingdom, **man from the lion**, and the **lion from the bear**, and the bear again from the **shrew**; in the vegetable species, the **oak from the hazel**, and the **hazel from the bilberry**, and **vervain from betony**, and **sage from thyme** and the rest; and in the mineral, **gold from lead**, **lead from antimony**, and so on—this occurs because of the infinite proportions and degrees by which matter differs from its form. For in some, the form is exalted in such a degree in one creature over that of another because of the obedience of that material nature, and the disobedience of this one. 

The disobedience of a species can happen in two ways: namely, where that enclosed **essential light** is so very small that, although the matter is sufficiently rare, thin, and workable, its form is not powerful enough to govern it and promote it toward the goal of perfection. Thus, **phlegmatic and melancholic creatures** move more slowly than **sanguine or choleric** ones; thus **houseleek** and **hemlock** reach maturity more slowly than warmer vegetables. Alternatively, it happens where the matter is extremely disobedient, thick, hard, and not at all porous, binding its soul—even if that soul is not small in quantity—as if with **chains**, and entirely hindering and prohibiting its power and the actions of its vigor. 

We conclude, therefore, that the softer and more obedient the substance of the body is, the more the invisible light enclosed within it proportionally renders its composition more noble. Moreover, just as the proportion of any material thing was to its form in the first creation, so also its generation from the beginning of the world to its end continues in the same proportion of mixture and under the same species by the divine will of the Creator; for **sparks of light** are continually rained down from above.

### C H A P T E R VIII.

->What is artificial or common fire? How does it participate in celestial fire?<-

That this lower fire of ours, which we call **common and artificial**, derives its origin from that celestial light, is proved both by the reasons of the ancient Philosophers and by their very examples. We do not hesitate to most easily confirm their opinions while we also strenuously pursue our own intention. For that **immense, uncreated light**, the head of the world, created the **primary light**, from whose super-celestial source rays are sent down into that solar body and the other stars. For the splendor of the **Empyrean heaven** undoubtedly communicates continually with these bodies, from which shining rays are infused into this artificial fire of ours. From this it is manifest that this fire has not only a participation with the super-celestial light, but also a certain likeness and presence of the uncreated light itself, since to the Ca—

...evil spirits <note>original: "codæmones"</note> are weakened and put to flight by the approach of fire, just as good spirits are refreshed and made stronger by the sight of it. For this reason, the ancients placed lit candles

and lamps next to the bodies of the dead and did not allow them to be removed until the sacred purifications were finished and the bodies were placed in tombs. This was done, namely, to drive away the **light-fleers** <note>original: "Lucifugos," spirits that avoid the light</note> and evil spirits serving **evil magicians** <note>original: "Cacomagis"</note>, or to block their approach, as is found in *Apuleius’s Golden Ass*. Similarly, the Vestal Priests, according to Roman rites, always had burning fires next to their altars. Finally, the true worshipers of GOD, as found in the sacred scriptures, are commanded according to the old law of GOD to offer sacrifices with fire, and that the fire should burn continually upon the altar; indeed, even to this day, among the followers of the Christian Roman religion, carefully observing that **anagram of Pythagoras** <note>likely referring to a symbolic or geometric representation of the divine flame</note>, it is perceived to burn unceasingly in the temples. But what this burning light is, which they call common and artificial fire, or how it acts destructively upon the subject it occupies, we shall briefly declare here. *Pythagoras* posited only a single fire penetrating all things, which *Pliny* called a great portion of natural things; we have called this the "essential light." But this fire is found to be stronger or weaker in its action within any subject according to the greater or lesser resistance to its actions. Thus, in the **Empyrean heaven** <note>the highest, most spiritual part of the universe</note>, because of the thinness of the substance of that place and its slight resistance, it is immensely dilated, and it warms most mildly and sweetly, being exalted in the highest degree of spirituality and perfection because it is freer there. In the middle heaven, because of the thicker consistency of the ethereal parts, it is more intense and hotter, because the composition of that body more greatly resists the actions of the **super-celestial fire** sent downward; yet it does not heat in such a way as to lead to the ruin and destruction of a creature. Rather, because of the moderation of its temperature, it is constantly occupied with the conservation and multiplication of those lower creatures. However, the more this fire verges downward and hastens toward the center, the more its operative power is resisted, and its rays are narrowed and compressed due to the corpulence of the substance of the lowest heaven, which grows thicker step by step toward the center. Being compressed, they act more violently, since a **united force is stronger** <note>original: "vis unita fortior"</note>. Thus we also see that in the narrower channel of a river or torrent, the waters move more swiftly and fiercely. And it is from this that among *Theologians*, that infernal and cursed fire is said to be—due to the excessive narrowing of the descending rays and the compression and condensation of the substance of the descending light—destructive beyond all imagination, burning with immense pain and horror, torturing with a suffering that will never cease. Because of the narrowing of the cursed matter containing it, it is said to be marvelously dark, horrendous, and gloomy. Indeed, the intermediate fire participates both in that heavenly fire and also in that of hell, according to the disposition of the thicker parts of the lowest heaven which it occupies. From this it happens that the fire of this lower heaven both conserves and causes things to sprout, but in different ways. From these things, it is certain that the one fire extending itself through all things—since in itself it is hidden and unknown, as *Dionysius* maintains—differs in its operation and reveals itself more or less according to the disposition of the intervening matter it occupies. For it is by the resistance of this matter that the nature of fire is manifested as both conservative and destructive. Indeed, it breaks apart **heterogeneous things** <note>things of a different nature or kind</note> and those differing from the nature of its own <term>radical moisture</term> <note>the fundamental fluid believed to sustain life and vitality</note>, so that it may find its true food and, as it were, its nourishment; not otherwise than animals seeking the central substance of a nut pull apart its shells and skins so that they may choose the marrow for their food, by which they are nourished. Therefore, just as that heavenly light, clothed in a "windy body" called air and spirit, is not only moved by its own heat and performs its operations, but also requires the pure and thin fatness of the ether for its food (for nothing can subsist without nourishment), so the innumerable rays of light or heavenly fire, as if for the sake of hunting, [reach] into the lowest region of the world...
