### Definitions

*Hypotenuse line* <note>original: Linea Hypothenusa</note> is that which is not raised perpendicularly from the point of the base, and is always found in a triangular figure.

*Perpendicular line* <note>original: Linea perpendicularis</note> is a line raised above the base at right angles; hence it is called "orthogonal" <note>meaning 'forming a right angle'</note>. It is also called the *cathetus* <term>cathetus<note>In geometry, a cathetus is a side of a right-angled triangle that is adjacent to the right angle; essentially, the height or the base when the other is the vertical.</note></term>.

# ON THE THEORETICAL PART OF GEOMETRY

A <term>diameter</term> <note>from the Latin 'diametrus'</note> is a line that, by attaching its endpoints to the edges of a figure, divides it into two equal parts. For this reason, it is called a <term>diameter</term> from <gloss>dia</gloss> <note>original: διὰ</note>, which means "through," and <gloss>metron</gloss> <note>original: μέτρον</note>, "measure," because it measures through the middle. This line is called a <term>diameter</term> when found in a square, a parallelogram, or a circle; in a sphere, it is called the <term>axis</term>; but in polygons, it is called the <term>diagonal</term>, so named as if it were touching two angles.

It should be noted, however, that every *hypotenuse* <note>the longest side of a right-angled triangle</note> is the actual <term>diameter</term> of an implied or imaginary parallelogram.

Points a. and b., therefore, with respect to Triangle a. b. c., are called the *hypotenuse*; with respect to square a. b. c. d., they are called the *diameter*.

*Proportion* is a certain relationship between two dimensions of the same kind according to their quantity.

### Proposition V.

*Every <term>parallelogram</term> <note>a four-sided figure with opposite sides parallel</note> is found to be larger or smaller according to the length of its <term>diameter</term> <note>original: "Diametri"; in this context, it refers to the diagonal line crossing the shape</note>.* For in the following demonstration, since every right-angled triangle (by the preceding proposition) is half of a parallelogram, it is necessary that its other part be conceptually considered, by which the square surface is completed. We say, therefore, that by the increasing of the diameter, the dimension of the parallelogram is increased, and consequently the <term>area</term> of the triangle, which is the half-part of the parallelogram.

The parallelogram *a. b. c. d.* is therefore smaller than the one labeled *a. b. e. f.*, and that one is smaller than the square *a. b. e. g. & h.*

### CHAPTER IV.
-> *On the generation of clouds.* <-

<insert>P</insert>ERIPATETICS <term>Peripatetics: Followers of the philosophy of Aristotle, who typically taught that physical phenomena resulted from the movement of the four elements.</term> define a *cloud as a vapor, raised from the earth into the middle region of the air; there it is constricted by the force of cold and, as if frozen, is driven and agitated here and there by the various motions of the winds.* But because the reality of this Meteor's generation is far different, I shall explain it first by experiment, and then by sufficiently clear philosophical reasons. While I was traveling from Venice toward Augsburg in Germany through the Alpine mountains, I perceived a very thin mist appearing at the summit of a certain rock of immense height, which the solar rays were striking forcefully. By thickening more and more, it was finally reduced into a very dense cloud clinging only to the front peak of the mountain; yet I saw the other parts of the rock free from the cloud and shining with solar rays. I noticed, therefore, that the cause of this kind of Meteor arose from the wind blowing strongly against that side of the rock or mountain peak. By its blast, the wind drove the thinner air before it and compressed it against the rock (which held back the escaping air due to the rock's hardness) in such a way that it always placed the succeeding parts of air against those preceding them. Due to the resistance of the mountain, it gradually condensed them into the consistency of a cloud; immediately, the solar rays striking the peak of the rock dissolved it into drops, bringing on rain. mountains or rocks are not found at all: to which it must be replied that the condensation of air is produced by a similar compression, albeit by different instrumental means. For two opposing winds blowing at the same time—even if one is stronger than the other due to its dominance in the air—regularly compress and condense the thinner air and turn it into rain, according to the nature of the wind or the exhalation. Both of these winds, if they act and resist each other more forcefully, produce a sound in the air similar to two rivers violently falling into the same bay or abyss with contrary motion.

I remember also when I was on a ship plowing the sea with sails spread, making my way and journey toward England with a stronger wind blowing; as it blew more weakly by turns, I observed a wind opposite to it and adverse to our journey driving the sails backward, until that wind which was favorable to us, by overcoming the strength of the other opposing one, finally carried us happily into England. Meanwhile, however, various clouds were gathered and resolved into rain. Finally, if we bring forward more evident philosophical reasons, *we will perceive that those arguments of the Peripatetics <note>original: "Peripateticorum"; these are the followers of Aristotle, whose traditional views on physics the author is challenging</note> demonstrating the generation of clouds are to be considered as nothing; for if the origin of a cloud were from the attraction of vapors into the highest region of the air, it would follow that clouds would be more frequent in the summer time than in the winter:* both because in summer the Sun, with its more direct rays, more easily attracts vapors upward, and also because in the warmer time, the terrestrial pores <note>small openings in the earth's surface</note> which vomit forth such vapors allow the fumes to exit without any impediment of cold obstructing the way. Indeed, we see that the air in summer time is very thick because of the constant vapors rising from the earth and water; in fact, ponds, springs, and rivers are either entirely or for a large part converted into the substance of air through thinning; just as in winter, they are filled again by thickening, when the coarser part of the air is condensed by the power of cold, and the air is converted first into clouds, and then into rain. Hence ponds, springs, and rivers are refilled in the winter time by the change of air into water and rise up as a torrent: and from this, the entire surface of the earth, dried in summer, is rendered moist and slippery in winter.

From these things it is evident that it is not vapor immediately elevated <margin>§</margin> into the middle region of the air, but the condensed air itself that is the cause and origin of the substance of a cloud, and that clouds are produced more in winter than in summer, both because of the contrary blowing of opposing winds, and because the blasts of the northern winds <note>original: "ventorum borealium"</note>, whose nature is to freeze, are more frequent; although it may not always be named as such, perhaps because of the more evident blasts of an opposing wind; and finally, because the air is prepared and fit for such impressions, and the nature of the middle region of the air, because of the absence or more remote distance of the Sun, is well-disposed to freeze the parts of the thick air and sustain them in the manner of ice, until they are dissolved into drops by the power of the stellar rays. *If, therefore, vapors are elevated during the daytime, experience constantly teaches us that they produce mists after sunset and not clouds.*

Finally, various effects are produced in the generation of clouds from the blowing of the winds; for where the *South Wind* <note>original: "Auster", the warm, moist wind</note> predominates, yet with the *North Wind* <note>original: "Borea", the cold, dry wind</note> blowing secretly, clouds are resolved into rain because of the freezing disposition of the one, with cold and dryness acting upon the substance of the cloud, and the dissolving quality of the other, which by its warm nature destroys the freezing works of its opposite. But where the *North Wind* has dominion, the cloud cannot be entirely dissolved by the *South Wind* blowing imperceptibly, but is turned into snow or hail; but if the *South Wind* is still stronger, it generates part snow and part rain. The Western wind, however, for the most part produces warmer and drier clouds, which are accustomed to sustain the solar rays and those of the other stars without the dissolution of their parts; hence they appear bright and serene: *where, however, a single and simple wind blows, or at least finds a transverse wind that is very weakly contrary to it, there for the most part the air is found without clouds.* If this is not enough for the wise man, what is to be thought of a cloud carrying lightning in its bowels, which, appearing at the furthest edge of the Horizon, is perceived to move against the motion of the wind?

We can also draw out many hidden truths from the nature of this instrument by carefully considering the proportion of its low and high sounds. For string *A. B.*, at the same size and length, would sound in the thinnest spirit of the upper heaven just as string *C. D.* would in the middle airy region of the lower world; that is, string *A. B.* would produce a sound as high and excellent as that of *C. D.* The reason, however, why string *A. B.* sounds so low in this airy medium is because the medium is too thick and drowns out the clarity of the sound, and the **moving soul** <term>moving soul (Latin: *anima movens*); the spiritual force that initiates motion or sound</term> is found to be too weak to refine that thick matter. Note, therefore, that the soul of sounds in a string proceeds from the action of the one playing it; the medium, however, through whose dimensions the sound is produced, is the substance of the air itself, receiving the modulations of the soul through vibration. For the same string, when stretched or loosened, gives off various voices, no differently than is seen in the human voice, which produces various notes when raised through the same **windpipe** <note>original: "trachea arteria"</note>. Air is therefore the medium, and as it were the instrument, in which Music is made; hence, just as a very small instrument usually produces higher voices and a large one lower voices, so also thinned and refined air produces more refined sounds; and conversely, thick air produces lower sounds. <insert>It is not the string, therefore, but its soul—sent into the medium or instrument by the vibration of the string—that produces the sounds; nor does the principal power of sounds reside in the windpipe, but in the **vital soul** <term>the life-force that animates the body</term> pushing against the surrounding air.</insert>

Indeed, just as a thicker medium breaks and hinders the rays of sight the thicker it is (as can be seen in foggy and cloudy air), while in a clearer and thinner medium the effects of sight are sharper and more certain; so also a thick medium offers lower sounds to the hearing, and more rarely higher ones, so much so that the thinner the medium, the more excellent the sounds produced. Furthermore, we see that when the soul of the player mixes itself with the string by striking it vigorously, the string itself produces harder and more intense sounds by a stronger vibration; but where that soul presses the string more weakly, there it forces the string to emit a lower voice with a more relaxed vibration. This is also seen in the human voice: by a stronger impulse of the moving soul, more intense and clearer sounds are produced, but by a weaker impulse, they are more relaxed and obscure. Likewise, we see the wind penetrating some crack in a house forcefully produces a higher and sharper voice, while immediately the same wind blowing weakly always stirs up a lower sound through that same crack. This is also clearly demonstrated in the manner of sounding a trumpet. <insert>The reason for this matter, therefore, consists in the weaker or more intense powers of the moving soul, and consequently in the medium into which the soul enters through the vibration of the string or voice;</insert> for a weaker moving soul does not have enough power to refine the air so as to produce higher sounds; and conversely, a motive soul acting powerfully produces higher and more sublime voices in the air, because of its great force and virtue in the **refinement** <term>subtiliation; the process of making something less dense or more spiritual</term> of the air, whence the sounding soul dilates itself more and more easily in the air and acts more sharply within it.

The demonstration of this matter is seen in the stronger and weaker striking of a string and its vibration, and especially in the rising or falling of the human voice. Similarly, a string performs the same thing in another way through the tightening and loosening of the sound; namely, when the motive soul contracts the string itself with greater force, it sounds higher, because according to the greater force and proportion of the contracting soul, it vibrates with greater violence, and by its vibrations it refines the medium, so that higher and sharper voices are produced. In the same way, a string of lesser thickness requires less power from the motive soul to bring forth high and elevated sounds than a larger string does, since it makes its way into the air with an easier motion and lighter vibration because of the slenderness of its body. Whence it fills less space in the air, and yet its force extends widely and sharply. ### CHAPTER VI.

> *How through the pipe, an art invented for Music, all the aforesaid*
->*is demonstrated more clearly?*<-

BEHOLD before your eyes a notable demonstration, hardly perceived by the inventor himself; through which it appears clearly that great and even immense secrets often lie hidden in common things; the reason and root of which, however, common eyes by no means perceive, looking at things superficially rather than at their roots.

<margin>→</margin>From this musical instrument, called a <term>fistula</term> <note>original: "fistula"; a pipe or flute, often used in Renaissance philosophy to represent the divine breath moving through creation</note>, the true proportion of the whole world is gathered. It is divided into three regions; the two lower ones have three holes, denoting the beginning, middle, and end of each region; the highest region, however, consisting only of one large hole, designates the nature of the super-celestial heaven, of which every part is of the same condition, as if most full with divine unity. But truly, just as this instrument in its own nature and by itself does not sound, move, or have any power without a soul to move it; so also neither the world nor the parts of the world can move or act by themselves without the excitation of the immense mind. Therefore, as the highest mind, GOD, at the apex of the whole machine, and as if outside the extreme surface of the world, makes the structures of the world exhibit its music—lower in the inferior part, and sharper and clearer the more and closer they approach the summit itself—so also, with the musician blowing life and motion from outside the pipe’s containment and at its summit, the further the holes are from his underlying blowing power, the deeper the voices they emit; however, the higher one ascends toward the bellows of his spirit, the more excellent the sounds rendered. And just as that single hole, A <note>likely referring to a diagram of a cosmic flute where 'A' represents the highest point</note>, gives as if life and soul to the others below it (since they do not render voices without it), so also the <term>Empyrean heaven</term> <note>the highest, most spiritual part of the heavens, thought to be composed of pure light or fire</note> <margin>→</margin>gives life to all the lower spheres. Oh, how great and how celestial would this contemplation be in so frivolous a matter, if it were considered diligently and a bit more deeply by an intelligent mind!

### CHAPTER V.

->*On elementary music.*<-

**I**t is established that there is a certain harmony even in the elementary part of the world; its consonances proceed more from the proportions of the heat of the celestial fire—which is not of the true essence of light, but rather forced and external—than from that essential [light]. Therefore, they produce symphonic compositions whose harmony, because of the scarcity of the true luminous form within them, is indeed not permanent, but transitory and vanishes with a certain sudden speed. However, that every element is arranged by natural consent according to musical proportions—both in its own heaven and in any composite of the heaven—we shall perceive more clearly than light itself, if we look more exactly and deeply into their natures and positions. For it is certain that their matter, or bulk, is thicker, and consequently heavier and harder; or thinner, and therefore lighter and softer. This occurs according to the greater predominance of the cold of the earth or the heat of the fire within it. Since, therefore, coldness has dominion only in the earth (whence, because of the absolute absence of fiery heat, those four quarters of coldness are present, which are as if the entire nature of the earth); but truly the element of water possesses no more than three quarters of coldness, joined with a single one of fire (which happens to it because of its participation with the middle sphere of humidity); similarly, the middle sphere of humidity contains only two portions of coldness and just as many of heat; finally, the element of air has acquired only a single portion of humidity, while it embraces three quarters of the quality of fire from the neighboring element; it is necessary that the earth be denser, heavier, and harder than water, and water than the impure sphere of equality, and that finally than the air, which is the upper part of that humid sphere.

### TREATISE I. BOOK III.

...and consequently, the coldness, density, and heaviness of the earth relate to those of water in a <term>sesquialter proportion</term> <note>original: "sesquialtera"; a 3:2 ratio, which in music produces a perfect fifth.</note>; and these same dispositions of water relate to the middle sphere of humidity in a sesquialter ratio; finally, the condition of this matter is related to that of the air in a <term>double proportion</term> <note>original: "proportione dupla"; a 2:1 ratio, which produces an octave.</note>. Therefore, the consonance from the convex surface of the base to that of water is found to be a <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>A perfect fourth.</note>, and from that water to the other sphere of humidity it is measured as a <term>Diapente</term> <note>A perfect fifth.</note>; from which all the way to the concave surface of fire, the <term>Diapason</term> <note>An octave.</note> extends itself, so that between fire and earth a <term>Disdiapason</term> <note>A double octave.</note>, which consists of a <term>quadruple proportion</term> <note>A 4:1 ratio.</note>, is produced. For in the sphere of false and corruptible equality, by ascending, the <term>Diapente</term> concludes after the <term>Diatessaron</term>, which joined together constitute the <term>Diapason</term>. Furthermore, by descending from the sphere of fire—in which there are four degrees of accidental heat—those degrees combined with the three degrees of air produce a formal <term>Diatessaron</term>; and the aforementioned three degrees of air, joined to those two of the sphere of humidity, make a <term>Diapente</term>. These two, when united, generate a formal <term>Diapason</term>. Moreover, those two-quarters of heat from the sphere of equality, coupled with the single part of air, bring forth another <term>Diapason</term>. From this, in the element of air, the <term>Diapason</term> of matter agrees symphonically with the <term>Diatessaron</term> of form; and in the middle sphere of humidity, the <term>Diapente</term> of matter matches the <term>Diapente</term> of form, which there also resounds as a <term>Diapason</term>. Because of this, it is the most perfect <term>seat of the elements</term> <note>original: "elementorum sedes"</note> and a <term>temperament</term> <note>A balanced mixture of qualities.</note> toward justice. In the element of water, a <term>Diapason</term> of form with a <term>Diatessaron</term> is perceived by the ears of reason to resonate. Therefore, these elements, when arranged in physical bodies according to these musical proportions, produce the best temperaments in them. But where they are poorly ordered—that is, with a less harmonic consensus—they cause a <term>dyscrasia</term> <note>An imbalance of the bodily humors.</note> and <term>intemperance</term> <note>An excess of one quality over others.</note>; they stir up strife and discord, generate diseases and illnesses in bodies, and finally lead to most certain corruption unless they are swiftly corrected. # CHAPTER VI.

->*Concerning the intervals of each element, and concerning the consonances which arise from them, by which the elements peacefully converge toward composition.*<-

---

In the general treatise on Music, we have proved that the **Fourth** <term>Diatessaron: a musical interval of a perfect fourth</term>, which is an imperfect consonance, is found only because of its impurity in every sphere of the lowest region of the world. In this place, however, we shall provide a most clear demonstration of this matter, through which we will evidently show that every sphere of this elemental region is composed of the entire consonance of the **Fourth**. Moreover, unless in the middle of the extremes a "sphere of friendship"—namely that of equality—were interposed as a spurious link <note>The author uses "spurious" (spuria) here to mean an intermediate or transitional zone that is not "purely" one element or the other</note>, it would be impossible for one of these to correspond to another in symphonic melody. For by reason of this middle sphere, all the aforementioned consonances are rendered both less perfect and more perfect, as appears most clearly in the following demonstration; where we have outlined three regions of the terrestrial globe:

One region is central, and simply cold and dry, and preeminent in weight, whose interval we have compared to a **tone** <term>tonus: a whole step or whole tone in music</term>. 

Another is intermediate, namely between the central and the surface regions, which we call the mineral region, verging more toward the simplicity of the center than toward the nature of water; whose interval we have also compared to a **tone**, from which we have now found the terrestrial **Major Third** <term>Ditonum: literally "two tones," forming a major third</term>. 

And the final region is the surface, which communicates more with water than with the purest nature of the center; from its circuit springs burst forth and plants arise, whose nourishment is water and air. We have assigned the space of this region of the earth to a **semitone** <term>semitonium: a half-step or half-tone</term>. From these terrestrial intervals, the consonance of the **Fourth** arises.

Similarly, we have also demonstrated that every sphere of the transparent elements is distinguished into three regions; in such a way, namely, that the lower region of water is muddier and more dreg-filled, communicating with the nature of earth, to whose interval we attribute a **tone**. Next is its middle region, imbued with the saltiness of the earth; it is as if "burnt water," whose subtler parts are extracted and evaporate, and are joined with fresh water. Therefore, this portion of water participates in both extremes—namely in the nature of terrestrial dregs and the nature of fresh water—wherefore its interval is also compared to a **tone**. 

The upper region, however, is fresh water, participating in the purer region of the salty orb and the cloudy nature of thick air, and joining itself with the sphere of spurious equality—which we call so in respect to the sphere of most pure and incorruptible equality, which we have called <gloss>a</gloss> the sphere of the World Soul. And thus, from these final intervals of the watery sphere, a **Minor Third** <term>Semiditonus: literally a "half-double tone," or minor third</term> arises, which, together with the tone of its lowest region, composes another **Fourth**. 

Furthermore, ascending even higher to the sphere of air, we find there also three regions: the lowest, somewhat inclined toward the nature of water, we compared to a **tone**; the middle, also to a **tone**; and the highest, more occupied by fire, we compared to a **semitone**. These intervals joined together constitute a third **Fourth**. 

Finally, the sphere of fire is also divided into three regions: to the lowest, which is familiar with the air, we attribute a **tone**; and likewise to the middle, where a simpler portion of the element of fire exists, we have given another **tone**. But the space of that highest region, participating with the **Fifth Essence** <term>Quinta essentia: the Quintessence or Aether, the celestial substance of the heavens</term>, we compare to a 
->minor<- **semitone**.

<summary>This page describes the musical structure of the four elements, arguing that each element (Earth, Water, Air, and Fire) is divided into three internal regions that correspond to the musical intervals of two whole tones and a semitone, together forming a perfect fourth (Diatessaron).</summary>

<page-num>99</page-num>
->ON THE MUSIC OF THE WORLD.<-
<note>original: "DE MUSICA MUNDANA." This refers to the concept of the "Music of the Spheres" or the harmony governing the physical and spiritual universe.</note>

## ON THE MUSIC OF THE WORLD.

...we have related in a smaller <note>likely referring to a previous section or a smaller volume of the work</note> account. From these things, it is clear that in the pure natures of the elements, no harmony is found except for that which is imperfect. The method for finding these intervals is as follows: at every step, the further one ascends from the earthly nature toward the fiery nature, the more the matter is altered as it rises, due to the gradually increasing operation of fire. Because it is certain that these operations are found perceptibly in the three locations of the said elements, we have therefore taken the intervals of our musical harmonies from these degrees of alteration.

In order, therefore, that all these <term>Diatessarons</term> <note>A "Diatessaron" is the musical interval of a Perfect Fourth.</note> may act upon one another naturally and peacefully, it is necessary to link the two "corporeal" ones—which belong to the visible elements—to the two belonging to the invisible elements. We shall clearly demonstrate that this connection arises from the <term>sphere of spurious equality</term> <note>A cosmological term used by the author to describe a transitional zone between the physical and spiritual realms.</note>, to which we have assigned the interval of a whole tone, which is indeed the most perfect interval. If this tone is joined with the *Diatessaron* of the watery sphere, a less perfect harmony is produced by this link and coupling; when this is united with the earthly *Diatessaron*, it gives birth to that most perfect corporeal harmony called the <term>Diapason</term> <note>A "Diapason" is the musical interval of an Octave.</note>.

Similarly, by ascending upward to the invisible elemental regions, if the *Diatessaron* of the airy sphere is joined with the perfect interval of the "sphere of spurious equality," an airy harmony of a less perfect sort will immediately be produced. When this is joined with the fiery *Diatessaron*, it will constitute an incorporeal—that is, an invisible—*Diapason*.

In this manner, therefore, fire will communicate with air in an *Diapason* (Octave) composed of a *Diatessaron*, the airy *Diatessaron*, and the interval of the middle sphere. Fire in the air communicates with water in an Octave composed of the *Diatessaron* of air, fire (animated by the preceding Octave), the tone of the middle sphere, and the *Diatessaron* of water—for these constitute another Octave. Finally, fire in the air and air in the water (acting as vehicles for the invisible elements) communicate with the earth through a third and lowest Octave, composed of the tone or interval of the middle sphere, the *Diatessaron* of the watery sphere, and the earthly *Diatessaron*; all of these joined together produce an Octave.

By this path, it is most clearly demonstrated by what chains the elements are linked to one another, and why fire exists more in air, less in water, and least of all (or in the smallest portion) in the earth. From this it is also declared how one element is, as it were, the matrix, vehicle, and receptacle for another—specifically for whichever is immediately above it: such as air for fire, water for air, and earth for water, which for this reason is the receiver of all elements. Thus, the earth is not undeservedly called by the Philosophers "the mother of all elements." This, then, is that elemental harmony, by the virtue of whose consonances the parts in a mixture of composition are connected most exactly and according to weight, and are peacefully preserved within it.

---

We conclude, therefore, that the true method which connects the proportions of contrary elements to one another in a composition is the "sphere of equality." Its "tone" is the interval that fills the natural ligament <note>A "ligament" here means a binding force or tie.</note> between the superior and invisible elements and the inferior and visible ones, without which the four elements can in no way concur to form any natural composition.

...vital actions and movements; for this reason, this is the most effective of all the aforementioned harmonies for the exact perfection of material things. *Mars* also, although it is very useful in its own nature and by itself, is nevertheless an unlucky star for lower living beings because its <term>Diapason<note>original: "Diapason"; the musical interval of an octave, which Fludd relates to the proportions of the cosmos.</note></term> extends to the sphere of water. Because of its contrary nature to water, it produces operations against life that are rebellious and malicious toward these lower regions, and it is held by Astrologers to be the **Lesser Misfortune** <note>original: "infortunio minori"; in astrology, the planet Mars is traditionally called the Lesser Malefic.</note>. 

*Jupiter*, however, immediately embracing the sphere of *Mars* with its own orbit, is benevolently received by the sphere of air, which is wonderfully delighted by its melody consisting of a double proportion <note>The "dupla" or 2:1 ratio, which creates the octave.</note>. For they agree in every way in the proportion of their natures and qualities, except that air participates in a lower nature, while the sphere of *Jupiter* participates in a higher one; for both are hot and moist. It is for this reason, therefore, that they primarily contribute to animal life; and that aerial orb has its benevolent disposition from *Jupiter*, who is therefore called the **Greater Fortune** <note>original: "Fortunium maius"; the planet Jupiter is known as the Greater Benefic.</note> by Astrologers, and from *Venus*, who is called the **Lesser Fortune** by the same. 

Finally, the last interval of this region is governed by *Saturn*, which stands in a double proportion—in which the **octave** consists—to the interval of the element of fire. But truly, since the nature of *Saturn* and that of the fiery sphere are contrary, such a melody, although it may perhaps be of use to one or another species, is nevertheless turbid and unpleasant, and indeed malicious to the animal race. For as the cold nature of *Saturn* terminates in that heat of fire, the quality of heat is repugnant to coldness; and so, even though that quantitative proportion is harmonious on the <term>World Monochord<note>The "monochordo mundano," a central symbol in Robert Fludd's work representing the universe as a musical string tuned by the hand of God.</note></term>, the contrary qualities of the giver and the receiver produce no small <term>dyscrasia<note>A medical or philosophical term for an imbalance of humors or qualities; a discord.</note></term> in that concord, which living things very easily feel and perceive because of the weakness of their forms. Hence it is that *Saturn* is called the **Greater Misfortune** by Astrologers, for the same reason that they call *Mars* the **Lesser Misfortune**.

<margin><<<</margin> From these things, therefore, it is clear that the *Sun* and *Moon* transmit a general worldly Music into these lower regions through their influences, while the other stars transmit a more particular music. Furthermore, some of these stars emit their melodies into these lower regions luckily, and some unluckily. Those that flow luckily, flow clearly, purely, and simply; but those that flow unluckily send their natures down into these lower regions through the intervals of the **octave** in a broken way, and these act in a very interrupted manner upon all bodies, unless they are very well disposed.

Finally, the natures of the stars also concur by a certain harmonic consent with the natures of the Planets themselves. Thus *Leo* <note>The zodiac sign Leo, the Lion.</note>, because of the singular vitality of its life, receives the *Sun* as its Lord; hence *Leo* is, as it were, in unison with the nature of the *Sun*. So also *Cancer* with the *Moon*; *Aries* with *Mars*, and so on for the rest. For any house of the Planets must be conformable and, as it were, in unison with the nature of its Lord—that is, it must resonate with its Lord in the same sound. Therefore, they flow in the same way and with the same harmonies as their Lords.

Finally, as far as the <term>Diatessaron<note>original: "Diatesfaron"; the musical interval of a fourth.</note></term> of the upper region is concerned, it must be understood that the higher Hierarchy pours its virtues into the middle, and the middle into the lowest. This lowest hierarchy communicates with the ethereal heaven, which expects and receives not only its splendor from that fiery heaven, but also the messengers and commands of GOD from its creatures, and carries out what has been received. <margin>-></margin> These operations are indeed carried out by the power of spiritual harmonies, in which that fiery love, filling the entire <term>Empyrean<note>The highest heaven, the dwelling place of God, associated with fire and light.</note></term> heaven and extending itself as far as the center of the Sun, is contained. By its harmonies, all spiritual and rational things descend into well-disposed bodies, <margin>-></margin> mediated by that ethereal vehicle. Concerning these things, since we shall discourse more widely in our books on the **Macrocosm**, we shall omit them in this place so that we may more properly move on to more natural matters.

->CONCERNING THE MUSIC OF THE WORLD<-

# CHAPTER VIII.

### *On the practice of elemental melody, and its effect, both in simple and composite bodies, and on its discordance and strife.*

---

<margin>--></margin> Just as the subtler arrangements and natures of the higher realms are infused into the lower bodies, so too is it necessary that bodies be composed in a way that allows them to aptly receive such influences. This occurs within the region of the "material pyramid" <note>A concept in Fludd’s philosophy where matter is represented as a pyramid growing broader as it descends, while light is an inverted pyramid narrowing as it descends.</note> of substance, which is divided into the elements. Furthermore, this material composition receives its essential form not from the elements themselves, but from heaven itself; <margin><--</margin> as I have experienced firsthand by seeing such things with my own eyes. For I have separated the four distinct elements from a living thing; then, in the final stage, I perceived and saw with most open eyes the life of the thing, which I recognized to be from heaven, from the <term>Quintessence<note>original: "Quinta essentia"; the "fifth essence" or purest element that transcends the four terrestrial elements.</note></term>, and from the solar nature, once I had set the four inferior elements aside.

Our intention here, therefore, is to treat the proportions and those consonances by which an apt connection of one element with another is made in the mixture and composition of worldly bodies. Thus, in the "Music of the Elements," Earth stands in relation to the sphere of Water as 4 to 3, since there exist in Earth four parts of the "fourth degree of coldness" compared to the three parts found in Water. This is because a single part of the element of Fire (along with the peak of the "luminous pyramid") exists within the sphere of Water; indeed, if more parts of heat existed within it, it would be of a thinner substance and thus would be converted into Air. For that reason, its sphere would neither remain closest to the Earth, nor would it be burdened with such heaviness or weight. That it contains some heat—that is, a fiery form—is witnessed by its transparency and fluidity, as was said before in its proper place.

Because of this <term>sesquitertial proportion<note>The ratio of 4:3, which in music produces the interval of a Fourth.</note></term>, Earth harmonizes with Water; however, this combination of the said elements is imperfect and less than absolute, because the moist parts of one are contrary to the dry parts of the other. Nevertheless, they sound together through the consonance of a <term>Fourth (Diatessaron)<note>The musical interval of a fourth.</note></term> because they agree in the active qualities that predominate within them. 

So also, in relation to the "sphere of false equality" (in which there are two material parts and just as many of fire), Earth stands in a <term>double proportion<note>The ratio of 2:1, which produces an Octave.</note></term>—namely, as 4 parts of Earth to 2 of that same sphere; for the nature of Earth produced these moist parts by the power of the light joined with it, which dissolved and refined it. Similarly, Water relates to that sphere of equality as 3 to 2, from which the <term>sesquialter proportion<note>The ratio of 3:2, which in music produces the interval of a Fifth.</note></term> arises. And thus we have obtained the Fourth, the Fifth, and the Octave of the terrestrial pyramid.

Similarly, the sphere of equality relates to the sphere of Air by comparing the two fiery parts of the sphere of equality to those three portions of Air; from this, a fiery <term>Fifth (Diapente)<note>The musical interval of a fifth.</note></term> arises. And the three fiery parts of Air compared to the four parts of the sphere of Fire produce the consonance of an <term>Octave (Diapason)<note>original: "consonantiam Diapason"; although 4:3 is mathematically a Fourth, Fludd here classifies the completion of this elemental scale as an Octave.</note></term>. 

Therefore, Earth agrees with Water in a Fourth, and with the sphere of equality in an Octave. Water agrees with the sphere of false equality in a Fifth, and the sphere of false equality agrees with Air in an Octave—namely, because they are held in a double proportion. So also Fire agrees with Air in a Fourth, and with the sphere of equality in an Octave; and Air agrees with the sphere of equality in a Fifth, and the sphere of equality with Water in a double proportion or Octave. Thus, the two visible elements concur most excellently for composition through the bond of the consonance of the Fourth, and the two invisible elements mix themselves with them by virtue of the embrace they have with the bodily proportions. Now, this sphere of equality connects those invisible elements, which are chained together by formal harmonies, to the visible elements through corporeal bonds or concords. Similarly, the air is joined to the earth in a quadruple proportion, and consequently fire, also glued to the air by the bond of a Fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>, is accustomed to being united with earth and water; yet they are joined to one another in such a way that the proper seat of the concords and the legitimate order are observed, lest discord and strife arise between them. For this reason, the <term>corporeal concords</term> <note>physical harmonies governing dense matter</note> ought to regard the more corporeal elements, and the fiery concords the fiery ones. The reason for this is that the region which is more earthly and visible, as well as the fiery and invisible one, is bounded and perfected by the most perfect concord. Hence, the limit of the corporeal or visible <term>pyramid</term> <note>a reference to the author's theory of two intersecting pyramids of light and shadow/matter</note> is within the corporeal Octave; and likewise that fiery pyramid is within its own less corporeal Octave. But truly, insofar as both Octaves are joined by the power of the middle sphere, the corporeal elements are joined and chained to those invisible ones. Therefore, one proportion must not look toward another outside its own region; for otherwise, discords would arise instead of harmonies. For example: fire consists of 4 parts of heat, and water of three parts of coldness; although there is a <term>sesquitertia</term> <note>a ratio of 4:3, corresponding to a musical Fourth</note> proportion here, it nevertheless exists poorly between bodies that are ill-disposed by reason of their qualities, and a progression occurs from the fiery kingdom to the corporeal one, whose natures are entirely opposite. Similarly, the earth relates to the air as 4 to 3; but for the same reason, they can in no way agree; hence fire is enclosed by air, through the mediation of which (by the sphere of equality—which is to be held as a medium for joining fiery and airy forms with aqueous and earthly bodies, just as the <term>ethereal spirit</term> <note>the vital breath or pneuma that bridges the soul and the body</note> is regarded as such in the conjunction of the soul with the lower body) the air passes, and is gathered with its fiery soul and with water, which water is most easily and naturally joined with the earth by the power of the concord of a Fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>. And this is that harmony by which the composition of mixed sublunary bodies is made. However, bonds of this kind are dissolved by strife and discord; for the proportion of <term>Martial fire</term> <note>heat influenced by the planet Mars, often associated with aggression or fever</note>, increased beyond the due nature of its concord, very quickly absorbs the moisture of its airy vehicle, and from its prison—the concord of the Fourth having been violated by the fiery proportion—it breaks out into the aqueous region and causes war instead of peace in the compound; hence desperate and incurable diseases arise, and that fiery nature, violently penetrating through the water and earth and breaking out from them, snatches away with it the celestial soul, which is closest to it in the composition because of the familiarity and kinship of the ethereal heaven with the sphere of fire; and in this way the compound is dissolved, suffers corruption, and is gradually reduced back into its first matter. <header>ON WORLDLY MUSIC.</header>

### CHAPTER IX.

->*On worldly discords.*<-

**A**FTER we have dealt with worldly concord, it follows that we should establish a discourse concerning its discords and the reasons for them. From the preceding sections, it has been clearly demonstrated that chaos, before the completion of the world, was composed of litigious proportions, and that there was nothing of concord in that rude mass, according to the Poet: *Cold things fought with hot, moist things with dry* <note>original: "Frigida pugnabant calidis, humentia siccis," a famous line from Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* describing the state of Chaos.</note>. From these causes—the hostile incursions of the Macrocosm <term>Macrocosm: The "great world" or universe, viewed as a large-scale reflection of the human being (the microcosm).</term> and its peaceful friendship—various effects are produced. For in the beginning, when heat was born, its opposite, cold, also arose. Between these two, while they waged war against each other, humidity intervened as a third something, a mixture of those two primary qualities, yet not entirely agreeing with either extreme; it participates in both extremes and therefore holds the middle place between them. Hence, dryness, never departing from either extreme, is in perpetual war with its contrary, humidity, so that one pursues the other in an unending enmity. 

Interrupting these hostile clashes in the nature of the Macrocosm, infinite nature made distinct and balanced things out of the indistinct. Once this was done, light things flew up to the higher regions, while heavy things settled beneath the moist sands, so that each of them was carried by a fiery spirit into its proper and proportional place, to speak in the words of *Trismegistus* <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the *Hermetica*.</note>. With things thus arranged in the ethereal heaven, every Planet was found in its own proper exaltation <term>Exaltation: An astrological term referring to the specific zodiac sign where a planet’s influence is most powerfully and harmoniously expressed.</term>. Indeed, they were so situated in the celestial Zodiac that those of contrary conditions were placed furthest apart from one another. Hence, the *Sun* found its exaltation in *Aries* at the first instant of its creation; the *Moon* had its exaltation nearest to it (since the Sun bestowed something of his own substance upon her, she being like a wife or female) and possessed *Taurus*. Similarly, *Jupiter*, the greatest friend to the Sun and Moon, was exalted in *Cancer*; *Mercury* in *Virgo*. But *Saturn*, who is most malicious toward the *Sun*, was distant from him by the entire diameter of the whole heaven, being exalted in *Libra*. Finally, *Mars*, exalted in *Capricorn*, was equally distant from both the Sun and Saturn. Thus were all these creatures of heaven arranged, so that no manifest strife existed between their qualities. 

However, after they fell into malevolent aspects <term>Aspects: The angular relationships between planets (like squares or oppositions) that astrologers believe cause tension or harmony.</term> through their natural motion—which has commonly happened every year since their origin—they produce rebellious effects in these lower regions. By these, lower compositions are either utterly destroyed and uprooted, or wonderfully afflicted and weakened. This occurs because of the malevolent influences of the Planets when they regard each other poorly; these influences are more depraved when the planet which is stronger and more powerful at the time of the aspect is itself of a more depraved nature. Now, they call *Saturn* and *Mars* the "evil" Planets; for they naturally extend their "double proportions" <note>This likely refers to the "diapason" or octave, here used in a dissonant sense.</note> downward into spheres that are incongruous and contrary to their natures. From this, they create a corrupted harmony and produce effects in these lower things (especially living creatures) that are accidental rather than natural, as was said before. For all Planets are good in themselves, but their influences—even though they too are good in their own right—work evil effects in bodies that are not fit to receive their natures, particularly in the case of these two [Saturn and Mars] for the reasons already alleged. Thus, the fault is not in the giver, but in the receiver. This is also confirmed by *Iamblichus* <note>Iamblichus was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on theurgy and the divine nature of the cosmos.</note> in these words: *Celestial things are not evil, though here they are received as evil; for all the powers of the celestial beings descend as good from that place, but in this mixture of contraries they are changed; therefore, the quality which causes harm on earth is something other than that which*...

...which had arrived from heaven until now; the reasoning of which is confirmed by the effect of our Philosophy. For first, speaking universally, the sphere of water received the influences of *Mars* through the <term>Diapason</term> <note>original: "consonantiam Diapason"; a musical interval of an octave, signifying a perfect harmonic relationship</note> consonance, but it received those things contrary to the nature of that sphere. Hence, fire fights invisibly with water, and by resisting, the water is preternaturally disturbed. Thus *Saturn* sends out its influences in the same proportion into fire, which in the reception of them similarly acts and suffers in more specific ways. 

<margin>[</margin>We see that the power of *Saturn* is restrictive and by accident frequently hinders, namely when it is received by colder matter: for then it does harm, because it is received for the most part by way of freezing. Similarly, we recognize that the power of *Mars* is motive <note>originating motion or action</note>, and we see its influences hinder, specifically when it is received by more fervent <note>hotter or more volatile</note> matter; and then it harms because it is received through heat. Indeed, these harms do not occur because of a wicked operation of the influences themselves, but because of the <term>bad disposition of the matter</term> <note>original: "malam materiæ dispositionem"; the idea that the "soil" (the physical body) is not prepared for the "seed" (celestial influence)</note>. Similarly, even the density and rarity of matter can be at fault. We also find sometimes that the weakness of the subject is the cause, so that good rays and influences produce bad effects in it; for it happens sometimes that the light of the *Sun* offends the eyes of the weak, and its heat and summer rays hurt even the stronger and more bilious <note>those with a temperament dominated by yellow bile, associated with heat and irritability</note>. 

Thus we also find that the influxes of *Mercury* and *Venus* sometimes agitate blasts and winds in the air; and experience teaches that in a bilious nature mixed with superfluous phlegmatic humor, through the influences of *Mars* and the *Moon* in a bad aspect—such as a square, conjunction, or opposition as they look upon each other—foul ulcers are birthed, since the fiery nature of *Mars* with the watery nature of the *Moon* continually works toward corruption until purulent <note>pus-filled</note> matter is produced. Similarly, *Mars* and *Saturn* themselves, finding contrary subjects in one man or animal, affect it for the most part with plague, putrid fever, or similar diseases, while other animals of the same species in the meantime—due to a lack of matter contrary to the *Martial* and *Saturnine* nature—receive the influxes of those Planets freely without danger and without any manifest alteration. 

From which it is clear that although all celestial influxes come as healthy in themselves, nevertheless sometimes the perversity or weakness of the subject cannot tolerate the natures of the higher powers. By the same reasoning in the Elementary region: after every nature in it (once indistinct and disturbed) had been reduced into consonant proportions by the rules of concordances, the earth obtained a place further removed from fire as its contrary. Similarly, water was placed between air and earth so they would not contend again; indeed, even a "spurious sphere of equality" <note>an intermediate zone of balance that prevents extremes from meeting</note> interposed itself between the coldness of water and the heat of air; and so, by reason of this middle sphere participating equally in both, peace is maintained between these elemental spheres opposed to one another, as was said above. 

Where, therefore, such bonds of peace in simpler bodies are broken, there we see in the elements the effects of strife and discord. For example, if fire is mixed with water, thunder and lightning are caused; if fire is in the air in too great a proportion, flashes, Comets, and other ignited <term>Meteors</term> <note>original: "Meteora"; in the 17th century, this referred to any atmospheric phenomenon including rainbows, lightning, and falling stars</note> arise. If the coldness of the earth is in the air, snow and hail are driven and gathered in the air; if water is in the air, mists and clouds. And so sometimes a confusion of consonances—indeed of the tones themselves—occurs; all of which accidents produce diseases of simpler bodies or elements in the lowest region of the world. 

Furthermore, even in composite bodies, a great strife sometimes arises, fatal to the body, which happens either because of the violation of the elemental ligaments contained in the composite, or because of the inequality of the proportion of one element to another—about which to debate more extensively in this place is not our purpose, since that would be more tedious due to the spacious field of that subject than suitable for this our Musical discourse. We therefore conclude this <term>World Music</term> <note>original: "Musica mundana"; the ancient and Renaissance theory that the universe is governed by mathematical and musical proportions</note> of ours with this axiom:

# CHAPTER I.

## *Concerning the distinctions of the spiritual creatures of the Empyrean heaven, according to both the ancient Philosophers and the Fathers of Theology.*

The word **DEMON** is used not only for the Devil alone, but for a spirit, so called from the property of the word <note>original Latin: *ex vocabuli proprietate*. The author is referring to the Greek root *daimon*, which was historically associated with "knowledge" or "wisdom" before it took on a purely negative connotation in Christian tradition.</note>, as if meaning "knowing, intelligent, and wise." It is known by this name of intelligence because it is an intelligent substance, free from all bulk of coarse bodies subject to decay; it is immortal, beyond physical sensation, present to all things, and influencing all things. However, it is sometimes called an *Angel*, that is, a "messenger," because it is ordered by God to reveal His commands to humans. Thus, the name "Demon" seems to be a general term pertaining to all spiritual creatures, the soul alone excepted; though I am aware that some have existed who distinguished Demons from other creatures of the highest heaven. Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on theurgy and the divine hierarchy.</note>, making mention of four orders of celestial spirits—namely, the first being *Gods*, the second *Demons*, the third *Heroes*, and the last *souls*—called these three latter groups the "attendants of the Gods." He demonstrates that one of these orders is more powerful than another, and that according to their dignity, they each possess more excellent places or regions of this heaven (which we named "elements" a little earlier), as he declared at great length in his descriptions and distinctions of their properties. Elsewhere, the same author distributes the choir of celestial spirits into eight species or distinctions: namely, Gods, Archangels, Angels, Demons, Heroes, Principalities, Princes, and souls; although the tradition of the Magi <note>Referring to the "Magicians" or practitioners of Hermetic and Neoplatonic natural magic who sought to communicate with these spirits.</note> seems to include all these species—excepting the outermost, or rather the last—under the name of "Demon" (taking the word "Demon" for a knowing, intelligent, and wise spirit). Hence, they would call spirits both pre-celestial and celestial, as well as the lower ministers, "Demons."

Theologians (among whom I name Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century theologian whose *Celestial Hierarchy* defined the standard Christian angelic orders.</note>) wished to condense these species of Demons into three hierarchies; each of these they distinguished into three orders differing in rank and property, which they called "choirs." In the upper hierarchy, therefore, which Dionysius calls *Epiphania* <note>meaning "Manifestation" or "Appearance from above"</note>, the first order is the *Seraphim*, the second the *Cherubim*, and the third the *Thrones*; in the middle hierarchy, called by him *Epiphononia* <note>A term implying a secondary or echoing manifestation</note>, are the *Dominations, Virtues, and Powers*; in the lowest (to him, *Ephionia* <note>Likely referring to the lowest tier of spiritual manifestation</note>) are the *Principalities, Archangels, and Angels*. Finally, all who have written on divine matters have been accustomed to divide Demons into the good and the evil. Those who are good are called "celestial" by Iamblichus; he asserts that such beings are beneficent and strive for and work toward nothing but good itself. Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD), one of the last major Greek philosophers, who heavily influenced medieval angelology.</note> says that the evil Demons are material and earthly; and that the good Demons are more open to the mind, while the evil and earthly ones must be driven away with the most diligent caution we can muster. Therefore, so that we may agree with the ancient Philosophers and the modern Theologians of this age, the celestial or spiritual...

The good they have arranged into three hierarchies; the bad, however, whom Plato calls *Cacodæmones* <note>original: "Cacodæmones," a Greek term for "evil spirits"</note>, deserting angels, and cultivators of crimes and impiety, they have named Lucifer with his associates, of whom there are infinite legions. *The good again are called angels of light, the bad indeed angels of darkness.* <margin>⮕</margin>The Soul, however, is the lowest species of the intelligences; which is proven by the fact that it is naturally accustomed to mingle itself with lower bodies, so that it might adorn them as an essential form.

### *On the composition of Demons and Angels; How they are said to be incorporeal? Several arguments proving the composition of demonic substances.*

**A**ugustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a central figure in Western Christianity</note> in his work *On Genesis*, *says that Demons are aerial and fiery animals*: By "aerial" he denotes pure spiritual matter; by "fiery" he understands the form. *Damascenus <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749 AD), a Syrian monk and polymath</note> in book 2, chapter 3*, calls Angels "intellectual lights," which *Pythagoras* <note>The famous Greek mathematician and philosopher who believed in the divinity of numbers and elements</note> judged to be made of fire alone. These are said to be brighter than the Sun, Moon, and other Stars, for this reason: because they drew their origin from the thinnest fire enclosed in the most subtle spirit; whereas those [celestial bodies] took their rise from a thick fire participating in air or ethereal humidity. Wherefore it is manifest that Angels do not participate in the matter of the lower heavens at all, as is held in *book three of "On the Soul"* <note>Likely referring to Aristotle’s De Anima</note>, but are certainly a formal spirit, whose matter—in respect to lower substance—is entirely "form," and fused as if from a single essence. Hence *Dionysius* <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a mystic whose writings defined the celestial hierarchy</note> calls Angels *Agalmata* <note>original: "Agalmata," Greek for "images" or "statues"</note>, that is, the clearest mirrors, receiving the light of GOD, representing His image, and revealing the secrets of things, as he testifies in his *book on the Divine Names*. That these spirits differ from one another in rank, dignity, and splendor, *Iamblichus* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher interested in theurgy and the divine</note> tries to prove by their appearances to priests in this manner: *The visions of the Gods,* he says, *appear to us extremely bright, shining to the highest degree, and wonderfully distinct in their splendor. Archangels have around them, in front and behind, a great multitude of fire, and a light precedes them which is divided in itself. The light of Angels is shining, but less than that of Archangels, and is divided. Demons appear as if they were a cloudy fire. Heroes <note>In ancient philosophy, semi-divine spirits between gods and men</note> have a light mixed from many sources. The light of Principalities is purer. Princes possess a light confused from dissimilar and contrary things. Souls yield a light full of many generations and mixtures, and divided; they have these differences according to their position: for the closer they are to* GOD, *the brighter they are; the more remote they are, the darker.* <margin>⮕</margin>From these things, therefore, one may gather that Demons are composed of the matter of the most subtle elements of the spiritual heaven—which matter, in respect to lower things, is the simplest and aerial—and from a divine form, emanating from the most splendid blessedness of GOD. Their composition, if compared with the creatures of the lower heavens, is called incorporeal; but in respect to the simplicity of the light-filled substance of the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest point of heaven, believed to be composed of pure light or fire</note>—in which, with which, and from whose elements they were created on the first day—they were made (no differently than plants, herbs, and their seeds were made on the third day with the earth, the opposite of the Empyrean heaven) <margin>⮕</margin>as a body fused from spiritual elements.

<summary>This page discusses the classification and physical composition of spiritual beings, arguing that while angels and demons are "incorporeal" compared to us, they possess a subtle spiritual "body" made of the purest celestial fire and light.</summary>

must be held. And hence it is that Augustine asserts they possessed aerial bodies <note>original: "corpora aërea"</note> from the beginning of their creation; that is, they were formed from the upper part of the air, suited for acting and not for suffering <note>In scholastic philosophy, "suffering" or "passion" refers to the capacity to be acted upon or changed by an external force</note>; and Basil affirms this same thing moreover: What, indeed, could more clearly denote the composition of Demons than their actions and passions? As to the fact that they act and suffer (Theological Resolutions, treatise 2, chapter 2), since they both receive and give forth illuminations again, and produce the act of understanding and also receive it, I certainly think no one is so grossly blind or deluded as to deny it. It is certain, therefore, that there is one thing in them which acts, and another which suffers; and indeed that by which they act can be nothing other than the act, which is called **form**; nor is that by which they suffer anything other than power <note>potentiality</note>; this is called **matter**. Furthermore, it must be especially observed here that the composition of matter and form, according to the diversity of the three heavens, has a twofold aspect. For in lower bodies, matter is subject to form, quantity, and contrariety <note>the opposition of qualities like hot and cold</note>; in celestial bodies, however, it is subject to form and quantity, but not to contrariety; but in spiritual creatures, it is subject to form, but in no way to corporeal quantity or contrariety. We conclude, therefore, that among all creatures, Demons are of the most subtle composition, and more radiant and clear than all others, because they are more full of formal essence, and consequently more spiritual, more noble, and as it were incorporeal, always mobile, free, and participants in immortality, as Damascenus <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century theologian</note> says. For their essence, from which they exist, is most simple, and as it were immaterial, lucid, pure, distinct, and discrete; their virtue, from which they have power, is free, intelligent, lovable, and everlasting; finally, their operation, through which they are exercised, is voluntary, sudden, useful, and honest; for they work without delay or hindrance, and serve us entirely without ceasing, as is found in the *Theological Resolutions*, treatise part 2.

## CHAPTER III.

->*How are angels said to be in a place?*<-

IN THE second chapter of the first book, we declared that God is in a place differently than Angels, and Angels differently again than corporeal creatures; since **GOD** is said to be here and everywhere only according to His presence—namely, in the **Empyrean heaven** <term>Empyrean: the highest part of the heavens, believed by medieval scholars to be composed of pure light and the dwelling place of God</term>, as if in His blessed tabernacle, and in any part of the world as if in a part of His empire. Angels, however, without the assumption of bodies, are judged to be in some part of the world not only by presence, but also **definitively**; and when they have assumed corporeal substances, they are there both by presence and definitively, as well as **circumscriptively** <note>original: "circumscriptivè"; to be in a place by filling the space and being bounded by its limits, like water in a glass</note> within some concave surface. Whence Angels, according to the resolution of the Theologians, are said to be **formally** in a place, that is, through their presences; yet they cannot be everywhere at the same moment of time, because they are said to be in a place definitively; nor indeed are they necessarily in a place, because they can be moved even when no containing body exists: for they can exist outside of all corporeal nature. And hence it is that they are said to be in a place **potentially**; for they have the power of existing in some containing body, but not in act, because they do not cause the sides of the container to stand apart, nor do they produce any containing surface in act. From these things, therefore, it is clear that Angels, on account of their composition, in a certain...

## CHAPTER VI.

### *On the differences of Spirits, and their duties, according to the tradition of both the ancient and more recent Magi.*

**T**HE MAGI <note>The "Magi" here refers to practitioners of "High Magic" or esoteric wisdom, such as Agrippa or Ficino</note>, establishing three types of spirits <note>original: "Dæmonum"; used here in the classical sense of mediating spirits, not necessarily evil demons</note> and intelligences—for according to them, some are *pre-celestial*, others *celestial*, and the rest *ministers of lower things*—called the pre-celestial ones "minds," being entirely separated from the body. They are like intellectual spheres, worshipping the one **GOD** as their most stable point and center; indeed, they claim them to be full of **GOD**, and as if intoxicated with divine nectar. They believe these spirits occupy themselves around **GOD** alone, and they think they take no care at all for worldly bodies, nor do they believe they serve the administration of lower things in any way. They conclude, however, that it is their duty to pour the light received from **GOD** into the lower orders, and to distribute individual duties to each. And this species of spirits is undoubtedly that which *Iamblichus* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the mysteries of the Egyptians and Chaldeans</note> calls **GODS**, *who follow the first God (the giver of all things to all) and who themselves bestow certain things upon all*. This is also the first and superior Hierarchy of Angels, comprising the orders of *Cherubim*, *Seraphim*, and *Thrones*, whose duty is to contemplate the order of divine providence; for the Angels of the first order look into the goodness of **GOD**, the second into the essence of **GOD** as a form, and the third into His wisdom. These, finally, are the Angels closest to **GOD**, whom they magnify with continuous hymns and everlasting praise <margin>→</margin> and *they pray to* **GOD** *for our salvation, as Athanasius says*. <margin>←</margin> *The Sages call the celestial intelligences "mundane spirits"* because, beyond divine worship, they are assigned to the spheres of the world and preside over each of the heavens and stars. From this it follows that they are distributed into as many orders as there are orbs in the world and stars counted in those orbs. And hence it is that some are called *Jovial* <note>associated with the planet Jupiter</note>, others *Saturnian* <note>associated with the planet Saturn</note>, and so on. Such spirits *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the "Hermetic" wisdom of Egypt</note> in his sacred discourse calls **GODS**; he says that after the heaven had shone forth in seven circles, they were seen in the patterns <note>original: "ideis"</note> of the stars with their zodiac signs, and it is said that the stars were numbered according to those **GODS** who inhabit them. These are undoubtedly those spirits of *Iamblichus* whom he calls "ministers of the Gods," acting as architects in the workshop of the world, who give expression to those things which are ineffable and hidden within the Gods. These are also those Angels who are placed in the middle hierarchy, having dominion over the middle region of the world. They are called by *Abbot Trithemius* <note>Johannes Trithemius, a famous 15th-century occultist and cryptographer</note> "secondary intelligences," which, by the ordering of the first intellect (that is, **GOD**), are said to govern the ethers and the orbs <margin>→</margin> of the Planets. The Magi call the spirits of the lower order "ministers," who are directed toward those things which must be arranged in the lower regions. These, *Origen* <note>An early Christian theologian</note> calls certain "invisible powers," through which any earthly things <margin>→</margin> are arranged. He asserts that they are visible to no one, and that they complete our business, direct our journeys, turn away the dangers of battles while being present, and prevent the outcomes of secret ambushes...

...and to provide the desired success to friends, namely by bringing about prosperity and breaking down adversity. In this species of spirits <note>original: "Dæmonum"; here referring to the Neoplatonic "daimones" or intermediary spirits rather than evil beings</note>, we judge that the "Heroes" of Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on theurgy and the soul</note> are to be counted. Their duties, as he believes, are exercised concerning earthly things; for they bring them to life, grant them reason, and guard their souls, which they also loosen and set free from these same things. From these points, it seems particularly suggested that these Heroes are mostly concerned with souls. 

However, theologians have placed this lowest kind of intelligences entirely within the final Hierarchy, called the "Ephionia" <note>A term likely derived from Hebrew or a specific esoteric tradition used to denote the choir of Angels closest to the material world</note>. Its spirits or Angels descend as ministers to care for lower things. They asserted that the office of this first order of the hierarchy is public—namely, to care for princes, magistrates, provinces, and kingdoms. The duty of the second order is to take part in sacred rites and to carry the prayers and sacrifices of men to God. Finally, the third order of Angels is commanded with the province of arranging all smaller matters appropriately; for they are present as individual guardians to individuals, and they supply the proper virtues to herbs, minerals, and all lower things. 

From the preceding, we therefore conclude that just as the elements of the lower heavens received their forms and essences from the shining fountain of the upper heaven, so also their creatures, molded and composed from those elements, are ordered, directed, and preserved by the creatures of that spiritual heaven. And this is also confirmed by Augustine, who proclaims that no visible thing exists among us which does not have an Angelic power presiding over it, and he constantly decrees that all bodies are ruled through a rational spirit of life. Origen also seems to agree with this, as in his commentaries he assigned a proper spirit not only to humans, but even to brute animals, plants, minerals, and the growth of all other things.

## CHAPTER V.

->*Concerning the evil Angel Lucifer, his rebellion and pride against God, and his expulsion along with his companions from the Empyrean heaven.*<-

<margin>Gregory:</margin>
<margin>Augustine, *Book on Questions of the Old Testament.*</margin>
<margin>Isaiah 14.</margin>
Lucifer <note>meaning "Light-bringer"</note> was created on the first day of creation, so named because he outshone all the Angels in clarity and splendor, as *Gregory* says: For just as he was the first Angel, preceding all others in creation, so he stood out far above all in the excellent quality of his light. And from this it happened, as supported by Augustine in his *Book on Questions of the Old Testament*, that he was blinded by his own elevation and desired to become like God—that is, so that he might preside and rule over everyone. Hence *Isaiah 14* says in the person of Lucifer: *I will ascend into heaven and I will be like the Most High.* This malice of Lucifer, which according to Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major medieval Scholastic theologian</note> began from self-love and was perfected in hatred of God (which was the greatest possible sin), is determined by theologians to have three states: *Beginning, increase, and completion.*

The *beginning* came from presumption; for as soon as he contemplated his own beauty, he immediately became presumptuous. The *increase* took root in ambition; for when he had first become presumptuous, he further desired—driven by a certain ambitious air—that which was entirely above him and which he could not possibly obtain. Its *completion* ended in the most destructive feelings of hatred and envy. For when that most foul ambition had tickled him with a burning desire for divine command, and he saw that it was truly impossible to attain it by any efforts...

...would follow, he was subsequently inflamed with an abominable envy against **G O D** the Best: **Whence** that Angel, on account of that horrendous pride, along with the others of an inferior order who showed themselves to be impious fellow-soldiers in the same *Theomachia* <note>original: "Theomachiæ"; a war against God</note>, was most deservedly cast down from the Empyrean heaven and its most blessed seat of light by the good Angels. Indeed, both he and his companions fell, cast headlong downward, and were enclosed and imprisoned in the dark air, or a horrendous and opaque shadow that glided beneath with a slanting motion, with not even the smallest spark of hope remaining for recovering their former state. Thus Lucifer—so named from his extraordinary light and splendor—fell through his excessive pride from Angelic radiance into Diabolical darkness; he migrated from the seat of love into the hatred and envy of all things, and tumbled from the highest peak of prosperity into the lowest abyss of unhappiness and misery, as Gregory <note>Likely Pope Gregory the Great, a foundational theologian for the Middle Ages</note> says. Therefore, after he had fallen in this manner, he is no longer called Lucifer, but from *to diaballein* <note>Greek: τῷ διαβαλεῖν</note>, that is, "to cast down," he is called *Diabolus* <note>Devil</note>, as if cast downward because of the weight of his pride. And by this name also the remaining soldiers of such noble Dynasts <note>original: "Dynastæ"; here meaning high-ranking angelic rulers</note>, stained by the same mark of treason, are designated.

But it will not be out of place if we observe with the Theologians that there is a threefold order regarding the sin of Lucifer and the rest of the Angels who fell with him. The first is *in the degree of gravity*; for the sin in him was heavier, whence it happens that he fell to the center, much deeper than the others, and from Lucifer was made **Lucifugus** <note>literally "one who flees the light"</note>. The second is the *order of occasion*, because he provided the way and occasion of sinning to others. The third is the *order of duration*; for Lucifer first presumed and opened the sentiment of his mind to certain other Angels, of whom indeed some supplied help to the horrendous wickedness, while others, abhorring such a great crime, clung to **G O D**, as was proper.

Hence the most powerful creator of all things retained the innocent Angels in heaven, shining with most brilliant glory, but drove the traitors out of his kingdom, walled in by perpetual darkness. Furthermore, for these Angels, a seat of exile—either lighter or heavier—is established according to the nature of their sin. For some are nearer to the Empyrean heaven, namely the *Fiery and Aerial* ones; others indeed are more remote, namely the *Watery and Terrestrial* ones, for they flee the light of heaven as much as possible because they are weakened by its presence. Whence they are called *Lucifugi* <note>light-fleers</note> by Marcus <note>Likely referring to Marcus Eremita or a similar early Christian writer on the soul and demons</note>, as we shall demonstrate below.

After Lucifer with his associates was cast down from the face of the Empyrean heaven into the lowest heaven, from that time he is certainly sometimes called a slanderer or *accuser*, because he pecked at the good with false calumnies: Whence *Revelation 12: The accuser has been thrown down*. Sometimes he is called by the name of *Dragon and Serpent* on account of his poisonous cunning; he is also compared to a *Lion* because of his bold violence: whence Peter, in his first and last [chapters], says: *As a roaring lion, etc.* And because he is stubborn and rooted in his wickedness, he is even sometimes named a *Boar*, as in *Isaiah 25*. He is also called a *Snake*, inasmuch as he hides under darkness. Augustine, in his commentary on Genesis, book 8, marks him, along with Plato, with the name of *Cacodemon* <note>Greek: "Evil Spirit"</note> as if with a brand. But Plato calls all subterranean and dark demons "deserting angels," "evil demons," and finally "wicked spirits," because they are driven by a certain wonderful and voluntary zeal for doing harm, as we shall declare in the following chapter.
