### CHAPTER VI.

->*Concerning the bodies, sufferings, properties, and types of evil demons.*<-

---

<margin>Augustine, *On Genesis* <note>original: "August. super Genes." refers to *De Genesi ad litteram*, where Augustine discusses the nature of angels.</note></margin>
**I**T IS necessary that these demons, according to the nature of the place to which they are banished, accidentally take on bodies that are either thicker or thinner; for the Fiery ones are more <term>subtle</term> <note>meaning less dense or more refined</note> than the Aerial ones, and these more than the Watery ones, and those again more than the Terrestrial ones. Although I am of the same opinion as **Augustine**, that all Angels at the beginning of their creation had aerial bodies, this same point also seems to be confirmed by **Psellus** <note>Michael Psellus (c. 1017–1078), a Byzantine philosopher whose "Dialogue on the Operation of Daemons" was a primary source for Renaissance demonology.</note>. He says that the bodies of the good Angels are as if they were immaterial, but he asserts that the bodies of the evil demons are in some way compacted of matter and are like the bodies of shadows. He proved through various examples in his booklet that these are even subject to <term>passions</term> <note>In this historical context, "passions" refers to physical vulnerabilities or the capacity to be acted upon by external force.</note>: they can be cut and divided by the blow of a sword (feeling pain in such a division), can finally be burned by fire, and even turned into visible ashes. For without a doubt, if they had only aerial bodies, it would be necessary for them to be entirely subject to such physical effects, just as experience constantly teaches that the air itself, if it is struck anywhere, must suddenly recede, make a sound, and be divided by the blow. Truly, they could not yield or give way to such sufferings in respect to their original composition, which was the same as the substance of the Angels (which we said a little earlier was fashioned from the spiritual elements of the <term>Empyrean heaven</term> <note>The highest part of the heavens, believed to be composed of pure light or fire and the dwelling place of God.</note>). Rather, they are vulnerable because of their participation in corruptible and material elements, with which they are mixed and more or less burdened according to the gravity of their sin. **Orpheus** also clearly confirms this from various descriptions of demonic bodies; he affirms that those of the Earthly Demons are certainly more visible to us, and more frequently met and encountered by our senses. **Agricola** also made mention of these in his book *On Subterranean Animals* <note>original: "Agricola in lib. de animalib. subterran." Georgius Agricola (1494–1555) was a scientist famous for his work on mining; he included spirits like "kobolds" in his classification of underground creatures.</note>. The natures and properties of these demons exist as utterly opposed as possible to the Great God and His creatures. For when the Devils had unsuccessfully tempted the Divine Majesty, they immediately turned their malicious thoughts toward this goal: since they could not harm God, they would at least lay wicked snares for His most excellent creatures, those endowed with the divine image. <note>A handwritten mark, perhaps a checkmark or arrow, appears here in the left margin.</note> For they harass quiet and innocent people, bringing them loss, misery, and harm; and, unless their great audacity and malice were restrained by the good Angels, everyone to a man would daily feel their implacable tyranny. For, as **Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> says, there is no evil that they do not dare to commit, for they have diseased and entirely violent habits. Furthermore, it happens not infrequently that their malice is exercised—by divine permission—in punishing impious men. Hence the **Platonists** called the dark demons the "avengers of crimes and impiety" (looking toward the ordering of divine justice). But here the merciful and most divine goodness of GOD offers itself to our consideration. For what is more cruel than this troop of demons? What is sharper or more inclined toward any kind of malignancy? For according to **Isidore** <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), an encyclopedist of the Middle Ages.</note>, they know some things by the subtlety of their nature, understand others by the passage of time and experience, and perceive others by revelation from the good Angels; and they most greedily desire the ruin and unhappiness of men. But behold, by their own strength they conquer no one and overthrow no one, only seducing the minds of men with certain disguised and deceitful persuasions, as **Gregory** testifies in Book 32 <note>Referencing Gregory the Great’s *Moralia in Job*.</note>. Sometimes, therefore, they lull human minds to sleep with sluggishness; at other times they vehemently disturb their peace, either by violently agitating the elements or by...

From this name, Apollo is called *Pythius*, and the woman in the book of Samuel <note>The "Witch of Endor" from 1 Samuel 28.</note> is called *Pythia*, who had a Python in her belly. This kind of Demon meddles in oracles and creates deceptions for the human race through uncertain and doubtful divinations or predictions.

<margin>7</margin> In the seventh degree are the *Furies*, the sowers of evils, the mothers of discord, war, and ruin; and their prince is *Abaddon*, that is, "the exterminator and destroyer."

<margin>8</margin> The eighth dwelling is possessed by the *accusers and slanderers*, whose prince is called *Astaroth*, who joyfully and swiftly exaggerates and insists upon our sins before GOD.

<margin>9</margin> The last place is filled by the *Tempters or Lurkers*, who are present as individuals to every individual human, and have received the name of *Genii* <note>In Roman mythology, a 'Genius' was a guardian spirit or personal daemon assigned to a person at birth.</note>. The *third* is "terrestrial," which dwells mostly around the earth and opposes all human plans and machines.

# CHAPTER VII.

->*Which region of the lower heavens does Lucifer, with his angels, most frequently inhabit?*<-

The Devil, the Prince of rebellion, once called **Lucifer** <note>literally "Light-bringer"</note>, but now called **Lucifugus** <note>literally "Light-fleeer"</note>, stays more in the Northern parts of the earth with his legions who are closest to him in the gravity of their sin. This agrees with Holy Scripture, where we are taught that Satan holds his seat in that part of the world; which indeed would be by no means difficult to confirm, both by manifest reason and by living examples. For if we exactly consider the nature of that extreme part, we will see its location agrees perfectly with the disposition of the Light-fleeing demons. For Olaus Magnus <note>A 16th-century Swedish historian and cartographer famous for his descriptions of the North</note> says that the region of Biarmia <note>A historical region on the northern shores of the White Sea</note> has the Arctic North Pole for its zenith and the Equinoctial for its horizon. He says further that in its outer parts (namely those looking toward the Tropic of Cancer), only a single natural day shines in the solar year. For there the year is divided into two equal parts: into a single artificial day, and then also into a single night. Day emerges when the Sun enters Aries <note>the spring equinox</note>; night begins when it leaves Libra <note>the autumn equinox</note>. But in parts further from the Tropic, and placed more under the Pole and beyond it, a certain immense part of the earth is found where the Sun never shoots its rays, but which is obscured by perpetual darkness and gloom. Freigius <note>Johann Thomas Freigius, a German humanist scholar</note> also asserts this in his *Geography*, stating that the part of the Frigid Zone closer to the pole is never illuminated nor warmed, but bristles and stiffens with cold and darkness. Hence it is demonstrated by manifest reason that these Light-fleeing demons take greater pleasure in this region of the earth, since they naturally hate the presence of light as an image of GOD; to avoid it <margin>Apuleius, Book 2 of the *Metamorphoses*</margin>, they withdraw into its dark places. And the ceremonies of the ancients seem to confirm this, as it was their custom to place very large lamps, with sufficient oil for light, next to the corpses of the dead, so that demons of this kind serving <term>Cacomagis</term> <note>From the Greek "kakos" (evil) and "magos" (magician); refers here to evil spirits or the dark arts</note> might be deterred by the great glare of the light and restrained from their usual slaughter. But in this place, since it always provides the absence of light, it is a wonder how they gather there in swarms; which, since it has been so ordained by the most high GOD, can in no way be avoided. Moreover, here the misery of these demons, and—

### C H A P T E R VIII.

#### *Concerning the various names of the soul, and the uncertain opinions of the ancient Philosophers regarding its essence.*

The lowest species of spiritual creatures is called the **Soul** <note>original: 'Anima'</note>, insofar as it grants life to all things. Whence some of the Gentiles called it wind and spirit. It is also called the **Mind** <note>original: 'Animus'</note>, insofar as it possesses a certain will; **Reason**, insofar as it judges directly; likewise **Spirit**, in respect to breathing; and finally **Sense**, while it perceives, as **Isidore** <note>St. Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), an encyclopedic scholar of the Middle Ages.</note> testifies in *Book 15, Chapter 14*. But so that it may be more fully understood by everyone what this final species of intelligences is—since the ancient **Greek**, **Arab**, and **Latin Philosophers** who labored in the exploration of its nature brought forth opinions about it that were not so much certain as they were diverse and wavering—we therefore deem it worthwhile to first explain their opinions in this place. For some were pulled here, some there, and all, distracted by diverse sentiments, brought forth various judgments concerning it. **Plato**, therefore, defines the soul as an essence living in itself; **Aristotle** as the act of a physical organic body having life in potentiality; **Zeno** as a number moving itself; **Xenocrates** as a number moving in itself; **Aristoxenus** as the principle of number; **Pythagoras** as harmony and the concord of melody—with whom **Dinarchus** agrees, asserting it to be the principle of the four elements in the body with which it is joined, their most beautiful temperament and harmony; **Hipparchus** as fire or a fiery force; **Heraclitus Ponticus** as light; and **Another** of the same name as a stellar substance...

...a certain spark; *Posidonius* calls it an "idea," insofar as it is the form of a living species; *Asclepiades* imagines it as a kind of string <note>original: "chordam," suggesting a musical string or tension</note>, providing the five senses with the faculty to carry out their functions; *Hippocrates* considers it a subtle spirit, dispersed through all the passages of the body; *Democritus* <note>The Latin text reads "Democrates," but refers to the atomist philosopher Democritus</note> believes it is an uncertain subtle spirit made of the smallest and indivisible little bodies, which he calls atoms, running together and clinging to one another. *Tertullian* and *Avicenna* claim that the soul is born from a soul just as the body is procreated from seed, and that it multiplies in the same way that the light of many candles is lit from a single flame. *Thales of Miletus* calls it the motive power <note>original: "virtutem motivam"</note> of every thing; and from this is derived his opinion that a magnet is animated because it draws iron plates to itself. *Alcmaeon* compared it to the celestial bodies because it is a most mobile thing—indeed, always in motion—and he says that from this disposition its eternity can most easily be discerned. *Parmenides* wants it to be made of earth and fire; *Epicurus* of fire and air; *Empedocles* and *Ericrates* say it is the strongest thing in the body. Finally, some feel it is the brain, *others* the blood (such as *Critias*); *others* believe it to be vapor and moisture; *certain others* altogether deny that it is a substance at all. However, although the assertions of these ancient philosophers seem for the most part to disagree very seriously with one another, we shall clearly declare from the writings below that some approach closer to the truth than others, and indeed some even agree with the truth itself.

# C H A P T E R IX.

## What is the soul? And concerning its properties.

<margin>Agrippa book 3, ch. 37</margin>
ACCORDING TO the opinions of *Augustine, Damascene <note>John of Damascus</note>, Isidore, Bernard, Remigius, Chalcidius,* and nearly all philosophers, both Pagan and Christian, we gather that the nature and disposition of the soul is explained in a twofold way: either it is considered by itself—that is, separated from the body—or insofar as it is joined to the body and gives it form <note>original: "informat," a technical term for the soul acting as the organizing principle of the body</note>. Therefore, as it is understood in its own proper and free disposition, it is described as: I. Being a certain divine light <note>original: "lux quædam divina"</note> created according to the first exemplar—that is, in the image of the uncreated light—and adorned with a kind of angelic beauty. <margin>Damascene's sermons and Bernard; Damascene in the same place; Seneca; Augustine.</margin> II. A spiritual substance, emanating from divine fountains; simple, indissoluble, immortal, free, incorporeal, and invisible; lacking size, shape, weight, and color. III. *A rational intellect.* IV. *An intellectual spirit, partaking in reason, always moving and tending toward happiness by its own nature.* V. *Finally, a divine mind, understanding all things and assimilating itself to all things.* And indeed, in this description, its properties are outlined with great precision. *One* of these properties is to illuminate knowledge: hence, in the *Theological Resolutions (tract 2, part 2, portion 3, question 2)*, the intellect is called the *light and reason* of knowing, since it is the *active* principle of knowledge. *Another* property is to lead the <term>Microcosm (the "little world," a term for a human being who reflects the structure of the entire universe)</term> back to GOD by its presence, as is held in the first chapter of *Genesis*; hence we defined the soul as a light created in the image of the uncreated light. Its *third* property is that, since it is a most pure, simple, spiritual, invisible, and incorporeal substance, it has communication with the higher intelligences, and—to speak with *Iamblichus*—through the harmonies of its essence and actions, it sometimes reconciles itself to the divine. The *fourth* is that, while it is enclosed in the body, it never permits it to die, because it is life itself, nor is it ever destroyed by the violence of death (as *Porphyry* speaks most excellently). Hence, with the Sages, we call it immortal and indissoluble. But it is, moreover, distinguished by another property,

<insert>←</insert> [the soul is constituted] so that it may always remember itself and never fail to understand itself. For it knows nothing so well as that which is present to it, and nothing is more present to the mind than the mind itself; as *Aurelius Augustine* <note>The author refers to St. Augustine of Hippo</note> testifies in *books 10 and 14, chapter 10* of his works. Whence, by its essence, the soul is likened to the earth; by its imagination, to water; by its reason, to air; and by its intellect, to the firmament <note>This describes a hierarchy of the soul's functions matching the four elements and the heavens.</note>. Its *sixth* property follows, which is, according to *Bernard* <note>Likely St. Bernard of Clairvaux</note>, to be the companion of Reason. The *seventh* is that it tends by its own nature toward blessedness, which *Porphyry* calls the "divine life" itself; the contemplation of this state merges the contemplator into one with that which is contemplated, as can be seen in the aforementioned author. It is for this reason that *Bernard* called the human soul a participant in blessedness and an heir to salvation. <insert>←</insert> The *ninth and last* of its properties, which we have observed from the previous definition, is that it is moved always and without ceasing. Therefore, it is certain that the soul is a most lively form and a primary act; hence it is called by *Plato* in the *Phaedrus* "a number moving itself," and by *Xenocrates* "a number acting in itself"; for the soul is moved within its own spirit. From these things, therefore, it clearly appears that the first of the aforementioned properties concurs with the opinions of *Hipparchus*, both *Heraclituses*, and *Epicurus*. Through the third property, the wisdom of *Plato* and the depth of *Alcmaeon* shine most clearly. Finally, the sentiments of *Thales of Miletus*, *Aristoxenus*, and *Xenocrates* agree with the ninth property.

Furthermore, insofar as the soul is joined to the body, we have described it in two ways: either with respect to the Microcosm <note>The "Little World," a common Renaissance term for the human being as a reflection of the entire universe.</note> alone, or insofar as it relates to animals and plants. As it is joined with the body of the Microcosm alone, the Soul, along with its vehicle <note>term: *vehiculum* — a "subtle body" or spiritual carriage that allows the immaterial soul to interact with the physical body.</note>, is defined as an incorporeal principle, a proportional number, and a primary act adapted to our bodies, by whose presence we live, feel, move from place to place, are endowed with reason, understand the first principle, and are capable of good or bad will. From this description, we have observed certain properties of the soul regarding the disposition of the human body: of which the *first* is that it is a principle connecting the four elements in composition so aptly and congruously that it imparts to them a most beautiful temperament and a sweet harmony. The *second* property is that, insofar as it is a proportional number, it has the power to rightly arrange the parts of the body through a certain harmonic consensus for the purposes of life, sense, motion, and action. And this kind of proportion in the human body produces "human Music" <note>original: *humanam Musicam* — the Pythagorean and Boethian concept that the healthy human body and soul exist in musical harmony.</note>, which is nothing other than concord, through which the soul loves the body and its parts. Whence the opinion of *Pythagoras* was not unsound when he considered the Soul to be a concordance of melody. *Third*, it is necessary that the body where this soul is found lives, feels, moves, and reasons. *Fourth*, that in its motion it is always capable of good or bad will; for although when free and separate from the body it never ceases to remember itself and understand itself, as has been said, yet insofar as it is involved in earthly things, which it draws in through the senses, it is never accustomed to perform that quite so exactly. And here indeed we think the sentiment of *Iamblichus* should by no means be rejected, by which we are taught that whatever passions of animals exist, they do not reside in their souls, but in the body, which possesses a certain quality under the soul by which it acts and suffers. <insert>→</insert> Its *last* property is that it universally rules and governs the body, according to the opinion of *Remigius*, no differently than a sailor governs a ship; or according to *Chalcidius*, just as a spider remaining in the center of its web is perceived to move the whole web by its own motion, so also the soul, hiding in the heart—which is the center of the body—is accustomed to move the entire mass of the body. However, as this spiritual creature relates to animals, its definition

of it, belongs to all these [animals] just as much as to humans; except that it does not bring them intellect and reason. This is the <term>specific difference</term><note>The defining characteristic that distinguishes one species from another in Aristotelian logic.</note> that separates humans from the brute animals, which are called irrational because they lack these faculties. Therefore, through the presence of this soul, they live, feel, and move locally in the same way as a human; yet they understand nothing, but only distinguish and recognize certain things through their senses. Similarly, the soul in plants is defined in the same way as in brute animals, except that it does not provide them with sensation. Therefore, just as the soul does not make beasts participants in reason, so it leaves plants devoid of sense. This description of the soul, then, applies to any species of animal: namely, that it is a certain sensible force, or a spirit giving life to an animated body and granting it the sense by which it perceives and discerns material, sensible things—that is, the corporeal forms of bodily things, whether present or absent, internal or external. 

As it applies both to animals in general and to plants, it is defined by <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749), a Syrian monk and theologian.</note>Damascene in Homily 26 and by Aristotle himself: it is a certain force in the body, the heart of life, imparting growth and generation. That is to say, it is a certain power, or <term>first act</term><note>Original Latin: *actus primus*. In Aristotelian philosophy, the soul is the 'first actuality' of a natural body that has the potential for life.</note>, in a living organic physical body, converting nourishment into the substance of the thing nourished so as to preserve it in its being, bring it to its proper size, and allow it to generate its like in species. In this description, indeed, three powers of the vegetative faculty are expressed, namely: *to nourish, to increase, and to beget*. From this description of the soul, we can gather many other properties; since these are readily known to those who study philosophy without further elaboration, we shall refrain from speaking of them in this place.

# TREATISE I. BOOK IV.

->*Just as the world and the parts of the world consist of body,*<-
->*So a spirit stands between them as a medium, which they call*<-
->*Neither body nor soul, but that which alone, participating*<-
->*In both, reduces these extremes into one and the same.*<-

The world therefore has a soul, as do the heavens, the stars, and the elements, with which they generate a soul in those lower and mixed things; because, to use the argument of <term>Augurellus</term> <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello (c. 1441–1524) was an Italian humanist and alchemist; his most famous work, *Chrysopoeia*, sought to reconcile alchemy with Christian theology.</note>, bodies are perfect; and it is necessary that their perfection proceeds from a certain soul. What doubt is there, then, that the world lives, as it were, and moves with a natural motion, since it is a most noble body, and consequently possesses a most vigorous soul? This soul suggests life and motion to the world by means of a certain most pure spirit, which is the vehicle and medium by which the soul is transferred to lower things. 

But as to what this soul of the world might be—although we have already spoken enough in the chapters regarding the universal form and the description of the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest part of the celestial world, believed by ancient and medieval cosmologists to be composed of pure light or fire and to be the dwelling place of the Divine.</note>—we will nevertheless briefly examine in this place what several others think of it, along with a light touch of our own opinion. This world soul is, according to some, a certain essence filling all things, penetrating everything to the very center, binding and connecting all things so that it renders the entire machinery of the world as a single unit. It is like a single <term>monochord</term> <note>A musical instrument with one string used to determine mathematical relationships between musical intervals; here used as a metaphor for the harmonious "tuning" of the universe.</note> resonating through the three kinds of creatures <note>Likely referring to the Intellectual (Angelic), Celestial (Heavenly), and Elemental (Earthly) realms.</note> by a single breath and a single life alone. In the specific parts of this definition, both the aforementioned opinions of the ancient Philosophers and those of the moderns are excellently depicted, as is declared more at length in the previous chapters on the soul. 

According to others, the world soul is described as the power of <term>GOD</term>, and as it were the <term>GOD</term> of nature itself, or the intermediary soul of nature, through which <term>GOD</term> is said to be everywhere in the world, filling it, governing it, and continually preserving it. And this is that divine power which <term>GOD</term> liberally rains down upon created things from the perennial fountain of His Spirit, by which all things live, are sustained, grow, and multiply; which world soul they believed to be located chiefly in the Sun. For many philosophers assert that the solar body received its extraordinary splendor and beauty from there; and they report that there is nothing in heaven that more reflects the likeness of <term>GOD</term> in its light and clarity; indeed, they judge that any thing, insofar as it is capable of light, claims so much of <term>GOD</term> for itself. 

We conclude, therefore, that this world soul is, as it were, the act and essence of the light created on the first day, submitting itself from the Empyrean heaven through the sieve of the Crystalline heaven into the lower regions. On the fourth day, it gathered itself in the Sun as if in the center and heart of the ethereal heaven, and from there it shoots and extends itself everywhere in a circular motion. <term>Augustine</term>, in his *Book on Free Will* <note>original: "Augustinus in lib. de lib. arbit."</note>, seems to argue that this formal nature of light is the "form" of every thing, and the soul for this reason. For he says that light holds the first place in bodies, which is the very disposition of the soul itself. Furthermore, in the book *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* <note>original: "in libro super Genesin ad literam"</note> and elsewhere, it is said that light is of such nobility that even corporeal things are judged more noble and perfect the more they participate in light, as is clearly seen in the elements. For there is nothing in the whole world more worthy than light, since it is a certain simple act, converting all things to itself with life-giving heat, permeating all Beings, leading their qualities and virtues through all things, and finally dispelling all darkness and gloom. And hence it is that the Sun—on account of the excellence of its clarity, like an ethereal King and Emperor of the corporeal world holding the scepter and rudder—is placed in the middle of it, illustrated excellently with radiance above the rest of the world's creatures, inspiring and pouring life, sense, motion, and vegetation into the lower things

->through its rays and<-
->infusions.<-

### CHAPTER XI.

->*That the intellectual soul, although it is composed in the same way as many Angels, nevertheless differs from them for several reasons, and concerning the immortality of the soul.*<-

Almost all philosophers, both ancient and more recent, testify that the **SOUL** is composed of matter and form. But a composition of this kind does not arise from pre-existing matter, as is the case with things that are generated and corruptible, but rather from nothing—that is, from matter that did not exist before and was produced through creation. From this creation, the Empyrean heaven <note>The Empyrean was considered by Renaissance thinkers to be the highest part of the universe, a place of pure light and the dwelling place of God and the blessed.</note> and its creatures—among which souls are numbered—are derived, as is more extensively declared in *Theological Resolutions*, treatise 2, part 2, portion 3, question 3. And although the composition of souls and angels is the same, it has been found by both philosophers and theologians that these two pre-celestial creatures differ in species for many reasons, as stated in the aforementioned treatise. The *first* of these reasons is because the more noble a created form is, the more it is multiplied through specific degrees; this is also confirmed by Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote extensively on the soul and the divine.</note>, who distinguishes intelligences into four degrees. Since the intellectual creature is the most noble, it must have many species; consequently, the Angel and the Soul are not of the same species. The *second* reason is because their manner of understanding is different: it is greater in Angels and lesser in souls. The *third* is because the Soul is sometimes discursive <term>discursive: the process of reasoning step-by-step from one premise to another, rather than knowing a truth instantly through intuition.</term>, specifically insofar as it is in the human body; whereas an Angel is always intuitive and without discourse. The *last* reason is because the Soul is the perfecter of the body; whereas an Angel brings nothing to the perfection of the body.

<margin>☞</margin>
From these points it is clear that the Soul is a lower species of intelligence, closest to humans and most suited for governing their bodies, yet it is immortal and survives perpetually after the corruption of its body. For although the power of composite matter is naturally corruptible and grows old with time, the operation of the rational Soul and mind is by no means consumed by the passage of time, nor does it become older; on the contrary, it seems to grow younger and to bloom again in a wonderful manner. For wisdom flourishes in the elderly, and prudence increases with the lapse of time. Furthermore, since understanding is a rational operation of the soul that does not depend on the body—because no bodily organ determines it—it is certain that the soul itself is incorruptible. It is also incorruptible insofar as it naturally desires blessedness <note>Original: *beatitudinem*, referring to the ultimate state of spiritual fulfillment or union with the Divine.</note>, as was said before; this natural desire is not in vain, since the Soul is capable of possessing blessedness. Wherever there is blessedness, there is security; where there is security, there is immortality and incorruptibility, as found in *Theological Resolutions*, treatise 2, portion 3, question 2. In these arguments, authors certainly seem sometimes to mean the Mind, sometimes the rational spirit (insofar as it desires blessedness), and not infrequently the mind together with the spirit, from which the composition of the rational soul is made.

<margin>☙</margin>
We conclude, therefore, in addition to the aforementioned reasons, that the soul is incorruptible due to the nature of its composition; for no contrary elements meet in its composition, since the spirit—which is, as it were, the matter of the soul—is airy, while the mind—which is the form of the composite—is fiery, being of the spiritual substance of light. Since air and fire are most friendly to one another, and one is like the food of the other, while the other is like the life and soul of its nourishment, they are joined together in a natural marriage by what are like perpetual bonds. They act upon and are acted upon by each other without the destruction of one or the other, just as a man and woman coming together. Furthermore, the abundance of the light-filled form has so satisfied the appetite of the spiritual matter that it does not desire a new form at all; it is so "formal" <note>In this context, meaning the substance is completely defined and filled by its spiritual form, leaving no "room" for change or decay.</note> in its substance that Wise men have written that it even divinely gave form to the thick little body of the Microcosm <term>Microcosm: literally "little world," a term used to describe the human being as a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</term> made of earth and mud.

# CHAPTER I.

->*On the substance, nature, and disposition of the stellar body.*<-

Almost all philosophers agree on this point: that stellar bodies consist of the specific substance of the middle heaven. Aristotle also, in his book *On the Heavens* <note>Latin: *De Caelo*</note>, maintains that the stars are made of the same material as the heaven in which they are placed. However, we do not entirely agree with them; we say instead that the solar body is derived from a dark mass driven out from the upper heaven, as we shall declare in its proper place below. Regarding the constitution of the other stars, it is necessary that some degree of density and opacity exists within the stellar body so that it may be rendered visible; such density, however, can hardly be found in the thin substance of the sky. And this is what those most skilled in the science of Optics have argued. *For*, says Algazel <note>Al-Ghazali, an 11th-century Persian philosopher and scientist</note> *on the nature of the mirror, no part of the celestial sphere is an object for the power of sight, nor capable of receiving and retaining the light of the Sun, except for its denser part, which we call the star itself.* He gives the reason that since the rest of the sphere is thinner, the light projected toward it is not bright—that is, it is not illuminated—because it lacks color, and consequently, it is not visible. For Hatten <note>Alhazen, or Ibn al-Haytham, a pioneering physicist often cited in medieval and Renaissance optics</note> says in Book 1 of *Perspectives* <note>Latin: *De Aspectibus*</note> that an object without color cannot be seen because, as he says, *a visible thing is only seen according to the light within the object, and visible light only occupies that which is colored.* Furthermore, the aforementioned Hatten gives another reason why the thinner part of the sphere is not seen: because it is necessary for the thing seen to offer resistance to the sight. Specifically, it must not be transparent, or if it is, it must be much thicker than the transparency of the air between the eye and the object; such a subject cannot exist without color or something similar. From these points, therefore, it is certain that a <margin>→</margin> somewhat opaque and colored body is required to receive and retain rays of light. The thinner matter of the middle heaven, as it was created on the second day, could not be of this kind because of its excessive transparency. Rather, after the Sun was positioned in the heart of heaven on the fourth day, the nature of the Sun converged to form all the other wandering stars <term>wandering stars|The planets, distinguished from the "fixed" stars of the firmament</term>. For the Sun attracted the subtler parts of the lowest heaven upward toward itself and joined them with the substance of the middle heaven, gathering the bodies of the other planets according to their different positions, as we shall teach a little further below. 

But because some matter is more suitable than others for receiving light, we believe it must be asked what substance nature chose as most fit for building stellar bodies. It is necessary that they incline toward the nature and disposition of the place where they are enclosed; therefore, they must be free from all earthly filth and opacity—except for a certain small darkness to blunt their excessive transparency. Thus, although the solar body is fashioned from the material of the "earthly shadow" in a spiritual way, it must shed its decayed and elemental form so that it may better and more easily put on a new and heavenly one. <margin>←</margin> For we see *decayed wood* <note>Latin: *ligna putrida*. This refers to bioluminescence, commonly known as "foxfire," where decaying wood glows in the dark</note>, the greater part of which is proven to be air or spirit by the way it floats on water, attracts to itself light dispersed invisibly through the air at night, as if seized by a greedy desire to take on a luminous form; which indeed [continues to next page]

Similarly, the *scales* of certain fish do this very same thing; for, on account of their moisture, they easily reveal invisible light through a certain magnetic power, when decaying by the heat of the air. There are also other bodies which, because of the complete perfection of their substance, naturally and even gradually attract solar rays to themselves, and firmly retain those rays once attracted. For *according to the merit of the matter*, as **Plato** says, *form is given*, <note>original: "secundum meritum materiæ... datur forma"</note> since form acts according to the disposition of the matter. Therefore, <term>Gold</term> and the <term>Carbuncle</term> <note>A legendary red gemstone, often identified as a deep red garnet or ruby, believed to emit its own light in the dark.</note> are of this kind of species. There are also still some other bodies which, although they are not perfect, nevertheless contain a certain spirit within them so close to the body of the Fifth Essence—due to the purity of their disposition—that they are perceived to shine at night. An example of this is that part of the <term>Glowworm</term> <note>original: "Cicendulae"</note> which makes its entire worm-like body visible in the darkness. 

Other bodies are found which, although they are transparent, are accustomed to evidently attract solar rays in such a way that they pass from a crystalline form to the likeness of a Ruby; such a spiritual humor I myself have extracted from a most noble body, and I observed its wondrous transmutation in the Sun. Indeed, I remember seeing that spirit, on account of its natural heat acquired from the sun, ascend by itself with its newly assumed tint into the head of the alembic <note>A glass apparatus used in distilling chemicals.</note> like a most brilliant Ruby, without any violence from elementary fire. But, to speak truly, after the entry of the solar light into that Spirit—or rather, the mating of the male with the female <note>An alchemical metaphor describing the union of solar "male" light with a "female" material substance.</note>—it was rendered somewhat thicker and more opaque. From this, the ignorance of those who have judged the light of the sun to be a mere accident <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property that does not change the essence of a thing; the author is arguing here that light is a physical, material substance.</note> and not at all material, is made clear.

But to approach the matter even more closely, and to ascend as if by three steps to the summit of the middle heaven, we shall deal briefly first with the <term>meteor</term> which they call a falling star; secondly, with the matter of the <term>Comet</term>; and lastly, with the substance and constitution of the <term>Milky Way</term> or <term>Galaxy</term>.

<margin>Sulphurous spirit, separated from digested linseed oil.</margin>
I myself, while walking through the fields at night under a clear sky, *beheld a meteor star falling near me; I finally found its substance through watchful investigation, touched it with my hands, and kept it until the next day. Looking at it carefully at the following dawn, I observed that it was composed of a very viscous and slippery substance, having a consistency like frog spawn.* <note>The author is likely describing "Star Jelly" or *Nostoc*, a gelatinous algae that was historically believed to be the remains of fallen stars.</note> For its matter was whitish and obscurely transparent, spotted with many tiny dark specks. Without a doubt, therefore, the substance of this thing was made from a vapor enclosing a terrestrial spirit; it was not "on fire" as some claim, but like a mirror receiving the brightness of the stellar rays—just as stars represent the true image and brightness of a natural star through the light-rays of the spiritual heaven and solar clarity. Undoubtedly, those spots included within its cloudy transparency rendered that transparent matter more fit to receive the rays of light into its substance; indeed, if I am not mistaken, they act as wicks for the transparent humor, providing light to it in no other way than wicks provide flame to the oil of a lamp. For this same thing can be seen in the substance of the moon, in whose body denser and darker parts appear even to our eyes, not much different from the branches of a tree.

Does that which the Philosophers tell of the substance and constitution of the <term>Comet</term> differ much from this? They say that *a Comet is a subtle exhalation, not in flame, but shining from the light of the sun and stars incorporated within it*; which exhalation they say is generated in the bowels of the earth, especially when the pores are constricted by cold, but exits when the aforementioned pores are loosened and opened by heat.

We have emphasized above and quite often that these varieties of matter flow from a greater or lesser portion of "form" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the organizing principle that gives matter its properties—here, the author associates it with light.</note>.

## CHAPTER II.

### *That stellar bodies are not subject to decay.*

ALTHOUGH every substance of this world, both visible and invisible, arises from first matter <note>original: "materia prima," the formless "stuff" of the universe before it is organized</note> already led into action, which is suited by its own nature to hunger for form, and for this reason is always changeable and subject to decay where that form is found to be weaker; nevertheless, if it ever reaches a place where it finds form sufficient to fulfill its hunger, then it certainly rests—that is, it hungers no further. For every natural thing has an inclination toward perfection, in which its hunger finds its end and completion. But truly, since the measure of all perfection consists in the essence of formal light, matter rejoices in light's embrace and is, as it were, snatched up into heaven; for unless matter is in heaven, its hunger is in no way completed. It is for this reason, I say, that although the bodies of the stars, and indeed the dark substance of the entire heaven, were formed and led into action by the presence of light; nevertheless, because of the presence of a proportional form—since there are two parts of light and just as many of matter—it is necessary that the thickness of that substance be completed in its hunger and rendered perfect. Just as also, where the proportion of form overcomes matter, it is said to be "more-than-perfect" and spiritual; a substance of this kind is found beyond the convex surface of the etherial heaven. From this, therefore, it is manifest that both the form of the middle heaven (called secondary light) and that of the spiritual heaven, protect whatever substances are found in their regions from rot and the injuries of corruption, preserving them always in the same state and making them perpetual according to the laws of nature; although it is necessary that the continuation of every thing depends upon the eternal will of GOD, as under His command

# CHAPTER III.

## *That it is likely the fixed stars were created on the second day of creation; Of their origin, place, and diversity, as much in size as in brilliance.*

I t was demonstrated in the preceding sections that light was created on the first day, and that it filled the entire concave surface of the highest heaven. In this way, the light inhabiting the highest region—which we have called <term>primary light</term><note>original: "primariam"; refers to the first, pure divine light before it interacts with matter.</note>—was separated from the darkness. This light thickened the darkness in the lower parts by driving it toward the bottom and the center of the whole by its presence and action. Thus, the first day (meaning the first light) occupied the <term>Empyrean heaven</term><note>The highest part of the universe in ancient and medieval cosmology, believed to be composed of pure fire or light and the dwelling place of the Divine.</note>, and night (meaning darkness) occupied all that space interposed between the base of this heaven and the center of the whole. Next, when the light was established in its spiritual heaven, it was most active and never resting. On the second day, by its power, it acted most sharply against its opposite—namely, the dark matter thrust down below the base of the highest heaven—hostilely repelling it downward from its boundaries as its greatest adversary.

Consequently, countless parts of this primary light penetrated the <term>diaphragm of the crystalline heaven</term><note>original: "caeli crystallini diaphragma"; a theoretical boundary or dividing membrane in the celestial spheres.</note>, disturbing the rest of the darkness in the middle region. Although this darkness resisted the invasions of the light rays strongly enough, it was nevertheless gradually forced to descend in an oblique revolution down to the concavity of the lower heaven, where it joined with the darkness there. Thus, the mass of darkness in the lowest region was made powerfully dense, thick, and opaque, because the darkness of the other heavens was mixed with it. And so on the second day, there was "day" in both upper regions, which are now called the "heavens"; but "night" possessed the lowest region. That light which we have called <term>secondary light</term><note>original: "secundariam"; light that is derived or reflected from the first source.</note> (as it was derived immediately from the primary light) filled the entire concavity of the middle heaven; hence, the substance of that region is called <term>ether</term><note>The subtle, fluid-like element that was believed to fill the space of the heavens above the sphere of the Moon.</note>.

Finally, on the third day, some rays of the secondary light already illuminating this region—specifically, a third part of it—penetrated into the lowest region, which was still unformed. They reverberated all its smoky and even pitch-black vapors around the center of the universal machine. This happened with the assistance of the element of fire, arising accidentally from the motion of the heavens and the bending of the rays. There, by the power of the cold contained within the matter, these vapors were constricted into a hard mass. Now, therefore, a great doubt can arise: by what means was that ethereal heaven illuminated on the second day, and the lowest heaven on the third, since we have stated elsewhere that light is invisible in itself? We have said that it is present abundantly in every part of this heaven and the middle heaven, even during the nighttime, and yet it appears in no way to the eyes.

Therefore, so that a distinction may be made between darkness and light, it is necessary that an object of sight—both privative [the absence of light] and positive [the presence of light]—be required. This cannot be had in invisible things. Therefore, it is necessary that that invisible light be produced visibly. For this to happen, certain bodies must be sought out to act as instruments and polished mirrors, manifesting the form that lies hidden invisibly in the medium or "common spirit." The substance of these bodies must be suitable and naturally disposed to gather and multiply the multitude of light rays that are secretly hidden. Such are the stars and heavenly bodies, as we explained in the first chapter of this book. Since, however, in the middle heaven

# ON THE CREATURES OF THE ETHEREAL HEAVEN.

After that region <note>The ethereal heaven.</note> was purified from its dark and foul dross, no such bodies are found there except for those of the stars. Because the other parts of this region are so thin and refined, it is necessary that certain stellar bodies serve as the organs and instruments through which that secondary light—which is luminous only to itself—shows itself visibly to illuminate the other substances of the world. Therefore, it does not seem far from the truth that the fixed stars were created on the second day, before the completion of the creation of the ethereal heaven; for without these, it does not seem agreeable to reason that a visible "day" could appear in this heaven. For the stars are like breasts through which <term>Divine Nectar</term> <note>original: "Nectar divinum"</note>, <term>Super-celestial Ambrosia</term> <note>original: "Ambroſia ſupercœleſtis"</note>, or a "luminous milk" are poured into the lower regions, as if from a nipple overflowing with light. And the "Son of the World," whom they call the <term>Sun</term> or <term>Phoebus</term>, is nourished and suckled by this after his birth. For this kind of celestial milk is prepared in the breasts of the upper heaven, and its breasts swell before the birth of the Sun, just as a woman's breasts swell before they give birth.

*But here someone will object: was it really necessary for light to appear visibly on the second and third days, seeing as sensory beings <note>i.e., animals and humans with eyes.</note> had not yet been created?* To this, we can respond in three ways: *First*, that day could not be distinguished from night, nor light from darkness, without a visible manifestation of light; *Second*, because the celestial light descended visibly and tangibly toward the center to expel the darkness and for the vegetation of the plants arising from the earth—since three things are required for their essence: light, heat, and influence; *Third and finally*, that the Sun appeared visibly in the heaven even before the production of animals, and consequently, it is not necessary to require a sensory organ for a thing to be "visible" by its nature. From these points, it is manifest that light was manifest and visible before the creation of seeing animals.

Nor will it suffice for such doubters to assert that the holy Scriptures of **Moses** are contrary to this opinion—wherein it is found that *God made two great lights on the fourth day, and that the other stars were also made on that same day.* For here it is likely that that Sacred Prelate <note>Moses.</note> understood the other "planets" or "wandering stars," since immediately before he had made mention of the two more principal ones <note>The Sun and Moon.</note>. Even **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with hermetic philosophy.</note> seems to verify this in his sacred discourse, where he says *that when all things were in confusion, the light things were carried to the upper regions by a fiery spirit, and immediately the heaven shone in seven circles;* from which it was manifest that the seven Planets were made immediately after the ascent of fire into the highest region; however, he makes no mention of the other stars. Furthermore, it would be an irregular order if creatures were created on the same day as the <term>Empyrean Heaven</term> <note>The highest, fiery heaven.</note>, and similarly, if some creatures of the Earth were produced on the day of its creation, yet no creatures were granted to inhabit the Middle Heaven on the day of its own creation.

But perhaps someone will doubt the manner in which the mass of these stars was forged: *namely, by what path or from what subject their bodies could be produced, and raised on the second day into that place called the <term>Firmament</term>, and there remain fixed as if adhering to it;* similarly, *by what reasoning they are distinguished by such diversity of light and magnitude of body?* To which, so that I may respond to all things probably and philosophically, it must be known that immediately after the penetration of light through the "diaphragm" of the crystalline sphere—as if through a sieve—a massive conflict arose between the rays of light and the matter of dark shadow found there. This was due both to the actions of the one substance and the dullness and forced motion of the other, and also because of their contrary qualities. For the rays of light acted strenuously upon the passive substance of the darkness, pushing it downward and pursuing it so greedily and vividly that sometimes some part of the light was submerged in the bowels of the shadow and became captive, as if in the snares of a certain viscous Spirit (which is the true matter of shadow). Then, the contiguous rays, trying to redeem and liberate their "brother" from prison, lifted this darkness up on high by the greediness of this aid, as well as through the rebound and reverbe- <note>The text continues on the next page with "rationem" (ration/reverberation).</note>

But here, along with the very part of light which it contains—like a body moving toward the motion of its own soul—it is carried upward, like the substance of a Comet, to the concave surface of the **crystalline sphere**, where, by the congealing power of that sphere, it is coagulated and hardened into the form of a dark crystal, or perhaps with darker spots of shadows tending toward opacity (as we find in the matter of a **falling star**), and it clings to the substance of that sphere in the manner of ice. Simply put, <term>formal light: "lux formalis," the essential, divine light that gives shape and life to matter</term> is attracted by any part of the middle heaven to the fulfillment of its desire. Hence, whatever the nature of the middle heaven is, such also is its luminous form, since the composition of this heaven is forged from an equal proportion of the material heaven and the spiritual heaven. Therefore, if the matter of the heaven exists invisibly, it is necessary that its light also be invisible; since visible existence proceeds from the visibility and appearance of light, and the visibility of light comes from a colored object of matter. 

But, because any part of the middle heaven is forged from an equal substance of matter and light, it is necessary that where the matter is invisible due to its thinness, there the light also shines invisibly and secretly; since such matter is too transparent <note>original: "diaphana"</note> and bright, and consequently not colored. However, the thicker the matter is, the more visible its light will be. For any dimension of this heaven never ceases to desire until its appetite is filled by an equal part of light. Therefore every part of it, even the denser part, has a portion of light similar to itself, by which it may be led to the goal of perfection and freed from the door of corruption. If, therefore, the matter is visible because of its dimension, I say it is necessary that its **formal light** also appears to the eyes. 

And it is from this that those stellar bodies, on account of their greater or lesser thickness, are more or less luminous, and because of their clarity are more subject to the power of sight than the other parts of the **ethereal heaven**. The probability of this thing is shown by a common demonstration: for thin air is invisible by itself because of its subtlety; but if it is condensed into a cloud or mist by the force of cold, it takes on a visible form, sometimes bright and flashing with splendor, sometimes whiter, and sometimes fiery, or tending toward blackness or a leaden hue, according to the greater or lesser predominance of light within it. 

That the body of one star is larger and denser than another occurs according to the quantity of viscous matter enclosing the light; just as we see in this lower heaven larger or smaller vapors or exhalations rise up, according to the more effective power of the light or soul enclosed within them, which is fit for lifting a greater or lesser weight upward. But as to why the substance of one star is less bright than another, we have explained the reason above: for we said that it is more luminous or more shadowy on account of its greater or lesser opacity, according to the nature and disposition of the celestial matter. ### CHAPTER V.

*That every Spirit of Darkness carries away a little of the lucid essence of its region with it. Concerning the generation of minerals and vegetables. That the work of the third day is, as it were, a prelude to that of the following day.*

**O**n the **FIRST** day of creation, immediately after the production of the essential light in the higher heaven, it was necessary that the darkness of that same region should give way to the place of that substance of light—which is contrary to it—and be thrust downward into the depths of the second and third regions by light's life-giving activity; yet in such a way that some part of the aforementioned light was held captive in its belly, on account of its very deep penetration into the spiritual matter of that darkness. So also on the second day of creation, the darkness of the middle region is driven downward into the lowest region by the active power of the lucid rays penetrating them (which we called secondary light above), and for the reasons mentioned before, they also hold a portion of those rays imprisoned in the womb of their spiritual matter. Finally, on the third day, the three species of darkness joined and gathered together in the lower place, constituting the crude and undigested <term>Philosophers' Chaos</term> <note>original: "Chaos Philosophorum"; the primordial, unformed matter that alchemists believed was the starting point of all creation</note>, were reverberated toward the mathematical center of the machine by the power of the third light, with the help of the <term>sphere of fire</term> <note>original: "sphaera ignis"; in the traditional geocentric model, the layer of the element fire located just below the moon's orbit</note>, and were compressed into a heavy, dense, and opaque mass called the <term>physical center of the world</term> <note>original: "centrum mundi physicum"; the Earth itself</note>. The clearing out of not only these darknesses but also of the matters included within them from the aforementioned heavens was entirely necessary, since without it, the operations of light—which are to purify, illuminate, and refine—could in no way have been completed in those regions of the world. Therefore, from the retention of light in the spiritual matter of the lowest darknesses (which matter is the coarsest of all), metals and minerals of every kind are procreated; just as from the greater or lesser sparks of that same light in the spiritual matter of the darknesses of the middle region, different species of vegetables arise, and plants growing out of the earth emerge. For because the light of the middle heaven was not as effective as that primary light which is included in the spirit of the darkness of the first region, and consequently does not have the same benefit of heating, refining, and dispersing; therefore, the thickness of the earth and the humidity of the water resist it more; but, since it is the nature of every lucid thing to tend upward as if toward its natural fatherland, and because the rays of every heaven (both visibly and invisibly) join themselves with the imprisoned rays by penetration (through which union the power of both is made stronger), it follows that a <term>lucid soul</term> <note>original: "anima lucida"; the vital, spiritual spark of light that gives life or form to matter</note> of this kind, included in the spirit of the middle darknesses, gradually tends upward and raises itself from the bosom of the earth. But since this light is most familiar with the element of fire, and is bound as if to its <insert>spurious brother</insert> <note>Fire was often considered a "spurious" or lesser version of the divine celestial light</note> by a certain closeness, it is necessary in its ascent that a portion of the element of fire should accompany it; further, because the sphere of fire is touching the middle spirit, which is the vehicle of the aforementioned light, the element of fire adheres to it by the bonds of nature and is raised above the earth with it; and because the element of air is touching and annexed to the sphere of fire, therefore no [ascent] can happen...

<margin>decorative flourish</margin> That **immortal light**, which we said above—veiled in darkness with the superfluous and thicker spirit of the <term>Empyrean heaven|cœli Empyrei</term> <note>The Empyrean was considered the highest, most refined part of heaven, composed of pure light or fire.</note>—was snatched to the center of the universal machine (namely when the rude and unrefined **chaos**, fused from a triple mass of darkness with a triple kind of light, was collected at the center of the machine), having laid aside every form of corruptibility in its own proper receptacle and vehicle, is exalted into the heart of the middle heaven. This follows the opinion of **Hippocrates**, who in his *Book on Principles* speaks in almost these words: *The greatest part of that immortal thing, which we call the hot, when all things were disturbed, retreated to that supreme region, which the ancients seem to call the ether.* <note>original: "Plurima illius immortalis pars, quod calidum vocamus..."</note> And certainly it was necessary that such deformed spirits should descend to the center, since they could lay down their obscurities and impurities in no other place except in that sole seat of corruptibility and darkness, namely the unrefined mass which we have called **earth**. Similarly, it was also <margin>>></margin> necessary that the **luminous soul** be contained in such a spirit, since without its action that spirit or body could not have been purified and regenerated from its horrific filth, nor exalted into its ethereal seat; since nothing at all is rendered clean, or sublimated to the summit of perfection, if portions of light are either entirely lacking or present in too small a quantity. And hence it is that **Trismegistus** <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of Hermeticism and alchemy.</note> in his *Sacred Discourse* <margin>>></margin> writes thus: *When all things were unrefined, all things began to be distinguished and weighed, and light things were carried by the fiery spirit, and flew forth into the high region, and immediately the heaven flashed forth in seven circles.* <note>original: "Cùm omnia essent indigesta res omnes distingui & librari cæperunt..."</note> For these reasons and others of this kind, it is probable that by the will of infinite nature, the denser part of each heaven, overwhelmed by darkness with some particles of its own light enclosed in the hiding places of its darkness, fell headlong toward the center of the universal structure by the action of the rays of the primary light, and was condensed into a terrestrial mass by the constrictive faculty of cold; in which the lighter spirit of the darkness of the ultimate heaven is held to be purer and simpler than all the rest, both because of the excellence of the place from which it flowed downward, and also because of the nobility of the fire or Light which it includes. But truly that Light, although most noble in itself, yet on account of the perpetual presence of night in the womb of the earth...

And from this it follows that, just as in plant life the thick ethereal spirit is bound to fire in its ascent, so also it is necessary that this thicker super-celestial mass be connected in its elevation to the thicker part of the ethereal mass by the <margin>ℯ</margin> chains of nature; with which mass the elements also mix themselves to a greater or lesser degree, and especially Air. Moreover, the reason why these substances of each heaven adhere to one another so gradually is the extremity of appetite, by which the <margin>☛</margin> matter of one heaven, in ascending upward, desires to seize and retain the form of another; since every spirit, of whatever density, naturally tends toward the goal of perfection. It was raised up to the middle of the ethereal heaven under the form of a most polished body, attracting the ethereal body from every side by a magnetic force so that it might appear more splendid—as is clearly explained in the experiment written below. There it holds the scepter and the rudder of the entire visible world, encompasses its action within itself, and acts as the Universal Emperor; it claims for itself the names of *Phœbus, Apollo, Titan, and the Sun.*

# ON THE CREATURES OF THE ETHEREAL HEAVENS.

Many objections could indeed be brought against this opinion of ours. Among these, someone might begin by asking: if the substance of this spiritual mass were *originally* <note>original: "originaliter"</note> from the highest heaven, why does it not return again to that heaven, since it is of the same *nature* and *condition*? But an answer to this is very easily provided: namely, because the substance of the upper heaven cannot become thicker due to the immense dominance of light within it, and also because the gathered spiritual matter mentioned before is too dense to ascend higher, yet too thin and spiritual to descend lower. For this solar mass is sustained in the middle of heaven, both in respect to its matter, which it received from the earth, and primarily by its formation. For the spiritual matter of each heaven, which we mentioned before, ascends from the earth into the heaven in a manner like a pyramid; *(we are not speaking of a mathematical pyramid having a thin point and a base, but we understand a certain physical body rising circularly from a thick central base, becoming ever sharper and thinner toward the circumference)*. It ascends pyramidally, I say, in a physical way, in the manner of a tree, from whose root the dimension of its bulk always decreases as it ascends upward; the lower part of the trunk is thicker than the upper, and the branches are smaller the higher they reach; finally, the leaves and flowers are the thinnest of all its parts. And so also stands the spiritual tree of the heavens; for the earth is the thickest of all, followed by water, then air, and fire, which are compared to the small branches and foliage. The planets surrounding the Sun correspond to the flowers, and in the solar body the true seeds of this tree are gathered, through which all natural things flourish and multiply.

And certainly, if we look more closely at the anatomy of a tree, we find that a certain earthy disposition is the only obstacle hindering its other parts from returning to their proper places; for all the elements are found distinctly within a tree. Indeed, we shall even find a portion of the <term>Fifth Essence</term> <note>original: "Quintæ essentiæ"; the pure, incorruptible element that makes up the celestial bodies</note> there along with its soul, by whose motion the plant is raised upward. For if a great mass of some tree is cast into the fire and turned to ashes, we will find the quantity of earth in it to be very small. From this, it certainly seems quite probable that a certain spiritual tree, rising from the earth, is liberated from its earthy bonds by the power of the rays of natural light, just as a burnt tree is, in which the spiritual parts of whatever thickness are liberated by the power of elementary or spiritual fire. By the support of this spiritual tree, the solar seed is retained in the heart of the middle heaven, partly in the manner of plant seeds, and partly by the restraint of the permanent light of its body (whose nature is always to be the same, and therefore to keep its body in the same place with the same lasting power), because it cannot ascend higher due to its thickness.

Moreover, that there is such a power of essential light, we are taught by both natural and artificial effects: for animals are moved to the operations of their souls; similarly, by the activity of artificial fire, heavy things are known to be carried upward and retained there for the duration of that fire's vigor, and by its failure, they are known to descend again to the natural place of heavy things. We conclude, therefore, that the Sun received its matter from the earth or from condensed and coagulated chaos, but derived its form from heaven, flowing through the solar mass according to the doctrine of <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Greek-Egyptian figure credited with the foundational texts of alchemy and philosophy</note>. We say further that it was necessary for its substance, since it was denser than that of the air, to descend toward the earth, where it would set aside its shapeless darkness so that it might receive the celestial and cool form without obstacle. For since darkness in the beginning was universally dispersed through the vast <term>vortex of hyle</term> <note>original: "hyles voraginem"; Hyle is the Greek term for raw, unformed matter</note>; and since the <term>cosmic mechanism</term> <note>original: "mundi machina"</note> could not be built and shaped without gathering the aforementioned deformity into a lowlier place, it was necessary that all the darkness of the machine be driven to the center of the mechanism, as the lowlier place; because it is further removed from the seat of light, from which perfection arises. But since darkness in itself is either nothing, or like a mere accident of some subject, and consequently cannot move downward without a vehicle

# CHAPTER VII.

## *Physical and Chemical, as well as Theological reasons, defending the probability of the preceding opinion.*

**A**LTHOUGH this our opinion concerning the origin of the solar body will perhaps seem new and unheard of to the Philosophers of this age; nevertheless we shall strive to demonstrate, by some Physical and Chemical as well as Theological reasons, that it rests upon probable arguments. For what must be thought of the density of the body of the Planets, since on account of the gathering of many spirits it has a dark and in a certain way opaque shape, so that it might be more capable of receiving visible light? This is no different than how invisible air, when condensed, produces a visible, shining cloud. Since, therefore, according to the said *Philosophers*, the matter of a hailstorm cloud evaporates from the womb of the earth and in its density is altogether likened to a subtle earth, why then should that solar body not be fashioned from the most subtle matter of its "belly," since the earth is called the <term>parent of all things</term> <note>original: "rerum omnium parens." A common alchemical and Hermetic trope referring to the Earth as the womb from which all material forms are birthed.</note> which are created after it? Do not meteors, or "corruptible suns" <note>This likely refers to parhelia or "mock suns," atmospheric phenomena that look like the sun but are temporary.</note>—which are not much different from that figure of the incorruptible Sun—appear in the upper region of the air from the exhalations of the earth? Their bodies could not ascend higher into the ethereal region because of their spurious impurity. <margin>A handwritten bracket and symbol, possibly a reference mark for a specific commentary.</margin> Is it not also by the authority of almost all the aforementioned Philosophers that fire is converted into air, air into water, and water into earth by a certain thickening? By this it is also very easily seen that, conversely, earth is transmuted into water, water into air, and air indeed into fire through refinement! And that fire has something in common with the ether. Moreover, since all things are from water, what is the difference between gross water and that which is subtle, except that the latter belongs to the part of the most subtle spirit, and the former to the part of earth? <margin>A handwritten arrow pointing to this sentence.</margin> Whence it is certain that the thickness of the Sun is of the nature of earth. Indeed, this assertion of ours rests and is supported by the very words of certain Philosophers, as it is found in *Hippocrates*: *A part of that immortal thing, which he called heat, when all things were disturbed, departed to the highest periphery, which the ancients called the ether.* That is, when the triple portion of darkness of the triple heaven <note>The "triple heaven" usually refers to the division of the universe into the Elemental, Celestial, and Intellectual realms.</note>—enclosing the bright rays and constituting a rude and indigested chaos—had been gathered into the lowest heaven, the light, which they call the *Immortal Heat*, ascended, etc. Which certainly *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational "Hermetic" texts on alchemy and philosophy were attributed.</note> seems to confirm in his sacred discourse, where he speaks thus: *There was an infinite shadow in the abyss; moreover, water and a thin intellectual spirit were within the chaos by divine power; and when all things had been indistinct, the light things soon flew up to the high region, while the heavy things settled under the moist sand, and once things were distinguished and balanced, which were carried by a fiery spirit, the heaven shone forth in seven circles.* For what else would that Wise Man mean by these sayings, than that light and essential spirits, through the word of God, were in the chaos of the lowest heaven, and that then the light things—that is, the spiritual things enclosed in the chaos—were carried up into the celestial region by a fiery spirit (that is, by the bright rays enclosed in the chaos)? By which act the Sun and the rest of the Planets shone forth. From those words of *Trismegistus* it also evidently appears that chaos is a mass of darkness of all the heavens, compacted into the lowest part with captive rays. For he says: *light things are carried by a fiery spirit into the high region, that is, into heaven.* He himself emphasizes this in almost the same sense—
