# TREATISE I. BOOK V.

...speaks in his <term>Pimander</term> <note>The *Poimandres* is the first treatise of the *Corpus Hermeticum*, a foundational text of Western esotericism attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note>, where he says that a certain terrifying shadow, by a slanting revolution, **slid down and moved into a moist nature, and from the depths of that moist nature, a pure and light fire immediately flew out and sought the heights, etc.**

---

<margin>☞</margin> But setting those things aside, what should we think about the constant communication of the Sun with the earth? Since the Sun daily joins with the earth, as if with his female, or at least with some moist spirit retained in the earth—disposed as a passive recipient—which acts the part of the female or the same womb. By their annual coupling or coitus, infinite things differing in species are produced, and each species is multiplied in itself. This, surely, could not be accomplished unless there were a great affinity between the spirit of the terrestrial <margin>←</margin> and solar bodies. That affinity, without a doubt, exists on the part of the matter, whose source is the earth, and not from the form, since its source is found in the opposite part, namely, in the <term>Empyrean heaven</term> <note>The highest, most spiritual level of the universe, thought to be made of pure fire or light.</note>. Finally, since the solar body is visible, and therefore half material, it is necessary that its more corporeal part be derived from the source of matter, which we have demonstrated above to be the earth. What else did the <term>Chemical Philosophers</term> <note>Early modern term for alchemists.</note> mean, who almost with a unanimous consent said that this most noble offspring of the Sun—which **they called the son of the sun and the terrestrial Sun—received its substance from the earth and the other elements, but its form from heaven?** <margin>←</margin> Did not also <term>Behemius</term> <note>Likely referring to Johannes Behem, a writer on the customs and nature of the world.</note> call the earth, in the lamentation of Nature, the mother and nurse of all things, who conceived in her womb from fire—that is, from light? To finally come to the reasoning of Holy Scripture, if we consider more diligently the time of the creation of the earth and the solar body, we will perceive a great mystery in the order of creation.

<margin>«««</margin> For on the third day of creation the earth was made, and its purely vegetable creatures; and after the creation of the earth, on the fourth day, the spherical body of the Sun is produced, in whose dimension the rays dispersed everywhere in the heaven are gathered on that same day. Since, therefore, the Sun is a body to be placed many infinite degrees before the earth, why would nature not have made it infinitely before the fabrication of the earth? For creation began from the most perfect creature, namely light, and the ethereal heaven was finished before the creation of the earth—a creature far more excellent than the Sun. Why, unless nature preferred to choose the mass of the Sun's body from the earth to receive such a most noble form, and to make the invisible and hidden rays of the middle heaven manifest and visible? Indeed, this creation of the Sun is deeply mystical, and a clear sign of the future uncreated good that would come to men. <margin>←</margin> For just as the created super-celestial light descended from heaven into the earth—that is, into the shadow by means of the spirit—and was buried there for three days in the abyss of darkness and earth in the manner of a vegetable body after the creation of the Empyrean heaven, and then, with the assistance of the higher rays, casting off the corruptible filth of the earth, it was glorified with its own body and, as if reborn, ascended into the ethereal heaven on the third day after its inclusion in the shadow; from which place it now rains down life, form, and the power of growth upon all vegetable bodies, gifted every year with a shining scepter and diadem: **So that <term>Uncreated Light</term> <note>A theological term for the eternal light of God/Christ, which exists independently of the created world.</note>, the true and only offspring of the uncreated Father, descended to earth by divine will, took on the nature of a human body, and died according to the corruptible flesh; but through its divine and uncreated essence, it rose again on the third day after death, with its body now purified from all mortal corruption and glorified beyond human intelligence. From there it ascended into the Empyrean heaven with unspeakable splendor, where, exalted at the right hand of its Father, brighter than all clarity, it daily and liberally rains down spiritual gifts upon human souls, illuminating them with its divine light and defending them from the rage of <term>Cacodæmons</term> <note>Evil spirits or demons.</note>; indeed, washing those men who were about to perish with the water from the fountain of life, regenerating them by spiritual washing, and redeeming and saving them from the corruption of sin. Therefore, no one should consider it impossible for this created solar essence to have descended to the earth, so that it might there lay aside the opacity and filth of its vehicle or body into which it descended.** <margin>»»»</margin>

### CHAPTER VIII.

->*That the entire substance of the middle heaven <note>The "middle heaven" (cæli medii) refers to the ethereal region between the sublunary elemental world and the highest firmament of the stars.</note> was denser and darker before the production of the Sun than after its appearance.*<-

That Light, the first creature, although it served in place of the Sun for three days before the production of the celestial lights—as **Dionysius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist whose writings on celestial hierarchies were highly influential in the Renaissance.</note> testifies—was nevertheless more imperfect than the Sun, as is affirmed in the *Theological Resolutions, treatise 2, part 2, portion 2, question 1.* For it was dispersed and dissipated within a greater quantity of matter; thus, on account of the vastness of that matter, it could not manifest its effects—namely, light and heat—as powerfully to the world, since the disposition of the matter always resisted the actions of the <term>form<gloss>In Aristotelian philosophy, 'form' is the active principle that gives shape and qualities to 'matter.'</gloss></term>. It follows, therefore, that before the creation of the Sun, this light did not possess such an effective power (flowing from its heat) to thin out and dissipate the condensed matter, since a united and gathered force is always stronger. Hence, the matter of the heavens was denser before the fourth day than after it.

Wherefore it is manifest that the "day"—which the divine Philosophers <note>Often referring to the Mosaic or Hermetic traditions of philosophy.</note> held to exist before the rising of the Sun as a quality (that is, as mere light) and not as a quantity or measure of time (inasmuch as time only took its origin from the fourth day, as the previously cited *Theological Resolutions* testifies)—was far gloomier and darker due to the thickness of the ether before the Sun’s creation than after its production. For after the third day, that entire mass of secondary light, which had been diffused through the vast capacity of the middle heaven, contracted itself into the solar body. Indeed, according to **Dionysius** in *On the Divine Names, chapter 4,* it is asserted that this light was the very substance of the Sun, but not yet fully formed.

It is certainly probable that this light, which was everywhere dispersed, was gathered into that purified and exalted solar mass for the reasons declared in the second-to-last chapter preceding this, and that it produced more vehement effects in that part of the world through which it passed than when its light was scattered in every direction. Thus, it 
<margin>❧</margin>heats, thins, dispels, and illuminates more effectively. By these actions, the thicker parts of this heaven, which were equally diffused before the Sun’s rise, are now—after its manifestation—reverberated both upwards and downwards in that same region to a greater or lesser degree. By the resistance of these parts and the action of this solar body, the various spherical bodies of the Planets are produced, as we shall declare below.

# CHAPTER IX.

### *On the production of the other Planets.*

In the chapter on the constitution of the Sun, we described how the Spirit of darkness <note>original: "Spiritum tenebrarum"</note>, retaining a portion of that same light from the highest region of the world, was reverberated with the darkness of the lower heavens toward the center of the machine <note>The "machine of the world" (*machina mundi*) was a common Renaissance metaphor for the universe as a designed, functional system.</note>. There, it shed its foul and black impurity and was exalted into the heart of the ether by the power of the celestial light. We also described how the rays dispersed on the second day through the vast capacity of the ethereal heaven were gathered and collected into its substance—partly by the magnetic power of the solar matter (which seeks form), and especially because of the bright soul retained in that place, which enticed its surrounding "brothers" <note>Referring to the scattered sparks or rays of light.</note> to its aid. This is not unlike a most clever fowler who, to deceive passing birds, shuts a little bird in a cage; by its presence and songs, others of that same species are enticed into the same snares.

Therefore, once a multitude of bright rays had been collected and occupied the mass of that Spirit equally, the thicker parts of this heaven were dispelled by the power of those united rays (whose nature is to refine). They were thrust down gradually—that is, in varying degrees—toward the outer parts of this heaven. For this reason, the parts of that heaven further from its center (where the solar body is suspended) are colder, and consequently thicker and denser, especially at that extremity which tends further downward—that is, toward the center. And this is why the Planets in those extremities produce cold effects, due to the dense disposition of the place.

In the lowest concavity of the middle heaven, the thicker part of the ether is reverberated by the power of the Sun's essential rays. Because of its proximity to the sphere of moisture, it is very humid; and because of its contact with the sphere of fire—beyond which it cannot descend due to the purity of its substance—its coldness is strengthened through <term>antiperistasis <note>A philosophical concept where a quality is intensified by being surrounded by its opposite, such as cold intensifying heat or vice-versa.</note></term>. 

Thus, this lower sphere of the middle heaven stands in relation to the middle part (where the solar body moves) as the element of water in the lower heaven stands to the element of fire. Hence, the coldness of the thick ether of this sphere, by resisting the actions of the solar rays, excites an upward motion as far as the midway point between this sphere and that of the Sun. For that motion is met by another motion—namely, that of the descending solar rays. Because these descending solar rays are equal to the ascending vaporous matter, the struggle between both natures is proportional. Therefore, the power of the light is not sufficient to prevent the ascent of the vaporous Spirit to that midway point, nor are the forces of that ascending exhalation strong enough to further repel the actions of the bright rays descending to that middle point. 

Consequently, they struggle against each other with proportional forces at the same point, and by struggling, they are moved in a double circular motion: namely, from west to east according to the appetite of the matter, and from east to west following the progress of the primary light. And from this, the thicker substance of that sphere is gathered, added to, and assimilated into a single globe by the swift motion of one nature against the slow (though strongly resisting) motion of the other. This is not unlike how two opposing winds blowing together create a cloud by thickening the air. This same process occurs in every sphere of this heaven immediately before the birth of its Planet. Therefore, by the action of the descending rays and the resistance of the ascending vaporous Spirit, a double circular motion is created in the midway path between the lowest sphere of this heaven and that of the Sun; and from there is born the

That bright globe, which we call the Planet **Mercury**, is one into which solar light is visibly gathered by a certain magnetic force, and by the presence of this light, its body becomes visible to our eyes. Similarly, by the constant bouncing back of rays from this Mercurial body, certain thinner vapors are stirred up from its body and driven upward to the midpoint between the solar body and that of Mercury. At that same point, another motion meets these vapors to prevent the further ascent of the aforementioned vaporous Spirit—namely, the descent of rays from the solar body. Therefore, the equality of the nature of the **Sun** with the equality of the nature of **Mercury** generates a middle sphere between them. By the dual circular motion of this sphere, its thicker matter is gathered into one spherical mass, which Astrologers have called **Venus**. This is the reason (namely, the closeness of the nature of the matter of these two planets to the essence of the Sun) why their natural motion differs less from the solar motion than those of the other planets, as we shall explain more fully below.

There is also another motion from that lowest sphere upward toward the globe of **Mercury**, and another from the body of **Mercury** downward toward that same sphere, such that in the middle of their path, the motion of one is opposed by the motion of the other. By the equal struggle of these forces, a dual motion is excited in that middle region; by its positioning, that spherical mass is gathered from the equal nature of the Mercurial body and the moist disposition of the lower sphere, which is called the **Lunar Body**, the **Moon**, *Phoebe*, *Diana*, *Cynthia*, *Lucina*, etc. <note>The author lists several names for the Moon derived from Greek and Roman mythology, associating the planet with the goddesses of the hunt and childbirth.</note> Because its body is close to the region of corruption <note>The "sublunary" world—the Earth and its atmosphere—where things are born, die, and decay, unlike the supposedly eternal heavens.</note>, and also because it receives only a tiny amount of bright form from its neighbor Mercury, it yearns more and more for the solar form. Although the Moon is adorned by this light equally (that is, in the same proportion as it is offered), its illumination appears more or less visible to us according to its distance from or proximity to the solar body. From this, it is manifest that the greater part of it is, in a way, opaque, and consequently, a certain opacity is required for the visibility of stellar bodies. Similarly, it is certain that this body is forged from the denser substance of this heaven, since it cannot be totally penetrated by solar rays. In this way, we have three planets moving in their own proper spheres, arranged at proportional distances and order from one another between the convex surface of the lowest heaven, whose bodies must be considered thicker and denser the further they exist from the solar body.

Since there are also as many planets found above the solar body (namely, between the place of the fixed stars and the sphere of the Sun), we must diligently investigate how and by what reason they could be produced there in their distinct spheres. From this, the thicker portion of that interval is gathered into one round body, which *we call Saturn*. ## CHAPTER X.

### *Concerning the natures of the Planets, and their dispositions, by which they act upon these lower regions.*

---

ALTHOUGH it is sufficiently clear from the preceding sections that the bodies of the three lower Planets and the three upper ones <note>The "three lower" usually refer to the Moon, Mercury, and Venus; the "three upper" to Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, with the Sun in the middle.</note> proceeded from the power of the Sun, we shall here provide another reason. By this, we shall declare both that the creation of the solar body was prior in order to the bodies of the other wandering stars, and also that it was the first to receive the formal arrangement of light. For almost all Philosophers have agreed on this: that light is in the *Sun* as if in a thing luminous in itself, but in <margin>→</margin> other Planets by participation <note>original: "participativè" — meaning they share in or reflect the Sun's light rather than producing it themselves.</note>. Since the light of a star is its essential form, without which a star cannot exist or even be named, and since the remaining Planets received this light from the Sun itself as if from their own giver of form, it is necessary that the *Sun* precedes the other Planets in the order of creation, just as a beginning precedes that which begins from it. Therefore, the light sent downward from the highest heaven through its common diaphragm <note>original: "diaphragma" — a dividing membrane or boundary between the spiritual and material heavens.</note> <margin>←</margin> was received into the Solar body on the fourth day and is guarded there, as *Basil* <note>St. Basil the Great, a 4th-century Church Father who wrote on the six days of creation.</note> testifies. 

The *Sun* bestowed a certain portion of this light to every Planet, both above and below it; he gave more or less according to how near or far that body was from his seat, and also according to the disposition of the planetary body to which he gave it. And hence it is that, according to *Iamblichus*, all celestial virtues reside in the Sun; and, as *Proclus* testifies, at the sight of the Sun the powers of all celestial things are gathered into one. We believe these powers are finally scattered into this lower world through his fiery vents <note>original: "spiracula" — breathing holes or pores through which spiritual energy flows.</note>. For this reason, the *Platonists* believed the soul of the world was enclosed within the Sun. Therefore, *Phoebus* <note>A name for Apollo, the sun god.</note> sits in the middle, shining with golden hair, holding a scepter and a helm like a King and Emperor. He is most full of the light of all the stars, which he received from the intelligible world <note>The "intelligible world" refers to the higher realm of pure thought and divine ideas.</note> above all other stars because his soul is more capable of receiving intelligible splendor, as some of the *Platonists* maintain. 

Furthermore, his primary royal disposition reveals itself clearly both by reason of its composition and its effect. For he is composed of an equal part of spiritual matter ascending from the earth and of an essential luminous form descending from the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest, most refined part of heaven, associated with fire and light.</note>. Because of this, his orb is called the *sphere of the soul and of equality* by *Artephius* <note>A famous, possibly legendary, medieval alchemist.</note>. From these things it is clear that his temperament is warm in the sweetest degree (which he received from the arrangement of secondary light) and imperceptibly moist (this coming from the nature of his spiritual body). But because the abundance of his form completely satisfied the "appetite" of his matter, heat certainly predominates in his body. By the benefit of this heat, not only did the Planets receive their natural dispositions, but so did every lower thing. 

It is for this reason, then, that *Mercury*, receiving one part of his nature from the Sun and another from the moist and cold mass scattered downward in a sphere, has three parts of coldness and moisture and an equal amount from the temperament of the Sun. Therefore, *Mercury* is much more moist and cold than he is warm, because in the arrangement of the Solar body, we said that one part of the body joins with one part of the luminous soul. And hence it is that *Mercury* is so variable in his nature and so inconstant that he sometimes joins himself to good planets and sometimes to evil ones, and [will join] their natures...

...is said to take on natures both good and bad. For since it has much cold matter in its composition, and only a tiny amount of "form" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the active principle that gives identity to "matter."</note> in respect to its substance, it seeks to take on the natures of the other planets; and whichever it encounters, or whichever it has some aspect toward, it willingly receives their impressions. Hence, in its own nature it is greatly helpful, and more moist than hot. 

The *Moon* (*Luna*), however, since it is composed on one side of the nature of *Mercury* and on the other of the cold and moist mass of that same heaven, is extremely cold and moist in respect to the celestial bodies. This is because it has received only one part of heat from *Mercury*, along with one part of coldness and moisture, and two parts from the cold and moist sphere itself; hence it constantly seeks and receives help and light from the solar body through participation. 

The nature of *Venus*, moreover, because it consists of equal parts of the *Solar* nature and *Mercury*, has three parts of the Solar disposition, but only a single part of the lower cold and moist sphere which it received from *Mercury*. Therefore, she is beneficial and life-giving in her nature and fortunate for living things; for she moistens more than the Sun, and heats more than *Mercury*. Thus, she is hot in the second degree of sweetness and moist in the first. 

*Jupiter*, however, differs from *Venus* in this: that in his nature he is hotter and more masculine, on account of the proximity of *Mars*, to which he is contiguous. For he participates in a way in that nature, since he was joined with the Sun in his composition. Similarly, he is drier than *Venus* due to the proximity of the sphere of *Saturn* in the upper part and *Mars* in the lower part. Hence, his nature is clearly hot and moist, fashioned from an equal disposition of the *Sun* and a part of the thicker ether pushed toward the concave surface of the highest heaven or the crystalline sphere. This occurs because the substance of that sphere—congealed by the power of the "glacial heaven" <note>The *Cœlum Glaciale* or Crystalline Heaven was thought to be a frozen or watery sphere in the geocentric model.</note> and agitated by the power of the solar rays—meets those rays as they descend into the "middle way" <note>The region between the spheres.</note> to offer resistance. This produces the same effect in this heaven as the nature of the Earth produces in the lower heaven when combined with the heat of the element of fire descending into the middle way: namely, moisture. But because heat exerts greater power in ascending (that is, it heats more strongly), *Jupiter* therefore heats somewhat more than he moistens.

*Mars*, however, is produced from the simple action and passion of *Jupiter* and the *Sun*. Hence, his nature consists of three parts of the Sun's nature—namely, one from *Jupiter* and two from the *Sun*. He also has a portion of the cold and dry sphere which he received immediately from the disposition of *Jupiter*. Therefore, on account of the heat of *Jupiter* and the *Sun*, he has three "testimonies" of heat; indeed, he is very hot and dry—that is, he has an entirely fiery nature. This is because the nature of the *Sun* heats more while ascending than while descending, which is also proven by the nature of artificial fire placed on the grate of some wind-furnace; for below the grate it heats only a little, but above it heats vehemently. For a fiery nature is always carried upward with great violence, imitating the disposition of its origin from which it was first derived. 

But because the "malignity" of the sphere of *Saturn* reflects the nature of *Mars* from the other side, it both makes him drier through its own dryness and also, through <term>antiperistasis</term> <note>Antiperistasis: A philosophical concept where a quality is intensified when surrounded by its opposite (e.g., a cold environment making internal heat more intense).</note> from that side, inflames the nature of *Mars*, pushes his powers downward, and causes them to reverberate. It grants him a malignity fatal to human nature, not unlike a cloud enclosing lightning; it multiplies the rage of that lightning by its own contrary disposition, and renews the exhalation enclosed in its belly by the contrariety of natures, illuminating it and bringing its destructive qualities into action.

*Saturn* has a nature participating in that cold and dry ethereal mass, pushed toward those margins by the force of the Sun's rays, and in the constitution of *Jupiter*. Hence, he has three-quarters of "styptic" <note>Original Latin: *stipticæ*. Meaning astringent, contracting, or binding.</note> coldness and only one of solar heat, which he received from the nature of *Jupiter*. And from this, his constitution is very fixed, cold, and dry, greatly reflecting an "earthy" disposition and drawing his congealing coldness from the crystalline heaven. Therefore, this planet is greatly opposed to *Jupiter*, *Mars*, the *Sun*, and *Venus*, and is a vehement adversary to the generation of lower things, [snatching away] the moisture...

...absorbing the **radical moisture** <note>original: "radicale," referring to "radical moisture," the life-sustaining fluid thought to exist in all living things</note> by its dryness, and blunting the innate heat with its immense coldness. Here it should be noted in passing that the fixed stars themselves take on the natures of these Planets, or rather have possessed similar dispositions since their creation; these stars differ from one another according to the mass of their vaporous matter and the proportion of their lucid form from which they are composed. Similarly, because of the proximity of one star to another of the same or contrary condition: thus, it is learned through experience that any Planet passing under a fixed star or stars of its own condition (which they call **signs**) has a more powerful effect on these lower regions; and then it is said *to be in its house of exaltation or joy*; and if it moves under signs of a contrary condition, its strength and power over lower things are weakened; and then the **Astrologers** say that *it is in its fall or detriment*. The fixed stars, therefore, act upon the bodies of the Planets, either to hinder their virtues and natural influences, or to strengthen them and make them more effective.

---

### CHAPTER XI.

->*That it is necessary for two extremes to be produced before any middle point can be assigned.*<-

SINCE in the preceding chapters we have dealt with many "middles" <note>intermediary points or spheres</note>, which cannot be held to exist without extremes, it is necessary that the extremes be produced first in the order of creation before a middle can be reached; for nothing can be called a middle which is not placed between two extremes. For instance, heaven was not called "the middle" before the lowest heaven was created; just as **GOD** also created the **empyrean heaven** <note>the highest part of heaven, thought to be composed of pure fire or light</note> and the earth before He suspended His glowing and glorious fire in the middle space between both extremities. Nor did He produce the sphere of humidity <note>likely referring to the element of Water or the atmosphere</note> in the midst of the lowest heaven until the Fire and Earth were first revealed, between which it might move. So also **Mercury** hangs in the middle of the lowest part by the virtue of two extremes—namely, the ethereal sphere of cold and moisture, and the solar body. Similarly, it was necessary that the **Sun**, and the sphere of cold and dryness <note>Saturn</note>, precede the birth of **Jupiter**, to whom a middle place between them is assigned. Finally, since the origin of the aforementioned middles arises from the mutual action and passion of the extremes, it is necessary that the extremes be produced first by the order of nature, rather than the middles which are composed from them.

---

And certainly, they do not wander far from the truth, since we are compelled by constant experience to recognize the wonderful operations of these influences. We shall, therefore, briefly discuss in this place the nature and fourfold character of this influx of the stars. Thus, we call the "influence" of any Planet that which occurs when a spark of its lucid soul...

But if it finds matter of a contrary condition, it undoubtedly works destructively upon it. For either the obstinacy of the receiving subject receives it perversely, or its weakness cannot easily tolerate the influence. For example: <insert><u>*Saturn’s* force is indeed retentive;</u></insert> <insert><u>*Mars’s* is truly motive;</u></insert> and the former [Saturn] frequently hinders by accident when it is received by colder matter; while the latter [Mars] does so when received by hotter matter. ### CHAPTER XIII.

->*That although the heavens and the stars may be governed by "intelligences" <term>intelligences: spiritual beings or angelic movers traditionally thought to guide celestial bodies</term>, as is the opinion of the ancients, it is nevertheless not likely that they are moved by them, but rather that a capacity for motion was naturally infused into them from the beginning by the divine will.*<-

**I**t is the opinion of all the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle's philosophy</term> that the stars do not move by their own motion, but by the circuit of their sphere; and they teach that the sphere is moved by an intelligence, or its *daemon* <note>original: *dæmonio*; here referring to a guiding spirit or guardian rather than an evil entity</note>; and that these spirits received their motion from the first mover, GOD. But, as it seems to me, in things that move naturally, the cause of their motion must always be called natural, and not supernatural. For from the beginning of heaven and earth, GOD bestowed upon all creatures a "first act" <term>first act: the fundamental state of being or capacity for action</term>, as a most beautiful gift, from which they are brought into their own existence, and are led by themselves either from one state to another, or from one place to another, according to the creature’s nature. 

Since light—which we have called above the first and principal creature of GOD—is the first act, most swift in its motion, granting form, life, and motion (whether greater or lesser) to every creature by its presence, who will doubt that some light and ethereal body, whose appetite has been satisfied by the presence of formal light, has the power of moving by itself and from its own form? For have we not experienced our own eyes seeing inferior natural bodies, in which a smaller portion of that luminous form exists, performing this very same thing? Indeed, we see animals move here and there by the action and agitation of their own internal light. Furthermore, since a twofold motion is perceived in animals (for sometimes they are led by the lust and appetite of their body, and at other times by the will of the moving soul), why should it be impossible for the stars—in which the quantity of light is a thousand times greater than in animals, and from which that light of animals descends—to be led from west to east according to the appetite of their matter, and also to be carried in the opposite way from east to west according to the disposition of their luminous form? 

Yet far be it from us to try to prove that the heavens and stars are *living beings* <note>original: *animalia*; in the sense of "ensouled beings"</note> according to the decrees of the Platonists and the Astrologers, whether they be *Arab*, *Egyptian*, or *Chaldean*, since the stars are to be preferred to animals by infinite degrees of perfection. What should we think even of a subject far lowlier than an animal—namely, a plant or a tree—in whose growth motion is found from one point to another, and according to the three dimensions of its body, without any help from "intelligences"? 

But, to descend to even lowlier things, what shall be said of artificial objects, when by the action of some light or a lit candle, images that are otherwise immobile immediately move and are led around by the effect of that light, as is shown in the experiment demonstrated below? <note>The author likely refers to a "magic lantern" or a similar optical device where heat or light creates motion in paper figures.</note> Since, therefore, our artificial and elemental fire, which is derived from the effect of light, can perform such things, who will be of such a dull wit as to deny that a stronger power lies hidden in the efficient cause of fire? For according to that old axiom of the philosophers, *Whatever makes a thing such, is itself even more so.* <note>original: *Quod facit tale, est magis tale*; a principle stating that the cause of a quality must possess that quality more intensely than the effect.</note> Since all these things can be performed both by nature and by art regarding the prompting of some intelligence in these lower regions; without doubt, in the ethereal heaven, they can be perfected and completed better and more exactly because of the multitude of never-resting light which predominates there. That is to say, it is possible for a long-lasting, tireless motion—and, according to natural probability, a perpetual one—to be produced without the assistance of "intelligences." Nor do we thus [exclude] the *intelligences* or spirits of the second order, which, *as in Book 2.*

<header>CONCERNING THE CREATURES OF THE EMPYREAN HEAVEN.</header>

<margin>Chapter 4.</margin> The tradition of the *Magi* <note>The author refers to the "Magi" as ancient wise men or practitioners of hidden wisdom, often associated with Persian or Hermetic traditions.</note> has called them celestial and worldly; thus, we exclude them from the bodies of the stars, as if they possess no office or dominion within them. For we confess, following the opinion of the ancients, that beyond divine worship, they are assigned to the spheres of the world, and each presides over the heavens and the stars. They are distributed into as many orders as there are heavens in the world and stars in the heavens. For this reason, the wiser *Magi* designated some spirits as *Saturnine*, others as *Jovial* <note>Related to the planet Jupiter</note>, and so on. Nor, indeed, was that opinion of the *Platonists* far from reason, which asserts that *infinite Daemons inhabit the spherical substances of the stars, no differently than animals inhabit the earth*. They divide these into legions, over which they say kings, princes, or governors are placed. And this is the very same thing that the Abbot *Trithemius* <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a famous German abbot and occultist</note> seems to confirm, saying: *seven spirits were set over the seven Planets from the beginning of heaven and earth.* <note>original: "septem Planetis spiritus septem à principio cœli & terræ esse præfectos"</note> Of these spirits, the governor of the kingdom of *Saturn* is called *Orifiel*; of *Jupiter*, *Zachariel*; of *Mars*, *Samaël*; of the *Sun*, *Michael*; of *Venus*, *Anaël*; of *Mercury*, *Raphael*; and of the *Moon*, *Gabriel*.

We conclude, therefore, that the motion of the planetary bodies no more consists in the power of the Daemons inhabiting and occupying them than the spherical motion of the terrestrial body consists in man—who stands as the noblest among all its inhabitants and Lord over all earthly things. Rather, we affirm more confidently that the planet derives all the power of its motion from its own soul and essential form. We say this because we find in *Augustine* and the *Theological Resolutions (tract 2, part 3, question 1)* that God has *so administered the things He created, that He allows them to be driven by their own motion.* <note>original: "quas condidit, sic administrasse, ut eos proprio motu agi sinat"</note> Since God gave to the stars and His other creatures those things which suffice for their operation, they are able to have their own operations without special illumination or the assistance of [external] intelligences. For the soul of every movable body is the "prime mover"—that is, it moves spontaneously and by itself—since its matter is quite ineffective on its own and falls far short of the soul itself.

### CHAPTER XIV.

->*Why the heavens are moved in a circle, and concerning the duration of the daily motion—that is, the revolution of the heaven in the space of twenty-four hours.*<-

I fall into a very great error, if I am not mistaken, those who say that *the substance of the Empyrean Heaven is immobile*. Indeed, we said in *Chapter 2 of Book 2* that the Spirit of the Lord moved first of all in that place; by whose motion, furthermore, it is certain that the most simple Spirit of that place moves, no differently than we perceive the air to move at the motion of an inferior fire. By the presence and ineffable power of that uncreated moving Spirit, the sacred Scriptures also report that this first creature—the swiftest and most vital of all, and the enemy of stillness—was produced as if by the radiance of that same Spirit. For that *Royal Psalmist* says: *By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the breath of his mouth all their power.* <note>original: "Verbo Domini cœli firmati sunt, & Spiritu oris ejus omnis virtus eorum" (Psalm 33:6)</note> Since, therefore, light is the first and foremost power of the heavens and the universal world, it must necessarily proceed immediately from that divine and inexplicable Spirit. *The Spirit of the Lord was carried* <note>A reference to Genesis 1:2</note> in the spiritual Heaven over the waters (or the physical heaven), bounding them and attributing to them a spherical shape by its motion, as is evidently demonstrated to rational eyes by the effect.

From these things it is manifest that the motion of that same divine Spirit was not straight, but circular, so that by its motion it might make that mass of <term>hyle</term> <note>Hyle: a term for primordial, unformed matter.</note>—which it surrounded and separated from the other parts of matter excluded from the world—round and spherical. This was done because a spherical figure of this kind, insofar as it has neither beginning nor end, is in a certain way likened to the Creator; for every effect necessarily... <note>The text cuts off mid-word "quan-", which the catchword "dam" (forming "quandam," meaning "a certain") would complete on the next page.</note>

...is accustomed to have a likeness to its own cause; then also, because such a figure <note>The circular shape</note> is the most noble, useful, perfect, and convenient of all others, since it is far more capacious than the rest. Immediately, therefore, after the action of this Spirit, that first creature <note>The first light mentioned in Genesis</note> began to shine, proceeding as if from the motion and brilliance of the **uncreated light**; it is probable that it moved in the same way and with the same logic of motion, by imitating the acts of its first cause. Furthermore, the effect seems to reveal to us the path of this circular motion—that is, the starting point and the destination—namely, that it was from the East to the
<margin>/</margin> West, or rather from the right hand to the left, while facing the north pole. (For the terms **East and West** received their names from the creation of the Sun). This occurs for two primary reasons. The *first reason* is because human nature, in which that divine light predominates more than in any other animal, is accustomed to move the right hand (so to speak) with a divine appetite for its own light, and to exercise it in every manual operation as being more excellent and noble. Through this, it is manifest that the natural appetites of the primary light are moved from the right side of the heavens. The *second reason*, which indeed seems infallible, is because the "rapt" <term>raptus: the 'snatching' or driving force of the outermost heaven</term> and swiftest motion of the heavens is perceived to tend from that side toward the west. 

And since the **created essential light** proceeding from that uncreated light is said to be the most noble (because nothing is more mobile or subtle), according to most philosophers and even those most skilled in Theology—among whom I name *Augustine in his Literal Commentary on Genesis*—and is even called by him in that same place the *foundation and principle of the supreme natural motion*, it is necessary that the more grasping and swifter motion of the whole heaven be derived from its source. Consequently, it follows that the **diurnal motion** <term>diurnal motion: the 24-hour rotation of the sky</term>—by which the entire material world is revolved from the **East** (contrary to the *opinion of Copernicus*) to the **West** in the space of twenty-four hours by the power of that bright spiritual source—flows from the light itself. *Trismegistus* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage to whom many mystical and scientific texts were attributed</note> also seems to confirm this in his *first sermon* with these words: *The creative Mind, together with the Word, encompassing the circles and turning them with swift speed, turned its own machine toward itself and commanded it to roll from the beginning to the end without end.* <note>original: "Mens quidem opifex, unà cum Verbo circulos continens, & celeri rapacitate convertens suam ad se machinam flexit, eamque volvi à principio ad finem absque fine præcepit"</note> By "the beginning," he seems to mean the rising [East], and by "the end," the setting [West]. Do we not also see that Sacred Scripture, in almost every place, always puts the name of the **East** before the **West**, as in *Genesis 13:14, Psalm 50*, and infinite other places? Furthermore, in all adoration, the worshippers turn themselves toward the **East**, as in *Ezekiel 8:16, Matthew 11, Luke 13:29*, and many other places. Similarly, *that star declaring the coming of Christ* appeared in the **East**.
<margin>/</margin> And so also the coming of the Lord will be from the east toward the west (*Matthew 24:27*). By these things it is sufficiently demonstrated that the **uncreated Light** moved from the **East** toward the **West**. For what could be clearer than this? Especially since the effect of that thing is perceptible to the senses. Are we not certain that a soul is in a man or some other animal, although invisible, while we perceive his body to move here and there by itself? Do we not recognize a visible act to be included in a plant when we see it flourish and germinate? Are we not also certain that an **intellectual soul** exists above the surface of the corporal world, while experience testifies that the world itself gathers together and revolves in a natural day? The matter of this world, since it is ineffective of motion by itself, could in no way perform this motion except through the motion of the **luminous source**, which is the foundation, source, and origin of any natural motion. Consequently, it is certain that the circular motion of that first bright creature was from East to West; this motion was the primary one of all, and swifter, nobler, and more powerful than the others, since it arose from the source of universal action.

# ON THE CREATURES OF THE ETHEREAL HEAVEN.

We conclude, therefore, with the opinion of **Trismegistus** <note>original: "Trismegisti"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure to whom the *Hermetica*—a body of Egyptian-Greek wisdom—is attributed.</note> put forward in his **third discourse**, that a wider circumference in the aerial circle was carried by the harmonious divine Spirit—indeed, from the beginning toward the end—and that by the action of its brilliance and the resistance of the moist matter, a threefold circular motion is created in heaven. Of these, <margin>1</margin> the *first* is this motion from East to West, or from right to left, which we have already said is driven according to the arrangement of the first heaven's shining source. <margin>2</margin> The *second* has its cause in the matter of the stellar body and the heavens, as we shall declare below; namely, that motion which occurs from West to East, or from the left part of heaven to the right. <margin>3</margin> The *third* takes its origin from the mutual action and passion of form and matter, which we call the **motion of trepidation** <note>original: "motum trepidationis"; a term in pre-modern astronomy for a hypothetical oscillation of the equinoxes.</note>. <margin>4</margin> There are also circular motions proper to the creatures of heaven, which are stirred up by the action and passion between the matter of a star's substance (tending upward) and its form (seeking downward); of such a kind are their motions in their own **Epicycles** <term>Epicycle: A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger circle; used in ancient astronomy to explain the complex observed paths of planets.</term>, which we will also discuss more broadly below.

### C A P U T  XV.

<margin>❦</margin>#### *On the error of Copernicus and Gilbert, who assert the daily revolution of the earth.*

**C**oncerning the daily revolution, various disputes arise among the Philosophers, and it is a controversy not easily settled. Some wish for the entire machine of the world to be revolved in the space of twenty-four hours by the hurried motion of the **First Mover** <note>original: "primi mobilis"; in the Ptolemaic system, this was the outermost sphere that moved all the inner spheres.</note>, and they think that this motion occurs from East to West. Such is the opinion of the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> and almost everyone of our age, with only a few of the contrary opinion excepted. In the ranks of these exceptions, we find numbered and named from the ancients **Heraclides Ponticus** and **Ecphantus** (both **Pythagoreans**), **Nicetas of Syracuse**, and **Aristarchus of Samos**, along with several others of that same kind. From the moderns, however, we find **Copernicus**, that most skilled Astronomer, and **William Gilbert**, our colleague—who for many years has been a studious investigator of **magnetic power** <note>William Gilbert (1544–1603) was a pioneer in the study of magnetism and, like the author Robert Fludd, was a member of the Royal College of Physicians.</note>. Their opinion is that the daily revolution is in no way caused by the First Mover, nor does it move from East to West; but rather that the globe of the earth itself [rotates] from West to East according to

...while they constantly affirm that the natural progress of the Planets revolves naturally in a space of 24 hours. <margin>1</margin> therefore, it would be miraculous if all the Planets of the heaven moved according to the latitude of the world, while the terrestrial sphere—far more base and ignoble than they—constantly completed its natural course every natural day under the same elevations of the pole <note>The "elevation of the pole" refers to the latitude of a fixed observer on Earth</note>, and consequently was irregular in its motion compared to all other celestial globes; for it is certain that no place on earth is raised higher or depressed lower,
<margin>2</margin> but always possesses the same seat of latitude. *Second*, if the circular motion of the earth were completed in the space of 24 hours, the earth would move infinitely many times faster than the swiftest horse hastening on its course, a stick violently struck, or a cannonball <term>cannonball<note>original: "globo tormentario"</note></term> coming forth from the fiery mouth of a bombard <term>bombard<note>original: "bombardæ," an early type of heavy cannon</note></term>. But the violent run of a horse seems in some way to hinder the rider's breathing through the compression of the air and its resistance; a stick driven through the air by a strong arm is perceived to give out a sound and stir up no small noise; and it is proven by the testimony of experience that a ball ejected from a bombard by the power of fire induces an even greater noise while flying through the medium of the air. Yet the motion of all these things could in no way be compared with that which the earth would stir up by its daily revolution (if it were ever moved by such a motion); consequently, from that swifter motion of the
<margin>1</margin> earth, by which it would finish its daily revolution, men standing perpendicularly on the surface of the earth, great cliffs and those protruding very high from its surface,
<margin>r</margin> trees reaching into the heights, and proud palaces and towers reaching even to the clouds, would produce a far more vehement noise and clangor <note>The author argues that the friction of the atmosphere against a rotating Earth would create a deafening, constant sound</note>
<margin>*</margin> through the striking back and resistance of the air. Since all these things can be perceived by no sense, we judge that the earth is moved by no such swift motion.
<margin>.</margin> For it is not enough to respond that the air itself is also moved with the motion of the earth and gives place to it in its motion; since we sometimes perceive winds blowing violently from the east to the west, whose blasts, sent against the motion of the earth, would likely induce horrible whirlwinds and tempests on account of the opposing motion of the earth; because these things do not happen, they evidently demonstrate that the earth does not move
<margin>3</margin> by itself in a daily revolution. *Third*, we shall prove that the natural motion of the earth itself is by no means to be compared in speed to the motion of the heavens, by these experiments drawn from nature itself.

### TREATISE I. BOOK V.

For it is clear that the Earth is the center of the heavens; because the Sun and the other stars are known to maintain the same distance from the Earth in their natural motion as they do here in our hemisphere; this is surely something that could not happen if, as some falsely claim, the center of the whole were in the Sun. And we further confirm this by the following reasoning: that which is more coarse and heavy should be the center of the world. Now, the Earth is more coarse; which is proven by the fact that the higher one ascends from the Earth, the thinner and more subtle the mediums are always found to be; thus water is thinner than earth, air than water, fire than air, and the <term>Fifth Essence</term><note>The "Quinta Essentia" or Ether, the pure, incorruptible material that makes up the celestial bodies.</note> or ethereal matter thinner than fire, etc. Therefore, we say that the preceding experiments clearly demonstrate that the outer parts of the globe—that is, those tending more toward the circumference—are by nature more fit for movement than the parts closer to the center; for they are surrounded by a more agile soul than those at the center. Consequently, it is demonstrated that the Earth itself moves more slowly by nature, since it is the physical center of the entire <term>macrocosm</term><note>The "great world" or the universe as a whole, often contrasted with the "microcosm" or the human being.</note>. Wherefore it is more likely that the daily motion of the world-machine proceeds from the circumference rather than from the center; and this is clearly proven by two reasons. First, because a hundredth part of the vigor that proportionally moves the center will move the circumference; just as is clearly seen in those artificial machines described above, and likewise at the end; for it is certain that their motion, although fashioned by art, nevertheless follows a natural logic. Second, because we have declared above that in the beginning of the world, action originated from the highest fountainhead of forms; from whose source only the smallest part could descend to the Earth, both because of its great distance from the <term>Empyrean heaven</term><note>original: "cœlo Empyreo"; the highest heaven, traditionally thought to be composed of pure light or fire and the dwelling place of the Divine.</note> (for the center is quite far from its circumference) and because of the Earth's immense coldness; for in it there are four degrees of coldness <note>The author refers to the Aristotelian system of "qualities" (hot, cold, moist, dry) measured in degrees of intensity.</note> and nothing of heat, unless it comes to it accidentally, namely either from the light enclosed in the darkness at creation, or from the influences of the stars flowing into the bowels of the earth, as we said above. ### CHAPTER XVI.

->*On the nature of the natural motion of the Planets—that is, from West to East—and against those who say that the stars move according to the motion of their spheres, whence arises the observation of Astrologers regarding the motion of the Epicycle.*<-

**T**HE motion of the heavens of the middle region from East to West is not called their natural motion, but a violent and **forced** <term>raptus; literally "snatched" or "carried away" by the rotation of the outer heavens</term> motion (although in its own nature—that is, with respect to the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest, fiery heaven of pure light and the dwelling place of God</note> from whose lucid source it is derived—it also occurs naturally). For the natural motion of bodies is to follow the motion not of its source, but of that mass in which the movement occurs. And here indeed a great mystery is to be observed; namely in this: that just as the celestial motion is distinguished from inferior motions because of the excellence and perfection of its essence, and has a motion contrary to them in every way—namely, the circular, which suits all the perfections of the parts of the world; so also between the heavens of the more perfect part of the world, a great contrariety of motion arises. For although in both the superior heavens, whether spiritual or corporeal, there is no difference in the order and shape of their motion, nevertheless, in their starting points <note>Latin: "terminis à quo"</note>, there is the greatest contrariety; since the former—namely the spiritual—is carried from the sunrise [East], and the latter—the material—is carried from the opposite point of the same hemisphere [West]. This opposition of circular motion is derived from that difference which exists between matter and form; it is natural for each of these, because of the separation of one from the other, to effect contrary motions. Hence heavy things, on the part of matter, tend to move downward (as was said in the discussion on the mass of darkness), while light things move upward toward the natural seat of light (as we have sufficiently declared in the discussion on the fiery disposition and the production of the Sun). But truly, where there is the best proportion—in the embrace of the agitated and ascending matter and the descending form—there the lucid and radiant form is not sufficient to repel the ascent of the vaporous matter below; nor indeed is the ascending matter able to rise higher, since it is hindered by the rays descending proportionally. From this it happens that a double circular motion is induced in the same body, because of the different dispositions of the things concurring in its composition, namely, matter and form. For it is necessary that the ethereal bodies move circularly, because of the equal proportion of their parts, which hinders universal motion upward or downward. How the first motion, which we called *forced* <note>raptus</note>, is induced, we described above. Here, however, we will speak briefly of the motion opposite to it, namely from West to East, which we have called the *proper motion of the stellar bodies*. Although it is the office of the form to give a name and being to the body in which it resides, we nevertheless call that whole thing which moves a "body" and "mobile." If it moves by itself, it is moved by that intrinsic active principle which we called natural motion—that is, by which any body is moved according to the appetite of its nature. If, however, it has motion from an external principle—of the kind that "forced" motion is—in that case it is not natural, but motion by acci[dent]...

From this, therefore, those planetary motions are described by Astrologers as occurring in an *Epicycle* <term>Epicycle: a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle, used in pre-Copernican astronomy to explain the complex paths of planets</term>, which they call *direct, stationary, and retrograde* <note>In 'direct' motion, a planet moves forward through the zodiac; 'stationary' is the brief pause before it appears to move 'retrograde' or backward</note>, on account of the inequality of the proportion between the light and the Spirit <note>original: 'Spiritum'; here referring to the subtle, vital substance Fludd believed permeated the cosmos</note> of which all planetary bodies consist, except for the Sun. For this reason we say that the Sun has no *Epicycle*, but always maintains the same distance in its motion, because it is composed of an equal and similar proportion of condensed spiritual matter <note>original: 'materiæ spiritualis'</note> and that light. For this reason, the Sun exists as more perfect, more stable, and more regular in its motion than all the aforementioned bodies.

# CHAPTER XVII.

## *On the opposite movement of universal form and matter, and on their proportion in any heaven, and a most effective demonstration of the position of the true Sun in the middle heaven.*

---

Since in the previous discourse we demonstrated that formal light <note>original: "lucem formalem"; in this context, "formal" refers to the spiritual principle of "Form" which gives shape and life to matter</note> becomes smaller and weaker the further it tends downward, whereas matter becomes thinner, more spiritual, and smaller in its proportion the further it ascends upward, it is certain from this that the formal splendor descends from its source—that is, from the summit of the Empyrean heaven—in the manner of a pyramidal cone from its base, descending toward the earth, so that its base is touching the concave surface of the Empyrean heaven, while its point (the cone) reaches the earth. For GOD is its root, fountain, origin, and father. 

On the contrary, however, because matter arose from the abyss of darkness, and all darkness is gathered into the terrestrial mass (of which the Devil is the prince), the result is that its motion is opposite to the motion of light. The base of its pyramid is pressed into the center of the earth, while its point is raised all the way to the concave surface of the Empyrean heaven. 

From this, therefore, arises the composition of each heaven out of matter and form; thus, the heavens are more "formal" <note>spiritual and light-filled</note> the more sublime they are, and more subject to matter the lower and closer to the center they are. 

From this also comes the most luminous description of the soul, which is of a middle nature, and the most excellent demonstration of its reasoning and composition. From this arises the position and arrangement of the Sun in the midpoint of that middle nature; hence its nature is exactly tempered and life-giving, infusing <term>natural heat</term> <note>the vital warmth necessary for life</note> and <term>radical moisture</term> <note>the fundamental fluid of an organism that sustains its vitality</note> into the lower things. 

From this arises the harmonic proportion of the world and the heavens, and even the various dispositions of the elements themselves. From this come the lives of creatures and the receptacles of those lives; in short, everything brought into action proceeds from a mixture of this kind. Even the infinite differences between species arise from the infinity of points emanating from the rays or diameters of these pyramids. 

For from this come the orders of angels, where some are more eminent in administration and place than others, and closer to GOD; from this come the various temperaments of the ethereal bodies; and from this the distinction of the sublunary elements, from whose diverse natures diverse creatures are born, some hotter or colder than others, some moister or drier. 

But also in this place, as if in a mirror, a wonderful mystery shines forth, by which it is clear that all these things flow from the one and only GOD; for outside the convexity of the ultimate heaven, no angle is found except for that one and only one, who is entirely incomprehensible. And because the inner side of the Incomprehensible Triangle has its position within the convexity of the <term>Empyrean heaven</term> <note>the highest heaven, composed of pure light and fire</note>, it is declared by this very fact that GOD communicates Himself to the world—as it is by His verbal and spiritual essence that the heavens and all their power are strengthened. 

Thus, the two angles of the one triangle are contiguous and, as it were, continuous with the convex surface of the Empyrean heaven; from their rays the light of the world is derived, and by their presence (as uncreated beings), its most spiritual matter is already informed and created out of nothing. So, we say that GOD is present everywhere, which is to say that His rays are seen as if in a mirror within the <term>Universal Spirit</term> <note>the "Spiritus Universalis," a cosmic soul that connects the divine to the material</note>. 

From this it is clear and manifest that GOD Himself, both outside the world and insofar as He exists present within the world, is one and triune, whose <term>Monad</term> <note>The "Unit" or "One," signifying the indivisible source of all things</note> or the head of the triangle descends all the way to the earth, so that by His presence He might restrain all darkness into the bosom of the earth. And so, since His trigonal <note>triangular</note> form is dispersed through the capacity of the entire <term>universal machine</term> <note>original: "universæ machinæ"; a common early modern term for the structured universe</note>, GOD is said to be present everywhere—not indeed that He is contained by any place, since He Himself...

### TREATISE I. BOOK V.

He himself contains all things in Himself; but just as in the unity of some triple light, rays are seen in a mirror to illuminate the mirror itself, so the image of that triple uncreated form in the material spirit of the world, illuminated by its presence, returns a triangular form of light; whence the wise have called the world the "image of God." For according to <term>Trismegistus</term><note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom a series of influential philosophical and magical texts (the Hermetica) are attributed.</note>: <note>original: "DEVS ante mundi creationem in seipso tantummodò reluxit, & in seipsum reflexit ardorem suum."</note> God, before the creation of the world, shone only in Himself, and reflected His own heat back into Himself.

Hence it is, therefore, that the real Trinity exists outside of all things, and its reflection is within all things. Yet that formal and lucid pyramid <note>Fludd often illustrates the universe as two intersecting pyramids: one of Light (descending from God) and one of Matter (ascending from the Earth).</note> is so present in the world that it is not separated from that which is outside the world; for the base of one is also the base of the other. So continuous is the splendor of the Trinity from its real and incomprehensible essence, as the rays of the Sun are to its body. And here is perceived that immense strength of God, who presides over light, above that of the Devil, the Prince of Darkness; for even the <term>Light-shunner</term><note>Latin: *Lucifugus*, a name for the Devil or a creature that flees from the light.</note> hiding in the center of the earth is not outside the ray and power of God. But insofar as he exists as a creature, to that extent only does the base of one material pyramid arise from him; for he is contained and does not contain. For the base of the material pyramid is drawn from the center of the earth to any part of the spiritual circumference, so that clearly the Devil is known to have nothing of infinity within himself.

**Plato**, however, in his *Timaeus*, seems to understand the soul as a portion of the spiritual pyramid composed with the formal splendor of its place; indeed, for this reason he calls it a **harmonic number**, because it is constituted from the <term>monad</term><note>The number one; the indivisible source of all numbers.</note>, the **binary**, the **ternary**, and the **quaternary** number. From the **monad**, namely from the ray of the unique mind; from the **binary**, for the substance of the primary spiritual light, which is intellectual and rational, is forged from purely formal light and material spirit; from the **ternary**, because the life-giving substance of the middle heaven is made from a double portion of the Empyrean heaven and the simple ethereal spirit; from the **quaternary**, because three those parts constituting the middle heaven, and the simple spirit of the lowest darkness, concur to the constitution of the Elementary heaven. Thus **Pythagoras**, not differing much from the opinion of Plato, asserts that the **soul is composed of simple, double, triple, and quadruple proportions, and as if from a point, line, surface, and cube**—understanding the simple as mere uncreated form, the double as the first composition of two, the triple as the second of three, and the quadruple as the third made of four, or the elementary body—just as appears in the following pyramid.

# CHAPTER I.

## A brief recapitulation of the subject of the preceding books: *On the nature of generation in these lower regions.*

---

**I**n the preceding pages, it has been clearly explained that, just as GOD <note>original: "DEUS"</note> was the source and highest origin of goodness, so too did He freely and by His divine will choose to impart His goodness first to the world, and then to the creatures of the world. Therefore, resolving to create the world from nothing, He set apart a spherical mass, confused and formless, from the womb of matter <term>hyles <note>from the Greek word for "prime matter" or "substance"</note></term>; wishing to adorn this with His goodness, He created a luminous form on the first day. By the presence of this light, those formless shadows were separated from the face of the abyss and thrust into the center of the sphere. From their thicker spirit arise the substances of the four elements (which pass and change from one into another), from which we say the substance of the ethereal heaven differs—both by the abundance of its luminous form and by its own living activity. Wherefore it is manifest that the *ethereal heaven* is the masculine part of this material world, and the active, generating, and multiplying nature; for it is hotter, more virile, and partakes more of the lovely heat of the Empyrean heaven <term>Empyrean <note>the highest, most fiery part of heaven in ancient cosmology, thought to be the dwelling place of God</note></term>. *The lowest elemental part, however, which is thicker and colder, is as if it were the female*, and the more passive portion of the world; its womb <term>matrix <note>a term used in early biology and alchemy for the womb or place of origin</note></term> is the earth itself, in which, and from which, all transitory creatures are formed. This heaven, therefore, is carried and moved everywhere above the elemental parts, so that in the manner of animals it may be joined and mate with the lower parts, as if with its female or passive partner.

And just as the things to be produced in the lower regions are drawn into the womb of the earth, as if into the womb of the entire female; so also every faculty of generating is gathered into the single spherical body of the ethereal heaven, which we call the *Sun*, so that its essential light and heat may be distributed through the whole Macrocosm <term>Macrocosm <note>the "great world" or the universe as a whole, viewed as a reflection of the human "microcosm"</note></term>. And, because that boundless Architect <note>original: "Opifex"</note> wished to introduce varieties and changes of things into these lower regions, He therefore commanded that glowing fire (into which He contracted the nature of the middle heaven, and upon which the life of all lower things depends) to move here and there, so that by its variable presence and absence, things might more aptly receive their constant changes in generation <term>generation <note>the act of being born or coming into existence</note></term> and corruption <term>corruption <note>the process of decaying or ceasing to exist</note></term>.

These things having been understood, one must examine with a keen mind how the mating of the higher with the lower occurs—that is, by what means the soul <note>original: "anima"</note> is emitted from heaven, and by what path it is received by a well-disposed earthly body. To understand this more easily, one should know that there is a double descent of the soul in its spirit to these lower regions: one, namely, in the days of creation, and the other after the completion of the perfection of the world and its creatures. The descent of the luminous soul before the completion of creation was in a spirit veiled by darkness, as was said above. For the sparks of primary light were captured and are held in the first mass of darkness, or in its hidden spirit, from which [arose] the Solar body <note>original: "Solare corpus"</note>, as we have previously stated;

## CHAPTER II.

->*How vegetative souls, after the completion of creation, are daily infused from heaven into lower things; and concerning the magnetic and attractive property of matter.*<-

Since the life of lower creatures is derived from that very <term>luminous soul</term> <note>original: "anima lucida"; the divine spark of life-force.</note>, and because that soul originates from a celestial source, we must diligently investigate by what path or by what vehicle this soul is transferred through the ether to these lower regions—contrary to the natural inclination of its own essence—and how it is infused into earthly bodies. This is a mystery because such bodies are entirely opposed to the nature of the soul; they are derived from the dark mass which is the opposite of light, and they are completely inert, making them the total opposite of the soul’s active, mobile power. It is manifest, therefore, that just as the spiritual substance of the "middle heaven" is placed between the lowest heaven and the luminous source, so too no spark from that source can descend into the lowest region of the world unless it first passes through the <term>Spirit of the middle region</term>. 

However, because all matter is forever hungry to reach the goal of its own perfection, and since the "motor" or driver toward that goal is the essence of light, it is necessary that every material portion of the middle heaven’s Spirit receives every passing spark of light as its "form" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the organizing principle that gives matter its specific identity.</note>. The Spirit then carries this spark downward to the lower realms, wrapped within its own glue-like and tenacious substance. This happens partly because of the great connection between the substance of the middle heaven and the lower heaven, and partly because matter, through a certain <term>magnetic virtue</term> <note>original: "magnetica virtus"; an attractive force thought to pull spiritual influences into physical objects.</note>, draws the soul and form toward itself. 

Furthermore, because the substance of the ether is more subtle than a physical, airy body, it very easily penetrates a "spermatic body" (which is perfectly prepared to receive it) without any hindrance. Thus, that soul is enclosed within a double vessel: first within the airy spirit, and finally within a terrestrial body. In this way, the ethereal spirit—serving as the vehicle for the soul—is locked within the physical body just as the soul is locked within the spirit. And just as the soul moves within the whole and every part of its spirit, so too the Spirit, along with its soul, is dispersed throughout the entire body and every part of it, generating a movement toward the goal of perfection or maturation. 

In this manner, spirit is added and joined to spirits, and their souls to the souls of others, daily and generously into bodies well-disposed to receive them. From this process, the <term>multiplication of things</term> <note>original: "multiplicationes rerum"; the reproduction and proliferation of life.</note> and generations occur steadily in every part of the world. From this comes the increase of a single grain into a vast multitude; <margin>$\rightarrow$</margin> from this comes the infinite growth of a single animal; and from this, finally, comes the "hurrying" of minerals toward the perfection of gold—that is, their inclination toward <term>fixation</term> <note>original: "fixatio"; the alchemical process of making a volatile spirit stable and solid.</note>. It is truly wonderful to contemplate how this luminous nature, after the work of creation was finished, can descend from its high place with an ethereal and spiritual vehicle into the lower realms, since light and every fiery thing naturally and greedily seek higher places...

And although the animal and vegetable kingdoms are richer in multiplication than the mineral; nevertheless, they cannot approach the goal of perfection any more than a man corrupted by greed and wealthy with much money can reach the pinnacle of immortality. For in every addition and union of a new form with the seed of the same species, new corruptible parts of the elements are also added and applied, due to the porosity of its species; which indeed cannot happen in the mineral kingdom because of the hardness and fixation of that substance, or the constriction of its parts; whence its treasure, acquired from the Sun and the rays of the Planets by the magnetic property of its matter, is diligently stored and reserved for the perfection of its body; wherefore every year it appears more radiant, and more and more <margin>→</margin> similar to those solar rays, and it grows and multiplies in perfection and fixation, though <margin>→</margin> imperceptibly—that is, it is more fully adorned with formal beauty, <margin>→</margin> as will be more clearly explained in the following chapters.

With these things known, it remains evident that the earth is the mother of both simple and composite bodies, carrying them in her womb in the beginning, before their production, no differently than a female carries her offspring. Regarding the simple bodies of the elements, we have dealt with them quite abundantly in the preceding sections. Here, therefore, we shall briefly discuss the differences among composite bodies, into which—when well-disposed—certain sparks of essential light are continually infused. The ancients generally divided composite and mixed bodies into 
<margin>{</margin> five species of composition; the first two of 
<margin>1</margin> which embrace inanimate bodies. For mixtures of the first composition are **Meteors** <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note>, formed from fumes, 
<margin>2</margin> vapors, and exhalations. Those of the second composition are **metals** and other minerals. The later species are animate; for mixtures of the third compo-
<margin>3</margin> sition are **plants** and vegetables; those of the fourth are **irrational animals**; and those of the fifth or 
<margin>4</margin> final composition are the **rational animal**, man, the most noble of all creatures. On account of his 
<margin>5</margin> great similarity to the greater World <note>the Macrocosm</note>, he is called the **Microcosm** <note>meaning "Little World," reflecting the idea that the human body contains all the elements and principles of the entire universe.</note>. It must be carefully 
<margin>巛</margin> observed, however, that celestial light abounds more in perfectly mixed bodies and is more firmly retained in them than in those that are imperfectly mixed. Similarly, this light is more abundant in animate things than in perfectly mixed inanimate things; and purely sensitive animate beings <note>animals</note> are richer in that celestial gift than those that are purely vegetative or irrational. And this is what the Philosophers seem to imply when they assert that in intellectual beings, **fire** predominates; in sensitive beings, fire is equal to **air**; in vegetative beings, **water** is weighed in similar scales with air—though in these, the dignity of the air is diminished because of the cold disposition of the water. Finally, they maintain that minerals are composed mostly of **earth** and water. From this it is manifest that in humans, that celestial fire prevails more insofar as they are intellectual; then in other sensitive beings insofar as air and fire predominate in them; and afterwards, at a still more diminished level, in vegetables, insofar as their aerial parts are tempered by the coldness of water; and finally, that the smallest portion of the luminous form is found in minerals, since earth and water hold dominion in them, and consequently they admit a smaller portion of fire into their composition.
