### CONCERNING THE CREATURES OF THE ELEMENTAL HEAVEN.

Philosophers generally define the material cause of minerals as a "smoky matter," a mixture of watery vapor and earthy exhalation. Specifically, they identify their "proximate and proper" <note>This refers to the immediate physical components as understood in Aristotelian and alchemical physics.</note> matter as *sulfur and quicksilver* <note>original: "sulphur & argentum vivum"; in alchemy, these are the two fundamental principles that combine to form all metals.</note>, concluding generally that their efficient cause is threefold: First, celestial heat, which mixes the watery and earthy elements and gradually "cooks" or ripens them within the veins of the earth. <margin>Pliny, Ptolemy, Calcidius.</margin> For the depths of the earth are most precious, since all celestial influences flow into its bowels, and a heat effective enough to produce metals and precious gems is generated near the center of the earth. Second, they assert that a "formative virtue" for metals and minerals exists within the matter itself, derived from the light of the stars and the heavens; the heat of this light gathers similar substances together and separates the dissimilar ones. The final cause is the mutual proportion of celestial and terrestrial powers, which is effective in subduing and shaping metallic matter—for according to all authorities, heaven is the father and earth is the mother of all minerals, carrying them within her womb like an unborn child. For our part, in accordance with our current purpose, we shall deal briefly with the origin of minerals first, and then with their life, growth, and multiplication, drawing from the traditions of the aforementioned philosophers. Earlier, in *chapter four of the preceding book*, we declared that the *solar body* <note>original: "corpus solare"</note> was born from the Spirit of Darkness cast down from the depths of the Empyrean Heaven <note>The highest, most spiritual region of the universe.</note> on the first day, while retaining a portion of that same heaven’s essential light. Similarly, the *vegetable body* <note>The realm of plants.</note> was formed from the Spirit of Darkness driven down from the middle heaven by the presence and power of light, and from the secondary light of that region. In the same way, we have said that the *mineral body* is forged from the Spirit of Darkness of the lowest heaven, containing a very weak spark of light which we have called the "third-day light" <note>original: "lux tertiana"; the author links the three levels of creation to the first three days of the Genesis narrative.</note>. For at the beginning of the third day of creation, the light of the second heaven (called "secondary light") penetrated downward and acted upon the threefold dark mass that had been driven into and reflected back from the lowest region. But because two parts of that mass—one from the upper region and the other from the middle—seized a sufficient quantity of light from their own regions, the remaining part of that mass belonging to this lowest region embraced only a small amount of this pursuing light flowing from the source of secondary light.

<insert>
But because the nature of light is to thin or refine (wherefore, the greater its proportion and power, the thinner and more subtle it renders bodies), and since light in the other heavens is stronger and more powerful than in the lowest heaven, these portions of "third-day light" are not sufficient to refine and purify the dense and rebellious Spirits of the lowest darkness. From this it happens that, in such a mixture, the matter completely overcomes the form; the form of the light is miserably and perpetually imprisoned within the belly of this matter because of the excessive constriction or smallness of the pores in its body, and the great tenacity of its viscous Spirit. From this comes the body’s coarseness, weight, and solidity; from this also comes the scarcity of the living soul's substance compared to the body, the sluggishness of its Spirit, and the difficulty or imperceptibility of its ability to generate and multiply—what is thought to be its sterility. For with its heterogeneous parts wrapped in dark filth, the mineral's contaminated soul is hindered in its movement because of the density of its Spirit, the strong composition of its bodily parts, and the untamed hardness and solid freezing of the body. Therefore, the heating power of the enclosed light is too meager to drive away the injuries caused by the cold of the mineral body; thus, it is not perceived to evidently live or grow in the manner of plants, nor is its soul, enclosed in its coarser Spirit, able to lift its head above the surface of the earth and strive toward its natural place <note>The heavens.</note> after the example of plants. This is both because its power is weaker than that of plants, and because it is locked and held by firmer bonds in the center of the mineral body. But since it is the desire of every corporeal thing to strive toward the goal of perfection, and since no perfection can be acquired unless...

### CHAPTER V.

->*On the origin of the insensate or vegetative animated body, and how it grew on the third day immediately after the existence of minerals.*<-

---

**A**LTHOUGH the matter of *vegetables* <note>original: "vegetabilium"; in this context, it refers to all plant life, characterized by the "vegetative soul" which governs growth and nutrition.</note> is softer and more manageable than that of minerals, and its heat more effective and free to carry out its operations; nevertheless, because it was necessary for the earth to be firmed and very well founded before things could flourish from it; and since the more solid part of the earth—such as the shadow of the lowest heaven—would fall more quickly to the center due to its weight than those parts which are lighter and thinner, it followed necessarily that after its natural rest, the sparks of that same light, though small and weak at first, began to act according to the order and appetite <term>appetite|In early modern physics, "appetitus" refers to an inherent natural inclination or drive within an object to seek its proper place or state.</term> of nature. Subsequently, the sparks of the parts of the earth that are closest to this in weight [began to act]; for those were firmed and came to rest in their destined place immediately after the first ones, such as the matter of the shadows of the second heaven. For it is certain that created things had their origin so much sooner as they had less heat in their beginning. For a greater quantity of enclosed light makes the spirit of the shadow enclosing it lighter; hence minerals existed before vegetables, and both were made on the same day, since the presence of the Sun was not required for their creation. Afterward, animals [were created] after the sublimation <term>sublimation|A process of purification where a substance is raised or refined to a higher state.</term> of the Sun in the heart of the ethereal heaven, because a greater power of light and heat was necessary for sensitive beings. 

The vegetative body, therefore, although it consists of the four elements, yet water and air predominate within it; but the dignity of the air is diminished by the presence of water. Moreover, it acquired its Soul and Spirit in its origin in this way: <margin>-></margin> namely, when the secondary light of the second heaven had reflected off the shadows, and sparks of the same were caught in the bonds of their more tenacious spirit, these shadows or darknesses of the second region, joined with those of the final region, gradually grew together into the substance of the earth, according to the gravity and weight of each. Once this spiritual subject of vegetables was placed and confirmed near the outer part of the earth, the sparks of the soul, or enclosed light, begin to act upon it, and by their action they strive to tend upward with their vehicle toward the beginning of their source: but, because there is great proximity between the substance of the ether and that of the higher part of the lower heaven, therefore the element of fire accompanies the aforesaid ethereal Spirit with its soul, and rises and is sublimated with it from the earth. And since one nature of an element always embraces and chains together the nature of the element closest to it, therefore the heat of the air is joined to the heat of the fire, and the moisture of the water to the moisture of the air, and the coldness of the earth to the coldness <margin>—></margin> <margin>-></margin> of the water (which is clearly demonstrated by experiment below), and consequently the subtle part of the earth, being more volatile, mixes itself with the parts of water and ascends <margin>-></margin> within them. 

The soul, therefore, enclosed in the spirit of plants, naturally desires to ascend upward: and it had help in its exaltation before the creation of the Sun from the wandering stars <note>the planets</note>, and from the rays of light sent out from the higher heavens, and after the creation of the Sun from the Sun itself, which on the fourth day drew to itself both the visible and invisible rays dispersed through the concavity of the middle heaven. For the rays proceeding from it penetrated the dense surface of the earth, and opened its pores—which had been constricted by coldness—with their heat; and they provide a way of exit for the vegetables. Whence, the stronger and more perpendicular the solar rays are, the better and more quickly things come forth from the earth, and the more easily and higher they are extended above the ground. This is the reason why in the springti- <note>The text cuts off here at "verno tempo-", likely completing as "verno tempore" or "springtime" on the following page.</note>

### TREATISE I. BOOK VI.

In spring and summer, plants and herbs rise above the earth, growing and multiplying. The reason for this growth (<term>vegetation</term>) is as follows: the solar rays, stretching out from the east, <margin>>>></margin> join themselves with the light enclosed within the <term>vegetable vehicle</term> <note>The "vehicle" refers to the subtle substance or "carrier" that holds the life force within a plant.</note>, and they lift it up gradually but invisibly, drawing it upward through the pores of the earth. The fire within such a plant is linked to the <term>Fifth Essence</term> <note>Also known as the Quintessence; the purest, most heavenly element that transcends the four physical elements.</note>; thus, as the light and its vehicle move, the fire must also be carried upward. To this heat, air is a close relative and embraces it; therefore, because air is in contact with fire and bound to it by the bonds of friendship, it rises immediately after the fire. Similarly, water follows the air, and earth follows the water. But since earth cannot naturally rise from its place because of the heaviness of its substance, it is necessary that the base and foundation of the plant be fixed in the earth as its <margin>></margin> natural place. Hence, while the soul of the plant (<note>original: "anima plantæ"</note>) tends upward with its Spirit toward its own proper seat, it is hindered by the weight of the root of its body fixed in the earth, and it cannot reach higher than the habit of its species allows. The eastern Sun, looking upon that shining spark of the plant, is perceived to extend and increase the plant little by little <margin>></margin> every day; this is why things are said to grow and flourish. 

Here it must be especially observed that since the coldness of the earth is joined to that water, it is likely that the subtle part of the earth rises with the parts of water. By mixing with them, it constitutes the visible body of the seed—or "egg"—of the plant, in the center of which the soul is contained with its Spirit. Similarly, the other two invisible elements are hidden within the aforementioned visible ones: namely, fire in the earth and air in the water. The vigor of this soul is dispersed through the entire vegetable body, just like that of an animal; for it is virtually present in the whole and in every part, through which every part of the plant grows and increases equally and proportionally with every other part. 

As for why the multiplication of the plant's "egg" or seed should happen infinitely, the reason is certainly at hand: for since all multiplication proceeds from the vigor of the soul, it is necessary that there also be an increase of the soul itself, since a single soul of one individual cannot animate many individuals. But <margin>{</margin> since this soul is nothing other than a spark, as it were, of the essential light of the <term>middle heaven</term> <note>In Fludd’s cosmology, the "middle heaven" is the sphere of the Sun, which provides the vital light to the world.</note>, it is necessary that this spark be increased and strengthened by the addition and joining of other sparks from the same fountain, proportional to the species. By these sparks, infinite bodies of the same species are usually animated, which is indeed achieved through the mediation of the solar rays; for rays are joined to rays and spirits to spirits no differently than sparks of fire to sparks, and drops of water to drops. From this, therefore, it follows that from one grain, infinite grains come forth, and from one seed, innumerable others; and from this it also happens that seeds buried in the matrix of the earth are wonderfully affected and delighted by the approach of the sun, through which they become enriched, grow, and multiply. 

Indeed, this is that Nature which generates all things, nourishes that "ligament" of the elements, and is the power of mixing which completes the <term>mixtures of the elements</term> in every thing of this <term>sublunary world</term> <note>The "sublunary world" refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, the realm below the moon where things are subject to change and decay.</note>. It imprints the form appropriate and proportional to its species, by which every thing is distinguished and separated from every other. We conclude, therefore, that where the matter is thinner and softer than that of minerals, and the heat of light is stronger, there that composition will lift itself upward above the surface of the earth, and will have a root as its foot and base; this we call a plant, or a vegetable. Because of the softness of this composition, the ethereal light and heat enclosed within it are more agile, free, and lively than those in a mineral composition. For the thinness and subtlety of the body is the cause of the soul's greater freedom, liveliness, and agility. Regarding the virtue of individual vegetables—both hidden and manifest—and their <term>chemical preparation</term>, we shall treat of these in Treatise 4 of the second volume.

# CHAPTER VI.

## On the origin of the sentient living body.

The animal is also composed of a simple nature—namely the ethereal—and an elementary composition, no differently than the vegetable body; however, a greater portion of celestial heat was required for the creation of sentient beings than for vegetables, since the acts of the senses are derived from a stronger power of heat, and their failure proceeds from too much numbness and stupor caused by cold. And it was for this reason that, during the days of creation, the animals were not created before the rising of the Sun. For the heat dispersed everywhere through the regions of the world, and especially through the firmament <note>The sphere of the stars or the sky.</note>, was weak before the fourth day, so that it did not have the power to communicate sensation to creatures. The acts of the senses arise from an abundance of heat, whereas the heat before the Sun only provided vegetative life and imperceptible motion; by this power all vegetables were created on the third day—that is, before the production of the Sun. Yet, under that same species, they perpetually receive multiplicative and generative power from the Sun, possessing no more heat than **GOD** attributed to them in the first creation. Hence, according to <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "Aristotium"</note>, creatures of this kind have three parts of coldness and only one fourth part of heat; for water predominates in them. 

But indeed, on the second and third days after the placement of the Sun <note>The fifth and sixth days of the biblical creation.</note>, all animals are created—and of these, the more imperfect ones immediately on the following day. For on the first day after the Sun's appearance, the terrestrial coldness strongly resisted the warm actions of the Sun; therefore, the colder irrational animals—namely those of the water—were established in the earlier part of that day, and the warmer ones in the latter part of the same day—namely the terrestrial and winged creatures lacking reason. These animals possess sensation above and beyond all the gifts of simple vegetables because, due to the application of the Sun's rays, they are far warmer in their creation than vegetables. For this reason, according to all the Philosophers, animals are said to be more "aerial" <note>Composed of the element of Air, which was considered hot and moist.</note> than vegetables, and accordingly far warmer. 

Yet, if these irrational creatures are rightly compared to those with intellect, we shall find them greatly diminished and lowered by fire <note>The "fire" of the intellect.</note>; while in these latter beings, we perceive Man to be exalted to a far more sublime degree. Therefore, the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>literally "Little World"; a common Renaissance term for Man as a reflection of the entire universe.</note>, or that intellectual animal, was created on the final day, acquiring not only the benefit of the solar heat now predominating more strongly over the earth, but also claiming for his own essence a portion of spiritual light and an enlightened intellect, as the divine will so commanded. And this is why, while other animals naturally look toward the earth because they lack this super-celestial light and are prone toward it, Man reaches upward toward the heaven and the stars. His head, like a little flower in which the most noble seeds of reason are enclosed, chooses for itself the highest seat of the whole body; for that divine light always raises Man up and entices him to contemplate higher things. Whence the Poet says:

->He gave to man an uplifted face, and bade him behold the sky,<-
->And to raise his upright countenance toward the stars.<-
<note>original: "Os homini sublime dedit, cælumq; tueri, / Jussit, & erectos ad sydera tollere vultus." A famous quote from Ovid's Metamorphoses.</note>

Hence, of all sentient creatures, he was made the most noble and **Lord** over the others. With the animal having been created, it is manifest that a twofold equality of nature concurs for its continuation and the preservation of its species; one of these is a manifest and extrinsic equality, the other an occult and intrinsic equality. That extrinsic equality consists in the equal composition of the body itself from the <term>four humors</term> <note>The bodily fluids thought to determine health and temperament in ancient and medieval medicine.</note>, namely: *blood, yellow bile, phlegm, and black bile* <note>original: "sanguine, cholera, phlegmate, & melancholia"</note>. This equality is the cause of the union of the soul with the body. However, this *intrinsic* equality is the nature of the vital soul itself, consisting of an equal portion of celestial heat and its innate or spiritual moisture. Therefore, where a strong and great departure from that manifest equality occurs, the bond of the soul with the body is corrupted, and then it happens that the soul is separated from the body; which separation is called *death*. But if that departure from equality is only weak, and in quantity...

...from a small quantity, sickness and disturbance of the body perhaps happen. To ensure that the proportion of the aforementioned qualities is maintained in weight or at least in justice, a double **nutriment** <term>nutrimentum</term> <note>In this context, nourishment refers to both physical food and the "spiritual" fuel required to sustain life.</note> is required for the preservation of the whole composite: namely, *spiritual or ethereal and corporeal or elementary: That spiritual* food enters the body, either by means of a thin and invisible body—namely air—or by means of a thick and visible body, such as that common nourishment, namely animal and vegetable. That invisible nourishment retains within itself some portion of solar light and ethereal spirit, by which the Vital Spirits <note>The "vital spirit" was believed to be a subtle substance that animated the body, carried through the arteries.</note> hiding in the arterial veins of the animal are wonderfully and at every moment refreshed. Therefore, food of this kind—namely air—is drawn into the innermost chamber of the heart during respiration, and its more essential parts are received for the refreshment of the vital spirits; but the remaining parts, as if excremental and superfluous—namely the watery substance of the air itself—are exhaled. Also in its visible and corporeal nourishment, which is usually either animal or vegetable, a double subject is found, fit for feeding both equalities. One of these is of the nature of heaven, which is called the essential or ethereal part of the nourishing thing—namely, the radical moisture <note>Radical moisture was seen as the "lamp oil" of life, a fundamental fluid that determined a creature's lifespan.</note> with its innate heat. The other is of the nature of the elements, namely its more corporeal part, from which a portion of the element of fire is drawn and separated for the proper nutrition of the choleric humor <note>The "humors" were the four fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile (choler), and black bile (melancholy)—that governed health.</note> in the thing to be nourished. Similarly, by the substance of the element of air, the animal's blood is nourished; and by the element of water, the substance of natural phlegm is conserved; finally, the coarser parts of the food strengthen the melancholy. Since the composition of the entire animal body is made from these elements, it is necessary that its more solid parts be extracted from the more subtle parts of the body's nourishment for its preservation in the state and vigor of a natural and well-disposed body, and that its coarser and more dross-filled portion, as if useless, be expelled either through the bowels or through the urine. Hence it is that from a defect of this kind of elementary nourishment, the animal body withers; indeed, it is rendered weak, and with its strength utterly cast down, it falls into wasting <note>Original Latin: *tabem*, referring to a progressive wasting away or consumption.</note>, just as happens to those urged by the sharpest hunger. From these things, therefore, it becomes manifest that that old axiom of the Philosophers is most true: *That like rejoices in like, and nature is not improved except in its own nature.* <note>Original: *Similia nempe similibus gaudere & naturâ non emendari, nisi in natura sua propria.* This is a fundamental principle of Hermetic and early medical philosophy.</note> We conclude, finally, that if the matter of a creature be purer and more subtle than that of vegetables, and its essential light more powerful, a work far more beautiful and noble is produced than that vegetable which is called an animal, in which air and fire work wonderfully. Concerning the virtues of particular animals, both hidden and manifest, we shall treat in Volume 2, Treatise 4.

# C H A P T E R VII.
## From where does the difference of species of creatures arise, and why are some hotter, colder, wetter, and drier than others?

IT IS CERTAIN beyond doubt that the universal difference of all things flows from their souls or essential forms, which we called substantial sparks of light included in the spirit above, since matter by itself is only in potentiality, nor is it brought into action unless it be informed by light. Some Philosophers call these **Influences** <term>influentias</term> <note>Influences refer to the celestial or divine forces that "flow down" and shape material existence.</note>, which descend through the element of earth even to its center, in a manner so varied and by a reason so diverse, that they produce different generations in the bowels of the earth through different impressions. Such a bright soul, I say, makes the whole, without which no action is found in the body. It draws, therefore, fire from the earth of the creature, and from the water that light and airy spirit which we call air, so that if there be a great quantity of earth in the creature and a small amount of water, with a strong portion of essential heat making the mixtures, then the element of fire will show itself in that composition and will have dominance. But if the heat be small in the predicted measure of earth, and little water, the earth will have...

But if in that same composition the heat is found to be even stronger and more powerful, the compound will be drier, and from such a mixture a <term>fatty body</term><note>Latin: *corpus pingue*. In early chemistry, "fat" or "oil" referred to the flammable or cohesive principle of a substance.</note> will arise. 

For this reason, when the <term>soul</term><note>Latin: *anima*. The vitalizing spark or life-force.</note> descends upon such matter, clothed in a spiritual, aether-like garment <note>original: *veste spirituali ætheri familiarissima induta*</note> (without whose dryness the soul and the compound body would never meet, be compatible, or be joined to one another), it moves that matter with its most temperate heat. It alters it in various and diverse ways, producing various habits and species of things according to the greater or lesser proportion of that same light, and the differing "obedience" of the material subject into which it enters. 

For a multitude of <term>form</term><note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the organizing principle that makes a thing what it is.</note> brings greater perfection, activity, subtlety, and purity to a body, provided the matter is well-prepared to receive it; and in this way, vegetables and animals are born. But if the body is rebellious, coarse, and disobedient to the quantity of its form, in that case the vigor of the soul is hindered in its actions, and it produces a mineral species. 

Where, however, in the three-fold division of things mentioned above, any individual species has its own distinction—such as in the animal kingdom, **man from the lion**, the **lion from the bear**, and the **bear from the mouse**; in the vegetable species, the **oak from the hazel**, the **hazel from the bilberry**, and **vervain from betony**, and **sage from thyme**, and others; and in the mineral, **gold from lead**, **lead from antimony**, and so on—this occurs because of the infinite proportions and degrees by which matter differs from its form. For in some, the form is exalted to such a degree in one creature over another because of the "obedience" of that material nature, or the "disobedience" of this one. 

The disobedience of a species can happen in two ways: 
1. Where the enclosed essential light is very small, so that although the matter is sufficiently rare, thin, and manageable, its form is not powerful enough to govern it and push it toward the goal of perfection. Thus, <term>phlegmatic</term> and <term>melancholic</term><note>The "humors" or temperaments believed to govern health and personality.</note> creatures move more slowly than <term>sanguine</term> or <term>choleric</term> ones. Thus **houseleek** and **hemlock** reach maturity more slowly than warmer vegetables. 
2. Or where the matter is extremely disobedient, thick, hard, and barely porous, binding its soul—even if that soul is not small in quantity—as if with chains, and entirely hindering and prohibiting its power and vigorous actions. 

We conclude, therefore, that the softer and more obedient the substance of a body is, the more the invisible light enclosed within it proportionally renders its composition noble. Furthermore, just as the proportion of every material thing was set to its form in the first creation, so also its generation from the beginning of the world until its end continues in that same proportion of mixture and under the same species by the divine will of the Creator; for sparks of light are continually rained down from above.

### CHAPTER VIII.

->What is artificial or common fire? How does it participate in celestial fire?<-

That this lower fire of ours, which we call common and artificial, traces its origin from that celestial light, is proved both by the arguments of the ancient philosophers and by their examples. We, too, pursuing our purpose vigorously, do not hesitate to easily confirm their opinions. For that immense, uncreated Light, the head of the world, created the primary light, from whose super-celestial source rays are sent down into the body of the sun and the other stars. For the splendor of the <term>Empyrean heaven</term><note>The highest heaven, believed to be the realm of pure fire and light.</note> undoubtedly communicates constantly with these bodies, from which shining rays are poured into this artificial fire of ours. From this it is manifest that this fire not only has a participation in the super-celestial light, but even possesses a certain likeness and presence of the uncreated Light itself, since to the light...

...evil spirits are weakened and driven away by the approach of fire, just as good spirits are refreshed and made stronger by the sight of it. For this reason, the ancients placed lit candles and lamps next to the bodies of the dead, <margin>Bartholomaeus, Book 11 <note>Likely referring to Bartholomaeus Anglicus, a 13th-century encyclopedist.</note></margin> and did not allow them to be removed until the sacred purifications were finished and the bodies were placed in their tombs; this was done, of course, to drive away the **Light-fleers** <note>original: *Lucifugos*</note> and evil spirits who serve **Evil Magicians** <note>original: *Cacomagis*</note>, or to block their approach, as is found in *Apuleius's Golden Ass*. Similarly, the Vestal Priests, according to Roman rites, always kept fires burning next to their altars. Finally, the worshippers of the true GOD, as found in the sacred scriptures, are commanded according to the old Law of GOD to offer sacrifices with fire, and that fire should burn continuously upon the altar; indeed, even to this day, among the followers of the Roman Christian religion, who diligently observe that **anagram of Pythagoras** <note>A reference to Pythagorean symbolic teachings on perpetual light or the "Y" representing the paths of life.</note>, fire is perceived to burn without ceasing in the temples. But what this burning light is—which they call common and artificial fire—or how it acts destructively upon the object it occupies, we shall briefly declare here. *Pythagoras* posited only a single fire penetrating all things, which *Pliny* called a "great portion of natural things"; we have called this the **essential light**. But this fire is found to be stronger or weaker in its action depending on the subject, according to whether there is more or less resistance to its actions. Thus, in the **Empyrean Heaven** <term>Empyrean: the highest part of heaven, believed by ancients to be made of pure fire or light</term>, because of the thinness of the place's substance and its slight resistance, the fire is immensely expanded; it warms most mildly and sweetly, and is exalted in the highest degree of spirituality and perfection, because it is freer there. In the middle heaven, because of the thicker consistency of the ethereal parts, it is more intense and hotter, because the composition of that body more strongly resists the actions of the **super-celestial fire** sent downward; however, it does not heat in a way that leads to the ruin and destruction of a creature. Rather, because of its moderate temperament, it is constantly occupied with the preservation and multiplication of the lower creatures themselves. But the more this fire turns downward and hastens toward the center, the more its operative power is resisted, and its rays are narrowed and compressed. This is due to the thickness of the substance of the lowest heaven, which grows denser step by step toward the center; these compressed rays act more violently, since a united force is stronger. So we also see that in a narrower channel of a river or torrent, the waters move more swiftly and fiercely. And this is why, among **Theologians**, that infernal and cursed fire is said to be destructive beyond all imagination—burning with immense pain and horror that will never cease—because of the extreme narrowing of the descending rays and the compression and condensation of the substance of the descending light. <margin>Bartholomaeus, Book 11</margin> Because of the crowding of the cursed matter containing it, it is said to be miraculously dark, horrific, and gloomy. The "intermediate" fire, however, participates both in that celestial fire and also in that of hell, according to the arrangement of the thicker parts of the lowest heaven which it occupies. From this it follows that this fire of the lower heaven both preserves things and makes them sprout, but in different ways. From these facts it is certain that the single fire stretching through all things—since it is hidden and unknown in itself, as *Dionysius* <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential Christian philosopher.</note> maintains—differs in its operation and reveals itself more or less according to the disposition of the intervening matter it occupies. It is by the resistance of this matter that the nature of fire is revealed as either preservative or destructive. For it separates **heterogeneous** things <note>Things of a different or "other" kind that do not belong together.</note> and things different from the nature of its **radical moisture** <term>Radical moisture: the fundamental life-fluid or "fuel" believed to exist within all living beings to keep them alive and hydrated against the heat of life.</term> so that it may find its true fodder and, as it were, its nourishment; not unlike animals seeking the central substance of a nut, who strip away its husks and skins so they may choose the marrow for their food to be nourished by. Therefore, just as that celestial light, clothed in a "windy" body called air and spirit, is not only moved by its own heat and performs its operations, but also requires the pure and thin fatness of the ether for its food (for nothing can subsist without nourishment), so the innumerable rays of the celestial light or fire move into the lowest region of the world as if for the sake of hunting...

# CONCERNING THE CREATURES OF THE ELEMENTARY HEAVEN.

[re]gion, they descend and, being compressed, they long for denser nourishment; for this reason, they invisibly seek out those subjects that are softer and easier to penetrate, in which a greater part of that **ethereal fatness** <note>original: "pinguedinis illius æthereæ"; a term used in alchemy to describe the oily, flammable essence of substances</note> which they seek is usually hidden; and especially those things whose forms have flown away and left their dwellings. It is from this, therefore, that dead animals and plants suddenly rot by the invisible presence of these rays; from this comes the dissolution of a corpse into its primary elements; and from this comes the stench and the foul, unwelcome odor of the air surrounding a corpse, which is a clear sign of its dissolution into fire and air. 

Nevertheless, for this type of action, it must be understood that fewer rays of light are gathered than for that of **artificial fire**, in which there are infinite rays; indeed, in its nature and operation, rays are no more continuous with rays and sparks with sparks than drops of water are when a drop is submerged in some body of water; hence it produces an effect that is prompter and swifter in its execution. For where that dense fire, imprisoned in thicker bodies, is drawn out by the collision of two hard bodies, it is visible because of its coarseness and easily clings to a gross body which, because of its softness and subtle fatness, is fit to be inflamed, to receive the **hungry fire**, and to serve it as food. As soon as this hungry fire begins to taste its food, it suddenly summons to itself the rays invisibly surrounding it; these fly to it like birds of prey or flies, whose multitude around dead corpses increases by degrees; for the presence of one summons another, then a third, and so on infinitely, until the entire corpse is covered with flies; or perhaps because there is a magnetic virtue in the substance of the denser fire by which rays are joined to rays and fire to fire. 

In any case, it is certain that the substance of such sparks is not from nothing, but from the matter of **celestial fire** <note>The author views fire not just as a chemical reaction, but as a heavenly substance descending into the material world.</note> which, because of its thinness, lies hidden in the air. Because of the abundance of food upon which that dense fire acts, it is gathered from every surrounding part to the passive subject, and by the application of many rays, it is condensed—in the manner of the fire acting previously—is rendered visible to us, and is multiplied infinitely by the constant union of arriving rays, provided that the quantity of food and fuel is sufficient to satisfy their appetite. But if the passive matter fails, the parts of that fire are gradually scattered through the spirit of the vast air and vanish; and once the subject is destroyed and its **radical moisture** <note>original: "humiditate radicali"; the vital fluid thought to sustain the life and structural integrity of all living things</note> consumed or invisibly snatched away by them, they tend toward their natural place. 

And certainly, a great mystery seems to lie hidden here, and a massive doubt arises: whether these gathered rays that constitute common fire devour these lower bodies so greedily because of a great enmity between the opacity of matter and its coldness, or so that they, being hungry, may be refreshed by that ethereal nourishment contained within the patient; or at least, so that they may redeem and liberate their imprisoned brothers with their ethereal vehicles, so that—since this cannot be done without the destruction of the elementary body—they seem to perform that work primarily by the dissipation of its parts. And truly, as it seems to me, that invisible and thinned fire can be content with its natural food when it is dispersed through the widely spreading ethereal sea, the substance of which is very simple and acts as the **radical moisture** of the whole world; the substance of air comes closest to this, by which the fiery nature is also fed, although it is thinner and not as "fat" as that of the ether, and is polluted by the raw exhalations and vapors of the earth and water. But truly, when an infinite number of scattered sparks are contracted together into one flame, a denser food is required; this is most easily demonstrated in the life of an animal; for because of the moderate disposition of its celestial fire, the air it breathes is not enough for its food, but solid nourishment is also required for its preservation, without which it cannot long subsist.

->**THE END of Book Six concerning the creatures of the elementary heaven.**<-

<page-num>183</page-num>

# CHAPTER I.

->*That imperfect mixtures, or Meteors, are not according to the nature of the Macrocosm, but are preternatural, and like passions and diseases, afflicting its lower parts.*<-

---

Just as we have shown above that perfectly mixed things exist naturally in the Macrocosm <note>The "Great World" or the universe as a whole</note>; so we shall declare that its Meteors <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars</note>, which are called imperfectly mixed things, happen to it not according to, but contrary to the world's nature. Indeed, these are like accidental hindrances and afflictions of that elementary mass, which we otherwise call diseases in animals. For what has the world or the nature of the world to do with *comets, flashes of light, lightning, thunder, leaping goats <note>original: "capris saltantibus" — a historical term for a type of flickering or "skipping" atmospheric light</note>, burning spears, halos, parhelia <note>sundogs or mock suns</note>, or will-o'-the-wisps?* What has it to do with *dry or moist clouds, hail, snow, mists, dew, frost, or with the eruption of springs and floods?* What likewise with *winds and breezes, moist or dry, hot or cold?* What with *earthquakes or the gaping open of the same?* Do all these things usually happen by necessity to the Macrocosm, or can they not rather, in the manner of an accident, be present or absent without the destruction of the lower world and its parts? It is indeed certain and beyond doubt that the elementary region of the world and its creatures suffer and are afflicted by their presence.

For how many calamities *Comets* have brought to the air and earth, infinite experiences prove; since histories also testify more than enough that by their appearance the temperament of the air changed into a pestilential state, and great changes occurred on earth, and even entire cities and regions were as if destroyed by famine. Likewise, by *lightning* temples and palaces have burned, and crops, herbs, and trees were scorched and withered. By *Thunder* cities, towers, and tall trees were leveled to the ground, and also the serene face of the air is veiled as if with darkness by the presence of *clouds*, looking upon these lower things with a mournful countenance. An excessive abundance of *rain and snow* brought floods and inundations, which were followed not only by the ruin of houses and cities, but also the slaughter of all animals, and even the corruption of the earth itself. Furthermore, by *Hail* trees and fruits are spoiled, and many other evils are brought in. The subversion of towns, temples, and houses accompanies *Winds*, along with the stirring up of the sea and swollen waves to the destruction and ruin of both ships and the men traveling in them. By a *Whirlwind* tall trees are cast down to the ground; by an *Earthquake* the earthly mass is shaken and is wounded as if by a gap; cities are swallowed up either in part or in whole, and trees are torn up by the roots, and innumerable other evils are brought in. Therefore, not in vain or inappropriately do we say that the meteors of the greater world are contrary to nature, and bring the greatest harm to its creatures, and for that reason are not undeservedly held to be diseases within it; just as we shall clearly demonstrate in the second volume that all the *meteors of the Microcosm <note>The "Little World," referring to the human body</note> are its diseased afflictions.*

<header>TREATISE I. BOOK VII.</header>

# CHAPTER II.
## *On imperfectly mixed bodies in general.*

**I**mperfectly mixed bodies are those of the first composition which are called *Meteors* <note>In early modern science, 'meteors' referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and rainbows, not just falling stars.</note>; those which the ancient Philosophers said were forged from vapor or exhalation; although we shall prove that some of them originate from elsewhere, as we shall say below in the description of the *cloud*. Moreover, Philosophers have distinguished this type of composition into fiery, watery, and intermediate; of which there are various subdivisions for each, distinguished from one another both by their *form of appearance* and by their *place of generation*. For in the *upper region of the air* they place perpendicular fire, the burning spear or beam, the lit candle, flying sparks, leaping goats <note>original: "capras saltantes"; a classical term for flickering, leaping lights in the sky</note>, the Comet, etc. In the *middle region*, the *lightning bolt, the flash, and thunder*. In the *lowest region*, that *ignis fatuus* <note>literally 'foolish fire'; often called 'will-o'-the-wisp'</note>, etc. The Meteors which they call *intermediate* contain *wind, earthquakes, and whirlwinds*. The *Watery* ones contain the *cloud, the little cloud, mist, rain, dew, hoarfrost, snow, and hail*; to which also *springs, hot springs, rivers, and the sea* with its saltiness and tide are connected because of their affinity. All of which we do not intend to treat thoroughly in this place, because nearly all Philosophers have dealt with them, but we shall bring to light only those whose generations and natures the ancient *Philosophers* explained not quite correctly, as it seems to me, and as truth itself would require; such as the *Comet, cloud, wind, thunder*, etc. We shall also discourse briefly in passing on rivers and springs.

---

# CHAPTER III.
## *On the composition of Comets and other Meteors located in the upper region of the air.*

**T**he opinion of Philosophers regarding the generation and appearance of the *Comet* is manifold. While *some* say that it is raised little by little from the bowels of the earth into the *upper region of the air* by the power of the stars, consisting of terrestrial vapor or exhalation—thick, fatty, and viscous—and of densely compacted parts, and there it is expanded, kindled, and set aflame; and they maintain that it lasts until its entire matter is consumed by burning. *Others* describe it as an exhalation, not thick but subtle, not illuminated from within but shining from the light of the Sun and stars incorporated into it; and they say that meteors of this kind have their origin from the action of the stars in the bowels of the earth, especially when the pores are constricted by cold. But in these opinions of the Philosophers, as it seems to me, many impossibilities occur. For since the nature of an exhalation is hot and dry (for smoke is defined as *hot and dry* <note>original: "calidus & sicca"</note>), it is impossible for it to pass through the sieve and the cold and humid diaphragm of the middle region of the air; since there is an immense contrariety between the nature of one and the other. Whence it must be that the immense quantity of the cold substance of the middle air region denies passage to the tiny portion of exhalation tending upward, and violently and vehemently represses it downward. Therefore, from exhalations of this kind, winds rather, or lightnings or thunders and flashes originate—

### Proposition VIII.

*Two parallel lines differing in dimension <note>Meaning they differ in length.</note> can be divided proportionally by straight lines falling from the height or perpendicular to the base.*

---

Therefore, just as the large <term>parallelogram</term> <note>A four-sided figure with two pairs of parallel sides.</note> $a.b.e.f.$ relates to the smaller parallelogram $a.c.d.t.$, so the larger triangle $a.e.f.$ presents itself to the smaller $a.c.d.$ By similar reasoning, the parallelogram $a.k.g.e.$ is compared to the smaller $a.c.n.s.$, and consequently triangle $a.e.g.$ to triangle $a.n.c.$ Likewise, parallelogram $a.l.e.h.$ is referred to that of $a.c.o.r.$, and consequently triangle $a.e.h.$ is related to $a.c.o.$: And because the bases $e.i.$ and $i.h$, and $h.g.$ and $g.f.$ are in proportion, as the base of one is to the base of the other; therefore by this 8th proposition—which is also the same as *Euclid’s Proposition 1, Book 6* <note>original: "propositione 1. lib. 6. Euclidis." This famous theorem states that triangles of the same height have areas proportional to their bases.</note>—the triangles $a.e.i.$ and $a.i.h.$ and $a.h.g.$ and $a.g.f.$ are equal in proportion, and consequently, because the bases $c.p.$ and $p.o.$ and $o.n.$ and $n.d.$ are equal; all the triangles also, raised upon those bases under the same height, are equal.

# ON THE THEORETICAL PART OF GEOMETRY.

Four parallelograms equal to parallelogram *a. b. f. c.* make up the larger parallelogram *a. b. d. e.*, or four parallelograms of the size *a. g. d. h.* will fill the same area. Therefore, triangle *a. c. i.* is a sixteenth part of the parallelogram *a. b. d. e.*, because it is half of the parallelogram *a. g. i. c.*, which is a quarter of parallelogram *a. b. c. f.*, which in turn is a quarter of parallelogram *a. b. d. e.* For side *a. d.* multiplied by side *d. e.* will produce 16 squares of the size *a. g. i. c.*, according to the first rule of Arithmetico-Geometric multiplication. Thus it is clear that the diameter <note>original: "Diametrum" — in this context, refers to the diagonal line connecting opposite corners</note> of square *a. g. i. c.* is also a quarter of the diameter of square *a. b. d. e.*, according to the first rule of division and production in the same book. This demonstration of the proposition is also confirmed by *Proposition 43 of Euclid’s 1st Book, and Proposition 4 of his 2nd Book.* <note>Euclid was an ancient Greek mathematician whose work "Elements" served as the primary textbook for geometry for centuries.</note> From these facts, we conclude that a smaller parallel line is compared to a larger one (or the base) in the same proportion as the part of the perpendicular line <note>A line meeting another at a 90-degree angle.</note> rising above the smaller parallel is to the total height. But since, according to Euclid’s *second definition in Book 5*, this is a multiple proportion (for it concerns a larger dimension in respect to a smaller one), we call it a "quadruple" proportion; because the base, or major parallel, contains the smaller one four times. Similarly, the proportion of part *a. c.* of the orthogonal <note>Meeting at right angles; perpendicular.</note> line *a. d.* to the whole line *a. d.* is quadruple; because the segment *a. c.* is contained in the whole line *a. d.* four times, and so on.

TREATISE II. PART III. BOOK I.

# BOOK TWO
## Concerning Geometric Instruments.
### CHAPTER I.
### *Concerning our Geometric Staff.*

Let there be a staff exactly squared, namely A.B., six feet in length and one inch in thickness; at its top, a slit or joint is to be made, in the hollow of which the <term>Hypotenuse</term> <note>original: "Hypothenusa"; in this context, it refers to a movable diagonal arm used to form a triangle for measurement</note> is to be placed. This ruler is to be attached and tightened by a wooden peg in such a way that it can be moved up and down at the craftsman’s pleasure. 

Next, let that same last foot toward point A be divided into two equal parts, and at the point of intersection—namely at C—let a hole be made through which a <term>Sliding Ruler</term> <note>original: "regula Cursoria"; a movable component that allows the user to adjust the scale or sighting</note> can be pushed forward or backward, establishing a line parallel to the base. At the midpoint or center of the small peg A, a string is to be fixed, at the end of which a <term>lead weight</term> <note>original: "globulus plumbi"; a plumb bob used to ensure the instrument is perfectly vertical</note> is to be hung and connected. By observing the position of this weight, the staff can be raised upright at right angles on a flat surface and held steady.

### Rule III.

Therefore, in every series of products, except for the lowest one, the difference Plus <note>P</note> towards the left is always to be expressed without Minus <note>M</note>, just as happens in standard multiplication, as is demonstrated in the preceding example above.

### Rule IV.

When the multiplication is complete, a Cossic addition <note>an algebraic addition of like terms</note> of all the products is always performed, as was stated in the abstract; and this is made clear in the preceding demonstration.

### Rule V.

When the multiplier is larger than the multiplicand, then the multiplier should be moved into the place of the multiplicand, and the multiplicand into the place of the multiplier; then one must proceed as before, just as in the following example.

# CHAPTER VI.

## On the division of Cossic numbers.
<note>The term "Cossic" comes from the Italian "cosa," meaning "the thing," which was the early Renaissance term for the unknown variable in algebra.</note>

<margin>In this operation, 4 things are to be noted</margin>

- **Difference, which**
    - If { Unlike, they are to be added / Like, they are to be subtracted } **First Rule.**
    - By multiplying themselves, they are either:
        - Like, as in multiplying { **P.** by **P.** / **M.** by **M.** } **Produces P.** } **Rule 2.**
        - Unlike, as in multiplying { **P.** by **M.** / **M.** by **P.** } **Produces M.** }
- **Characters**
    - The subtraction of one character from another } **Third & fourth rules.**
    - Finding the remainder, and its arrangement }
- **Arrangement of numbers**
    - Where nothing remains at the beginning after subtraction is done, Rule Five.
    - Where in the last place the divisor is larger than the dividend, Rule Six.
    - Where a fractional number is left over once the partition is complete, Rule Seven.
- **The Proof, which is done by**
    - Dividing the dividend by the quotient number, Rule Eight.
    - Multiplying the quotient by the divisor, Rule Nine.

---

### Rule I.

> *Where unlike differences <note>The author uses "difference" here to refer to the algebraic signs of the terms.</note> occur together, there the numbers are to be added, as is held in the rule for subtraction; on the contrary, numbers are to be subtracted where the differences are alike.*

### Rule II.

> *The first number of the quotient toward the left claims for itself the difference **P.** <note>original: "P." for "Plus"</note> (as it is in the third rule of multiplication) which, when led into **P.**, will give **P.** Similarly, **M.** <note>original: "M." for "Minus"</note> into **M.** will give **P.** The second difference, multiplied by its opposite, will produce **M.** by the second rule of the same. Moreover, **M.** by **P.** or **P.** by **M.** is added. But **P.** by **P.** or **M.** by **M.** is subtracted, by the fifth rule of subtraction.*

### Rule III.

> *In the subtraction of a lower number from an upper one; the value of the lower <term>character</term> <note>In early algebra, "characters" were specific symbols used to represent different powers of the unknown (e.g., $x$, $x^2$, $x^3$).</note> must also be taken away from the upper (namely, from the dividend), and the <term>character</term> of the remaining value must be expressed. It must always be understood, however, regarding the first <term>character</term> toward the left of the number whose quotient is sought. For the <term>characters</term> toward the right do not diminish the values of the upper ones. It should also be noted that the remainder of the value of the upper <term>character</term> is to be placed in the quotient, with its difference arranged according to the second rule of this section.*

### Rule IV.

> ***Q.** is the smallest Cossic sign or character that is divisible: for **R.** is just like unity, which cannot be divided. <note>In the notation likely used here, "R" (Radix/Root) represents the first power or the constant unit, while "Q" (Quadratus) represents the square. The author suggests the constant unit is the fundamental building block.</note> Moreover, the remainder of the value, which the sign re-*

The divisor 3 is found twice in the dividend 6. Therefore, 2 must be noted in the quotient, as is done in the division of abstract numbers. Then, according to the 4th rule of this type: when a Root is taken from a square <note>original: "R. sublata à q." — essentially dividing $x^2$ by $x$</note>, a Root remains, which must be set down after the 2 in the quotient. Afterward, because by the second rule the difference of the first number toward the left, for both the divisor and the quotient, is a Unit <note>original: "D" for Drachma</note>: multiply them, as in abstract numbers, saying "two times 2 is 4," and a Unit times a Unit makes a Unit according to the aforementioned proposition. Then, the Unit is subtracted from the Unit by the second rule of subtraction: therefore, when 4 is subtracted from 19, the remainder will be 15, which must be written above with the Unit designation.

Finally, let the divisor be moved one step toward the right, proceeding as in the previous steps. For 3 is found five times in 15; therefore, the number 5 must be noted in the quotient toward the right, and the Root is canceled by the Root. From these 5, then, 10 are made; and five times 3 are 15, which when subtracted from the numbers above leave nothing.

<meta>Continuing from the detailed exposition of algebraic symbols and basic operations. This page serves as the concluding summary (epilogue) for the section on "Cossic" mathematics, which we now know as algebra.</meta>

->ON COSSIC ARITHMETIC<-
<note>original: "DE ARITHMETICA COSSICA"; the term "Cossic" derives from the Italian "cosa" (thing), which early mathematicians used to refer to the unknown variable, much like we use "x" today.</note>

### EPILOGUE.

As for the reduction of Cossic fractions and their various types <note>original: "species"; in early mathematics, the basic operations were often referred to as species.</note>—namely addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division—as well as the "Rule of Three" (which practitioners call the "Golden Rule" because of its unique utility), the extraction of roots, and the Algebraic rule known as the "Rule of Equation," I believe you should be referred to Michael Stifel, Robert Recorde, and countless other authors who have written most brilliantly on these subjects.

I am content to have written here, openly and clearly, only about these principles or primary operations. Regarding these, other writers—acting as if they begrudged the world this sublime and hidden science and feared it might one day become common knowledge—have treated them far too briefly and obscurely. For when the principles of any science remain unknown, the science itself is rendered entirely hidden and concealed. This is why this art, so distinguished and noble, is discovered with such difficulty and by so few. 

Now, however, with these four operations explained clearly enough to the world, it will be very easy to investigate the rest that follow them through the sharpness of one's own mind, and to bring the entire science under the control of anyone who desires it.

->[A decorative tailpiece featuring a bearded face surrounded by leafy scrolls marks the end of this section.]<-

<summary>In this concluding passage, the author justifies his focus on the fundamental principles of algebra, arguing that previous writers intentionally obscured them. He directs advanced students to established authorities like Michael Stifel and Robert Recorde for complex operations.</summary>

# BOOK FOUR.
## On Geometrical Arithmetic.
### CONTENTS OF BOOK IV.

<margin>
In geometric numbers, two things are to be noted, namely:
</margin>

*   **Names, for some become**
    *   **Linear** <note>Numbers represented as a sequence of points in a single dimension</note> **and these are either**
        *   Straight.
        *   Circular.
    *   **Superficial** <note>Also known as "plane numbers," representing two-dimensional shapes like squares or triangles</note>
        *   **Regular**
            *   Triangular.
            *   Quadrangular <note>Square numbers</note>.
            *   Pentagonal.
            *   Hexagonal.
            *   Circular.
        *   **Irregular, such as Trapezoidal.**
    *   **Corporal** <note>Also known as "solid numbers," representing three-dimensional shapes</note>
        *   **Pyramidal**
            *   Triangular.
            *   Square.
            *   Pentagonal.
            *   Round.
        *   **Columnar** <note>Prismatic numbers, which have a polygonal base and a set height</note>
            *   Trigonal <note>Three-sided</note>.
            *   Tetragonal <note>Four-sided</note>.
            *   Pentagonal.
            *   Hexagonal.
            *   Round.
*   **Types of calculation**
    *   **Simple**
        *   Addition.
        *   Subtraction.
        *   Multiplication.
        *   Partition <note>Division</note>.
        *   Reduction <note>Simplifying or converting units</note>.
    *   **Mixed**
        *   Addition with subtraction.
        *   **Multiplication with**
            *   Addition.
            *   Subtraction.
            *   Mediation <note>The process of halving a number</note>.
            *   Division.
        *   Division with Progression.
        *   Progression <note>The study of sequences and series</note>.
    *   **Composite**
        *   Rule of three proportions <note>A method to find a fourth value given three known values (A is to B as C is to X)</note>.
        *   Extraction of the root <note>Square roots</note>.
        *   Extraction of the cube <note>Cube roots</note>.

---

**A** linear number is that which, beginning from two and always adding a unit, constitutes a line; one must therefore begin from two, because just as a line is constituted from points, so a number is constituted from units. <note>In this period, "one" was often considered the "monad" or source of numbers rather than a number itself; thus, the first "line" requires at least two points.</note>

A superficial <note>planar</note> number is one contained by two sides, namely length and width, or it is a number beginning from three; because no surface is enclosed by fewer than three lines.

<term>Geometrical Arithmetic</term> — the study of "figurate numbers" where quantities are represented by geometric shapes.
<term>Linear Number</term> — a number representing a one-dimensional sequence.
<term>Superficial Number</term> — a plane number representing a two-dimensional area.
<term>Corporal Number</term> — a solid number representing a three-dimensional volume.
<term>Rule of Three</term> — a fundamental mathematical rule for solving proportions.
<term>Mediation</term> — an ancient arithmetic operation specifically for halving numbers.
<term>Extraction</term> — the mathematical process of finding roots (square or cube).

## ON GEOMETRIC ARITHMETIC.

*A <term>triangular number<note>original: "Numerus triangularis." These are "figurate" numbers that can be represented as dots arranged in an equilateral triangle.</note></term> is one which, when described in width according to its units, is contained by 3 angles and sides arranged in equal dimensions.*

->15.<- ->21.<- ->28.<-

*A <term>square number<note>original: "Numerus quadratus." A number formed by multiplying an integer by itself, represented as a square grid of dots.</note></term> is one described in width according to its units, with 4 angles and sides arranged in equal dimensions.*

*A <term>pentagonal number<note>original: "Numerus pentagonalis." A figurate number that extends the concept of triangular and square numbers to the five-sided pentagon.</note></term> is one which, when described in width according to its units, is contained by five angles and sides arranged in equal dimensions.*

*A <term>corporeal number<note>original: "Numerus corporalis." In modern mathematics, we call these "solid numbers."</note></term> is, or a solid, which is contained by three dimensions, namely length, width, and depth: Or it is that which, when its units have been arranged in length and depth, will represent the figure of some solid body.*

*A <term>pyramidal number<note>A figurate number that can be represented as a pyramid with a polygonal base and a sequence of decreasing layers.</note></term> is composed of its units in the manner of a physical pyramid; specifically, it begins from a wide base and continually decreases as it rises until it reaches a single unit, which is its <term>apex<note>original: "conus," referring to the peak or vertex of the solid.</note></term>.*

*A <term>columnar number<note>A number representing a prism-like shape where the base and the top are the same size, maintaining a constant width throughout.</note></term> is composed of its units in the manner of a physical column, such that it rises from a wide base to the top with an equal width, neither decreasing nor increasing.*

## C H A P T E R IV.

### On Partitioning.

### Rule I.

**L**et a square be circled around its surface by dividing one of its sides into 4 equal parts A, B, C, and D. Then, by drawing a circle from its center touching the intersections B and D, the capacity <note>original: "capacitas", here meaning area</note> of the circle will be the same as that of the square.

### Rule II.

*The center of a square is found if it is divided into 4 equal parts by two diameters <note>The author uses "diameters" to describe diagonal lines</note> drawn from corner to corner; for the point of their intersection will be the center of the square, namely point "e".*

### Rule VI.

*If the diameter is divided into 14 equal parts, and if a perpendicular line is raised from the eleventh part to the circumference, and from that point where it touches the circumference a straight line is drawn to the beginning of the first part, that straight line will be the side of a square whose area will be the same as the area of the circle.* <note>original: "Diametro in 14. equales partes diviso..." This describes a geometric method for "squaring the circle"—finding a square with an area equal to a given circle. This was one of the most famous challenges in ancient mathematics. This specific method relies on the approximation of pi as 22/7.</note>

# CHAPTER V.

## On Transformation.
<note>original: "De Reductione" — in 17th-century geometry, "reduction" refers to transforming one geometric shape into another of equal area, such as "squaring a circle."</note>

### Rule I.

*A triangle is transformed into a rectangle of the same area, where the base is contained six times within its height <note>original: "linea ejus orthogonali" — literally "orthogonal line," referring to the vertical altitude</note> if, at the end of the third part of the height, a perpendicular line equal to the base is raised at right angles; then, in the usual way with the other side, a parallelogram is formed, whose area is identical to that of the triangle.*

#### Examination.

Because <term>a. b. e. f.</term> is part of the triangle <term>a. b. d. f.</term>, and because a part of the rectangle—specifically <term>a. b. c.</term>—is equal to <term>b. d. e.</term>, the rectangle <term>a. c. e. f.</term> is therefore of the same dimension as the tri- <insert>angle a. d. f.</insert> and is transformed into the parallelogram <term>a. c. e. f.</term>
<note>This section explains a geometric proof where pieces of a triangle are rearranged to form a rectangle of equal area, a process known as "dissection."</note>

---

### Rule II.

*A triangle of the aforementioned dimension is transformed into a circle if its base, or the sixth part of its height, is used as the radius <note>original: "semidiameter"</note> of the circle.*

### Rule III.

*Two unequal squares are reduced into one if the sides of one and the other are placed at a right angle, and a straight line is extended from the extremity of one to the other, forming a triangle. For that hypotenuse <term>hypotenuse: the longest side of a right-angled triangle, which sits opposite the 90-degree angle</term> will measure the sides which must constitute the square containing the area of the two aforementioned squares.* <note>This is a practical application of the Pythagorean theorem to combine the areas of two squares into a single larger square.</note>

### Rule IV.

*The area of a square is reduced into a parallelogram <term>parallelogram: a four-sided figure with opposite sides parallel; in this geometric construction, Fludd is specifically describing a rectangle</term> if the bottom side of the square is lengthened to whatever quantity you wish your figure to have; let the top side of the same square also be extended to the same dimension, and let two parallel lines be fixed so that they form a quadrangle, let it be a. c. d. e. Then let a straight line be drawn from angle c. to angle e. and where this transversal line intersects the side of the square b. f., let it be marked g. For the length of line g. f. will be the width of the parallelogram equal in area to the given square.*

->PROOF.<-

Through the midpoint of the <term>perpendicular line<note>A line drawn at a right angle (90°) from the base to the highest point of the triangle to determine its height.</note></term>, let a line be drawn parallel to the base and equal to the length of the base; let it then be reduced into a <term>parallelogram<note>A four-sided shape with opposite sides that are parallel and equal in length.</note></term>, the area of which will be the same as that of the <term>scalene triangle<note>A triangle in which all three sides are of different lengths.</note></term>.

---

Similarly, because triangle **a.b.c.** is equal to triangle **c.e.d.**, triangle **d.e.f.** is also the same as triangle **f.g.h.** <note>This refers to the geometric proof shown in the first diagram, where pieces of the triangle are "moved" to fill a rectangle, proving their areas are identical.</note>

## Rule III.

*Triangles also, of which two angles are equal <note>These are isosceles triangles.</note>, are measured by the preceding rule: namely, by erecting a perpendicular line and multiplying the base by half of its height. The same is to be done where all angles are equal <note>These are equilateral triangles.</note>, as follows:*

---

->PROOF.<-

Take half of the base, and let that be the width of the parallelogram; or, take the midpoint of the perpendicular line, and let that be the height of the parallelogram.

<note>This table provides numerical examples of the area formula (Base × 1/2 Height). In the first case, 12 multiplied by 3 equals 36; in the second, 8 multiplied by 5 equals 40.</note>

Furthermore, all the shaded triangles <note>original: "trianguli obscuri"</note> outside the boundaries of the true triangle are equal to the triangles within the true triangle, as is evident from the preceding examples.

## Rule IV.

*A polygonal surface is measured by multiplying the sum of all its sides (or the bases of the internal triangles) and then multiplying that product by half of the perpendicular line <term>orthogonal line: also known as an apothem; a line drawn at a right angle from the center of a polygon to the midpoint of one of its sides</term> drawn from the central angle to the middle of the base.*

---

## Rule V.

*A trapezoidal surface, in which there are no right angles, but two sides are equal <note>This refers to an isosceles trapezoid.</note> and the ends are of unequal length, is measured by taking the average of the ends added together and multiplying that average by the length of the side.*

---

### I N V E S T I G A T I O N.

For if that trapezoid is reduced into a parallelogram and then measured according to the second proposition of multiplication, the resulting area <term>capacity: here used in the sense of two-dimensional area or "room" within the shape</term> will be the same as was previously demonstrated.

## Rule VI.

*In a trapezoid <note>A four-sided figure with at least one pair of parallel sides.</note> where two right angles are included: if half of that portion of the line by which the longer side exceeds the side opposite to it is added to that opposite side, and the surface is reduced to a parallelogram, you will most easily measure it by multiplication; for triangle a. b. c. is equal to triangle d. e. c.*

### Rule II.

In much the same way, the height of an object is perceived in a mirror <note>original: *speculum*</note> by approaching the mirror until the summit of the tower appears in the center of the mirror; then, by multiplying the interval from the center of the mirror to the foot of the tower by the height of the eye, and dividing the product by the distance from the person's foot to the center of the mirror. ### Rule III.

By a similar process, the accessible height of a tower is also gathered geometrically <note>original: *quadratè*, likely referring to the use of a geometric square or quadrant</note>: Because, if you multiply the distance from yourself to the base of the tower by the intercepted points of the <term>reversed shadow</term> <note>The "reversed shadow" (*umbra versa*) refers to markings on a surveying instrument like a quadrant or shadow square used when the object is taller than the observer's distance from it.</note>, and divide the product by 12, the quotient will be the height of the tower. Let the distance be 18 feet, and the intercepted points 4, as in Number 2.

->### Rule IV.<-

**The height of an inaccessible tower is found** if you divide 12 by the number of points cut off—namely 3—and you keep the quotient, which is 4. Then, having marked the location of your station, move backward to select a second station, and divide 12 by the points cut off there—namely 6; the quotient will be 2. This second quotient is then subtracted from the first quotient, provided the second is smaller than the first, and the remainder is kept. (However, where the second quotient is larger than the first, the first must be subtracted from the second.) For example, when 2 is taken from 4, 2 remains. Finally, let the distance between the first and second station be measured—which here is 40 feet—and this distance must be divided by the remainder <note>In this example, 40 divided by the remainder of 2 equals 20.</note>. To this quotient, the height of the observer’s own body must be added—let it be 5 feet—and the sum will be the total height of the object.

<note>The "points" mentioned here refer to the divisions on a <term>Geometric Square</term> or the <term>Shadow Square</term> on the back of an astrolabe or quadrant. These instruments used a scale of 12 parts to help surveyors calculate ratios of height to distance without needing complex trigonometry.</note>

[A diagram illustrating geometric height measurement of a tower using lines of sight to a reflection point or marker on the ground, labeled with numerical values 6, 18, and 16.]

## Rule III.

You shall divide a <term>right-angled triangle <note>original: triangulum rectangulum</note></term> into as many equal parts as you wish if you construct a square based on its <term>perpendicular line <note>original: lineam orthogonalem; the altitude of the triangle</note></term>. Divide the area of this square by 4, then extract the <term>root <note>original: radicem; the square root</note></term> of the resulting number. This value, when measured from the <term>apex <note>original: cono; literally 'cone', referring to the top vertex</note></term> of the triangle toward the base, will mark the first quarter of the triangle's area. The second quarter is found by taking half of the square's area and extracting its root; this root, measured downward from the apex toward the base, will identify the second quarter equal to the first. Finally, the third quarter will reveal itself by extracting the root of three-quarters of the square's area, always measuring from the apex toward the base, and so on for any further divisions.

[A geometric diagram of a triangle divided into segments labeled 1 through 8, used to illustrate Rule III.]

->For example.<-

## Rule IV.

In this same manner, we can divide non-right-angled triangles into equal parts by treating the side that most closely approaches a perpendicular line as the side of the square.

[A complex geometric diagram showing two overlapping triangles with horizontal dashed lines and numerical markers (6, 8, 10, 12), illustrating Rule IV.]

## CHAPTER XII.

->*On progression or proportion.*<-

### Rule I.

**T**he doubling of two correctly found stations of a three-foot <term>Jacob's staff<note>original: "baculi Jacobi"; a medieval and Renaissance surveying instrument used to measure angles and distances.</note></term> (whose <term>slider<note>original: "cursor"; the movable cross-piece on the staff.</note></term> shall be half a foot) will be the measure of the height of the object; for twice the distance from *a.* to *b.* will be the height of the tower, *c. d.* For the relationship of *a. b.* to *c. d.* is the same as 2 to 4, and 3 to 6.

->*For the sake of example.*<-

---

### Rule II.

*The length of an object is also gathered from the proportion of its width: for as the triangle A. B. C. is related, so also is the triangle of the instrument c. d. e. proportioned. Therefore, the side of triangle A. B. C., namely B. C., is similar to the side c. d. e. of the instrument. Thus, side C. B. differs from side A. B. by a <term>sesquiquartal ratio<note>A mathematical ratio of 5:4, where one value is 1.25 times the other.</note></term>; therefore, divide side A. B. into 5 equal parts, take away one, and the result will be the length B. C. We have demonstrated this extensively in the third book of our Geometry, where we made ample mention of a similar Jacob’s staff in every type of measurement, and where we also spoke fully about the use of the quadrant and the instruments we invented. You will find an example of this rule in that place, where a single length is investigated from a single station.*

### Rule III.

*The proportion of weights and moving objects is continued by a natural progression; if its orders are successively multiplied by themselves, they will produce the weights of the locations in geometric proportion, as is shown in the following figure.*

### Rule VI.

->For spheres or globes whose diameters are in a double proportion <note>original: "proportio est dupla"; meaning one diameter is twice the length of the other</note>, their ratio of volume and weight will be eightfold <note>original: "proportio octupla"</note>. Thus, if a larger sphere weighs 50 pounds, a smaller one <note>with half the diameter</note> will consist of 6 and 1/4 pounds.<-

---

### Rule VII.

->Once the weight of a cannonball <term>globus bombardalis</term> <note>from "bombarda," an early type of large-caliber cannon</note> is known, its measurement and diameter can be determined by a progressive proportion along a line or a flat surface. Therefore, let a one-pound globe be prepared from the same metal from which you wish to cast your artillery ball <term>tormentarium</term> <note>referring to siege engines or gunpowder artillery</note>. Let it be perfectly round, with a diameter marked A.B., the circumference of which you shall draw upon a flat surface.<-

The progression is therefore as follows: specifically, the fourth part of the circle of the one-pound globe, namely A.C., will be the radius <term>semidiameter</term> of the globe that ought to weigh two pounds. Furthermore, a fourth part of the circle of that two-pound globe will be the radius of a three-pound globe, and the fourth part of the three-pound globe will constitute the radius of a four-pound globe, and so on, progressing infinitely.
