## *Concerning the rule of three proportions.*

### Rule I.

When **t**wo proportional numbers are known, the third will also be determined through this rule. For if five parts of the parallel line A. B. correspond to 14 parts on the line C. D., then 40 parts of line A. B. will give 112 parts of line C. D. For the triangle A. B. E. shares similar angles with the triangle A. C. D. E. And the equally divided parts of the line or side A. B. are proportional to the divided parts of line C. D.

## On the extraction of the Root.
<note>original: "De Radicis extractione." This refers to the mathematical process of finding the square root of a number.</note>

### Rule I.

A number of two digits has only a single figure for its <term>root</term> <note>the number which, when multiplied by itself, produces a square</note>, because the largest square number of two digits or figures is 81, whose root is 9. For example:

### Rule II.

The root of any square number composed of two figures is found by multiplying that digit by itself whose product comes closest to the square number. For that digit will be the square's root, just as 6 is the root of the square 36. Similarly, 8 is the root of the square 64, because 6 <insert>when</insert> multiplied by itself produces 36, which no other digit can produce. So also eight times 8 makes 64, which is its square number, and so on for the others; concerning which [see] this wheel below, whose outer sphere denotes the roots, and the inner the squares.

## Rule IX.

*If after the extraction of a root <note>The "root" here refers to the square root, the side length of a square area.</note> some remainder is left over (which always happens when the number is not a perfect square), the remainder will be explained by fractional numbers, as in the case of 10, which contains 9 as its greatest square, whose root is 3. One unit, however, will remain, as appears in the following demonstration.*

-> [Diagram of a 3x3 square with a 10th unit excluded] <-

Therefore, the tenth part is excluded from the square (since the number nine is a square number), which is to be divided into 6 equal parts; these 6 are to be attached to the smaller squares of the two sides of the larger square. Such a number, however, cannot be perfectly squared, because of angle A, which is left empty. <note>This explains why the square root of 10 is an irrational number; geometrically, when you try to add the "remainder" to the sides of a square, you are always left with a tiny missing corner (1/6 x 1/6) that prevents it from forming a perfect larger square.</note>

-> [Diagram showing the division of the remainder unit into segments around the square] <-

## Rule X.

### Rule II.

*The root of a cube is also found without the preceding wheel <note>original: "rota"; referring to the circular volvelle diagram which functions as a visual look-up table for roots, squares, and cubes</note>, for a number is produced that closely approaches the value of the cube by multiplying some root <term>radix</term> by itself; the square <term>quadratus</term> which is the product, being multiplied again by the root, will be the cube <term>cubus</term> of that square; or by multiplying any square number by the root, the product of which comes closer to the value of the cube. ## Rule IX.

## Rule 12.

### Rule III.

*To determine the total sum of any pyramidal formation with an even number of ranks, consult the second rule of common Arithmetic progression, as follows:*

->12<-

<note>This calculation adds the first and last rank (1+12=13) and multiplies by half the number of ranks (6) to find the total number of soldiers (78) in a triangular formation.</note>

*If, however, the ranks are odd, let us seek counsel from the third rule of the same.*

### Rule IV.

*The number of soldiers in any Rhomboidal <term>Rhomboidalis: A diamond-shaped formation where the ranks widen to a middle point and then taper back down.</term> formation is determined by doubling the pyramid and subtracting the larger number or rank from the sum, as follows:*

->78 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 156<-
->2 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 12<-
->--- &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; ---<-
->156 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 144<-
<note>By doubling the triangle (78 x 2 = 156) and subtracting the shared middle rank (12), one arrives at the 144 soldiers needed for a diamond shape.</note>

### *The use of this type of formation.*

This arrangement of soldiers, which the French call *pointed battalions* <note>original: "Bataillons en point"</note> or *lozenge-shaped* <note>original: "en lozange"</note>, is very little in use today, except where necessity compels it. This occurs when the level ground of a location offers a path for the cohorts <term>cohortes: tactical units of infantry</term> whose entrance or exit is very narrow—being almost entirely surrounded by rocks, mountains, woods, rivers, marshes, or lakes—through which it is necessary for the army to pass. Similarly, such a form is required when invading a town as an enemy, especially where the streets are too narrow.

### Rule V.

*Cohorts are quickly arranged into a battle-line or square shape if you extract the square root <term>radix quadrata</term> of the total number of men. The extracted root will indicate the number of men in each rank or file. For example, let the number of soldiers be 625; the root of which is 25.*

->25<-

## Rule VI.

*Whoever wishes to arrange <term>cohorts</term> <note>A cohort was a standard unit of the Roman army, though in this Renaissance-era context, it refers generally to a body of soldiers.</note> in battle so that the formation has a length double, triple, or quadruple its width, should divide the total number of cohorts into as many parts as the factor by which he wants the length to exceed the width. For example, if the length should be three times the width, the number of soldiers must be divided by 3; the <term>square root</term> <note>original: "radix"</note> of the result will be the number of soldiers in each rank and file. If four times, divide by 4, and so on. Suppose, therefore, the number of soldiers is 2,310. When divided by 3, the result is 770. The square root of this is 27, and 41 men remain, who can be employed for other duties. The demonstration follows below.*

## Rule IX.

*The circumference of a circle shall be three times its diameter* <note>original: "triplus suo diametro." The author uses a simplified value for Pi (3 instead of 3.14) for easier calculation during troop maneuvers.</note>, for where the diameter is seven, there the circumference will be 21; and so it is for other internal circles. But the best method of all in the formation of round battle lines will be to first find the diameter of your circle and arrange it in the first place, then complete the entire circumference with three times that number of men. It must also be observed that the smaller diameter will consist of 3, as follows:

---

*(Diagram of concentric circular military formations showing the relationship between diameters of 3, 5, and 7 and their corresponding circumferences of 9, 15, and 21 men)*

---

This form of battle is necessary when the enemy is nearby, so that the first ranks may resist the adversaries while the inner ones form themselves; the <term>Front-rank Leader</term> <note>original: "Antesignanus" — historically a Roman elite soldier, but here referring to the commander or veteran officer positioned in the center to direct the formation.</note> must always be placed in the center, and let the smaller circle be composed of soldiers who carry short weapons, such as swords with small shields, halberds, etc. Indeed, the Germans and Dutch tend to order this disposition of soldiers more by continuous practice than by an accurate method or written rules of the military art.

## Rule X.

*Once the arrangement of the circular order is known, an oval figure can be established very easily.* Let the diameter of some round battle figure be the side of a certain square of men; let the round cohort be divided into equal parts, of which the middle part is joined to the head or front part of the square, and the other part to the rear, or "tail," and the battle figure will be oval, as follows:

## Rule XII.

*The ladder by which soldiers may scale the walls of a town protected by a <term>moat</term> <note>original: "fossâ"; a ditch or defensive trench</note> is best adapted in this way: Let the exact length be measured from the edge of the moat to the foot of the wall; likewise, measure the height of the wall. For a straight line crossing the moat will create a <term>right angle</term> <note>original: "angulum rectum"</note> with the foot of the wall. Therefore, the length of the diagonal line, by which the ladder must be measured, is determined by the method taught in <term>Geometrical Arithmetic</term> <note>original: "Arithmetica Geometrica"; the application of arithmetic to solve geometric problems, specifically the Pythagorean theorem in this context</note> in the chapter on multiplication and subtraction, under the first rule.*

# CHAPTER I.
## On Musical Proportion.

**To add** proportions is to multiply them. To subtract, however, is to divide them. To *double* is to multiply by itself; therefore, multiplication and division do not function in the same way in proportions as in simple arithmetic, because proportions do not admit the number one; for one cannot descend below the double proportion <note>The "double proportion" refers to the 2:1 ratio of the octave.</note>. The demonstration of this rule can be seen by the eyes, as it were, in the division of the Monochord <note>A one-stringed scientific instrument used to measure musical intervals.</note>.

A "multiple proportion" is one in which a larger number is compared to a smaller quantity and measure.

How all the remaining proportions relate to one another is shown in the book on numeration, in the chapter concerning proportions.

### Rule VIII.

*The "acute" <note>high-pitched</note> letters are to be found in exactly the same way as the "grave" <note>low-pitched</note> ones: namely, by dividing the remainder of the string from G to Π into 9 parts to find the location of the high letter A; then the distance from A to Π into another 9 parts to find the location of the high B, and so on for the rest.*

### Rule IX.

*We shall proceed by the same progression to find the "superexcellent" <note>the highest register in the medieval musical scale</note> or extremely high letters, as will appear more extensively in the following demonstration.*

### Rule X.

*The proportion of a whole tone to another tone is as 9 to 8. But the proportion of a semitone to a tone is the superpartient proportion <term>superpartient: a complex mathematical ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number plus several fractional parts—in this case, the Pythagorean "limma" (256:243)</term> of 256 to 243. For example, if a monochord is divided into 324 parts, that number represents a tone; but the second tone is 288. The semitone is 256. The **Diatessaron** <term>Diatessaron: a perfect fourth</term> is as 4 to 3. The **Diapente** <term>Diapente: a perfect fifth</term> is as 3 to 2. And the **Diapason** <term>Diapason: an octave</term> is as 2 to 1, as is clear in the following example.*

### Rule XI.

*From an <term>octave</term> <note>original: "Diapason"; an interval of eight notes</note> combined with a <term>fifth</term> <note>original: "Diapente"; an interval of five notes</note> arises a triple proportion, or a "double-sesquialter" proportion <note>original: "dupla sesquialtera"; this refers to a 3:1 ratio, which creates the musical interval of a twelfth</note>. From a double-octave comes a quadruple proportion <note>a 4:1 ratio</note>, and from a triple-octave arises an octuple proportion <note>an 8:1 ratio</note>. The <term>fourth</term> <note>original: "Diatessaron"; an interval of four notes</note> consists of a <term>four-to-three ratio</term> <note>original: "sesquitertia"; where the larger number is 1 and 1/3 times the smaller</note>. The fifth, however, remains in a <term>three-to-two ratio</term> <note>original: "sesquialtera"; where the larger number is 1 and 1/2 times the smaller</note>, as is clearly shown to the eyes of the viewers in the preceding demonstration.*

### TREATISE II. PART I. BOOK VI.

The numbers encompassing musical consonances were discovered from the weights of hammers. <note>This refers to the legend of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who supposedly discovered the mathematical basis of music by listening to the different pitches produced by hammers of various weights in a blacksmith's forge.</note> Just as there were four hammers, so there are four numbers found from their weights, as has been said, which contain almost the entire power of music. These numbers are 6, 8, 9, and 12. In these four numbers, you will find just as many proportions, and through these, just as many perfect consonances. These proportions are: *Double, One-and-a-half, One-and-a-third, and One-and-an-eighth*.

*Double proportion* <note>original: *Dupla proportio* (2:1 ratio)</note> occurs whenever the larger number, compared to the smaller, contains it twice within itself, such as 6 to 12, 4 to 8, 2 to 4, and 1 to 2. Under this proportion falls the consonance called the <term>Diapason</term> <note>The interval of an octave.</note>, as is demonstrated below on the <term>monochord</term> <note>A scientific and musical instrument with a single string and a movable bridge, used to demonstrate the mathematical properties of sound.</note>.

If you wish to prove this, whether on strings, pipes, small bells, or large bells and all sounding things, it is necessary that one thing be double the size of the other, and thus the half will undoubtedly sound the <term>Diapason</term> in relation to the whole.

*One-and-a-half proportion* <note>original: *Sesquialtera proportio* (3:2 ratio)</note> occurs whenever the larger number, related to the smaller, contains the whole smaller number within itself, and half of it besides, such as 12 to 8, 9 to 6, 6 to 4, and 3 to 2. From this proportion arises that consonance which is called the <term>Diapente</term> <note>The interval of a perfect fifth.</note>. Wherever the <term>Diapente</term> is found, its lower voice will always contain the entire other part and its half.

*One-and-a-third proportion* <note>original: *Sesquitertia proportio* (4:3 ratio)</note> is when the larger number compared to the smaller contains it whole, and a third part of it besides, such as 12 to 9, 8 to 6, and 4 to 3. From this harmony of numbers consists the <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>The interval of a perfect fourth.</note> consonance, where its lower voice contains the whole of the other part and its third part.

*One-and-an-eighth proportion* <note>original: *Sesquioctava proportio* (9:8 ratio)</note> is when the larger number related to the smaller contains the whole smaller number and an eighth part of it, such as 9 to 8 (where the difference is a single unit); in this proportion the tone is encompassed. Do not doubt that its lower voice contains the entire other part and its eighth part.

*Note*, that wherever the aforementioned consonances exist, you will undoubtedly find those proportional numbers by which alone—and not by others—we divided the monochord as shown above. By these numbers, all musical instruments are formed, such as pipes, cymbals, and small or large bells; by these, harps, lyres, and viols resonate. Finally, whatever in the world resonates musically will in no way deviate from these proportions of numbers.

---

->CHAPTER IV.<-

->*On temporal proportion.*<-
<note>Temporal proportion refers to the speed and rhythmic relationships between different musical notes.</note>

->Rule I.<-

**I**N double proportion, two small notes are equivalent to one of the same name and quantity, such as two <term>minims</term> <note>A short musical note; in modern notation, similar to a half note.</note> equaling one, and two <term>semibreves</term> <note>Originally the shortest note, but by this period it functioned as the primary unit of time, similar to a whole note.</note> equaling one. Similarly, in triple proportion, 3 notes are equivalent to one. In quadruple, 4 notes are equivalent to one in measure and quantity, and so on for the others.

->Rule II.<-

->*Quintuple proportion is represented by the semibreve.*<-

->Rule III.<-

->*Sextuple proportion, because of its speed, cannot easily be expressed by the fingers or lips through the minim.*<-
->Therefore, this proportion must always be composed using the semibreve.<-

### CHAPTER IV.
->ON THE DISCOVERY OF THE CONJUNCTION, OPPOSITION, AND QUADRATURE OF THE LUMINARIES.<-

Add as many days to the **Epact** <term>Epact: The age of the moon in days on January 1st, used to synchronize solar and lunar calendars.</term> of your year as the number of months that have passed since the beginning of March. Subtract 30 from this total if it exceeds 30, and the remainder will be the day of the **conjunction** <term>Conjunction: The New Moon, when the Sun and Moon are at the same celestial longitude.</term> for the month in which the conjunction is sought. By adding seven and a half to these days, the first day of **quadrature** <term>Quadrature: A moon phase where the Moon is 90 degrees from the Sun; the first or last quarter moon.</term> will result; by adding another seven and a half to those, the day of **opposition** <term>Opposition: The Full Moon, when the Moon is directly opposite the Sun in the sky.</term> will be born; finally, by adding 7 and a half to these, the second quadrature will be produced.

Let the year, therefore, be 1600, whose Epact is 15. Let the month be July, in which the time of the conjunction is to be sought, which is the fifth month starting from March: therefore, 5 must be added to 15.

# ON ASTRONOMICAL AND ASTROLOGICAL ARITHMETIC.

## CHAPTER V.

### On the Discovery of <term>ASPECTS</term> <note>The angular distances between planets that astrologers believe create specific "harmonies" or "tensions."</note> in the <term>Zodiac</term> <note>The 360-degree circle of the heavens divided into twelve signs.</note>.

The **Z**odiac consists of 360 parts [degrees]; halving it denotes the aspect of <note>The text shows conjunction symbols ☌ — ☌, but the math indicates the 180-degree aspect, known as an Opposition ☍.</note> opposition; but if it is divided by 3, the resulting number will be a third part of the zodiac, making the △ (trine) aspect: if by 4, it will produce the □ (square) aspect; if by 6, it will denote the * (sextile) aspect as many times as it goes in.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 3 6 0 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; (180.

## CHAPTER VI.

### On finding the true hour of any day in which a conjunction (☌), opposition (☍), square (□), trine (△), or sextile (*) occurs between two planets.

**B**ecause it is necessary to erect a celestial figure <note>A horoscope or birth chart.</note> for the hour of an aspect, either for predicting changes in the weather or for preparing <term>elections</term> <note>The practice of selecting the most spiritually or physically auspicious time to begin a task, like a journey or a building project.</note>. This is therefore done in this way: *One must examine the Ephemerides <note>A book or table listing the daily positions of the planets.</note> of the given year and month, where the planets that are due to make an aspect are closer together; one must also observe whether both are in direct motion, or both retrograde, or whether one is direct and the other retrograde.*

*Where indeed both are direct or retrograde, their daily motion must be considered: which motion of theirs is either equal or unequal. If they are indeed unequal, the smaller number is to be subtracted from the larger, and the remainder will be the first term of the "rule of three" <note>A mathematical method of finding a fourth value from three known values using proportions.</note>. If, however, the motions of both are equal, then the daily motion will be the first term of that rule. For example, a conjunction (☌) of the Sun (☉) with the Moon (☾) in the year 1600 occurs on February 14. The daily motion of the Sun is 1 degree; while the Moon's is 14 degrees and 27 minutes.*

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; ☾. &nbsp;&nbsp; 14 deg. &nbsp; 27 min.  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; ☉. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 1 deg. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 0 min. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 13 deg. 27 min. **Z** <note>original: "Z°" likely standing for the Zenith or the calculated difference.</note>  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 13 deg. &nbsp; 27 min.  

*The second term will always be 24 <note>Representing the 24 hours of a day.</note>.*

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 13 deg. &nbsp; 27 min. **Z** 24 [hours].

*The final term is collected by subtracting the motion of one <term>meridian</term> <note>The position of the planet at noon.</note> from the motion of the other. The noon motion of both is taken for that day in which the planets behold each other. Whatever remains from the larger number will be the third term. Therefore, the Moon's motion at the noon hour was 21 degrees and 40 minutes; while the Sun's was 24 degrees and 38 minutes.*

### CHAPTER VII.

->On finding the ALTITUDE OF THE SUN.<-

*The declination of the degree of the Sun, in which the sun is found on the day the question is raised, must be considered. If the declination is northern <note>original: "septentrionalis"</note>, it must be subtracted from the latitude of the region; if it is southern <note>original: "meridiana"</note>, it must be added to the latitude. The resulting sum must then be subtracted from 90; what remains will be the altitude of the sun for that day.*

---

### CHAPTER VIII.

->On finding the NUMBER OF DEGREES FOR UNEQUAL HOURS.<-

*Divide the portion of the <term>diurnal circle</term> <note>the arc the sun travels above the horizon</note> by 12, and the quotient will reveal the number of parts for the hours of that day. This same process must also be followed when the number of parts for the hours of the night is desired—namely, by dividing the portion of the nocturnal circle by 12.*
<note>"Unequal hours," also known as planetary or seasonal hours, divide the period of daylight and darkness into 12 segments each, meaning an "hour" varies in length depending on the time of year.</note>

ON ASTRONOMICAL AND ASTROLOGICAL ARITHMETIC

## C A P. IX.

->*On finding* EQUAL HOURS *for any day.*<-

**D**ivide the portion of the day’s circle <note>In traditional astronomy, the full circle of the sky is 360 degrees; dividing by 15 results in the 24 hours we use today.</note> by 15, and the result will be the number of equal hours of the day. In this same way, the equal hours of the night are found, if the nocturnal portion is divided by 15.

---

## C A P. X.

->*On the conversion of equal hours into unequal hours.*<-

**M**ultiply the equal hours by 15, and divide the product by the degrees of the hours for that day <note>This refers to the "seasonal" length of an hour for a specific date.</note>; you will then have the unequal hours <term>unequal hours: also known as "planetary hours," these divide the period of daylight into 12 equal parts regardless of the season, meaning an "hour" is longer in summer than in winter</term>.

---

## C A P. XI.

->*On the conversion of unequal hours into equal hours.*<-

**M**ultiply the unequal hours by the parts <note>degrees</note> of the hours of that day, and divide the result by fifteen; you will then have the <insert>equal</insert> hours. <note>The original text contains a correction where "unequal" was struck through and replaced with "equal".</note>

---

## C A P. XII.

->*On finding the* DAILY MOTION *of any* PLANET.<-

**O**ne must consider the motion of the planet: namely, is it retrograde <note>appearing to move backward across the sky</note> or direct? For if it is retrograde, the minutes and seconds must be subtracted. But where the planet is direct, the minutes and seconds are to be added. For example, Saturn <note>original symbol: ♄</note> is retrograde on the fourth day of November. The difference in its motion from the 3rd to the 4th is between 39 and 34. Similarly, its direct motion on the 3rd of July is between 24 and 13.

| Saturn retrograde: 39 | Saturn Direct: 24 |
|------------|---------------|
| 34         | 13            |
| ---        | ---           |
| 5 daily motion | 37 daily motion |

---

## C A P. XIII.

->ON THE CALCULATION OF THE MOTION OF THE PLANETS FOR ANY GIVEN HOUR.<-

**T**he daily motion of any planet and the hours elapsed since noon must be reduced to minutes. Then, multiply the minutes of the one by the minutes of the other, and divide the product by 24. Again, divide the resulting number by 60, and the quotient will signify the true motion of that planet. For example, let the daily motion of the Sun be 58 minutes, and the hours in question be 20 hours and 30 minutes past noon.

## CHAPTER III.

### On Duplication and Multiplication

**D**uplication occurs when any figure is found twice in the same chart—that is, in different "Houses" <note>The 'Houses' are the twelve or sixteen positions in a geomantic chart, each corresponding to a different area of life, such as wealth or family.</note> of that same figure. Multiplication is when the same figure is found even more frequently in the same chart.

### Rule I.

*The first figure found in the second House portends riches and profit; in the third, it signifies something good from parents; and so on for the others, according to the nature of the Houses in which they are found, as in Figure 4.*

### Rule II.

*If any figure is multiplied within the Shield <note>The 'Shield' (or 'Scutum') is the central part of the geomantic diagram containing the core figures of the divination.</note>, it signifies the good or bad fortune of the seeker, according to the nature and disposition of the figures that appear so frequently, such as:*

## CHAPTER IV.

### On Increase and Decrease.

**I**ncrease and decrease occurs when the total number of points in the 16 figures of the Shield either exceeds the total number of all simple geometric points (which is 96) or is less than that number.

### Rule.

<insert>Hand-drawn arrow in left margin pointing to this paragraph</insert>
*When the slowness or speed of a future event is required, first ask whether the sum of all the points in the geomantic chart, when added together, is greater or less than the given number 96. For the smaller it is, the swifter the event of the question will be, and vice versa. For example, if a prognosis were to be made regarding the length or shortness of some illness, and such a chart occurred to us as in Figure 5.*

## CHAPTER V.

### *On projection.*

<margin>☞</margin>
**G**eomantic projection is performed by taking the odd points <note>Geomantic figures are made of rows containing either one or two dots. For the specific house and the figure within it to which the final number is assigned will be the "conjunction" <note>The focal point or primary answer</note> of the inquiry. The upper circle of the wheel described above denotes the number of the letters of the names; the circle placed below that contains the elementary letters themselves; the third circle from the circumference indicates the number of the days of the week; and the circle designated below it, the names of the days. Finally, a line in the form of an axis passing through the middle of the entire sphere, and dividing it into two equal parts, is like its <term>Horizon</term> <note>The dividing line between the "living" (upper) and "dead" (lower) sections of the chart.</note>, distinguishing one hemisphere—namely, the upper—from the lower. Furthermore, the numbers positioned above that diameter promise prosperous fortune; truly, those below it promise misfortune. The <term>prognostications</term> <note>predictions or forecasts</note> drawn from this wheel are of this sort:

-> *To know which of the combatants shall obtain the victory.* <-

Take the name of one and likewise the other who are to fight between themselves, and collect the numbers assigned to each letter; next, collect the number of the day on which the fight ought to happen; similarly, the number of the <term>Moon</term> <note>referring to the age of the moon in the lunar cycle (e.g., 1st day of the moon, 2nd day, etc.).</note>—namely, if it be the first day of the Moon, take 1; if the second, 2; and so on. Let these numbers be added together and divided by 30; having done this, seek whatever remains over 30 within the hollow of the sphere. If it is found in the upper hemisphere, he will be the victor; if in the lower, he is the defeated.

-> *Concerning a fugitive, whether he shall return or not, or if he shall be found.* <-

Proceed with his name just as you did in the preceding account with each of the combatants, and divide the total sum of the name of the fugitive, the day, and the Moon by 30, and seek the remainder. For if it is found in the upper hemisphere, he shall return or be found; but if in the lower, the opposite.

### *Whether a pregnant woman will give birth to a male or a female.*

Calculate the numerical value of the name of the woman and her youngest son, or, if she has no son, calculate the value of her husband's name, add 15, and divide by 9. If the number is even, a male will be born; if it is odd, a female.

### *Whether the husband or the wife is to die first?*

Calculate the value of their names by the letters <note>This refers to onomancy, where each letter of a name is assigned a numerical value</note>, and divide by 9. If the remaining number is even, the man will bury his wife; if odd, the wife will bury her husband.

### *Whether in a one-eyed man his right or left eye is missing?*

Calculate the numerical value of his name by dividing by 9 and adding one to the remainder. For if, after the division is made, an even number remains, it will be the right eye; if odd, the left.

This sphere is divided into three circles and a single center <note>Latin: *ventrem*, literally "belly" or core</note>. ->Use of this sphere.<-

->*Concerning fugitives: will they return or be found, or not?*<-

Calculate the value of the fugitive's name by its letters and divide by 30; to this, add the age of the Moon <term>age of the Moon: the number of days passed since the last New Moon</term> and the number of the day on which they fled, then divide the total by 30. The same method is to be observed as in the previous case, namely by calculating the letters of the name and dividing by 30, and adding the age of the Moon for the day of the battle or the start of the journey, and simultaneously adding the number of the day itself, finally dividing the aggregate by 30. For the upper part of the sphere will denote victory, while the lower part denotes the contrary.

### CHAPTER X.

By this same art, the superstitious also predict the *friendships or enmities* of men; they even pass judgment *concerning litigious matters, good fortune or misfortunes, captivity and imprisonment, titles and honor, plague and slaughter*, and other such things. All of these I have omitted in this place because I would not wish for too much faith to be placed in this science <note>original: "huic scientiæ," referring to onomancy/divination</note>, on account of the uncertainty of its principles.

## Rule II.

*The aforementioned places will also very easily retain a series of two numbers through a mental image <note>original: "conceptum"</note> if a double action is performed in each place, namely from its lower part to its upper part, in this manner. Let it be imagined that in the first place a man or a girl is positioned, waiting for apples, nuts, or some other fruit to fall from a tree. In the second place, however, let a mental image be formed such that some people appear to be ringing bells hanging at the top of a very tall tower. In the third, a wolf or a fox greedily gazing at men hanging from a gallows. You will visualize it in that manner, as shown in Figure 1 immediately following.*

## Rule III.

*If there are more series in addition, subtraction, or multiplication above the roof of this square, it is necessary to add three places of another square, filling them also with a double mental impression. For in the first part of that square, you should visualize a bridge in your mind, upon which a fisherman will stand, who appears to be pulling a fairly large fish out of the river with a hook. Similarly, if more places are required in these operations <note>original: "speciebus," referring here to the "species" or types of arithmetic</note>, it will be necessary to connect the places of one square to those of another side-by-side, either simply or doubly, according to how many series there are to be added, as shown in the following Figure 2.*

## C H A P T E R II.

->On addition.<-

### Rule I.

**Suppose** then that the numbers to be added are 164 and 335. <note>In this mnemonic system, the author assigns specific objects to digits: 1 is a spear, 3 is a tripod, 4 is a square cap, 5 is a horn, and 6 is a snail.</note> Let the imagination conceive of a man covered with a square cap <note>original: *pileo quadrato*; representing the number 4</note>, who, greedily desiring the fruit of a tree, has violently thrown his horn <note>original: *cornu*; representing the number 5</note> against the fruits, and by the force of that blow broke it into tiny pieces, the broken parts of which will tear his cap. In the second place, let it be imagined that a snail <note>original: *limacem*; representing the number 6</note> has wounded a man ringing a bell with its horns; seeing this, the bell-ringer, by knocking a tripod <note>original: *tripodem*; representing the number 3</note> down upon him, killed the snail. In the third place, let it be impressed upon the intellect that a wolf is attempting, with a spear <note>original: *hasta*; representing the number 1</note> and by other means, to cut the halter of a hanged man; while he is about to do this, a tripod <note>here acting as a gallows or *patibulum*; representing the number 3</note> terrified and put him to flight by falling.

### Rule II.

*Moreover, the aforementioned figures are added by the conversion of two figures into a third.* <note>The "metamorphosis" is the process of adding the two digits to produce a new symbol representing the sum.</note> For the cap and the horn of the first order are transformed into a serpent <note>representing the number 9, the sum of 4 and 5</note>; the snail and the tripod into a dog's tail <note>representing the number 9, the sum of 6 and 3</note>, with which the serpent, because of the liveliness of the action, will do battle. Similarly, under the third series of places, the third metamorphosis—or the transformation of the spear and the gallows into a square book <note>representing the number 4, the sum of 1 and 3</note>—will be expressed, as shown below.

# CHAPTER III.
## *On Subtraction.*
### *Rule I.*

**S**ubtraction in this art is performed by the same means, namely by subtracting the bases of the positions from the upper series, and placing the transformed result in the <term>fundamental place</term> <note>The "fundamental place" is the primary mental workspace or "memory palace" used by the practitioner.</note>. Thus the character 4—namely, the **hat**—subtracted from the character 5—the **horn**—generates the character 1, the **spear**; and so it goes for the others, just as is held in common Arithmetic.

---

# CHAPTER IV.
## *On Multiplication.*

**I**n multiplication, where the multiplier is a single unit, the method is clearly the same. But because a multiplier is sometimes composed of many units, the <term>fundamental place</term> is divided into three or more equal parts according to its length: one of these will be **green**, another **white**, and the third **ruddy red**. For by these distinctions, the numbers to be multiplied can be set out better and more clearly, and this is also explained in the following example. Whatever the total sum of the multiplication might be, it must be expressed in the **black** section.

# CHAPTER V.
## *On Division.*

**B**ecause practitioners very rarely use this final species of Arithmetic in this art—both due to the difficulty of grasping the concept quickly, and because of the great number of operations involved, which would generate confusion in the Artist's imagination—we shall make no mention of it in this place. Instead, we shall leave it to be discovered by the sharper investigations of others, while we hasten our steps toward <term>lighthearted arithmetic</term> <note>original: "Arithmetica jocosa," referring to recreational mathematics or mathematical puzzles intended for entertainment.</note>, by which we may finally refresh our minds, which have long been weary from these vain imaginings.

# BOOK ELEVEN.

## Concerning Jocose Arithmetic.
<note>Original: *Arithmetica Jocosa*. This refers to "playful" or recreational mathematics—a genre of literature popular in the 17th century that used arithmetic for magic tricks, puzzles, and social entertainment.</note>

---

->CHAPTER I.<-

<margin>Decorative woodcut initial S</margin>
*IF there are three men, of whom one has gold, another silver, and the third lead, it will be very easy to guess by the following rule who among them has the gold, who the silver, and finally who the lead?* You shall give the name "one" to one of them, "two" to the second, and "three" to the third. Then, command that the one who holds the gold double his name-number; let the one who has the silver multiply his by 9; and let him who possesses the lead multiply his by ten. Next, the resulting product must be investigated, and it must be observed how much or by how many units it differs from 60. Afterward, it must be noted how many times 8 is contained in that number; for how many times it is contained will infallibly demonstrate who has the gold. For if it contains 8 once, the first person has it; if twice, the second; if three times, the third person holds the gold. It must likewise be observed what remains after the division by 8; because from this, knowledge of the possessor of the silver arises: if one remains, the first has it; if two, the second; if three, the third. Once these are known, the possessor of the lead is very easily identified.

---

->CHAPTER II.<-

<margin>Large initial S</margin>
*IF a ring is held secretly on some finger and you wish to know upon which finger it rests?* First, the number one is to be given to the thumb as its number; let two be given to the index, three to the middle, four to the ring finger <note>original: *medico*, the "medical finger," so called because of an ancient belief that a vein ran from this finger directly to the heart</note>, and five to the little finger. Afterward, command him to double the number of the finger on which the ring is placed; to this doubled value, let the numbers of the other fingers be added. Then, subtract 15 from the total sum, and the remainder will show the finger upon which the ring is found.

---

->CHAPTER III.<-

<margin>Large initial C</margin>
*IT IS ALSO known, by the wonderful aid of this art, in which hand two coins—one of even value, the other odd—are separately hidden.* For if a three-denarius coin and a two-denarius coin are handed to someone to be hidden in their hands, the coin hidden in the right hand must always be tripled, while the one enclosed in the left must be doubled. Let the tripled number then be added to the doubled one; if the total number is even, then the even-valued coin will be found in the left hand; but if it is odd, it will be found in the right.

->THE END.<-

## A MOST LUMINOUS
# DESCRIPTION OF THE PREFIGURED TEMPLE.

**Concerning** the structure and situation of this temple, the Poets would sing marvelous things—they whose intentions are usually and constantly occupied with fables and fictions. Indeed, they would pursue this subject much more eagerly since Music derives its name from their Goddesses, namely the Muses, just as is held in the etymology of the word <note>The word "Music" comes from the Greek *Mousike*, meaning "art of the Muses."</note>. I therefore beg leave of them if I allow myself to be led in the description of this temple by the stimulus and invention of "poetic fury" <note>original: *poëtici furoris* — a Renaissance concept referring to divine inspiration or a state of creative trance</note>, though not by its poetic meter <note>Fludd is explaining that he will use the vivid, imaginative language of poets, but will write in prose rather than verse</note>.

Let us imagine, then, this Musical Temple constructed upon the summit of Mount Parnassus <note>A mountain in central Greece which, according to mythology, was the home of the Muses and sacred to Apollo</note>, the seat of the Muses; adorned on every side by groves and fields flourishing with everlasting greenness, and surrounded by crystalline springs flowing gently here and there. The murmur of these springs often induces peaceful sleep in those passing by, while the little birds frequenting those parts and inhabiting the woods seem diligently to provide a base or foundation for the temple with their sharper songs—doing so that they might pour out diverse consonances of sounds more symphonically. By the melody of these birds, the Nymphs themselves around the temple, the Satyrs led by Sylvanus <note>The Roman god of the woods and uncultivated lands</note> through its groves, and the Shepherds (with Pan <note>The god of the wild, shepherds, and flocks, often associated with the rustic music of the pan-pipes</note> as their leader) through the fields are moved to dance. 

Amidst these delights, therefore, that divine gift of Apollo is established, preserved, and indeed worshipped with the adoration of all souls. All its constituent parts, dedicated to peace and concord, are so bound to one another by the mysteries of harmony and symphony—which include the concordances of the heavens and the elements—that it would be necessary for the whole universe to perish and be reduced to nothing by the strife of discord before the temple's consonances should either fail or be corrupted.

<summary>This page introduces an allegorical "Temple of Music" situated on Mount Parnassus, describing it as a divine structure where the laws of harmony mirror the eternal order of the universe. Fludd uses poetic imagery of gods, muses, and nature to illustrate that musical consonance is a fundamental, indestructible force of creation.</summary>

-> The Presiding deity or GODDESS of this temple is *Concord*, <-
the ineffable Concord, the great offspring of the Being of Beings <note>original: "Entis Entium"—a Neoplatonic term for God as the ultimate source of existence</note>, by whose adoration small things grow, and by whose contempt great things fall into ruin <note>This is a reference to a famous Roman maxim by Sallust: "concordia parvae res crescunt, discordia maximae dilabuntur."</note>. Its Guardian
<margin>/</margin> or priestess is *Thalia*, the sweetest of the nine Muses; through her
teachings, the hidden mysteries of harmony are explained to those traveling through and to those who humbly seek her Oracles.

<margin>/</margin> Therefore, the man of science will observe with eager eyes every part of this structure, nor will he despise its smallest portion, because that harmonic soul of Apollo <note>Apollo was the god of music and leader of the Muses; Fludd suggests a divine "soul" inhabits the laws of music.</note>, and that spirit of Music, moves within every part just as it does in the whole. It is accustomed to breathe through all the nerves of this structure like the West Wind <note>original: "Zephyri"</note>, soothing and gladdening the souls of living creatures, carrying away human desires, and by its sweetness restraining the madness of malignant demons, imbuing them as if with a certain humanity. Eagerly, I say, you should gaze upon the spiral revolution of the tower of the larger temple,
<margin>/</margin> which denotes the motion of the air after it is struck by a sound or voice.
<margin>/</margin> Two golden doors signify the organs of hearing <note>The ears</note>, without which
<margin>/</margin> an emitted sound is not perceived; nor is there any entry into this temple
<margin>/</margin> except through them. In the second place, you will observe its three smaller towers, representing the arrangements of the notes, <term>B-round</term> <note>original: "b rotundi"—the soft hexachord, source of the "flat" sign (♭)</note>, <term>B-square</term> <note>original: "♮ quadrati"—the hard hexachord, source of the "natural" (♮) and "sharp" (♯) signs</note>, and the Natural; and alongside the observation of these, three parallelograms are to be sharply inspected (each built under its respective tower, to which it is naturally related), demonstrating the various natures, names, and places of the aforementioned notes within the <term>system</term> <note>The "system" or "gamut" refers to the full range of notes used in music at the time.</note>. Furthermore, the pipes or organs expressed at the summit of these parallelograms denote the differences of voices and sounds in each parallelogram. 

Nor should the division of the column of this temple be despised, since it outlines the true proportions of the <term>monochord</term> <note>A one-stringed instrument used by ancient and Renaissance theorists to mathematically demonstrate musical intervals.</note> and the various types of consonances. The clock <note>original: "horologium"</note> must also be weighed diligently, lest time slip away unexpectedly, or proceed with too slow a foot (that is, with no proportion or measure observed). This clock, therefore, is like the guardian of the regular time of the notes, and a most ample mirror of their simple value. Why should the triangle of commensurable quantity not also be inspected? It examines the diversity of the proportion of times in both diminution and augmentation, and clearly demonstrates the perfection and imperfection of the notes. <note>In Renaissance music, "perfection" and "imperfection" referred to triple or duple rhythmic divisions.</note> Finally, the symphonic triangle of the system of intervals must be inspected with no small care, as the final mystery of all the rest; for through it, and from it, all musical consonances are drawn, without which no symphony is made. # BOOK ONE,
## Concerning the Subject of Music.

---

### CHAPTER I.

->Concerning the Definition, Etymology, and Inventors of Music.<-

<margin>In Music, we first consider its</margin>

<margin>Definition, which is taken</margin>
> *Generally, it is defined* as a divine science by which all worldly things are connected with an unbreakable bond, and by which, in every single thing, like is related to like in equal proportion. This definition of Music applies to the cosmic <note>original: "mundanæ"</note>, the human, and the instrumental.
> *Specifically, it is defined* as the science of singing well, the skill <note>original: "fides"</note> of playing instruments, and the art of composing songs well and fittingly, in both low and high pitches. And it is the subject of this Music that we shall treat within this temple.

<margin>Etymology, for its name is derived either</margin>
> From *Moys*, which is "water" in Latin <note>This refers to an old, though linguistically incorrect, medieval belief that the word for "water" in Egyptian or Greek was the root for "music" or "Moses"</note>, as if it were a science discovered near water, because without the benefit of moisture, no song or delight of the voice can exist.
> From the *Muses*, according to the myths; and the Muses are named from *muso*, that is, "I seek," because, as the ancients believe, the power of songs and the modulation of the voice were sought after. This is also confirmed by Socrates in Plato’s *Alcibiades*, who testifies that the Muses were the first presiding deities of the musical art, from whom Music took its name. And it is for this reason that we have fashioned *Thalia* as the guardian of this temple, who far excels the other eight of her order in joyfulness.

<margin>Inventors. For according to</margin>
> *Moses, Tubal* of the lineage of Cain was the inventor of this art before the Great Flood.
> The *Greeks, Pythagoras* discovered the first principles of this art from the sounds of hammers and the striking of stretched strings. He labored long over this science but could not find anything certain about it; while tossing about in this uncertainty and endlessly revolving many ideas in his mind, he finally came to a certain blacksmith's shop. There he saw men striking one anvil with five small hammers, and he perceived that they created a certain harmony <note>original: "consonantiam"</note> with their strokes. Consequently, he ordered the hammers to be weighed. Casting aside one which was discordant with the others, he weighed the remaining hammers: the first weighed 12 units, the second 9, the third 8, and the fourth 6. From these numerical weights, the harmonies are born upon which the whole art of Music stands, namely the <term>Diapason</term> <note>the interval of an octave</note>, the <term>Diapente</term> <note>the interval of a perfect fifth</note>, and the <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>the interval of a perfect fourth</note>, as we have discussed more extensively in our *Musical Arithmetic*.

# ON THE SUBJECT OF MUSIC.

> After *Pythagoras*, *Boethius* <note>An influential 6th-century Roman philosopher whose "De institutione musica" was the standard music theory textbook for a millennium.</note> flourished and left behind wonders in this art. Then came *Guido the Monk* <note>Guido of Arezzo (c. 991–1033), the inventor of modern staff notation.</note>, who was the inventor of the system. He was succeeded by *Franco* <note>Franco of Cologne (mid-13th century), who developed "mensural notation" where the shape of a note indicates its rhythm.</note>, who established the alteration, perfection, and imperfection of figures in measured song.

As for the origin of Music and the invention of musical instruments, a great controversy arises among writers. For *Pythagoras* himself asserts that this discipline was not invented by men, but by the Architect of the world himself; He caused the celestial spheres to be moved by a certain harmony of intervals and motions, from which Pythagoras affirms that human Music flowed forth. The Poets make *Apollo* the leader and moderator of this science; and certainly not without reason, since among them the Sun is the leader and prince of the spheres and the moderator of the other lights—the mind or soul of the world, and the very heart of heaven. *Heraclides Ponticus* makes *Jupiter* (Jove) the inventor of songs. *Amphion*, the son of Jupiter and Antiope, invented the lyre, and *Terpander* was the first to publish the rules of the lyre. *Apollo* invented the cithara <note>A professional version of the lyre, often associated with formal song.</note> and the flute <note>original: "tibia," an ancient double-reed instrument similar to an oboe.</note> according to *Macrobius*. *Pythagoras* was the first to discover Music, a view which we shall follow more closely. But according to *Pliny*, *Amphion* and *Cethione* first revealed it. According to some, *Lamisus Heroneus*, son of *Chabrinus* (who was numbered among the seven sages of Greece in place of *Periander*), wrote the first book on Music. *Tyrrhenus* invented trumpets, the *Phrygians* the flutes, the *Latins* the cithara, *Mercury* the lyre, and *Phanius* the panpipes <note>original: "fistula," also known as the syrinx.</note>.

---

## CHAPTER II.

### *On the divisions of Music.*

Music is either:
- **Worldly (Mundane)**: Which pertains to either the:
    - Celestial spheres.
    - Elemental regions.
- **Instrumental**, which is either:
    - **Harmonic**, consisting of:
        - **Human Music** <note>The internal harmony of the human body and soul.</note>.
        - **Melody**.
        - **Symphony**.
    - **Rhythmic**, which is created by:
        - **The number of syllables**; in this way the Lyric poet composes songs.
        - **Arithmetic proportion**, distinguishing the intervals of a temple.
    - **Metric**, which is created by:
        - **The measurement of syllables**, about which the Poets write.
        - **The metrical arrangement of feet**, which dancers use.
        - **The measurement of intervals and musical notes**.

That **M**usic of the world <note>original: "Musica mundana," the Pythagorean concept of the Harmony of the Spheres.</note> is produced from the essential effect of the Planets and the elements; for their excellent order and proportional arrangement undoubtedly produce a great symphony in those regions, if we give any credit to the opinions of *Plato* and *Cardano* <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian polymath.</note>. They say that the finest harmony is generated from the clustering and rotation of the spheres, which cannot be perceived by our ears because of the greatness of the distance. Similarly, the elements themselves are bound by such a chain that their enmity is made peaceful through the interposition of friends, and chaos—once a formless mass—is now essentially and distinctly shaped by a sympathetic arrangement.

<page-num>166</page-num>
<header>TREATISE II. PART II. BOOK I.</header>

In a not dissimilar way, the soul is connected with the body of the Microcosm <note>The "Microcosm" or "Little World" is a traditional philosophical concept where the human being is viewed as a miniature reflection of the entire universe (the Macrocosm).</note>; from this connection proceed the wonderful actions of life, and the consensus of the humors <term>Humors: The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which pre-modern medicine believed governed health and temperament</term> both for the purpose of giving life and for growth. Indeed, one function aids the other sweetly and kindly. That species of Music, however, which is called **instrumental**, is occupied with discerning and knowing songs. It contains, therefore, **Harmonic Music**, whose role is to distinguish sounds into the deep and the high. And this consists of numbers and figures. It is therefore either *spatial* (according to the proportion of sounds and voices in continuous quantity) or *temporal* (according to the proportion of long and short figures in discrete quantity). From these things it is clear that *harmonic Music* is the discernment of modulation and the science of singing truly, an easy path to perfection, and the science and consonance of several dissimilar but proportional voices; or rather, the science of number as it relates to sounds. From these things it is established that **Melody** and **Symphony** are contained under Harmony; of which Melody is the harmony of sounds, inflected by a certain system and mode according to the singer's emotion; while Symphony is the concordant harmony of distinct sounds and melodies. Furthermore, universal harmony is brought into action either by the percussion of the voice—which is called the **natural instrument**—or by the vibration of strings, as in the lute; or by the collision of air through the openings of some hollow body, such as a pipe. These latter two species are **artificial instruments**. Under instrumental Music, *Rhythmic* and *Metric* Music are also included; of these, *Rhythmic* is that part required in the scanning of poems created for songs, to determine whether the words to be used in singing and reading cohere well or poorly; while *Metric* Music shows the measures of various meters by probable reason, as is seen in Heroic, Iambic, Elegiac meter, and similar forms.

### C H A P T E R III.

->*On the operation of Music in the soul and body.*<-

The operation of Music is certainly admirable, and its power in the soul and body is marvelous; wherefore, according to the opinions of several Philosophers, knowledge of it is necessarily required for the arrangement of human life and morals. For:

*   It penetrates the inner parts of the mind and strikes the soul most vehemently.
*   It brings a certain becoming shape, through which anyone who is rightly educated in Music is made graceful and beautiful.

<margin>Plato in the third [book] of the *Republic*.</margin>
For this reason, he concludes that Music:
*   Should be handed down to children, so that they may be rendered gentler and more harmonious, and more ready for acting and speaking.
*   Should be employed in the state, so that it may produce more civilized and gentle customs; but one must abstain from voluptuous Music.

<margin>The harmony of Music according to Marsilio <note>original: "Marsilium." Refers to Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), a famous Renaissance Neo-Platonist who revived the study of "musical therapy."</note> through:</margin>
*   The movement of subtle air, it penetrates vehemently.
*   The body's airy nature, set in motion, moves the body.
*   The purified air stirs the spirits <note>In this context, "spirits" refers to the *spiritus*, a subtle vapor thought to act as the bridge between the physical body and the immortal soul.</note>, and the airy knot of the soul and body.
*   It affects the sense of emotion.
*   It acts as meaning upon the mind.
*   It sweetly soothes contemplation.
*   With a certain marvelous pleasure, it floods both spiritual and material nature with a conforming quality, and simultaneously seizes and claims the whole human being for itself.

## CHAPTER V.
### Concerning the matter or subject of Music, and concerning the sense of hearing.

**T**he matter or subject of Music is *sound*, which is the unbroken striking of the air <note>original: "indissoluta aëris percussio"</note> and the violent vibration of the same across low and high pitches <note>original: "in gravibus & acutis"</note>. By its spiral and rolling motion in the air, tending upward hither and thither in an oblique ascent (according to the disposition of the medium), sound finally penetrates the ears through the forced revolution of that same medium and invades the inner senses. And this is why we have fashioned twin temple doors at the summit of the system, in the manner of the pair of ears. For without the sense of hearing, the entrance to the *Temple of Concord* <note>original: "Concordiæ templum"; an allegorical representation of the ear and musical harmony.</note> does not lie open. Likewise, we have represented the spiral revolution of the air after the production of sound above both doors, so that the dissolved motion of the air might be better understood by the mind; all of which we have described in this place.

TREATISE II. PART II. BOOK II.

# BOOK SECOND

->Concerning the Musical System.<-

### INTRODUCTION TO BOOK II.

**W**e call that square of the Temple of Music—which we have described below as being composed of three parallelograms—the **Musical System**; it is nothing other than that subject-matter established by lines and clefs, in which the logic of sounds and the melody of song consist. Without a knowledge of this square surface and its steps, it will be impossible to enter the door of this temple. For without the governing and governed notes <note>original: "notis imperantibus & imperatis" — likely referring to primary and secondary notes or the hierarchy within the hexachordal system</note> along with the syllables and clefs, both principal and less-than-principal (through whose differences the Musical system is discovered), no one can undoubtedly reach the perfection of this science. 

The first parallelogram of the square, toward the left, denotes the clefs and voices of the song or system of the **soft B** <note>original: "b. mollis" — referring to the hexachord containing B-flat</note>. Hence it is depicted beneath a "round tower," in which soft sounds or bells sounding deeply are imagined to hang or ring, according to the variety of syllables and instruments. 

The second or middle parallelogram distinguishes the natural notes; this is also clearly depicted beneath a tower in the form of fire, which is to say, ascending sharply (since the nature of fire itself is described this way by the Philosophers). In this tower, one might imagine bells or voices sounding between the deep and the sharp. We have therefore depicted the summit of the tower as more sharp, as if projecting between the two variations of the **round b** <note>original: "b. rotundum" — the flat sign</note> and the **square b** <note>original: "♮" — the natural or sharp sign</note>. 

Moreover, we have placed the third parallelogram beneath a "square tower" because "square" sounds are produced from this type of **hard system** <note>original: "systemate duro" — the hexachord using B-natural</note>. Therefore, such bells are found in this tower that sound harshly and "squarely." This part of the Musical Temple is depicted here by itself, and we will devote this entire second book to its explanation.

<header>ON IMPERFECTLY MIXED BODIES.</header>

Without a doubt, this type of <term>meteoron<gloss>an atmospheric phenomenon; in this era, "meteorology" included study of all things in the sky, including wind and rain</gloss></term> is born at the intersection of both horizons from the breath of two winds blowing in opposite directions. One of these was stronger in one horizon, and the other held dominance in the other. That wind in the "hidden" horizon, blowing more upward and more strongly from the opposite side, is perceived to move the cloud that causes thunder against the breath of the weaker wind in the visible horizon. We conclude, therefore, that a cloud is formed by the compression of the thinner parts of the air, caused by the breath of winds moving toward opposite regions of the world. We say, contrary to the opinions of the <term>Peripatetics<gloss>the followers of Aristotle, who dominated scientific thought at the time</gloss></term>, that wind is found in the middle region of the air as well as the lowest, since the bodies of clouds are moved by their breath, just as the Peripatetics themselves wrote.

# C A P U T V.
->*On the winds.*<-

**T**he ancients also wrote in various ways regarding the origin of the winds, from which their uncertain knowledge of the cause of this phenomenon is easily recognized. For the Peripatetics said the matter of wind was a "hot and dry exhalation," moving laterally around the earth. <term>Bede<gloss>referring to the Venerable Bede, an 8th-century Anglo-Saxon scholar</gloss></term> called it "vaporous air," stirred by smoky matter exiting from the earth. <term>Constantine<gloss>likely Constantine the African, a famous medieval translator of scientific texts</gloss></term> defines wind as a cold and dry vapor, dissolved and separated from earth or water, which moves the air vigorously by the power of heat. Others have proposed that the origin of winds comes from the violent motion of clouds pushing the air before them. Others maintained that the wind had its origin from the reverberation of the parts or "arms" of the sea, coming from any region of the earth; they say the southern arm turning toward the north brings in the Eastern or <term>Subsolanus<gloss>the Latin name for the wind blowing from under the sun, or the East wind</gloss></term> wind, and so on for the others. Some others write that winds come forth from caverns and caves. 

We, however, are taught by certain practice that the origin of winds is primarily derived from two things: namely, either from enclosed air breaking out simply and violently from the belly of the earth, or from the water itself, dissipated into hot vapor by the force of the <term>central fire<gloss>a common early modern belief in a heat source at the Earth's core</gloss></term>. Furthermore, the air enclosed in the earth is expelled by its "subtiliation" <note>original: "subtiliatione," meaning the process of making something thinner or less dense</note> caused by the central heat, just as is shown in the following experiment; and then, because of the small amount of matter, it excites only a light wind, the kind we see blowing in summer.

->*Experiment I.*<-

### TREATISE I. BOOK VII.

For water at the center [of the earth], thinned by the force of heat, seeks a more spacious place to contain its body, since it cannot remain in its former seat due to the expansion of its mass. Therefore, partly because of the expulsive nature of fire and partly because of its own now-subtle substance, it very easily bursts forth into the region of the air. It agitates the air here and there by its presence and motion and—on account of the <term>sulfurous spirits</term><note>In early modern science, "sulfur" was often used to explain flammability and heat-generating properties in minerals.</note> retained within those vapors—it generates thunder, lightning, flashes, and other such meteorological phenomena. From this kind of hot vapor is derived that wind which they call a **Typhon** <note>original: *Typhonem*</note> because of its fiery nature.

We can prove that these causes of the winds are certain and infallible, not only by the artificial examples described above, but also by natural experience. For in **Dalmatia**, as **Pliny** and **Pomponius Mela** <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (Pliny the Elder) and Pomponius Mela were famous Roman geographers and natural historians.</note> relate, there is a lake in a very deep cave with a vast, steep opening. They write that if even the lightest stone is thrown into it, even on a calm day, winds are suddenly stirred up and storms like whirlwinds arise. Here, without a doubt, a vast quantity of air is trapped at the base of the hollow, and the multitude of waters blocking the mouth of the cave prevents its exit. Therefore, when the stone thrown downward makes a penetration, a great part of the air is pushed outside, forced out by the entry of some portions of the water.

Indeed, in the **province of Cyrenaica** <note>A region in modern-day Libya.</note>, a certain rock is said to be sacred to the **South Wind**; and from the region of **Aeolia**, winds are observed to blow constantly because of the multitude of infinite caverns and caves contained within it. Hence the Poets imagined its first king, called **Aeolus**, to be the GOD of the winds; for through such caves, the earth more easily emits the smoky material of the winds.

Indeed, some inhabitants of the **Promontory of Puteoli** <note>Modern-day Pozzuoli, near Naples, Italy—a highly volcanic area.</note> who are still living have said they remember in this latest age that a horrendous earthquake occurred on their promontory. They testified that winds and sulfur, accompanied by stupendous thunder, were stirred up for the space of 48 hours; that the earth was moved from one place to another, and a mountain was raised up in one spot which they called **Cineritium** <note>Literally "The Ashy One." This refers to the formation of Monte Nuovo in 1538, the youngest mountain in Europe.</note>. They further witnessed that in the nearest part, a significant portion of land—and even the greater part of the city of **Cumae**—was submerged by sea waters (->a wondersome spectacle of this time<-).

I myself have seen all these things, and I attribute the reason for this event to an immense quantity of sulfur burning under the earth. By its destructive power, the greater portion of the sulfurous earth in that part was turned to ashes and gave way to the weight of the earth hanging above it. This earth, plunged into the bowels of the globe down to the burnt ashes, forced the trapped hot air to burst out. By the violence of this air, the aforementioned earthquake, flaming winds, lightning, thunder, and other mournful accidents were undoubtedly brought about.

Therefore, sulfurous vapors of this kind are most often the authors of fire-vomiting winds. Thus, in those regions where the bowels of the earth are either visibly inflamed or where the air is regularly tainted by these vapors through invisible exhalations, lightning flashes and thunder occur most frequently.

We conclude, therefore, that winds are usually excited by:
1. The extrusion of air trapped in the bowels of the earth, or by its thinning (which then stirs the weak wind called the **Zephyr**); 
2. Or when its entire substance bursts from the womb of the earth, either due to the violent entry of waters occupying its seat, or due to an immense portion of earth plunging downward toward the center (by whose fall and presence the air retained there is suddenly thrust out, inducing a vehement agitation of both earth and air);
3. Or by the thinning of waters in the womb of the earth arising from sulfurous heat. 

Winds of this kind are perceived to blow more often from the Southern part because of the Sun's constant familiarity with it. The Sun's fiery faculties are removed in the winter time because of the vehement resistance of the northern blast; hence thunder and lightning are not produced as frequently in winter as in summer. Winds arising from thinned air shaken out of the belly of the earth are also more frequent in summer; but those arising from air driven out of the earth in its integral nature occur more in the spring...

Furthermore, the cause of the winds blowing from one region of the world to another—that is, their lateral blowing—are the motions and mutual aspects of the Planets, which stir up both exhalations and vapors, driving that sublunary spirit <note>original: "spiritum istum sub lunarem"; refers to the atmosphere and elemental forces below the sphere of the Moon.</note> here and there according to the disposition of their natures. And in this way, according to the disposition of the Planets, various winds are brought in at various times of the year, as we shall teach below.

# CHAPTER VI.
### On lightning and thunder.

THE PERIPATETICS <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> write that thunder and lightning occur when a hot and dry exhalation is raised by the heat of the Sun along with a moist and watery vapor into the upper part of the middle region of the air. There, they claim that exhalation is surrounded and enclosed on all sides by the vapor, and condensed into a cold and thick cloud. Being unable to endure the injuries of that intense cold, the enclosed exhalation is driven here and there as if in indignation, seeking an exit. At last, through this agitation and <term>antiperistasis</term> <note>A philosophical concept where one quality is intensified by being surrounded by its opposite, such as heat becoming more concentrated when surrounded by cold.</note>, it ignites like tow <note>original: "stupæ"; coarse flax or hemp fibers used for tinder.</note> and bursts the sides of the cloud by its fiery force. Thus, the cloud, being fractured and disrupted, gives forth a huge crash, which they call *thunder* <note>original: "tonitru"</note>, while simultaneously calling the light of the ignited exhalation a *thunderbolt* <note>original: "fulmen"</note>, *lightning* <note>original: "fulgur"</note>, and *flashing* <note>original: "coruscationem"</note>.

Indeed, we cannot entirely disapprove of their opinions, for we say that the "patient matter" <note>The passive substance acted upon.</note> which produces the crackling is air reduced into the substance of a cloud; but the "active form" which induces the crash is that sulfurous and windy matter, ignited by the force of both cold and moisture. This matter, illuminated according to the nature of the enclosed fire, seeks the open air, and to satisfy its appetite, it bursts its prisons and flies out into a more spacious and thinner place and vanishes, where it can live more freely. Thus we also see that the substance of <term>Saltpeter</term> <note>original: "Salis Petræ"; potassium nitrate, a key ingredient in gunpowder.</note> is nothing other than air congealed by cold; to which, if some portion of sulfur is added, though it be very small, it produces a huge noise and emits artificial lightning, as is demonstrated by the following experiment.

> *Upon saltpeter <note>original: "salem nitri"</note> (D) melted in a pot (A, B, C) by a charcoal fire and sprinkled with sulfur, I threw in a burning coal (E); suddenly I heard a great noise and perceived a massive conflict between the nature of the saltpeter and that of the fiery coal with sulfur. From this, artificial thunders arose along with the appearance of lightning. Having observed these things, I judged more precisely the arrangement of natural thunders.*

Furthermore, this very thing is sufficiently demonstrated in the action of gunpowder <note>original: "pulveris bombardici," literally "bombard powder"</note>. From these facts it is manifest: that thick air containing a nitrous disposition within itself is the material cause of lightning and thunder, and that a sulfurous exhalation is their formal cause <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "material cause" is the substance something is made of, while the "formal cause" is the pattern or essence that makes it what it is.</note>. How this condensation of air occurs we have already clearly enough explained in the section on the generation of clouds, where we contended against the opinion of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy, whose meteorological theories the author is challenging.</note>. For when the South wind blows—whose vaporous matter we have said is mostly drier and more sulfurous because of the Sun's proximity to that region, especially in summer time—sulfurous vapors are frequently and more significantly (though invisibly) lifted upward by the Sun's perpendicular attractive power. These vapors, moved toward the North and encountering the North wind blowing at that same time, are whirled and massed together in a cloud formed by the opposition of these winds. All its parts, formerly scattered, are reduced into one dense mass. Thus force is joined to force, and sulfurous atoms to atoms, until finally—through the resistance of the very cold nitrous nature, both by the percussion agitating the sulfurous mass and by the active power of the fiery mass itself—they are ignited and fortified through <term>antiperistasis: an ancient and medieval scientific concept where a quality is intensified when surrounded by its opposite, such as heat becoming more intense when compressed by cold</term>. The parts of the sulfur, which previously operated only in potential, are now brought into actuality and refined by the ignition. This occurs with such vigor, due to the subtleness of their parts, that they penetrate downward through the cloud's exterior, violently bursting through its sides, and are perceived to emit a massive crash, which we also call <term>thunder</term> <note>original: "tonitru"</note>. That a sulfurous mixture can be ignited and lit through *antiperistasis*—that is, because of resisting cold—the following experiment confirms.

->Experiment II of this chapter<-

*Take an egg and extract its contents through a small hole made in it. Let its interior surface be dried, and let an equal amount <note>original: "ana q. s." / "ana quantum satis," a prescription term meaning "of each a sufficient quantity"</note> of saltpeter, sulfur, and quicklime <note>calx viva</note> be placed inside, and let the hole be stopped up again with wax. Let this artificially prepared egg (A) be thrown into a stream (B), and suddenly a flame will emerge from the water itself.*

Finally, we do not say that the blast and nature of the South wind alone produce sulfurous and drier vapors of this kind, but also the other winds blowing from any quarter of the world, provided they partake of sulfurous spirits. And these things will be perceived more clearly if we diligently observe the movement of a cloud that thunders and vomits forth lightning. For a cloud emitting lightning is observed to be agitated against the movement of clouds that lack sulfur; and then, for the most part, a crackling sound is produced when both clouds have come together into one mass and have firmly and powerfully enclosed the sulfurous vapor accompanying the opposing wind. Here it must also be observed that in the opposing clash of clouds, that cloud burdened with sulfurous spirit even moves the contrary cloud against its own motion, on account of the multitude of "living fire." This occurs in the manner of a most powerful soul moving its body; by its vigor, the power of the other contrary cloud is repelled, no differently than when a stronger man carries a weaker one somewhere against his will and despite his struggles. Hence, therefore, is the origin of the struggle in which—since the disposition of the sulfurous cloud is fiery and sulfurous, while the constitution of the cloud moving against it is extremely cold—the sulfurous nature is inflamed. This occurs according to the reasoning shown in the previous demonstration regarding artificial fire in water <note>original: "ignis artificiali in aqua." This likely refers to a chemical experiment, perhaps involving quicklime or a phosphorus-like substance that ignites when dampened, used here as an analogy for how the "hot" sulfur ignites when compressed by "cold" clouds.</note>.

We conclude, therefore, that common experience has sufficiently and evidently demonstrated that the formal origin of thunder and lightning is certain sulfurous vapors dispersed invisibly in the air. When these are gathered together, they are brought into action—that is, they are ignited. For while lightning and flashes are scattered through the air, strongly sulfurous odors are perceived; indeed, the true nature of sulfur is discerned even by ordinary eyes, both in the color of its flame and in the condition of its effects. We have furthermore seen in exotic regions that thunder is more frequent near those places where sulfur mines or sulfurous mountains are found ignited by some accident, as in Sicily and around Naples; similarly in rocky regions, where the solar rays are powerfully focused against the peaks of mountains. Finally, what could more clearly show the origin of thunder than that horrendous production of the Ash Mountain <note>Referring to Monte Nuovo near Pozzuoli (Puteoli), which formed suddenly during a volcanic eruption in 1538.</note> at Puteoli, of which we spoke in the preceding chapter.
