### C H A P T E R VII.

->*How the superior bodies act toward the production of such meteors?*<-

In the preceding sections, we have made mention only of the more "proximate causes" <note>Immediate physical causes, such as the vapors themselves.</note> of <term>meteors</term> <note>In the 17th century, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note>. Here, however, we shall briefly explain by what means the stars and Planets produce these "imperfect mixtures." Since it has been determined among all Philosophers that the superior things <note>The celestial bodies.</note> constantly act upon these inferior things to produce new things, it is certain that such celestial bodies are the primary causes of the production of any meteor and the positioning of its substance in its proper place. But we shall here review in passing what the <term>Astrologers</term> think and strenuously affirm in this matter; then we shall conclude with our own opinion. Some Astrologers teach that Comets for the most part imitate the nature of <term>Mars</term> and <term>Venus</term>, and for this reason, they claim they portend wars, heat, and tumults. Others say that they have their origin from some unfortunate position of the stars, such as the conjunction of the superior Planets and an Eclipse, and especially when <term>Saturn</term>, <term>Mars</term>, and <term>Mercury</term> look upon the Sun or Moon with unfortunate "aspects" during an Eclipse—most especially if some [event] also preceded...

an ill-omened conjunction of the higher powers: *Appianus* <note>Peter Apian (1495–1552), a celebrated German astronomer and mathematician.</note> predicted that such a **Comet** would come in the *year 1532.* They also teach that foul mists are produced and resolved into dust when the **Moon**, after its conjunction or aspect with the **Sun**, seeks out **Saturn** (acting as the disposer of the heavens) and regards him with some aspect. Finally, they hold that a stronger **Mercury** in the celestial chart, when joined with the **Moon**, generates huge and rapid winds; they also affirm that some winds arise from the power of the **Moon** passing through a "dry house." They affirm that snows in winter happen by some predominant aspect of **Saturn** with the **Moon**, and that hailstorms with thunder occur when a strong **Saturn** looks upon **Mars** in the summer, and so on for the rest. From these assertions of the astrologers, we conclude that our aforementioned opinions concerning the origin of **Meteors** <note>In the 16th century, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and rainbows, not just falling stars.</note> are not fictions, but are very close to the truth itself.

For in the composition of a **Comet**, they say the natures of **Mars** and **Mercury** concur, and they have spoken the truth: for a spark of **Martial** substance flowing down from on high is like the soul and life of the **Comet** itself. Its body and substance, however, is entirely **Mercurial**—that is, gathered from the inconsistent substance of the most subtle air, having the aptitude (in the manner of **Mercury**) to take on any form or impression. What can better prove the generation of **clouds**—namely, while the air is thickened by the blast of opposing winds, which condensed air we have called a **cloud**—than the fact that they are primarily generated from the aspect and opposition of different Planets, which excite distinct winds in these lower regions by their diverse influences? For in the aspect of the **Moon** with a predominant **Saturn**, the moisture of the one is repugnant to the dryness of the other. From such a conflict, a contrary motion arises in the air, compressing it so that a cloud is generated therefrom. Similarly, two **winds** of contrary condition are produced in the summer time from the opposition, conjunction, or other malevolent aspect between a predominant **Saturn** and **Mars**. For **Mars**, on account of its familiarity with fire, gathers sulfurous vapors and moves them by its power in the form of a wind against the breath produced by **Saturn**, just as its own body moves against that of **Saturn** in the ethereal heaven.

However, since **Saturn** is cold, it is opposed to **Mars** not only in motion but also in quality. Wherefore the coldness of **Saturn** ignites the sulfurous matter gathered by **Mars** in no different a way than the water of a spring ignites that other artificial mass <note>The author is comparing planetary interactions to a chemical reaction where water triggers a fire.</note> *described in experiment 2 of the preceding chapter;* from this, thunders exist. But because **Saturn** is stronger, **hail** also falls. Similarly, if **Jupiter** has dominion in the heavens and looks upon **Mars** in the summer time with some malevolent aspect, it induces diverse and opposing motions in the air, because the moisture of **Jupiter** is contrary to the dryness of **Mars**. Therefore, that moisture of **Jupiter**, although it is warm, ignites the flammable matter gathered by **Mars** in no different a way than the moisture of saliva ignites that *described in experiment 3 in the preceding chapter,* in which the moisture of the saliva, penetrating and submerging itself into that fire-bearing body, leads back that fiery force (which was hidden and existing only in potential) into a flammable act; the composition of which is this:

This, therefore, is the reason why drier exhalations and vapors rising from the earth move the air more easily here and there, according to the desire of the Planet exciting such motions.

### CHAPTER VIII.

->*That rains, snows, thunders, lightnings, winds, and finally*<-
->*earthquakes and springs sometimes proceed from supernatural*<-
->*causes.*<-

IT IS CERTAIN, and proven by experience itself, that meteors <note>The author uses 'meteors' in the Aristotelian sense to mean any atmospheric phenomenon: rain, wind, or lightning.</note> of every kind happen sometimes by divine will or permission beyond the laws of nature; For the sacred Scriptures testify that sometimes Almighty GOD appeared in a cloud, and descended in horrendous thunder and ineffable lightning, and sometimes preceded the Israelites in the form of a pillar of fire, and demonstrated Himself in a bush under the form of fire, and that a spring gushed forth from a dry rock at the command of His divine power, and that infinite things of this kind have happened. Sometimes even evil angels, by the consent of the Most High, can stir up storms and lightning; for the aerial powers, which we said *in book 4* are those Demons of the sixth order, mix themselves with thunders, lightnings, and thunderbolts, corrupt the air, and stir up tempests. From this order are those four angels described *in the Apocalypse* <note>The Book of Revelation</note>, to whom it was given to harm the earth and the sea, holding the four winds blowing from the four corners of the earth; indeed, in this order of Demons is contained that Prince spirit whom we previously called *Meririm*, that is, the "noon-day Demon," a spirit burning and raging at midday, whom Paul *to the Ephesians* calls the Prince of the power of this air, as we mentioned before. According to Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, a 11th-century Byzantine scholar famous for his classification of demons</note>, aerial Demons also disturb the air to human ruin and loss, and stir up waves and tempests in the sea and lakes, by which they utterly sink ships loaded with men and overwhelm everything present with waters. There are even others still who cause chasms and the trembling of the earth and stir up flame-vomiting winds. For it is read *in chapter 1 of Job* that the Devil, by divine permission, stirred up a violent wind blowing from the desert, by whose blast the house in which Job's children were feasting was prostrated to the very ground. What also must be said of the nefarious and Diabolical power of the <term>Cacomagi</term> <note>From the Greek 'kakos' (evil) and 'magos' (magician); practitioners of black magic.</note>, when so many true and non-fictional histories have written entire volumes about their frequent use of stirring up tempests and other wickednesses perpetrated by the Demon; among whom Remigius <note>Nicolas Rémy, a 16th-century judge and author of 'Daemonolatreiae libri tres'</note>, in *book 1, chapter 25*, says he heard from the free and spontaneous [confession] of two hundred Cacomagi...

...by the assertion that on fixed and certain days they were accustomed to go in groups to the bank of some pool or stream, where very often, having received a rod from a Demon, they were used to beat the waters for a time until they stirred up vapors and smoke in abundance; when these were carried high and they perceived themselves to be enclosed in thick, dark clouds. In what manner, or by what reason these malevolent angels are accustomed to move these storms, this much is certain: they have not wished to reveal it to men, but act sophistically <note>They act with deceptive or misleading logic.</note> with them and their servants, the Magi; for it is not likely that a rod, or dust, or some incantation could have such power; but rather, by the invisible motion of these Demonic bodies, the quiet and tranquil air is agitated, and winds of every condition are suddenly stirred up, and clouds, thunder, hail, and other things of this kind are brought on as if in a moment of time. What wonder then if the weak grasp of men is daily deceived by Diabolical subtlety, since all that the Devil does, he performs secretly and invisibly, and tries to withdraw human nature from divine worship and make it rebellious to its creator, whether by the allurements of flattering words or even by threats? *Truly, since only* GOD *the Best and Greatest can resist these attempts, and repress his rage, and see and look deeply into his hidden works, the King of Kings and Lord of the world must be assiduously entreated from the innermost depths of the heart, that he might mercifully preserve us—exposed to every kind of misery—from the tyranny of that adversary and his serpentine cunning, and restrain his untamable wickedness with the reins of his justice and goodness, since without his protection nothing at all is safe, and nothing is immune from destruction. For the Lord alone is our highest helper, without whose aid we cannot be delivered from evil.*

->On the origin of springs.<-

*Finally, there is one unique experiment which we expressed at the beginning of this treatise, in the observation of which a marvelous secret concerning the flowing of springs from the earth will be perceived. For air enclosed within the earth moves toward the empty center of the earth through <term>rarefaction <gloss>the expansion of a substance into a larger volume</gloss></term>, and water similarly flees the solar force through thinning. While the Sun remains perpendicular over the earth, bringing on the season of summer, that denser air and the water hide away in the bowels of the earth around that center; but truly, as the Sun recedes from that summer region and winter approaches, the thick air and water return once more from the center to their former place—that is, to the surface of the earth—and they flow as they did before.*

And indeed, this is a most evident demonstration, by which no one of sound mind can deny that springs flow more or less from the veins of the earth by reason of the sun’s presence or essence; yet it is certain that their increase comes from the reasons mentioned above. For in winter, the **central heat** <note>original: "calor centralis"; a common belief in early modern science that the Earth possessed an internal fire or heat source.</note> is increased through <term>antiperistasis</term> <note>original: "antiperistasin"; a historical scientific concept where a quality, such as heat, is intensified when it is surrounded by its opposite, such as cold.</note>. Thus, that same <term>rarefaction</term> <note>original: "subtiliatio"; the process of a substance becoming thinner or less dense, such as when water or air is heated.</note> which the Sun caused on the earth's surface during the summer time, is conversely caused by this heat in the earth's center and bowels during the winter. 

Consequently, it produces the same effects, namely by driving waters and air through rarefaction toward the surface of the earth, from which they had receded during the previous summer. Similarly, rain, which falls more frequently in winter because the thick air is frozen into clouds by the force of the cold, enters through the pores of the earth and drives the trapped air out of the earth's caverns. It also happens in many places that this same air, expelled into a passage where it encounters water, thrusts the water out and occupies its place, just as we have demonstrated above in the preceding experiments.

## CHAPTER X.

->*A brief summary of the entire treatise brought together into one.*<-

**H**ow great an admiration and divine speculation—following a pious contemplation of the whole Archetype <term>Archetype: The original divine blueprint or "master model" of the universe existing in the mind of God before creation</term>—must be considered due to those two principles of created things! These are, namely: the Dark Mass of matter, and that Substantial Light granted to the world, its parts, and living things to be created on the first day by the inexplicable and divine will of the Creator himself. It is no doubt clearer than the midday sun to all of you endowed with a more sagacious mind, who look somewhat more deeply into the hidden causes of things with your keen, lynx-like eyes <note>original: "lynceis vestris oculis"; a common Renaissance idiom for sharp-sightedness or scientific penetration</note>; for we can find absolutely nothing in this entire universe that does not participate in one or the other of these aforementioned principles. For, just as those two primary substances are contrary to one another in nature and disposition, so also whatever is discovered in this world adheres more to one of them, and is thus utterly opposed both to the opposite principle and to everything governed by it. There is, therefore, Light, to which Darkness is opposed: we have GOD, the Father of Light, and we have the Devil, the Prince of Darkness. For us and for the world, the day shines forth, to which we find the night of darkness to be an opposing veil; Light produced the heavens for us, converting the purer part of the dark mass into its own substance, while <margin>→</margin> darkness left for us and the Macrocosm <term>Macrocosm: The "Great World" or the universe at large, which was believed to be mirrored in the "Microcosm" of the human body</term> the earth, burdened by the depth of blackness and obscurity. The essence of Light infused into us the sparks of life, but the body of darkness maliciously encloses, retains, and imprisons that same substance. It compels the splendor of the mind both to suffer and endure the most wretched tortures of the flesh, and—seduced by various deceptions and traps—to deviate and wander from the truth and the right path, as if blinded by ignorance. From Light, finally, we have fire, form, essence, perfection, life, generation, motion or action, and beauty; but from Darkness we receive water, matter, privation, imperfection, death, corruption, rest, and ugliness. Similarly, who doubts that whiteness, exaltation, love, virtue, good, truth, knowledge, riches, and other things of that kind proceed from the messenger of the highest Creator? For it is manifest and certain without any controversy that blackness, depression, hatred, vice, evil, falsehood, ignorance, poverty, and similar opposites proceed from darkness by the messenger of the Devil. O, how great and how deep is the dimension of these principles, and how inscrutable are their secrets! Although these cannot be investigated in any way through "a priori" demonstration <note>A priori: Reasoning from theoretical principles or causes rather than from observed effects</note>, God has nonetheless granted us permission to contemplate them "a posteriori" <note>A posteriori: Reasoning based on observations and known facts after they have happened</note>. Indeed, happy is he who can rightly know their mysteries, upon which the most profound of the Pagan <note>original: "Ethnicorum"</note> Philosophers used to consume not just a year or two, but the entire span of their lives; for they were driven by a greater wonder and more vehement study to inquire more deeply into these mysteries the more they found something probable within them.

<margin>→</margin> We conclude, therefore, that if anyone wishes to judge our preceding subject rightly and not rashly, he will perceive this opinion of ours to be not only probable but also (unless I am mistaken) not far distant from the truth itself. In the meantime, however, I will most gladly accommodate and submit myself to the judgments of all those better versed in this Divine Philosophy, asking them again and again that...

<header>ON MUSICAL TIMES.</header>

# ON MUSICAL TIMES.

*Simple notes* are the characters used for Durations <note>original: "Temporum"; referring to the length of notes</note> expressed without connections or dots; they are the *Large, Long, Breve, Semibreve, Minim, Fusa,* etc.

The *Large* (or *maxima*) is the greatest among all measurable shapes.
The *Long* is half of a Large.
The *Breve* is half of a Long.
The *Semibreve* is half the quantity of a Breve.
The *Minim* is half the quantity of a Semibreve, of which half is the *Semiminim*.

*Unequal proportion* or "odd time" consists of unequal space <note>uneven rhythmic divisions</note>, yet it is contained within the same motion of the <term>tactus</term> <note>the 'tactus' was the steady down-and-up motion of the hand used by conductors to keep a constant pulse</note>. From this, it follows that its notes have unequal forms.

A *Ligature note* is the joining of two or more note shapes together.

A *Dotted note* (with the dot to the right) is the value of that note plus half of its value; for example, <term>𝄀.</term> denotes ♢♢♢, which are 𝄀 plus ♢ <note>A 'Long' with a dot equals three 'Semibreves' instead of two</note>.

The figure to be kept silent is called a *Pause* <note>original: "Pausa"; today known as a "rest"</note>, which is nothing other than the omission of the vocal sound for the proper duration of a note, just as if it had been performed in some way.

The *internal sign*, which indicates time, is found in the unusual blackening of a note <note>a technique called "coloration," used to change the rhythmic grouping of notes</note> or the doubling of rests.

The *external sign*, which is also an indicator of time, is placed at the beginning and consists of circles, dots, and numbers, as we shall demonstrate below <note>these are the ancestors of our modern time signatures</note>.

The *Fusa* <note>likely equivalent to a modern eighth or sixteenth note depending on the context</note> is half of a semiminim.

***

-> [An intricate engraving of a musical "compass" or chronometer. It illustrates the mathematical subdivisions of time—1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128—around a central compass rose. The device is housed in a grand architectural frame topped with a small dial and an hourglass, symbolizing the measurement of fleeting sound through mechanical precision.] <-

***

TREATISE II. PART II. BOOK IV.

## C H A P T E R I.

### On simple figures to be expressed by the voice.

**A**mong the ancients, the Minim <note>original: *Minima*</note> relates to time as unity relates to number, or a point to a line. For just as unity is not a number, nor a point a line, but rather their starting principle; so the Minim is not Musical Time, but the principle of measured time. From this it is clear that the Minim is the head of mensural music <note>music where the duration of notes is strictly measured</note>; just as unity is the head of number, which cannot be divided. The moderns, however, have found even smaller notes and have fundamentally overturned that aforementioned opinion of the ancients. Among them was <term>Philippe de Vitry</term> <note>a famous 14th-century French composer and theorist</note>, who was called the "flower of the whole world" in music; he is said to have discovered the crotchet <note>original: *chrochutam*</note> or semiminim, which we also called the semiminim above. Others after him produced even smaller notes through their art, such as the <term>Fusa</term>, the <term>Semifusa</term>, and its half-part, which we will discuss below. I would prefer to approve and follow the method of Brother <term>Robert Brunham</term> <note>a 14th-century English musical theorist</note> in this matter; he set forth three species of square figures from which 6 species of simple notes are formed. From the largest square consists one species, which is called the <term>Large</term> <note>original: *Larga*</note>; from the middle square come two second species, namely, the <term>Long</term> and the <term>Breve</term>; from the highest square the three remaining species arise, namely, the <term>Semibreve</term>, the <term>Minim</term>, and the single note or <term>Fusa</term>. We have explained all these in the following shield, adding a seventh and eighth note.

---

a. Maxima, or Large.
b. Long.
c. Breve.
d. Semibreve.
e. Minim.
f. Semiminim.
g. Fusa.
h. Semifusa.

---

Among the aforementioned simple notes, some are "less simple" and others "more simple." For long notes are called simpler than breves and semibreves and others of this kind. This is because Breves, semibreves, Minims, and so on are more difficult to pronounce <note>to perform or sing</note> than Longs.

---

## C H A P T E R II.

### On the ligature or composition of notes.

**I**n the <term>Ligature</term> <note>a group of notes joined together in a single symbol</note> of notes, two forms are observed, one of which is straight and the other oblique; both of these either ascend or descend. Furthermore, each of these forms is either truncated or possesses a small stroke or tail, which is either raised or lowered. Now, this ligature occurs in three places: namely, at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end. Thus one is initial, another medial, and another final; regarding which the following Rules apply.

<summary>This page defines the hierarchy of musical note values, crediting Philippe de Vitry and Robert Brunham with expanding the system from the "ancient" foundations into modern, smaller subdivisions. It also introduces the concept of ligatures, which are multiple notes combined into a single written figure.</summary>

<header>ON MUSICAL DURATIONS.</header>

# ON MUSICAL DURATIONS.

## Rule I.
### Regarding the duration of initial notes.
*The first note lacking a tail is a <term>Long</term><note>A 'Longa' or 'Long' was a note value in medieval and Renaissance music, typically equal to two or three 'Breves'.</note> when the second note is descending.*

## Rule II.
Every <term>ligature</term><note>A 'ligature' is a grouping of two or more notes written as a single connected shape, common in early music notation.</note> that ascends without "property"—that is, without a tail—starts with a <term>Breve</term><note>A 'Brevis' or 'Breve' was the standard unit of time, shorter than a Long but longer than a Semibreve.</note>, as in:
*The first lacking a tail, but with the second ascending,*
*is a Breve.*

## Rule III.
*The first note with a tail on the left-hand side pointing downward is a Breve.*

## Rule IV.
*The first note with a tail pointing upward is a <term>Semibreve</term><note>A 'Semibreve' is half the value of a Breve; in modern music, it is known as a whole note.</note>, as is the note following it.*

### Regarding the duration of Middle notes.
## Rule.
*Any note in the middle [of a ligature] is a Breve, and the next one attached to it that has an upward tail is considered a Semibreve.*

### Regarding the duration of Final notes.
## Rule I.
*Every final note in a ligature that ascends is a Breve.*

## Rule II.
*Let a final square note that hangs downward be a Long to you.*

---

# GENERAL RULES.

## Rule I.
*The value of a <term>Maxima</term><note>The 'Maxima' was the longest note value in the system, usually equal to two or three Longs.</note> cannot be varied, because*
*a Maxima is a Maxima at the start, the middle, and the end.*

## Rule II.
*The Long is never tied in the middle [of a ligature] but only at the end,*
*and the Breve rightly occupies all positions at the beginning.*

## Rule III.
Every descending ligature that has a stroke from the first point, descending from the left side, is called a ligature "with property" <note>original Latin: 'cum proprietate'. This is a technical term indicating that the first note follows the standard expected duration—usually a Breve in a descending ligature with a tail.</note>.

## Rule IV.
Every ascending ligature, if it lacks a tail, is said to be "with property."

## CHAPTER III.

### *On the simple value of temporal figures, the dots of notes, and likewise on the figures of silence.*

The <term>simple</term> <note>original: *simplex*</note> value of the temporal notes, together with the rests—which are the figures of silence—is gathered from the three outer circles of the Temple Clock; just as it appears at the beginning of this book, and will be demonstrated more clearly in the following demonstration. The <term>Larga</term> <note>literally "the large one," the longest standard note value in this system</note> is measured by two Longas, and is described as a long square with a "property" <note>original: *cum proprietate*; a technical term in medieval notation referring to the presence of a tail or stroke</note>, that is, a tail toward the right, in this manner 𝆶. The simple <term>Longa</term> <note>literally "the long one"</note> is weighed as two Breves, and has an exactly square body with a "property" or stroke, either ascending or descending toward the right; it is described in this manner 𝆷 or 𝆷. The <term>Brevis</term> <note>literally "the brief one"</note> is an exactly square figure without a property or tail, which is measured by two Semibreves; we have depicted it in this manner 𝆸. The <term>Semibrevis</term> <note>literally "the half-brief"</note> is a diamond-shaped <note>original: *rhomboidale*</note> body lacking a stroke or tail, which is measured by two Minims. It is expressed in this manner 𝆺. The <term>Minim</term> <note>original: *minima*, meaning "the least"</note> is the body of a Semibrevis with an addition, namely having a stroke drawn either above its head or falling down from the lower angle, and is measured by two Crotchets or drachmas; it is depicted thus 𝆹𝅥 𝆹𝅥. The <term>Crotchet</term> <note>original: *crochuta*</note> does not differ from the Minim except in the color of the diamond-shaped body: while that of the Minim is white, the body of the Crotchet is black. It is made up of the value of two Fusae, and is expressed in this manner 𝆺𝅥𝅯 𝆺𝅥𝅯. The <term>Fusa</term> <note>equivalent to a modern eighth note</note> is half the part of a Crotchet, produced from two Semifusae. It differs from the Crotchet only because the top of its stroke is hooked, in this manner 𝇁. The <term>Semifusa</term> <note>equivalent to a modern sixteenth note</note> differs from the Fusa only because, just as the Fusa's stroke is hooked once at the top, the end of the Semifusa's stroke is hooked twice, in this manner 𝇂.

It also very often happens that dots are found in music, placed next to the right side of the notes; these increase the notes by half their value. For example, if 𝆶 signifies two Longas, then 𝆶. will denote three Longas. Likewise, 𝆸. denotes the value of 𝆺 𝆺 𝆺, and so on for the others.

As for the voices to be kept silent, which are called <term>Rests</term> <note>original: *pausae*</note>, it is certain that there are as many species of them as there are temporal notes in Music—namely eight. One of these signifies the quantity of a Larga to be silenced, which is the omission of the sound of a Larga figure; the second is for the Longa; the third for the Brevis, and so on for the rest. The <term>Larga rest</term> is marked by touching four lines of the music with a vertical line, or when two vertical lines touch three lines in this manner:

---

<insert>
[Diagram: Five-line musical staff showing two forms of Larga rests: a single thick vertical stroke crossing four lines, and two vertical strokes crossing three lines.]
</insert>

---

The <term>Longa rest</term> is marked by the contact of three lines of the system <note>original: *systematis*; the musical staff</note> or scale by a single vertical line, or when two vertical lines touch two lines of the scale, as in the following example:

---

<insert>
[Diagram: Five-line musical staff showing the Longa, Brevis, Semibrevis, and Minima rests, along with smaller rests.]
</insert>

---

The <term>Brevis rest</term> is marked by the contact of two lines of the scale by a single vertical line. The <term>Semibrevis</term>, however, is marked by half the vertical line of a Brevis hanging down from a line of the scale; similarly, the <term>Minim</term> rest is formed from the same half-vertical line ascending upward from a line of the scale. From these, the smaller rests are also composed, as will appear clearly in the following example, along with the simple value of all the notes.

**W**HEN I was traveling through foreign and overseas regions—having previously attained the degree of Master of Arts—for nearly six full years throughout France, Spain, Italy, and Germany, I devoted my primary efforts to the liberal arts. Indeed, I was encouraged by several princes and noble friends of mine, especially the French, to instruct them in some manner in those sciences.

First of all, therefore, I composed the compendium of <term>Arithmetic</term> <note>The science of numbers and calculation.</note> described in this treatise for <term>Charles of Lorraine</term>, <note>Charles of Lorraine (1571–1640), the 4th Duke of Guise, a prominent French noble.</note> Duke of Guise, and I dedicated it to him, and also privately instructed him in the knowledge of it.

<term>Geometry</term>, however, as well as <term>Perspective</term> <note>The mathematical study of sight and how objects appear in space.</note> and the secrets of the <term>military arts</term>, I compiled for a most noble youth of the greatest promise and a magnanimous Prince, <term>Francis of Lorraine</term>, <note>François de Lorraine, the younger brother of the Duke of Guise.</note> Knight of Guise. He was, alas, violently snatched from human society by an untimely death, being unhappily torn apart by an ill-fated piece of artillery. Under my instruction, he not only grasped these sciences with wonderful speed, but also exercised himself in their practice with such delight of mind that he even strove to surpass me, his own teacher, in them. Furthermore, I dedicated <term>Music</term> and the <term>art of memory</term> <note>A system of mental techniques, often involving "memory palaces," used to recall large amounts of information.</note>—of which quite a full mention will be made in the second volume—to the <term>Marquis of Orizon</term> and the <term>Viscount of Cadenet</term>, seeing as they were kindled with a wonderful love for learning those sciences. Finally, I presented my <term>Cosmography</term> <note>The study of the mapping of the universe, including both the earth and the heavens.</note> to my father, who was at that time the Treasurer in military affairs throughout France and the Low Countries <note>original: "Belgium inferius"</note> under <term>Elizabeth</term>, Queen of England, of pious and never-sufficiently-praised memory (may his soul be blessed). I presented it to him as the one from whom I drew the origin of my life and from whom I received the necessary support to taste the honey-sweet nectar of the Muses, so that I might be raised on feathered wings to the circumference of the upper heaven by a most sweet and delightful breeze. I did this, moreover, with the intention that he might all the more easily and better [understand] those regions...

# AUTHOR'S LETTER

...so that he might be able to observe the positions and layouts of the overseas lands <note>original: "Ultramarinarum"</note> which he was about to visit: This, I say, my **Cosmography** <term>Cosmographia: A field of study that combines elements of geography, astronomy, and mapping to describe the main features of the universe and the earth.</term> I have also corrected, expanded, and assigned a singular place for it in this my treatise.

Just as I presented all these works individually to those whose names were mentioned above, I now gladly and willingly share them with you in general, dear Reader. I hope that you will receive this labor of mine with a cheerful and serene countenance, since everyone knows that no perfect knowledge <margin>-</margin> can be acquired or obtained without an understanding of the liberal arts. Therefore, I ask that you look upon these nocturnal studies <note>original: "lucubrationes"; literally "work done by candlelight," implying late-night scholarly devotion.</note> of ours with an impartial mind. If any error occurs in them (as will undoubtedly happen in so great a work), do not attribute it entirely to our lack of skill or ignorance. Instead, attribute it partly to the weakness of our body, which is almost exhausted by unremitting labor and thus unable to examine everything with such an exact balance <note>original: "trutina"; a metaphorical scale for critical weighing of facts.</note>. Attribute it also, in part, to our other occupations, by which we are called away to various tasks. Thus, led by a fiery love, restrain yourself from the viperous tongue <margin>-</margin> which is a servant of darkness, malice, and even the Devil himself. Approve and praise those things you find well and rightly written, but correct all errors (which I know are not few) with a calm face and a judgment removed from all envy. Do not act toward me in this matter otherwise than you would wish to be dealt with in a similar case. If you do this, you will deserve to be called a son of light, and this book of ours will emerge more fortunate through your goodness. Farewell.

# BOOK ONE.
## On number and numeration.
### CHAPTER I.
#### On Physical and Mathematical number.

**Number is twofold:**

*   **Physical**, which is likewise twofold:
    *   *Numbered or material.* <note>The actual objects being counted, like stones or sheep.</note>
    *   *Numbering, or formal, and it is twofold:*

            *   For the act or operation of the numbering soul.
            *   For the concept of the distinction of that act; thus time is called number, that is, the distinction of "before" and "after" in space. <note>This draws on the Aristotelian definition of time as the "number of motion."</note>
            *   For the sign and the numeral word, such as one, two, three; and this indeed is called **Mathematical number**.
*   **Mathematical**, in which two things are observed:
    *   *Unity, which is the principle of numbers.*
    *   *The Subject matter, of which there are two parts:*
        *   The collection of Units, from which number is made
            *   Abstract, and this is:
                *   Absolute, which is:
                    *   Even
                        *   Simple,
                        *   Composite.
                        *   Each of which is either:
                            *   Evenly even. <note>A number that can be divided by two repeatedly down to one (e.g., 8, 16).</note>
                            *   Evenly odd. <note>An even number which, when halved, results in an odd number (e.g., 6, 10).</note>
                            *   Unevenly even and odd.
                    *   Odd,
                        *   Simple.
                        *   Composite.
                *   Relative, which is:
                    *   Commensurable.
                    *   Incommensurable.
                *   Figural or Geometrical.
                    *   Linear,

            *   Contracted <note>Also known as "applied" or "concrete" numbers used in specific contexts.</note>, which is taken for:
        *   Arithmetic, which contemplates the subject of numbers, and is:
            *   Proper.
            *   Improper.
            *   Common.
            *   Cossic or Algebraic.
            *   Geometrical.
            *   Military. <note>Arithmetic applied to fortifying camps, arranging troops, or calculating ballistics.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of natural philosophy, moving into the classification of numbers and their relationship to the soul and geometry.</meta>

<page-num>6</page-num>

### TREATISE II. PART I. BOOK I.

<meta>Catchword: CHAPTER</meta>

**N**umber in Physics is a measure by which we judge the difference between a smaller or larger quantity of some substance.
We call that the numbered or material number which is a specific thing or a numbered multitude, such as a pile of bricks, a handful of barley, and so on.

However, we call the rational soul itself the primary *numbering number* <note>original: "numerum numerantem"</note>, because it distinguishes species and individuals from one another; from this, it is manifest that the souls of brute animals <note>Animals lacking human reason</note> are able to number or discern nothing at all.

That the soul is a number is confirmed by *Plato* in his *Timaeus*, where he calls it a harmonic number for the reason that it is constituted from the Monad (or unity), and the numbers two, three, and four. Nor does *Pythagoras* dissent from *Plato’s* opinion; he asserts that the soul is composed of simple, double, triple, and quadruple proportions, and as if from a point, a line, a surface, and a cube. By this Pythagorean symbol, the intellect of the soul and its powers seem to be signified. For the Monad <note>The number one; unity</note> signifies the intellect, which is most simple and unique. The Binary <note>The number two</note> signifies knowledge discerning two things—namely truth and falsehood. The Ternary <note>The number three</note> signifies a doubtful opinion judging among three things: namely truth, falsehood, and probability. The Quaternary <note>The number four</note>, however, expresses the senses; for these perceive only corporeal things, since incorporeal things are not at all presented to the senses. Finally, the elements of species are denoted through numbers, which the soul, conceiving them as known, numbers and discerns either through principles or through the effects of principles.

*Mathematical number* is discrete quantity, collected from two or more units. Therefore, no number is unity, because the smallest number is greater than unity.

Unity is the limit from which every number is derived and in which it ends. Just as in Geometry the limits of lines are points—for as a line is formed from the flow and series of points—so also is number formed from the gathering of unities.

Unity in Arithmetic and the point in Geometry are indivisible. For indeed, unity multiplied by itself produces nothing <note>Meaning it does not increase the value; 1x1 remains 1</note>; that which cannot be multiplied can in no way be divided.

*Abstract number* is that which has no denomination attached to it, such as 5 or 10 without any other thing joined to them.

*Contracted number* is that which has some denomination coupled with it, such as 5 lines or 10 degrees.

*Proper contracted number* is a whole number such as 6 or 10. *Improperly called contracted number* is a fractional number, which is less than a whole unity, such as 2/3 or 7/9.

*Absolute abstract number* is that which has no respect or relation to another but is considered by itself alone and absolutely.

*Absolute even number* is that which can be distributed into two equal parts; such as 4, 6, 12, 20, etc.

*Evenly-even number* is that which is divided into equal parts all the way down to unity, such as 16 into 8, 8 into 4, 4 into 2, and 2 into 1.

*Evenly-odd number* is that which cannot be reduced to unity by equal division, such as 18 into 9 and no further; likewise 10 into 5, etc.

*A number both evenly-even and odd* is that which when divided gives even numbers, but those members when subdivided produce odd parts, such as 60 into 30 (which parts are even), and 30 into 15 (which are odd).

*Odd number* is that which cannot be separated into equal parts without a fraction of unity: thus 9 equally divided will produce 4 and 1/2. And fifteen will give 7 and 1/2 in the quotient.

OF NUMBER AND NUMERATION.

## ->CHAPTER II.<-

### ->*On Algorithmic or common numeration.*<-

<margin>Two things coincide for the numeration of abstract numbers <note>original: numerorum abstractorum</note></margin>
*   **The Figure, which is of either**
    *   **Units, such as 1.**
    *   **Numbers**
        *   **Significative <note>Meaning figures that represent a specific quantity on their own.</note>, which is twofold**

                    *   10.

                    *   40.
                    *   50.
                    *   100.

                    *   1024.

        *   **Non-significative, such as the cipher 0.**
*   **The value of the Figure.**
    *   **Fixed <note>original: Certus</note>, which is found in digits alone.**
    *   **Relative <note>original: Incertus; literally "uncertain," meaning the value depends on the placement.</note>, in which two things must be noted, specifically**
        *   **Place, and in this two things must be observed.**
            *   **The Numerator <note>Here referring to the digit itself that occupies a place.</note>.**
            *   **The Denominator <note>Here referring to the power of ten or the specific place value, such as "hundreds."</note>.**
        *   **The order of places counting from the right, of which**
            *   **The first is the place of units**
            *   **The second of tens <note>original: denariorum</note>**
            *   **The third of hundreds <note>original: centenariorum</note>**
            *   **The fourth of thousands**
            *   **The fifth of ten-thousands**
            *   **The sixth of hundred-thousands**
            *   **The seventh of millions <note>original: millies millium</note>.**

---

**N**umeration is the process by which the due value of each number is estimated, and by fitting figures and proper places is either increased <note>original: exaltatur; literally "exalted"</note> or decreased <note>original: deprimitur</note>.
A *significative figure* is one by whose value a unit or a digit is signified.
A *non-significative figure* signifies nothing by itself, such as the cipher <note>the zero</note>. What a *unit* is, and what a *number* is, was stated above.
A *digit* is every simple number which is contained between a unit and the first simple article, such as 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. 9.
An *article* is every number that is divided into ten equal parts without a remainder, such as 10. 20. 30. 40. 50. 100. 1000.

<meta>catchword: Nume-</meta>

<summary>This page defines the "Algorithmic" (Arabic) system of writing numbers, categorizing them into digits, multiples of ten (articles), and composite numbers. It introduces the concept of place value, explaining how a digit's position determines its total value from units up to millions.</summary>
<keywords>numeration, algorithms, digits, articles, zero, cipher, place value, units, tens, hundreds, thousands, millions</keywords>

--- Page 436 ---
<meta>This page continues the definitions of basic arithmetical concepts, focusing on place value and the role of the zero.</meta>
<page-num>8</page-num>
<header>TREATISE II. PART I. BOOK I.</header>
<meta>catchword: NV MERA- (Numbers)</meta>

*A mixed or composite number* <note>original: "Numerus mixtus seu compositus"</note> is one which is constituted either from simple significant figures alone, such as 12 or 345, or partly from significant and partly from non-significant figures, such as 470 or 24,021.

*A cipher* <note>original: "Ciphra"; the digit zero</note> is that which by itself, or placed on the left side of any digit or digits, signifies nothing, such as 04 or 037; however, when placed on the right side of a digit, it signifies as many tens as the preceding digit denotes units, such as 40, 50, 240, etc.

*The fixed value of numbers* <note>original: "Valor certus numerorum"</note> is when any digit is considered by itself and in its own nature—that is, according to the quantity of units it contains, such as 2, 3, 4, or 5 taken by themselves. For 2 has the value of two units, 3 of three, and so on.

*The variable value of numbers* <note>original: "Valor numerorum incertus"; literally "uncertain value"</note> is when the same digit expressed in different places has a different value and estimation. For example, in this number 142: the 2 signifies no more than two; the 4, however, signifies forty; and the 1, one hundred. Yet by expressing the same digits in this way, 214: here the 4 signifies only 4 units; the 1, ten; and the 2, two hundred.

*Place* <note>original: "Locus"</note> is the seat or interval in which each individual figure of any number is expressed. For as many figures as are established in a number, so many "places" are attributed to it, the orders of which the following wheel <note>referring to a diagram likely on the next page</note> will clearly explain.

A <term>Numerator</term> <note>In this historical context, the "numerator" is the digit that counts how many of a certain power of ten are present</note> is the estimator and value of each digit in the place of a ternary division <note>the grouping of numbers into threes, such as hundreds, tens, and units</note>.

A <term>Denominator</term> <note>Historically, the "denominator" gives the name or category to the group, such as "thousands" or "millions"</note> gives the name and the boundaries to every place of the ternary division and its figures, by which the numerator can precisely estimate them. For the first ternary division is of units, the second of thousands, and so on. For example, in this number 204, the denominator is "units," because it is a ternary division of the first order. But in 204,000, the denominator is "thousands," while the "numerator" is 204. For it is a ternary division of the second order.

It must be noted that a denominator of this kind differs from that used for "contracted numbers" <note>original: "numerorum contractorum"; these are concrete numbers tied to specific units like weight or length</note>. For the former is specific to the ternary places of figures, but the latter refers to things joined to the naming of the figures—as when I say 4,000, here "thousand" is the denominator and 4 is the numerator; but if I connect pounds, inches, or feet to the said number, there will be a double denomination: the first is proper to abstract numbers, and the second is that which makes abstract numbers "contracted" or concrete.

->*How, by the benefit of this mirror, may the value of any number be found?*<-

When a number of many places is presented to us, which we cannot readily name, we must proceed in a continuous counting order from right to left, observing the places of threes <term>ternarios</term> <note>referring to the practice of grouping digits into sets of three, like 1,000,000</note>, of which there are three numerators and one denominator.

Therefore, in every division of three, there are three numerators, of which the first toward the right is of units, the second of tens <note>original: denariorum</note>, and the third of hundreds <note>original: centenariorum</note>. The naming <note>original: Denominatio</note> of the first division of three is of units, the second of thousands, and the third of millions.

The nine lower spheres are of the digits <note>original: digitorum</note>, which are to be found in the aforementioned places.

**A** proportion of equality is when two equal numbers are compared together; however, this uses the name "proportion" less strictly <note>In classical mathematics, a "ratio" usually implied a difference between numbers; if they are equal, some argued it isn't a "ratio" in the sense of a relationship of inequality.</note>.

**A** proportion of inequality is when two unequal numbers are compared together, such as 4 to 2, or 3 to 5.

**A** proportion of *greater* <note>The original Latin text mistakenly says "minoris" (lesser), but the context and examples like 5 to 3 indicate the author meant "majoris" (greater).</note> inequality is when a larger number is compared to a smaller one, such as 5 to 3 and 15 to 12.

**A** proportion of *lesser* inequality is when a smaller number is compared to a larger one, such as 2 to 8 and 3 to 5; here it should be noted that the reasoning for greater and lesser proportions is the same.

**A** simple multiple proportion is one that contains the smaller number exactly two or more times within itself.

<margin>Proportion, therefore:</margin>
> **Double** encompasses the smaller number exactly twice, such as 4 to 2, 6 to 3, and 12 to 6.
> **Triple** embraces the smaller number three times, such as 6 to 2, 9 to 3, 12 to 4.
> **Quadruple** contains the smaller number four times, such as 4 to 1, 8 to 2, 12 to 3, etc.

**A** superparticular proportion encompasses the whole of the smaller number plus one certain part of it.

# CHAPTER I.

->*How many concordances are there, and how do they differ from one another?*<-

**S**ix types of musical concordances are enumerated, differing in quantity, namely: the *<term>Unison</term>*, the *<term>Minor Third</term>* <note>original: "Semiditonus," literally "half-two-tones"</note>, the *<term>Major Third</term>* <note>original: "Ditonus," literally "two tones"</note>, the *<term>Fifth</term>* <note>original: "Diapente"</note>, the *<term>Major Sixth</term>* <note>original: "Tonus cum Diapente," literally "a tone with a fifth"</note>, and the *<term>Octave</term>* <note>original: "Diapason"</note>. From these it is clear that the *unison* is not a "consonance," since a consonance is a harmony of dissimilar voices brought together into one. Consequently, it is manifest that not every concordance is a consonance, nor vice versa. It also follows that nothing harmonizes more perfectly than two voices singing in *unison*. From this, it is clear that among these aforementioned concordances, there is a great discre-

...[discre]pancies; for they are distinguished in two ways: namely, either by the nature of the sound, and thus some are called *equisonant* <note>original: *æquisonæ*</note>—specifically those which, sounding together, produce a single sound, such as unisons—and others are called *consonant* <note>original: *consonæ*</note>, that is, sounding sweetly in a mingled succession, like the remaining concordances. Or they are distinguished by the nature of their proportion and succession, and thus some are *perfect*, namely the Unison and those born from it, such as the 8th or *Octave* <note>original: *Diapason*</note>, the 15th or *Double Octave* <note>original: *Disdiapason*</note>, and the *Fifth* <note>original: *Diapente*</note>, and those which arise from it, such as the 12th and 19th. Among these, the Unison and the *Octave* are the more perfect consonances, while the *Fifth* and those derived from it are less so. Now, the reason why such concordances are called perfect is varied; for the unison is called *perfect* because of its stability <note>original: *immobilitatem*</note>, and it is a concordance of equality. Truly the *Octave*, which is the eighth voice, is so called because it claims for itself the double proportion <note>A 2:1 mathematical ratio</note>; the *Fifth*, which is the fifth voice, because it is unfailingly made in the <term>sesquialter proportion|A 3:2 ratio, where the larger number contains the smaller plus its half</term>. The remaining consonances are called imperfect because of their instability; for they move from place to place, and their proportions are not found by themselves among the others; of this kind are the *Minor Third* <note>original: *Semiditonus*</note> and the *Major Third* <note>original: *Ditonus*</note>, and those which arise from them, the 10th and 17th. For the *Minor Third* and the *Major Third*, which hold the third voice, vary in different ways as the song ascends. Truly a *Whole Tone* <note>original: *Tonus*</note> with a *Fifth* always makes the sixth voice, but the sixth voice is sometimes a *Fifth* with a *Whole Tone*, and is called an imperfect concordance, and sometimes it is a *Fifth* with a semitone, and is called an imperfect discordance. Therefore the Sixth and those arising from it—namely the 13th and 20th—are called imperfect consonances.

## CHAPTER II.

->*On the intervals of the Triangle in general, which receive concordances and produce dissonances, and how many of them are sufficient for the human voice?*<-

**T**he intervals by which concordances are measured are 11, namely 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 13, 17, 19, and 20, which are described in our Interval Triangle in white squares along with their proportions. Just as the 9 dissonances—namely 2, 4, 7, 9, 11, 14, 16, 18, and 21—are designated by shaded and dark little squares. Now, the white squares of the Triangle are those from which the harmony of melodies is derived, just as from the darker ones a discordant symphony is produced, unless its entry into the <term>symphonic harmony|A multi-part musical arrangement</term> is managed with no small amount of skill; for in that harmony, discord is sometimes expressed with great subtlety and to the delight of the listeners, as will be taught below. Of these consonances, an octave is made from a unison by adding an octave; a tenth is made from a third, a twelfth from a fifth, and a thirteenth from a sixth. Likewise, a fifteenth is made from a unison by adding a double octave; a seventeenth from a third; a nineteenth from a fifth; and a twentieth from a sixth. From the teaching of the preceding chapter, it is clear that intervals 1, 8, 12, 15, and 19 are perfect intervals, because they measure perfect consonances, while the rest are imperfect. Of these intervals, eight were usually sufficient for the human voice, namely 2, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 13, and 15. The rest are assigned to musical instruments, which are perceived to sound higher and lower than human voices, which are tightened and loosened by nature <note>Referring to the physiological range of the vocal cords</note>.

It maintains the Boethian tradition of arithmetic commonly used in music theory and natural philosophy during the Renaissance.</meta>

<page-num>14</page-num>
<header>TRACTATE II. PART I. BOOK I.</header>

# TRACTATE II. PART I. BOOK I.

->*That every kind of proportion can be extended to infinity according to the order of this mirror.*<-
<note>original: "speculi." The author likely refers to a "mirror" as a systematic table or a conceptual model that reflects mathematical truths.</note>

### Rule I.

In **multiplicative proportion**, an even number, multiplying itself or any odd number, will produce infinite **double** proportions, where the number to be multiplied is taken as the smaller, and the product is held as the larger proportional number. Thus, two multiplied by two makes 4 to 2; and 4 multiplied by 2 will produce 8 to 4; and 8 multiplied by 2 will give 16 to 8. Similarly, 3 multiplied by 2 will produce 6, and 6 to 3 is a **double** proportion; as are 12 to 6, and 24 to 12.

A **triple** proportion is also produced to infinity by multiplying any digit by 3 in the preceding manner. Therefore, multiply 2 by 3 and it will give 6, and 6 to 2 is a **triple** proportion: And 6 multiplied by 3 will make 18, which is also a **triple** proportion to 6: Thus 3 multiplied by 3 makes 9 to 3, and 9 by 3 makes 27 to 9.

The same reasoning must also be observed in **quadruple** proportion by multiplying any digit by 4; in **quintuple** by 5; in **sextuple** by 6; and so on for the rest.

### Rule II.

*If two even numbers are compared in equal proportion, such as 4 to 4, 6 to 6, 8 to 8, etc., and a half-part of the first is added, then between those relative numbers there will be a **sesquialtera** proportion;* <term>sesquialtera: a ratio of 1.5 to 1, or 3:2, where the larger number contains the smaller plus its half</term> thus the half-part of 4 is 2, which numbers joined together make 6, and 6 to 4 will give the aforementioned proportion: also 4 added to 8 makes 12, which is related to 8 by the preceding proportion.

Similarly, where 3 is compared to 3, or where two equal numbers composed of 3 are related, such as 6 to 6 and 9 to 9; if a third part of one is added to the first, it will give a **sesquitertia** proportion, <term>sesquitertia: a ratio of 1.33 to 1, or 4:3, where the larger number contains the smaller plus its third</term> such as 4 to 3, 8 to 6, and 12 to 9.

This same thing applies to **sesquiquarta**, where a fourth part is always added; and **sesquiquinta**, where a fifth; and **sesquisexta**, where a sixth part of one is added to the other.

### Rule III.

*Every **superpartient** proportion <term>superpartient: a ratio where the larger number contains the smaller plus more than one of its fractional parts (e.g., 5:3)</term> has respect to the parts of the smaller number: such as the **super-two-part**, that is, the smaller and two of its parts. The **super-three-part**, that is, the smaller and three of its parts. The **super-four-part**, that is, the smaller and four of its parts, and so on for the rest.*

Similarly, the naming of these kinds of proportions is made through the smaller number; for instance, the **super-two-part thirds** proportion signifies the smaller and two-thirds of it <note>This equals a 5:3 ratio</note>, and the **super-two-part fourths** proportion requires the smaller and two-quarters of it, and so on for the rest.

In the same way, the **super-three-part fourths** denotes the smaller and three-quarters of it <note>This equals a 7:4 ratio</note>, the **super-two-part fifths** denotes the smaller with two of its fifths, etc.

### Rule IV.

*The **double sesquialtera** proportion <term>double sesquialtera: a ratio of 2.5 to 1, or 5:2</term> can be expressed in a threefold way: namely as 5 to 2, or 5/2, or 2 1/2.*

Similarly, the **triple sesquiquinta** proportion <term>triple sesquiquinta: a ratio of 3.2 to 1, or 16:5</term> can be expressed under these formulas: 16 to 5, or 16/5, or 3 1/5; and we can observe this kind of order in every other proportion.

## Rule V.

The same proportion takes on different names depending on how it is viewed. For what is called "four-parts over thirds" <note>original: *Super quadrupartiens tertias*; this refers to the ratio 7:3, because 7 contains 3 twice with 1 left over, or expressed as a fraction: 2 1/3</note> is the same as the "double sesquitertia" proportion <note>original: *duplex sesquitertia*; a ratio of 2 and 1/3</note>, such as 7 to 3 or 14 to 6. Likewise, "four-parts over tenths" will be the "two-parts over fifths" proportion <note>7/5 or 1 2/5</note>, and "four-parts over twelfths" will be "one-and-a-third" <note>original: *sesquitertia*, the ratio 4:3</note>; and "five-parts over fifths" will be the "double" proportion <note>ratio 2:1</note>, and "six-parts over thirds" will be "triple" <note>ratio 3:1</note>; and so it follows for the others.

## CHAPTER IV.
### On figurate numbers.

- **A figurate number is either**
    - **Geometric**, which pertains to:
        - **All figures of Geometry**; for it is a number that is:
            - **Linear.** <note>A number represented as a simple line of units.</note>
            - **Superficial** <note>Surface or two-dimensional numbers</note>, such as:
                - Triangular.
                - Square or Parallelogram-like (with equal sides).
                - Pentagonal.
                - Hexagonal.
                - Oval.
                - Circular.
            - **Solid**, such as:
                - Cubic.
                - Pyramidal, and others of this kind.
        - **Refers only to three forms of Geometry**, which are the foundations of <term>Cossic</term> <note>From the Italian *cosa* ("the thing"), referring to early algebra where the unknown variable was called "the thing."</note> numbers, namely:
            - **The Root or side**:
                - Of a square, which is a line.
                - Of a cube, which is a square surface.
                - A square or a four-sided figure of equal sides.
            - **The Cube**:
                - Simple.
                - Composite, such as:
                    - A square made of cubes.
                    - A cube made of cubes.
    - **Non-Geometric**; for it represents no exact Geometric figure, and is either:
        - Geomantic. <note>Relating to 'Geomancy,' a system of divination using patterns of dots.</note>
        - Memorial. <note>Numbers used as mnemonic devices for memorization.</note>

**A** figurate number is one that represents the form or figure of some thing, whether it be a geometric object (regular or irregular) or a non-geometric object.

A linear number is one that creates only length by its progression, such as 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8.

A superficial number produces both length and width by its increase, such as a parallelogram-like number.

<page-num>215</page-num>
<header>ON THE PARTS OF POLYPHONIC MELODY <note>original: "DE SYMPHONICÆ MELOD. PARTIBUS"; here "symphonic" refers to the harmonious blending of multiple voices in polyphony rather than a modern orchestral symphony.</note></header>

### Rule IV.

> Nevertheless, perfect intervals should usually be mixed with imperfect ones in such a melodious way that an imperfect interval is cast between two perfect ones, and vice versa. <note>In early music theory, "perfect" intervals include the unison, fifth, and octave, while "imperfect" intervals include thirds and sixths.</note>

### Rule V.

> In sequences of perfect intervals, a "hard" voice should not be set against a "soft" one; rather, soft should harmonize with soft, and hard with hard or "natural." <note>This refers to the hexachord system: "hard" (dura) involved B-natural, "soft" (mollis) involved B-flat, and "natural" (naturalis) avoided B entirely.</note>

### Rule VI.

> Multiple sixths are not continued while ascending, but they may be in descent, provided a perfect twelfth follows; although a tenth may also follow a sixth.

### Rule VII.

> The sixth is rarely used except in music with many voices, for it does not sound as sweet and pleasing as the third.

### Rule VIII.

> Dissonances are sometimes used in song, namely the 2nd, 4th, 7th, and 9th. But this does not happen except in the fastest rush of musical figures—that is, in the <term>Fusa</term> <note>an eighth note</note> and <term>Semifusa</term> <note>a sixteenth note</note>—because then they are not perceived due to the speed. For in such cases, the error of the discord is hidden.

### Rule IX.

> A dissonant <term>Semibreve</term> <note>a whole note</note> is rejected unless it is diminished by half.

### Rule X.

> It very often happens and is approved that a discord over the same sustained Bass note is "broken" into a concordance. <note>This refers to the practice of "division" or "diminution," where a long dissonant note is divided into smaller notes that resolve into a harmony.</note>

### Rule XI.

> To a stationary voice in the Bass, many moving consonances can be fitted, both in ascending and descending.

### Rule XII.

> A "breaking" <note>original: "ruptio"</note> in the higher parts from a 6th to a 5th harmonizes best over a solid Bass note; similarly, a Bass note can be "broken" from a 6th to a 5th against a sustained note in a higher part.

### Rule XIII.

> A note in a higher part over a sustained lower note (or a lower note under a sustained higher one) can be divided into as many parts as it contains smaller rhythmic units: Thus a <term>Breve</term> <note>a double whole note</note> can be divided into two semibreves, or 4 Minims, or 8 Semiminims, or 16 Fusas; or into two Minims and one Semibreve; or into one Semibreve, one Minim, and two semiminims; or into two minims, two semiminims, and four fusas; and so on with the rest.

### C H A P T E R  V.

#### On the Special Rules for the parts of a song.

### Rule I.

**A**ll symphonic harmonies of a melody are expressed above the <term>plainchant<note>Original: "planum cantum." The foundational, often slow-moving melody (cantus firmus) upon which other parts are built.</note></term> or the Bass.

### Rule II.

*The <term>Discant<note>The highest vocal part, equivalent to the modern Soprano.</note></term> shall begin above the plainchant with intervals of the 8th and 4th; below the 8th will be the 5th and 6th intervals; below the 8th will be the 3rd. Above the 8th, an 8th below the Discant is equal to the plainchant, and a 3rd above the Discant is a 10th from the plainchant, and a 5th above the Discant is a 12th above the plainchant, and a 6th above the Discant will be a 13th from the plainchant, and an 8th above the discant will be a 15th <note>A double octave.</note> to the plainchant.*

### Rule III.

*The <term>Alto<note>Original: "Altus." The high male voice part, situated between the Soprano and Tenor.</note></term> will for the most part finish on a perfect chord, namely with a 5th, and then its <term>penultimate<note>The second to last note in a musical phrase or cadence.</note></term> note will be a 3rd.*

### Rule IV.

*If the plainchant descends and ends Mi, Re, or Fa, Mi, or Sol, Fa <note>These are syllables from the Guidonian hexachord system, representing specific melodic steps.</note>; then the Discant ends with an 8th, having a 6th before it: Similarly, if the plainchant ends in Re, Ut, then the higher Discant will end in a 12th, having a 10th before it.*

### Rule V.

*When the Tenor is closed with the song in Mi, the penultimate note shall leap back from a 3rd into a 5th. But if the Tenor glides from a 6th to an 8th, the penultimate note being led from a 3rd into a 3rd, and the <term>Counter-tenor<note>Often interchangeable with the Alto in this period, providing harmonic fullness.</note></term> being led from a 3rd into a 5th, it creates a pleasing harmony.*

### Rule VI.

*To the Discant and Tenor in unison, the Bass sounding a 3rd below and the Alto a 3rd above harmonizes musically. There are also infinite other observations in this part of Music which are better perceived and taught through practice and experience; we shall pass over them lightly in this place, so that we may more quickly descend to the use of our Triangle.*

# THE MIRROR OF COSSIC NUMBERS,
### in which their value is perceived by those who regard the nature of their roots more than their forms.
<note>original: "Numerorum Cossicorum Speculum." The term "Cossic" comes from the Italian "cosa" (the thing), an early name for algebra. This "Mirror" is a visual tool for understanding powers and roots.</note>

---

## Rule I.

->The same procedure should be followed with mixed roots as with single digits or simple roots.<-

## Rule II.

->By what method do we find the root of any number?<-

You must inspect the nature of the number—specifically, of which <term>denomination: the power or category of the number, such as square or cube</term> it is. The given number must be sought in the "arc" of that quantity. Once found, one must also seek the root within that "sphere" <note>likely referring to the concentric circles in the accompanying diagram</note> where the said number is located. For in the arc of roots, and within that same sphere, you will find the radical number of the given number. 

For example, let the given number be 7776. This will be the "numerator" <note>here meaning the value itself</note>, while its "denominator" <note>the category or power name</note> will be the <term>Sursolid: an archaic term for a number raised to the fifth power (x⁵)</term>. Therefore, the said denominator must be examined in the arc of the Sursolids—namely, the number 7776. Then, you must proceed through that same sphere toward the left; for the root found there will be the radical number of the given value 7776: namely, 6. 
<note>The math checks out: 6 × 6 × 6 × 6 × 6 = 7,776.</note>

<summary>This page introduces the "Mirror of Cossic Numbers," a visual guide for identifying algebraic powers and roots, and provides a step-by-step rule for finding the fifth root of a number using the diagram.</summary>
<keywords>algebra, cossic numbers, sursolid, fifth power, roots, mathematical diagram, arithmetic rules</keywords>

## Rule III.

*However many times the root is found in the aforementioned numbers—all of which are produced through the multiplication of a multiple root—that is how many times the radical line exists in that geometric form; for instance, this root* <insert>[diagram: square with unit points]</insert> <note>original: "radix hæc"</note> *is found four times in this square* <insert>[diagram: wireframe cube]</insert> *and eight times in this cube* <insert>[diagram: shaded cube]</insert>*, and in 16, and so on.* <gloss>by multiplying the multiplication of 7.</gloss>

---

## Rule IV.

*The progression and increase of numbers contained in the Mirror* <note>The 'Mirror' likely refers to a specific table or diagram earlier in the text showing numerical relationships.</note> *occurs by multiplying the smaller number immediately preceding it by the root. By this method, every number of each sphere originates from the preceding one in the same sphere, led by the root found in that sphere; for example, the number preceding the cube is the square. Thus, by multiplying the square by its root—namely, the root of the same sphere—the cube of said sphere is produced; and it is possible to proceed in this way into infinity.*

---

## Rule V.

### Concerning the alteration of the names of certain numbers.

*Those who have commonly explained the Cossic art* <term>Cossic art: From the Italian 'cosa' (thing), this was the early modern term for algebra, where the unknown variable was called 'the thing'.</term> *have assigned names and symbols to them according to the nature of the roots rather than their geometric forms. But I shall name them based on their similarity to geometric forms, so that the demonstration of this art may become clearer.*

*Therefore, a "square of squares"* <term>x⁴ or biquadrate</term> *is commonly called so because its root is a square number: for instance, the root of 16 is 4, and the root of 256 is 16. But if its geometric form is considered, it will be called a "long cube," because it has the width and depth of one cube, but the length of two or more; for which reason it is not improperly called a "line of cubes." In the same way, an architect calls a line of bricks or tiles a "wall." Also, the "surde-solid"* <term>x⁵ or the fifth power</term> *as it is commonly called, if we look at its geometric composition, should be called a "square of cubes"; for it has a square figure whose parts are arranged so that each unit is a cube in itself.*

*It is also produced from the multiplication of a square and a cube together, as by multiplying 8 and 4, the surde-solid number [32] will be produced.*

*The "square of cubes"* <term>x⁶ or the sixth power</term> *as it is commonly called because it is made by multiplying a cube by itself, will be named a "cube of cubes" when considering its geometric form and composition, because it is arranged in geometry in such a way as a larger cube is constituted from smaller ones.*

*The "bi-surde-solid"* <term>x⁷ or the seventh power</term> *we shall also call a "long cube of cubes" for the preceding reason; for its figure is constituted of two composed cubes, connected together.*

*A "square of squares squared"* <term>x⁸ or the eighth power</term> *is by the same consideration called a "square of cubic cubes," because two long cubes composed of cubic cubes joined together form such a square figure.*

*Here, however, we shall describe and delineate the names of the Cossic numbers...*

### CHAPTER IX.

->*On the nature of the four Temple windows, and how the same may be*<-
->*achieved here in the mechanical composition of song, as*<-
->*in the Triangle.*<-
<note>The "Triangle" refers to a diagram previously discussed in Fludd’s work used for calculating musical intervals. "Mechanical composition" refers to a rule-based, systematic method of writing music.</note>

In the four Windows, seven low letters are described, opposed to as many high letters; each of these windows denotes a specific concordance <note>original: "concordantiam"; a harmonious musical interval</note>. The first two, counting from the left, demonstrate the dimensions of two perfect concordances, measuring them from the low letter to the higher letter. The two later windows, however, designate two imperfect concordances and their proportions from letter to letter. And this must always be observed in this teaching: that the letters expressed toward the right in said windows convey to us the intervals of the Bass <term>Bass: the lowest part in a musical composition</term>—that is, the spaces and lines distinguishing them. The others, however, placed opposite them in the same arches, designate the intervals of the parts or melodies in spaces and lines which ought to be built upon that Bass. From here, therefore, arise the foundations of this teaching: namely, that any parts of a song, divided into proper intervals, should have both the lower and higher letters expressed before them. From which the proportion and measure of any string or consonance may be more clearly discerned, so that an exact melody and harmony <note>original: "concentus"</note> of parts may be achieved.

We find that the first note is expressed in low G <note>original: "G. gravi"</note>, above which letter we desire to build the notes of the other two parts harmoniously <term>symphoniacè</term><note>Meaning "in symphony" or "harmoniously," referring to the vertical alignment of notes in counterpoint.</note>. The **Discant** <note>The highest part, or soprano.</note>, however, will begin with a 3rd; wherefore, the G of the Bass being found in the 3rd "window" <term>fenestra</term><note>The author uses "windows" as a metaphor for a lookup table or chart used to find corresponding harmonic intervals.</note>, you will perceive that *b* must be noted. 

Next, we shall proceed to the two second notes of the Bass, which, because they complete the measure of a **Semibreve** <note>A rhythmic value, historically a "half-brief," which functioned as a standard pulse in this period.</note>, are expressed between two parallels. Over the first of these, I shall erect an octave proportion in the Contratenor; for this, the eighth window must be inspected, where the letter D being found will show its opposite letter, namely *d*. Therefore, that same note will be expressed on the *d* space of the Contratenor. Truly, the second note of the Bass is to be sought in window 3, namely C, and its opposite letter will be *e*. Therefore, the same note of the Bass will be written upon the *e* line of the Contratenor. Finally, two similar notes of the Discant will harmonize with those of the Bass in a 5th and an octave. One must proceed in the same way with the rest of the notes of the Bass, diligently observing the right-hand letters of the windows, which show the locations of the harmonies of any upper part, as if by the finger of truth itself.

Then, in the windows toward the right, those letters—showing the notes of the given parts—will show the Bass letters on the opposite side. # ON THE PARTS OF MY SYMPHONIC SONG.

The use of the aforementioned staff or ruler <note>original: "baculi seu regulæ"</note> is as follows: namely, let this ruler be extended over some paper on which you desire to draw the four musical scales; then, let the scales serving the four parts be marked out, in such a way, however, that the interval between the parts, and likewise their lines and distances, match in all respects with those of the ruler or staff by which they ought to be directed and governed, just as we shall explain below. Once this is done, let the **Bass** part be composed according to your will, upon which the other upper parts may be symphonically composed. To do this, the lower end of the staff must be placed upon the "seat" <note>the specific line or space</note> of the first note—that is, either on the line G, B, D, F, or A, or on the space F, A, C, E, G, or B. For example, in the preceding illustration, the seat of the first note is on G; let the staff, therefore, stand perpendicularly upon the G line; and it will point out, as if with a finger, the concords and their locations in each upper part. 

For if you wish the **Countertenor** to begin with a 12th or 5th interval <note>consonance</note>, that interval will fall upon the second space. If you wish the **Alto** with a 3rd or 10th, you will find this proportion above the second space of that part. If you wish the **Soprano** <term>discantum: the highest vocal part, often called the descant</term> with a 15th or **Octave** <term>diapason: a Greek term for the interval of an octave</term>, you will also perceive that concord placed on the second line of the same song. Then the bottom end of the staff is raised so that it stands perpendicularly over the third line, in which the second note is expressed. The upper sections of the staff will denote the proper concords and their corresponding positions for the upper parts, according to their degrees of height or depth. 

Here, however, it must always be observed that the sequence of notes in the same song is smoother and sweeter the closer the following note is to the preceding one—except for the **Bass**, where the ascent is often made most pleasantly by intervals of an 8th or 5th. And in this same way, one must proceed with all the other notes of the **Bass**, wherever they are placed—namely, by either raising or lowering the end of the staff, provided that the staff is always held perpendicular to the given underlying note.

->END OF THE FIFTH BOOK.<-
