<note>The following three points conclude the interpretation of the figure **Populus** (The People), which began on the previous page.</note>

Thirteenth: A multitude of profit for one who goes to some Great person; <note>The "Great person" refers to a nobleman or high-ranking official.</note> of loss, of change, and of similar things.

Fourteenth: A multitude of people gathered together, either for good or for evil, according to the figures neighboring it.

Fifteenth: A multitude of good or evil for the petitioner, a gathering of people for good or for evil, according to the figures from which it arises; for if it comes from good figures, it denotes much good; if from evil, the contrary.

**Note**, that this figure <note>original: "haec figura", referring to *Populus*</note> found in the first house signifies a merchant of diverse things traveling through the countryside.

## XIV. Of the Way. <note>original: "De Via". *Via* is a geomantic figure represented by a single vertical line of four dots, symbolizing a path or journey.</note>

**First House:** A good journey, little profit, thoughts of small fruits. <note>In geomancy, "fruits" refers to the results or successes of an endeavor.</note>

**Second House:** Loss or gain, according to the neighboring figures.

**Third House:** Brothers, neighbors, water, a good journey, light business matters, journeys for a brother or relatives, the comparison of riches.

**Fourth House:** Parents, labors, lands, the concealment of stained things, the end of matters, poverty, poor parents, poor inheritances.

**Fifth House:** Letters, messengers of small importance, small fruits, poor attire, poor children, little joy.

**Sixth House:** Poor beasts, bad fortune, unstable servants, a sudden increase of illness, liberation from illness, the misfortune of beasts.

**Seventh House:** Thieves, poor women, little sense, poor and weak enemies, a harlot, the death of thieves.

<margin>The Way denotes in the house...</margin> **Eighth House:** Poverty in a foreign land, loss of inheritances proceeding from death.

**Ninth House:** A change of letters, messengers of little knowledge, a good journey, the benefit of the Church, smallness of gain and profit.

**Tenth House:** Very small offices, little gain from Lords and noble women, an old judge, little wisdom, the loss of some thing.

**Eleventh House:** Poor friends, very small fortune, little profit, gifts of merchandise, and letters of joy.

**Twelfth House:** Useless beasts, poor friends, a light exit from prison, liberation from debts or from misery, and sometimes death in prison, according to the good or bad figures nearby, and those from which it is generated.

**Thirteenth House:** Profit of journeys and changes.

**Fourteenth House:** Loss and departure from some matter, according to good or bad figures.

**Fifteenth House:** The way, a good outcome, according to the figures from which it comes.

**Note**, that when the Way <note>original: "via"</note> is found in the first house, it signifies a man who is changeable, false, and poor.

## XV. *On Conjunction.* <note>original: "De Conjunctione." In geomancy, this figure—represented by two points over two points—symbolizes joining, communication, and the planet Mercury.</note>

<margin>Conjunction denotes in the house...</margin>

> *The First House*, in a person: sense, good speech and eloquence, subtlety, skill, and goodness; and if it is joined with favorable figures, it signifies goodness of heart and of friends.
> *The Second*, the acquisition of good fortune and profit in trade.
> *The Third*, good sense among relatives, and a gathering of parents and neighbors.
> *The Fourth*, a good life, a good end, a good friend, profit from inheritances, and in legal proceedings, documents regarding inheritance.
> *The Fifth*, letters, messengers, and a gathering of goods.
> *The Sixth*, long illness, bad servants, and thieves.
> *The Seventh*, marriage, a good gathering, but also thieves and subtle, eloquent enemies, whether in a lawsuit or in battle.
> *The Eighth*, a gathering for the purpose of dividing the property of the deceased.
> *The Ninth*, knowledge, a bad road, thieves upon the path, and knowledge and eloquence among Clerics and men of the Church.
> *The Tenth*, service to Lords and Kings, and profit in mastery or one's profession.
> *The Eleventh*, good fortune, the gathering of all things, and the union of lovers.
> *The Twelfth*, prisons, a bad road, a bad gathering of men, and a bad life.
> *The Thirteenth* <note>The 13th through 15th positions in a geomantic chart are the Witnesses and the Judge, which summarize the reading.</note>, good and profit from one’s Lord.
> *The Fourteenth*, much fortune for the sake of love, much fortune and labor.
> *The Fifteenth*, good fortune in good matters, and bad in bad matters, according to the [other] figures.

*Note*, when this figure is found in the first house, it signifies a prudent man, a scribe, or one occupied in an office of money; a person of average build, who consumes his fortune as quickly as he acquires it, skilled in the liberal arts, and so on for the rest.

## XVI. *On the Prison.* <note>original: "De Carcere." This figure—one point, two points, two points, one point—symbolizes restriction, boundaries, and the planet Saturn.</note>

> *The First*, loss and the imprisonment of men; a person who is fearful and sad, sadness of heart, secret thoughts, and the hindrance of a journey abroad.
> *The Second*, the preservation of all secret things, and thoughts regarding the love of money.
> *The Third*, love of parents and of profit, the love of God, the hindrance and delay of a journey, and greedy brothers and neighbors.
> *The Fourth*, inheritances, hidden treasures, underground houses, a hidden and dark place, and good inheritances.
> *The Fifth*, few children, a pregnant woman, the writing of letters and messengers, rude men, raw foods, filthy garments, and treacherous loves.
> *The Sixth*, illness within a prison, a pregnant woman, a useless servant, a bad man and woman, death or a long illness, illness in the secret parts of a person, and bad or useless beasts.

### *General Rule.*

It must be noted that through any given house, good or evil, profit or loss is promised according to the nature of the figures with which the figure of each house is joined, or from which it is generated.

## CHAPTER IV.

### *Regarding the meaning of the 16 figures when they appear twice in a reading—that is, when identical figures are found in different houses, such as two "Ways," two "People," etc.*

*Second* <note>Referring to the second house in the chart.</note>, position, and especially so if it is a fixed, fortunate figure; if it is an unfavorable figure, it indicates the opposite. This principle should be observed through all the remaining houses.
*Third*, a good matter involving relatives, brothers or parents, sisters or neighbors.
*Fourth*, a bad change, though not excessively so, unless the figure is <term>Cauda Draconis</term> <note>original: "Cauda Draconis"; The Dragon's Tail, a figure usually associated with endings or bad luck.</note>.
*Fifth*, joy, companions for drinking and eating, new clothes, music, melody, an ancient object, and a result so well-suited to the heart's desire that the matter could not be better even by wishing—unless the figure is <term>Cauda Draconis</term>.

# ON GEOMANTIC FIGURES

<margin>A figure found or existing in the first house signifies, when it repeats itself in the [following] house:</margin>

The Sixth house: sickness, tribulation, and fear.

The Seventh house: fearful matters regarding an army or a wicked woman; it signifies every good thing unless <note>original: "Cauda aut Via"</note> the Dragon's Tail or the Way <note>Geomantic figures: the Dragon's Tail is generally ill-omened, while the Way suggests change or movement.</note> are present there, which denote every kind of evil in this house—unless the question was asked concerning a gathering, a marriage, or enemies, for otherwise they show danger.

The Eighth house: evil, great anger, or death, or a physical blow, loss, insulting words, and bad tribulations; but if it is a "good" figure, it signifies the acquisition of inheritances from the dead.

The Ninth house: some good, a firm and stable change to acquire something for another, and the handling of some religious or Church business, or dealings with nations or Churchmen, or with messengers, or those returning from a pilgrimage—unless <note>original: "Cauda & Rubeus"</note> the Dragon's Tail and the Red <note>The Red (Rubeus) is a figure associated with passion, blood, and violence.</note> appear in a question regarding a journey.

The Tenth house: entirely good, such that things could not be better, especially for acquiring honor and dignity, unless the Dragon's Tail and the Red are present.

The Eleventh house: good, so much so that there is no better result for a question; for it signifies hope and a good friend, provided the figure is <note>original: "Major, Via, vel Acquisitio"</note> Greater Fortune, the Way, or Gain.

The Twelfth house: the petitioner will fall into some tribulation, or a grave illness, or the loss of something, or harm from enemies; nor can matters be worse than if the figure is the Dragon's Tail.

---

<margin>A figure existing in the second house signifies, when it repeats itself in the [following] house:</margin>

The Third house: profit from parents, specifically brothers, sisters, or neighbors, if they are good figures; but if they are bad, the opposite.

The Fourth house: that the petitioner expects to profit from his father, or from some great Lord, if the figure is good; if bad, then evil.

The Fifth house: that the petitioner is thinking of earning a living, or clothes, or of messengers who will come to him with letters, or of damage by fire.

The Sixth house: future illness of the family, or some loss, or dread, or great tribulation, or sickness, or some other bad thing.

The Seventh house: marriage, loss caused by a woman, great enmity for the petitioner, or robbery, or thoughts of women through concupiscence or lust, or brawls, threatening words, and moving from place to place.

The Eighth house: the return of an absent person, or someone else from the family.

The Ninth house: profit for the petitioner of a religious or ecclesiastical nature, or a priest, or some other similar matter.

The Tenth house: <term>necromantic</term> <note>original: "Negromanticas"; refers to magic involving spirits or the dead, often used broadly in this period for "hidden" or "black" arts.</note> arts, or that the petitioner will go to win the love of some woman or a Lord, or great Majesty, or sciences, according to whether the figures are good or bad.

The Eleventh house: fortune in that house, or in the family, or through the family, or through profit, or friends, or trade; for this is the strength and power of the entire question.

The Twelfth house: the imprisonment of someone from the family, or a grave illness, grave harassment, or the destruction of that person from the family whom you have gained, great accidents, or future tribulation and anguish.

---

The Fourth house: <note>This section appears to begin a new sequence, perhaps if a figure repeats in the third house.</note> brothers, sisters, companions, neighbors, messengers to the petitioner, profit for those who ask, or loss, according to the nature of the figures.

The Fifth house: joy, gladness, fast news from friends, letters, and messengers.

<margin>The figure of the sixth house signifies, when it repeats itself in the following house:</margin>

The *Seventh* signifies illness, and that a servant, or the seeker's woman or companion, will suddenly become angry and fall among enemies; or that the seeker and his woman will fall into the hands of thieves, or suffer infamy, which they will nonetheless escape if they can.

The *Eighth* signifies that servants or the seeker's beasts <note>livestock or work animals</note> will fall into danger or tribulation, pain or sadness, and that he will be beaten or lose some object, and will be absent in the company of the house's enemies, or the seeker's woman will be intimate with someone else.

The *Twelfth* signifies illness of the beasts, or that the seeker himself will fall into illness or be occupied with prisons; he will suffer loss either through useless beasts or through a long journey.

The *Twelfth* signifies the management <note>original: "occupationem"</note> of large beasts, and that he will fall into a grave and long illness, or into imprisonment, or a long journey, or poverty; or that certain letters will bring him loss in a short time, which ought to be kept well and secretly for proof.

The *Twelfth* signifies secret enemies of the seeker who work hard to burden him, or that the absent person is imprisoned or sick, or that a prisoner will die.

<margin>The figure of the ninth house <note>The house of travel, religion, and dreams.</note> signifies, when it repeats itself in house:</margin>

A figure existing in the eleventh house signifies, when it duplicates itself in the twelfth house: prison, the hatred of enemies, or a similar matter; or, through this duplication, the question will turn out fortunately for the seeker.

->Rule.<-

The fulfillment of a matter is granted either more quickly or more slowly according to the nature of the figure. The first figure is of a light element, namely fire; if this is found in the fourth house <note>The house of endings and the grave; traditionally a "slow" house.</note>, it denotes misfortune and long duration, for the fourth house signifies the slow completion of all things.

### CHAPTER V.
### Regarding testimonies—that is, regarding the thirteenth and fourteenth figures of the Geomantic shield—from which the Judge, or fifteenth figure, arises, in which three figures the entire judgment consists.

<margin>The figure *Populus* <note>Latin: "The People"; a geomantic figure representing a crowd or stability.</note> acting as the Judge signifies gatherings arising from two:</margin>
*Minor figures*, a gathering of the king’s army, a prince, or a powerful Lord, or a large gathering of women.
*Major figures*, a matter of the King or a great Lord or a Knight, and also every person existing in law or justice, men of science, and a gathering of noble women.
*Sorrow figures* <note>original: *Tristitiis*</note>, a gathering of melancholic men, obscure, dark, and heavy matters, dead things, and sadness of the heart.
*Joy figures* <note>original: *Latitiis*</note>, a gathering of Prelates and churchmen, men of the council of great prosperity, knowledge, and holiness, who possess the joy of the world. Likewise, men of great perfection.
*Gain figures* <note>original: *Acquisitionibus*</note>, profit for men who love reason, the completion of trade, a judgment of truth, and of all good things.

# ON GEOMANTIC FIGURES

**Loss** <note>original: "Amissionibus"</note> signifies a change from one's own proper place, home, and land into a foreign place.

**The Dragon's Tail** <note>original: "Caudis"</note> signifies a multitude and gathering of all evils, namely thieves, assassins, deceivers, and false men, as well as every evil and interruption upon a journey.

**The Dragon's Head** <note>original: "Capitibus"</note> signifies the correction and gathering of a secret council, hidden things, prayers and religious gatherings in one place, weddings, and the union of companions.

**The Boy** <note>original: "Pueris"</note> signifies a gathering of infants and small children, as well as women for the sake of love; a gathering for luxury and feasts for the comfort and joy of men and women; instruments of song and music; and a gathering of servants for weddings and similar events.

**The Girl** <note>original: "Puellis"</note> signifies servants, a multitude of vain and luxurious talk, the faults of men, women, and harlots, betrayal within a family, dishonesty, lying men and women, those drunk in luxury, fornicators, and Sodomites.

**The Red** <note>original: "Rubeis"</note> signifies spilled blood, specifically in battle; if it arises from "bad" figures, it is a negative omen, but if from "good" figures, that shedding of blood is interpreted more favorably <note>likely referring to medical bloodletting or a necessary sacrifice</note>.

**The White** <note>original: "Albis"</note> signifies white things, written books, silver letters, profit, and the agreement of many people.

**The Way** <note>original: "Viis"</note> signifies channels, rain, a multitude of poor people, the path and journey of small beasts, and anything light, unstable, or of little importance.

**Conjunction** <note>original: "Conjunctionibus"</note> signifies something of many colors, writing, weddings, ointments or fatty substances, complaints, death, graves, falsehood, and changeable words.

**The Prison** <note>original: "Carceribus"</note> signifies a gathering of ships, pregnant women, prisons, deep ditches, words spoken over graves, and dark or hidden things.

---

<margin>The Way, when it is the judge, signifies outcomes arising from:</margin>

**The People & The Way**, weddings and accidents, though these are good and faithful; pilgrimages, sudden paths, rains, waters, joy, and consolation. It is a bad sign for the promises of Lords or for firm and stable things; it signifies bad weddings and sudden legates or messengers.

**Loss & Gain** <note>original: "Amissione & acquisitione"</note>, frequent going and returning, especially in trade, resulting in neither profit nor loss; this is a "light" judgment and denotes peace in all matters, but a bad change of location.

**The Tail & Sorrow**, poverty, loss, and malice regarding a journey or the acquisition of a desired thing. It is good for someone who is meant to return from their native country; it signifies a great exit in trade, a path of little profit, good winds at sea, but a bad sign for collecting debts.

**Greater Fortune & Lesser Fortune** <note>original: "Majore & minore"</note>, a good return of an absent person and the discovery of a lost man. It is good for large beasts but dangerous for weddings; it signifies freedom from prison, yet is a sign of confusion and loss for those currently traveling.

**The White & The Girl**, journeys by land, a good sign for the return of an absent person, messengers, and the company of one who will return after their arrival.

**The Dragon's Head & Joy** <note>original: "Capite Drac. & Latitia"</note>, dignities, honors, a stable journey, sudden and good fortune before judges, the fulfillment of promises made by Kings and Lords, and the completion of one's own desire.

**Conjunction & The Prison**, good weddings, good fortune, and good fellowship. However, it is a bad sign for travel and change; it suggests imprisonment after liberty, sickness after health, and sadness after triumph.

<header>ON PRACTICAL GEOMETRY.</header>

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the measurement of height or distance using similar triangles. On the right is a tall vertical pole or tower labeled 'e' at the top and 'd' at the base. On the left is a smaller measuring apparatus with a vertical component labeled 'a' and a base labeled 'c'. A dashed horizontal line connects the base of the device to the base of the pole. A solid diagonal line (hypotenuse) extends from the top of the measuring device to the top of the pole, creating a large right-angled triangle. The measuring device itself contains a smaller, similar right-angled triangle.</image-desc>

In this same way, the diagonal <note>original: "Diameter"</note> of a square is investigated to recognize and find the height of scaling ladders <note>original: "scalarum altitudinem"; likely referring to military scaling ladders used to breach fortifications.</note>, as will be demonstrated in the treatise on fortifications. For just as the diagonal of a smaller parallelogram relates to its base or side—or, as the hypotenuse <note>The longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.</note> of a smaller triangle relates to its sides (which is the same thing)—so will the diagonal of the larger square, or the hypotenuse of the larger triangle, relate to its sides.

### CHAPTER V.

->*On finding any width from two stations using a device similar to Jacob’s Staff.*<-
<note>Jacob’s Staff, or the *Baculus Jacobi*, was a common 17th-century tool for measuring angles and distances in navigation and surveying.</note>

Place the cross-piece <note>original: "transversor"</note> or cursor at the end of one of the six divisions of the staff; then, with your eye positioned at the end of the staff, move forward or backward until you see the outer boundaries of the acquired width through both ends of the cross-piece (whether using the smaller or larger ends). Once these are seen, mark the location of that first station with your foot or some other object. Then, move the cross-piece from that section of the staff, either to the next section closer to the eye or to the next section further away. If the cursor is moved to a section toward the eye, then it is necessary to approach the object being measured until you again see the boundaries of the width through the extremities of the cursor. However, when the cursor is moved to the next section away from the eye, you must move backward until those aforementioned boundaries...

<term>Albus</term> <note>original: "Albo"; the White figure, associated with peace and wisdom</note> and <term>Laetitia</term> <note>original: "Latitia"; Joy</note> signify great profit, victory, virtue, and the fulfillment of one's will; health to the sick, good news for those absent, letters, and messengers.

<term>Puer</term> <note>original: "Puero"; the Boy</note> and <term>Tristitia</term> <note>Sorrow</note> signify old age, poverty, hindrance in affairs, poor men, and bad brothers; however, the end will be good, and sometimes it is even a sign of rest.

<term>Amissio</term> <note>original: "Amissione"; Loss</note> and <term>Via</term> <note>the Way or Path</note> signify loss and a lack of things to be acquired, which will nonetheless later turn into profit; the return of an absent person to profit and health; a hindrance to a journey, yet eventual profit.

<term>Via</term> and <term>Amissio</term> signify health for one making a journey and profit, good fortune, riches, and the reception of letters and messengers.

<term>Carcer</term> <note>original: "Carcere"; the Prison</note> and <term>Fortuna Minor</term> <note>original: "minore"; Lesser Fortune</note> signify fame and the honor of a great man, good for a petitioner seeking favor from a King or Lord, the increase of all profit, and the collection of debts.

<term>Fortuna Major</term> <note>original: "Majore"; Greater Fortune</note> and <term>Conjunctio</term> <note>original: "conjunctione"; Union or Conjunction</note> signify the fulfillment of a promise, aid in receiving merchandise, and denote good company, profit, acquisition, and joy.

<term>Fortuna Minor</term> and <term>Carcer</term> signify stability in a person, and healthy love, faithfulness to promises, the acquisition of lands containing houses and other such things; it is a sign of a powerful man and of good stability in marriage.

<term>Puella</term> <note>the Girl</note> and <term>Laetitia</term> signify gain in trade, profit in wheat and beasts, and loss to those who are in remote places, but the end will be good.

<term>Puer</term> and <term>Cauda Draconis</term> <note>original: "Cauda"; the Dragon’s Tail, often a volatile or negative sign</note> signify the recovery of a lost thing, the obtaining of a promise, profit and advantage, earthly matters and minerals, silver and riches; however, it affects the petitioner heavily, for it is a sign of labor, pain, and fear or dread, but the end always comes to safety.

<term>Caput Draconis</term> <note>original: "Capite"; the Dragon’s Head</note> and <term>Albus</term> signify honor and security, the possession of goods, victory over enemies, and advantage and joy in every matter.

<term>Tristitia</term> in <term>Rubeus</term> <note>original: "Rubeo"; the Red figure, associated with passion and conflict</note> signifies many stable things, pregnant women, and the liberation and labor of the sick from "hot" diseases <note>likely fevers or inflammations</note>, or from blood, or incantations; it is good for trade, but it is a very unhappy figure for those who are imprisoned.

<term>Populus</term> and <term>Acquisitio</term> are good for trade and a good end; it is a healthy sign, good for beasts, and for every useful thing.

<term>Conjunctio</term> and <term>Fortuna Major</term> signify the stability of things, but much labor in acquisition; it is good for one making a journey and for the recovery of debts.

<term>Laetitia</term> and <term>Puella</term> signify good profit, and especially in trade, acquisition in every matter, and health and rest; it is good for those in prison, and for the acquisition of honor and exaltation from a King.

<term>Cauda Draconis</term> and <term>Puer</term> signify that it is bad to have a promise, for it prolongs promised things; yet it fulfills them in the end; it is a sign of slowness and dread, but all things eventually reach a good end.

<term>Caput Draconis</term> and <term>Albus</term> signify great joy and power in trade, good for victory, honor, and glory; acquisition, joy, and the exaltation of that which is sought.

<term>Rubeus</term> and <term>Tristitia</term> signify the hindrance of secrets, secret things, great or arduous knowledge, and also hard things and matters of great importance.

## ON GEOMANTIC FIGURES

*Conjunction and People* <note>original: "Conjunctione & populo"</note> portend marriages, are good for tournaments and for journeys, and are favorable for many matters.

*Greater Fortune and Gain* <note>original: "Majore & acquisitione"</note> signify the acquisition of livestock and profit, near-term gain, stability in many things, the recovery of lost property, and the fulfillment of a promise after a period of despair.

*The Head and Sorrow* <note>original: "Capite & Tristitia"; referring to the figure 'Caput Draconis' or the Dragon's Head</note> indicate fear in all things and destruction among one's friends; it is a sign of receiving gold, silver, and similar objects.

*The Girl and The Boy* <note>original: "Puella & puero"</note> signify a gathering and marriages, friendship, and loss, except in the case of livestock.

<margin>Conjunction, when it acts as the Judge <note>The 'Judge' is a final figure in a geomantic reading that summarizes the outcome.</note>, signifies what arises from</margin>
*Life and Prison* <note>original: "Vita & carcere"; 'Vita' likely refers to the figure 'Via' or The Way</note> portend a great journey, the joining of feminine matters, treasures, horses, and are good for a pregnant woman and for a social gathering.

*Gain and Greater Fortune* <note>original: "Acquisitione & majore"</note> signify travel for feminine matters, a sign of treasures, a gathering of fine horses, joy for pregnant women, a long journey, and occasionally delay and pain.

*Loss and Lesser Fortune* <note>original: "Amissione & Minore"</note> signify confidence, security, victory, virtue, power and honor granted by the King, rest, and are good for marriages.

*The Boy and The Girl* <note>original: "Puero & Puella"</note> signify hope and love between brothers and sisters; it is good for illness and for receiving gold, silver, and other such things.

*Sorrow and The Head* <note>original: "Tristitia & Capite"</note> signify the completion of marriages, a beautiful woman, and are good for the return of an absent person, though there will be hindrance and fear, the end of which will nevertheless be good.

*Red and White* <note>original: "Rubeo & Albo"</note> signify the shedding of blood and contention, the color red, escape from evil, the return of an absent person, and a good end after a delay.

*The Tail and Joy* <note>original: "Cauda & Laetitia"; referring to 'Cauda Draconis' or the Dragon's Tail</note> signify fortune, a happy and great man, victory, usefulness and grace, virtue, a promise, and sometimes poverty.

*Lesser Fortune and Gain* <note>original: "Minore & acquisitione"</note> signify marriages, joy, good fortune in everything, and the return of an absent person.

*White and Red* <note>original: "Albo & Rubeo"</note> signify the return of an absent person and profit, various colors, gain, and are good for any ambiguous matter or anything about which one has doubt.

*Joy and The Tail* <note>original: "Laetitia & Cauda"</note> signify a great man, good fortune and love, but a sickness of the heart, such that even one who is healthy may suffer.

<summary>This page lists the divinatory meanings of various pairs of geomantic figures, covering topics such as marriage, financial gain, health, and travel. It serves as a reference guide for a practitioner to interpret the "Judge" or final outcome of a geomantic reading.</summary>

# CHAPTER IV.

->*Concerning the meaning of the 16 figures when they multiply themselves in a question.*<-

---

When a figure multiplies itself in a question <note>In the practice of <term>geomancy</term> (divination by patterns of earth or dots), "multiplication" occurs when the same figure appears in multiple "houses" or positions within the reading chart, intensifying its influence.</note>:

*   **<term>Sorrow</term> <note>original: *Tristitia*; a geomantic figure associated with weight, grief, and the element of Earth.</note>, which is the misfortune of Saturn**
    *   **It signifies** { A man bowing his head toward the earth, pensive and greedy; the speeding up of a desired matter; likewise, either death or recovery for the sick; harm to a pregnant woman and the loss of her offspring; and especially when the question concerns such matters, harm to a prisoner; the sinking of a ship at sea, particularly if it is found in the third or ninth <term>house</term> <note>The "houses" are twelve specific positions in a geomantic chart, each representing an area of life such as travel (3rd and 9th) or health (6th and 11th).</note>; disease if it should be in the eleventh house; the permanence of a lost object; and the capture of a thief.
    *   It fares poorly in every house, except for the fourth, eighth, and twelfth.
    *   **It possesses** {
        *   Its <term>Exaltation</term> and <term>Fall</term> <note>Astrological terms indicating where a figure's power is at its highest (exaltation) or lowest (fall).</note> in the 5th house.
        *   A value that grows greater the more it is multiplied.

*   **<term>The Prison</term> <note>original: *Carcer*; a geomantic figure representing limitation, binding, or focus.</note>, which is likewise a figure of Saturn**
    *   **It signifies** { A sorrowful master and the restricted <note>original: *clausam*; literally "closed" or "locked."</note> release of a prisoner; a good journey for a traveler; and concord or reconciliation between enemies.
    *   It fares well in no house, except for the twelfth. Its worst location, however, is the sixth house.
    *   **It possesses** {
        *   The same Exaltation and Fall as Sorrow, since both are figures of the planet Saturn.
        *   The color black.

### ON GEOMANTIC FIGURES

<margin>Multiplying itself in a question <note>This refers to a figure appearing multiple times in a geomantic chart, which changes its interpretation.</note></margin>

- **Gain <note>original: "Acquisitio"</note>, which is a figure of Jupiter**
    - { **It signifies** }
        - Gain, harm to the imprisoned and the sick, hindrance of a journey, the restoration of lost property, and robbery or theft.
    - It remains very good in the first house <note>The "houses" are twelve divisions of the chart representing different areas of life, such as the self, wealth, or health.</note>, but poorly in the seventh and eighth houses.
    - { **It has** }
        - Joy in the eleventh house, exaltation in the fourteenth house, and its fall <note>A point of weakness in astrological/geomantic dignity.</note> in the tenth house.
        - A color <note>The Latin "calorem" (heat) is likely a typo for "colorem" (color).</note> mixed of redness and whiteness.

---

- **Joy <note>original: "Laetitia"</note>, which is the fortune of Jupiter**
    - { **It signifies** }
        - Shouts, quarrels, and petitions for things; and sometimes battles and brawls amidst merriment—for instance, among guests and banqueters—a decrease in the crowd, a precious thing for the petitioner, delight for the petitioner of judgment and testimony, the exaltation of his honor, and the healing of disease.
    - It remains well in all houses, except for the sixth, eighth, and twelfth; it is better the more it is multiplied.
    - { **It has** }
        - Joy, exaltation, and fall the same as "Gain" <note>Acquisitio</note>.
        - A color between whiteness and yellowness.

---

- <note>The text here describes **Loss** (Amissio), though the name is omitted in this section of the manuscript.</note> { **It signifies** }
    - Loss and the shedding of blood, superfluous business difficult to accomplish, the severity of a disease, long imprisonment, but profit from a king to the petitioner, the destruction of a thief; Likewise, if "Loss" <note>original: "amissio"</note> should be its companion, it signifies fire and thieves; but if "Greater Fortune" <note>Fortuna Major</note> or the "Head" <note>Caput Draconis, the Dragon's Head</note> itself precedes it, it signifies hope or a red thing in a favorable sense.

### <term>Rubeus<gloss>Latin for "The Red One"</gloss></term>, which is the misfortune of Mars

This figure is situated very poorly in the fourth and seventh houses (specifically indicating the shedding of blood for the <term>petitor<gloss>The seeker or person asking the question</gloss></term> there) and in the first house, where it indicates fear for the seeker.

**It holds**
- Joy in the sixth house, exaltation in the tenth, and its <term>fall<gloss>A position where the figure's influence is weakened or corrupted</gloss></term> in the fourteenth.
- A quality of redness over blackness; it is considered better the more it is multiplied within a reading.

**It signifies**
- Wailing, change, great difficulty, fornication, delights, lustful behavior, cheerfulness, the readiness of a pregnant woman to give birth, harm to ships at sea and to sailors, hindrance of travel by land, the subversion of a matter, madness, delirium, and fury; it is an ill omen for those imprisoned.

---

### <term>Puella<gloss>Latin for "The Girl"</gloss></term>, which is the misfortune of Mars

<note>original: "Puella, quæ est infortunium Martis." In most geomantic traditions, Puella is associated with the planet Venus and is considered favorable; however, this text uniquely categorizes it as a "misfortune of Mars."</note>
This figure is well-placed in the second and seventh houses, but nowhere else.

**It holds**
- Its joy, exaltation, and fall are the same as Rubeus, since both are considered figures of Mars in this system.
- A red color; it is better the more it is multiplied.

**It signifies**
- Harm to the sick, foreign men, four-legged animals, liberation from prison, the return of one absent from their homeland, the shade of trees, and the recovery of stolen goods.

---

### <term>Major<gloss>Latin for "The Greater"</gloss></term>, which is the misfortune of Mars

<note>This likely refers to "Fortuna Major," the figure of Greater Fortune, though the author continues to link these figures to Mars's more volatile influence.</note>
This figure is well-placed in the first house, which is the house of its name; it is poorly placed in the seventh house.

**It holds** joy in the ninth house, exaltation in the first, and its fall in the seventh.

## TREATISE II. PART XI. BOOK II.

**Multiplying itself in the question** <note>original: "Multiplicans sese in quæstione." This refers to a geomantic technique where a figure appearing in multiple "houses" or positions in a chart creates a specific connection or "pass" between different areas of the seeker's life.</note>

---

### Albus, which is the fortune of Mercury

*   **Significance**
    *   It indicates a matter that is dissolved and frustrated, levity, and harm to the sick. However, if it is followed by the figure Rubeus <note>Rubeus, "The Red," is a figure of Mars and usually indicates passion or violence.</note>, it signifies good results and liberation for those imprisoned, but harm to the petitioner <note>The person asking the question of the oracle.</note>.
*   **It dwells well in the fourth house; poorly in the first.**
*   **It possesses**
    *   Its Joy <term>Gaudium: a specific house where a figure’s influence is most naturally expressed</term> in the Ascendant <note>The first house.</note>, its exaltation in the sixth house, and its fall <term>Casum: the position where a figure’s power is most weakened</term> in the twelfth house.
    *   Its color is a perfect white, and its flowers are green.

---

### Conjunctio, which is the fortune of Mercury, and is neutral between male and female

*   **Significance**
    *   Knights, men who recite histories with eloquence in the presence of Kings, carpenters, tailors, victory, struggles, evil for the imprisoned, and hindrance for those making a journey. It signifies profit for those who conspire in fraud and betrayal, but also mortality, harm, and is especially dangerous for pregnant women.
*   **It dwells well in the sixth house and many others, but poorly in the eighth and twelfth.**
*   **It possesses**
    *   Joy, Exaltation, and Fall just like Albus, since both are figures of Mercury.
    *   Its color is white and black.
*   **It is strengthened in good or evil by the figure that is six places distant from it.**

---

### Populus, which is the fortune of the Moon

*   **Significance**
    *   Change and battle in every way, serious matters, and bad business; although, when it stands alone, it signifies health for the sick.
*   **It dwells well in the tenth house; poorly in the fourth, as that is its opposition.**
*   **It possesses its Joy in the third house, its Exaltation in the second, and its Fall in the eighth.**
*   **It is strengthened by the house six places distant from it, whether distant to the right or to the left.**

# ON GEOMANTIC FIGURES <note>original: "DE FIGUR. GEOMANT." Geomancy is a method of divination that interprets patterns formed by dots, often associated with the elements and planets.</note>

When the figure of **The Way** <note>original: "Via"</note>, which represents the fortune of the moon, multiplies itself in a question:
- **It signifies:** Abstinence, the delay of a request, a "corrupt woman" <note>likely referring to a woman of ill-repute or a situation that has soured</note>, and retardation—though its singular nature can bring freedom from illness.
- It is well-placed in the fifth <term>house</term> <note>In geomancy and astrology, "houses" are twelve divisions representing different aspects of life, such as wealth, health, or travel.</note> and poorly in the eleventh, which is its opposite. It shares its joy, exaltation, and "fall" <note>astrological terms for the relative strength or weakness of a planetary influence</note> with the figure known as **The People** <note>original: "Populus"</note>, as both are lunar figures.
- It is strengthened by the fourth figure following it.

---

**The Head** <note>original: "Caput," referring to the Head of the Dragon or the North Node of the moon</note>, which belongs to Jupiter and Venus, represents the fortune of the Dragon and the sign of Virgo:
- **It signifies:** Stable business matters, the fulfillment of a petitioner's request, the confirmation of royal edicts and answers, health for the sick (even in the case of daytime illnesses), and the certainty of pregnancy or conception.
- It is well-placed in the sixth house and poorly in the twelfth.
- **It has:** A yellow color. It bears a resemblance or similarity to the figure called **Greater Fortune** <note>original: "Major," referring to Fortuna Major</note>.

---

When the figure of **The Tail** <note>original: "Cauda," referring to the Tail of the Dragon or the South Node of the moon</note>, which is the figure of Mars and Saturn and the sign of Sagittarius, multiplies itself in a question:
- **It signifies:** Business matters that are snatched away from the petitioner's power, a change of path, fortune for a King, liberation for the imprisoned, and the speeding up of a sick person's recovery.
- It is well-placed in the seventh, ninth, twelfth, and fourteenth houses, and poorly in the eleventh and fourth.
- **It has:** A red color mixed with yellow.

## C H A P. VII.

### *Concerning the forms and figures of the body, and likewise concerning the qualities of the soul, which the Geomantic figures signify in human persons.*

**Acquisitio <note>The figure of "Acquisition" or "Gain," often associated with the planet Jupiter and the gathering of resources.</note> signifies a person by reason of:**

*   **Soul or character**: Of great modesty, tenacious, or one who does not laugh easily <note>original: "nihil alteridantem"</note>, cautious in trade, and a lover of beautiful, white garments.
*   **The body**: Of medium stature, with a beautiful face, a small and narrow mouth, slightly bowed forward in the upper body, having very small ears, a long neck, thick hair, and large eyes that look toward the ground. The front teeth are larger than the others (up to the middle of the jaw), with narrow shoulders, and a well-groomed appearance.
*   **Fortune and condition**: A gatherer of money and riches, established in a position of dignity, such as a knight, wealthy and powerful.

---

**Amissio <note>The figure of "Loss," the inversion of Acquisition, representing the expenditure or loss of energy or wealth.</note> signifies a person by reason of:**

*   **Soul or character**: Desirous of honor, simple-minded, prone to lying, and easily moved to anger.
*   **The body**: Neither too large nor too small, yet short and stout, robust, having a long neck, a large head, broad shoulders, a round face, a very small mouth, beautiful eyes, large feet, thick hair, and most often a scar or a cleft.
*   **Fortune**: One departing from all good things and all evils; it also signifies blood <note>In traditional medical astrology, this might indicate bloodletting or a sanguine temperament.</note>.

---

**Letitia <note>The figure of "Joy," usually associated with the planet Jupiter or the Sun, representing success and a cheerful disposition.</note> signifies a person by reason of:**

*   **Soul or character**: Intelligent, of good character like a religious or ecclesiastical person, a lover of white clothing, truthful, a lover of GOD, and perhaps presumptuous.

# ON GEOMANTIC FIGURES

<margin>Joy <note>original: "Laetitia," a geomantic figure formed of dots representing a "U" shape or a bridge, usually associated with the planet Jupiter</note> denotes a person by reason of:</margin>
**Of the Body:** Walking honorably and having a modest appearance, looking toward the ground, of a full stature, with large feet, a round face, large eyes, a broad forehead, coarse hair, a thick neck, a long nose, wide nostrils, and two prominent upper teeth.

---

<margin>Sorrow <note>original: "Tristitia," a geomantic figure that is the inverse of Joy, associated with Saturn</note> denotes a person by reason of:</margin>
**Of the Mind or Character:** Keeping malice in the heart for a long time and living without law; a liar, easy and prone to anger, and not laughing easily.

**Of the Body:** Having a long and thin body, a dark complexion, large teeth, a long and black face, an ugly form, large feet, a mark on the ankle, and coarse hair.

---

<margin>The Dragon’s Head <note>original: "Caput Draconis," representing the North Node of the Moon, generally considered a favorable or "increasing" influence</note> denotes a person by reason of:</margin>
**Of the Mind or Character:** Chaste, honorable, and of good will.

**Of the Body:** Of medium stature, having beautiful eyes, a beautiful and round face, a long nose, a large mouth, large teeth, and much hair; it also signifies the house, beasts, and secret fields <note>original: "acres secretas," possibly referring to secluded lands or hidden assets</note>.

---

<margin>The Dragon’s Tail <note>original: "Cauda Draconis," representing the South Node of the Moon, generally considered a decreasing or unfavorable influence</note> denotes a person by reason of:</margin>
**Of Mind:** Evil.

**Of the Body:** More beautiful from the back than from the front, having a long face, a large jaw, a sharp chin and beard, long and thick legs, a long belly, a long and thin body, a long nose, a large mouth, and large teeth; in general, it also denotes weapons, false rumors, anger, and strife.

---

<margin>The White <note>original: "Albus," a geomantic figure associated with Mercury and the color white, representing peace and wisdom</note> denotes a person by reason of:</margin>
**Of the Mind or Character:** Loving peace, faith, and charity, as well as the color white; modest, acquiring many friends but retaining few, and spending more than he earns.

**Of the Body:** Thicker in the upper part than the lower, of medium stature, having a large head, a forehead that sweats often, a round face, a sufficiently long beard, thick skin on the face, very small eyes, and a mark in the eye; it also signifies, in general, books, writings, and everything that is white.

### TREATISE II, PART XI, BOOK II

<margin>**Rubeus <note>Latin: "The Red." In geomancy, this figure is associated with the planet Mars and represents passion, fire, and potential violence.</note> denotes a person by reason of:**</margin>
- **The mind or character**: Very cunning, prone to foul language, and a stirrer of discord.
- **The body**: Having a rough face, a fierce look, a red or brownish complexion, and very often red spots or pustules on the face; sparse hair in the beard, and a voice threatening like thunder.

---

<margin>**Puer <note>Latin: "The Boy." This figure is also associated with Mars (specifically in Aries) and represents youthful energy, impulse, and sometimes recklessness.</note> denotes a person by reason of:**</margin>
- **The mind or character**: Ferocious, easily moved to anger, fond of adorning their face and striving for its brilliance; likewise, men and women who love foolishly and seek out fornication.
- **The body**: Handsome, fleshy, sufficiently strong and of medium height, with sweet speech (and occasionally foul); having beautiful eyes, beautiful eyebrows, a long neck, a large head, a round face, a very small mouth, and broad shoulders.

---

<margin>**Puella <note>Latin: "The Girl." This figure is associated with the planet Venus and represents harmony, beauty, and social grace, though here it is also linked to discord.</note> denotes a person by reason of:**</margin>
- **The mind or character**: A sower of discord and an instigator of battle among all nations; if the subject is male, he will love women; if female, she will love men; likewise, a prostitute, etc.
- **The body**: Neither too fat nor too thin, having a short and thick-set body, a beautiful face, a brown or red complexion—and indeed quite often a deep redness in the face—sparse beard hair, small eyes, and poorly aligned teeth.

---

<margin>**Major <note>Latin: "Fortuna Major," or Great Fortune. A figure associated with the Sun, representing success, inner strength, and nobility.</note> denotes a person by reason of:**</margin>
- **The mind or character**: Beneficent, modest, honest in speech, a lover of laws, of light <note>original: "levium," which can mean light-hearted, agile, or sometimes fickle</note> manners, seeking high things, and somewhat proud; generous in spending, and a squanderer of wealth.
- **The body**: Lean, of medium height, having a round face, delicate teeth, large eyes, a beautiful complexion, one leg thicker than the other, and a face verging toward a yellowish hue.
- **Life or condition**: Of good and powerful status, like a nobleman or a Lord; of a fine craft or profession.

## ON GEOMANTIC FIGURES

<margin>Minor <note>original: "Fortuna Minor," meaning Lesser Fortune.</note> denotes a person by reason of:</margin>
**Of the soul or character** { Bold, proud, loving God, modest, and walking honestly; presumptuous, high-minded, and generous.

**Of the body** { Fleshy, of medium size and stature, having a round and white face, a large and long nose, black eyes turned toward the ground, a beautiful complexion, a broad forehead, thick and coarse hair that is spread out, a thick neck, wide nostrils, and a medium beard.

---

<margin>Populus <note>original: "Populus," meaning The People or The Crowd.</note> denotes a person by reason of:</margin>
**Of the soul or character** { Finding joy in walking about, and not liking to rest in one place.

**Of the body** { Neither too large nor too small, yet leaning more toward being tall; having a beautiful and kind face, a thin body, slender legs, a certain spot in the eye—or one eye larger than the other—a dark complexion, large teeth, a long face, an unattractive form, a large beard, and a wound or some other mark that shall never leave him. It also signifies plants, herbs, waters, and a gathering of people.

---

<margin>Via <note>original: "Via," meaning The Way or The Path.</note> denotes a person by reason of:</margin>
**Of the soul or character** { Slow to anger, yet monstrous when anger boils over; loving to move from place to place without ceasing.

**Of the body** { Neither too large nor too small, thicker in the middle upper part than in the lower parts, having one eye larger than the other (or at least with a spot), a white complexion, tiny teeth, and a forehead that frequently sweats.

**Of fortune and condition** { Poor. It also signifies, among other things, a journey and trees.

---

<margin>Conjunctio <note>original: "Conjunctionis," meaning The Conjunction or Union.</note> denotes a person by reason of:</margin>
**Of the soul or character** { Loving reading, eloquent, of good will, acquiring many friends, generous (or rather, consuming more than he earns), lying, pleasure-seeking, ingenious, and a despiser of laws.

**Of the body** { Beautiful or handsome, having a thin and lean body, of medium stature, a beautiful and long face, beautiful eyes, a beautiful but small beard, a thin nose, and thin shins. It also denotes things of various colors, such as cloth and the like.

It is noteworthy that aperture C can also be placed at a distance of one-quarter of a foot from the small pin A; specifically when the distance to be measured is too long for the slider in the lower aperture to encompass. The reasoning for this is derived from the final proposition of this first book. For the higher the slider is raised in its measurement—provided it remains parallel to the base—the more the base will be extended. Consequently, the further the base extends, the higher the slider must be raised. <note>The author is describing the principle of similar triangles: as the "base" (the distance on the ground) increases, the "cursor" (the sliding cross-piece) must be moved further up the staff to maintain the correct sighting angle.</note>

**A.** is the pin joining the <term>Hypotenuse</term><note>original: "Hypothenusam". In early modern surveying, this refers to the diagonal sighting arm that forms the long side of a right triangle against the vertical staff.</note> rule at its junction with the staff, in the center of which is attached a thread with its lead weight. <note>A plumb line used to ensure the instrument is perfectly vertical or to measure angles of elevation.</note>

### CHAPTER II.
#### Concerning the description of the Hypotenuse Ruler.

**T**he Hypotenuse Ruler <term>Hypotenuse Ruler: The diagonal arm of the instrument, named after the longest side of a right-angled triangle</term> shall have a width of half an inch, a thickness of a quarter of an inch, and a length of one and a half feet <note>original Latin: "sesquipedalem"</note>. Its joint is to be fixed into the slot of the staff, fitted with a small wooden peg as previously described. At each end, along the straight line extending from the peg, two sighting vanes <term>sighting vanes: also called pinnules, these are small upright plates with holes used to align the instrument with a target</term> (each having a hole through which the lines of sight must pass toward the object) are to be accurately glued in place.

A & B. The length of the Hypotenuse Ruler.
A. The joint to be placed into the slot of the perpendicular staff, and held there by a small peg through hole o.
C. & C. are the two perforated sighting vanes through which the lines of sight pass.

---

### CHAPTER III.
#### Concerning the drawing of the Sliding Ruler.

**L**et this Ruler <term>Sliding Ruler: A graduated scale that moves along the main staff to measure distances or angles</term> be one and a half feet in length and exactly square in cross-section. Its thickness should be about half an inch, and let the outer end be sharp, where a certain raised copper point must meet the sighting vanes at right angles. This slider should then be divided into exactly equal parts, counting from that copper point toward the other end. Experience or practice will determine the distance between these divided parts; however, it should be done so that the first distance corresponds to a specific number of whole feet or cubits <note>original Latin: "ulnarum," a traditional unit of length often based on the forearm</note>. The remaining divisions will be proportional to the first, following the eighth proposition of this first book.

### CHAPTER IV.
### *Regarding the foot or guardian of the orthogonal staff.*

**W**e call this part of our Staff the "guardian," because it firmly keeps the staff standing perpendicularly, lest it create an acute or obtuse angle through the instability of its position—that is, so it does not tilt too far to the right or left, which would destroy the alignment of the right angles.

Therefore, let this foot or guardian be one foot in width, square in shape with equal sides. Its center must be pierced with a hole suitable for receiving and firmly holding the foot or lower end of the <term>orthogonally <note>meaning "at a right angle" (90 degrees) to the ground</note></term> raised staff, in this manner:

## CHAPTER V.

### *How this instrument should be handled, and what must be added to it when it is tilted to the side?*

**A**t both ends of the <term>staff</term> <note>original: baculus; the main longitudinal rod of the instrument</note>, and likewise at both ends of the sliding <term>rule</term> <note>original: regula; the cross-piece</note>, two perforated <term>sighting vanes</term> <note>original: pinnulae; small plates with sighting holes used to align the instrument with a target</note> are to be attached. So that this may be done better and more readily, holes suitable for the aforementioned purpose should be left at both ends of these parts, so that the perforated openings correspond to one another in a straight line.

Let *a* and *b* be the <term>sighting vanes</term> of our <term>staff</term>. Similarly, let *c* and *d* be the <term>sighting vanes</term> of the <term>slider</term> <note>original: cursor</note>.
It must be observed here that the <term>sighting vanes</term> of the <term>staff</term> can always be kept fixed in the <term>staff</term> without hindering the primary measurement—that is, when the <term>staff</term> is held upright at right angles. Likewise, <term>sighting vane</term> *c* should always remain fixed in its place. However, <term>sighting vane</term> *b* can be removed or attached at the craftsman’s pleasure, so that the <term>slider</term> can be more easily extended or contracted; and furthermore, so that the view of the metal points through the vanes of the <term>hypotenuse</term> <note>original: Hypothenusa; refers here to a specific diagonal rule or the line of sight representing the longest side of a right triangle</note> rule is not obstructed.

### C A P. VI.

#### *On the construction of a staff similar to the Jacob's Staff.*

**L**et there be a straight staff having the shape of a long rectangular prism <note>original Latin: "parallelogrammi longi"; here describing a three-dimensional rod with a rectangular cross-section</note>; the length of which shall be three feet, the width one inch, and the thickness indeed half of an inch. Moreover, let each foot be divided into two equal parts, so that the entire length of the staff consists of 6 half-feet.

The slider <term>Cursor<gloss>a sliding cross-piece used to measure angles by moving it along the main rod</gloss></term>, which must run upon the aforementioned staff from one half-foot mark to another, shall be a rule made of solid wood, having a length of one foot, a width of one inch, and a thickness of a fourth part of an inch. Let this rule be divided into four equal parts, the two outer parts of which are to be distinguished from the two inner parts by a certain decorative craftsmanship. Around its center, let a square hole be made, suited to receive the body of the staff itself tightly. This hole must also be reinforced on one side with a thicker piece of neatly polished wood, so that the staff may be held more firmly at right angles with the slider. In this manner, therefore, they are represented in the illustration.

### Concerning the description of our parallelogram instrument.

**T**his instrument does not differ much from the preceding one, except that its parallel line, which in the previous instrument acted as a mobile slider, is found in this one to be stationary. This line, however, is divided into just as many equal parts as that mobile one was, and performs clearly the same function. Let its length be 6 feet and its width two feet. Therefore, let its opposite sides be equal. Let the parallel line be distant from the small peg of the <term>Hypotenuse</term><note>The longest side of a right-angled triangle; here, it refers to the movable diagonal rule used to calculate distances or angles.</note> by a quarter of one foot; this area must also be divided into equal parts following the straight movement of the Hypotenuse-rule. Let its guard <note>The frame or support structure.</note> be one foot in width and two in length. Let there be spots at the ends of the parallel line suitable for receiving two <term>sights</term><note>original: *pinnulae*; small metal plates with slits or holes used to align the instrument with a distant object.</note>, just as two are also found permanently fixed at each end of the parallelogram itself, directly opposite one another. Let the Hypotenuse also be made of wood or copper, one finger wide, as thick as a knife-blade, and two and a half feet long. It should also have its own thread with a lead weight <note>A plumb line used to ensure the instrument is level or to mark a vertical axis.</note> attached to it, as is described below.

*A. B. are the <term>sights</term> attached to the side of the parallelogram and permanently fixed.*

*C. D. is the <term>numbering line</term> or <term>numerator</term>, which is assigned to this instrument in place of the sliding rule.*

*In K. is depicted one of the holes into which a certain sight can be fixed at the craftsman's pleasure. The numerator also has another hole for a second sight, which, because it lies hidden beneath the Hypotenuse-rule, is not visible to the eyes in this position.*

### C H A P. VII.

### *On the description of the Quadrant.*

**O**ne should take some metallic body, such as tin or copper, or for lack of those, some hard wood: let this body be flat without any concavity or convexity, and upon its surface draw a circle, the diameter of which shall be as you please, either larger or smaller. Let it be divided into four equal parts; of which one (whichever you prefer) is to be chosen, which is to be divided into two equal parts by a line passing from the center to the circumference. Near the margin or circumference let two parallel lines of unequal width be made; the width in the first of these is to be divided into 18 equal parts, and each of those is again to be subdivided into 5 <note>18 multiplied by 5 equals 90, representing the 90 degrees of a right angle.</note>. Then, a portion of the side of the quadrant must be taken, beginning from the center; let that portion (the size of which shall be as you please, though the larger it is, the better) be the side of an equilateral square. According to the dimension of this side, through that proposition of <term>Euclid|The ancient Greek 'father of geometry' whose 'Elements' was the standard textbook for over 2,000 years</term> regarding equilateral squares, you shall construct a square by dividing its two interior sides into 12 equal parts. Of these sides thus divided, the one to the right is called the <term>straight shadow|original: umbra recta; a scale used in surveying to measure heights when the observer is close to the object</term>, while the other toward the left is called the <term>turned shadow|original: umbra versa; a scale used when the distance to the object is greater than its height</term>. This being done, let the other three quarters of the circle be cut away, carefully preserving this prepared quarter. Finally, on one of the outer sides, let two perforated <term>sights|original: pinnulæ; small plates with holes used to align the instrument with a target</term> be attached, through which you may observe an object, yet in such a way that the hole of one sight corresponds in a straight line of the side itself with the hole of the other. Lastly, a certain silk thread is to be fixed in the center of the quadrant, at the end of which a buckle or a small lead weight is attached. All these things are expressed more clearly in the demonstration 
->following.<-

**A. B. d.** is the fourth part of a circle <note>A quadrant, representing a 90-degree arc.</note>. **B. d. x. y.** The two spaces between the parallel lines **B. d.** and **e. f.** are divided into 90 parts <note>These represent the degrees used to measure angles of elevation.</note>.
**G. H. K.** are the two inner sides of the square **A. G. K. H.**, of which one is the **straight shadow** <note>original: "umbra recta"; a scale used for calculating heights when the object is higher than the observer's 45-degree line of sight.</note>, and the other is the **turned shadow** <note>original: "umbra versa"; also called the "back shadow," used when the object is lower than the 45-degree line.</note>.

# BOOK THREE.

## On Geometric Practice.

### DEFINITIONS.

**Altimetry is** <note>Latin: Altimetria</note>, that through which we measure the height of bodies according to their length.
**Planimetry** <note>Latin: Planimetria</note> is that through which flat surfaces and their areas are described.
**Polymetry** <note>Latin: Polymetria</note> is that through which the depth <note>in this context, the volume or three-dimensional thickness</note> of bodies is exactly investigated.

---

## CHAPTER I.

->*On finding the height of a body with our staff from a single station.*<-

**L**et his orthogonal staff <note>Latin: baculus; a surveying rod or cross-staff used for measuring angles</note> be laid out upon the stool <note>Latin: scamnum; the supporting bench or tripod shown in the diagram</note> so that the <term>Hypotenuse</term> <note>The longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle; used here as the line of sight.</note> projects above: Then, by the rule of Geometric Arithmetic, when two numbers are known, the third may be found by the rule of three <note>A mathematical method of finding a fourth value from three known ones based on proportions (a:b = c:d).</note>, as is taught below.

Treatise II, Part III, Book III.

### *How to determine this using a single position with the two aforementioned instruments.*

Just as the base of the triangle formed on the staff or <term>parallelogram</term> <note>a geometric frame or instrument</note> by the <term>hypotenuse</term> <note>the diagonal rule or sight-line</note> relates to the perpendicular line of that same triangle produced by the sliding rule; so the distance between the eye (or the joint of the hypotenuse) and the base of the tall object will relate to the height of that object. But the base of the smaller triangle is compared to its perpendicular in a <term>sesquitertian</term> ratio <note>original: *sesquitertia*—a mathematical ratio of 4:3, where one value is 1 and 1/3 times the other</note>. Therefore, the distance from the instrument to the base of the tower is in that same ratio to its height. This operation is clearly demonstrated by the eighth and ninth propositions of this book.

### *Another way to do this using a similar Jacob’s Staff.*

Place the <term>cursor</term> <note>original: *cursor*—the sliding cross-piece on a surveyor's staff</note> on one of those six divisions of the staff. Then, with your eye positioned at the end of the staff, look through both ends of the cursor toward the base and the lowest part of the wall or object to be measured. Once these are sighted, you must carefully note how many parts distance the cursor is from the eye. Then, the distance between your feet and the base of the height should be divided into that many parts. For example, the height of the tower will be a fourth part of the distance if there are four parts between the eye and the cursor. If only three parts lie between them, the height will be a third part of the distance; if two, then half; and so on for the rest.

->*An example follows.*<-

->How the same result is achieved by the <term>right shadow<note>original: "umbra recta"; refers to the vertical scale on a quadrant used when the angle of elevation is greater than 45 degrees.</note> or inverse shadow<note>original: "umbra versa"; the horizontal scale on a quadrant used when the angle of elevation is less than 45 degrees.</note> of the quadrant.<-

The distance must be multiplied—for example, 5 feet by 12—making 60. This must then be divided by the intercepted points <note>The points or marks read on the quadrant's scale.</note>, let us say 6, and you will have the height of the object.

Multiply the distance between yourself and the base of the tower: For example, let the distance from you to the tower be 40. This must be multiplied by the number intercepted on the inverse shadow, namely 6, which makes 240 feet. Divide this number by 12, and the quotient will be 20, which is the height of the object; to this, add the measure of your own height, namely 5 feet. I say, therefore, that the height of the object will be 25 feet.

## CHAPTER II.

->On determining length from a single position.<-

<margin>see Number 1.</margin>
By using our staff <note>Likely referring to a Jacob’s Staff or cross-staff, a common surveying tool of the period.</note>, the lengths of surfaces are determined from a single position, both by comparing the base—that is, the <term>cursor<note>The sliding cross-piece on a surveyor's staff used to align sight lines.</note></term>—to the perpendicular line, and by that "rule of three" <note>The mathematical rule of proportion.</note> according to the proposition of Arithmetical Geometry, *see Number 1.*

For as line *c. d.* relates to *c. a.*, so the total length *b. e.* relates to the length of the staff *a. b.* Therefore, as many times as *a. c.* is contained within *c. d.*, just as many times the staff *a. b.* is contained within *b. e.* Or like this: if one part of the cursor yields 11 feet, how many will 7 parts yield? The answer is 77. This chapter is demonstrated by the 7th and 8th propositions of this first book.

<margin>see Number 2.</margin>
The length of an object is also captured in the same way with our <term>parallelogram<note>A drawing or surveying instrument (like a pantograph) used for scaling and proportions.</note></term>. *See Number 2.*

### *Another method with a similar Jacob's staff.* <note>original: "baculo Jacobi"</note>

**D**istances <note>literally "lengths"</note> cannot be investigated with this staff unless by calculating the heights or widths found at their far ends. Thus, if we wish to determine a distance on the ground, it is necessary that we first measure the width or height of an object situated at the end of that distance. Once you have marked the distance between those two observation <term>stations</term> <note>specific points where the surveyor stands to take a reading</note> (as will be described below in the section on finding widths): For example, if the <term>cursor</term> <note>original: "Cursor sive transversor"; the sliding horizontal cross-piece of the Jacob's staff</note> was set at the fourth division during the first station, and if at the second station we move closer to the height situated at the end of the distance, the difference between the first and second stations will be the height of the object, as will be taught below. We will find, therefore, the <term>cursor</term> at the second station at the fifth division from the eye.

We conclude, then, that just as the length of the <term>cursor</term> is contained five times within the space of the staff between the cross-piece and the eye; so the space between my two operations or <term>stations</term> is contained five times within the total distance to be measured.

It must be noted here, however, that where height or width is measured with this staff using the ends of the smaller cross-piece (the length of which is <term>half a foot</term>), we are accustomed to measuring it in this way; for if the lines of sight <note>original: "radii"</note> pass through the ends of the larger cross-piece (the length of which is a full foot), then the space between the two stations must be doubled. For double that interval will correspond to the height of the object, and consequently, the total distance to the object will include ten times the interval between the two stations.

## Two sliders on one body. See Number 1.

## Demonstration of length measured with the aforementioned staff. See Number 2.

->*Achieving the same result with a quadrant.*<-

One should look through the sights <note>original: "pinnulas"</note> of the quadrant toward the end of the distance to be measured. Once this point is sighted, if the plumb line <note>original: "filum"</note> falls upon the straight scale <note>term: scala recta; the vertical part of the "shadow square" on the instrument</note>, the proportion of the eye's height to the distance being measured will be the same as the proportion of 12 to the number where the line falls. For example, if the line falls on 6 of the straight shadow <note>term: umbra recta</note>, the distance will be only half the height of the eye. However, if it falls upon the shadow or "turned scale" <note>term: scala versa; the horizontal part of the shadow square</note>, the opposite occurs; if the line falls on six on that scale, the distance will be twice the height of the eye, and the same logic applies to the other numbers. See Number 3.

## CHAPTER III.

->On the measurement of lengths from two stations with our staff.<-

**THE** staff should be tilted to the side so that the far end of the distance <note>original Latin: *longitudinis extremitas*</note> can be seen through the attached sights <term>pinnulae: small metal plates with slits or holes used for aligning the instrument with a target</term>; once this is done, and while the staff remains immobile, some mark chosen by the Artist <note>the surveyor or practitioner</note> should be observed through the sights of the staff itself. Next, the staff must be moved to that marked spot, while also marking the location of the previous station. After this, one should look back through the sights of the staff to see the mark of the first station. Having seen it, and while the staff still lies fixed, let the end of the length to be measured be viewed through the sights of the hypotenuse <term>Hypothenusa: the diagonal side of the sighting triangle formed by the instrument</term>. Once that is in view, form a triangle on the hypotenuse with the cursor <term>cursor: a sliding component on the staff used to mark a specific point on a scale</term>. Therefore, the base of that triangle on the instrument will relate to the side created by the cursor in the same way that the distance between the two stations relates to the length being measured, as will be seen in the following example.

Therefore, just as the base **a. b.** relates to the side **c.**, so the interval between the two stations—namely the base **b. d.**—relates to the side **d. e.** Now, the base **a. b.** is contained within the side **b. c.** <note>The text likely refers to the ratio of the instrument's components</note> two and a half times; therefore, the space between the two stations is contained that many times in the resulting length, according to the eighth proposition of this first book. Consequently, if the distance between **b.** and **d.** is 50 feet, the space of the length to be measured will be 125 feet <note>50 x 2.5 = 125</note>.

Therefore, just as triangle *a. b. c.* is related, so is triangle *b. e. d.*, because through the fifth and eighth proportions <note>original: "quintam & octavam proportiones"; likely referencing geometric rules from Euclid's *Elements* or a similar textbook.</note> the square *a. b. c. g.* is proportional to the square *a. d. e. f.* Since, however, the triangle within each square is half of that square according to the "square proposition" of Book 1, it follows that the triangle of the smaller square is proportional to the triangle of the larger square. For this reason, side *a. c.* is proportional to side *d. e.*, and side *b. g.* to side *b. d.* We conclude, therefore, that the base of triangle *a. b. c.*—namely *a. c.*—relates to its side *b. g.* in the same way that the width *e. d.* relates to the length <note>In this context, "longitudo" refers to the distance between the observer and the object.</note> *b. d.* Once the length from the acute angle of the instrument to the closer extremity is known (by the method in Chapter 2), the desired width will be very easily determined.

Similarly, the height of an object is gathered with an instrument of this kind: for, just as the side *e. d.* of the larger triangle relates to its side *b. d.*, so too does side *a. c.* of the instrument’s triangle relate to its side *a. b.*

## CHAPTER V.

### *Concerning finding any width from two stations using a device similar to a Jacob’s Staff.*

<term>Jacob's Staff: Also known as a cross-staff, this was a popular 16th and 17th-century tool for measuring angles between objects, used for both navigation and land surveying.</term>

Next, move the slider from that section of the staff, either to the next section closer to the eye or to the next section further away from it. ### *Another way to find the depth of a well using a quadrant.*

The edge of the water is sighted through the sights <term>pinnulas: small metal plates with slits or holes used to align the instrument with a target</term>, and if the plumb line <note>original: "filum"; the weighted thread that hangs from the center of the quadrant to indicate the angle</note> falls upon point 12, then the width or diameter of the well (if it is round) or the side (if it is square) will be equal to the depth. But when it falls upon the direct scale <term>scala recta: the vertical portion of the "shadow square" on a quadrant, used for calculating heights and depths through ratios</term>, the depth will exceed the width in proportion to how much smaller the number intercepted by the line is than 12. On the contrary, if the line falls upon some number of the inverse shadow <term>umbra versa: the horizontal portion of the shadow square, used when the measured angle is greater than 45 degrees</term>, then the further that number is from 12, the smaller the depth is compared to the width.

->DEFINITIONS.<-

**O**ptical science is that part of Natural Philosophy which demonstrates the principles of seeing.

*Sight* is the sensory power, located in the optic nerve, for perceiving the form of that which enters the crystalline humor from the likenesses <note>original: *similitudinibus*</note> of colored bodies; these "idols" <note>The term *idola* refers to the visual images or forms transmitted from an object to the eye, a concept common in pre-modern physics</note> travel through transparent <note>original: *diaphana*</note> and radiant bodies to the surface of the eyes.

*Simple vision* is that by which a single object is seen in its true and simple likeness—that is, through straight rays in the same medium, namely air.

*Composite vision* is that which perceives a visible thing through a double and reflected image—that is, where the ray falling obliquely is either reflected or broken <note>refracted</note> upon meeting a medium of a different transparency.

A *direct, straight, or perpendicular ray* is one whose impact upon a surface leaves right and equal angles on both sides.

A *visual ray* is nothing other than the "form" <note>original: *species*</note> of the visible object extended in a straight line.

An *oblique ray* is defined as the opposite of a straight and perpendicular one.

*Reflected ray* is the name for one which, upon meeting an opaque surface, is thrown back toward its origin along the same or a different line, much like a ball bouncing off a wall; however, it is not the exact same ray that is reflected, but a new one generated from the primary luminous object.

A *refracted ray* is the name given to one which, upon encountering a medium of a different transparency <note>original: *perspicuitatis*</note>, is not extended in a straight line.

*Light* <note>original: *Lux*</note> is a visible quality in a luminous body, moving according to the motion of that in which it exists, and not depending on anything external; or, it is the action of a luminous body insofar as it shines; or, it is the first of all visible things, which by itself brings the images of other visible things to the sight.

*Radiance* <note>original: *Lumen*</note> is the action of a transparent medium insofar as it is clear, yet bounded by something opaque; or, it is a quality generated by Light [source light]; or, it is the image of light, and its first and primary derivation.

<vocab>Optics, Sight, Ray, Source Light (Lux), Radiance (Lumen), Refracted, Reflected, Eye, Transparent, Clarity</vocab>

<keywords>optics, vision, lux vs lumen, reflection, refraction, visual pyramid, anatomy of the eye, natural philosophy</keywords>
