# ON DEFINITIONS.

Shadow is the interception of light by an opaque body <note>original: "corpus opacum"</note>.
Darkness is the privation of light, which is recognized by the absence or deprivation of those things that occur to the sense of sight.
Color is the boundary of a transparent body within a bounded body; *or* it is a quality at the boundary of a bounded or opaque body which touches a transparent medium <note>In Aristotelian physics, color was often defined by how light interacted with the "limit" or surface of a solid object when meeting a clear medium like air.</note>.
The *radiant pyramid* <note>original: "Pyramis radiosa"; this refers to the cone of light or "visual cone" that artists and scientists used to map how light enters the eye.</note> is a physical surface under which an object is seen, the base of which is on the object being viewed and the peak [cone] of which is within the eye of the observer.
The *axis of the radiant pyramid* is a radiant line which passes through all the centers of the eye's membranes <note>original: "tunicarum"</note> and fluids <note>original: "humorum"; referring to the aqueous, vitreous, and crystalline humors of the eye.</note>; we have previously called this axis the visual ray.
The *cone of the radiant pyramid* is the center of sight.
The *base of the pyramid* is the surface of the colored or seen object.

### *On the Constituent Parts of the Eye.*

Regarding the three humors <note>The fluids that fill the chambers of the eye</note>, in which first, three things are to be noted regarding the first humor, namely its:
- **Names.** It is called:
    - **Aqueous** <note>original: "Aqueus"</note> from its similarity to water.
    - **Albugineous**, because it is similar in both substance and color to the white of an egg <note>original: "albugini," the Latin word for egg white</note>.
- **Uses,** for:
    - It moistens the **crystalline lens** <note>the lens of the eye</note>, lest it be corrupted or dried out by the dryness of the tissue surrounding it.
    - It irrigates the entire eye.
    - It defends and protects the crystalline lens from external accidents.
    - Also, placed here between the <term>aranea</term> <note>literally "the spider-web," a historical term for the delicate membrane or capsule surrounding the lens</note>, it guards the crystalline lens from the hardness of the <term>cornea</term> <note>the transparent front layer of the eye</note>.

->On the three humors of the eye.<-

The **glacial or crystalline humor** <note>original: *humor glacialis sive cristallinus*; this refers to the lens of the eye.</note> is white in color, transparent, and shining; its substance is moderately hard, yet it is the most delicate of all. Its shape is not exactly spherical, but tends toward a lenticular <note>lens-shaped or like a lentil</note> form. Presented by itself and freed from all the parts surrounding it, it is described in this way: See Number 1.

The **aqueous or albugineous humor** is similar to the white of an egg <note>original: *albumini ovi*</note> in both color and substance, except that it is somewhat thinner. It is described below, both by itself and with the crystalline humor enclosed in its middle; see Number 2.

The **vitreous humor** is contained within a texture of veins, from whose blood it takes a reddish tint. It "digests" this blood and sends the processed result to the crystalline-like body for nourishment. <note>The author is describing an early theory of how the eye's internal fluids were replenished by blood.</note> These two humors are separated by a certain thin membrane, called the "spider-web" <note>original: *tela aranea*</note> because of its resemblance. In its center, it holds the middle part of the crystalline body, just as the aqueous humor takes the other half. It is described in the following way, viewed both directly and from the side; see Number 3.

### Concerning the Tunics <note>The membranes or layers of the eye</note>

The *adnate tunic* <note>The conjunctiva; the outermost layer connecting the eye to the socket; original: *Tunica adnata*</note> is strong and fatty, so that the humors cannot freeze or leak out in any way. Its posterior part is called the *Sclerotica* <note>The sclera, the tough white outer layer of the eyeball</note>. Although this tunic is white, it is not transparent; therefore, it has an opening <note>original: *foramen*; referring here to the space for the cornea and the pupil</note> in the front part, so as not to block the entry of images <note>original: *specierum*; in early optics, "species" were the visual forms or "likenesses" of objects that traveled to the eye</note>. It likewise has an opening in the back part, so that the images may reach the optic nerve.

### TREATISE II. PART IV. BOOK I.

The <term>cornea</term> <note>the transparent front part of the eye; the name comes from the Latin word for "horn-like"</note> is clear, bright, hard, and solid, composed of many small fragments; it also consists of four delicate membranes and is transparent, so that images may pass through it. Some call the posterior part of this layer the *Cerusina* <note>original: "Cerusinam," a term used by early anatomists to describe the inner layers of the cornea</note>, while others simply call it the "hard part." The <term>uvea</term> <note>the vascular middle layer of the eye, including the iris; the name refers to its resemblance to the skin of a grape</note> is smooth on the outside and velvety on the inside. This likewise has an opening in the front part, so that images may pass through. They call the outer portion of this membrane the <term>secundina</term> <note>original: "Secundinam," a term traditionally used for the choroid membrane due to its resemblance to the placenta or "afterbirth"</note>. It is depicted with the crystalline lens in this way, see *Number 1.*

The <term>spider-web membrane</term> <note>original: "Tunica aranea," now known as the lens capsule</note> is said to be the specific membrane of the <term>crystalline humor</term> <note>the lens of the eye</note>, for it surrounds and encloses that entire fluid.

# BOOK TWO

## Concerning direct rays.

### Proposition I.

*The direction of rays remains straight only within a medium of a single nature and density; see Illustration No. 1.*
*The reason is that a change in the medium causes the refraction of rays, as will be demonstrated in the third book.* <note>Refraction refers to the bending of light as it passes from one substance to another, such as from air into water.</note>

### Proposition II.

*The <term>species</term><note>In historical optics, "species" refers to the formal image or likeness of an object that travels from the object to the observer's eye.</note> of visible things are received through both eyes, and yet a single object does not appear to be two; see Illustration No. 2.*

...received by the eye, they appear not as two but only as one; because the <term>visual image</term><note>original: "species". In medieval and early modern optics, this refers to the form or likeness of an object traveling through the air to the eye.</note> passing through nerve *c* and likewise the other through nerve *b* meet together at center *a*, namely in the <term>common sense</term><note>original: "sensu communi". This was thought to be a faculty in the brain where the data from all five senses were integrated into a single perception.</note>, where they are united according to the form of that which is presented.

### Proposition III.

*Where the two axes of both sights <note>meaning the eyes or lines of vision</note> are joined on some surface of the seen object, there the surface of the seen object will be the common base for both <term>radiant pyramids</term><note>original: "pyramidibus radiosis". The cone-shaped volume of light rays extending from the object to the eye.</note> formed between the two centers of both sights; and that seen object and the two axes, which are between it and the two sights, are perpendicular to the surface of the two sights.*

Here, the two axes of both eyes, namely *c.b.* and *a.b.*, are joined on the surface of the seen object *d.e.* at point *B*. Therefore, the surface *c.d.* is the common base for both radiant pyramids, namely *a.e.d.* and *c.e.d.*, which are formed between the two cones or vice versa, namely *c.a.* Therefore, the two axes *a.b.* and *c.b.*, which are between the thing seen and the two eyes, are perpendicular to the surface of the two eyes. From the definition of the center of sight, it is known that it is the center of the pyramid.

### Proposition IV.

*The closer a colored or visible thing is, the larger the object appears.*

-># ON DIRECT RAYS.<-

This proposition is proven by the preceding demonstration; because the shorter the <term>pyramid<note>In early optics, the "visual pyramid" refers to the cone-shaped volume of light rays extending from the eye to the object being seen.</note></term> is, the stronger it becomes, as it possesses a wider and more <term>obtuse<note>An angle greater than 90 degrees. A wider angle here implies the object is closer and thus perceived more clearly or "strongly."</note></term> angle at its apex. For this same reason, stars appear very small to us because of the narrowness of the angle of the cone.

### Proposition V.

*Between any <term>object seen<note>original: "visum"</note></term> and the <term>center of vision<note>The point within the eye where the rays are thought to converge.</note></term>, there exists an <term>imaginary pyramid<note>A geometric construct used by scholars to map how light travels to the eye.</note></term>, whose apex is the center of vision and whose base is the surface of the object being seen.*

### Proposition VI.

*The <term>perception<note>original: "comprehensio"</note></term> of a visible object occurs by means of a <term>radiant pyramid<note>A pyramid formed by rays of light.</note></term>; however, the <term>certainty<note>original: "certificatio" — the process of gaining a clear, detailed, and accurate image.</note></term> of that perception is achieved when its axis is moved across the visible object.*

### TREATISE II. PART IV. BOOK II.

On the front part of a fixed table, positioned between your eye and the city or house to be depicted <note>original: *describendam*, meaning to draw or map out</note>, let a frame filled with small squares <term>grid: a lattice or "veil" used as a drawing aid to divide a view into manageable sections</term> be erected perpendicularly. Once this is done, you should lay out your paper—which is also filled with small squares—upon the same table. Finally, you must proceed in this manner:

The entire site of the city will be viewed from the small ball of the sighting post <note>original: *styli globulo*, referring to the aperture or tip of the sighting device</note>. Then, when you wish to draw any small portion of the city or house, you shall sketch it using the distinct square as a guide. For just as that part of the city is found within a specific square of the frame, so too must it be depicted in the square of the same number on the paper. Next, the neighboring square of the frame must be observed, and whatever you see within it must also be transferred into the square of the same number on the paper. And in this way, you shall proceed with all the remaining squares.

# BOOK THREE.

->Concerning refracted rays.<-

<margin>There are two causes of refraction</margin>
One on the part of the ray, namely its weakening arising from its slant; for as much as the slant <note>original: *declinatio*; refers to the angle at which light hits a surface</note> of the ray is greater, so much also its weakening is greater, just as the warming effects of solar rays are either strengthened or weakened by their directness or slant. It follows, therefore, that the more the slant of the ray occurs, the more its refraction <note>The bending of light as it passes from one medium to another</note> also occurs.

The other is on the part of the medium, namely the difference in transparency <note>original: *diaphanitatis*; the quality of a substance that allows light to pass through</note>; for as much as the medium is denser, so much more it resists. Therefore, the passage of light is not proportional in a denser medium as it is in a thinner one, unless a greater refraction occurs. For the denser the second media are, the more it is necessary for objects to appear larger or smaller.

## Proposition I.

The refraction of a ray occurs only at the very surface of the second medium. The demonstration of this matter will be clear below; but the reason for it is that light, by its nature, moves in a straight line in every transparent medium <term>diaphano</term>; but in the place where two transparent bodies are touching, a deviation from that straightness usually occurs, as is sufficiently described in the causes of the refraction of rays.

## Proposition II.

*A colored object will appear outside its own place through refracted rays.*

<header>TREATISE II. PART IV. BOOK III.</header>

The reason for the aforementioned proposition is that the location of images is at the intersection of the perpendicular lines drawn from the thing seen, according to Proposition 4, Book 5 of *Common Perspective* <note>original: *perspectiva communi*; this refers to the widely used medieval textbook on optics by John Pecham</note>. For, on account of the perception of the ray through which a thing is represented to the eye, the object is thought to be at the end of that same ray when extended in a continuous line. For example: Let *a.* be the eye in the air; *B.* a colored object within the water; and let *b. c.* be the ray through which the form of the colored object travels toward the eye. This ray would proceed toward *g.* if the medium had been of the same nature; but on account of the difference in the medium, it is now <term>refracted: the bending of light as it passes from one substance, like water, into another, like air</term> away from the perpendicular line *f. e.* and falls into *a.* Therefore, let the visual ray be drawn in a continuous and straight line until it touches the perpendicular line that can be raised from the colored object *b. d.* at point *h.* For *h.* will be the place where the colored object appears, even though in reality it is at *B.*

### *A problem confirming the preceding proposition.*

In the primary city of the Ligurians, *Genoa*, I met a certain Empiric <term>Empiric: in the 17th century, this referred to a person who relied on practical experiments and observation, often a self-taught practitioner or even a traveling "showman" of science</term> who, boasting that he was rich in many secret experiments of the world, demonstrated this one thing to me and my companion after we had finished dinner. In the middle of the bottom of a certain earthen vessel, he placed a gold coin; the vessel was of moderate height and placed on the ground. This being done, he ordered me to step back, while keeping my eyes fixed on that coin, until the coin was completely hidden from my sight by the sides of the vessel, so that it no longer appeared. However, while I remained fixed and immobile in that spot, the Empiric filled that vessel with clear water; and that coin—whose direct rays could not reach my eyes because of the obstruction of the opaque vessel—was now clearly revealed because of the refraction of the rays. Indeed, we were all amazed. I, however, since I was somewhat experienced in Philosophy <note>In this context, "Philosophy" refers to "Natural Philosophy," what we would call science today</note>, sought out the cause of the matter and found the explanation in *Propositions 15 and 16 of Book 1 of Common Perspective, and Propositions 4, 5, and 7 of Book 3 of the same work*, the essence and marrow of which I have distilled into our preceding proposition.

# BOOK FOUR.

## Concerning Reflected Rays.

### DEFINITIONS.

**PRIMARY LIGHT** is that which originally passes from a luminous body, such as the light in the Sun.
**Secondary light** is that which, upon the arrival of primary light, departs from a colored object; for luminous rays are inherent within color. <note>The author suggests that objects don't just reflect light, but that "color" itself contains a latent luminous quality activated by the sun.</note>

**Regular surfaces** are those that have a uniform arrangement in all their parts, such as flat surfaces, convex surfaces, and the like. Smooth bodies, because of this regular surface, reflect rays uniformly.

**Irregular surfaces** are those found on rough bodies; light falling upon these is scattered and pulled apart because of the roughness.

### Proposition I.

*Primary and secondary light—whether pure or mixed with colors—are reverberated and reflected from the surfaces of dense bodies. See Number 1.*

For a ray of light and color is naturally suited to travel through a transparent medium <term>diaphanum<note>From the Greek 'diaphanes,' meaning transparent; used here to describe any medium like air or glass that light can travel through.</note></term>. However, when it encounters a dense body, such as a mirror made of iron or one coated in lead, because the power of the radiating source and the influence of the radiant flow are not yet finished, yet cannot pass directly through, the ray returns by reflection toward the place from which it came. This is just like a ball: when it is thrown against a wall where it cannot pass through in a straight line, it returns by way of reflection so long as the force of the thrower <term>virtus impellentis<note>Literally the 'force of the impeller,' referring to the momentum or energy behind the moving object.</note></term> persists.

### Proposition II.

*Only those reflections made from regular surfaces are perceived by the sense of sight; the reason is seen in the definitions of regular and irregular surfaces. See Number 2.*

<summary>This page introduces the fourth book on optics, focusing on the nature of reflection and defining the differences between primary and secondary light, as well as how regular and irregular surfaces affect the path of light rays.</summary>
<keywords>optics, catoptrics, primary light, secondary light, reflection, regular surfaces, irregular surfaces, transparent media, mirrors</keywords>

### Proposition III.

*Reflected lights and colors are weaker than those radiating directly. The reason is because of **obliquity** <note>The term "obliquity" refers to the slanted or angled path light takes when it hits a surface and bounces, rather than traveling in a straight, uninterrupted line.</note>; for direct motion is the proper motion of light.*

### Proposition IV.

*Lights and colors reflected from a mirror show objects to the eye, of which they are the <term>species</term> <note>In the scientific language of the time, "species" were the invisible "likenesses" or "forms" that objects were thought to constantly emit. These species travel through the air to enter our eyes, allowing us to see the object's shape and color.</note>.*

# ON MIRRORS.

Every mirror used in optics <term>optica: the science of light and vision</term> is either:

*   **Regular**
    *   **Flat (Plane),**
        *   **Simple,** in which an object can be seen where it actually is.
        *   **Composite**
            *   Either one where the edge of one mirror is joined to the edge of another at right angles.
            *   Or one that is fashioned from many non-continuous pieces of glass on the same surface.
    *   **Irregular,** <note>original: "difforme"</note> of which there are five types:
        *   **Concave,** which makes an object appear larger than it really is.
        *   **Convex,** representing an object as smaller than it is.
        *   **Pyramidal,** } which make objects
        *   **Columnar,** } appear elongated.
        *   **Spherical,** which renders things wider than they are.
*   **Composed from regular types**
    *   Flat in one part, and concave in another.
    *   Composed of many concave sections.
    *   Made from flat, concave, and convex parts.

---

# EXPERIMENTS CONCERNING MIRRORS.

### *Experiment 1. Concerning a simple flat mirror in a dual medium.*

Let some flat mirror be taken, made either of iron or some other material, and let it be placed into a small vessel filled with very clear water so that it is submerged. Then, let it be exposed to the shining sun, and a "bright star" will be perceived in it; this is not actually a star, but a secondary image of the sun <note>original: "idolum solis"</note> reflecting from the interface of the different surfaces of the mirror and the water.

<note>The accompanying engraving shows a personified sun casting rays into a water-filled bowl on a decorative table. Inside the bowl, a submerged rectangular mirror reflects a focal point of light upward.</note>

### *Experiment II. Concerning plane mirrors joined at a right angle.*

When two flat mirrors are so placed that one is set upright at a right angle <note>original: "orthogonaliter"; at 90 degrees</note> upon the other, the appearances of things show up in the upper mirror as they truly are, but in the lower one, they are represented backward; this occurs due to the reflection of the upper mirror in the lower mirror.

### *Experiment III. Concerning a concave mirror, in which images will appear outside.*

A common convex mirror should be chosen, and the lead <term>lead backing: early mirrors were coated with lead or a lead-tin amalgam to create a reflective surface</term> should be scraped away with a knife from its concave side. It should be noted, however, that it is very tedious to perfectly scrape away all the lead in this way without the risk of breaking the glass. But if you wish to clean it well and remove its lead cleanly, let the lead be smeared with quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury</note>, which will immediately adhere to the lead and penetrate it very easily, so that we can shortly separate the lead from the glass. 

Therefore, let this glass—cleaned of its lead in the aforementioned way—be placed in a certain box that is not too deep, in such a way that the convex side is toward the bottom of the box. Let there be, however, some black cloth placed between the bottom and the mirror, so that the visual ray <term>visual ray: in historical optics, this was the imaginary line along which sight was thought to travel</term> may be better reflected. Once this is done, if you look carefully into the mirror, you will perceive the image extending outside the box and "idols" <note>original: "idola"; in this context, the term refers to optical phantoms or virtual images that appear to float in space</note> appearing outside in the cylindrical <note>original: "columnali"</note> and pyramidal mirror, as is taught in the study of perspective <note>original: "perspectiva"; at the time, this term referred generally to the science of optics</note>.

->*Experiment IV. Concerning a mirror in which many moving images will appear from a single position.*<-

Take this deep box <term>pixis</term> <note>In this period, a "pixis" usually refers to a cylindrical vessel or apothecary jar used for scientific instruments.</note>, and place at its bottom a common convex mirror. Next, you must choose six or seven other convex mirrors of the same size. Their lead backings <note>original: *plumbeæ substantiæ*; 17th-century mirrors were typically glass coated with a lead or tin amalgam. Scraping this off allowed the glass to become partially transparent or to reflect light differently.</note> should be scraped off in the manner described in the third experiment. Once all these mirrors are well cleaned, they should be arranged at an angle within the box, each in a different position. Arrange them so that one edge touches the first mirror while the opposite edge is a finger's width away from it. The remaining mirrors should also be placed at various angles around the central mirror. On the very top surface of the box, however, you will place one last cleaned mirror—just like the others, but set straight and not at an angle. These must be fitted together so precisely that nothing can be seen except the topmost mirror. 

Then, if you look into the mirror, you will see within it as many images as there are mirrors. If you rotate the device, you will see how one image always remains steady in the center and in one spot, while the other images circle around it as if they were revolving on a tripod <note>original: *tripodem*; here referring to a rotating stand or a mechanical base that allows for circular motion.</note>.

### *Experiment 5. Concerning the burning mirror.*

Take a common convex mirror, and scrape away the lead—as described above—from the concave side. Then take a sheet of tin <note>original: *folium stanni*</note>, fit it to the size of the mirror, and place it upon the convex side of the glass. Afterwards, coat the sheet very thinly with mercury <term>quicksilver; original: *argento vivo*</term>; for if this is not done delicately, once it has been soaked with the mercury, it tends to peel away easily. Then place this mirror into a small box, turning the concave side outward; there will appear within it a most distorted image <note>Latin: *idolum turpissimum*. In early optics, "idolum" referred to the reflected image or "specter" of an object, which appears "foul" or "ugly" here due to the extreme spherical distortion of the mirror.</note> of a very small size. When you wish to burn something with it, hold it against the rays of the Sun and observe where the primary point caused by the Sun's reflection appears. After a short time, you will see the object to be burned catch fire at that spot.

->THE END OF THE SCIENCE OF OPTICS.<-

### PART V.

# BOOK ONE.
## On the Theoretical Part of the Art of Painting.

---

### CHAPTER I.
->What kind of person a painter ought to be.<-

**P**ainters must obtain no small gifts from heaven to be seen as worthy of their art; indeed, without these, one can by no means truly be called a painter. For an artist to be considered skillful and refined in his duty, it is necessary, *firstly*, that he be well-versed in all the arts, and that he be <term>literate</term> <note>original: "literosus"; implying a deep education in the humanities and classics</note> and outstanding in his knowledge of many subjects, myths, and histories. *Secondly*, it is required that he be eager for praise and studious, since ambition in the arts tends to spread perfection through the craftsman; for education can achieve nothing without a desire for acclaim. *Thirdly*, it is required that he be <term>liberal</term> <note>original: "liberalis"; meaning generous of spirit and possessing the character of a free man, rather than a mere laborer</note> and not at all "sordid" or mean-spirited; for greed and filth debase and cloud the power of invention. *Fourthly*, he must be prudent and not at all foolish, so that he understands that there is a certain fixed reason or logic in all things. *Fifthly*, he must be extremely well-versed in antiquities, so that he may correctly depict ancient histories. For example, he should be able to give the reason why *Venus* is depicted as armed among the *Spartans* <note>original: "Lacedæmonios"</note>, black among the *Arcadians*, and <term>bearded</term> <note>original: "barbara"; here referring to the "Bearded Venus" or Aphroditus of Cyprus, who possessed both masculine and feminine traits</note> among the *Cypriots*, distinguished by a masculine scepter and feminine attire. And so it is with infinite other things of this kind, all of whose causes the painter must hold exactly and perfectly. *Sixthly*, it is necessary that he be endowed with an excellent imagination, so that he can imagine in his mind the infinite appearances of one who is laughing, or sick, or dying, or in danger, and the like; he must be able to hold and render those mental concepts of all the things he desires to express. *Seventhly*, it is necessary that he be excellent in the "caution of imitation" <note>the careful, disciplined study of nature and masterworks</note>; and *finally*, it is also required that he has prepared and acquired for himself an exact knowledge and science of <term>lineaments</term> <note>the fundamental outlines or "bones" of a drawing</note>, symmetry, Geometry, Perspective, and other things of this sort.

---

### CHAPTER II.
->On the types of painting.<-

**S**ince *painting* is generally described as the art which—by means of simple lineaments, the illumination of colors in their variety, and by carving or statuary—delineates the likeness of any thing, it will not be useless here to discuss each of these types in a few words. 
Regarding, then, the *first type of painting*, we say that *lineaments* are the straight drawings of fitting lines used to demonstrate the appearance of each thing. The lines that run together to form this appearance are either "outer lines," which they also call "environging" because they embrace the outermost parts, or "intermediate lines," because they expre- <note>The text breaks here; the catchword "expri-" suggests the next page begins with "expriment," meaning "express" or "represent."</note>

<page-num>320</page-num>

-> TREATISE II. PART V. BOOK I. <-

...express [these things], and are accustomed to distinguish the joints of the limbs. Furthermore, the method for representing the surrounding outlines <note>original: "Ambientium"</note> is manifold and almost infinite due to the variety of actions. For example, in the depiction of the human head, whether through a triangle or a square, there are infinite demonstrations, any one of which makes the view different from another. In these line-drawings, all things are explained vividly in two ways: namely, by the modeling of either shadows or light, and especially the heights <note>In this context, "heights" refers to the relief or three-dimensionality of the body.</note> of bodies. In this specific type of painting, *Parrhasius* <note>Parrhasius of Ephesus (5th century BCE), a celebrated Greek painter known for his mastery of contour lines.</note> won the palm among the ancients; for he surpassed all his contemporaries in making white and black line-drawings, and especially in the descriptions of curled hair.

The second species is the **illumination of things, achieved with simple and compound colors**; in this species, *Apollodorus* <note>Apollodorus "Skiagraphos" (the Shadow-painter), an Athenian who pioneered the use of light and shadow in the late 5th century BCE.</note> surely excelled among the ancients; it is reported that he was the first to discover this species of painting, along with the method of applying colors with a brush.

The third species, however, they call **sculpture**, the praises of which *Pomponius Gauricus of Naples* <note>Author of "De Sculptura" (1504), a famous Renaissance treatise on the art of bronze and stone.</note> sang so greatly. Indeed, the use of this art was very well known in all ancient ages, in the histories of both the Greeks and the Barbarians. Moreover, the subject or material from which statues were usually formed was either wood from hard trunks, ivory, clay, wax, gypsum, stones, or metals. Sculptors working in wood were called *carvers* <note>original: "defectores"</note>; those who put their effort into clay were named *molders* <note>original: "fictores"</note>; those who worked in marble were called *marble-workers*, and so on for the others. In this species, they say that *Prometheus* so excelled that, on account of the excellence of his art, he was even said to have brought a vital spark snatched from heaven into the mud.

---

## CHAPTER III.

### *On the arts most necessary to the painter, and first, on Symmetry.*

**S**ince Symmetry <note>In the classical sense, "Symmetry" refers to the proportional relationship between parts of a whole.</note> contributes a great deal to painters, we shall now discuss it briefly. In considering human **Symmetry**, one must examine the **matter** and its proportional image or form, just as in any other natural thing. By **matter**, I mean the body itself divided into three dimensions: namely, length, width, and depth. The **form**, however, or the human image, is comprised of the line-drawings we discussed above.

By *Symmetry*, therefore, we understand that most admirable proportional measure which we ought to contemplate and love, not only in man himself, but also in every natural thing, since it clearly appears to be nothing other than a certain harmonic instrument, most perfect in all its numbers, so that all things are composed of parts distributed everywhere by the most exact dimension—and especially that noble human body above all others.

The dimensions of the human face, then, are three. *One* is from the top of the forehead, where the hair begins, down to the eyebrows; *the second* is from the eyebrows to the bottom of the nose; and *the last* is from the bottom of the nose to the chin. Of these, the *first* is the seat of wisdom, the *second* of beauty, and the *third* of goodness. These parts, multiplied by themselves, will yield the entire stature of the human body in proportions, however great it may be. Of these, the *first* will be the face, the *second* the chest, the *third* from the top of the stomach to the navel, and the *fourth* from the navel to the bottom of the thigh; the hips to the back of the knee will contain *two* [units], and *just as many* will be numbered from there to the ankle; however, this *lowest* part, which is from the ankle to the bottom of the sole, and that throat, which is from the top of the chest to the bottom of the gullet, as well as...

# CHAPTER IV.
## On Geometry.

The knowledge of geometry is especially useful to painters, since their entire art usually revolves around geometric figures, both regular and irregular. Therefore, I advise those who intend to spend their lives in this art of painting that, at the beginning and upon their entry into this art, they should first apply their efforts to the drawing of circles and squares of every kind, as well as oval figures, cylinders, and other such solid and plane shapes. These will be of great benefit in their earliest works, and will wonderfully assist and sharpen their reasoning regarding symmetrical proportion <note>original: "Symmetrica", referring to the balanced relationship between parts of a whole</note>. Likewise, they should learn how to draw one straight line intersecting another straight line at right angles. Through these kinds of geometric operations, the new painter or <term>novice</term> <note>original: "tyro", a beginner or student in a trade</note> will perceive an easier and more certain way to outline any object symmetrically and without error.
    The method for constructing these figures geometrically, and their practical use, will be demonstrated more clearly in the following book.

---

# CHAPTER V.
## On Perspective.

It is at the very heart of the painter's craft to use perspective correctly and in its proper place, as well as in its true explanation. This is usually expressed with lines that are either finer or thicker according to the imitation of nature; for indeed, the further a visible object is from the eyes, the smaller it appears to us, and consequently, the lines constituting it are rendered finer to our sight. This is the path to be followed, and the same reasoning is used by artists in their description of *Perspective*. Artists divide this part of painting into two, asserting that it pertains either *to the whole* or *to individual parts*. That which pertains to the *whole* work comes first and is judged by the sight initially; that which pertains *to the parts* proposes for consideration only those specific things that occur within the viewing.
    Furthermore, this part of pictorial *perspective* which we said pertains to the *whole work* is threefold: namely, *proceeding straight ahead*, when the sight is extended to the furthest heights and the lines of the feet, which is called <term>Optics</term> <note>original: "Optica"</note>; *looking upward*, which is raised toward the middle of the horizon above the head and is called <term>Anoptics</term> <note>original: "Anoptica"</note>; and *looking downward*, which is cast below the feet and is called <term>Cathoptics</term> <note>original: "Cathoptica"</note>.
    There is also *perspective from the side* and *from the back*, but since <term>Pomponius Gauricus</term> <note>A 16th-century Italian humanist and art theorist famous for his treatise "De Sculptura," which discussed perspective and proportion</note> has treated all of these well, we will refrain from discussing them here.
    Finally, the Germans call a branch of this species <term>Landscapes</term> <note>original: "Landschips"</note>, which are never or rarely drawn by themselves, but sometimes with forests, cities, cliffs, mountains, rivers, and other such things.

## CHAPTER VI.

### On the instruments necessary for the art of painting.

**T**here are those who, because of the shortness of time allowed to them for painting, or even due to an unskillfulness in noting the true proportions of a given object, fill the proposed picture with various small squares, and likewise divide the paper on which it is to be drawn into similar squares. They draw these lines—either with black lead <note>original: "plumbum nigrum"; in this period, this often referred to graphite or a lead-tin alloy used for drawing</note> or willow charcoal—so that they may be easily erased, in this manner:

---

*Some others place paper soaked in lamp-black <note>soot from a lamp used as a pigment</note> over clean white paper, and place the picture to be copied on top of it; they then press with a wooden stylus upon all the lines of the picture, which remains fixed and immovable.* <note>This is a 17th-century description of the "transfer paper" or carbon paper method.</note>

*There are also some others who use a thin, transparent sheet of horn <note>original: "cornu tenui diaphano"; animal horn was shaved into thin, translucent layers before the invention of clear plastics</note>, upon which they may trace the underlying picture; these inventions are indeed very useful for beginners in this art.*

There are also certain other things extremely necessary to this art, which are also constantly used by those more skilled in this science. Such items include *black lead* sharpened and fixed in the hollow of a quill, which serves best for making the rough and initial sketch of the painting. Similarly, *willow charcoals* <note>original: "carbones salicis"</note> shaped to a point perform the same task; for that wood yields a finer charcoal, and consequently is accustomed to make a finer line. Furthermore, a *straight ruler made of copper or solid wood* is required, and likewise *compasses* <note>original: "circini"</note>, by which symmetrical proportion is usually observed. Moreover, *white bread crumbs* <note>original: "medulla panis albi"</note> should be at hand for removing lines made with the aforementioned lead or charcoal. Finally, *brushes* <note>original: "penicillos"</note> must be ready, with which the paintings can be quickly shaded.

# BOOK TWO.

->On the Geometric use in the art of painting.<-

---

## CHAPTER I.

->*On the essential aids of this art.*<-

**P**AINTINGS <note>original: "Picturæ"</note> or the proportions of objects are outlined with a twofold aid, namely either with the *help of Geometric figures*, or without them *by the power of the Idea and imagination alone*: <note>In the Renaissance and Early Modern periods, the "Idea" referred to the artist's internal mental concept or divine inspiration that guided the hand before any physical lines were drawn.</note> The Geometric figures that are most helpful to painting are two straight lines intersecting at right angles, the equilateral Triangle, the quadrangle, and the oval, circular, and cylindrical figures. Concerning the operation of the *idea* in the irregular proportions of things, we shall treat more extensively *below in chapter 5 of book 3*; meanwhile, we will briefly discuss the composition and use of certain Geometric figures in this art.

---

## CHAPTER II.

->*On the intersection of lines at right angles, and on their use in this art.*<-

*Let a straight line be drawn on some flat surface, whether on paper or on any other flat object. Next, fix one foot of the compass <note>original: "circinus," the drafting tool used for circles and measuring.</note> at one of its ends, and extend the other to its other end; let a small arc of a circle be made above the center of that line, and while the foot remains fixed, let a similar arc be made below the center of the same. Then, using the same distance <note>keeping the compass set to the same width</note>, let another small arc be made intersecting the first arc, with the foot of the compass remaining on the opposite end of that same line: that small arc must be intersected both above the line and below it. You ought to mark the points where the intersections occur; then, having placed a ruler over both opposite points, a straight line is to be drawn, which will intersect the given line at right angles. Let the given line therefore be A. B. Thus, with one foot of the compass placed on A, the other ought to be extended to B; and let arcs C. D. and E. F. be made. Then, with the same foot placed on B, let other arcs be made intersecting the previous ones, namely G. H. I. L.*

# C H A P T E R  I V.

## On the Quadrangle.

The formation of quadrangles—both the oblong and those with equal sides—is also found in this art, and is extremely useful both for apprentices <term>tyronibus: beginners or students in a workshop</term> and for those more experienced. To form such an equilateral figure <note>a square</note>, one must proceed as follows:

*Let a straight line be drawn according to the requirements of the object being depicted, either vertically, or with an inclination or slant. Then, placing one foot of the compass on the end A, let the other be extended to the other end B, and let a faint circle be made; then again, let one foot be fixed on the other end B, and let another faint circle be made. Once these are finished, let two perpendiculars be raised above each end until they touch the concave surface of the overlapping faint circle, and then let them be joined at the top; this will be an exact square.*

->[Diagram of a square construction using circles and vertical lines from points b and a]<-

*Through this type of figure, the symmetrical proportion of a person's full face is outlined, as will be explained below.*

*An oblong square <note>a rectangle</note> is also made by raising the outer sides perpendicularly, and by a vertical straight line reducing the whole into a parallelogram figure, in this way:*

# CHAPTER V.
## On the method of forming a double oval figure.

**L**et the legs of the <term>compass<span>a mathematical instrument used for drawing circles and measuring distances</span></term> be extended according to the size you wish your oval figure to have. Then, draw a faint circle and label it A.B.G. Afterward, from the top or vertex and the *Zenith* <note>original: "Zenith"; refers here to the highest point of the circle</note> of your circle, draw a faint straight line through its center to the opposite point of its circumference—namely the *Nadir* <note>original: "Nadir"; refers here to the lowest point of the circle</note>—and label it A.D. At the point of intersection D, fix one leg of the compass and, keeping the same distance, draw another circle, namely E.F.G. Where one circle intersects the other, specifically at point H, fix one leg of the compass and extend it toward the opposite intersection, namely I, and join the outer curves of the two circles with an arc. Once this is done, move the compass leg to intersection I and join the opposite parts of the circles with a similar arc. Finally, let the desired oval figure be clearly traced with a pen; it will be A.B.F.G.E.

The use of this specific shape serves primarily to frame the <term>portrait<span>original: "effigiem"; an image or likeness of a person</span></term> of an individual, and it is constantly employed and practiced by painters in their daily work. There is, however, another type of oval figure where one end is sharper than the other. Since this is used to paint the full view of a face with correct symmetry, we shall explain the geometric method of drawing it here for the benefit of <term>students<span>original: "tyrones"; beginners or apprentices in the craft</span></term>.

## C H A P T E R VI.

### Concerning the circle.

**F**or the composition of a circle there is no need for much instruction, since its drawing by means of compasses is known to everyone. However, there are many things in this art to be performed and delineated with the help of this geometric figure—as for example, the depiction of the *celestial Sun*, the painting of a round eye, and also the formation of a round face.

It also happens sometimes that two, three, or more circles are required in the same proportion of a single thing, just as we join three circles for the description of a child’s face, in this manner.

## CHAPTER IV.

### *On the use of the circle in this art.*

**C**ircles are valuable in this art for the composition of things that naturally possess a round form. In this process, it will not be unsuitable to also use lines intersecting one another transversely at right angles, so that the object may be depicted with more certain <term>proportion|The harmonious relationship between the parts of a whole, a central concept in Renaissance and Baroque art</term>. For example, *if I wish to depict the figure of the Sun*, I shall draw a faint circle with black lead <note>original: "plumbo nigro," likely referring to a lead point or early graphite</note> or charcoal; in the center of this, I make two straight lines intersecting each other at right angles. These lines will guide the beginner <note>original: "tyronem," meaning a novice or apprentice student</note> not only in the proportional shaping of the larger rays but also in correctly sketching the nose and eyes of the solar figure, just as it appears in the following illustration.

Similarly, other things are very easily depicted using only a semicircle. For example, *if I wish to sketch a bowl* <note>original: "craterem," meaning a vessel, chalice, or large cup</note>, I can easily depict it in this manner, and similarly a *child’s face*.

### CHAPTER V.

->*Concerning objects which have no regular relation to geometric figures.*<-

**T**here are certain objects in which regular geometric shapes <note>original: "regulares figuræ Geometricæ"</note> will be of no use at all to artists, but which are guided and outlined more by the arrangement of an idea than by any geometric dimensions; such things include the lion, the horse, the eagle, and others of this kind. Therefore, use your own judgment in these matters, and through constant practice, you will compare the truth of their proportions more and more every day. However, so that you may reach such perfection all the sooner, first think carefully about the object you wish to sketch <margin>/</margin>, and delineate and form it in any way you can with black lead <note>likely graphite or a lead point</note>, or red lead <note>sanguine or red chalk</note>, or charcoal <margin>/</margin>. Once this is done, set that proportion you have drawn aside for one day. Then, on the following day, reviewing it again, weigh within yourself where you have erred most, and correct it according to that idea in your mind, whether in a specific part or in the general proportion. Then, set that picture aside again until the next day, and correct it once more. Do this for 5 or 6 days, thus successively and gradually amending all parts, even down to the very veins. In this way, forty sheets of various subjects can be worked on at the same time. Afterward, compare any of these figures with the work of some most excellent master <note>original: "opificis alicujus præstantissimi"</note> of the same species, and where you find a fault or defect, correct it lightly. By this path, it will not be difficult to gradually remove and avoid all errors; however, it must be observed that a strong imagination and a sufficient memory are required to perform this very work, for these two are, as it were, the nurses and midwives to this art.

Let us proceed; *Shadows, therefore, or shadings* <note>original: "Umbræ igitur seu obumbrationes"</note> required in this art are manifold: some are **simple**, others **double**, and some **triple**. Furthermore, **some of them are made with points alone, some with lines, and some with points and lines mixed together**. Again, **those which are formed of lines alone are made with straight and oblique lines**. Regarding each of these, we shall say something separately in its proper place.

**Simple shadows are sometimes accustomed to be made with points alone**, both where denser and where subtler shadows are required to delineate an object. For the multitude and density of the points makes the shadow darker, just as, conversely, the fewness or rarity of them usually constitutes a lighter shadow; this is required where the body ought to appear more luminous, and it is done, for example, in this way, **see Number 1.** <note>This technique is known today as stippling.</note>

**Simple shadows with lines alone** are also made either rarer or denser according to the number of lines. These shadows are also to be depicted where the bodies or surfaces are more illuminated, either by their own nature or by the position of the place, **see Number 2.**

**Shadows made with points and lines mixed together** on a surface are demonstrated in this way, **see Number 3.**

**Shadows with double lines** <note>This refers to cross-hatching.</note> are made for the most part where parts of the object are suddenly turned away from the light; the more that part is turned from the light, the darker the shadow must be, as in the depiction of a wheel's surface, or in that of a column, **see Number 4.**

---

**Shadows made with three lines** <note>Triple-hatching, where three sets of lines intersect to create deep blacks.</note> are necessary there where the things to be described are further distant from the light, such as, for example: the depth of a well, holes and caverns in the earth, the interior part of a gate or window, fissures, parts of any body quite remote from the light, the darkness of forests, and infinite other things. For an example, **see Number 1.**

**Oblique lines** are also employed in many types of shadings: mostly, however, where objects are round; and similarly where clouds and other things of that sort are to be expressed, as in the following examples, **Number 2.**

### CHAPTER VII.

->*On the practice of perspective.*<-

Since perspective is very often required in the practice of the art of painting, we shall say something briefly here about its practical application, and thus bring this part of the present treatise to an end.

Artists are accustomed, when they wish to depict some thing or object in perspective <term>perspective: the technique of representing three-dimensional objects on a two-dimensional surface to give the right impression of their height, width, depth, and position in relation to each other</term>, to extend straight lines from a given center, spaced equally and wandering according to their own pleasure. They then depict objects according to the progress and extension of these lines by looking back toward the center point; by which way we shall perceive that the perspective itself is delineated and explained. For example:

# BOOK ONE
## On fortifications and bulwarks.

---

### C H A P T E R  I.
### *On the Types of Fortifications.*

Fortified places are strengthened either solely by nature, or solely by art <note>In this context, "art" refers to human engineering and construction (artifice) rather than aesthetic art.</note>, or by both nature and art joined together. A place is said to be naturally fortified when it is rendered almost inaccessible by nature itself. Natural fortification occurs through two primary means: namely, either by the position of some rock or cliff, which makes access difficult and dangerous, or by some wide and deep body of water surrounding a place, guarding it from any land-based invasion as if in a protective embrace.

Regarding the first type of natural defense, we call that fortification "strong" which is located not far from **Trento** <note>original: "Tridento"</note> under the dominion of the **Venetians**, situated on the river **Adige** <note>original: "Adicen"</note>; no one can enter or leave it except by a certain large basket which the guards raise into the heights or lower from above with a rope as they please. Nor is it possible for those traveling directly from **Venice** to **Augsburg** <note>original: "Augustam Germaniæ"</note> in Germany to avoid this passage guarded by the aforementioned fortification.

**Quintus Curtius** <note>A Roman historian famous for his biography of Alexander the Great.</note> also makes mention of a certain rocky mountain called **Dorius**, so fortified by nature and the river **Indus** that, because of its inaccessibility, a very few Persians disrupted the entire army of **Alexander the Great** and did not fear in the least to resist his hostile fury. 

In this same regard, the town of **Orvieto** <note>original: "Orvetum"</note> in **Tuscany** <note>original: "Thufciæ"</note> is said to be naturally fortified. For it is situated on the flat summit of a high and precipitous mountain without walls; in their stead, it is encircled on all sides by steep and high rocks, created by nature in such a way that from the highest ledge, the view looking down into the depths is truly horrific. An image of this town is depicted below. In a similar way, several citadels are fortified above the city of **Aden**, the great trading port of **Arabia Felix** <note>Literally "Happy Arabia," an ancient name for the fertile southern region of the Arabian Peninsula.</note>, standing out upon the highest peaks of the rocky cliffs.

---

<summary>This page introduces the classification of fortifications, distinguishing between natural defenses—such as cliffs and water—and man-made structures. It provides historical and contemporary examples of naturally "impregnable" locations like Orvieto and the mountain passes near Trento.</summary>
<keywords>fortification, military engineering, natural defenses, Orvieto, Trento, Alexander the Great, Adige River, Aden, Quintus Curtius</keywords>

--- Page 612 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of fortification theory, transitioning from natural defenses to the necessity of a specialized vocabulary for modern military engineering.</meta>

<page-num>346</page-num>
<header>TREATISE II. PART VI. BOOK I.</header>

The second type of natural defense is provided by the nature of the subject itself—namely, water—which surrounds locations with its depth and width. This is best demonstrated by the positions of **Venice** in Italy; **Zierikzee** in the Netherlands <note>original: "Germaniæ inferioris", referring to the Low Countries</note>, which was besieged by the **Spanish** in the year 1576; and **Mexico City** in New Spain. There is also such a fortress in the middle of the Rhône river near **Rochemaure**, and another in the sea not far from **Marseille**, which is called **the Château d'If** <note>original: "le Chasteau Dec."</note>; and so it is with others.

In purely artificial fortification, we do almost nothing except imitate nature. For we either protect towns and cities by surrounding them with water, or we fortify them against enemy invasions with earthworks and bulwarks, or we defend them using both at once. It is with such fortifications that **Milan** is defended (namely the **Ramparts** with 9 bastions); similarly **Peschiera** and **Lucca** in Italy; **Calais**, **St. Omer**, **Arras**, and **Péronne** in France; and **Zaltbommel**, **Gorinchem**, **Flushing**, **Ostend**, and countless other towns in the Netherlands.

Both natural and artificial fortifications are commonly those which have an irregular shape, so that art may more easily harmonize with the natural site. Such fortresses are found in many places where nature seems to offer aid through her own tools—namely, water or cliffs. It must be observed, however, that "art" (engineering) is most required in those parts of a site where nature appears to have been more negligent. Examples include the correction of the walls in the citadel of **Brescia** in Lombardy on the side facing the city, and in **Marseille** on the landward side; the positioning of the earthwork or <term>Bastion|A projecting part of a fortification built at an angle to allow defensive fire in several directions</term> in the part of **Bologna** facing the mountain; the elevation of the Bulwark at **Crema** in Lombardy toward the torrent to guard the bridge; and in countless other places where the vulnerability of a certain section is aided by <term>Curtains|The straight wall of a fortification linking two bastions</term> and Bastions, or by earthworks alone, or by <term>Spurs|Projecting V-shaped defenses</term> and <term>Ravelins|Triangular fortifications located outside the main ditch</term>, or by the diversion of water, or by the elevation of a <term>Cavalier|An interior fortification raised higher than the main wall to allow firing over it</term>, and many other such inventions.

---

# CHAPTER II.

->Concerning the vocabulary necessary for this science.<-

**E**very part of a fortification, whether it be interior or exterior, requires its own technical term so that it may be distinguished from another. These terms cannot be derived from Latin because, in the times of the ancient Romans, this doctrine of fortification was entirely unknown. Since these fortifications have been invented in recent years—during which <term>bombards|Early large-caliber cannons</term> and larger engines of war have come into widespread use—to resist the immense power of said machines (which the old Roman walls could not have long endured), we have fashioned technical terms that sound like Latin. However, we have derived their sound and substance from those nations where they were constantly used in military discipline. In this way, readers who are somewhat experienced in military affairs may more easily understand my intention. I have not disdained to imitate the vocabulary of the French and Italians, among whom I have had much conversation regarding this art. For that part which the French call a *Bastion* and the Italians a *Bulvardo*, we also call a **Bastion** or **Bulwark**; what they call *Casemates*, *Flanks*, *Shoulders*, *Curtains*, *Parapets*, *Counterscarps*, and *Banquettes*, and what the Italians call *the covered way* <note>original: "battre le strade"</note>, *Ravelins*, and *Cavaliers*, we call **Casemates**, **Flanks**, **Shoulders**, **Curtains**, **Parapets**, **Counterscarps**, **Banquettes**, **Ravelins** (or spurs), and **Cavaliers**. We shall speak copiously regarding the descriptions, natures, and uses of these parts below.

### CHAPTER III.

#### *Concerning the things necessary in the construction of a fortification.*

**A**mong all things, the excellent judgment of the Engineer <note>original: *Ingeniatoris*; a term for a military architect or designer of war machines</note> is required to foresee future dangers; for otherwise, the greatest error and irrecoverable loss would follow. Therefore, it is necessary to choose a site suitable for one's purpose, in which he must carefully observe its position, and weigh the approaches to it, as well as offensive and defensive positions, in equal balances; and especially, he must consider whether it might be attacked from any higher surrounding ground. Next, the time in which the begun fortification can be finished must be considered; for sometimes necessity compels a bulwark <note>original: *propugnaculum*</note> to be raised suddenly, beyond all the enemies' expectations. From this it should be noted that a fortification with fewer bastions <note>original: *bastionum*</note> may be erected more quickly and at a lower price than one consisting of many. Let all things necessary for war also be prepared, such as provisions or food required for the set term, and let it be such that it is preserved from spoilage for a long time. Furthermore, let it be well-armed with cannons <note>original: *tormentis*; literally "engines of torsion" but here referring to artillery</note> with the necessary powder and shot; and especially let it be guarded by industrious men, excellently trained in war, who are ready and fit both to attack the besiegers and to receive and repel their assaults. Finally, let the best and most proportional order be observed in all parts of the fortification, and especially that the curtains <note>original: *Courtinæ*; the straight walls connecting two bastions</note> be neither too long nor too short, but of moderate size. For then the arquebusiers <note>original: *harquebuzei*; soldiers armed with an early type of long gun</note> will be better able to guard the flanks <note>original: *Flanquos*</note> and the sides of the bastions, as will be said more clearly below. Here, however, we have briefly expressed certain rules necessary for both the attackers and the besieged.

-> Rule I. <-

*He who knows not how to destroy fortifications like an enemy, knows not how to fortify them; likewise, he who knows not the method of attacking fortifications shall also be judged utterly ignorant of the art of fortifying.*

-> Rule II. <-

*In the siege <note>original: *obsessione*</note> of all places, one must proceed at the beginning with force, diligence, and fury, both to stun the besieged and so that not the slightest opportunity is given to them to fortify themselves further. Hence follows an admonition for the besieged to note: that nothing be left unfinished in their defenses <note>original: *fortificationibus*</note>, but that all things be completed according to expectation, all things well-fortified, and that no opportunity be offered to the besiegers by which they might bring any harm to them or to the bulwark.*

-> Rule III. <-

*A place well reconnoitered is almost conquered <note>original: *expugnatus*</note>.*

### Rule I.

> *The interval between two bulwarks should be neither too long nor too short; for if the bulwarks are too close, the Casemate and Shoulders will be weak; if they are too far apart, they cannot be well flanked <note>original: "flancari," meaning to be protected by crossfire from the sides</note> by arquebusiers <note>original: "Harquebuzeis," soldiers armed with an early form of long gun</note>.*

### Rule II.

*There are round bastions <note>original: "propugnacula rotunda"</note> that do not form an angle at their front. Although these are strong enough, they are not praised as much as others; first, because they more easily receive the strikes of artillery <note>original: "tormentorum ictus"; refers here to heavy siege engines or early cannons</note>; second, because the front section cannot be effectively <term>flanked</term> <note>Flanking fire allows defenders to shoot along the face of a wall from a protected side position to prevent enemies from scaling it.</note> due to its roundness. The bastions of the city of Augsburg <note>Augsburg was a major center for military engineering in the Holy Roman Empire.</note> are built in this way; see Diagram Number 1.*

### Rule III.

*A bastion is sometimes double—that is, one inside another—and in such cases, both have their own <term>parapets</term> <note>A low protective wall along the edge of a roof or balcony; in military terms, a barrier to shield soldiers from fire.</note> or <term>counterscarps</term> <note>The outer slope of a ditch or moat facing the fortification.</note>, as can be seen in the bastions of the city of Augsburg; see Diagram Number 2.*

### Rule III.

### CHAPTER IV.

### *On the exterior parts of a fortification.*

The **Moat** <note>original: "Fossa"</note> is a proportional excavation of the earth, the outer edges of which stand at an equal distance from the base of the fortification. Its use is to hinder the approach and sudden invasion of attackers. Its figure follows below.

---

A **Ravelin** <note>original: "Ravellina"; a triangular fortification located outside the main ditch</note> is a certain triangular embankment, raised within the moat in front of the middle of the curtain wall, not far from the edge of the ground or the Banquette. This member is extremely useful in every fortification; especially where some part of the Rampart is overlooked by some high ground, or is weak and easily accessible <unclear>see Number 1.</unclear>

The **Banquette** <note>original: "Banquetta"; a step or ledge behind a parapet for soldiers to stand on while firing</note> or **Retrenchment** <note>original: "Retrenchamentum"</note> is that which is constructed along the length of the edge of the moat with its own counterscarp; it shall be 6 feet in height.

Its use is to impede the enemy, so that they cannot approach the moat at the beginning of a siege. The Banquette defends the Ramparts, and the soldiers occupying the Banquette—who for the most part are Harquebusiers <note>original: "Harquebuzei"; soldiers armed with an early type of long-barreled firearm</note>—are also made secure by them. ### CHAPTER VI.

#### *On the shapes of Defenses.*

**A**s the shape of a defense <term>munimentum: a general term for a fortification or defensive structure</term> may be regular or irregular, we call that one regular which has a regular surface—that is, one which is composed of equal Bastions and Curtains <term>courtina: the straight section of a defensive wall that connects two bastions</term>. Such a figure is called regular because it is drawn upon a regular Geometric surface. This type of Geometric figure, which is angular and according to which fortifications are built, has many variations. For *some are triangular*, *others Quadrangular*, *a third Pentagonal*, *a fourth Hexagonal*, *a fifth Heptagonal*, *a sixth Octagonal*: and so on for the others, in which all angles and sides are equal. The specific types of these figures follow below.

### TREATISE II. PART VI. BOOK I. ###

And figures of this kind are usually only drawn on an open field or level ground, because an uneven surface—owing to its protrusions in one place and its hollows in another—will make the <term>curtains</term> <note>original: "Courtinas"; the straight sections of a defensive wall connecting two bastions</note> and <term>bastions</term> <note>original: "Bastiones"; the angular structures projecting outward from the main wall to allow for defensive fire</note> sometimes longer and sometimes shorter, depending on the layout and the roughness of the terrain. Consequently, the parts of the fortification will fail to meet the required proportions, which is considered a defect in this art <note>The "art" refers to military engineering or "architectura militaris."</note>. There is also one type of irregular figure with which fortifications and their components are sometimes designed, and it is what they call the oval, which is described here.

---

But this type is quite rare. There are also other variations of regular figures which are also used in many places, according to which fortifications are built, such as the <term>rhomboid</term> <note>a parallelogram with unequal adjacent sides and oblique angles</note> and the star figure, which are depicted here.

An *irregular figure* is one which has no proportion among its parts. Because of the unevenness of a site, fortifications are very often constructed according to this kind of surface shape. This varies according to the invention and judgment of the Engineer <term>Ingeniator: a term for a military architect or designer of "engines" and defenses</term>, who, depending on the location's site and layout, is accustomed to finding infinite types of such shapes. All of these are known by the general name of Trapezoids <note>original Latin: "Trapezeæ"; here referring to any four-sided figure without parallel sides</note>. And although these types are not as highly praised as those called "regular" <note>Ideal geometric shapes like squares, pentagons, or hexagons which were favored in "trace italienne" fortification theory</note>, nevertheless, regarding the natural strength and inaccessibility of the location where they are drawn, they far exceed those purely artificial defenses in strength. This is because such ramparts are never built except where nature itself sufficiently strengthens the place—either because of its position elevated upon a cliff, or because it is protected on all sides by deep water or marshy ground. These kinds of figures are explained below.

---

## CHAPTER VII.

### *On the method of sketching and depicting any shape of a fortification upon the level surface of a field.*

**F**irst, it will be necessary to prepare a piece of flat, exactly square wood. In this, two lines <note>grooves or channels</note> will be carved to the width of a certain cord, so that two cords may very easily enter and exit without hindrance in both grooves. Let these lines be extended with such width that they form an angle upon the flat surface with two equal sides—either a right angle to describe a four-sided figure, or a more obtuse angle to describe a fortification with many angles. Where those two wide lines form the angle, both cords are to be fixed as if at a center. It will also be necessary for a thread, hanging perpendicularly with its lead weight <note>a plumb bob</note> near the openings of the lines, to act as a faithful guardian of the direct and true movement of each cord. Thus, when the thread is moved over its perpendicular line, the cord is then held immovably until, following its direction, lines are dug from the angle of the wooden surface to the other end of the cord upon the flat surface of the earth, or marked out with some iron instrument. At this point, it should be noted <meta>catchword: is,</meta>

Let A be the center or the meeting point of the two sides of the instrument, forming an angle at point A, to which the cords <note>original: "chordæ"</note> AF and Ag are attached.

The method of operation is as follows: Have a wooden board ready, upon which some polygonal <term>polygonia<gloss>a many-sided geometric shape</gloss></term> surface is to be drawn. Then, let the aforementioned compasses <term>circini<gloss>drafting dividers or compasses used for measuring and transferring distances</gloss></term> or forceps be placed, and let the center of their head be fitted to one of the angles of the polygonal figure, and lightly fixed there with a small nail. Once this is done, the compasses should be opened until their sides BC and DE are equal to the width of the two sides of the polygon. After these steps are completed, take the compasses and draw the polygonal figure on the ground in the previous manner—namely, by fixing center A to the ground and extending the two cords; one along the edge of one leg of the compass, namely BC, and the other along DE. In this way, it will not be difficult to depict any figure upon a flat surface without hesitation.

### CHAPTER VIII.

->*By what method are the internal and external parts of a simple fortification <term>munimenti<gloss>defensive walls or earthworks</gloss></term> drawn proportionally, so that they may be properly arranged in their correct places? And concerning the types of regular fortification shapes.*<-

Therefore, once the shape of the fortification has been produced upon the field or a specific location according to the teaching of the previous chapter, any of its sides must be divided into six equal parts, the four interior of which shall be the length of the **Curtain Wall** <term>Courtinæ<gloss>the straight path of a wall between two bastions</gloss></term> of that side. The **Bastion** <note>original: "Bastio"</note> with its parts is also made in this way: at both ends of each curtain wall, let the two outer parts—which remain from the said six aside from the four for the curtains—be raised perpendicularly <term>orthogonaliter<gloss>at a right angle or 90 degrees</gloss></term>. The height of these perpendiculars will therefore be one-sixth part of the side of the figure. This is described in a four-sided figure as follows, *Number 1.*

Furthermore, each part raised perpendicularly (namely 1 and 6), when divided equally, will establish the width of the **Casemate** <term>Cassemattæ<gloss>a vaulted chamber in a bastion for firing cannons</gloss></term> and the **Shoulder** <term>Humeri<gloss>the corner or "joint" of the bastion where the flank meets the face</gloss></term>, which must be of the same dimension. When these are finished, faint lines are to be drawn from the internal angle of one perpendicular through the peak of the other on the same side. This must be done on every side of the figure; from this, all the **Bulwarks** <term>propugnacula<gloss>the projecting parts of a fortification, such as bastions</gloss></term> will be produced, as will appear in the following demonstration, *Number 2.*

## *On fortifications built upon triangular and quadrangular shapes.*

### *Rule I.*

Fortifications built on triangular and quadrangular shapes are not frequently used, because the fronts of their bastions have angles that are too sharp <note>In military architecture, acute angles were avoided because they were easily shattered by cannon fire and provided less space for defenders.</note>.

### *Rule II.*

*However, fortifications of this kind are of great value where necessity forces one to defend themselves quickly against the onset of an approaching enemy, or where a narrow space or a specific passage must be held to block the enemy’s crossing or to avoid their raids.*

But while these types of fortifications are built more easily and in less time than those with more bastions, they are not expected to endure as long against the fury of the enemy.

The method for sketching the parts of any fortification, both internal and external, is the same for every other shape as it was for the quadrangular shape previously discussed. For example, a Pentagonal fortification <note>A five-sided fort.</note> is sketched in this way, *Number 1.*

A *Hexagonal* fortification <note>A six-sided fort.</note> with its various parts is also described in this way, *Number 2.*

# ON FORTIFICATIONS AND BULWARKS.

The same method also applies to sketching other polygonal fortifications, whether they are simple or composite.

->*On Pentagonal and other polygonal fortifications.*<-

### Rule I.

These kinds of fortifications, consisting of equal bastions and curtains <term>courtinarum: the straight defensive walls connecting two bastions</term>, are always constructed in flat plains, much like how towns in Flanders are most often fortified. They are quite convenient for controlling the paths along a region's borders or the narrow passages of a river, and for quickly fortifying a position when necessity compels.

### Rule II.

The more bastions a fortification has, the larger it is in its constituent parts—provided that proportional order is maintained. Therefore, the larger the troop of soldiers (both cavalry and infantry), the larger and more multi-pointed the Bulwark <term>Balvarda: a bastion or projecting part of a fortification</term> must be.

### Rule III.

Cities and larger towns require more bastions according to the size of their perimeter.

---

## CHAPTER IX.

->*On the irregular shapes of fortifications and their parts.*<-

### Rule I.

Irregular or trapezoidal fortification shapes vary according to the specific terrain of the site. The landscape forces a change in shape, either because of water surrounding it—as seen in the fortification called **Schenck-Schantze** <note>A strategically vital Dutch fortress located at the split of the Rhine and Waal rivers</note> situated in the middle of a river—or because of the uneven sides of a rocky surface, as shown in the Castle or Citadel in **Brest** <note>A major port city in Brittany, France, known for its rugged coastal geography</note>.

### Rule II.

In these types of fortifications, one must ensure that no part, if possible, is overlooked or "commanded" by any overhanging high ground. Furthermore, they must be protected by sufficiently deep ditches, as is evident in the following description of the fortification of **Siena** <note>A city in Tuscany, Italy; the author likely refers to the Medici Fortress or the city's complex Renaissance defenses</note>.

# CHAPTER X.

## *On composite fortifications.*

**A** <term>composite fortification</term> <note>original Latin: *munimentum compositum*</note> is so called when smaller shapes are contained within larger ones, upon which other smaller and interior defenses are usually raised, for longer-lasting resistance and for the easier repelling of the enemy. For, if the outer <term>bastions</term> <note>the angular structures projecting from the main curtain wall of a fort</note> are invaded, the enemy nonetheless cannot advance further because of the interior fortifications, but are always driven back by them. And these interior <term>ramparts</term> <note>original: *propugnacula*; the defensive stone or earth walls of the fort</note> are very well protected by ditches and <term>counterscarps</term> <note>the outer slope or wall of the ditch facing the fort</note>.

It is yours, O **Nature naturing** <term>original: *Natura naturans*; a philosophical term describing Nature as an active, creative force—God acting through the natural world</term>, infinite and glorious, to regenerate my soul, which is wasting away in ignorance, by the power of your splendor. It is yours to awaken, bring to life, and raise to the true peak or summit of knowledge the sparks of reason—those which survived after the **fall of Adam** <term>original: *Adami lapsum*; the biblical loss of innocence and perfect knowledge</term> and have been most miserably submerged for a long time in the abyss of bodily darkness—through the wonderful clarity of the Holy Spirit of discipline. 

May your will be done in the celestial and immortal part of me, a man, just as in the earthly and mortal part, so that whatever is produced by them and in them may all, through due consideration, be a participant in your goodness. Thus shall this heartfelt offering, consecration, and, as it were, sacrifice of mine be pleasing to your most holy divinity: thus the fruit of your goodness in me, receiving the rays of its own growth flowed in from your bright fountain of all and only goodness, with your divine Spirit leading the way, shall fly away in a true **resurrection** <note>The author likely refers to an intellectual or spiritual "rising" rather than a physical one.</note> with its whole self transformed into the heights, and may it rejoice to visit its super-heavenly homeland, in which you, **Highest Prince and greatest Emperor**, live and reign forever. Be favorable and gracious to me, O good God, you who live forever.
