# A MOST LUCID EXPLANATION
## OF THE EMBLEM AT THE 
### BEGINNING OF THIS VOLUME.

[Initial A] Before the creation of things, the incomprehensible and almighty Maker of the Macrocosm <term>Macrocosm: The "Great World," referring to the universe as a whole.</term> divided the entire mass into three parts, differing in their level of purity, by His immense power. From the purest of these, He ordained that the Cherubim, Seraphim, Archangels, and all the other orders of Angels be created; from the less pure, He created the heavens and the ethereal regions; and from the most impure, He created the elements and all sublunary things <note>Things "under the moon," referring to the earthly realm of change and decay.</note>, saying: *Let them be, and they were made* <note>original: "Fiant, & facta sunt"</note>. 

However, because of the simple purity of its substance, He placed the first division of matter beyond the reach of natural understanding. It is indeed metaphysical and supernatural, which modern <note>original: "neoterici"</note> writers of philosophy confirm is bounded by the Empyrean heaven <term>Empyrean: The highest, most celestial part of the universe, often described as being made of pure light or fire.</term>, that is, the burning and fiery realm. But the remaining parts of the less pure mass—namely the ethereal and the elemental—are rightly called "natural," because they are subject to the governance of Nature (who serves as the governess of the Microcosm <term>Microcosm: The "Little World," or humanity, viewed as a reflection of the larger universe.</term> under God). 

Two efficient causes contained within this fabric of the Macrocosm are enumerated: namely, Nature, and her "Ape," which we call Art <note>In this period, "Art" (human craft and technology) was seen as a way of imitating or "aping" the processes of Nature.</note>. The Father and Lord of Nature is God, the Best and Greatest; she is closest to Him, and from Him we know all her virtues and effects are derived. She is, as it were, the knot and bond of the elements; she possesses the power to temper the mixture of elements in their proper proportions, to mingle them aptly in every composition, and to impress the appropriate form upon every species. 

Nature is also a certain infinite force procreating like from like, being the fertile mother of all qualities and things, which she increases and nourishes. To describe her in a single word according to the opinions of Zoroaster <note>An ancient Persian prophet often cited by Renaissance scholars as a source of hidden wisdom.</note> and Heraclitus <note>A Greek philosopher who believed fire was the fundamental substance of the universe.</note>, she is the invisible fire, which they call the Soul of the World <term>Soul of the World: "Anima Mundi," the vital spirit that was believed to animate all of nature.</term>. We have depicted her visibly in much the same way as some more recent philosophers have done, and we did so with the intention that her power might be better understood by the reader's mind. 

Thus, we have imagined her as a naked virgin in her tender and blooming youth, with star-bearing and beautifully gilded hair, possessing a most clear and admirable gaze, and a lovely blushing color in her cheeks. This virgin was so remarkable in the whiteness of her whole body, and so sweetly decorated with all the gifts of the Great Maker, that poets could not prefer Pallas <note>The goddess Athena.</note>, Venus, Juno, or any other goddess, however graceful, to her beauty. By her singular prudence, the First Mover <term>Primum Mobile: In the geocentric model, the outermost sphere that moves all the inner celestial spheres.</term> is governed, as is the eighth sphere...

<summary>This page introduces an emblem of Nature, describing the creation of the universe from three levels of purity and defining Nature as the "Soul of the World" and the intermediary between God and the physical realm. It describes Nature personified as a beautiful, celestial virgin who governs the movements of the heavens.</summary>

*The sphere adorned with stars is handled and turned by her hands, and the influences of that same sphere are daily prepared and arranged by her fingers for the generation of elemental things. The bodies of the Planets also serve as instruments for the works of Nature; they are, as it were, the small hammers by which metals are produced in the terrestrial mines.* The region of the heart and breast of this virgin is the true seat and womb of the celestial Sun, and her belly is filled with the lunar body. From her breasts, she perpetually instills and suckles all the creatures of the elements with <term>innate heat and radical moisture</term> <note>These were considered the two fundamental fluids necessary for life in medieval and Renaissance medicine: heat provides energy, while moisture provides the substance.</note>, from which their life and growth arise. By a certain golden splendor of her heart, the stars—both fixed and wandering—are illuminated, borrowing their souls, lives, and beauties from it. Their imperceptible influences are infused into her womb by the <term>Mercurial Spirit</term> <note>original: "Spiritu Mercuriali"; often identified by alchemists as the "Spirit of the Moon," a universal medium that carries celestial influences down to Earth.</note> and are carried downward to the earth, penetrating even to its center. Through these impressions, diverse generations, differing in both location and species, are continually brought forth. By the actions of this Nature, the Planets come together, and through this union, they produce various things differing in species across the animal, vegetable, and mineral kingdoms. Starting from the lower parts, from the loins, the four Elements are encompassed; for her right foot occupies the earth, while her left occupies the water, signifying the conjunction of her sulfurous and mercurial nature. By this, it is argued that nothing can be generated or grow without the union of both.*

*This Nature, I say, is not a GODDESS, but the closest minister of God. She has beneath her a handmaid or follower who, by imitating her mistress and impressing upon herself the likenesses of the things produced by her through consensus, follows and imitates her tracks and outlines in a wonderful manner. And it is for this reason that we have depicted her in the form and habit of an **Ape** at the feet of Nature; whom we call by the even more worthy name of <term>Art</term> <note>original: "Artem". The "Ape of Nature" (Simia Naturae) was a common Renaissance metaphor for how human art and science attempt to mimic the creative power of the natural world.</note>. This beast (I mean Art), arising from human ingenuity, learns many secret, beautiful, and remarkable things from the diligent observation of her mistress, with which she is accustomed to enriching men in every kind of doctrine; so also, conversely, she brings no small utility and benefit to that same teacher and mistress. For unless Art, produced by human ingenuity, occasionally gives aid in certain matters, Nature herself would soon fail in the perfection of her operation. For Art sometimes corrects and supplies Nature—indeed, in the discourse of mineral things, Art even seems to surpass her, if only we give some credit to those Chymical Philosophers <note>alchemists</note>. This is especially true since it is certain and proven by experience that in the animal circle, eggs can hatch more quickly and silkworms can be multiplied; in their growth, they can be transformed into various shapes like Proteus, and bees can be procreated from the head of an ox. In the vegetable circle, crops grow and multiply through the artifice of the plow, by which fields are cultivated and harrowed, trees by grafting, and herbs and other vegetables by planting. In the mineral circle, metallic bodies and lesser minerals are prepared for medicine as well as for other uses, cleansed of their dross, and the <term>Physician’s Stone</term> <note>original: "Lapis Physicus"; commonly known as the Philosopher's Stone, believed to perfect base metals and heal all ailments.</note>—of whose praises the Philosophers preach so much—is forged. It is our purpose in this volume to discuss these two efficient causes of the <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>The "Great World" or the universe at large, as opposed to the "Microcosm" or the human being.</note> both clearly and extensively.*

# TO THE BENEVOLENT READER
## AND THE SINCERE SON OF PHILOSOPHY,
### FROM THE HOLY SPIRIT OF UNDERSTANDING,
->enlightenment.<-

TO YOU, my friend, I most willingly offer these my writings to be read; certainly not to <note>In Greek mythology, Momus was the personification of mockery and unfair criticism.</note>Momus or any other overwhelmed by the darkness of ignorance or envy. For it is the nature of such people to use their impure mouths to corrupt everything adorned in the garments of truth, and thus also to impiously profane, for the most part, the very rites of the uncreated Creator. Furthermore, I do not believe this subject of ours should be submitted to the judgments of those who claim it is too deep and divine for human grasp, and for that reason decree that these sacred secrets are in no way to be investigated by us. They diligently drum in that old axiom: *What is above us, is nothing to us* <note>original Latin: "Quæ supra nos, nihil ad nos." This proverb was often used to discourage people from studying divine mysteries or "forbidden" knowledge.</note>. Indeed, by striving to withdraw us entirely from the contemplation of divine things in this way, they seem to suggest clearly enough that humans—made in the image of the immense Creator—differ little or nothing from brute beasts devoid of all reason.

But is it not found in the Holy Scriptures that the Wise Man shall rule the stars? <note>Referring to the popular Maxim "Sapiens dominabitur astris," common in astrological and alchemical texts.</note> And has not the very offspring of the uncreated Creator promised us that the way will be opened to those who knock? I shall pass over in silence for now the fact that even that immortal spirit, breathed into man at the first creation by the divine mind, made him closest to that same mind through this breath of life. It permitted him to look more deeply into the works of the mind, and to contemplate and investigate them with his soul. This is truly what the most divine of all philosophers, and the one closest to Moses, <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure from whom "Hermetic" philosophy takes its name; he was believed to be a contemporary of Moses and a master of alchemy and magic.</note>, confirms in these words in the first discourse of his *Pimander*: *“When man,”* he says, *“having power over all things in himself, observed the creations of the seven governors; these governors, rejoicing in the meditation of the human mind, each made man a participant in their own order—”*

<summary>In this preface, the author defends the study of divine and alchemical mysteries against critics who argue such knowledge is "above" humanity. He asserts that because humans are made in God's image and possess a divine spark, they have a right and duty to investigate the secrets of creation, citing Hermes Trismegistus as an authority.</summary>

May the Almighty mercifully grant this to you, to me, and to all, through the merits of his only-begotten Son, Amen.*

-># P R E F A C E,<-
->## IN WHICH IT IS DEMONSTRATED,<-
->### HOW CAUSES ARE INVESTIGATED THROUGH THEIR EFFECTS,<-
->### THAT IS, BY DEMONSTRATION<-
->### *a posteriori* <note>original: *a posteriori*—a method of reasoning that works backward from observable effects to discover their underlying causes</note>.<-

*SINCE it is impossible for even the wisest or most gifted person to demonstrate or know* **GOD** *himself—the author of the fabric of the Great World <term>Macrocosm: from the Greek 'makros' (large) and 'kosmos' (world), referring to the universe as a whole</term>—through *a priori* <note>original: *a priori*—reasoning from causes to effects, or knowing something by its internal essence rather than its outward results</note> means, because it has never been granted to anyone to define Him by His essence (not even to the divine leader Moses), nor shall it be granted in any age (so omnipotent and incomprehensible is He in His very being!), it is therefore necessary that He be sought *a posteriori*. In this way, our understanding may approach Him through His more excellent effects. The Psalmist <note>Referring to the author of the biblical Psalms, traditionally King David</note> teaches us in Psalm 19:4 to gaze upon His more noble effects in the heavens, and His glory in the firmament, as if in a most polished mirror, with universal eyes. To reach a knowledge of these things, since they are placed above us, it will be necessary to ascend through the elementary stages, moving from the more complex toward the simpler by means of analysis <note>original: *resolutionem*—the process of breaking down a complex substance or idea into its basic components</note>. Nor should any rest be allowed in this ascent until those first principles are reached, which, because of their absolute simplicity, cannot undergo any further analysis. This journey is therefore immense, very thorny, and dangerous; and indeed, it is not easy to find the ladders by which we might reach the summit of this invisible height without the help of divine light and the illumination of the Spirit. Therefore, most Merciful **GOD**, creator of all creatures and my helper, I humbly pray and implore that it may not displease Your dignity that I, an unworthy sinner, beg for Your mercy. Deign to enlighten me in the knowledge of created things, so that, since You are unknown beforehand <note>original: *per prius*</note>, You may at least be known from what follows—namely, through Your glorious effects. For indeed, You promised to open the door to those who knock diligently, and You have never forbidden anyone from eagerly searching the fountain of goodness. This is especially true since that Spirit of life, which You breathed into our father Adam, warns and urges us every moment to strive toward the bright fountain of blessedness and the ultimate goal of divine knowledge. It moves us no less than the heat of the Sun (Your most noble creature) breathed into some raw and unripe fruit is perceived to move that fruit steadily toward mature perfection. Indeed, by this very breath <term>spiraculum: a Latin term for the "breath of life" or divine inspiration</term> of Yours, adorned with a divine mind, daily [the minds] of men...

# P R O O E M I U M.
<note>original: "Prooemium" — Preface or Introduction.</note>

...contemplation is carried away to that third heaven <note>The "third heaven" was traditionally considered the "Empyrean," the dwelling place of God and the highest celestial sphere.</note>, the dwelling place of the blessed, and is beautified by beholding your inexplicable glory, and grows rich with spiritual riches: Enlighten, I say, O good GOD, me your servant, though unworthy, with the splendor of your light, so that without interruption from darkness or the Devil, I may rightly and effectively know you and your creatures for the love and merits of our Lord JESUS CHRIST your son, who lives and reigns with you forever and ever.

*Since, therefore, one must arrive at the knowledge of causes through their effects, our inquiry must begin from the things better known to us, which are generally of two kinds, namely **matter** and **form** <term>materia & forma: the two fundamental principles of reality in Aristotelian philosophy; matter is the "stuff" and form is the "organizing principle" or soul.</term>. Moses and the divine Peter <note>The author refers to Genesis 1:2 and 2 Peter 3:5, interpreting them to mean that the universe was originally composed of water.</note> have left us the teaching that **water** is the matter of all things; which we perceive by the senses to be as much more subtle as it ascends higher, and as much coarser as it is more inclined toward the center. For the earth, which is the dregs and the thicker and more shapeless part of the dark waters, has visible, sensible, and dense water falling upon its surface.*

*Similarly, that thick and visible water has a thinner and more invisible water floating above it; the more subtle part of which, overflowing higher up, fashions the **sphere of fire** because of its heat and subtlety, which is the portion of the waters of the lower region more subtle than all the rest. And so, without a doubt, in the same proportion up to the summit of the upper heaven, the watery mass ascends in the form of a **pyramid** <note>The author likely refers to the "interpenetrating pyramids" of light and matter, a famous visual concept used by Robert Fludd to explain how spirit descends into matter.</note>, always sharper and thinner at the top. Whence it is certain that the lowest water is of the same substance as the upper water, which is purely Spirit, but differs from it only in form—which we shall demonstrate below to be the **light** created on the first day: namely, by whose more abundant presence the waters were made thinner; but with a smaller abundance, they are rendered more thick and dense.*

*Moreover, the portion of light contained in the lowest heaven is of the same nature and essence as that of the upper heavens, but differs only because of its composition; since the density of matter hinders the active disposition of the lower light, and constricts its rays so that it makes them destructive and burning, just as is seen in artificial fire. These things being known, then, will it be impossible—through **experiments** and conclusions made in water both visible and invisible, and the fiery light of the lower region of the world—to investigate also the natures of those subtle waters and the most thin light of the upper heavens, since there is no difference between them except in the proportion of their bodily density?*

*For we see that a smaller machine performs the same work as a large one, though not in the same proportion. Our coarse fire makes images painted on paper move by its power; and so also the bright nature of the sun moves its light and ethereal body from the west to the east. Similarly, a spindle is driven upward by the power of artificial fire and moved hither and thither; thus that fire sent from heaven into animate bodies drives them hither and thither and makes them move. Finally, we perceive the sun itself by the effect of its light making denser things subtle; will the faculty of elementary and artificial fire not also perform this same thing? Through experiments of this kind, therefore, and from the action of the heat of the lower, thick light in the same region's...*

# CHAPTER I.

### *On the infinite nature and the creator of all things.*

**I**NFINITE NATURE, which is the immense Spirit, inexpressible, beyond understanding, outside all imagination, above all essence, unnamable, to be proclaimed by the heart alone, most wise, most merciful, FATHER, WORD, and Holy SPIRIT, the highest and only good, incomprehensible depth, the unity of all creatures, which is more powerful than all power, greater than all excellence, worthier than all praise, the indivisible TRINITY, the most splendid and unutterable light, *finally the divine mind*, free and separated from all mortal composition <note>original: "concretione mortali"</note>, the glory of all, divine nature, necessity, the end and the renewal; <margin>Hermes, *Sacred Sermon*</margin> *This, I say, God most high and greatest of all, whose name be blessed forever, most skillfully established the wonderful machine of the entire <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>The "Macrocosm" refers to the entire universe or "great world," viewed as an ordered system.</note>, and most beautifully decorated its structure:* This is what almost all philosophers, both ancient and more recent, assert with a nearly unanimous consent—except for the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, so named because they often walked while teaching.</note>, who would have it that the world has existed from eternity. These philosophers name this most divine founder of the universe with many titles, suiting every property of his actions. Among them, *Hermes calls him eternal*, *Thales calls him the oldest*, *Plato calls him the unbegotten principle of the world*, *others call him the infinite cause, both as if outside all things and yet within all things and everywhere*, *others the Being of beings, the first cause*, insofar as other causes and effects depend upon him, *the maker of all, the author, and according to Plato, the creative intellect*. From this, some others have called him the Prince of worldly things, the governor, the orderer, the first mover and the first moving force, and the unmoving principle; for all things are moved by him while he remains unmoving and subject to no passion, since he is always stable, fixed, and permanent; *Trismegistus calls him the principle of all things*, by which he seems to understand the sole creator of the work; finally, *Plato and Hermes Trismegistus* call him Father, insofar as he is the author of all fertility and the parent of all things; finally, the greater chorus of Philosophers (among whom I name *Orpheus and Democritus*) concludes that *God has every name, since all things are in him and he is in all things*; not otherwise than how all straight lines drawn from a center to a circumference are said to be in the center, or just as a number is said to be in unity, which is the common measure, source, and origin of all numbers, and contains every number uniquely joined within itself; hence the Pythagoreans and those most skilled in numerical science, adapted the *<term>monad</term> or unity to God* <note>The Monad (from the Greek "monas") represents the number one, signifying the ultimate source or God in Pythagorean philosophy.</note> the creator; both because before all things he was alone and unique, and also because he stood as the first actor and sole mover to complete the vast structure of the work; however, to his matter or subject—which was the second Being, upon which the creator acted for the perfection of the world—they attributed the *<term>Dyad</term> or duality* <note>The Dyad represents the number two, often associated in this context with the "otherness" of matter compared to the unity of the Divine.</note>; and finally to his spiritual power, or fiery and lucid form, through whose presence the said matter or subject of the world was brought from potentiality into act <note>original: "de potentia in actum," a standard philosophical phrase meaning to move from possibility to reality.</note>, and all the machines

The parts and regions, together with their creatures, were most excellently distinguished and arranged; they assigned the *Triad* <note>original: *Triadem*; a group of three, or a Trinity, representing the divine structure of the cosmos</note>, since in the construction of the universal workmanship, this essence claimed for itself the place of the third Being. From the opinions of these pagan philosophers, it is manifest that they did not wander far from the true knowledge of the divine mind. Among them, I can never sufficiently admire or praise the sacred revelation of *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>original: *Mercurii Trismegisti*; a legendary Egyptian figure believed to be a contemporary of Moses and a source of ancient wisdom</note> and his depth in divine mysteries. Indeed, in his *Pimander* <note>original: *Pimandro*; the foundational text of the Hermetic tradition</note>, he revealed to us things hidden by divinity and beyond human grasp—the secrets of <term>GOD</term> <note>In this context, the author uses the Latin *Deus* to signify the ultimate Creator</note> and His universal structure. However, although it is impossible to describe this three-fold Maker in His essence, He is nevertheless depicted to our eyes in this manner, according to the contemplation of several Doctors: namely, *in human form.*

We have therefore described **GOD** in this place insofar as He is said to be within all things—that is, insofar as He is said to be present everywhere. But indeed, since *Trismegistus* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage to whom the "Hermetic" mystical writings are attributed</note> called the *world the image of* **GOD** *Himself*, we say that the image and likeness of **GOD** Himself is seen in the Spirit of the world, just as a human likeness is glimpsed in a mirror. For nothing could be seen in the mirror of the world before **GOD** shone upon it; no more so than a man's likeness can be perceived in a mirror without the light of a fire or the Sun. **God**, however, before the creation of the world, shone only upon Himself, and reflected His own heat back into Himself, as *Trismegistus* testifies. But when He wished to create the world, He changed His form and all things were suddenly revealed, and all things were turned into light, as is found in the *1st Pimander* <note>The "Poimandres," the first book of the Corpus Hermeticum, which describes a vision of the creation of the universe</note>. Therefore, just as the face of a man is seen in a mirror through reflection, so the triple distinction of the one essence is reflected everywhere into the universal spirit of the world. ->*In how many ways God is said to be in a place, how he is present everywhere*<-
->*and fills all things? And regarding his chief seat*<-
->*in this world?*<-

**B**EFORE we discuss the proper seat or dwelling of <term>Nature naturing</term> <note>original: "Naturæ naturantis"; a term used by medieval and Renaissance philosophers to describe God as the active, creative force behind nature, as opposed to the created world itself.</note>, we must ask whether he can even be in a specific place, since he is infinite in his essence. To this doubt, the entire School of theologians responds by making a distinction: they say he is in a place *not definitively* <note>original: "non definitivè"; meaning his presence is not limited by the boundaries of a space, as a soul might be in a body.</note>, like intellects or spiritual creatures, nor *circumscriptively* <note>original: "circumscriptive"; meaning he is not measured or contained by a space like physical objects are</note>, in the manner of bodily things, *but only presentially*. Although <margin>according to Gregory</margin> **G**OD is said to be in all things in a *threefold* way; namely, either *presentially*, as he offers good to them, or *potentially*, namely through influence, or *essentially*, that is, through the intimacy of his essence. However, **G**OD is said to be everywhere insofar as his divine power permeates all beings, through which he defines the relationship of the entire universe's potentiality to himself: thus he is also said to fill all things, not so that he is contained by them, but rather that they are contained by him. *For it is*, says Ambrose, *the property of Divinity to be everywhere and in all things*. It is manifest, therefore, that **G**OD is not in all things in such a way that any thing can grasp him according to the measure of its own portion—as greater things contain the lesser—but he is said to fill all things in the sense that there is nothing where he is not. We understand, therefore, that **G**OD is within all things, but not enclosed, because he is infinite and immeasurable; and outside all things, but not excluded, insofar as he encompasses all created things by his uncircumscribed magnitude. And it is from this that all things created by **G**OD are said to be good because of him, by participation—that is, through his presence, or according to the degrees of essence by which angels are preferred over souls, and souls over animals. And yet, insofar as any creature has obtained more or less dignity according to the beauty of its form proceeding from the first nature or Being, to that extent, as *Iamblichus* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the soul and the divine.</note> testifies, it will possess a higher or lower seat in that goodness acquired through participation. But indeed, as "good" is understood absolutely, simply, and, to use the words of *Iamblichus*, "beyond essence," it is then taken as the cause of good—that is, as the principle of essential good. <margin>Hermes Trismegistus</margin> <note>original: "Mercurius Trismegistus"; the legendary figure to whom many mystical and philosophical texts were attributed.</note> treats this where he warns us to be careful not to call anything "good" except **G**OD alone. Therefore, all the works of the Creator are found to be participants in goodness—not that goodness "beyond essence" which belongs to **G**OD alone—but according to their essence, insofar as they receive essence, form, and substantial light from the fiery benevolence of the Creator. By his gifts they are illuminated, given form, and brought from potentiality into act, and consequently, they are said to be "participatively good." And indeed, the world and the world's creatures received this "essence-making" goodness from the Creator himself, not forced by necessity (as some philosophical traditions hold), but out of his free and most abundant will, wishing to perfect all his creatures, according to the mind of the Royal Psalmist: *Whatever the Lord pleased, he did in heaven and on earth*. Finally, the ancient philosophers placed the habitation of this "Nature naturing" in the heavens, because of the beauty and clarity of that place. Hence *Plato* *asserted that God dwells in a fiery substance*, that is, in the ether. Even more recent philosophers (among whom I name *Isidore*, *Bede*, and *Basil*, true worshippers of this Nature) seem to agree, calling the <term>Empyrean Heaven</term> <note>The highest, most refined part of the heavens, believed in ancient cosmology to be composed of pure light or fire.</note> the *dwelling place* of **GOD**. For although **G**OD is said to be everywhere (as stated above), yet properly and principally, that is,

God is said to be present with greater abundance in this heaven, where the works of His power shine more brightly, as if in a more worthy place and position where divine power operates more fittingly, as *John of Damascus* <note>original: "Damascenus," an 8th-century theologian influential in defining the nature of heaven</note> testifies. For **GOD** is not said to be above all things and outside all things by local distance, but by the excellence of His nature, as is held in the *Theological Resolutions, tract 1, part 1, question 4.* And hence it is that this heaven is called *intellectual*, because **GOD**, whose seat it is, is called the Intellectual Spirit. Some others have attributed this super-celestial region to angels and blessed souls, and therefore established another dwelling outside of this very one, which they called the *Heaven of the Trinity*, suitable for the Trinity alone—namely Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. They say this is **GOD** Himself in substance, but differs in reason. For according to *Albertus* <note>likely Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century philosopher-theologian</note>, this heaven is the excellence of divine power, which contains and circumscribes all created things. Whence *to be in this heaven is to be in the equality of the power of* **GOD**, *who creates, contains, and saves all things*. All these things are clearly explained through the vision of *Ezekiel*, where although these two regions—namely of the Intelligences and of the Trinity—seem to differ only in the purity and exaltation of their essence, the Prophet nevertheless denotes that they are contained within one Empyrean heaven (so called from its perfect illumination <note>The word "Empyrean" comes from the Greek "pyr" for fire, signifying a heaven of pure light or fire</note>), not otherwise than air and fire are contained in the ethereal heaven. For a single heaven, surrounding the convexity of the firmament, bore the likeness of a man, whose upper part from the loins of the image upward shone with a fire of amber form <note>original: "carabeae formae," referring to the "electrum" or glowing metal mentioned in Ezekiel 1:27</note>—that is, most thin and most spiritual; but the lower part from the loins downward sparkled with a fire somewhat denser and thicker. Through this partitioning of the place, he seems to indicate two regions differing in dignity: namely, the pre-celestial heaven proper to spiritual creatures, and that super-celestial one.

### CHAPTER III.

->*On the origin of first matter: is it created or <unclear>uncreated</unclear>?*<-

**A** GREAT disagreement arises among recent philosophers concerning the origin of the matter of the first creation; the larger chorus of whom says assertively that it was created; among whom *Artephius* <note>original: "Artefius," a name associated with several influential medieval alchemical texts</note> uses almost these words: *The Creator of all in the beginning, without the utterance of a word, said: "Let such a creature be," and afterwards nature itself, or first matter, was created by* **GOD**. But another, smaller chorus, in which *Paracelsus* <note>The famous 16th-century Swiss physician and occultist</note> participates with the rest of his school, calls this matter the *great mystery* <note>original: "mysterium magnum"</note>, which had no likeness to any created thing, nor was it even created, but only prepared by the highest craftsman, **GOD**. Both these schools, however, attempt to prove their arguments from the Holy Scripture brought forth by *Moses*, variously interpreting the nature and meaning of the word *Beginning* <note>original: "Principii"</note>. For *Artephius*, with others of his opinion, explains the start of the narrative of Genesis handed down to us by *Moses*—namely, *In the beginning* **GOD** *created the heaven and the earth*, etc.—in this way: *in the first things, or firstly,* **GOD** *created the heaven and the earth*. Attempting to refute this exposition of the word *Beginning*, the followers of *Paracelsus* propose three doubts to us: namely, whether by *in the first things or firstly* the interpreter intended to refer the name *Beginning* to *some time, or to order and time together, or whether he intended to designate the first place by it*. To which questions, they respond by denying them absolutely and confidently; to the *first*, indeed, because time did not yet exist, as it only had its origin from evening and morning; whence they in no way admit that interpretation of *beginning*. To the *second*, because it would be absurd to place the world in time and order before its ma-

Finally, they contend that the name of "Beginning" cannot be adapted to *Place*, using a reason taken from these words in the first chapter of the Gospel of *St. John*: *The Word was in the beginning*; for to wish to include the Word of **GOD** in a place is believed to be a wickedness by all the pious, since He is incomprehensible; and furthermore, even before the creation of the world, there was no place, because there was nothing placed. With these and similar arguments, I say, *Paracelsus* <note>The famous Swiss-German physician and alchemist</note>—along with some of his disciples—attempts to refute the aforementioned opinion of the opposing sect. He accepts the primordial words of *Moses* in this sense: *In the great uncreated mystery* **GOD** *created the heaven and the earth* <note>original Latin: "in mysterio magno increato creavit DEUS cælum & terram"</note>; that is, in the first matter—formless, dark, and potential—God created the heaven and the earth. And this Paracelsian opinion does not seem to differ from that of the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy</note>, who, existing with the view that the world is eternal, *established that prime matter is also co-eternal with the World itself*. Some philosophers also rise up against the creation of *Hyle* <note>A term for raw, unformed matter</note> with this argument: *What is formless is not created; but hyle is formless; therefore hyle is not created.* The major premise is clearly demonstrated by the fact that *creation is the bringing into actuality, and making something out of nothing: but hyle in its nature is nothing in actuality, wherefore it is certain that it lacks all form*. But referring all these ambiguous and controversial disputes of those philosophers to my superiors in Philosophy, and to those far more learned than me in these matters, I shall at least descend to the description of that matter.

## CHAPTER IV.

### Description of Prime Matter, or the Subject of the Universal Work.

**M**ATTER or the subject, in whose womb that greatest Architect of our Macrocosm <note>The "Great World," referring to the universe as a whole</note> arranged his structure, is that Philosophical <term>hyle <note>original Greek: ὕλη; the fundamental raw matter of the universe</note></term>; which physicists have called "absolutely first matter": because, just as nothing is more common, so also nothing is found more unknown than it. Regarding its investigation, two among the other ancient philosophers especially devoted their studious efforts: the first of these, namely *Thales* (with whom *Heraclitus* and *Hesiod* agreed), after long study and many sleepless nights, *constantly affirmed that water is the first matter of things*, and confirms the reason for his opinion, *because, he says, the seed and nourishment of all things is moisture*. Both *Pagans* <note>original: "Ethnici"</note> and *sacred writers* seem to approve of this sentiment. For the former, for this reason, consecrated *Neptune, Oceanus, and Thetis*; the latter, among whom I name that divine leader of Philosophy, *Moses*, called this matter the *abyss and water*; and *St. Peter* in 2 Peter 3 indicated to us that *the heaven and earth were from water and through water*. The other diligent investigator of this matter was *Anaxagoras*, who after much labor endured in this study, was of the opinion that *the first matter of things was a rude and undigested mass, called Chaos*, with whom the *Poet in the Metamorphoses* <note>The Roman poet Ovid</note> also seems to agree. Other philosophers have written differently about this matter: For indeed *Anaximander* established "infinite principles" as the material origin, *Anaximenes* "infinite air," *Diogenes* "air endowed with divine reason," *Plato* an "invisible and formless species," *Zeno the Stoic* the "substance of fire turned through air into water," the *Epicureans* "atoms," and *Empedocles* the "four elements"; nearly all of whom, on account of the hidden and concealed arrangement of this mystery—which without a doubt is truly and essentially known to **GOD** alone—wrote with uncertainty and indeterminately, contradicting one another, and

### ON THE PRINCIPLES OF THE MACROCOSM
->D<-

...whatever they strongly and probably conceived in their minds, they immediately set forth in their books. This is what *Plato* seems to sufficiently prove in his *Timaeus* when he describes this matter as "a thing perceptible without the senses, and scarcely believable by false reasoning." <note>original: "esse rem sine sensu perceptibilem, & ratiocinatione spuria vix credibilem"</note> From these words, it is clear that his knowledge in this matter is like a dream or mere imagination. In this regard, *Augustine* also seems to agree to some extent, as is evident from the following discourse: 
> When he says, "I conceive of something formless, I understand nothing before I understood it; just as darkness is seen by seeing nothing, and silence is heard by hearing nothing." <note>original: "Cum, inquit ille, aliquid informe concipio, prius nihil intelligo, quàm intelligebam; quemadmodum nihil videndo videntur tenebrae, nihil audiendo auditur silentium."</note>

*Aristotle* himself admits the difficulty of knowing this thing, asserting that this matter can neither be known nor described by itself, except by analogy—that is, through examples taken from external qualities. Hence, he and other Greek philosophers likened it to <term>Hyle</term> <note>original: "$\tilde{\upsilon}\lambda\eta\nu$"; a Greek term originally meaning "wood" or "timber," used by philosophers to describe raw, unformed matter.</note>, which is to say, a certain immense forest whose wood is fit for constructing any house, machine, or other object. For this reason, the divine *Moses* compared it sometimes to a void and empty earth, and sometimes to waters and the abyss. *Hermes Trismegistus*, in his *Pimander*, likened it to a certain horrendous shadow migrating into a moist nature. *Plato* called it the mother, nurse, and seat of generated things, because it contains and nourishes all. *Augustine* called it darkness and silence, as was said; *Pythagoras* called it duality. *Some* compare it to a mirror in which the soul of the world is seen; *others* to wax and clay, which are fit to receive any impression. *There are also those* who wish to compare it to an ointment, which is ready to receive and retain any scent. And from this, it follows that *Plato* called it "infinite," namely because of its inclination toward infinite forms—although this matter could also be called infinite as far as we are concerned, for only GOD knows how far this potential extends beyond the curvature of the world. *Aristotle* seems to understand this same point *in his book On the Heavens and the Earth*, where he says that outside the heaven there is neither place, nor body, nor dimension, nor fullness, nor time, nor number, nor measure of movement; and consequently, nothing exists outside the heaven except this formless matter, to which the aforementioned properties alone belong. Hence also, *Hermes Trismegistus* in his sacred discourse speaks these words: 
> "An infinite shadow," he says, "in the abyss, etc."

We conclude, therefore, from all the writings of both ancient and modern philosophers, that this first matter is the <term>Primordial Being</term> <note>original: "Ens primordiale"</note>: infinite, formless, having the potential to be either something or nothing. It possesses no quantity or dimension, since it can be called neither small nor large; no quality, since it is neither subtle nor thick nor perceptible; no property nor inclination; neither moving nor resting; and without any color or elemental quality. Yet, it is the first passive recipient of all actions and is capable of containing all things. For this reason, it is called the "Mother of the World," in whose womb the ethereal spheres—decorated with glowing fires—and the four elements suspended below near the center are contained, just as if in a mother’s uterus.

In this place, we have depicted an imaginary image of this formless matter, imitating the descriptions of *Hermes Trismegistus* and the truthful *Moses*, under the form of a blackest smoke, or a vapor, or a horrendous shadow, or a dark abyss, or finally, a certain raw, undigested, and imperceptible mass.

<summary>This page explores the concept of "First Matter" (Materia Prima) through the lenses of various historical authorities, defining it as a formless, infinite, and passive substance that serves as the "Mother of the World." It synthesizes views from Plato, Aristotle, Hermes Trismegistus, and Augustine to describe the primordial state of the universe before form was imposed.</summary>

## CHAPTER V.
### *On darkness and privation.*

**A**UGUSTINE, in his arguments against the *Manichaeans* <note>A dualist religious movement that viewed the world as a struggle between light/spirit and darkness/matter</note>, asserts that <term>privation</term> <note>the lack or absence of a quality that should normally be present</note> is nothing other than darkness, which is defined as the absence of light. But if the meaning of darkness is correctly considered, we will perceive that it extends more widely than the term "privation." For, as *Moses* bears witness, *darkness was upon the face of the deep* <note>referring to Genesis 1:2</note>, before light or form was created; <term>privation</term>, however, cannot be so named except in relation to some established state <note>original: "positionis"</note>, that is, where there is the absence of some form that preceded it. Therefore, to agree with *Augustine*, *every privation is darkness*, that is, [the absence] of form...

the removal of light; *but not the other way around*: From this it is clear that darkness, or "privation" <note>In philosophy, privation is the absence of a quality that should normally be present, like blindness is the privation of sight.</note>, happens only to things subject to corruption since the creation of the world. Such things include the elements and the things made from elements in the lower heavens. For since the "form" <note>The "form" is the internal design or essence that makes a thing what it is.</note> of the elements is not enough to satisfy the "appetite" of matter (which explains their volatility and imperfection), it is necessary that this same matter always craves a new form. Since it cannot satisfy this craving without the absence of the previous form, it follows that corruption or "putrefaction" <note>The process of breaking down or decaying.</note> must precede that new form. The old form must first be extinguished and stripped away. The signs of this are darkness, which is nothing other than blackness and obscurity, signifying the absence of light and form—the very things from which the beauty and essence of the putrefied thing were previously derived and known. 

The Chemical Philosophers <note>Alchemists.</note> have called this blackness by many names. Among these, they most often called this sign of putrefaction the *raven’s head* <note>original: "caput corvi." In alchemy, the "Nigredo" or black stage symbolizes the death of the old state and the beginning of the Great Work.</note>. By this, they understood a purely accidental principle and a medium that joins matter and form together, like a groom joining with his bride. This dark color perishes immediately after generation <note>The birth of the new substance.</note>. Here, therefore, it should be considered that when the matter of a thing is submerged in darkness, it exists as a thing stripped of form, much like the "prime matter" of the macrocosm <note>The universe as a whole.</note> before the production of light. For it has the potential for the presence and beauty of a certain light, without which it can never be led into "actuality" <note>The state of being fully realized or functional.</note>. 

It must be understood, however, that the word *darkness* has a double meaning among the Philosophers. *Sometimes* it is taken to mean a certain dark substance, such as dark and black air, or the shadow of some opaque body. *At other times*, it is taken as a mere "accident" <note>A property that can change without changing the identity of the thing, like color.</note>, specifically for the color of blackness. In the first sense, it is described by *Moses* as being "upon the face of the deep." In the second sense, it is held to be the privation of light. However it is taken, *darkness is always entirely opposed to light*. For darkness makes a thing hidden and concealed; it brings about fear and sadness, removes shame, invites sleep, and is a great friend to rest; thus, it is the companion of matter. Light, however, makes a thing known and manifest; it takes away fear and brings confidence, courage, and joy. It makes one feel shame, drives away lethargy and laziness, and does not allow an animal to rest, since it excites life and movement in its blood. For light is, as was said above, the origin of forms and actions.

***

# CHAPTER VI.
### *Concerning the universal essence, by which the Creator informed the matter of the universal work.*

The most wise Maker of the world, who said, *I am the light of the world, the true fire, and the father of lights* <note>original: "Ego sum lux mundi, verus ignis, luminiumque pater."</note>, decreed that this formless matter—this foundation of nature or the subject of the universal machine—should be made the *dwelling place of forms* and, to speak with Plato, their nurse. He did this so that by their presence, the mass of the entire abyss, which was overwhelmed by darkness, might be made visible and perceptible and brought into actuality. To accomplish this with ease, He first communicated the clarity of His fire to the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest, most spiritual heaven made of pure light or fire.</note> (for *his breath*, which *Mercurius Trismegistus* calls the GOD of fire and the divinity of spirit, *was carried over the waters*). Then, He communicated it secondarily to the ethereal heaven, the sun, and His other spherical creatures, so that through their power—acting as instruments—the ethereal heaven might be decorated, and form and life might be instilled into the lower creatures. 

This fiery creature, created on the first day according to the likeness of the divine idea and given as the first and most excellent gift from GOD for the perfection of the rest of His structure, *Moses* called LIGHT, *Artephius* called clarity, *Plato* called the Idea, and *Aristotle* called the divine and best principle. For Aristotle himself, in his book on the five substances, recognizes that light gives to all things their form, beauty, and being, since without it no matter can be manifested or known, but remains hidden and as if only in potential. This same thing *Mercurius Trismegistus*...

Finally, almost all agree with a unanimous consensus to call it the <term>prime act</term><note>The 'prime act' (actum primum) refers to the first realization or activity of a thing's essence in Aristotelian philosophy.</note>, *form, species, and essence*. This light, therefore, is a unique substance, and a corporeal one, existing simply in itself, the simplest of all things, the most worthy and noble; indeed, it is of such great nobility, according to the testimony of **Augustine** in his work *On Genesis*, that even corporeal things are judged more perfect and noble the more they participate in light; whence he asserts that light holds the first place among bodies. And this *Substance of Light* the same **Augustine and Dionysius** define—on account of its sweet heat—as *being a pure fire, unburnable, immeasurable, and indivisible, increasing and multiplying itself into infinity, extending itself everywhere, and present to all in a single moment, comprehending all things, yet not to be comprehended, always shining in itself, but invisible and unknown to others by its own nature:* <note>original: "ignem puram, incombustibilem, immensurabilem..."</note> because it never illuminates visibly unless some body intervenes whose matter is fit to be illuminated. And it is for this reason that the substance of the middle heaven, although it is very bright in itself and holds the first place among composite bodies due to the abundance of its light, nevertheless does not illuminate during the nighttime.

From the source of this super-celestial light is undoubtedly derived that invisible fire of **Zoroaster and Heraclitus**, from which they teach that all things were brought forth; whose power, though invisible, all animals and all other sublunary creatures—indeed, even the sea itself in its ebb and flow—seem to recognize and feel deeply by day and night. Finally, the Philosophers call this fire *simple act* because of its vitality; <note>original: "actum simplicem"</note> nothing is more mobile than it, or faster and more powerful in its motion, nothing more subtle, or more penetrating because of its subtlety, nothing more useful or full of virtue, nothing more beautiful or more uniform in its essence, nothing more capable of perfecting and exalting beings according to a greater or lesser degree, and nothing dissolves them more quickly or removes their bonds more easily, as **Chalcidius** testifies in his commentary *on the Timaeus*.

From these points it is manifest, contrary to **Damascene and Aristotle** (who in this matter somewhat contradicts himself), that light is not an <term>accident</term><note>An 'accident' is a property that can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist; the author argues light is essential, not just an added property.</note>, which is nothing in itself; hence it does not seem likely that it would make the substance in which it inheres more noble, since that is the function of an essential form, from which both the name of any body and its very being are derived. We conclude, therefore, that *light is either uncreated*, namely GOD giving nature to all things; (for in GOD the Father himself is the true light; then in his Son the illuminating and enriching splendor; and in the Holy Spirit the burning radiance surpassing all understanding) *or it is created by that uncreated light*, which is either the simplest soul, as it were, and true essential form of each of the three heavens, informing the clearest spirit as its bond and vehicle. 

Whence **Iamblichus**, on account of the clarity of the ether, thought that it was nothing other than light itself, even in any of their composite creatures: for in the angels there is a certain infused, shining intelligence, poured over all the limits of reason, yet received in different degrees according to the nature of the recipient; it descends thereafter to the celestial bodies, where it produces in them a life-giving power, whence life and effective propagation, along with a life-giving splendor, are bestowed upon lower things: In humans, it is the bright discourse of reason; in other animals, it is a hidden fire clearly governing the actions of life and sense; in vegetables, a certain bright soul hiding around their centers, causing growth and multiplication into infinity: in minerals, it is also a spark of splendor driving them toward the goal of perfection. Therefore, from the supernatural light created on the first day arise the differences of the macrocosm of the heavens and of the bodies existing in them (for they are distinguished by purity, simplicity, and dignity): for according to the degrees of excess or deficiency of this essence, the highest heaven differs from the lowest, and the lowest from the middle,

...and every element of each heaven is found to be either lowered or exalted by the presence or absence of this <note>The author is referring to the divine light or "formal" principle discussed previously</note>: for the further matter stands from the nobility of form, the coarser, more impure, darker, and unworthier it is. From these things it is manifest that, if clarity and light were removed from the world, one must believe that the world's matter would return to its first state and disposition, nor would any particle of it be superior to the others in dignity, location, or any other quality or quantity. ### TREATISE I. BOOK I.

Here, the shining form <note>original: "forma lucida"</note>, beginning to appear and shine forth in a circle within the womb of the abyss of primordial matter or of darkness, drives the particular darknesses and the thicker part of the matter contained within the circle of light toward the center by its own power. Thus, the watery spirits now begin to be revealed; they are thinner the closer they are to the seat of light, but thicker the further they are removed from that seat of light.

->*Demonstrations by which it becomes manifest that, if the action of the shining form should cease, or if it were entirely absent, the world and its matter must necessarily return to the first abyss and the dark primordial matter <term>hyle: a Greek term used by ancient philosophers and early scientists to describe the unformed "stuff" of the universe before God or Nature gave it shape</term>, according to the reasons expressed by us above.*<-

Since the presence of solar light is closest and most similar to the shining creature created on the first day <note>This refers to the "First Light" of Genesis, which many mystical philosophers believed was a pure spiritual light distinct from the sun</note>—given that, according to the Fathers of Theology, the solar body was made on the fourth day as a receptacle for all those same rays—we will therefore begin this demonstration of ours from its power and effect. By this, we shall prove that the presence of light itself caused this formal alteration in the primordial matter, and that in its absence, that same matter, once shaped, would return to its pristine—that is, unformed—state.

Therefore, let a globe <term>pila: here meaning a hollow sphere or bulb used in scientific apparatus</term> be made of lead, of sufficiently large capacity, such that the thickness of its material is not too thin—so that it is not easily broken—nor too porous, lest air penetrate through it. In its top, let a hole be made, into which a certain curved tube made of the same material is fixed, descending nearly to its bottom, in such a way that no air can enter or leave except through the hollow of that channel. Let the other end of the same channel or curved tube be extended nearly to the bottom of another vessel filled with water. Let the globe be A, the channel or tube B, and the vessel filled with water C. 

We conclude, therefore, that the sun’s rays, by heating globe A, will expel the thick and smoky air contained in globe A through channel B into vessel C, to the bottom of the water contained in that vessel C. This thick air, expelled by the power of the heat, will mix with the water of vessel C and create many bubbles, one after another. But as soon as the sun has withdrawn, or if some other object is placed between the sun and the globe, or if the globe itself is placed in the shade, the former state will return to the hollow of the globe through the absence of the sun and the cooling of the globe—namely, the same portion of thick and dark air that was in there before. 

The proof is as follows: since the vacuum cannot find air of the same nature in the water-filled vessel, it draws the water itself (which is even thicker) into the place of the air; necessity forces as much of this water to move up into the globe as the solar rays first expelled from it through the refinement and purification of the air. By this experiment, it is demonstrated, as if with a finger pointing, that all purification in this world and all inequality or diversity in thickness or thinness proceeds from the act of essential light itself, and by its presence, such a difference in state is maintained until the end of the world. By this very experiment, it is infallibly proven that if the light fails, all things will return to their pristine state. Two experiments written below, drawing their effects from elementary fire, declare this truth even to ordinary eyes. We have depicted the demonstration of this first experiment thus:

Similarly, the following pneumatic experiment <term>spirituali: 'spiritual' here refers to pneumatics or the study of air and 'spirits' (gases), rather than religion</term>, taken from the conclusions of Heron <note>Heron of Alexandria, a 1st-century mathematician and engineer famous for his mechanical inventions.</note>, confirms the preceding operation of nature: where dense air enclosed in the upper region of the hearth is thinned <term>subtiliatur: refined or made less dense through heat</term> by the presence of a fire lit above it. In this thinning, its sootier part is expelled through opening A into the lowest region, as if into a part further away from the active force <note>The 'active force' or 'actor' is the heat from the fire.</note>, so that the air of the upper region is illuminated and activated. But when the fire is extinguished, that sooty and thick portion of air, which had exited from the upper region, returns to its own former seat and joins with the thinned air, so that the aerial spirit then returns to its former state of bulkiness, just as it was before the arrival of the fire.

From these things, therefore, it is manifest that all things given form by essential light <term>lux essentialis: the divine light that gives shape and life to the material world</term> take on their formlessness again once the benevolent gaze of light and its formative presence have left and deserted them. Consequently, when light ceases, all things will lapse back into the former nature and disposition of dark matter <term>hyle: the Greek term for the primordial, unformed 'stuff' of the universe</term>.

# CHAPTER VII.

->*Concerning the two simple and primary qualities, derived from the two first substances;*<-
->*likewise concerning the two qualities arising from those simple ones.*<-

**F**rom each of the two aforementioned constituent parts arises a certain simple nature, which reflects the disposition of its source. For when the fiery spirit was carried over the waters (which we called the source of light and the origin of forms above), it produced a certain essential quality accompanying its actions. Therefore, the Philosophers <note>Likely referring to natural philosophers and alchemists such as Robert Fludd, who sought to explain the physical world through spiritual and chemical principles.</note> called this an active quality, as it were the effect of form or of most lively light; they also named it <term>heat</term> <note>original: "caliditatem"</note>. Its nature is to penetrate all the way to the center of thickness, and by penetrating, to open dense and solid things, and by expanding them, to dissolve and loosen them. After their dissolution, it scatters and separates the coarse from the subtle, and purifies them through rarefaction <note>The process of making a substance less dense, often through heating.</note> or thinning, making them volatile and light; thus they are elevated by nature and carried upward. Finally, it gathers together things of a similar kind <note>original: "homogenea"</note>, digests, matures, fixes, and perfects them; but things of a different kind <note>original: "heterogenea"</note> it cuts, scatters, drives away, and beats back. It performs all these things insofar as it is immediately derived from the most noble and subtle body of all, and accompanies its most thin and noble substance. Having thus declared the origin of this active nature, it remains for the quality or simple nature of the other constituent part—namely, the passive one—to be revealed, since no action can occur without a disposed capacity for being acted upon. Hence it is necessary that such a disposition [originate] from <term>hyle</term> <note>A Greek term for primordial "matter" or the raw substance of the universe before it is shaped by light or spirit.</note> or the primary macro-

...the matter of the cosmos <term>macrocosmi: the "Great World" or the universe at large</term> is derived, buried in darkness before the rise of heat. For with the first appearance of light, shadows began to move; and just as heat was introduced by the motion of light, so too—by the motion of the substance of the abyss <term>abyssi: the primordial, unformed chaotic state of matter</term>—another quality is produced. This quality is called "passive" (insofar as it is acted upon more than it acts) because it endures the actions of heat. This passive quality accompanies the thicker substance of matter and is intensified or diminished according to that matter's thickness, much like heat is perceived as more intense or more relaxed according to the abundance or scarcity of the essence of light. Therefore, the nature of coldness, revealed by the rise of heat, is entirely opposed and adverse to warmth. Because of heat’s subtle penetration, coldness resists it; by resisting, it gathers, restricts, and condenses the more impure, thicker, and darker parts of the substance of the abyss, drawing them toward the center of the cosmos.

This is because the central point of the earth is the part most distant from the world's circumference and, consequently, the seat in which coldness

Through the mutual action and passion <note>original: "actione & paſſione"—in this context, "passion" refers to the state of being acted upon or receiving an impression.</note> of these two, certain parts of the macrocosm are made more subtle (the upper parts) according to the retreat of cold and the approach of heat, while certain parts are thickened (the lower parts) according to the absence of heat and the presence of cold. Thus the world and its distinct regions were made; if these natures were to fail, it is necessary that all things return to their former state, reduced from "something in act" to "something in potency." <note>A reference to Aristotelian philosophy: "actuality" (the thing as it exists now) vs. "potentiality" (the raw materials or possibility of the thing).</note> From these simple natures or qualities, two other dispositions arise, which Artefius <note>Artefius was a medieval author to whom many alchemical and Hermetic texts were attributed.</note> called "the simples derived from simples": namely, moisture and dryness. The first of these, moisture, arises from the mixing and temperament of the two primary simples; for if heat is joined with an equal part of cold, the nature of moisture is created. We call "dryness" that quality joined with either heat or cold where moisture is entirely absent. It is clear, therefore, that dryness is nothing other than the absence of moisture, and thus these two qualities are called opposites; nevertheless, they are passive in respect to the primary simples, as we shall declare below in its proper place.

## CHAPTER VIII.

->*That two things concur for the existence of first matter: under what form first matter appears when brought into actuality? and that it is thick and subtle water.*<-

---

For the existence of first matter <note>original: "materia prima"; the fundamental, unformed substance of the universe in alchemical and Aristotelian thought</note>, two things are required: the first is a certain Being in potentiality <note>Something that exists as a possibility but has not yet taken physical form</note>, which is the subject of that hidden matter; the other is a sort of dark veil of the same, which removes the impression of any specific thing from it as long as it is present, which is called Darkness by Moses. By the presence of these things, beings are said to exist in potentiality, but by their absence, they are said to be brought from potentiality into actuality. This matter, while still unformed, **Moses** called the abyss <note>original: "abyssus"</note>, reporting that *darkness was over the face of the abyss*. But as soon as the Spirit of the Lord was said to move over the waters, bestowing a fiery vigor upon them, the darkness gradually departed; and what was previously called an abyss because of its gloom, now beginning to take form, claimed for itself the name of "waters." For it was seen to represent the appearance of water before it was reduced into spirit through refinement. This even the divine **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic writings are attributed</note> **in his Pimander** <note>The "Poimandres," the first and most famous book of the *Corpus Hermeticum*</note> seems to assert, saying that *a dreadful shadow, sliding down in an oblique revolution, migrated into a humid nature—that is, was converted into water; and in his sacred discourse, he says that an infinite shadow, and moreover water and a thin intellectual spirit, were in the chaos through divine power*.

Those things, therefore—namely the darkness—are dispersed by the presence of specific light; while this—namely the matter of the same—is purified from the dark gloom by the clarity of light. It is then called "subtle spirit," and from a thing once completely hidden and covered with the sooty face of dire gloom, it is now rendered visible, pleasant, very transparent, and indeed most clear. However, it is more so in one part than another, depending on its position farther from or nearer to the source of light. For its lower part is turbulent, and becomes thick and dense because it is compacted and defiled by humid vapors and earthy exhalations which the dark abyss vomited and exhaled from its depths. From this, winds are stirred up by the strenuous agitation of this matter, as are clouds, thunder, hail, and snow. Therefore, this part of the waters is called corporeal and corpulent.

The middle part, however, is not entirely bodily, nor plainly spiritual; but according to the **Philosophers**, it is as if not a body, but almost already a soul, or as if not a soul, but almost already a body—that is, it participates in both extremes. And because the luminous soul, possessing the upper part and rendering it entirely formal, deviates from its opposite—though without it, corporeal creatures cannot live—the Creator ordained this middle spirit, besides the purpose of separating the waters from the waters, to be a receptacle and vehicle for the soul. Through this vehicle, the soul may move toward lower things, so that it may be further introduced through them into bodies, and thus exhibit its powers to their limbs by means of this vehicle. And it is for this reason that **Philosophers** call it the spirit of the world <note>original: "spiritus mundi"; a vitalizing force that permeates the universe</note>, and **Albertus** <note>Likely Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century philosopher and theologian</note> calls it the Mercurial spirit, because it has the power of penetrating and altering bodies. Likewise, the **Greeks** name it air and ether, as if a burning spirit, as if they were saying...

## TREATISE I. BOOK I.

...a spiritual receptacle and container for the fiery soul, bright and clear, descending from the Empyrean heaven <note>original: "caelo Empyraeo"; the highest part of heaven, believed by ancient philosophers to be composed of pure fire or light</note>: therefore, in this spirit or **quintessence** <note>the "fifth element" that permeates all nature and is more pure than the four earthly elements</note>, every generative and seminal power resides. Finally, the supreme part of this spiritual matter was so purified by the newly created light, and made so spiritual by its inexplicable splendor—as if intoxicated by its lucid and enlightened nectar—that almost its entire substance is nothing other than pure **essential form**. This is especially true when compared to the lower parts, by which the other dark parts of primordial <term>hyle<note>A Greek term for the raw, unformed matter of the universe.</note></term> are brought from potentiality into actuality. 

If any spark of this formal mass should descend into its middle region, it is immediately received by the middle spirit—namely, the ether—and is wrapped in its thin little body. Then both, namely the vehicle and that which is carried, descending downward, are enclosed in the body of the lower region in the same way that the soul itself descended into the middle spirit, as will be more fully explained at the end of the second book of this treatise. 

From these things, therefore, it is manifest that darkness relates to matter in potentiality <note>matter that exists but has not yet taken a specific shape</note> just as light relates to matter in actuality. Matter that has not been brought into actuality is like a substance overshadowed and hidden by a cloud of darkness; that is, it is something between "something" and "nothing," a being hardly imaginable because it is unformed and unknown from its prior state. This matter is indeed clarified, informed, and manifested by the presence of light, and is known from its subsequent state to exist in the form of thin waters. This is in agreement with Thales, Hesiod, Moses, and Peter the Apostle <note>The author is reconciling Greek philosophy with Biblical tradition</note>. Of these, the lower region is called the **air**, containing water, which is called "thick air" <note>original: "aër spissus"</note>, and the spheres of the upper sublunary elements; the middle region is called the **ether** and the middle spirit; and the supreme region is called the home of light and fiery love, as we shall demonstrate more extensively in its proper place below.

From this it is manifest that the elements are made from the varying action and passion of these simple natures, since every portion of matter called an "element" is derived and distinguished from them.

### CHAPTER X.

#### *On Chaos, and the principles of the creatures of the lowest heaven.*

<margin>*Chaos, or matter as a confused and undigested mass, in which all things—namely the four elements—were confused and mixed together; because from among them, earth and water, which are heavier than the others, rose up as far as the sphere of the moon; whereas fire and air, being lighter, descended even to the center of the earth.*</margin>
M<gloss>ultiple</gloss> is the prime matter of things, as is manifest both from what precedes and what follows. Of these types of matter, that which we called <term>Hyle<note>A Greek term (ὕλη) meaning "wood" or "raw material," used by philosophers to describe the most basic, formless state of matter.</note></term> above is the most remote from any composition. *The second is the matter of the elements*, distinguished by the predominance of coldness or heat, and called by various names because of its various locations and operations. *The third is*—and this, according to some, was that unformed mass of the matter of heaven and earth, gaping open from the beginning, out of which all things later came forth one by one through various species and their own proper forms. For without doubt, this was an unformed mass on the first day of creation in both lower heavens, hidden under a veil of blackness, reverberated by the light acting within it, and on the second day compressed into the lowest heaven. We can more correctly define this as an unformed mass of darkness, or of waters lurking in the darkness, supplying the material for the entire <term>workmanship<note>Latin: "opificio"; referring to the Divine construction or "Great Work" of the universe.</note></term>, with a small portion of the radiant rays of each heaven retained in that dark prison by the stickiness of the said waters. Yet these portions of light could not give form to anything without the help of the eternal fountain of light (which they received step by step on the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth days—that is, more and more according to the divine will of the Creator). For as of yet, nothing held its own proper place; for the portion of light belonging to the <term>Empyrean heaven<note>The highest, most spiritual part of the heavens, associated with pure light and fire.</note></term> possessed the center of the dark mass contrary to its nature, and that other portion, which was proper to the middle heaven, was higher up—that is, above the imprisoned light of the Empyrean heaven toward the hollow

They maintained that diverse natures must necessarily be drawn from this matter, both for the perfection of the macrocosm <term>macrocosm: the "great world" or the universe as a whole, reflecting the same structure as the "microcosm" of the human body</term> and also for the completion of the philosophical work <note>This refers to the "Great Work" of alchemy, the creation of the Philosopher's Stone</note>. 

However, philosophers have called the fourth and final matter the "first matter," which is closer to physical bodies and from which the compounds of the lowest heaven are immediately generated and multiplied. In animals, this is recognized as sperm; in plants, as seeds; and in minerals, as sulfur and quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury; in alchemical theory, all metals were thought to be composed of varying proportions of sulfur and mercury</term>. We shall treat these matters more extensively below. Moreover, we describe the **Philosophical Chaos** according to their common intention, as a state where hot things fought with cold, and moist things with dry.
