# TREATISE I. BOOK I.

Although we are ourselves eyewitnesses to these things, we can provide a better demonstration of this matter through the dissection <note>original: "anatomisatione"; here referring to the chemical separation of a substance into its components, rather than a medical autopsy</note> of any part of that mass. For according to *Giles de Vadis* <note>Giles de Vadis was a 16th-century writer on alchemy and "The Art of Distillation"</note>, there remains in the world <margin>Handwritten arrow pointing left</margin> a certain part of that matter which is well known to everyone. Indeed, in the exterior part of this same mass, I clearly perceived at first glance—at the home of a certain friend of mine—a foul, deep black, and heavy earthly substance. By its blackness and its horrific veil, all the remaining elements, and even the substance of the Sun and the sky itself, were so covered over that no natural order could be found within them. I discovered that everything there was <margin>Handwritten arrow pointing right from the left margin</margin> positioned contrary to the laws of nature. Specifically, I perceived that things which were light were pressed down toward the center, while things which were heavy dwelt near the mass's outer edge. For by dissecting this deformed body with the most burning <margin>Handwritten double arrow pointing right</margin> knife of nature—that is to say, fire—I saw fluid water right next to this deformed, black, and earthy crust appearing on the outer part of the mass. Thus, that middle part of the water, being more involved and joined with this earthy nature, flowed out first of all, following that earthly coldness which it held within itself in a clear and raw state. However, I perceived another part of that same element, which was closer to the fire and the center of the mass and was tinted and mixed on every side with the aerial spirit, distilling after that raw nature. Thus, I observed that air was mixed equally with water in the lower part of the aqueous sphere—that is, the part tending more toward the center of the mass. Yet, the moisture of this kind of air was not free from the rebellious dryness of the black earth. This earth had spread its power not only on the edge of the mass, where it held its chief and most royal seat in the midst of the confusion, but also throughout the entire mass, dispersing the vapors of its nature through it, so that no part of the whole mass existed pure and free from that darkest pollution. After the airy fire rose out of the abyss <note>original: "abysso"; the unformed deep or chaotic state of matter</note> of that chaos, it was foul and ill-smelling because of the earthly pollution.

From these things, it is certain that this fire was in a continuous war and conflict with that part of the aqueous substance which was imbued with air; for while that fire naturally sought and attempted to be refreshed by its airy food, it repeatedly experienced the constant injuries of that hostile water mixed with the said air.

<margin>Handwritten double arrow pointing right</margin> But from the middle and innermost center of the entire unformed mass, as if from the very <margin>Handwritten vertical bracket on the right margin from "point" to "demonstrate."</margin> point of the abyss, I saw the solar substance of the mass rise up miserably and as if out of purgatory—as if rising from the dead—still struggling with the impurity of the mass and appearing as if sick. I saw it being refined <note>original: "sublimari"; a chemical process where a solid is heated into a gas and then recollected as a purified solid</note> by a marvelous operation of wit and philosophical industry. And indeed, some Philosophers have called this dark part of the mass the **Central Sun**. By its operation, we are taught the manner in which, in the beginning of the world, this celestial Sun of ours—after a purification was first made in this lower place—was exalted into its incorruptible place, that is, into the heart of the ethereal heaven, just as we shall demonstrate more clearly in *Book 4 of this treatise, in the chapter on the Sun's birth*.

Once these precious gems had been extracted from that blackest mass and seized as if by violence, I found a certain dreg-like and very black matter <margin>Handwritten double arrow pointing right</margin> left at the bottom. Its blackness was manifest, **but its redness was hidden, having a near-metallic nature. This, like Lucifer, having fallen from heaven, was cast down into the lowest abyss**, <margin>Handwritten arrow pointing left</margin> because it strove to preside and predominate even over celestial matter.

This process is used as an allegory for the creation of the cosmos and the fall of heavy, "Lucifer-like" matter to the depths.</summary>

## CHAPTER I.

### *Concerning the world and its division.*

**M**ARTIANUS <note>Martianus Capella, a 5th-century Latin author who wrote on the liberal arts.</note> understands the term "world" in three ways. First, for that which is called the *Archetype* <term>Archetype: the original "blue-print" or divine model of the universe existing in the mind of God</term>; its substance is incorporeal, invisible, intellectual, and everlasting. According to its example and the divine image, the beauty and form of the physical world was crafted, as *Boëthius* <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), a philosopher whose works bridged classical antiquity and the Middle Ages.</note> testifies; and this world remains eternally within the divine mind. Second, it is used for the corporeal heaven, which is that "greater world" <note>original: "mundus ille major"</note> which is bounded and contained by the concave surface of the *Primum Mobile* <term>Primum Mobile: the "first moved" sphere, the outermost shell of the universe in traditional astronomy</term>; and this world is also eternal by the will of GOD. Or finally, it is used for man, who is called the "lesser world" <note>original: "mundus minor"</note> or Microcosm; in respect to his form he is said to be perpetual, but in respect to his matter, he is corruptible. 

We, however, not differing much from *Martianus’s* opinion, shall treat of a twofold world: namely, the *Macrocosm* <note>The Great World or the Universe</note> and the *Microcosm* <note>The Little World or Man</note>. We distinguish the former from man (the Microcosm) by regarding the entire space of prime matter as the world, the Cosmos, or the Macrocosm—that space which the spiritual light, or the Spirit of the Lord moving over the waters, encompassed in its circular embrace. Indeed, this circular portion of the abyss—consisting of various combinations of light and darkness arranged into distinct levels of purity and impurity—is distributed into three parts differing in their essential nature. 

The upper part is that space of the world in which the fiery spirit was carried, and where the primary substance of light is contained; it extends from the inner boundary of the *Sphere of the Trinity* to the outer surface of the starry heaven. The substance of this part of the world, because of the abundance of its "form" or light, is so subtle and pure that, compared to us, it is considered insensible and entirely imperceptible. Hence, the Philosophers have called it intellectual and spiritual in the highest degree. 

The middle part, however, is adorned with fixed and wandering stars (the planets); for it occupies that entire hollow of the universe contained between the outer surface of the Moon’s sphere and the inner surface of the *Primum Mobile*. The substance of this region is corporeal when compared to the upper part. 

Finally, the lower part of the world is all that space which the inner surface of the Moon’s sphere embraces. From this it becomes clear that the mass of the world is divided into two principal parts: one which is incorporeal, spiritual, most pure, and most subtle (the upper part), and the other which is corporeal. This corporeal part is again subdivided into two: one which is subtle, thin, and incorruptible (the middle part), and another which is impure, gross, and subject to decay. This last is the lowest portion of the world, which we shall hereafter call the "sublunary" <note>The region "below the moon"</note> and "elemental" region. 

Both ancient Philosophers and sacred writers have called these regions of the Macrocosm "Heavens." For they named the upper one the Empyrean Heaven <note>original: "coelum Empyreum," from the Greek for "in fire"</note>, because it is filled on all sides with spiritual fire or the substance of light. And this was that "third heaven" into which *Saint Paul* confessed he was caught up in spirit, and which he himself called *Paradise*.

## CHAPTER II.

->*That GOD before the creation of the world shone only for himself: Concerning the gift of love, which GOD gave to that part of primordial matter which forms the world: Why is the shape of the world spherical?*<-

---

<margin>He made darkness his secret place, and made his tabernacle with dark waters, and veiled it with thick clouds. Here is signified the portion of primordial matter outside the world: Darkness and clouds are around him. (Psalm 97, verse 2.) <note>original Latin: "Fecit tenebras locum suum secretum..."</note></margin>
The **MONAD** <note>The Monad refers to the singular, indivisible "One" or the divine source of all things in Hermetic philosophy.</note> according to Hermes Trismegistus (who is the light of the world) begot a monad before the ages—that is, a GOD of fire—and reflected his own heat back into himself. For this Father of Lights, before the creation of the world, shone only within himself and did not wish to reveal his brightness until he thought upon the creation of the world. (Psalm 18, verse 11). Then, says *Hermes Trismegistus*, he changed his form; that is, he manifested his hidden essence, by which he suddenly revealed all things. (Psalm 18, verse 12: At his brightness the clouds and dark water fled). This Almighty GOD, therefore, freely and without compulsion, determined by his ineffable wisdom to build the Macrocosm <note>The "Macrocosm" is the great world or the universe, often compared in this period to the "Microcosm" or the human being.</note> and, before its construction, to mystically determine its matter, essence, figure, dimension, and the connection of its parts. He chose matter for this structure from the womb of infinite <term>hyle <note>original Greek: ὕλης; referring to the raw, unformed primordial matter of the universe.</note></term>, matter which was suitable to be adorned with various virtues and essential forms. He wished to freely impart a holy gift of love to it, proceeding immediately from himself. For in the act before creation, GOD breathed, and the Spirit of his mouth—that is, a passive breathing proceeding from him by way of a gift of love—was carried over the waters. This means it moved over the watery sphere, or rather moved around and over the whole material of the corporeal world, namely over the two lower heavens as yet unformed, whose primordial matter was water, as *Saint Peter* testifies (2 Peter 3). It was carried, I say, without doubt in a circular motion in the world, made by the spiritual presence of that same Spirit over the convex surface of the material world. This motion is the most noble of all, through which the matter of the corporeal world and its simplest spiritual substance is distinguished from that mass of infinite *hyle* or unformed matter thrust outside both worlds. Thus the corporeal world received its convex boundaries or margins and its most capacious and noble shape, namely the spherical. Indeed, this is that high gift of God’s divine essence which GOD gave to it, having an aptitude most full of the power of his procession so that it might be given; it proceeds only by way of the gift of love, in which all other things are given. For all common gifts are said to be by reason of the love of that Holy Spirit, which is the infinite love proceeding from the Father and the Word. From his simple act, therefore, all virtues and essences are distributed as gifts to every part of the world by the command of the divine will, according to the sentiment of the royal *Psalmist*: *By the word of the Lord were the heavens established, and all their power by the breath of his mouth*. *Saint Paul* also seems to confirm this same thing: *Through the Holy Spirit*, he says, *all things are searched out and each is distinguished by its degree*. This Spirit of the Lord, therefore, which is a fiery love, was carried over the waters, imparting to them a fiery vigor as the divine will so commanded. From this, the first creature of the world, the most subtle, simple, noble, and active of all, first shone upon the world. This Spirit, then, even the Pagans recognized: For the *Chaldean Oracles* <note>A collection of mystical oracles from the 2nd century AD, often attributed to Zoroaster or Julian the Chaldean.</note> called it a "fiery love" proceeding from the Father and the Word—

<page-num>458</page-num>
<header>TREATISE II. PART VII. BOOK II.</header>

*A. The main wheel. B. C. Weights of one side. D. E. F. Weights of the other side. G. The carrying rod. H. The support for the rod. I. The small lifting wheel. K. Its gear-teeth <note>original: "pecten," literally "comb," used here to describe the teeth of a gear or rack</note>. L. The crown wheel. M. The gear-teeth of the crown. N. The interrupted wheel <note>A "rota interfracta" or interrupted wheel is one with teeth only on certain sections of its circumference, used to create intermittent motion.</note>. O. The Shaft or Axle. P. The small pulley-disc. Q. The cord. R. A weight of 4 pounds.*

The main wheel is constructed in this manner: it is divided into 12 equal parts on both sides, and 6 pegs are fixed to each side, arranged at equal distances from one another. They are placed so that any given peg stands in the middle of the two pegs on the other side of the wheel, rather than side-by-side. With the 6 weights now attached (of which there are 3 on each side, yet all 6 are on one side of the wheel's center), this wheel is found to be burdened with a weight of 15 pounds. This is because weight C, in a straight line, equals 4 pounds; D and E are approximately 7 pounds; and B and F are 4 pounds. Added together, these produce 15 pounds, as is clear from the first rules of the first chapter, and the first and second rules of the second chapter of the first book.

The wheel is now moved so that the lowest weight approaches the peg of the carrying rod; this rod, positioned near B and F, receives this weight by its hook. While adhering there, the weight is carried upward, and the wheel, now emptied at the bottom, continues its course. Meanwhile, the next peg—which follows B—approaches, and in the same place where B just was, it receives the weight brought to it by the rod. Thus, the wheel is always loaded in the upper part and unloaded in the lower part. This is because every time a twelfth part of the wheel turns, the rod must ascend, and while another twelfth part turns, the rod must descend again. 

The rod is raised by the small wheel I <note>The text says "L" in this sentence but the legend and context suggest "I" or the mechanism associated with the crown L.</note>, which, by turning three times, reaches the full height of the rod, elevating it to the desired peg. This small wheel is turned by its gear-teeth K by the crown wheel L. The crown wheel itself is turned once by its gear-teeth M by the interrupted wheel N <note>The text also refers to this as O in the next clause</note>. This interrupted wheel always has teeth on a twelfth part of its surface, occurring six times. It has other empty intermediate spaces of the same kind to release the rod, which then falls by its own weight. This fall forces the pulley Q and the crown M to return to their positions. However, lest it fall with too much force, it is suspended by a cord Q attached to another rod through the pulley-disc P; because as much as one rod falls, the other ascends.

The interrupted wheel is fixed to the shaft or axle of the main wheel and is turned by its force. The reason that similar instruments are placed on the other side of the main wheel is so that work is carried out continuously, loading and unloading the wheel; for when a weight is removed from one side, it is attached to the other. Thus, the wheel always has 5 hanging weights, and one weight always on the ascending rod.

But, although this theory of the Swiss Engineer <note>original: "viri Helvetici." This likely refers to a contemporary mechanic or a specific person whose designs Fludd is critiquing.</note> is sufficiently ingenious and probable—suggesting that 5 weights attached to the wheel should easily be able to pull and raise a single weight—nonetheless, because the force is not proportionate to the time, nothing is achieved here. The ascending weight must travel through the space of 5 weights (or through the space of as many parts as it takes for one of them to move), and the single ascending weight lasts only as long as the other five by reason of its long transit. Therefore, it cannot overcome itself.

We have described this invention of the Swiss Engineer and his error in this place so that those curious in this science may examine the knowledge of proportions with greater diligence and observe them carefully.

### CHAPTER III.

#### *Concerning the first three days of creation.*

**U**nderstanding the arrangement of the days established before the creation of the Sun <note>According to the Book of Genesis, the Sun was not created until the fourth day, leading to much debate on how the first three "days" were measured</note> appears to be a difficult task, as there arises a significant disagreement even among the Church Fathers <note>The influential early Christian theologians whose writings established primary doctrines</note> themselves regarding the nature of those days. For Basil <note>original: *Basilius*; St. Basil the Great (c. 330–379 AD), who wrote a famous series of sermons on the creation called the Hexameron</note>, Damascene <note>original: *Damascenus*; St. John of Damascus (c. 675–749 AD)</note>, and other Greek authorities argue that the light created on the first day produced the "day" through the emission of light, and produced the "night" through its withdrawal, according to the Divine will. But the Doctors <note>Referring to the Western or Latin Doctors of the Church, whose views likely follow on the next page</note>...

# TREATISE I. BOOK II.
### Page 50

->TREATISE I. BOOK II.<-

Latin authors likely say that this light performed a circulation, similar to the one now made by the Sun, and illuminated the hemisphere in which it was present; and thus darkness was brought into the opposite hemisphere because of the obstruction of the thicker, denser, and blacker matter which existed in the middle of the whole unformed matter. We, however, shall offer a twofold interpretation of those days—neither of which, perhaps, if considered somewhat more exactly, will seem to wander far from the limit of truth. 

The first of these is that the "day" before the creation of the Sun can be considered as primary, secondary, or tertiary light, extending itself through the transparent universe. In this way, night is understood as the dominion of darkness in that part where no light had yet shone. Thus, the first day is taken for the brightness generally dispersed throughout the entire <term>Empyrean</term> <note>The highest part of heaven, believed by ancient cosmologists to be composed of pure fire or light.</note> heaven, specifically after that light had driven the darkness downward from its region and had purified and refined the spiritual matter of its heaven according to the proportion of its action. The "morning" of this day was the first penetration of divine light into its darkness, and the beginning of the action of light in the upper darkness; not otherwise than how "morning" is named among us as that time when the rays of the Sun begin to penetrate into the obscure and dark mass of night. Similarly, "evening" is the lowest surface of this heaven, in which dark vapors still exist, as if on the surface of the middle region, and there they still revolve in an oblique revolution and terminate the action of the first day; and so it is in the others. Certainly, this exposition is not to be entirely rejected, since both day and night must be considered in respect to the subject to which the aforementioned dispositions of the two times ought to be applied. But in truth, the <term>Empyrean</term> heaven was entirely luminous and clear after its creation: whence it also received its name from "fire" <note>From the Greek 'pyr', meaning fire.</note>, and for that reason neither night nor darkness was tolerated in it in any way immediately after its creation. And this same thing can be said of the substance of the ethereal heaven. 

However, our second interpretation—which seems closer to the truth to us, as it agrees directly with the Latin Theologians—will clarify itself from the following declaration. For it is probable that the Divine Spirit, sent forth and moved over the waters before any creation, encircled them with a triple revolution, and each of its circuits produced a spiritual or supernatural day. Thus, by the first circuit, it established the first day, in which it perfected the <term>Empyrean</term> heaven and drove the darkness downward by one degree. By the second revolution, it brought forth the second day, in which, by the double presence of divine virtue, the darkness was pressed down by a second degree; and in this way, the divine light and virtue shone in the middle and ethereal region of the world. Finally, by its third and last revolution, through the third degree and to the final limit from the circumference, the darkness was scattered by the power of the third divine impression. And thus the tabernacle of the entire world was completed, and all the virtues and essences of its regions were produced by the power of the Divine Spirit. Here, therefore, were finished those three spiritual days, measured by the act of the Divine Spirit and related to the number of persons of the <term>Trinitas</term> <note>The Trinity: Father, Son (the Word), and Holy Spirit.</note>, all of whom acted toward the creation of the world.

> *For GOD the Father spoke; and by His Word the heavens were made firm; and by the Spirit from His mouth, all their power [was created].* <note>original: "Nam DEUS Pater dixit; & Verbo ejus firmati sunt cæli; ac Spiritu ab ore ejus omnis virtus eorum." This is a reference to Psalm 33:6.</note>

Therefore, in the span of these days, and after their completion, the heavens were produced and given essence by divine operation, in which the universal spirit of the <term>Macrocosmus</term> <note>The "Great World" or the universe as a whole.</note> received form and being. Soon after, the solar days, which are concerned with the more corporeal things of the world, obtained their origin. To produce the kinds of these creatures, the first three of these solar days came forth, just as the three spiritual days first shone forth to build the dwellings of the three heavens. For on the first solar day, which is the fourth from the beginning of creation, the stars or wandering planets and the creatures of heaven were created; on the second, all irrational animals; and on the last day, the lesser world or <term>Microcosmus</term> <note>The "Little World," referring to Man as a reflection of the universe.</note> was created and completed; not otherwise than how the <term>Macrocosmus</term> was led to its perfection on the last spiritual day. Who, therefore, can almost doubt...

# ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE MACROCOSM.
<page-num>51</page-num>
G 2

Why should the motion of the Sun after the world’s completion not be the same as the motion of the Spirit was before its perfection, seeing as God, after the limit of three spiritual days, established his tabernacle in the Sun itself? Therefore, through the Sun itself, as if by the only demonstration from effect <note>original: "à posteriori"; reasoning from observed results back to causes</note>, we can arrive at the true motion of that divine Spirit, by which it moved on any given day toward the composition of the world. Indeed, no one should hesitate to believe that the following days in creation were equal in dimension to the preceding ones, and consequently, that the divine Spirit moved in its revolution in the same time that the Sun now moves in its own. Rather, it seems that the solar body is like a mirror and the heart of the world, into which the supernatural rays of the Spirit shining from the Trinity are poured. By the power of this radiance, and beyond all human reason, that solar body is made visible, and it always provides a constant and immutable motion by divine will, producing days of the same length at all times as those in which creation was completed.

It seems, therefore, that the Holy Spirit, who appeared to the apostles in the form of a radiant and shining dove, circled the waters in a spiritual form, illuminating their darkness by its motion and pouring its rays into them. By leaving these rays behind after its departure so that the waters might be shaped by them, the Spirit clarified and illustrated all things spiritually in an ineffable way by its presence, no differently than the Sun does physically by its presence. And (to turn to the opinion of the Latin Theologians) that uncreated light, by pouring light into created things, performed the same circulation during the first three days of creation which the Sun thereafter completed each day by its own motion. It illuminated its sphere in which it resided no differently than the Sun illustrates its own; similarly, darkness was made in the opposite hemisphere because of the interposition of grosser, thicker, and more opaque matter in the midst of the entire formless mass or "dreadful shadow." We spoke of the motion of the divine Spirit over the waters in the preceding chapter, at the end of which we also depicted its motion on the first day of creation according to human understanding; we explained the reasoning for that emblem near the end of this fifth chapter.

## CHAPTER IV.

->*On the creation and nature of light, and on its operation, and the constitution of the Empyrean heaven, or the first region of the world.*<-

THE LORD SAID; *Let there be Light*, and on the first day the highest heaven was made, filled with light. For the contents of this heaven are nothing other than the most essential and spiritual substance of light, fashioned from a large portion of soul and a tiny bit of the thinnest Spirit. Therefore, it is called the fiery Spirit and the <term>Empyrean heaven</term> <note>From the Greek 'empyros,' meaning 'in fire.' In ancient cosmology, this was the highest, most refined part of the universe.</note>—that is, fiery and burning, as *Isidore* says; not because it burns like elemental fire, but because it is bathed on all sides by the splendor and clarity of light.

For this reason, I do not agree with the opinions of those who thought this heaven was immobile and at rest; for these properties are entirely contrary to the substance of light from which this heaven is fashioned. Since light is the first and simplest act, nothing is swifter in its motion. (*His lightning illuminated the world, and the earth—that is, the darkness—seeing him, was terrified and fled: Psalm 97, Verse 4.*) Therefore, by the presence of this creature or fiery vigor, the darkness and gloom of that still formless and obscure upper part are driven downward through a slanted revolution. This happens for two reasons: the first is that the hidden and potential quality of the shadow is now revealed by the fiery activity of the light and takes the name of "coldness." Since its disposition is in every way contrary to the quality of luminous heat, it flees and turns away from the operations of light and its object. It follows from this that the cruder and thicker part of matter, on account of the predomin— <note>catchword: "prædomi-" referring to "prædominantiam" (predominance)</note>

...the coldness predominating in it, it retreated more and more toward the center of the universal globe, which is located further away from the habitation of the primary light. The second reason is that the same relationship exists between light and darkness as between form and privation <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the active principle that gives identity, while "privation" is the absence of that form.</note>: for this reason, the darkness, avoiding the sight of the light like a "horrid shadow," <margin>As *Hermes Trismegistus* says</margin>—to use those words—slipped away in an oblique revolution and sought the center of the circumference. It is from this that this heaven is purified and cleansed to the highest degree, separating the subtle from the dense, and is illuminated and made to shine beyond measure, by driving all gloom from its margin toward the center. 

Therefore, this heaven, or the supreme and supernatural region of the world, is the habitation of the fountain of light, and as it were the fatherland and native soil in which the first-created light—the primordial beginning of things—was first placed. Hence it is called the "foundation of the world," by whose formal presence the appetite <note>The inherent "desire" or tendency of matter to seek a specific state.</note> of all the matter of this heaven is filled to the highest degree. For it is certain that the matter of this heaven is exceedingly thin and subtle, since its entire substance is formal <note>Consisting mostly of "form" rather than heavy, physical "matter."</note>: For according to <margin>*Aristotle*, 4th book of *Metaphysics*</margin> *Aristotle* in his 4th book of *Metaphysics*, where there is more form, there is less matter, and consequently, the thickness of matter proves a scarcity of form. Indeed, the multitude of the radiant form, through its actions, constantly thins the purer part of the matter of the abyss—retained in this heaven by divine will—and extends its mass wider through this thinning process <term>rarefaction|the process of a substance becoming less dense</term>, just as is perceived in the chemical art. There, if a thick substance in a sufficiently large glass vessel, <margin>Hermetically sealed</margin> <note>original: *Hermeticè sigillato*; referring to a vacuum seal used in alchemy.</note> is refined by a more vehement fire, its thinned parts naturally seek a wider place; thus the glass is broken so that the thinned vapors may find a freer space. 

So also the clear matter of this heaven extends itself very widely, thinned by the lovely heat of this heaven. And hence it is that, according to <margin>*Basil*, book 2 of the *Hexaëmeron*</margin> *Basil* in the 2nd book of his *Hexaëmeron* <note>A commentary on the six days of creation.</note>, this heaven extends itself wider than all other heavens. We conclude, therefore, that this heaven is the most noble form of all, spiritual and simple beyond all imagination, the greatest of all in quantity because of the thinning of its matter, the brightest in quality, and most full of fiery vigor. It is most active in action, and swiftest in the motion of its radiant substance; it is most sweet in the heat derived from its motion, most temperate, lovely, not burning nor destroying, but connecting all lower things in harmonious peace with proportional bonds. It preserves these things in its own spirit—which can scarcely be perceived by the imagination due to its subtlety—moving and living by itself, and existing in its own natural seat without the contact of any foreign thing or the hindrance of any coldness. In shape it is spherical, which it received from the motion of the Spirit that was "carried over the waters," and from the radiant power proceeding from it by divine will. By name it is called the **Empyrean**, meaning "fiery," as stated above. It is also called **Olympus** because of its clarity. It is also called **supernatural**, because it is spiritual beyond the laws of nature as opposed to corporeality; and **intellectual**, because it is not visible to us, but only intelligible, and perceivable only by demonstration from its effects <note>original: *a posteriori*</note>, or because it is most full of angels and intelligences.

## Description of the instrument.

<image-desc>A technical engraving of a mechanized water-lifting system. On the left, a large overshot water wheel is turned by falling water. Its horizontal axle terminates in a small lantern gear (H) which drives a large horizontal toothed wheel (G) at the base of a central vertical shaft. Near the top of this shaft is another horizontal toothed wheel (F), labeled "Ped: 37" (37 feet), which drives a small lantern gear (E) on a horizontal axle. This axle also holds a chain wheel (D). ### Explanation of the letters.

A. The *lift* <note>original: "haustrum seu pompa"</note> or pump.

B. The *small wheel* fixed at the bottom of the lift, over which the *pistons* <term>pistella: small circular discs or "rounds" that fit tightly inside a pipe to push water upward</term>, or rounds made of leather, revolve smoothly so that they may more easily move upward; it is fitted with iron hooks.

C.C.C. The *pistons* or leather rounds, by whose help the water is raised within the pump.

D. The *small wheel* through which the aforementioned rounds are elevated on high.

E. The *lantern gear* <term>pecten: literally "a comb," but in 17th-century mechanics, it refers to a spindle or lantern gear whose rungs engage with the teeth of a larger wheel</term> moving the wheels D and B.

F. The *wheel* driven by the lower wheel G, by whose teeth the lantern gear E is rotated.

H. The *lantern gear* moving wheel G.

### The use of this instrument.

This instrument is numbered among the wheels of the "first order" <note>This refers to machines that utilize a primary external power source—in this case, flowing water—to initiate a chain of motion.</note>. It is extremely useful for many purposes, as there is no doubt that through this arrangement of multiple wheels, a great quantity of water can be carried upward with very little effort.

The length of the lift A is 35 feet, while its width is 1 and 1/2 feet.

TREATISE I. BOOK II.

# CHAPTER VI.

## *Concerning the middle heaven and its various names, and the reasoning behind them.*

The middle region of the world, completed on the second day of creation, possesses various names due to the downward-tending operations of the matter of light. When considered by itself—that is, in respect to its own proper matter—it is called the middle spirit <note>original: "spiritus medius"</note> after the dispersal of the darkness. However, in relation to the higher heaven (that is, the luminous substance) and its mixing with the spirit of that realm, it is called the ether <note>original: "aether"</note>. Furthermore, insofar as it relates to the four lower elements that appeared and were distinguished on the third day, it is called the Fifth Essence <note>original: "Quinta essentia," often called the Quintessence; the pure, incorruptible material of the celestial bodies</note>.

By itself, therefore—that is, in its own proper substance revealed on the second day and purified of its gloom—it displays the form of the subtlest waters and of a certain vaporous and never-resting smoke. For this reason, among the Platonists, it is called the middle spirit of the world <note>original: "spiritus mundi medius"</note>, which we called the receptacle, bond, and vehicle of the essential light and the soul of the world <note>original: "animae mundi"</note> above in Chapter 5 of Book 1, where we also demonstrated the reasoning behind that name. 

But insofar as this spirit is the bond of the light descending from the spiritual source, by whose action a life-giving and natural heat is stirred up, it is to that extent called the ether—that is, "shining," according to Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), an encyclopedist who provided etymologies for many medieval terms</note>—because there is perpetual clarity and brightness there. Or, it is called "fiery" according to Anaxagoras <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher</note>, who asserted that everything that burns is called ether, since ether is nothing other than inflamed air. Thus, according to Greek grammar, it is derived from <term>αἴθω</term> <note>aithō: to kindle, burn, or shine</note>, which signifies "I burn"; the spirit of the air is, as it were, "ether-air," which is to say, a burning spirit. 

Because of this, Orpheus calls it the "Fiery Breath" <note>original: "Pyripnon"</note>, and Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note>, along with other Platonists, calls it the spirit in the middle of which they placed the soul of the world. And from this it follows that, according to Marianus <note>Likely Martianus Capella, author of an influential late-antique work on the liberal arts and cosmology</note>, in the ether there is perpetual day, because darkness never approaches that place; although its simple substance, divided from the stellar bodies, is invisible—that is, not perceptible to the eyes of mortals—as we shall declare more at length in the following chapter. 

Finally, it is held to be a single element, just as Aristotle maintains in his book *On Meteors* <note>The *Meteorologica*</note>, where he asserts that the ether of that place is nothing other than a unique element. Hence, it is necessary that this unique element be outside the number of the four lower essences that were soon to be produced in the lowest region. And for this reason, it is also called the Fifth Essence by the philosophers, in which no corruption is found, since the two contraries that induce putrefaction <note>In Aristotelian physics, decay is caused by the conflict between opposing qualities like hot and cold</note> are not found in that same element. 

From the reasoning behind these names, it is manifest that the matter of this region—formerly primary, but now made secondary through its reduction into an active state <note>original: "in actum," a philosophical term for moving from potential to reality</note>—is nothing other than a purest vapor, or a certain most subtle mist, generally called "spirit." Its form, by whose presence it is brought into an active state, is that light or clarity essentially gushing forth from the perennial source of the divine and super-celestial spirit, totally filling the spiritual appetite of this middle matter, as will be declared below.

# CHAPTER VII.

### *The composition of the middle heaven: why is it called the sphere of equality? And why is this region called the corporeal heaven in respect to the one above?*

---

Just as the Empyrean heaven <note>original: "cœlum Empyreum"; the highest, most spiritual realm of the universe, associated with pure light and fire.</note> was created on the first day from a single thing—namely, from the substance of light—and was composed of three-quarters of the thinnest fire and one-quarter of the most subtle spirit; and whereas, in respect to the lower regions, it is entirely **formal** <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "formal" refers to the 'Form' or spiritual essence of a thing, which gives it life and identity, as opposed to its physical 'Matter.'</note> and is called "fiery" because of the predominance of fire within it: So too, the matter of this second heaven, since it is more corporeal than that of the first and highest heaven, corresponds to its own luminous form in that necessary proportion by which matter is usually weighed against its form on equal scales. 

Thus, it is composed of one part fiery and most thin light—descending from the fountain of the Empyrean heaven through the <term>diaphragm of the crystalline sphere</term> <note>original: "sphæræ cristallinæ diaphragma"; a theoretical dividing membrane between the highest heaven and the planetary realms.</note>—and an equal quantity of "first matter," <margin>1</margin> which has already been shaped and has taken the name of "spirit." This is also what Pythagoras seems to assert when he writes that the sun, moon, and other stars are composed of fire and air. For this reason, following the consensus of the ancient philosophers, Artephius <note>A legendary medieval author of alchemical and philosophical texts.</note> named this region the **heaven of equality**; within its center, the wise have placed the **sphere of the soul**. From these points, it seems likely that the constitution of this heaven consists of two quarters of "middle spirit" and two quarters of that most beautiful substance, the "luminous soul," which is perfectly suited to satisfy the longing of that same spiritual matter and preserve it from corruptible changes.

We can prove by many arguments that this region is more corporeal <note>Physical or material.</note> than the highest realm. One reason is that where there is less "form," there is more "matter"; but in this second heaven, there is less form than in the Empyrean heaven (whose entire substance is completely formal). Therefore, there is more matter in this heaven than in the Empyrean. The major premise of this argument is taken from the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Refers to Aristotle's foundational work on the nature of reality.</note>. 

Another reason is that the mass of "first matter," before the appearance of light, always maintained one and the same state; for it lacked an "agent" <note>An active force or power that causes change.</note> whose actions could lead it from one disposition to another. Hence, it could be called neither thinner nor thicker, since all its potential and imaginable parts must be judged to be of the same condition in one potential region of the world as in another. However, since the nature of light is such that nothing more subtle exists, and nothing penetrates and opens bodies more effectively, it must always seek to thin out the parts of thicker matter so that it may act and move within them more readily and without hindrance. Thus, the more "formal" a thing is, the more subtle its substance must necessarily be. The reason for this is purely philosophical: formal light is moved by its own act, and by its motion it excites heat, the nature of which is to thin, dilate, and dissipate.

From this, it follows that the perennial fountain of light, created on the first day in the upper region of the world, soon revealed the hidden matter of that region and brought it into "act" <note>Moving from a state of potential existence to actualized reality.</note>. It shaped a thin and most subtle part according to its own nature, while thrusting the thicker portion of it downward toward the center into the middle region. It did this so that it could govern the simplest substance of spirit (which it brought into a kind of universal form) and carry it through all the hiding places of the world without any obstacle. And thus it is that the half-corporeality of this shaped region, reflected back into the middle, makes the middle more corpo-

### CHAPTER VIII.

*Concerning the reflection of the double darkness of the middle heaven into the lowest region of the world, and concerning the disposition and effect of its light—that is, the heat arising from it—and that light shines invisibly through itself and in itself.*

**T**HE power or clarity of the supernatural heaven, descending through the openings or rather the breasts <note>original: "ubera"; Fludd uses this anatomical term to suggest the divine realm provides life-giving nourishment to the lower world.</note> of the watery sieve by the Creator’s decree, and pouring itself downward from its perennial source into the middle heaven—which was still potential and unformed—dispelled the gloom and darkness of this part of matter by its presence. It drove them down toward the lowest region, which was still invisible and hidden. By this means, it rendered the substance of the middle heaven visible and formed: pure, subtle, thin, and far excelling the mass of the lower heaven in perfection and beauty. Indeed, this is that luminous essence springing from the first super-celestial source through infinite streams into every part of the celestial sea, which the ancients called the *ether* <note>The "ether" was believed to be a fifth element, distinct from earth, water, air, and fire, making up the heavens.</note>; we, however, shall call it *Secondary light*, because it is derived immediately from the first root. Likewise, we shall call the rays of the Sun and stars that penetrate into the lowest region of the world *tertiary light*.

This light, therefore, although secondary, is filled with such active and most vivid power that it frees this entire heaven from its primal impurity, dispels its obscurity, and causes it to glide away like a horrific shadow into the lowest part of the world in an oblique revolution. It thrusts the more imperfect and thicker parts down to the lower depths along with the darkness, separating the subtle from the dense. It illuminates the substance of this heaven and makes it ethereal; it fills its material spirit with its own perfection and satisfies the entire appetite of matter, so that it is not subject to corruption or putrefaction and is least of all afflicted by contrary forces, because all its parts are of the same kind <note>original: "homogeneæ"</note>.

Finally, this was that secondary essence which, for three days from the creation of the world, performed the duties of the Sun. On the fourth day, as <margin>Dionysius</margin> *Dionysius* <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian philosopher whose writings on celestial hierarchies were highly influential.</note> maintains, it passed into the substance of the Sun. Indeed, this is that simple act by whose operation this ethereal heaven is most skillfully decorated with ruddy fires. From this arise its motions, differing in various ways—namely, the eastern, the western, and that according to latitude, which they call "trepidation." Finally, a benign heat, most friendly and entirely necessary to the life of creatures, is kindled. This heat is more intense and sensible in this location than in the higher heaven because of the thicker substance of this heaven; for the denser the matter, the more vehemently it resists the acting force, and consequently, the actor acts more strongly upon the recipient. But the matter of this heaven, as has been said, is thicker than that of the Empyrean heaven <note>The Empyrean is the highest, most spiritual level of heaven, associated with pure fire or light.</note>. Therefore, light acts more strongly upon it, and the matter resists it equally, and consequently produces hotter effects to repel the injuries of the cold—which was once hidden but is now manifest because of the presence of heat—since it is the nature of cold to always accompany thicker matter. This heat, therefore, just as it is more intense than the supreme heat, is likewise far more temperate, subtle, and simple in respect to the lower heat; for it follows the disposition of the form from whose action it immediately proceeds. We conclude, therefore, that just as the substance of the form of this heaven was born from an immortal parent and is in no way to be corrupted, being exalted and most noble in dignity due to its origin, breathing life and soul into worldly creatures and nourishing <note>original: "vovens," likely a typo for "fovens" (cherishing/nourishing)</note> them with its light; so also its heat...

Indeed, it is necessary for the continuation of living bodies that light should shine for them in some way at night. For according to the teaching of <term>Hippocrates<note>original: "Hippocratis"; the ancient Greek physician. The author here cites a traditional belief that the "spirit" of the air must be tempered by celestial influence to remain breathable.</note></term>, if the life of the stars did not temper the thickness of the air during the night, the bodies and the very spirits of living things would be suffocated; and yet this impression of the stars is not perceived at night—indeed, their splendor, dispersed everywhere, is distinguished only with difficulty, except in the lights themselves.

### CHAPTER IX.

->*That the poles and circles of this heaven are merely imaginary, artificial,*<-
->*and in no way naturally suited*<-
->*to it.*<-

THOSE skilled in Astronomy have discovered many things more useful to the art of <term>cosmography<note>The science that maps the general features of the universe, including both heaven and earth.</note></term> than they are true. Although these things are fictional and artificial, they are to be esteemed as true and natural because they more readily guide the student in the art. Among these, they have placed two poles on the periphery of this heaven, opposite to one another, which they have called the ends of a certain imaginary axis or diameter passing through the center of the world, and the "vertices" of the world. They imagined the globe of the heaven to be turned upon these poles. They also described *circles* upon them, both *greater* and *lesser*. Some of the *greater circles* they made *immobile*, and others *mobile*. They established only two *immobile* circles, which they called *external*: one of these is the *Meridian*, drawn through the poles of the world and the *Horizon*; the other they called the *Horizon*, which divides the upper hemisphere from the lower and limits our sight. They made this horizon either straighter or more oblique according to the depression or elevation of the pole. Furthermore, they called the *mobile circles*, which they devised as *internal*, either *greater* or *lesser*. All the *greater* circles, except for one, lack width, and they distinguished them into *parallel* or *non-parallel*. The greater parallel circle they called the *Equinoctial*, because of its division of the world into two parts (for it divides equally...

These circles, I say, along with the two poles of the world, are merely fictitious and conceived solely by the imagination as technical terms, and were in no way connected to the nature of this heaven from its origin. 

Nevertheless, they are intentionally delineated by astronomers and cosmographers upon the convex surface of the firmament and its center for the easier explanation of those arts; for they attributed to each of the aforementioned circles a certain property suitable to the cosmographic art: *Whence in the meridian circle the Sun creates midday and midnight; the Horizon separates the visible part of the world from the invisible; the duty of the Equinoctial <note>original: "Æquinoctialis"</note> is that, as the Sun passes through its intersections—which the Zodiac makes in Aries and Libra—the equinox occurs throughout the whole world; hence it is called the Equator of day and night; both Tropics encompass the extreme movements of the Sun according to latitude, and separate the temperate zone from the torrid; to the Polar circles is given the task of bounding the frigid zones and separating them from the temperate; the Zodiac demonstrates the path of the seven planets; finally, to the two Colures a double duty is assigned: namely, to mark for us the solstices—the summer and winter ones—and also to show the equinoxes, namely the vernal and autumnal. All of these things, because they pertain more to technical history than to Physics <note>In this context, "Physics" refers to the study of the natural world and the actual substance of things, rather than the mathematical models of astronomy</note>, we shall reserve for the treatise on Astronomy.*

### CHAPTER X.

->*Concerning the third heaven, and its various names; Why is this lowest region called "heaven"?*<-

**B**EFORE the action of light upon the third and lowest region of the world, its container was like a shadow or a most thick and foul smoke, endowed with no visible form, but distinguished in a way by the density of its substance. For it was thicker below because of the presence of light and heat; but afterwards on the third day, once the operation of light—tending downward toward the earth to create the mathematical center—was completed, this heaven, as shall be said below, was given various names by philosophers, both more recent and ancient. For some, wishing to signify its dimension, called it the **sublunary region of the world**, denoting all that space measured between the concave surface of the middle heaven (or the sphere of the Moon) and the convexity of the physical center (or the Earth). Others, considering its elementary orbs, with whose bodies the capacity of this heaven is filled, called it the **elementary region**; although we have declared above that the upper elements also fill the heavens in a certain way.

Certain authors have called it **corruptible**, <note>original: "corruptibile"</note> since its matter is prone and disposed to seeking new forms and leaving behind old ones. That it is indeed heaven is demonstrated by a twofold reason: namely, both because it is a portion of "heaven" taken in its general sense—that is, the part by which heaven is distinguished from the earth—and also because in many places of the Holy Scripture the birds are called "the winged creatures of heaven," <note>A reference to Genesis 1:20.</note> where the word "heaven" is used not in a broad sense, but a strict one. From this, therefore, the four elements arise, differing in their seat, nature, dignity, and perfection. <insert>This is the true explanation of the Hermetic enigma, which affirms that the things above are only as the things below, that the gross is subtle and the subtle is gross, and that the matter of all things, taken by itself, is one and the same.</insert> <note>This refers to the *Emerald Tablet* of Hermes Trismegistus, a foundational text for alchemy and Hermeticism.</note> And without doubt, if the light created on the first day were extinguished by the divine will, it would seem by no means impossible to the Philosopher <note>Usually referring to Aristotle.</note> that the matter of the entire universe would return to the same state. For all matters are perceived to differ from one another only by reason of their form, and without form they possess the same condition, as they are contained under the same potentiality; thus, no part of <term>matter</term> <note>original: "ὕλης" (hylēs). The Greek term for the fundamental "stuff" or prime matter of the universe.</note> exists as more worthy, thinner, thicker, or lighter than another, nor should any other difference or quality be thought to distinguish it from the rest.

## CHAPTER XI.

->*Concerning the element of fire.*<-

The sooty matter, covered in darkness, was driven down from the highest heaven by the power of the primary light on the first day of creation into the region of the middle heaven. Subsequently, on the second day, it was thrust down and contracted from the middle heaven by the power of the secondary light—along with all the darkness of that region—into the third and lowest heaven. In this inferior region, the matter is now rendered very thick, dark, and rebellious, so that the power of the natural light of the third order (which is merely an offspring of the second heaven) is not sufficient to propel and depress that foul, shapeless, and black matter into the center of the universe, because of the great amount of cold lurking within it. Hence, the greatest architect <note>God, as the "Opifex" or divine craftsman.</note> ordained that the natural faculties of the warm third-order light should be strengthened by accidental means. For He willed that a certain foreign heat should arise, not proceeding immediately from the light, but from the violent agitation or motion of matter. For by the circular and rapid vibration and rotation of the middle heaven from the east to its opposite side—proceeding immediately from the action of the primary light—an intense heat is excited in the upper part of the lowest heaven. This happens partly because of the readiness of the lower heaven's matter to receive any form (whether accidental or essential), partly because of the resistance of the cold in the thick matter which, through <term>antiperistasis</term>, <note>original: "antiperiftafin". A historical physical theory where one quality is intensified by being surrounded by its opposite, such as heat concentrating when surrounded by cold.</note> preserves and strengthens that foreign heat on the convex surface of the lowest heaven, and partly because of the density of the matter, causing a collision of one convexity against the concavity of another; and finally, it is caused by the reflection of the bright rays emerging from the middle heaven. Yet truly, as long as a proper proportion of natural moisture remains, alongside the <term>innate heat</term> <note>original: "calidum innato"; the internal "pilot light" of biological life</note>—which we call "vital"—the forces of that external, incoming quality are suppressed. Thus, they are prevented from entering the physical body against the laws of nature.

By unanimous consent, all have defined its nature as hot and dry for the reasons mentioned above. Nevertheless, it must not be denied that heavenly light is present within this element, since that light cannot descend into the lower realms unless it first penetrates the sphere of fire. # CHAPTER XII.

## *On the element of earth.*

**W**ith two powers <note>original: "virtutibus"</note> therefore united—namely, the natural and the added <term>adventitious|A term in medieval philosophy referring to a quality or force that comes from an external source rather than being inherent</term>—matter, which is rebellious due to its coldness, is strongly beaten back by them. By a certain natural instinct, matter flees the effects of light (both primary and secondary) that are sent out from the periphery and pursue its cold nature; seeking a seat most remote from the circumference of that light, it retreated into the form of a horrific and oblique revolution of a gliding shadow around the center or middle point of the spherical machine of the universe, where it contracted into a hard, solid, and opaque globe. In this place, it is much more secure from the actions of its adversary—namely, heat—and much more distant from the dwelling of light, since from the action of light that hostile heat arises. This movement of matter was not caused by itself, but by that aforementioned double action of light. For just as without the manifestation of light, the matter of the darkness was only something potential; so too without the presence of heat, which is the essential quality of light, that natural disposition of matter—namely, coldness—produces nothing in actuality and, consequently, no changes by itself.

Therefore, the coldness of matter is driven downward by the active power of both the primary light and the element of fire produced by the movement of matters; for without these, nothing at all is done. Yet that coldness, by suffering the repercussions of heat, seems to resist in a way, and by resisting, it reacts. By these actions and passions <note>In this context, "passion" refers to the state of being acted upon by an external force, the opposite of "action"</note>, other levels are produced in this lowest heaven, and intermediate regions differing in their disposition are established, which philosophers call the lower elements. From these things, therefore,

<margin>/</margin>that chief principle is explained: why heavy things cannot fall beyond the center of the world, and for what reason they rest there perpetually. This is because weight <note>original: "gravitas"</note> is the companion of denser and more compact matter. The cause of this thickness was coldness, which contracts scattered and thin matter from the fury of penetrating heat toward the center of the world, constraining it in that place and defending it against the invasions of light's rays. Since, however, the action of heat pursues the cold in every part of a thick thing (and especially where it is more dispersed around the center), and the rays of light (whose nature it is to penetrate bodies most easily) surround and besiege it everywhere, it happens that heavy things can in no way proceed beyond that center toward the natural dwelling of light, unless that cold (enclosed by nature in heavy things) is oppressed and violated by the violence of heat. And from this it follows that any heavy thing violently thrown upward naturally and of its own accord returns downward to the center, the seat of coldness.

It is manifest, therefore, that the entire substance of darkness—by whose presence the spiritual matter of the whole world was hidden and formless—is now finally, by the power of light, reduced and gathered into a dense and opaque mass around the center of the world, which is indeed called the element of Earth. The remaining spiritual mass of all the now-formed matter, which is clear and wonderfully transparent, extending from the margins of the earth even to the convex surface of the world, is known by the general name of "Heaven." Among the sacred writers, the most divine *Moses* confirms this at the very threshold of *Genesis*: *In the beginning*, he says, *God created* <note>original: "DEUS"</note> *the heaven and the earth*; that is, He separated the light from the darkness. For He made the heaven clear and bright, but the earth opaque—that is, He immersed the center of the world in darkness. The positive part of the days...

It provides a philosophical and mechanical explanation for gravity as the "weight" of matter that has been condensed by coldness.</summary>

...created the origin, and established the privative <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "privative" refers to a state characterized by the absence of a quality, such as darkness being the "privation" or absence of light.</note> part as the cause of nights. For unless the Creator had placed the earth in the center of the world, the world would not be fouled by any filth or impurity, everything would be bright, and perpetual day would shine forth. It is therefore not at all surprising that so many and such great corruptions and changes of things happen in this lower world; indeed, since in its center or heart hides that most corrupt mother of ruin and privation, that mournful and dark seal of the separation of forms and essences from composite creatures, and there is perpetually placed the truthful witness and messenger of the preternatural tyranny of the element in physical things once they were formed. Hence the most holy *Job* says: *And the dark land is covered with the shadow of Death* <note>original Latin: "Et terra tenebroſa cooperitur cum obſcuritate Mortis"</note>; and elsewhere; *the land is said to be of misery and darkness* <note>original Latin: "terram de miſeria & obſcuritate eſſe dicitur"</note>; indeed, this is as if it were a place of perdition, in which Adam with Eve, banished from the joys of Paradise, received for themselves and left to their heirs the sign of inevitable death. Indeed, the element of fire is like the fiery sword of the Cherubim, wielded by a celestial spirit to block the way to the tree of life—that is, to that divine and immortal nectar—and to bring either sudden or unexpected death to all who thirst too much for immortality. Finally, this central mass is a dire companion of sadness and error, due to its blind and stealthy condition, since an enemy not only of men but of the Greatest and Best GOD and the celestial intelligences is enclosed in the middle of its belly because of its horrendous rebellion. Therefore, woe to us wretched ones on earth, for whom such a crowd of miseries daily lies in wait, and such great danger to body and soul always looms! But you, O celestial creatures, and true inhabitants of the sweetest Paradise, you, I say, O thrice and more happy, and blessed beyond human understanding, who are free and immune from such miserable bonds of hardship through the ineffable power of light!

As for the arrangement of this central mass, although almost all Philosophers assert its natural quality to be dryness, and wish it to predominate in it, while stating its coldness to be plainly accidental and acquired <note>The author is refuting the Aristotelian view that Earth is primarily dry and secondarily cold.</note>—as if it were derived from the natural disposition of water—nevertheless, if we consider a little more accurately both our preceding intention and the possibility of nature itself, we will see that nothing wanders further from the mark of truth than that fantasy of theirs. For since the essential seat of natural light exists at the periphery of the world, and the origin of heat depends on the source of that same light, it is necessary that darkness, which is the contrary of light, and also coldness, which is opposed to heat, should obtain a place most remote from each other. Consequently, then, as the seat of original heat is in the highest heaven, so the primordial dwelling of cold is in the physical center of the same, as in the most remote place. From this it follows that coldness more naturally predominates in it, while dryness exists there as something more accidental; that is, because of the absence of natural moisture in that place, the parts of the earth are called dry; because moisture is made from a tempering of coldness with a portion of heat; which heat, for the reasons aforesaid, has no power or possession in that place. Furthermore, I think no one would be so foolish as not to call that body colder which possesses no portion of heat at all; but it is certain that in the element of water some part of aerial heat is present, since it derived its moisture (whence its fluidity) from the air itself, which is most certainly known to be moist and hot. But it is certain that the earth shares nothing with the air, because it has no fluidity in itself; nor does it have any commerce with fire, both because it is most remotely distant from its sphere, and also because water, which they make contrary to fire, is placed between it and fire. Finally, since the earth is far thicker than the rest of the elements, and indeed the disposition of coldness is to condense both heterogeneous and homogeneous things, it is infallibly proven by the effect that coldness abounds more in the earth. We have delineated the region of earth and fire in this manner.

## CHAPTER XIII.

->*Concerning the middle sphere, which is called the sphere of moisture, and concerning the elements of water and air.*<-

**T**HE sphere of moisture, situated in the middle between the center of the earth and the outer <note>literally "convex"</note> surface of fire, is called the *sphere of equality*, because it is forged from an equal portion of each of the two extreme elements <note>The "extremes" are Earth (cold/dry) and Fire (hot/dry)</note>; for neither the coldness of the earth by itself, nor indeed the heat of fire alone, is capable of producing moisture. Instead, the conjunction of both—acting much like the union of male and female—constitutes it. For just as terrestrial cold alone constricts the middle spirit <term>spiritus: in this context, a subtle, vaporous substance that permeates the universe</term> where it resides, it is the role of the heat descending upon it to dissolve and liquefy that frozen spirit, rendering it fluid. Similarly, heat by itself—that is, when joined to its own inherent dryness—would absorb the essence of that spirit...

...absorbs, or certainly by its own quality dissipates it into imperceptible parts; hence it deserves to be called a divider of <term>humidity</term> <note>The quality of "moistness" or "fluidity" in Aristotelian physics.</note> rather than a producer of it. Therefore, the violence of heat is blunted to a greater or lesser degree by the encounter with <term>cold</term>; whence the intense operations of both are hindered, and the <term>spirit</term> <note>In this context, "spirit" refers to a subtle, vaporous substance or "breath" that permeates matter.</note> is not permitted to be coagulated by the cold because of the presence of heat. Nor is it possible for heat, according to the property of its nature, to dissipate and scatter the parts of the moistening spirit, which happens because of the resistance of the present cold; hence the spirit is dissolved by the assistance of the heat. But once dissolved, it is not dispersed, nor is it thinned almost to nothing—which is completely achieved by the presence of cold—but it remains in the middle as a naturally flowing substance. Through its fluid nature and liquidity, it moistens all intermediate things, either more corporally and visibly (if it clings to a greater portion of cold) or more spiritually and imperceptibly (if it embraces a larger part of heat). And it is from this disposition of the <term>humid</term> that the two intermediate elements are derived, as we shall immediately demonstrate.

Therefore, the thick matter, as was said before, having been driven down from on high to the center, and retained there because of the immense cold with which it is endowed, desires to rest there. But truly, because it is the nature of heat to always attack cold with hostility and to pursue it with a certain natural antipathy—and because it is also the nature of any <term>subtle</term> <note>Refined, thin, or gaseous matter.</note> thing to penetrate—therefore this active quality (heat), driving that passive quality (cold) downward, pursues it there and continually attempts to penetrate its mass. And because the end of any thing is its opposite, and not only rest, but even motion is opposed to motion; therefore, to that motion intended downward toward the center or middle, another motion has succeeded: namely, from the bottom upward toward the element of <term>Fire</term>. This was stirred up by the resistance of the cold opposing the injuries of the heat, and by the reverberation of the rays of light fighting against it. 

Whence two parts of terrestrial cold, ascending upward to repel the injuries of the hot, encountered in the middle way between the center and the sphere of fire an equal number of parts of heat descending to fulfill that coldness. And by the union of these parts, the <term>sphere of humidity</term> is established, the middle part of which exists as simply and equally moist. For the forces of heat in its middle are proportional to those of cold, so that they are weighed as if on an equal balance, leaning toward neither side, and possessing the same strength and power of acting on both sides; that is, they tend neither more downward nor more to the side, and consequently while they are moved, it is necessary that they be carried <term>circularly</term> <note>original: "circulariter." Fludd is explaining why the celestial bodies and the elements move in circles around the center.</note>. 

However, the dimension of this middle sphere that tends downward toward its concavity is called the element of **Water**. Because of its proximity to the element of Earth and its greater distance from the sphere of Fire, it appears more terrestrial, thick, visible, and sensibly moistening. For its temperament is composed of three-quarters terrestrial cold (for it is much more contiguous to the earth) and one-quarter heat of fire; in which temperament, although the smallest portion of heat is present, it is nevertheless sufficient to hinder the coagulating disposition of the cold and to preserve this part of the sphere of humidity in its fluid quality. And this is the same reasoning that we put forward above: so that it may be most clearly evident that cold exists much more intensely not in water, but in earth, since water is frozen by the absence or diminution of that fourth part of heat and is reduced into ice—that is, a substance more terrestrial and non-fluid. 

But the other half of the aforesaid sphere, protruding upward toward the concave surface of Fire, because it is further distant from the earth and because of its vicinity with the element of Fire, is a great participant in heat and contains very little cold within itself by which its fiery heat might be tempered. For that reason, it is much more subtle, spiritual, and invisible than the lower part of the same, and because of its subtlety, it penetrates more and moistens more deeply. From which things it is gathered...

### C H A P T E R XIV.

#### *On the form of the elements.*

The **FORM** of this lower heaven is weaker than that of the higher realms because of its great distance from its origin <note>The "origin" refers to the divine source or the highest point of creation from which light and form descend.</note>; this is most easily proven by its effects. Consequently, it is certain that the matter of this heaven, the more it approaches the center, the coarser, more impure, and less worthy it becomes; according to that principle of *Aristotle* in his <term>metaphysics</term> <note>The branch of philosophy concerned with the nature of existence and the first principles of things.</note>, *where there is more matter, there is less form, and vice versa.* From this it is clearly evident that the matter of this heaven predominates because of the weakening of its form, and as a result, it constantly seeks a new form every day; for there is not enough form available in this region for the appetite of its matter to be satisfied or filled. # C H A P T E R XV.
### *Concerning the substance of the aforementioned elements.*

<margin>**I**</margin>
n the preceding chapters, we treated the degrees of the elements and their mutual dependence, and how they differ from each other with respect to the diverse quality of the mixture of earth with that of the element of fire; now, however, we shall relate a few things concerning their primary matter or substance. The spirits of darkness, cast out from the highest region into the center, which retained no portion (or a very small one) of the primary light, after they exited from the earth through its open pores following the flight of the solar spirit, they possessed the higher place of this inferior region. These were like the thicker parts or dregs of that mass from which the purest body of the sun, raised into the heart of the middle heaven, is separated. Indeed, these aforementioned parts of the spirits are compelled to dwell in that place—namely, in the sphere of fire—and to be carried in a circle, both because they lack a sufficient soul to raise them further, and because the form of the middle heaven cannot completely inform a greater quantity of matter, and finally because its mass is thicker and more impure (though the most subtle of all in the lower heaven) than the matter of the [middle] heaven.
<margin>—</margin>
Furthermore, those parts of the spirits of darkness from the middle region of the world, which enclosed some sparks of its secondary light, were reduced into vegetables and plants on the second day. The other parts, which possess almost no portion of the ethereal rays, since they are naturally contiguous to the super-celestial spirit, succeed the matter of the element of fire and fill the place of air. Finally, the spirits of darkness of the third and lowest region of the world, which are the thickest and heaviest of all, since they are contiguous and closest to the ether, succeed it in the order of nature; hence they possess the region of water and are called water. And if parts of this spirit include any portion of the light of this heaven, they produce minerals. And by this reasoning, in their retreat, the thicker spirits of darkness, driven out from the <term>Empyrean heaven</term> <note>The highest, most celestial part of the universe, characterized by pure fire or light.</note> as the highest region of all, constituted the element of fire; but those cast down from the middle region or ether escaped into the substan-

We conclude, therefore, that Earth is the dregs of the spirits of each heaven and a heap of substantial darkness; <insert>Water is that thicker spirit of the lowest heaven, almost void of light; for the spirits of that heaven that embrace light are converted into various metals, according to the greater or lesser proportion of light contained in them; hence, their radical moisture is found by Philosophers to be a thick and viscous water.</insert> Air is that spirit of the second heaven which escaped from the earth through refinement, whose denser part, embracing secondary light, produces warmer or colder vegetables according to the appropriate proportion of light and that fatty spirit; and finally, Fire is the spirit of the darkness of the **Empyrean heaven**, whose thicker substance, filled with primary light, constituted the solar body, as will be declared below.

### *An experiment with wine, from which the nature of each element*
### *can be gathered.*

We have made an experiment from the most excellent wine itself, which clearly shows us—as if with a finger or a rule of certainty—the substances of the elements and the fifth essence itself. For once the spirit was extracted from the wine by a well-known process, I then extracted an oil floating upon the spirit. Then, from the dregs of the wine, I extracted another oil and brought it to the highest purification through various refinements. Afterward, I frequently purified the phlegm that was distilled even after the extraction of the spirit. Finally, I cleansed the dregs of the entire wine from its muddy filth through many washings. I then placed all these into a round glass in equal proportions; this I sealed **Hermetically** <note>original: "Hermeticè"; airtight, using a method attributed to the legendary alchemist Hermes Trismegistus.</note>, as they call it. After this vessel had rested for an entire night, I found five regions in the morning: <margin><note>manicule</note></margin> the lowest was black and veiled in darkness; upon this resided a portion of phlegm; then the oil extracted from the dregs covered that; in the fourth place, the <insert>spirit of wine</insert> ascended above it; <insert>and finally, the oil extracted from that spirit covered it in the fifth rank.</insert>
