## CHAPTER XVI.

-> **Regarding certain experiments involving waters, demonstrating various arrangements in the constitution of the aforementioned heavens through the operation of light.** <-

**IT IS CERTAIN** that fire is included under the name of "light" and originated from light itself; for nowhere in the universal description of creation did our divine leader *Moses* <note>The author refers to the Book of Genesis as a scientific/philosophical text.</note> make mention of that most noble creature, fire, except when speaking of light. This is also more clearly declared in Book VI, Chapter 8. Furthermore, no one will doubt that air and water belonged to the substance of that mass—namely, the universal waters—since the Holy Scriptures testify that all things were forged from that mass. But now, because these aforementioned operations are undoubtedly viewed with suspicion by some who rely more on their senses than on reason, it remains to represent these operations to their eyes through effects derived from those two primary causes, namely water and light. Indeed, they will very easily perceive these visibly if they diligently observe the following experiments.

-> *First experiment regarding fire and air, or subtle water.* <-

With a fire lit in the upper part of a hollow and perfectly sealed instrument, at the bottom of which (opposite the fire) a very small hole or tube is placed, the internal air is thinned <note>original: "attenuatur"; meaning rarefied or made less dense by heat.</note> as it approaches the place of the fire. The thicker part of this thinned air, which is colder, tends to move from the working fire toward the lowest part of the vessel, as if moving away from its enemy. This is visibly evident because it is perceived to exit gradually in the form of a moist vapor through the tube or hole of that region.

From this we therefore conclude that thick air, on account of the coldness contained within it, flees from fire and moves toward the region most remote from its presence. ### *Experiment II.*

Let there be made, therefore, a certain globe of glass or copper, divided into three distinct regions, so that one encompasses the entire hollow of the other <note>Fludd is describing a set of three concentric spheres nested inside one another</note>; and let these regions have certain openings or tubes, protruding in the manner depicted below, and let the outermost surface of the globe be surrounded on all sides by a most lively fire. When this is done, it will be visible to the eye that the external fire imparts its more lively vigor to the upper <note>original: 'superiori', here referring to the outermost layer closest to the heat source</note> region, and that the air contained within it is wonderfully thinned <term>attenuated|The process of making a substance thinner or less dense, the opposite of condensation</term> because of its proximity to the living fire.

Furthermore, the second, middle region also receives fiery vigor from the first; but nevertheless, because that vigor is milder there than in the upper region, for that reason the air existing within it is less subtle and thin, as the fiery force is naturally unable to <term>rarefy|To make a substance (like air) less dense through heat</term> it further. Finally, the fiery power hiding in the middle region will also pour some force, though a small one, into the lowest <note>the innermost</note> region. From this, the previous proposition—and also that which is expressed after the end of the seventh chapter—demonstrates that the thick air of the upper region (of which there is a greater quantity), as well as that of the middle region (which is smaller in proportion), and finally even that of the lowest region (which is the smallest of all), tends toward the center and there gathers into drops <note>Fludd is describing condensation, where the 'fleeing' cold air is forced to the center and turns into liquid</note>. The demonstration follows.

## THE EXPERIMENT IS AS FOLLOWS.

In the beginning, the potential substance of the waters in the world was no different than if a portion of some artificial globe—divided into various cavities with specific gaps running from the outer edge toward the center, such as the arc *a.c.b.* shown in the previous demonstration—were filled with clear water or air. In this state, all parts of the water share the same density and arrangement. But if fire touches the outer surface of that arc, the denser air of the upper region (indicated by I), which is much larger in relation to that center, as well as the air of the second and third regions, becomes extremely thick and compact when it is reflected back toward the center. Indeed, it could not be contained in such a narrow space as the center in any other way. For the air that was previously held within the spaces *A. C. D. E.*, *D. E. F. G.*, and *F. G. H. I.* is squeezed into that tiny corner of the arc, narrowed down, and reduced into a thick and vaporous mass. From this principle depends that great mystery of the ancient Philosophers: the discovery of the weights and proportions of the elements.

<margin>/</margin> And indeed, it is for this reason that the entire world was fashioned into a spherical shape. The Archetype <term>Archetype: In Robert Fludd's philosophy, this refers to the divine "master builder" or the original divine mind that designed the universe</term> placed the heavier, thicker bodies toward the center of the cosmic machine <note>original: "machinæ centrum"; Fludd often describes the universe as a divine machine or engine</note> so that as those bodies became subtler through rarefaction <term>rarefaction: the process of a substance becoming less dense; expansion through heat</term> and thinning, they could always find a more spacious place for themselves as they ascended. As previously stated, dense objects require less space before they are dissolved than they do after they have been refined. Therefore, once this knowledge is mastered, it will not be difficult to measure the capacity of the heavens—provided the size of the earth is known first—nor will it be hard to determine the proportions of the elements relative to one another...

# CHAPTER I.

## *On the nature of worldly proportions.*

---

**F**ROM what has preceded, it is clear that just as the <term>Empyrean heaven<gloss>The highest part of the universe in ancient and medieval cosmology, believed to be composed of pure fire or light.</gloss></term> is the dwelling and seat of supernatural fire and light—from which natural fire proceeds directly, and that other more accidental fire proceeds indirectly—so also its opposite place, which limits and finishes the movement of its rays, is the receptacle of matter and darkness. Furthermore, since the relationship between opposites is the same, it is necessary for the sake of the world’s continuity that the disposition of the moist nature of darkness stands in the same degree and the same proportion to that fiery nature of light. Hence, as we have previously declared that the physical center <note>The Earth</note> is naturally cold in the fourth degree, most dense, most opaque, and most heavy, naturally seeking rest by its very self; so also the furthest region of the world-machine <margin>/</margin> is undoubtedly opposed to it in all things, not only in location but also in condition. Thus, by the equal action of the one and the proportional passion <note>In this context, "passion" means the capacity to be acted upon or to receive an impression.</note> of the other, all intermediate bodies are established; and according to the nature of the subject—that is, according to the abundance or poverty of the light predominating in it—they either resist deprivation longer or more quickly yield and are subjected to it. Who, therefore, will doubt that the supreme region of the Empyrean heaven is free and immune from every invasion of coldness, the property of which is to thicken? For it is the most subtle, purest, lightest, transparent in the highest degree of clarity, and is almost nothing else than fire sublimated to the ultimate <margin>/</margin> peak of the most sweet and amorous heat.

Without a doubt, therefore, those proportions of things induce a most noble worldly harmony, through which—as the virtue of the primary light works upon intermediate matter—an indissoluble concord of things is mediated, and the ears of the intellect are soothed by a certain inexplicable music. For the instrument of this melody, namely the machine of the world, is like a <term>monochord<gloss>An ancient scientific and musical instrument with a single string, used to demonstrate the mathematical relationships between musical intervals.</gloss></term>, whose string (through which the consensus of parts is introduced) is the intermediate matter of the whole world. The composer in this music, however, <margin>/</margin> is the <term>Soul of the World<gloss>In Latin, *Anima Mundi*; the vital force or spirit believed to animate the physical universe.</gloss></term>, or essence-making light. It is not otherwise than in that instrumental music of man, in which <term>Gamma<gloss>Represented by the Greek letter Γ, this was the lowest note in the medieval musical scale.</gloss></term> takes its beginning from the lower part of the system, ascending with deep, excellent, and super-excellent voices. Truly, such a progression also occurs in the world-monochord, namely by ascending proportionally from the earth to its <term>ee la<gloss>The highest note in the standard Renaissance musical scale (the 'Guidonian Hand').</gloss></term>, which is the limit of the furthest periphery. And as in Gamma the sound is heavier and deeper because of the extreme distance from *ee la*, from which the striking of the voice becomes more intense as it ascends; so also, the higher one ascends from the earth toward the Empyrean heaven, the stronger the effect of light and heat is found, and the <term>world spirit<gloss>The subtle, invisible substance that acts as a bridge between pure spirit and gross matter.</gloss></term> is rendered thinner by its virtue. Just as a greater force and therefore a greater <margin>/</margin> virtue of the luminous soul is required for the raising of the human voice, while in its lowering, altogether less is required;

### CHAPTER II.

#### *How the mundane proportions are drawn from the site and location of the parts of each pyramid?*

<margin>-</margin> SINCE in every part of **hyle** <note>prime matter</note>, and similarly in every portion of the most beautiful light, there was no difference at all but supreme equality before their mixing occurred: it follows necessarily from this that the alteration, both in the already-informed matter of hyle and in the already-created form itself, consists in a greater or lesser action and passion of these principles. ...observing that, if they are compared to that single portion of their pyramid which is found in the highest or *Empyrean* <note>The highest part of the heavens in ancient and medieval cosmology, believed to be the realm of pure fire or light and the dwelling place of the Divine.</note> region, they are found in a **double proportion** <note>A 2:1 ratio, which in music corresponds to the interval of an octave.</note>, and relate to one another as 2 to 1. And it is certain that these proportions of the material pyramid <term>material pyramid: a symbolic triangle representing the density and ascent of matter from the Earth upward</term> arise according to the multiplication or reduction of the parts of light; just as the proportions of the formal pyramid <term>formal pyramid: a symbolic triangle representing the descent of "form" or divine light from God toward the Earth</term> itself arise from the greater or lesser presence or absence of the material portion. For its source is purely formal and uncreated—from whose base the formal pyramid descends—and insofar as it is purely and absolutely formal, it contains no portion of matter within itself. Thus, it is known to consist of "four quarters of heat"—that is, of the most perfect simplicity and absolute homogeneity. If those three portions of created light in the highest region of the air—namely, the *Empyrean*—are compared to this fountainhead of the pyramid, they will stand in a **sesquitertian proportion** <note>original: *sesquitertia*; a ratio of 4:3, which in music corresponds to the interval of a perfect fourth</note>, namely, 4 to 3. Similarly, the three portions of light of that heaven, when compared with the two of the intermediate heaven, will constitute a **sesquialter proportion** <note>original: *sesquialtera*; a ratio of 3:2, which in music corresponds to the interval of a perfect fifth</note>, and will relate to each other as 3 to 2. 

<margin>$\rightarrow$</margin> Moreover, the two portions of the middle heaven are compared to that single portion of the lower heaven in a **double proportion**, relating to each other as 2 to 1. From these things it is manifest that the formal pyramid descends from its base to the earth by the same proportions with which the material pyramid ascends to heaven, and consequently, in their intersection, they relate to one another proportionally. 

<margin>$\rightarrow$</margin> From these general proportions, the musical consonances—both general and particular—of the **world monochord** <term>world monochord: Fludd's famous concept of the entire universe as a single-stringed instrument tuned by the hand of God</term> itself are produced, as we shall explain in the following chapter.

# ON WORLDLY MUSIC.

## CHAPTER III.

->*On the world monochord, and on the discovery of its harmonies, both simple and composite, from which the worldly harmony is composed.*<-

---

**SINCE** all those proportions in each aforementioned pyramid are worth nothing by themselves for producing musical harmonies without a mixing of the two (for neither is the lute <note>original: "barbiton," an ancient stringed instrument</note> sufficient without the musician, nor the musician without the lute to create musical harmonies), it is therefore necessary that both pyramids must concur to constitute the worldly harmony: namely, the material pyramid, which takes the place of the musical instrument, the string of the monochord, or the instrument and breath of the singer; and the formal pyramid, which performs the office of the soul striking or singing and producing the voice. Therefore, an increase of the formal substance <note>The "formal substance" refers to the light or spirit acting upon the world.</note> produces a sharper and more subtle air, and consequently brings forth more rarefied and excellent worldly symphonies; <margin>$\rightarrow$</margin> not unlike how a more intense human spirit or the string of an instrument will give sharper voices and more subtle air through more violent vibrations. However, its decrease creates a thicker air, and consequently makes a heavier <note>In this context, "heavy" means lower in pitch.</note> worldly harmony, just as a relaxed human voice or a loosened string of a monochord renders softer sounds; and this happens because of the excessive thickness of the air. <margin>$\rightarrow$</margin> Light, therefore, acts upon the matter of the world by the same means as the human spirit acts upon the air. From these things it is manifest that one nature, whether material or formal, is worth nothing without the other, and therefore Worldly Music arises from both pyramids being mixed at the most fundamental levels. For without the presence of light, moist matter would not have a pyramidal form, nor would a created form have its own without moist matter. Whence it is certain that they are mixed with one another according to "more or less," following the nature of the portions of each pyramid moving oppositely in the <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>The "Great World" or the universe as a whole, as opposed to the Microcosm (man).</note> and running together toward one another. Having learned these things, let us take our beginning from the matter of the world, <margin>$\rightarrow$</margin> which we have compared to the strings of the monochord (the great instrument of which is the <term>Macrocosm</term> itself), so that we may aptly compare every degree—by which any difference of locations between the center of the worldly instrument and its periphery is discerned—to musical intervals, both simple and composite. Wherefore it must be known that just as the string of an instrument is usually divided by metric proportions by reason of its ascent from Γ <note>The Greek letter Gamma, representing the lowest note in the traditional musical scale, or "Gamut."</note> through the intervals, so also both matter and its form are distributed by quantitative degrees, and distinguished by similar proportions that constitute musical harmonies. For if a monochord were imaginatively extended from the summit of the Empyrean heaven to the base of the earth itself, constituting the radius of either pyramid, we would perceive that it is divided into parts constituting harmonies; if its middle part were pressed, it would produce the <note>original: "Diapason"</note> octave harmony, just as experience teaches that this same thing happens in a physical monochord.

It must be considered, however, that in such a worldly monochord, harmonies both simple and composite, and similarly the proper intervals measuring them, can be delineated in no other way than when we divide a physical monochord into proportional parts. For the effect of coldness in the earth, and consequently the very matter of the earth, in its thickness and weight, relates naturally to the coldness and matter of the lowest region, in which there is but a single

A fourth part of light and natural heat is present, in a ratio of 4 to 3, which is the **sesquitertial proportion** <note>original: "proportio sesquitertia"; a ratio of 4:3, which in music defines the interval of a Perfect Fourth</note>, as was stated above. Within this proportion, the consonance of the **Diatessaron** <note>The musical interval of a Perfect Fourth</note> consists of three combined intervals: namely, water, air, and fire. For in "world music," Earth holds the same position as the number 1 in music, unity in Arithmetic, and the point in Geometry. It is, as it were, the starting point from which the ratio of proportional matter must be calculated, since it is the base and foundation of the material pyramid. 

Water, therefore, will occupy the place of one whole tone, and Air also the place of one further interval. The sphere of Fire, however—since it is nothing other than the ignited summit of the region of air—holds the place of a minor semitone. 

But insofar as two portions of this matter are raised upward in a pyramid shape toward the center-point of heaven to resist the actions of supernatural heat, and as an equal number of light-parts act downward in a pyramid shape upon those two portions of matter, they create the composition of the Sun's sphere. They naturally grant it the name "Sphere of Equality." To that extent, a **sesquialtera proportion** <note>original: "proportio sesquialtera"; a ratio of 3:2, defining the musical interval of a Perfect Fifth</note> is produced within it, specifically because the three parts of the spirit (or lower matter) of the middle heaven are related to those two parts of the solar sphere, and consequently produce the consonance of the **Diapente** <note>The musical interval of a Perfect Fifth</note>. 

Such is the difference between the Moon and the Sun: between the curve of this heaven and the middle of the Sun's sphere, there are four intervals—namely, the entire spheres of the Moon, Mercury, and Venus (compared to whole tones), and the half-part of the solar sphere, which we have composed of a semitone. 

Since the consonance of the **Diapason** <note>The musical interval of an Octave</note> is truly composed of the Diatessaron and the Diapente, it is necessary that this Diapason consonance be produced there. This is the more perfect consonance of matter, which can in no way acquire perfection unless it satisfies its longing through the solar form. 

Furthermore, although this middle heaven ends in its own heart—namely, the Sun—with a more perfect consonance of matter and begins its movement toward the formal Diapason, yet in its concavity, both above and below the "sphere of equality," it sounds nothing but the Diapente consonance. This interval is more suited to this location than others because, just as this consonance is less than "perfect" (being placed midway between the perfect and the imperfect), so too is this heaven: although it is perfect and free from decay, it is said to be less perfect in respect to the higher heaven, and it occupies a middle position between both heavens—the perfect and the imperfect. 

Moreover, the point of exact equality, which is the exact intersection of the two pyramids (marked as N. H. <note>Refers to a diagram in the original text</note>), is the true boundary of the more perfect consonance. Here, there is such a union and embrace of matter with form that a separation or division can never occur. 

But truly, because the parts of the pyramids in the ethereal region—both above the sphere of intersection (marked S. Q. O. P. and N. H.) and below it (namely, R. M. Q. G. and N. H.)—are equal enough for perfection, the ethereal matter outside the sphere of the soul has enough "form" to satisfy its appetite, even if not to the perfection of the solar sphere. Therefore, the proportion joining these intervals is called a "perfect consonance," but it is less complete than that of the Sun, which the most excellent Musicians have called the Diapente. 

And this was the sole reason why some of the Philosophers distinguished its substance by the name of the **Fifth Essence** <note>original: "Quinta essentia"; the "quintessence" or ether, the fifth element beyond the earthly four</note>, since its composition participated more in the consonance of the Diapente [the Perfect Fifth] in respect to both extremes of heaven. For descending from the sphere of the Sun, it relates to the lowest heaven in a 3:2 ratio, and ascending to the borders of the spiritual heaven, it is found in that same ratio. 

However, the upper consonance differs from the lower one because the former refers to "form" [light/spirit] and the latter to "matter." Therefore, just as form is more excellent than matter, so the nature of the upper consonances is more eminent than those of matter. Just as a Diapason was produced from the center to the Sun’s sphere (which was material), so another Diapason is raised upward from the head of the material pyramid to the highest peak of the **Empyrean heaven** <note>The highest, most spiritual heaven of pure fire/light</note>, which is spiritual. For the upper part of the middle heaven, starting from the sphere of intersection...

### ON WORLD MUSIC

The region of the triangles, in which the center of the sun exists, receding toward the crystalline region, is more spiritual than the lower region because of its proximity to the Empyrean heaven <note>The Empyrean was considered the highest part of heaven, composed of pure light or fire, and the dwelling place of the Divine.</note>; hence, the consonance produced therein is also spiritual. For insofar as two portions of the light of this upper part of heaven relate to those three portions that give form to the matter of the Empyrean heaven, to that extent we find their arrangement regulated by a <term>sesquialtera</term> proportion <note>A ratio of 3:2, which in music creates the interval of a perfect fifth.</note>. Indeed, from the part of the material pyramid contained between the sun's dwelling and the borders of the Empyrean heaven—due to the relationship and respect of each portion of light to the other—four intervals are drawn out from it, from which a spiritual <term>Diapente</term> <note>A musical interval of a perfect fifth.</note> consonance is composed and perfected. 

For from one portion of the solar sphere—namely the upper one, stretching from the sphere of the pyramidal intersection to the summit of the solar sphere—that interval is found which is compared to a minor <term>semitone</term>, so that the lower part of the same solar sphere retains the place of the minor semitone for the composition of the material fifth, and the upper portion serves for the minor semitone of the formal fifth. Truly, the double excess by which the two major semitones exceed the two minor ones—namely, two <term>commas</term> <note>A very small musical interval, the difference between two nearly identical notes in different tuning systems.</note>—concur toward the exact composition of the sphere of equality, in which the center of the solar body, the vehicle of the soul of the world, is suspended with balanced weights. 

Next, the sphere of *Mars*, and that of *Jupiter*, and finally even that upper sphere of *Saturn* are numbered as the three other intervals of the spiritual fifth, which we have compared to whole tones, since each of these spheres has distinct natures and operations both in the middle heaven itself and also upon these lower things. Upon this spiritual consonance, which is less than perfect, is founded that most perfect consonance of all, which is called the spiritual <term>Diapason</term> <note>A musical interval of an octave.</note>. 

And at this point, a divine mystery will reveal itself to those looking carefully: just as the formal octave is more excellent than the material one, so also its foundation is more excellent and far nobler, both in the proportion of its harmony and in its base. Therefore, just as the earth is far more ignoble than the solar body, so also the material octave and the consonances contained within it are to be placed far behind those spiritual ones. For the earth is the base of the material <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>A musical interval of a perfect fourth.</note> and the material fifth, which together constitute the material octave; but the solar sphere itself is the foundation upon which the spiritual fifth, fourth, and octave are raised. 

Furthermore, the fundamental consonance of the material octave is the fourth, which is the most imperfect of all accords; but the fundamental accord of the formal octave is the fifth, which is surely a perfect accord. From this, therefore, the degrees of all material things are seen as if in a mirror, and from there, the scale and spiritual order are made manifest to the eyes of the intellect. All generations, therefore, happen beneath the sun and receive their power from the lower minor semitone of the solar sphere, which we called "material" above; but truly, all regenerations have their origin from the upper semitone of the solar sphere, from which a sublimation occurs toward the summit of the spiritual realm. Accordingly, those things which have not reached the summit of the solar sphere cannot acquire the perfection of regeneration, nor become spiritual things from corporal ones. Blessed, therefore, are the bodies that are permitted to arrive at such great height and dignity. 

But, to return to our purpose, those three parts of light relating to one part of the thinnest informing matter—compared to those four parts that are purely formal and constitute the complete form, in which there is no matter at all (such as the nature of uncreated light)—agree in a <term>sesquitertia</term> proportion <note>A ratio of 4:3, which in music creates the interval of a perfect fourth.</note>, which constitutes the spiritual consonance of the fourth. The most subtle spirit of this consonance, as if transformed and liberated from bodily substance, is further divided into three intervals attributed to the three Hierarchies <note>The traditional ranking of angels.</note>; the two lower spheres of these are likened to whole tones, while the upper is likened to a semitone, insofar as the orders of the Epiphany—and especially the Seraphim, who are said to minister to **GOD** Himself—extend themselves beyond the limits of matter...

From these joined harmonies, therefore, arises the spiritual <term>Diapason</term> <note>An octave, representing the most perfect consonance in music with a 2:1 ratio</note>, the perfection of which cannot be grasped by human understanding, because it ends in the triangular nature of the purest form. It is, therefore, the highest peak of all earthly perfection, height, and purity, beyond which nothing exists except the one and only GOD.

<margin>←</margin> And this same consonance is produced as much from the side of matter as from the side of form: For if two parts of matter, which give substance to the ethereal heaven, are compared to that single corporeal volume shared with the <term>Empyrean</term> <note>The highest heaven, believed by ancient and medieval scholars to be the realm of pure fire and the dwelling place of the Divine</note> heaven, a double proportion will result, in which the <term>Diapason</term> harmony consists. From these things it is certain that there is a quadruple proportion between the earth and the curved surface of the spiritual world, since its <term>Semidiameter</term> <note>Radius</note> is composed of a double <term>Diapason</term>; in the following demonstration, we have imagined this to be the string of our <term>Macrocosmic</term> <note>Relating to the "Great World" or the universe as a whole</note> monochord. From this it is manifest that, just as a musical instrument called a <term>Monochord</term> <note>A one-stringed instrument used to demonstrate the mathematical ratios of musical intervals</note> will resonate a <term>Diapason</term> from its center to either end if it is pressed in the middle, so also the action in the middle height of the world—or the midpoint of the radius drawn from the center to its circumference, which is manifested especially in the body of the sun—is perceived to give out a double <term>Diapason</term> of harmony at its center. From this it shines out most clearly that the perfection of the spiritual heaven extends itself to the center of the sun, and that the earth seeks and receives from that solar boundary all the perfection it possesses, of whatever kind or amount it may be. Therefore, the motion of light tends downward so that it may impart perfection to the lower things; the boundary of this motion is in the Sun. Thus the solar body, which is the collector of the emitted rays of light, shoots them toward the surface of the earth in the same proportion. Therefore, the formal heaven gives the form, which the matter eagerly seizes.

<margin>☿</margin> <note>The symbol for Mercury, often associated in this period with the mediation between the spirit and the body</note> We conclude, therefore, that the Sun is the GOD of nature—but a created one—receiving all formal and light-giving power from the greatest GOD of all, the supernatural uncreated creator. This happens by the power of spiritual harmony, through the formal <term>Diapason</term> ordered proportionally with its intervals. The earth, in turn, receives the influences of that same GOD through the material <term>Diapason</term>, and thus has the same correspondence with the Sun as the Sun has with the most high GOD; <margin>←</margin> who is therefore said by the *Psalmist to have placed his tabernacle in the sun* <note>original: "regio condidisse tabernaculum suum in sole" — a reference to Psalm 19:4</note>. We have proved in this, our Music, that both <term>Diapente</term> <note>The musical interval of a perfect fifth</note> consonances are found in the intermediate part of the world, so much so that the Philosophers have called its substance the <term>Quinta essentia</term> <note>The "Fifth Essence" or Quintessence, a celestial element thought to be superior to the four earthly elements</note>; but both <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>The musical interval of a perfect fourth</note> consonances are established in the outer parts of the world, while the <term>Diapason</term> consonance is found in the Sun, and the <term>Disdiapason</term> <note>A double octave, representing a 4:1 ratio</note> is found in GOD himself. <margin>⋘</margin> This, then, is the natural harmony of the universal machine, which no one until now, as far as I know, has explained so succinctly and clearly. ## ON WORLDLY MUSIC.

The upper Fourth <note>original: *Diatessaron*</note> agrees with the material Fourth in this respect: just as the lower Fourth—though more perfect relative to the earth placed beneath it, because it possesses more of the form that shapes it than the earth does—is found to be imperfect when compared to higher things (that is, to the Fifth <note>original: *Diapente*</note> of its own nature), and can in no way be compared to the matter of the ethereal heaven (no more than the harmony of the Fourth can be compared to that Fifth), so too does the formal Fourth behave in all things. For if it is compared to the nature of the ethereal heaven, it is more perfect than it; indeed, it is even more perfect than its own formal harmony of the Fifth, insofar as the intervals of the latter are more material, while those of the Fourth are more spiritual. But if it is compared to the pure form above itself, the intervals of this harmony are still imperfect. Thus, this harmony is found there so that our intellect may see that this very region—even if it is the purest and most perfect of all the world's regions as far as we are concerned—is nonetheless removed from the perfection of the Heaven of the Trinity by an immense distance.

The logic of this World Monochord <note>original: *monochordum mundanum*; a single-stringed instrument used here as a metaphor for the harmony of the universe</note> is proven by its effect, which aptly explains to us that pyramidal proportion and quality of worldly matter. Let there be made, therefore, a musical instrument constructed in the shape of a pyramid, and from one point on one side of it, let a brass string be stretched to a point on the other side directly opposite to it. Then, let a second string be stretched from another point to its opposite, and then a third and fourth, proceeding through the rest until the thickness of the entire pyramidal instrument is filled with strings differing proportionally from one another. We say, therefore, that these same strings, stretched with equal force, maintain the intervals of <term>Whole Tones</term> <note>original: *Tonus*; the basic interval of a musical scale</note> and <term>Semitones</term> <note>original: *Semitonium*; a half-step, the smallest interval in traditional Western music</note>, such that from the base of the pyramid toward its peak <note>original: *conum*</note> we shall always ascend from lower sounds to sharper ones through those musical scales (which we more rightly call intervals), until the peak is reached. Beyond this, to ascend higher will be no less impossible than trying to penetrate further by going beyond the unit in Arithmetic or the point in Geometry. ### TREATISE II. PART VII. BOOK II.

**E**ven though wheels are not present in this place, nevertheless, because the Diameter of an imaginary wheel—namely E. G., whose center is H—completes almost the entire action of this experiment, we will speak briefly here about it and its description.

The water descending through tube A passes through the angular opening of the <term>shutter-valve<note>Latin: *claustrum*. A mechanical gate or stop used to control the flow of fluid.</note></term> H into tube C and lifts the wood covered with leather and proportionally weighted with lead. This weight is balanced according to the proportion of the height of the distance between the orifice of tube B and the exit of the pond. When the said weight in the <term>lantern-chamber<note>Latin: *laterna*. In early modern engineering, this refers to a cylindrical housing or cage, often containing a piston or gear mechanism.</note></term> E is lifted, it forces the water enclosed in tube D—which cannot recede—to seek an exit through tube B. And it works in this way for as long as it is forcing the water. 

The balancing of the shutter is achieved by a mechanism to which a small vessel is attached on one side; this vessel receives water drop by drop from tube A through a <term>vent-hole<note>Latin: *spiramen*.</note></term> made for this purpose. Therefore, when it is filled, it outweighs the counterweight of the other side of the balance and falls onto a nail fixed below, and opening its valve, the water is discharged. By the fall of this same vessel, the shutter-valve is turned in such a way that its angular opening—which previously corresponded to tube B and tube C—now makes an opening to the lower tube I and to C. 

As a result of the backflow of water from G into I, the weight lifted in the lantern-chamber E falls back down. However, since the lantern-chamber cannot be empty, it draws in water through the valve K (in the manner of a <term>siphon<note>Latin: *syphonis*. Here used to describe the suction or drawing action of a pump.</note></term>), because the upper valve is closed by this attraction, so that the lantern, tube D, and tube B are always full of water. Immediately, as soon as the weight of the lantern has dropped and the water of tube C is emptied, the shutter-valve is closed again. This happens because the counterweight of the balance has already regained its weight once the small vessel (as was mentioned) hit the nail and discharged its water; once the shutter-valve is closed, the effect is repeated. As we said at the beginning, these repetitions happen suddenly and quickly.

Thus, all the <term>foul water<note>Latin: *aqua putrida*. Refers to stagnant or wastewater being moved through the system.</note></term> enters the well Q. However, the water level cannot rise much from these sources—no more than two or three feet—because it seeks an exit through subterranean veins.

In well R, other water always arrives through its own veins.

It should be noted here that for the first time, tube D must be filled through the orifice N, which is immediately closed and always remains closed thereafter.

# BOOK THREE.
## Concerning motion generated from the natures of the four Elements.
### CHAPTER I.

->*On the nature of formal motion <note>original: "motus formalis"; in Aristotelian physics, this refers to motion dictated by the essential nature or "form" of an object, such as fire rising or earth falling</note>, and on the certain axioms of the Philosophers which demonstrate the reason for the diversity of motions originating from elementary bodies.*<-

->Rule I.<-

*According to the consensus of all Philosophers, a vacuum is not permitted in the nature of things.*

->Demonstration.<-

Since all elements are corporeal <term>corporeal: having a physical body or substance</term> substances (for they are the matrices <note>original: "matrices"; the source or "womb" where qualities are generated</note> of the primary qualities), it is necessary that every sublunary <term>sublunary: the region below the moon, where the four elements—earth, water, air, and fire—interact and change</term> place be filled either with elements or with things composed of elements. Because elements are dispersed everywhere and their parts are continuous, a vacuum—which is nothing other than the absence of a body—cannot exist in the nature of things.

->Rule II.<-

*Air, since it is a body, does not allow any other body to enter into its place until some part of it, or the whole of it, withdraws from that place.* This is demonstrated by the following experiment, which is widely known:

![Scientific diagram showing an inverted glass vessel (A) in a basin of water (B)](https://example.com/placeholder.png)

*A. A glass vessel filled only with air. If its opening, C, is pressed into the water of the basin B, no part of the water will be able to enter until some part of the air has exited; for the exit of the air is the entrance of the water.*

### Rule III.

> *Light elements naturally yield their place to heavier ones; for Fire gives way to air, air to water, and water to earth. The reason is that heavy things naturally tend downward, while lighter things are thrust toward the circumference <note>original: "versus circumferentiam." In the cosmology of the time, the "circumference" refers to the outer edges of the universe, where the lightest element, Fire, resides.</note>, as will be explained in the following experiments.*

---

It is manifest from the preceding experiments that the thick and heavy resists the thin and light; furthermore, a <term>subtle body<note>Subtle (subtile) refers to matter that is thin, rarified, or fine, like air or spirit, as opposed to "dense" matter like water or earth.</note></term> is more volatile and fleeting than a dense one. Thus it happens that it easily recedes and, because of its ability to penetrate, it departs through narrower passages. For at the top of the flask **A** is a certain hole, namely **B**, through which the receding air allows the water to enter through the mouth of the vessel. However, when that hole is blocked, the entry of water is immediately hindered; when it is suddenly opened, the water enters again and increases within the small vessel.

In the second experiment, it is manifest that water poured in through the opening of the tube **c. d.** compels the air occupying the region of the vessel **D** to fly out through tube **E**.

### Rule IV.

> *Sometimes heavy things are thrust out by trapped light things; this occurs where the path is blocked by heavier things, so that a light body, being pushed by another thick body and by the heavier body that is to be displaced, cannot depart from its place unless the less heavy body is displaced first, as appears more clearly in the following example.*

This rule seems to be contradictory to the previous rule, since the preceding rule suggests that the heavy pushes down the light <note>original: "grave detrudat leve"</note>. However, it must be understood that in this section we are not speaking of the simple motion of an element, but of <term>composite motion</term> <note>The action of one element upon another, and then that element upon a third.</note>. For in the first demonstration, sand poured through opening **A** into the region of vessel **B** gradually expels the air that fills said region through opening **C**. Both of these are refined and thinned by the fire, and are gradually pushed out through the small opening **k** until the air has completely refilled the vessel.

## *Rule V.*

*Fire also expels air through <term>subtiliation</term> <note>The process of thinning or rarefaction, where a substance expands and becomes less dense when heated.</note>. **A.** represents the fire heating region **B**, which is filled with air. This air, having been thinned, exits part by part into region **C**, where it seeks a more spacious area.

*Where air enclosed in any place is either evacuated or consumed, it is necessary that some new body fills that place, so that a <term>vacuum</term> <note>The classical belief that nature "abhors a vacuum" and will immediately pull matter in to fill any empty space.</note> is not permitted.* This is demonstrated by the following examples in *No. 2.*

In the second demonstration, a candle is fixed to the bottom of a vessel filled with water. Its flame enters the mouth of a flask <note>original: "phialæ"</note> when that mouth is pressed down at right angles to the candle; this will draw up into the flask a proportion of water from the vessel equal to the amount of air trapped in the flask that the flame has consumed. For air nourishes fire, and in nourishing it is consumed; and so that a vacuum is not admitted, water—which is the third element <note>In the ancient system of the four elements: Fire, Air, Water, and Earth.</note>—occupies the place of the consumed air.

### Rule VII.

*The substance of the element of water is joined to air by a tenacious bond, so that there is no distance between them; from this it follows that water is raised upward along with air.* This is demonstrated by the following examples.

---

In the first demonstration, the contact <note>original: "contiguitas"</note> of water with air is shown because when the end of a pipe or a hollow quill A is immersed in a cup, if the air trapped within the hollow of the quill is drawn out by the mouth, the air will lift the water up with it.

In the second, a channel <note>a tube or siphon</note> inserted through the side of a jar A, labeled c. d. e., will never stop emptying the water filling the jar through its opening e. until the water level has fallen to the end of the tube F. At that point, it will cease to flow: for the water poured into the jar expels the air that was in the tube C. E., and water takes its place. But when the water has descended to the mark F, then air is permitted to enter because of the absence of water, so that water no longer flows through E. There are certainly infinite examples based on the intent of this rule, some of which we recount in our practical section.

### Rule VIII.

*Water does not exit from a jar unless air and a similar body follow it: from which the marvelous industry of nature in the avoidance of a vacuum appears clearly to us.* This is shown by the following example, Number 1.

Suppose there is a vessel or some jar which has a hole at its top, but many holes in its bottom. Let that vessel be filled with water; as long as hole A is [blocked] by a finger...

This action lifts and then releases an axe, allowing it to strike an object on a stone anvil—a clear example of using water power to automate the sharpening of tools or the crushing of materials.

This rotates a wheel ('c') equipped with spikes or cams. As the wheel turns, these spikes catch a lever ('e') which is balanced by a smaller weight ('g'). This mechanism causes a wooden arm holding an axe to perform a repeated chopping motion, making the figure appear as if it were a living soldier or laborer.

### Experiment III.

The burning of houses, the lighting of altar sacrifices, the appearance of long-haired and bearded comets, the offering of incense, and many other such artistic effects can be achieved through the motion described in the first experiment. This is done if a candlestick, a lit candle, or a lamp is hidden within the hollow of the altar in such a way that the lit flame touches a copper plate that blocks a certain hole at the top of the altar. By the motion of a lead weight or of water at a specific time, that plate will be secretly removed, and the flame, emerging through the hole, will ignite whatever combustible material it finds upon the altar. Therefore, if paper or wooden palaces, or some fragrant and easily ignited wood, or incense mixed with wood are placed there, everything will burst into flames. This experiment will, therefore, be very useful for the artificial representation of the destruction of *Troy*, the burning of *Nero's Rome*, the immolation of *Sardanapalus* <note>A legendary Assyrian king who, according to myth, burned himself alive along with his palace to avoid capture.</note> with his palace, and other similar events.

In the first demonstration, weight A presses down on the sand B. Because the sand is expelled through the opening G, the weight gradually descends. Its extending arm <term>d<note>The Latin "excrescens d." refers to a protruding piece or extension labeled "d" in the diagrams that originally accompanied this text.</note></term> passes through a wooden slot so that the weight moves more steadily and directly; as it falls upon the wooden spatula E, it presses it down. In this manner, a figure <note>original: "imago," referring to a decorative mechanical character</note> will sometimes move in a circle and sometimes remain fixed in place.

The same mechanism can be achieved using the weight of water, as seen in the second demonstration. Here, water A flows from the channel B into a small vessel C, gradually filling it. Once filled, the vessel becomes heavy enough to overcome the lead weight E, causing the vessel's valve g to fall upon the key D. This causes the valve to open until almost all the water has flowed out. Consequently, the weight E easily lifts the vessel again, since it has been made lighter by the drainage of the water. It is therefore necessary that the moving cord turns the wheel G, by whose action a sphere placed above it is rotated.

### Experiment VI.

Music is produced, with specific harmonious sounds, both by the movement of sand and by the flow of water itself, whether by means of a wheel or without it; and this is indeed done in various ways, the first of which concerns sounds produced by a <term>pipe<note>Latin: *fistula*. This refers to any tube-like musical instrument, such as a flute or an organ pipe.</note></term>. Here, therefore, we shall briefly describe the mechanical artifice by which this can be accomplished.

First, it is certain that air is very easily expelled from a certain region of a vessel when a denser body intervenes, provided that a suitable and convenient exit is offered through which it may depart. Otherwise, the air does not permit another body—of whatever element it may be—into the place it occupies, as is sufficiently demonstrated by the second and third rules of this book.

Therefore, this sixth experiment will teach the method by which a <term>blast of air<note>Latin: *flatus*. In 17th-century mechanics, this refers to the pressurized air flow or "wind" necessary to power organs or automated sound-makers.</note></term> is created. For by this blast, organs and pipes will be heard to sound, bottles to "speak," birds to sing, snakes to hiss, and lions and bulls to roar and bellow. Moreover, this blast is produced either by the simple action of sand and water upon the air—namely, by expelling it from its place through an opening—or by a composite action, specifically the action of fire upon water, and then that water upon the air, as is manifest in the following demonstrations.

### *Experiment* VII.

The music of horns, trumpets, and other pipes, consisting of many harmonious parts, is produced by the following wheel <note>a pinned musical cylinder</note>, aided by the mechanical device described in the previous experiment. Therefore, let a wheel be constructed and divided into equal parts, so that each part serves for the musical duration known as a **semibreve** <note>original: "Semibreve"; equivalent to a modern whole note</note>. Then, divide each of these parts again into four equal sections; two of these together will represent the value of a **minima** <note>original: "Minimae"; a half note</note>, while each individual section represents a "black note" or **crotchet** <note>original: "cruchetam"; a quarter note</note>. From this, it is clear that the length <note>the circumference</note> of the wheel indicates the proportions of musical time, while its width represents the degrees of the musical system <note>pitch</note>.

Consequently, the width of the wheel must be divided into as many parts or "keys" as there are notes in the musical system, counted in their proper order: **Gamma-ut, A-re, B-mi**, and so on <note>the traditional "Guidonian" system for naming notes: G, A, B, etc.</note>. Thus, the pins <insert>or pegs</insert> must be skillfully applied across the width and length of the wheel, so that they are arranged according to the measure of time as well as their true position in the musical system, following the nature of the song. Finally, the wheel is set in motion according to the teachings of the fifth experiment, or according to the inventor's own arrangement, so that the pins on the wheel move and press down the keys of the pipes.

### Rule XI.

Water contained in one region of a vessel is pushed down and propelled upward, partly by the force of external water driving out trapped air, and partly by a hidden machine placed beneath the water's region. The reasoning by which water raises water by means of air is explained in Rule 4 of the third book. However, the hidden machine in the "belly" of the vessel is made from an iron wire, <term>wound like a spring</term> <note>original: "spiritaliter" — in early modern science, this refers to both the shape of a spiral and the pneumatic principles of air and pressure</note>, such that by the pulling of a cord hidden secretly beneath a table, that wire is contracted according to its height; by the relaxation of the same cord, it is extended at the whim of the Artist. Therefore, by the contraction of the cord, the water stops flowing and spraying in all directions; by its relaxation, however, it splashes everywhere.

These two experiments serve many remarkable machines and inventions, intended both to provoke laughter among guests at a banquet and for the construction of artificial fountains. The method by which both types are beautifully explained follows below.

### Experiment XII.

How, by the heat of a very gentle fire or of the sun heating a vessel, the air contained within it may be so rarefied <note>rarefied: made less dense; expanded</note> that, after the vessel cools, water is carried upward against its nature <note>The author refers to the Aristotelian idea that water's "nature" is to move downward toward the center of the earth; here, suction overcomes gravity.</note> and fills the space of the air that was thinned and expelled.

Let there be a leaden ball (or, if possible, a glass one), hollow inside, of moderate capacity, and of a strong build so that it does not break. Let this ball be perforated at its top. Also, let another sufficiently large vessel be made and filled with water. Afterward, let these two vessels be so arranged that one arm of a curved tube or siphon descends almost to the very bottom of the water vessel. Similarly, let the other arm enter the hole in the ball, which must be sealed so that air can neither enter nor exit except through this single tube.

Therefore, let the ball be exposed to the sun's rays, or to a fire very much like the sun's heat. When the ball has become heated, part of the enclosed air—now thinned by the fire—exits through the curved siphon into the water-filled vessel (as demonstrated by Rule 5, Chapter 1 of this book) and will mix with the water there, stirring up many bubbles one after another. 

However, when the sun moves away from the ball, or the fire is removed, or the ball itself is placed in the shade, the air (which was previously rarefied) seeks to reclaim its lost volume because of the condensing cold that begins to take hold. Because the air's path is now blocked by water, the suction lifts the water up and carries it over into the ball. This water will then rise again and flow back down into its own vessel if the fire or solar rays touch the ball a second time.

## Experiment XIV.

This same experiment is also performed using the heat of fire. If a structure in the form of an altar is built, into the middle of whose base one end of a straight tube <term>tube: original *tuba*, here referring to a pipe or conduit</term> enters, while its other end enters a globe placed beneath the altar, cast from lead, glass, or some other material, it must be constructed so that no air at all can escape from the belly of the altar or the hollow of the globe, except through this tube. 

Then, if one end of a bent <term>siphon: a tube used to convey liquid upwards from a reservoir and then down to a lower level</term> siphon enters into the sphere or globe and reaches down to its bottom, and its other end or terminal point likewise enters into a jar standing next to the globe, almost reaching its bottom (as will be demonstrated below), and if, furthermore, water is poured in through a hole at the top of the sphere—the hole being plugged after the water is poured in—and then finally a fire is lit upon the altar: We say that the air contained in the hollow of the altar, now thinned <note>original: *rarefactum*; in early modern science, 'rarefaction' describes air expanding and becoming less dense when heated</note> by the heat of the fire, seeks a larger space. 

Wherefore, through the tube E. F., this thinned air from altar A descends into sphere C and pushes out the liquid held in that sphere through siphon G.H. into the jar or flask I.K.L.M. But when the fire is extinguished, the thinned air retreats and ascends back to its original place. Once the air has departed, the water that was pushed into the jar also returns into the sphere, and it remains in that sphere in the same state it was in before. The demonstration follows.

*A. Altar. B. fire. C. sphere or globe.*
*D. The hole through which water is placed into the globe.*
*E. F. Tube shared by both vessels.*
*G. H. Bent siphon, shared by the globe and the vessel I. K. L. M.*

### Experiment XV.

I once constructed a pouring vessel <term>prochyta</term> <note>original: "prochytam"; a specialized pitcher or vessel designed for controlled pouring of different liquids</note>, which emitted first water, then wine, then milk, then saffron water, and finally ink in succession. I shall make mention of this later in the following book regarding the construction of machines; but here I will explain the experiment from which I derived the invention of the said vessel: the vessel *A. B. C. D.* In the top of the vessel, let there be a small channel, namely *G*, and on its side let there be another, specifically *H*. Also, in the upper part of the vessel, let there be 3, 4, or more different compartments <term>claustra</term> <note>original: "claustra"; internal enclosed chambers or sections</note>, let them be *I. K. L. M.*, which must be so fitted that air can neither enter nor exit from one to another; and let each compartment have a very small channel or tube above, and another below.

Therefore, the openings *G. F.* are to be blocked, and the upper part of the vessel *C. D. E. F.* is to be filled. Afterward, let each compartment be filled individually through the lower tubes which are under the tail of the vessel, namely *I. K. L. & M.*, and let their openings be blocked while the channels *G. H.* are opened. Only all the water which is in *e. f. c. d.* will come out. Now, let there be different liquids in the different compartments: for example, let there be water in *I*, beer in *k*, wine in *L*, and oil in *M*. If, therefore, the opening *I* is opened, water will flow out through channel *G*; and if opening *k* is opened, beer will flow through *G*; and if opening *L* is opened, wine will flow through *G*. And if opening *M* is opened, oil will flow through *G*. From these things it is clear that from the same tube you can receive any liquid coming out by the opening and blocking of the compartment channels; and if all are plugged, nothing will go out, just as was stated by the eighth rule in the first chapter of this book. The demonstration of this follows.

---

### Experiment XVI.

Let an instrument sometimes be made with a continuous blast on account of the drawing-over of air by fire. The instrument can be made in this manner.

Let some round copper vessel be made, quite strong; in the top of which let there be an opening in the manner of a mortar <term>bombarda</term> <note>original: "bombardæ"; literally a cannon or mortar, referring here to a wide, reinforced opening</note>, and let that opening be very well blocked with wood so that nothing escapes. From the side of the vessel, let a channel of the same material ascend, sufficiently narrow. Therefore, let a third part of the vessel be filled with water before that large opening is blocked, and then afterward let it be placed near a sufficiently strong fire so that the water boils; which, being rarefied <term>subtiliata</term> <note>original: "subtiliata"; the process of turning a liquid into a fine vapor or "thinning" the air through heat</note> along with the air, produces constant winds and blasts...

# BOOK FOUR

## Concerning the invention of our entire pneumatic machine.
<note>original: *machinæ ſpiritalis*. In this period, "spiritual" or "spiritalis" refers to *spiritus* (air or breath), indicating a machine powered by air or water pressure, commonly known as a pneumatic machine.</note>

---

### CHAPTER I.

#### *On the shape of the base of our pneumatic machine.*

**Q**UONIAM <note>Since</note> we desire this pneumatic machine of ours to revolve around the conditions of the seven Planets, for that reason we have arranged its base—according to whose proportions it must be raised upward—into a heptagonal <term>heptagonal: a seven-sided polygon</term> shape, so that each of its sides might correspond to the nature of one of the Planets. Therefore, let a circle described upon some flat surface, namely upon the ground or a pavement, be divided into seven equal parts: from each point of division to the next point of division, let a straight line be drawn, and in this way you will have a straight heptagonal figure. Once this is done, let a straight line be drawn to each angle of the heptagonal surface, which must be divided into seven equal parts. And this is to be done for every line drawn from the center to an angle. Then, from each point of division to the point opposite it, let a straight line be drawn, so that many heptagonal surfaces—one smaller in proportion than the other—are enclosed within each larger one. In the center of this surface, let there be a sufficiently large hole, through which a large bronze or iron tube <note>original: *tuba*</note> may emerge. Through this, water is to flow upward, and for that reason, that tube must ascend all the way to the top of the machine, so that by the rotation of the machine itself from one side to the other, water can very easily flow into any region of the machine. And this tube must also adhere firmly and immovably to the center of the base, so that the machine can be rotated upon it as if upon an axle <note>original: *axem*</note>. The partitions of this fundamental surface’s diameter, and consequently of its entire area into heptagons, denote the boundaries of each region of the machine, in which regions the natures of the Planets must be expressed, as we shall explain more extensively below. Here, indeed, we have described the heptagonal surface, ordered and arranged for the base of the machine.

<note>The vocabulary below defines the key technical terms used in the Latin original.</note>
**Pneumatic machine** <gloss>machina spiritalis</gloss>, **heptagon** <gloss>heptagonum</gloss>, **Planets** <gloss>Planetae</gloss>, **base** <gloss>basis</gloss>, **bronze tube** <gloss>tuba aenea</gloss>, **fundamental surface** <gloss>superficies fundamentalis</gloss>.

The design includes a central bronze or iron pipe for water distribution, serving as a fixed axle for the machine's rotation.</summary>

## CHAPTER II.

*Concerning the arrangement of the construction and form of this machine upon the aforementioned base.*

**T**he structure, which is to be built and erected upon this base, must follow the shape of the base itself: Let it therefore be divided according to its height into seven regions <note>These seven regions represent the seven classical planets: the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, and let there be a distance in height of three feet between each region; and let the width of each region be sufficiently appropriate and suitable for accommodating the actions and movements of the images, which can demonstrate the natures and conditions of the <term>planets</term><note>original: "planetarum"</note> through their actions. And in this way, it is necessary that from the base of the machine toward its summit there be a progression into a nearly <term>pyramidal</term><note>A tapering, tiered structure, similar to a stepped pyramid or a theatrical stage that narrows as it rises.</note> shape, so that each region, the further up it reaches, the smaller its capacity becomes; and consequently, where more actions and a greater number of actors are required, there the space is larger and exists closer to the viewer’s sight. Truly, on the flat surface separating the height of each region from the next, certain stories are to be painted, pertaining to the character of the Planet, which the ancient poets described, so that besides the actions of the moving images, the history and life of each Planet may be depicted on the ground <note>Likely referring to the floor or "stage" of each specific tier.</note>: Moreover, the entire substance of this machine, from the summit almost to its base, through

...the center of the base of the pyramid, looking toward its cone, must have a suitable opening so that the tube protruding from the center of the base can enter it. ### CHAPTER III.

->*Concerning the axis of the machine, which is fixed in the center of the base, on which the entire machine*<-
->*is turned lightly from one side to another.*<-

**H**ere, however, it must be noted regarding the axis of that <term>machine</term> mentioned previously, that a channel must be fixed and enclosed within it beneath the ground. This channel leads water from subterranean parts into the tube, so that the water can be propelled and spurt upward with sufficient force. Therefore, in the upper part of this axis, directly opposite the hollows of the regions where the historical scenes are painted, seven holes should be made—not too large—one for each region. This is done so that a single hollow part of the machine’s opening, out of the seven already mentioned, also has a hole in its own region. This hole is aligned so that the opening of the tube reaching it can inject or pour its water through, causing the internal mechanism to move. Upon its movement, the visible images will also move. This same process will occur with the holes of the other regions; indeed, it should be observed here that each side of every region must have such a hole in its midpoint. Furthermore, the summit or peak of this round tube must be secured with a round copper surface, constructed so that there is a hole in its center to manage the multifaceted motion of the upper <term>sphere</term>. Specifically, as the upper part of the machine is turned step by step, and containing the seven holes within itself, it ensures that in its circular motion, each of its holes gradually and successively joins its mouth with the orifice of the hole at the peak of the tube. Thus, the water exiting through the hole at the peak of the tube, and flowing upward through the hole adjacent to it, moves the internal mechanism, and by that movement, the sphere is also moved with its proper motion. In this manner, this <term>tube</term> <note>original: "tuba"</note> or <term>channel</term> <note>original: "canalis"</note> will be well-prepared to carry out the actions of the machine. Its description, including its holes, is sketched in this way.

## CHAPTER IV.

### *Concerning the frontispiece of the Planet Sun.*

**I**n the upper region of one side of the machine, a subtle arc of a sphere shall be depicted, in which a gilded man—clothed on all sides with rays in the manner of the Sun—is seated. Holding a lyre or <term>cithara</term> <note>A stringed instrument from the lute family, often associated with classical mythology.</note> in his hands, he will be seen to move little by little and step by step along the arc of his sphere. This ingenious device can be carried out through the experiments explained in the fourth and fifth sections of the preceding book.

Then, immediately after this movement of the Sun (or Apollo), Orpheus will suddenly appear in the lower region of the machine with his own lyre, by virtue of the aforementioned experiments. The music of the lyre will be perceived by those standing nearby, emerging from the hollow area of the lower region of the machine; because of Orpheus’s finger movements, the music will seem to be caused by Orpheus himself. In this way, a song of many parts <note>original: "cantilena multarum partium"</note> can be heard upon the brass strings of the instrument, a feat of ingenuity provided by the ninth experiment of the preceding book. However, once the song is finished, Orpheus will depart. 

From there, moving upward into the second region of the same side, there will appear a chorus of men holding trumpets to their mouths. The figures of that chorus will be seen turning themselves toward the spectators—

### CHAPTER VI.
->About the second side and the regions of the Moon.<-

**H**aving completed those actions of the regions of the *Sun*, the solar side will suddenly vanish, and after it, the Lunar side will appear; and this shall be done by the rotation of the universal machine <term>machinæ universalis (a large-scale mechanical device used for theatrical or allegorical displays)</term>. In the upper region of this side, therefore, let the figure of *Cynthia* <note>original: "Cynthiæ", a poetic name for the Moon goddess</note> be sculpted, supporting the shape of a crescent moon upon her head, clothed and adorned according to the fictional intentions of the Poets. She shall suddenly move in her region as if in the arc of a certain sphere in her own proper sign <note>The Moon’s zodiac sign is Cancer</note>, just as the *Sun* does in *Leo*. And this shall be done by the teaching of the fourth experiment of the preceding book.

And because this Planet is moist, and has dominion especially over the waters, we shall therefore treat in her regions those histories which have communication with water. *In the first* region, therefore, shall be the history of *Neptune*, *Aethis*, and *Glaucus* <note>original: "Gloci", likely referring to the sea-god Glaucus</note> upon the backs of Dolphins. *In the second* region, the *flood of Deucalion* <note>The Greek myth of a Great Flood</note> with rain falling from every side. *In the third*, *Diana with her Nymphs* bathing in a spring, with the appearance of *Actaeon* among the groves, observing the bathing *Diana* herself; so that, having perceived *Actaeon*, *Diana* suddenly vanishes with her Nymphs as if terrified. *In the fourth* shall appear a certain hunt, with some blowing upon horns that give out sound, and there at the end, the dogs of *Actaeon* pursuing him, shall finally tear him apart and kill him. *In the fifth*, the *Tragedy of Leander* with *Hero*, and the drowning of *Leander*. *In the sixth*, the *love of Narcissus*, and his drowning in the spring, and the rising of the *Narcissus* flower.

As for what pertains to the boards <note>original: "asseres", likely the mechanical panels or partitions</note> distinguishing the height of the regions, you could adorn them with pictures pertaining to *Cynthia*, such as her descent to the underworld and her reception by *Pluto*, etc., or other figures and actions suitable to each region. And now the sphere at the summit of the machine ought to move circularly, emitting water from its top through a fine pipe. All these actions, however, and the reasoning behind them, are easily drawn from the experiments of the preceding book, as well as from the elements expressed at the beginning of the third book, and finally from the inventions explained in the pneumatics of Hero <note>original: "spiritalibus Heronis", referring to Hero of Alexandria, an ancient engineer famous for hydraulic and pneumatic automata</note>.

### CHAPTER VII.
->About the third side of the frontispiece, namely Saturn.<-

**O**n the third side, the regions of Saturn shall be described, who, because he is a sad and Melancholic Planet, we have therefore adapted things in his regions suitable to his own nature. Hence, at their summit, we have placed *Saturn* moving in his sign, as above; and, because he was the inventor of agriculture, in the lowest region we have depicted a man with oxen directing a plow, who ought to move twice or thrice around his region. *In the second region*, let an altar dedicated to *Saturn* be placed, with the inhabitants of Italy and King *Janus* <note>The Roman god of beginnings, often associated with Saturn's arrival in Italy</note> worshipping him with the solemnity suitable to *Saturn*. *In the third*, let there be the image of *Diogenes* proving his melancholy in his *Amphora* <note>original: "Amphora", the large clay jar or "tub" in which the Cynic philosopher Diogenes lived</note>, which is proper to *Saturn*, before whom Athenian men shall stand. *In the fourth*, let there be snow and hail falling upon houses and cutting down herbs and trees, with moving cattle, and men lighting a fire.

## CHAPTER VIII.

### *Concerning the regions or frontispiece of Mars.*

**W**hen these actions are finished, the side of *Mars* will suddenly present itself, in which the figure of *Mars* himself will be placed in the highest region, and he will move as if in the arc of a certain sphere (which the figure of <term>Aries<note>The Ram, the zodiac sign ruled by Mars.</note></term> will occupy), holding a sword in one hand and a spear in the other. In *one part* of the lower region, a castle adorned with <term>bombards<note>Early forms of cannons or mortars.</note></term> will be formed; on the other side, however, ships with spread sails will move toward that castle. As soon as those ships begin to approach the castle, the bombards of the castle will be discharged step by step, and suddenly each ship in its turn will respond with its own tiny bombards, until all the bombards have been fired.

In the *second region*, two armies will appear fighting among themselves with spears and swords. In the *third* region, *Hercules* will be depicted battling against the *Hydra* and the *Lion*, whom *Hercules* will lay prostrate at the end. In the *fourth* region will be the love of *Mars* with *Venus*, and *Vulcan* will diligently observe him talking with *Venus*, covering and trapping them both in an iron net. One must deal with the outer panels just as in the preceding sections, by adorning them with paintings of things most suitable to these actions. Meanwhile, the sphere revolving at the summit ought to vomit fire from one side toward the end. And when these things are finished, this side too will vanish.

# BOOK ONE.
## On the types of Time.

---

### CHAPTER I.
### On the difference between time, age, and eternity.

<insert>P</insert>ost the history of motions, both natural and artificial, the order of our work requires that we discourse briefly on the nature of Time. Time is defined as the *number of motions of changeable things as a measurement, specifically according to before and after.* <note>original: "numerus motuum rerum mutabilium mensurans, & id quidem secundùm prius & posterius." This is the classic Aristotelian definition of time.</note> Indeed, it is that span drawn from the revolution of the heavens and the sun, by which we measure the movement and the changing states of all things that can move. From this it becomes clear that in time there is a "motion from a starting point toward a destination." By these conditions, time is distinguished from its two relatives or "kin": namely <term>Aevum</term> <note>Latin: *Ævum*. In scholastic philosophy, this is the "middle" state of duration for beings like angels, who have a beginning but no end.</note>, the condition of which is to measure the local motions of those things that have a beginning but no end; and <term>Eternity</term>, which is the infinite measure of that which has no beginning, no middle, and no end whatsoever.

Furthermore, this temporal "numbering" of motions, if compared to the motion as its efficient cause—such as a calendar day compared to the motion of the sun above the earth—is called the *numbered number* <note>Latin: *numerus numeratus*. This refers to time as a quantity resulting from a specific event.</note>. If, however, it is compared to the moving subject itself according to its parts—namely, present, past, and future—then it is called the *mediating numbering number*. Similarly, because this number measures motion according to what is "before" (the past) and what is "after" (the future), it cannot exist entirely in a single moment, since a moment is only a tiny portion of the present time. Thus it follows that, just as a number is composed of units and a line of points, so also is time constituted of tiny pieces or moments. Therefore, a <term>moment</term> <note>Latin: *momentum*.</note> is properly said to be the very act or substance of time itself, since moments continued without interval are nothing other than time itself. Time is generally divided into *years, months, weeks, days, hours, and minutes*, which we shall discuss in this book.

---

### CHAPTER II.
### On the Year.

**A** year is that span of time in which the sun, by its natural motion, passes through the twelve signs of the <term>Zodiac</term>. According to some (such as *Isidore* <note>Saint Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century scholar famous for his etymological encyclopedias.</note>, etc.), it is called *Annus* from *An*, which means "around," because in the circular motion of the sun, both ends of the circle are joined—that is, the Sun returns by its natural motion to the place from which it departed. And hence it is also that others have more correctly thought the name *Year* is derived from *annulus* (a ring) for that same reason. For this reason, even the *Egyptians*, before the invention of the alphabet, represented the *year* hieroglyphically by the sign of a *Dragon* <note>original: *Draconis*. This refers to the Ouroboros, the serpent eating its own tail, a common symbol for the cyclical nature of the year.</note> turning in a circle and biting its own tail, they signifi-
