<page-num>505</page-num>
# ON THE KINDS OF TIME.

This is properly called the *solar year*, because it is measured by the movement of the sun in such a number—namely, a span of 12 months, or 365 days, 5 hours, and 46 minutes. This year is distinguished from the *Lunar year*, which is so named in three respects: for it is taken either for that time in which the Moon completes its course through the entire Zodiac in 27 days, 7 hours, and 44 minutes; or for the span between one conjunction of the Moon with the Sun and the next; or for the span of twelve lunar revolutions, which it completes in 354 days. This year is shorter than the solar year by 11 days, and from this difference or excess of days is born the <margin>-></margin> <term>Epact <note>original: "Epactus"; the number of days by which the solar year exceeds the lunar year, used to determine the date of Easter.</note></term>, as was stated in our book on *Astronomical Arithmetic*. Thus, every third solar year will consist of 13 lunations. But the remaining planets <margin>-></margin> also have their own years; for the *year of Saturn* consists of 30 solar years, and the *year of Jupiter* of 12. The *year of Mars*, however, consists of two, and so it is with the others. There is yet another year, which is called the *great year and the year of the world*, which according to *Aristotle* will be completed when all the stars return to the places and points in which they first began to move. Regarding the determination of this span, philosophers disagree: for according to some, it will be completed in 36,000 solar years; according to others, 49,000. And according to *Macrobius*, among the *Platonists*, the span of this year is only 15,000 solar years. However it may be, <margin>-></margin> it is certain that the solar year is what the common people generally consider the true year, though nations vary on its beginning. For the *Jews*, *Persians*, and *Greeks* begin the year from the autumnal equinox—specifically from the conjunction of the Moon with the Sun closest to that equinox. The *Arabs* begin their year in midsummer, namely when the Sun is found in its own house, that is, in Leo ♌. The *Alexandrians* want the year to begin on August 26th. The *Romans* begin theirs on the first day of January; the *Venetians* theirs on March 25th, because their city had its beginning at that time of year. Finally, *Astronomers* begin the solar year in the month of March, at the very same instant the Sun enters the point of Aries. The ancient *Greeks*, however, used another span of time which they called the *Olympiad*, followed by *Diodorus Siculus* in his history. An *Olympiad* was that span of time that lay between certain anniversary contests in the city of Morea <note>original: "Moreae"; likely referring to the Peloponnesian region where Olympia is located.</note>, which were called *Olympic* because there was a statue in that city dedicated to *Olympian Jupiter*, in whose honor *Hercules* had instituted the said exercises; and that span of the Olympiad lasted from 4 to 4 solar years.

---

## CHAPTER III.
### On the Week and the Month.

The **W**eek is so named because it consists of 7 days dedicated to the 7 planets. For Sunday <margin>-></margin> is assigned to the Sun, because the Sun is the master of the first hour after the sun’s rising on that day; then Venus ♀ occupies the second hour, and Mercury ☿ the third, and so on, proceeding according to the order of the planets until the completion of 24 hours. Thus, Monday is attributed to that planet, because <margin>-></margin> the Moon ☾ possesses its first hour after the sun's rising, and so it goes with the others.

That span of the year called a *month* is usually taken in two ways: namely, for that span in which the Moon completes its course through the 12 signs of the Zodiac, and this is called the *lunar month*, which only the *Hebrews* observed; or for the span in which the Sun passes through a single celestial sign, that is, 30 degrees, and it is called the *solar month*, which is also how the common people understand it. Properly, it is that span in which the Moon, having departed from the Sun, catches up to it again. Such a span of time in—

Likewise *February* is named from *februando* <note>Latin: purifying or performing a ritual purgation</note>, which signifies a cleansing; for the *Februa* <note>An ancient Roman festival of purification and atonement</note> are celebrated in honor of the dead. Others will have it that it is called *February* as if *Plutonian* <note>Referring to Pluto, the god of the underworld</note>, to whom they offered sacrifices in this month. *March* received its name from *Mars*, which name the Romans bestowed upon it in memory of *Romulus*, whom they believed to be the son of *Mars*. *April* is named from the verb *aperire* <note>Latin: to open</note>, since in this month the earth opens itself and sends forth its fruits. *May* was so called from the *majores* <note>Latin: ancestors or elders</note>, that is, from the Senators, for it was out of reverence and honor for them that they wished this month to be so named. There are others, however, who establish that the name of *May* descends from *Maia*, the wife of *Vulcan* and mother of *Mercury*; it would be tedious to discourse further on these matters here, as they are common knowledge.

## CHAPTER IV.
### On the Day.

**T**hat space of time which is called a *day*, we divide into the *non-solar and the solar day*. The Holy Scriptures testify that the *non-solar* day existed before the creation of the Sun, since they count three days before the production of the Sun. But because the fathers of Theology <note>Early Christian scholars and writers, such as St. Basil</note> seem to disagree among themselves regarding this species of day, we shall therefore briefly set forth our opinion on the matter in this place, according to our proposal concerning the *Macrocosm* <note>The "great world" or the universe as a whole</note>. First, however, we shall declare the opinions of the said theologians on this subject. *Basil and Damascenus* <note>St. Basil the Great and St. John of Damascus, influential Greek theologians</note> along with other *Greeks* say that the light made on the first day caused day and night through the emission and retraction of light, performed by the divine will. The *Latins*, however, more probably say that this primary light performed the same circulation that is now done by the Sun, and thus it illuminated that hemisphere in which it existed, and darkness was made in the opposite hemisphere due to the interposition of grosser and darker matter in the middle of the whole unformed mass; and thus they will have it that this light performed the office of the Sun.

We, however, establish that this day can be understood in two ways: first, for that clarity pushing down the darkness in the beginning from the *Empyrean* <note>The highest part of heaven, thought by ancients to be composed of pure fire or light</note> region, and purifying and refining its spirit according to the proportion of its action, in which case night, since it is a privation of clarity, can be held as the darkness possessing the lower spirit. And so the first day was in the highest region of the world, and night in the two lower ones; similarly, the second day was in the highest and middle region, while night was in the lowest; and the third day was in all three said regions, and night was on the earth, after which the solar day began on the following day. And this exposition is not entirely to be rejected, since it is rightly established that day and night are to be understood with respect to the subject to which the aforementioned dispositions of the two times ought to be presented.

<margin>*</margin> But truly the *Empyrean* heaven after its creation was entirely luminous and clear, whence it also received its name from fire <note>The Greek word "pyr" means fire</note>.
<margin>*</margin> Hence, therefore, immediately after its creation, it does not suffer night, nor are any shadows ever admitted into its immense interval.
<margin>*</margin> And this same thing must also be said of the *Ethereal* heaven <note>The celestial region beyond the moon, often considered the fifth element or aether</note>, which always shines in itself (though to us invisibly). Morning, therefore, can be taken as the beginning of the first, second, or third work, whereby light gradually entered the region to be created and gave it day, not otherwise than the Sun induces day by its elevation in our <margin>--></margin> hemisphere. Evening, however, can be taken for the end of the work, whereby the rays descended further into the darkness of the middle region. Furthermore, *our second exposition* <margin>--></margin>

# ON THE TYPES OF TIME.

...agrees with the Latin Theologians; for the Spirit moving over the waters communicated, through that motion, its acts with each heaven. In this way, a greater light was, as it were, infused through the presence of that spirit, because it performed the same duty in the super-celestial realms during creation as the Sun performs in the celestial realms during generation <note>The author is drawing a parallel: just as the Sun gives life to plants and animals today, the Holy Spirit "animated" the heavens at the start of time</note>. Therefore, those first three days of creation were **spiritual days**, measured by the Divine Spirit, in which more spiritual things were created. The remaining days, however, were **solar days**, and pertain to those things which are more corporeal <note>Physical or bodily</note>. It was seen that the world was made by a triple circuit of the spirit, related to the circular Trinity, and that in each of its circuits—each constituting a supernatural day—one region of the world was forged. Once this was completed, the divine tabernacle was established in the sun; by its own triple circular circuit, which brought about three other **natural days**, the creatures of the world—both the higher celestial ones and the lower ones—were produced.

*Astronomers have divided the solar day into the "natural" and the "artificial": The **natural day** is that space of time which proceeds from sunrise to sunrise—that is, from one specific point back to that same point. This day is again divided into two other intervals or distances, one of which constitutes the day and the other the night (known as the **artificial day**).* Consequently, the natural day is divided into 24 equal parts, which we call **hours.** Regarding these, we shall write to your heart's content in the two following books.

## C H A P. I.
### Concerning the method of constructing the <term>Scioteric</term> rule.

**T**HIS rule, which is called <term>Scioteric</term> <note>original: "Scioterica"; from the Greek words for shadow and observer, referring to the science of sundials</note>, contains within itself certain equal divisions of a straight line. These are derived from the equal partitioning of two quadrants so that they may serve in the rapid drawing of sundials. This present commentary has been written on this matter so that the method of constructing the said rule and its use may be learned. Therefore, the rule is prepared in this manner:

Upon the straight line D. F. in the drawing placed below this chapter, let the quadrant D. G. F. be described from center F, which is to be divided into 24 equal parts. Thus, the sixth part of the quadrant divided in this way is for one hour <note>representing 15 degrees, the angle the sun travels in one hour</note>, the twelfth for half an hour, and the twenty-fourth part for a quarter of an hour. Each one of the hours, however, ought to bear a double numbering, as appears in the following figure. Once the quadrant has been divided in this way, one must decide on the length of the rule, which may conveniently be extended to six digits <note>original: "digitos" — a traditional unit of measurement approximately the width of a finger</note>. On the given rule (whether it be made of brass or wood) A. B. C. D., let line A. B. be taken at the said length of six digits, and according to this distance, let line I. H. be drawn parallel to line D. F., the radius of the quadrant D. G. F. just described; this should intersect the radius (extended as needed) at point I. Then, from center F, draw a straight line F. H. through the fifth or seventh hour marked on arc D. G., which intersects line I. H. at point H. From H, draw the straight line H. L. parallel to line F. I., which intersects line D. F. at L. Finally, line F. L. will be the exact width of the rule adapted to the given length. Now, align the rule with center F and simultaneously with each of the divisions of arc D. G., and let straight lines be drawn which intersect lines L. H. and I. H. into unequal portions as the geometry dictates. These small parts ought to be transferred onto the rule and distinguished there by their own numbers, as is evident in lines A. B. and B. C. In the following treatise, these segments are called "parts of the hour" and "hour-parts," and when they are needed, each is to be taken from the rule (maintaining the order from A toward B) and drawn on a given line from a given point, as appears on line D. E. in <term>Horizontal</term> and wall-mounted <term>sundials</term>. After this, upon line F. E., let quadrant E. G. be described from center F and divided into 90 parts, beginning at point G and ending at point E. From center F, through that degree of quadrant F. G. E., let the straight line F. K. be drawn, cutting line I. K. at K; let the straight line K. M. be drawn parallel to line F. G., which intersects D. E. at M. Line F. M. will give the width of the rule and will be found equal to line F. L. Then let straight lines be drawn from center F to each individual degree of the quadrant...

## CHAPTER II.

### *On the use of the Scioteric Rule.*

**F**or a fuller use of the rule, a knowledge of certain propositions necessary for the description of <term>Horologes</term><note>An archaic term for sundials or time-keeping instruments.</note> is required. Although the geometric operation of these is familiar and known to any beginner, since they can be derived from this rule without a deep knowledge of geometric elements, I have judged it not foreign to the purpose to propose them in this place. The propositions therefore follow.

### Proposition I.

*Upon a given straight line, from a given point, to make a straight line at right angles; or what is the same, how you may lead a right angle to a given point in this manner:* On the rule, take the <term>radius</term><note>original: "semidiameter." In this context, it refers to a standard reference length on the mathematical instrument.</note> of the rule from B to C and mark it on the given line; then take the <term>tangent</term> of any degree—that is, place one foot of the compass on letter C and extend the other to any degree on line C-D; for example, to the fortieth. With the compass thus extended, place one of its feet on point E of the given line and describe arc G-H. Similarly, measure the <term>secant</term> of the same degree, which is done by placing one foot of the compass on B of the rule and extending the other to the said 40th degree. Fix the other foot of the compass on F of the given line and describe arc K-L, which intersects arc G-H at B. Then the line drawn from B to E will be <term>perpendicular</term>.

---

### Proposition II.

*The method of drawing an angle equal to a given angle upon a straight line at a given point.*

**I**n this entire treatise, we understand no other angle besides the right and the acute: we have already spoken of the right angle in the previous proposition; it remains for us to deal with the acute angle, which can be described thus.

Let the given line be E-F, and let an angle of 50 degrees be drawn at point F. From F to E, let the radius of the rule C-B be measured; then let the <term>secant of the complement</term><note>The complement is the angle needed to reach 90 degrees; for a 50-degree angle, the complement is 40 degrees.</note> of the assigned degree be taken, and according to this distance from point F, let arc K-L be described. Afterward, take the tangent of the same complement, and from point E describe arc G-H, which intersects arc K-L at P: Then let the line be drawn from P to F, and the angle P-F-E will contain 50 degrees, and will be equal to the assigned angle.

### CHAPTER III.
## On the Horizontal Sundial.

**A** Horizontal <term>Sundial|horologium</term> is the name given to one that is parallel to the plane of the horizon, and it is drawn in the following manner. Let a straight line E. F. be drawn. From E toward F, the distances for the hours are measured, taken from a ruler on line A. B. <note>original: "ex regula desumptæ in linea ejusdem A. B." — referring to a standardized scale used for geometric projections.</note> From point E of the given line, a perpendicular line E. G. should be raised; and in that same line, from E to G, one must measure the <term>secant|In early modern trigonometry, this refers to a specific length on a scale corresponding to the secant of an angle</term> of the elevation of the pole (which throughout this entire treatise we presuppose to be 51 1/2 degrees). <note>A latitude of 51.5° suggests the author may be writing for readers in Northern Europe, possibly near London, Antwerp, or Cologne.</note> From point G to the individual markings on line E. F., straight lines are to be drawn, which may be extended as far as desired. From the same point G, a straight line parallel to E. F. is drawn. In this way, you will have the hour lines of the Horizontal Sundial described. To prepare the <term>style|stylus; the blade or rod of the sundial that casts the shadow</term>, the secant of the equinoctial <note>The equinoctial refers to the celestial equator; the angle used here is complementary to the latitude.</note> should be measured on line E. F. from E to H, <note>The Latin text reads "ab E. ad A.", likely a typographical error for "H" as indicated in the subsequent instruction and diagram.</note> and a line should be drawn from point G to H, which will represent the style. From this model, a complete Horizontal sundial can be transferred onto any designated surface.

## CHAPTER IV.
### *On the mural <gloss>wall-mounted</gloss> or vertical sundial.*

**A** mural sundial is one that is drawn upon a surface parallel to the plane of the vertical circle, which is why it is also called a vertical sundial. It is either Southern or Northern. Both can be transferred from the same model, the layout of which is as follows: On the straight line E. F., let the distances of the hours be measured, as was done in the previous section. Then let a perpendicular line E. G. be erected. From point E towards G, let the secant <term>secant: a trigonometric function used here to calculate the length of the shadow-casting parts based on latitude</term> of the elevation of the Equator be measured (which we assume to be 38.5 degrees <note>This latitude suggests the author may be calculating for a location in central Europe, likely near Frankfurt or Mainz.</note>). From point G to each of the individual hour sections on line E. F. [draw lines]. And in this way, the hour lines belonging to the mural sundial will appear. To find the stylus <term>stylus: the rod or pin, often called a gnomon, that casts the shadow onto the dial face</term>, let the secant of the elevation of the pole be measured from point E to H on line E. F., and the straight line drawn from point G to H will give the stylus.

---

It should be noted that a complete southern **mural sundial** must be transferred from this model, but this is not so for the Northern one. For the Northern dial only admits two hours before six and two hours after six. Those who live closer to the North have more hour lines; those who move closer to the South have fewer.

It must also be observed in the *Northern sundial* that the tip of the stylus always points upwards.

---

E. be formed which is equal to the angle of the polar elevation. In the line...

## CHAPTER VI.

### *On the Declining Sundial.*

**A** **declining sundial** is one that stands at a right angle <note>90 degrees</note> to the plane of the Horizon, but at an oblique <note>non-perpendicular</note> angle to the plane of the vertical circle. The amount of "declination" is determined by the arc <note>the degree of the curve</note> measured between the plane of the vertical circle and the surface of the wall where the dial is placed; this angle is always less than 90 degrees. A declining sundial is primarily named after the North or South, but with the addition of the other two cardinal directions; thus, a dial may decline from South toward the East, or from South toward the West, or from North toward the East, or from North toward the West. He who knows how to construct one of these knows how to make them all, because they do not differ in any essential logic; rather, all of them can be derived from one and the same model, provided the declination is the same. They only differ in the naming and placement of the hours. For example, if you draw a sundial on one side of a sheet of paper for a wall that turns from South toward the East, those same lines viewed from the other side of the paper will provide a dial that declines from South toward the West. By merely changing the labels of the hours, the remaining two types of dials will emerge from that same pattern.

A declining sundial is drawn in this manner: Let us suppose the declination is 40 degrees toward the East. Upon the straight line **E. F.**, let a perpendicular line **G. H.** be erected, dividing line **E. F.** at point **I.** Upon the line **E. F.** at point **I.** (on the left side, if the given surface declines from South to East or North to West; but on the right side, if it declines from South to West or North to East), let an angle be drawn equal to the <term>complement of the declination</term> <note>the "complement" is the remainder of 90 degrees; if the declination is 40°, the complement is 50°</note>, forming the angle **E. I. K.** On line **I. K.**, measure from point **I.** to **K.** the <term>secant of the pole's elevation</term> <note>a trigonometric value based on the local latitude</note>. From point **K.**, let line **K. L.** be erected perpendicular to **I. E.** at point **L.** From point **K.**, let line **K. M.** be drawn perpendicular to **I. E.**, dividing **I. E.** at point **M.** On line **G. H.**, measure from point **I.** to **G.** (if the declination is Southern) or from point **I.** to **H.** (if it is Northern) the <term>secant of the Equator</term>. From point **G.** to **L.**, draw a straight line representing the sixth hour. From point **G.** to **M.**, draw the <term>substylar line</term> <note>the line on the dial face directly beneath the gnomon</note>. From **M.**, draw line **M. P.** perpendicular to **G. M.** and equal in length to line **M. K.** A straight line drawn from **G.** to **P.** will give the <term>style</term> <note>the "gnomon" or rod that casts the shadow</note>. From point **I.**, draw line **N. I. O.** perpendicular to **K. I.**, extending it as far as possible. On this line, on both sides of point **I.**, the hours are measured and transferred from a rule. From point **K.** to each of the hour marks, draw faint lines that divide line **E. F.** into as many parts as possible. Straight lines drawn from point **G.** to the intersections on line **E. F.** will provide the hour lines we seek for the proposed declining sundial. Therefore, the style must be erected over the line **G. M. P.**; and from the following model, four declining sundials can be derived.

# CHAPTER VII.

## On the Reclining and Inclining Sundial.

**A** <term>reclining sundial</term> <note>original: "Horologium reclinans"</note> is one whose surface, representing one of the four cardinal points, forms an obtuse angle with the Horizon if it were to be extended. An <term>inclining sundial</term> <note>original: "Horologium inclinans"</note> is one that creates an acute angle with the Horizon. Each of these is divided into four types, according to the different positions of the four cardinal points; for a dial, whether reclining or inclining, is either Eastern, Western, Northern, or Southern. The degree of recline or incline is known from the arc contained between the Horizon and the designated surface. Reclining and inclining dials that face each other are essentially identical in nature and are constructed with the same skill and labor; they differ only in the naming of the hours and their placement, as will appear in the following sections. We shall first deal with the Southern reclining and Northern inclining dials, which are opposites, and afterwards with the Eastern and Western types.

If the Southern recline and the Northern incline are equal to the <term>polar elevation</term> <note>This refers to the latitude of the observer's location.</note>, it is named a **Polar Sundial**, and it is prepared in this manner: Let a straight line **E. F.** be drawn parallel to the Horizon, in the middle of which a perpendicular line **G. H.** is raised, which intersects line **E. F.** at point **H.** On line **E. F.**, on both sides of point **H.**, the hours are to be numbered according to a scale transferred from a rule; at each individual point, let straight lines be drawn parallel to line **G. H.**, and thus the hour lines of the polar sundial will appear. Let the <term>Style</term> <note>The "stylus" or gnomon; the part of the sundial that casts the shadow.</note> be perpendicular to the surface, and let its length be equal to the radius of the scale used. But if the distance of the hour lines described here does not fit the given surface properly, it can be either increased or contracted as the occasion demands, as we have taught previously in the description of the Eastern Sundial.

### TREATISE II. PART VII. BOOK II.

If the reclining or inclining angle is less than the elevation of the pole <note>original: "elevatione poli"; the observer's latitude</note>, subtract the reclining angle from the elevation of the pole, and let the remainder serve as the pole's elevation, according to which a **Horizontal** <term>Horizontal: A sundial whose plate is parallel to the horizon</term> sundial may be constructed, as we have previously taught. This will result in a Southern reclining dial, or a Northern inclining dial for the given reclining angle. But if the reclining angle is greater than the pole's elevation, subtract the pole's elevation from the reclining angle, and let the remainder serve as the elevation of the Equator; then construct a mural <note>a wall-mounted</note> sundial, as was said before, and this will be a Southern reclining and Northern inclining dial for the given reclining angle.

*Southern reclining and inclining sundials have their own specific forms proper to them;* if the reclining or inclining angle is equal to the elevation of the Equator, then the sundial has its own character and name, and is called an **Equinoctial Sundial** <term>Equinoctial Sundial: A dial whose face is parallel to the Earth's equator</term>, because it is placed on a surface parallel to the plane of the Equator, and it is prepared in this manner: Let a straight line E. F. be drawn, and on both sides from point E. toward F., let the distance of the hours be measured as taken from a rule <note>a measuring scale</note>. From point E., let E. G. be erected perpendicular to E. F., and with a length equal to the radius of the rule from point G., let straight lines be drawn to each hour section. From point G., let a straight line be drawn parallel to line E. F. In this way, the hour lines will present themselves for an Equinoctial sundial. The **stylus** <term>Stylus: The rod or "gnomon" that casts the shadow</term> must be erected from the center perpendicular to the surface of the sundial, extended to whatever length is desired.

->*Equinoctial Sundial, or Southern Reclining by 38 and 1/2 degrees.*<-

In the present sundial and in others of the same kind, it must be noted that a Southern reclining sundial may not obtain more than twelve hours; it can, however, have fewer. This happens when the inclination is less than the sun's midday height in the **Southern Tropic** <term>Southern Tropic: The Tropic of Capricorn, marking the sun's southernmost point in the sky</term>. For then, the meridian line <note>the noon line</note> will never be illuminated by the sun; and by the same reasoning, one may judge the others as the inclination is decreased.

Furthermore, if the Northern inclination is greater than the sun's maximum midday height in the Northern signs <note>the Zodiac signs of summer, like Cancer</note>, then the meridian line will never be illuminated by the sun, and so it goes for the others as the inclination is increased.

If the <term>reclination</term><note>the angle at which a dial plate tilts backward away from the observer</note> is less than the elevation of the Equator, add the reclination to the polar elevation, and by calculating the total as the elevation of the pole, a Horizontal sundial may be drawn as was shown before: And in this manner, a North reclining sundial will be produced, and consequently a South <term>inclining</term><note>tilting forward toward the observer</note> one.

If the inclination or reclination is greater than the elevation of the Equator, add the <term>complement</term><note>the angle needed to reach 90 degrees</note> of the reclination to the elevation of the Equator, and by calculating the total for the Equator, you should draw the sundial as previously demonstrated: And thus you will obtain the hour lines which you desire.

# C H A P T E R VIII.

## *Concerning East & West Reclining and Inclining Sundials.*

**J**ust as declining sundials can all be derived from the same model, so too can these which we are now discussing: whatever, therefore, was said of those before is also to be understood regarding these. The proposed sundials are thus to be delineated in this manner: Let us suppose the reclination to be 40 degrees toward the East: upon the meridian line G.H., let a perpendicular line E.F. be drawn to point I. Upon the line I.H. at point I, let the angle K.I.H. be established equal to the angle of reclination: On the line I.K., from I to K, let the <term>secant</term><note>a trigonometric value used in the geometric construction of the dial’s angles</note> of the Equator be numbered: From point K, let the line K.L. be drawn perpendicular to I.K., which should intersect line I.E. at L. From point K, let line K.M. be drawn perpendicular to I.E., which should intersect I.E. at M. On the line G.H., from I to H (if the reclination is toward the East, but if it were toward the West, from I to G), let the secant of the elevation of the pole be measured: From point H to L, let a straight line be drawn, which represents the sixth hour: From point H to M, let the <term>substylar line</term><note>original: "linea substylaris" — the line on the dial's face directly beneath the gnomon</note> be drawn: From point M, let the line P.M. be drawn perpendicular to H.M., equal to line M.K. A straight line drawn from H to P will give the <term>style</term><note>original: "stylus" — the shadow-casting edge of the gnomon</note>: From point I, let line N.I.O. be drawn perpendicular to K.I., which should be extended as far as possible: On this line, on both sides of point I, let the hours be numbered as taken from the rule: From point K to the individual hour marks, let faint lines be drawn, which should divide line E.F. into as many parts as can conveniently be done: Straight lines drawn from point H to the individual intersections of line E.F. will give the hour lines which we seek.

# BOOK THREE.

## On our clockwork machine.

---

### CHAPTER I.

### *Regarding the amphora or hollow space containing water, in which the indicator of the clock must move up and down.*

Let a vessel <note>original: "amphora"</note> be made of lead in a shape that is either round, pentagonal, or hexagonal; however, it is better to have a shape with sides rather than a round one for the purpose of marking the twelve hours upon it. This vessel should be fitted in such a way that all its sides are equal, and consequently all its angles are similar, with the same dimensions of hollowness in all parts. This is so that the floating <term>cursor</term> <note>A "cursor" is a sliding indicator or float that tracks the water level.</note> can be moved up and down within it exactly and without hindrance. That is to say, all the angles of the float's base and its sides should be aptly fitted to the sides and angles of the containing vessel, so that they move without obstacle, being lifted upward as water flows into the vessel and descending as the water flows out again.

In the middle of its base, there should be a hole of such a size that nearly all the liquid of the filled vessel can exit through it in the space of twelve hours. Indeed, so that this vessel can be filled again with a new supply of water, it shall have a tube protruding outside the vessel, rising slightly above the height of the vessel itself. The lower part of this tube shall enter into the lower part of the vessel's side; from there, once a valve <note>original: "clave," literally a key or stopcock.</note> of the <term>aqueduct</term> <note>The water supply system feeding the clock.</note> has been turned by a certain mechanical device (as will be shown below), the water exiting through the opening of the channel will fill that vessel or amphora little by little and step by step through the tube. When this is done and the valve is turned again, the water will once more glide out through the hole in the bottom of the vessel. In this way, without the contact of hands, that clock will always move and will demonstrate the hours of the day and night.

But since the water gradually decreases from the upper rim of the vessel down to its bottom over the space of twelve hours, we shall therefore divide one side of the vessel into twelve equal parts, counting from the aforementioned upper rim down almost to its foot. And indeed, this division ought to be made with distinct lines, always inserting a subdivision of each part into four other equal parts by means of fainter lines. For in this way, a single indicator point <note>original: "hypothesis"</note> on the float, descending gradually, will point as if with a finger to the number of the hours and their quarters. We have drawn an example of this vessel in the following manner.

## CHAPTER II.
### Concerning the internal part of this machine.

Let a base for the <term>moving instrument</term><note>The "basis instrumenti cursorii" refers to a float or piston that travels vertically as the water level changes.</note> be prepared from wood that is sufficiently solid but somewhat porous, imitating the angles and sides of the containing jar <note>original: "amphorae"</note>, yet in such a way that the base is adapted so that it can move up and down through the angles and sides of the said vessel without hindrance, and on such condition that it inclines in no way toward the right or left, but always performs its movement perpendicularly. The length of this column ought to be distributed into 40, 50, or even more parts—up to a hundred—which parts again ought to be subdivided into four others. These divisions will serve the musical timing for a song composed for bells, sounding at every twelfth hour, which melody will last through this ascent of the column from the base of the vessel up to its edges. ## CHAPTER III.

### *On the position and site of the bells, and on the construction and arrangement of the hammers striking them.*

**C**oncerning the order of the small bells, it should be known that there are two methods: one that is better suited and more fit for the mechanical construction of the instrument, and another that is more accommodated to the arrangement of the sounds. As for the former, because of the great number of bells, it is necessary to arrange and place them in a circular or round order, since that shape is the most capacious of all; or even, if preferred, according to the shape of the column or the whole machine itself, so that the striking keys <note>These "keys" or "pins" are the pegs on the rotating drum that trigger the mechanism.</note> may more easily reach the bell hammers. According to the order of sounds, they should also be established so that they represent the true series of the <term>Musical system<note>The "musical system" refers to the standard scale or gamut used during the Renaissance and Baroque periods.</note></term>, so that the preceding bell corresponds to the following in tone and semitone according to the tenor and norm of the <term>Monochord<note>A monochord was a single-stringed instrument used by scientists and musicians to mathematically determine the correct pitch and intervals of the scale.</note></term>, lest discords arise instead of harmonies. Therefore, the largest bell, which represents **Gamma Ut** <note>original: "Γ. ut." — This was the traditional name for the lowest note in the musical scale of the time.</note>, should be immediately followed by the bell next in size; and so on for the rest down to the smallest and last.

And since an object, the further it is from the center of a circle, claims more space and room for itself, the handles of the hammers, which follow the radius of the circular arrangement, must be somewhat long. This ensures that a wider interval is left for the circular placement of the bells; for otherwise, the iron pins fixed into the small column will be too close and cramped for the arrangement of the bells, and consequently, because of the lack of space, each iron pin will not be able to reach its corresponding bell.

The hammers should be made of iron, but not too heavy, so that the machine is not hindered when several different hammers must be raised at the same instant. The arrangement of the bells with their hammers is shown in the following illustration.

But to prevent the levers <note>original: *claves*, literally "keys," referring to the triggering components</note> from striking the other bells as this machine descends—except for those that serve as indicators for the hours and minutes—the front part of the handle of each small hammer <note>original: *marculi*</note> must be prepared in such a way that it gives way to the striking levers during the descent. ## CHAPTER IV.

->Concerning the channel or aqueduct, and likewise the valve, by the turning<-
->of which to one side water is released through the channel, while by<-
->another part the exit of the water is blocked.<-

**I**t remains now for us to explain the method by which this vessel fills itself again automatically after the twelfth hour. Let there be placed in the upper part of the column, on the side near the valve <note>original: *versorium*, a pivoting mechanism or stopcock</note>, a channel and an iron <term>trigger mechanism</term> <note>original: *hypothesis*; here referring to the mechanical arrangement or catch that initiates an action</note>. This is adapted so that at the moment the water is completely drained through the bottom of the vessel, it aligns with the protrusion on the valve and, through its contact, is able to turn it. Once this is done, the mouth of the channel will immediately be opened, and water will flow abundantly through the tube, quickly filling the container more and more. This gradually raises the internal column; when it reaches its maximum height and its highest point, another iron trigger—joining with the valve’s trigger during its ascent—will close the water passage. Thus, the flow of water into the machine's container is stopped until that water has again drained out through the lower hole, which, as previously stated, occurs over a period of twelve hours. The description of this follows here.

### CHAPTER V.

->*How the motion of the Moon can be accurately indicated by such a clock?*<-

**L**et a round Planisphere <note>A map of the celestial sphere projected onto a flat surface.</note> be fashioned near one side of the vessel, containing the twelve celestial signs divided into degrees. Through the center of this planisphere, let an axis pass that governs a pointer-rod; on the front of this rod, let the Moon be depicted with a finger or an index pointer. On the other side of the axis, between the side of the vessel and the Planisphere, let a wheel be made, carved with as many suitable teeth as there are degrees in the Zodiac <note>The author implies a wheel with 360 teeth to represent the 360 degrees of the ecliptic.</note>. This wheel must be so constructed that it can be moved by the descent of the column itself, but remains fixed when the column ascends. 

Therefore, small <term>mechanical pawls</term> <note>original Latin: "hypotheses"; here referring to the small levers or catching mechanisms that engage the gear teeth</note> must be adapted onto the rod descending from the top of the column, so that they firmly press the teeth of that wheel to move it; however, during the ascent, they should withdraw easily and apply no force to the teeth that would move the wheel. This can indeed be achieved if the joints, which we mentioned previously, are so adjusted that they yield easily during the ascent but resist strongly during the descent. 

This rod will therefore have seven <term>pawls</term>, corresponding to those seven degrees which the Moon, by its natural motion, usually completes and traverses in twelve hours. Thus, by a double repetition of that downward-tending motion of the rod, approximately fourteen degrees are counted each day, and fourteen teeth out of the three hundred and sixty existing on the aforementioned wheel are turned every natural day <note>While the Moon actually moves about 13.2 degrees per day, the author suggests 14 degrees as a practical mechanical approximation for this device.</note>. In this way, without great error, the motion of the Moon can be sufficiently well demonstrated and observed for any day of the month and in any sign of the Zodiac.

### TREATISE II. PART IX. BOOK I.
### CONTENTS OF PART IX.

---

In this part dealing with **Cosmography** <note>The science of describing the features of the universe, encompassing both astronomy and geography.</note>, two main subjects are proposed, namely:

*   **Cosmographical Principles dealing with the Earth**
    *   **By its Division**
        *   **According to longitude** <note>The author here uses 'longitude' in a historical sense to describe the divisions of the celestial and terrestrial spheres moving from the poles toward the equator.</note>
            *   The two polar circles
                *   Arctic } Distinguishing the frigid zones.
                *   Antarctic }
            *   The two Tropics
                *   Of Cancer } Describing the temperate zones.
                *   Of Capricorn }

# BOOK ONE
### On Cosmographic Principles.
---

->CHAPTER I.<-

> *How the celestial circles relate to the parts of the earth, and how they divide the earth in the same manner as they divide the convex surface of the celestial sphere itself.*

<margin>A</margin>STRONOMERS have imagined that the convex surface of the universal world is divided and distributed by circles, some major and others minor. Among the major circles, some are exterior and immobile, namely the *Meridian Circle* and the *Horizon*; others are mobile and interior, and these are categorized either by having width or being without width. The one that possesses width is called the *Zodiac* or the *Sign-bearer* <note>original: "Signifer"</note>. All other circles, however, whether major or minor—except for the two called the *Colures* <note>The Colures are two principal meridians that intersect at the celestial poles, marking the equinoxes and solstices.</note>—are parallel to one another. Of these, only one is a major circle, dividing the heavens into two equal parts along its length, and it is called the *Equator* or the *Equinoctial*. The minor circles consist of the two *Tropics*—specifically those of *Cancer* and *Capricorn*—and the two *Polar Circles*. The two *Colures*, just like the *Meridian*, intersect the poles in their circuit.

Regarding all of these matters—namely the name of the *Equinoctial*, its shared use with all the other circles, why the *Zodiac* is called an "oblique" circle, what constitutes a "right" or "oblique" *Horizon*, the variety of meridians, and all other things pertaining to the description of these circles—we shall not use many words in this place. This is because these topics are treated copiously by almost all authors who have written on Cosmography and Astronomy. Instead, we shall deal briefly with the division that these celestial circles project onto the terrestrial globe. 

Therefore, although the terrestrial mass is, in its circumference and periphery, like a mere point or a small supporting portion in relation to the entire "machine of the world" <note>Fludd uses the term "machina mundi" to describe the universe as a complex, divine mechanism.</note>, it is nevertheless necessary—insofar as it exists as the physical and bodily center of the entire spherical machine—that every circle of heaven divides it proportionally. This occurs in exactly the same way as it divides the outermost surface of the world. Since all straight lines drawn from the circumference to the mathematical center of the system maintain the same proportional relationship at the physical center (the smaller globe of Earth) as they do at the circumference of the universal machine, it follows that all its circular lines are impressed upon the earth just as they are in the heavens, as will appear more clearly in the following demonstration.

### *On the Use of these Circles on Earth for Distinguishing the Zones.*

**H**owever, these divisions on earth, formed from the imaginary circles of the sky, result in the distinction of the <term>Zones</term> <note>The five major latitudinal belts of the Earth: two Frigid, two Temperate, and one Torrid.</note>. For as many intervals as there are across the entire earth from pole to pole, proportioned to the aforementioned parallel circles, so many Zones are counted. For, counting from the Arctic Pole to its circle, that whole space is counted as one of the <term>frigid Zones</term>. But truly, that whole interval contained between the Arctic Circle and the Tropic of Cancer is called one of the <term>temperate Zones</term>, specifically the northern one. That which is measured between the Tropic of Cancer and the Equinoctial Line is the northern part of the <term>Torrid Zone</term> <note>The 'Torrid Zone' (Zona Torrida) refers to the tropics, which ancient and medieval geographers often believed were too hot for human habitation.</note>, which—

<summary>This page explains how celestial circles like the Tropics and the Equator are projected onto the Earth's surface to define the five geographical climate zones.</summary>
<keywords>Cosmography, climate zones, Arctic Circle, Tropic of Cancer, Equator, Torrid Zone, Temperate Zone, Frigid Zone, celestial projection</keywords>

--- Page 803 ---
<meta>This page continues a discussion on the division of the Earth into zones based on celestial circles, transitioning into a specific study of parallels and "climates"—a historical term for latitudinal bands.</meta>

<page-num>533</page-num>
->ON COSMOGRAPHIC PRINCIPLES.<-

...just as that space between the *Equator* <note>original: "Æquinoctialem"</note> and the *Tropic of Capricorn* is the other part of the Torrid Zone, namely the Southern part, so indeed—since that portion of the earth is divided equally by the line of the *Equator*—this Torrid Zone appears to be double. Thus, one may no less correctly count *two torrid zones, Northern* and *Southern*, just as two frigid zones and two temperate zones are numbered. Furthermore, that entire space contained between the *Tropic of Capricorn* and the *Antarctic circle* is called the *Southern* Temperate Zone, just as the entire gap extending from the *Antarctic* Circle to *its pole* is called the *Southern or Meridional Frigid Zone*. This, then, is the primary use of projecting celestial circles onto the terrestrial globe. From these circles, it is evident that the width of the frigid zones is 23 degrees and 20 minutes, while the width of the Temperate Zones is nearly 43 degrees. Both Torrid Zones, which Astronomers count as only a single Zone, have a width of 47 degrees. All these differences are caused by the closer presence of the Sun or its more remote absence; for the more the Solar rays incline toward right angles—that is, the more perpendicularly they fall upon the earth's surface—the more the heating power <note>original: "virtus calefactiva"</note> is intensified in that region of the earth. However, the more acute the angles it makes upon the earth's surface, the colder it usually renders the region. We shall not deal with these matters at greater length, as the authors who have treated <term>Cosmography</term> <note>The science of mapping the general features of the universe, including both heaven and earth.</note> have described them extensively.

## C H A P T E R III.

### On Parallels and Climates.

**W**e call those circles *Parallels* which are distant from one another by equal intervals. We distinguish these into *general* and *particular* types. The ancients established eight General parallels, which extend according to longitude through the peak of any given region, beginning from the *Equator* and ending with the start of the ninetieth degree of elevation or latitude; each of these parallels differs from the next in latitude by 10 degrees of the Meridian. The *particular parallels*, however, are certain imaginary lines on a terrestrial map used to distinguish regions, which also approach the poles as they progress from the *Equator*. There is also another division of these particular parallels, for the space of earth contained between two parallels, counting from the beginning of one to the end of the other, is called a <term>Climate</term> <note>In ancient geography, a "climate" (clima) was a latitudinal zone where the longest day of the year was of a specific duration; it does not refer to weather as the modern word does.</note>. Hence, as any parallel circle at its start is further from the *Equator* and closer to the pole, it always has a longer day than the others tending toward the *Equator*; thus a *Climate*, the further it is from the *Equator*, the more it increases that portion of the longest day of a parallel. From this, every parallel distant from the *Equator* toward the pole, counting up to the 14th parallel, has its maximum day longer than the maximum day of the preceding parallel by a quarter of an hour; but any Climate distant from the Equator will have its longest day exceeding the maximum day of the closely preceding Climate by half an hour. Here, however, it must be observed that from the 14th parallel up to the 19th, the progress occurs by half an hour, and at the 20th and 21st parallels, the maximum day consists of 20 hours.

As for what pertains to the Climates, *Ptolemy* <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), an influential Greco-Roman mathematician and geographer.</note> described only seven types of them; more recent authors, however, have established more, namely nine; all of which received their names from the more notable places through which they pass. Hence the first, stretching from the *Equator* to the North, is called *Diameroe* <note>original: "Diameroe," from the Greek "Dia Meroes," meaning "Through Meroe."</note>, since it passes through the island of that name surrounded by the *Nile*. The *Second* is called...

Here, however, it must be carefully observed that the spaces of the earth enclosed by climates or parallel circles are not equal; rather, they are larger the closer the parallels or climates are to the Equator or the middle of the world, and they are more contracted and smaller the further they are from the middle of the world and the closer they are to the poles.

### ->On the division of the parallels, and on their order, as observed by Ptolemy in Book 2 of the *Great Construction* <note>The *Almagest*.</note>, chapter 6.<-

**C**osmographers observe three types of parallels, which they distinguish by the behavior of their shadows. They call some parallels *Amphiscii* <note>From the Greek for "shadows on both sides."</note>—namely those in which the shadow is cast in both directions <note>North and South at different times of the year.</note>; these are all the parallels contained between the two Tropics, specifically the first six. Others they call *Heteroscii* <note>Greek for "shadows on one side."</note>—specifically those that cast a shadow in only one direction. The first of this kind is the parallel through Syene (the Tropic of Cancer), and the last is the thirty-second; there are twenty-six in total from the Tropic of Cancer to the Arctic Circle. Finally, they designated others as *Periscii* <note>Greek for "shadows all around."</note>, which cast a shadow toward all parts of the horizon in a circle on any given day. The first of these is the thirty-third, where the days are twenty-four hours long. There are seven other *Periscii* from the Arctic Circle all the way to the Pole, and there the entire Tropic of Cancer is seen above the horizon, while the Tropic opposite to it <note>The Tropic of Capricorn.</note> is entirely submerged.

<margin>The parallels of the Amphiscii number six, of which:</margin>
> The first is the Equinoctial <note>The Equator.</note>, which always maintains 12 hours of daylight, because the Pole is not elevated there; it passes through the middle of Africa.
> The second has 12 hours and 1/4; it is 4 degrees and 1/4 distant from the Equator. This passes through the island of *Taprobane* <note>Ancient name for Sri Lanka.</note> in the Indian Sea.
> The third has 12 hours and 1/2. Here the pole is elevated 8 degrees and 1/2. It passes through the *Avalitic Gulf* <note>The Gulf of Zeila, near modern Somalia.</note>, and in this way the *first Climate* is formed.
> The fourth has 12 hours and 1/2 plus 1/4 <note>12 hours and 45 minutes.</note>. The pole is elevated 12 degrees and 1/2. it runs through its own *Adulitic Gulf* <note>The Gulf of Zula, near modern Eritrea.</note>.
> The fifth has 12 hours <note>This is likely a scribal error for 13 hours, as the latitude for Meroë corresponds to a 13-hour day.</note>. The pole is elevated 16 degrees and 27 minutes; it runs through *Meroë* <note>An ancient city on the Nile in modern Sudan.</note> and constitutes the *second Climate*.
> The sixth has 13 hours and 1/4. The pole is elevated 20 degrees and 14 minutes.

<margin>First</margin>
> The seventh has 13 hours and 1/2. It is elevated 23 degrees, 51 minutes, and 20 seconds, and passes through *Syene*, constituting the *third Climate*.

<margin>Second</margin>
> The eighth has 13 hours and 1/2 plus 1/4. <note>The number 3 in the original is likely a printer's error for 13, following the progression of hours.</note> It is elevated 27 degrees and 40 minutes, passing through *Ptolemais of the Thebaid* <note>Ptolemais Hermiou, an ancient Greek city in Upper Egypt.</note>.

<margin>Third</margin>
> The ninth has 14 hours. It is elevated 30 degrees and 22 minutes; it runs through the lower parts of *Egypt* and constitutes the *fourth Climate*.

<meta>catchword: CHAPTER</meta>

### CHAPTER V.

->*On vertical circles or meridians.*<-

**M**eridian or vertical lines are circular lines that are not parallel, passing through the Zenith <note>The point in the sky directly above an observer</note> of any given region and meeting together at the poles of the world. Their primary use is to measure the latitude <note>Distance north or south of the equator</note> of terrestrial regions, just as the purpose of the Equator is to determine their longitude <note>Distance east or west</note>, counting from the meridian of the Fortunate Isles <note>The Canary Islands, which were used as the starting point for measuring longitude in early modern geography</note> to the region in question.

The terrestrial globe is usually divided by 24 of these lines, each of which encompasses the space of one hour. Therefore, it is certain that places located under such meridians differ from each other by a space or interval of one hour. Thus, of two places separated by only one meridian, the more easterly one will experience its midday, daytime, midnight, lunar eclipses, and the conjunctions and oppositions of the luminaries <note>The alignment of the Sun and Moon</note> one hour earlier than the other. If they are separated by two meridians, the difference is two hours, and so on for the rest.

And here it should be observed that a single degree of longitude is equal in its span to 4 minutes of an hour, as will be more easily understood through arithmetic calculation.

---

### CHAPTER VI.

->*On the method of drawing meridian and parallel circles*<-
->*optically in a hemisphere divided by*<-
->*the Equator.*<-

**L**et a round circle be made on any flat surface, of whatever size you wish, which will represent a portion of the Equator; let this be B. C. D. E. Let a space be made on its margin in which the numbers of the degrees of the Equator are to be written. This hemisphere should then be divided into four quadrants, and each quadrant subdivided again into three equal parts, and then each of those three parts further distributed into another three. In this way, you will have the vertical circles or meridians, the first of which is numbered from B—namely, from the Fortunate Isles, specifically the one passing through the westernmost *Canary* island. 

Then, to find the parallel of latitude on the meridian A. C., let "d" be the center, and let a ruler touch the point of the parallel F. Where the meridian A. C. is intersected, that is where one parallel circle shall pass. Next, while keeping one end of the ruler fixed on D, let the other be extended over point G; where the second intersection occurs on the radius A. D., the second parallel line shall pass. Then, let the ruler be turned to point H, and that intersection of line A. D. will, as if pointing with a finger, show the location of the third parallel circle. Similarly, from D to I for the fourth, from D to L for the fifth, from D to M for the sixth, from D to N for the seventh, and from D to O for the eighth. Afterward, with the foot of the compasses fixed at center A, let the parallel lines be drawn around from each intersection; in this way, you will have produced those eight parallel circles which we called "general" above.

->*The Second Treatise of the Macrocosm.*<-

...with those intersections of the <term>Equator<note>The great circle around the middle of the earth, equidistant from the poles.</note></term> occurring on the eastern part, just as was done on its western part. <term>Parallel<note>Lines of latitude running parallel to the equator.</note></term> lines in this kind of hemisphere will be expressed in this way: from the point E of the Diameter or Equator to the point O on the first meridian, a straightedge is extended, and an intersection is made on line A-D. Afterwards let it be extended to point M, and again to point L, and so to I, H, G, and F. And where the intersections were made on line A-D, it must be carefully observed; for from that intersection to its corresponding point, the center must be found: for example, the center for the first intersection and point O, for the second and point N, for the third and point M, and so on for the others. Then let the segment O-P be drawn through the first intersection, and N-Q through the second intersection, and M-R through the third, and so on for the others. And in this way you will recover the general parallels of the entire Hemisphere, and you will have both the vertical circles and the parallels optically described, as if the half part of any exactly spherical globe were pressed into a flat surface. Note, however, that although these two methods of sketching hemispheres are quite perfect according to the principles of optics, they nevertheless suffer a defect regarding the proportion of the parallels to the <term>great circle<note>A circle on the surface of a sphere that lies in a plane passing through the sphere's center, such as the equator.</note></term>; because in the final description, all regions situated around the poles of the world always appear smaller than they truly are.

# CHAPTER VIII.

## *By what method should any quarter of the world be mapped?*

**IN** the geographical mapping <note>original: "delineatione Geographica"</note> of any quarter of the world <note>In the early modern period, the "four quarters" of the world referred to the four known continents: Europe, Asia, Africa, and America.</note>, its exact longitude and latitude must be considered; and for its latitude, one must observe its distance from the pole that chiefly faces that part, measuring from its own parallel that ends that part to the parallel where it begins.

For instance, let us wish to depict a geographical map of *Europe*, to which geographers attribute a width of 40 degrees, beginning from the southern parallel of 30 degrees latitude, up to the parallel of 70 degrees toward the north.

We therefore draw A.B. as a straight line, which will represent the middle meridian of the given region: from this, you will take a certain length according to the size of the work to be constructed. Let A be the pole of the world, and B the crossing of the parallel 30 degrees below the given parallel; therefore, you will divide the whole of A.B. into 60 equal parts, which will signify the degrees of latitude for the given map, beginning from the parallel of 30 degrees and ending at the parallel of 70. Thus, the line drawn over 50 degrees will be the middle parallel of the entire map. Now, using the aforementioned pole as the center, you shall draw segments of circles through every ten degrees of latitude, which will give you the principal parallels of the <term>Equator</term> <note>The great circle of the celestial sphere, or the terrestrial line equidistant from the poles.</note> on this map. But since the limit of all Europe is set at 40 degrees (as stated above), of which a fourth part is ten degrees, I say that the parallels of 40 degrees and 60 degrees are the intermediate parallels; according to the proportions of these, the inclinations of the other meridians to the first must be placed without any noticeable error.

Furthermore, to find the proportion of these equally distant intermediate points, modern authors observe this geometrical method: they take from the figure placed below the straight line A.C., which contains 10 degrees on a great circle, and from B as a center, they construct a quadrant of a circle *c. l.* With this quadrant divided into 90 equal parts, you will count from *c.* toward *l.* 40 degrees up to *m*. Then draw the transverse line *m. n.* making right angles with *b. l.*, which will be equal to the arc C. H. for 10 degrees of longitude on the parallel of 40 degrees. Similarly, on the quadrant *c. l.*, let there be an arc *c. o.* of 60 degrees. Therefore, a line drawn at [right] angles with *l. b.* will be the line *o. p.*, the space of an arc of 10 degrees on the same parallel of 60 degrees. The remaining steps are as follows below.

If, however, the individual spaces of these two intermediate parallels, which are marked by 10 degrees, are divided into 10 equal parts, you will have the length of the degrees step by step. And thus it will not be difficult to map the other quarters of the world—namely Asia, Africa, and America—provided that those things said above are exactly considered.

## CHAPTER IX.
### *On the method of representing regions and islands in the aforementioned map of the world.*

**T**o depict any region of the world, this shall be the chorographic <term>chorography: the practice of mapping a specific region or district rather than the whole world</term> method. Seek out the region to be described in a larger geographical map or chart; once found, note its maximum longitude as measured by the degrees of the Equator, and likewise its latitude as marked by the degrees of the meridians <note>original: "per gradus meridianorum"</note>. Having found these, establish the latitude and longitude of the region as you please, and divide its meridian and its line of longitude into as many parts as the proposed region requires. For example, if our purpose were to depict *France* <note>original: "Galliam"</note>, we find that its greatest extent of latitude lies between the city of *Marseille* in Provence and the city of *Antwerp*; this spans 12 degrees of the meridian, beginning from its southernmost part—namely, from the 43rd degree counting from the Equator up to the 54th degree as one moves toward the north. Let these then be arranged in such a way that, by means of dark lines, a passage is made from one degree of both longitude and latitude to the degree opposite it. And by this crossing of lines, many small squares <note>The author is describing the creation of a coordinate grid</note> will be produced in the map of that same region, so that all parts of the aforementioned region may be more accurately and easily expressed and truly drawn in the said map.

# BOOK TWO
## On the construction of our Cosmographical Planisphere. <note>A planisphere is a map or instrument that represents the 3D celestial or terrestrial sphere on a 2D flat surface.</note>

---

### C H A P T E R I.
#### *On the parts of our Planisphere in general.*

This Planisphere of ours is divided into two notable and equal parts, each of which represents a hemisphere of the universal world with a full delineation of the terrestrial globe. Furthermore, the entire machinery of the world thus described in this hemisphere is divided by the Equinoctial <note>The "Equinoctial" refers to the celestial equator.</note>, and each portion of the upper or celestial world is joined with the terrestrial portion, so that the stars, signs, and houses of the heavens, and every part of them, correspond to the earth and its regions, and govern and rule over them: for this reason, we have imagined the sky to be extended above the earth onto a flat surface.

Therefore, each hemisphere of our Planisphere is divided into four parts, two of which are essential—namely the two lower parts—while the others are demonstrative: specifically, the small hour-sphere and the index of total latitude, called the rule or the visible meridian, as will appear below.

---

### C H A P T E R  II.
#### *On the lower or northern terrestrial part of the Planisphere, with the Zodiac on its margin.*

Let a board of the hardest wood be chosen, and one excellently seasoned by age <note>original: "maturitate optime confectus"</note>, so that it remains stable in its position, and let it have a width of one and a half feet. Then, according to that diameter, let a circle be made upon it, and let the remaining parts of the board be separated from that circle. Afterward, let it be very well covered with a parchment veil prepared in this manner: let a parchment skin be chosen that is very flat and smooth, and let it be quite white and clear. 

Then, following the diameter of the round board, let a circle be drawn from its center, which circle will be the margin of this entire Cosmographical instrument. Within that circle, let another circle be delineated, between which two circles the characters of the celestial signs or of the Zodiac ought to be expressed. Inside this circle, another circle not far distant from it must be painted, in which space the degrees of each sign of the Zodiac—namely thirty—ought to be described. Inside this circle, let another be drawn, the interval of which from its nearest outer circle shall be only of such a width as to be able to contain the numbers of the degrees expressed above. After this circle, let yet another interior one be drawn, wide enough to contain the names of the months, in such a way that—

There should be a small gap between the number of degrees of the signs and the region of this circle, in which the number of days for the month written below is also to be expressed. In this way, both the solar and lunar regions will be completed. Between the Equinoctial <note>The celestial equator</note> and this sphere of the months, a sufficiently large space must be left. In this space, the solar orb—upon which the track <note>original: *volutabrum*, a rolling path or orbit</note> of the moon itself is accustomed to move—must be drawn. This can be done according to the preference of the Artist and according to the size of the location or the spherical board. However, everything must be joined together so that all the things already described, as well as those yet to be described, can be explained within this area.

Having left this solar and lunar space, one must proceed to the Equinoctial circle itself. This should be laid out on this spherical surface after the aforementioned space, though with a small margin contained between two circles, in which the Equinoctial degrees <note>Degrees of longitude measured along the equator</note> ought to be expressed. Inside this margin, a sufficiently wide space is to be included with another interior circle, in which the degree numbers must be written. Afterwards, parallels <note>Lines of latitude</note> are to be drawn through every tenth degree of latitude, according to the teaching in Chapter 5 of the preceding book. The Equinoctial line must also be divided into 36 parts. Through each division, diameters are to be drawn to the opposite side through the center of the entire terrestrial sphere. These will represent the meridian lines <note>Lines of longitude</note>, so that the distance between any two meridians represents 10 Equinoctial degrees.

Once these tasks are finished, the Arctic Circle and the Tropic of Cancer are to be delineated. Note that the Tropic of Cancer must pass through the 23rd degree of latitude, just as the Polar circle passes through approximately the 67th. Therefore, the Radius <note>original: *Semidiameter*</note> of the Equinoctial circle must be divided into nine parts according to the teaching of Chapter 5 of the previous book—or, if you prefer, into equal parts. Each of these parts is to be subdivided into ten other parts, which comprise the degrees of the Meridian circle. Placing one foot of the compass <note>A drawing tool for circles</note> in the center, let its other foot be extended to the 23rd degree and 31st minute, counting from the Equator toward the Arctic pole. According to this measurement of the compass, the Tropic of Cancer shall be drawn. Then, by closing the compass while the foot remains fixed in the center, the Antarctic Circle <note>original: *Circulus Antarcticus*. In this context of mapping the northern hemisphere, the author likely refers to the northern polar circle—the Arctic Circle—but uses the term for the "opposite" circle relative to the equator</note> is to be drawn at the 67th degree. These circles should have enough width so they can be distinguished from the other parallels, which ought to pass through that first ninefold division mentioned above. In this way, you will have the northern part of the terrestrial hemisphere prepared, with its margins containing the celestial signs and the months of the year. Within this, every part or region of the Northern earth—according to both its true longitude and latitude—and all the seas of that same region and the more famous rivers are to be depicted.

**Note: First**, observe that this instrument <term>Planisphere: a map or instrument representing the celestial or terrestrial sphere on a flat surface</term> ought to be at least ten times larger than it is represented here, so that all regions, rivers, mountains, and seas, as well as their virtues <note>In the 17th century, "virtues" often referred to the specific astrological or spiritual qualities and influences associated with different geographical locations.</note>, may be depicted more clearly. I would wish, therefore, for the reader to take his examples from that planisphere by Petrus Plancius <note>Petrus Plancius (1552–1622) was a Dutch-Flemish astronomer and cartographer whose maps were famous for their detail and accuracy.</note> divided by the equator.

**Second**, observe that the number of days for each month should be divided into small sections, just as we have depicted under March for the sake of brevity. Therefore, it should be noted that:

*   **March**, having 31 days, begins at the 10th degree of **Pisces** and ends at the 10th degree of **Aries**.
*   **April**, having 30 days, begins with the 10th degree of **Aries** and ends with the 9th degree of **Taurus**.
*   **May**, having 31 days, begins with the 10th degree of **Taurus** and ends with the 9th degree of **Gemini**.
*   **June**, possessing 30 days, begins with the 10th degree of **Gemini** and ends at the 8th degree of **Cancer**.
*   **July**, having 31 days, begins with the 8th degree of **Cancer** and ends with the 7th degree of **Leo**.
*   **August**, having 31 days, begins in the 8th degree of **Leo** and ends in the 7th degree of **Virgo**.
*   **September**, having 30 days, begins at the 8th degree of **Virgo** and ends at the 6th degree of **Libra**.
*   **October**, having 31 days, begins with the 7th degree of **Libra** and ends with the 7th degree of **Scorpio**.
*   **November**, having 30 days, begins with the 8th degree of **Scorpio** and ends with the 7th degree of **Sagittarius**.
*   **December**, having 31 days, begins with the 8th degree of **Sagittarius** and ends with the 9th degree of **Capricorn**.
*   **January**, having 31 days, begins with the 10th degree of **Capricorn** and ends with the 10th degree of **Aquarius**.
*   **February**, having 28 days, begins with the 11th degree of **Aquarius** and ends with the 9th degree of **Pisces**.

# C H A P T E R  III.

### *On the construction of the Celestial Wheel.*

**T**his wheel must be so adapted that its convex surface can move beneath the concave surface of the circle of months. The width of this wheel, between the convexity of that outer sphere of the heavens and its own concavity, must be the same distance as that between the circle of months and the convex surface of the Equinoctial line <note>The "Equinoctial line" refers to the celestial equator.</note>. Upon this circle or space of width, two circles are to be drawn. The outer one should not exceed the capacity required to receive the numbers of the days of the lunar month, so that its breadth is not large, but narrow. Another space, however, must be composed in the shape of the head and tail of the Dragon <term>Head and Tail of the Dragon: In traditional astronomy, these (the lunar nodes) are the points where the Moon's path crosses the Ecliptic, often associated with eclipses.</term>, so that by a two-part division of it, the movement of the Moon in its waxing and waning—along with its quarters—can be indicated with very easy ingenuity. For this reason, half of this sphere, divided off-center, should be stained with blackness; the other whole part, however, should be adorned with whiteness. Thus, a rotating handle or crank <note>original: "volubrum sive manubrium"</note> wrapped around the width and containing the Moon's orb at its extremity will demonstrate the proper proportion of light or darkness of the Moon itself, as will be discussed in its proper place.

The interior parts of this celestial sphere are entirely empty and transparent, so that through their clarity the terrestrial Hemisphere may be more precisely observed—except that half of the Zodiac (namely the northern part) must be traced upon it. It is also necessary that the two upper diameters of this Hemisphere cross at right angles to support this celestial machine along with the semicircle of the Zodiac. Furthermore, this half of the Zodiac in the upper Hemisphere is to be drawn so that its divided ends touch the Equinoctial circle, and especially so that the part of the Ecliptic line <note>The Ecliptic is the apparent path of the Sun across the sky.</note> is positioned such that the middle of that Ecliptic part is adjacent to the Tropic of Cancer expressed on the terrestrial Hemisphere.

Therefore, for this to be done, a suitable center must be found so that a semicircular line of this kind can be drawn with its proper width, and this should be fixed upon some part of a meridian. Once finished, this semi-Zodiac should be divided into six equal parts, assigning the sign of Aries to the first, Taurus to the second, Gemini to the third, Cancer to the fourth, Leo to the fifth, and Virgo to the sixth. Next, each of these spaces for the signs must be divided into three equal parts, and each of those must again be subdivided into ten equal portions <note>This creates the standard 30 degrees for each zodiac sign.</note>. In this manner, the northern celestial Hemisphere will be completed, occupying the second series and order in this our Cosmic Instrument. It should be noted, however, that the pointer <note>original: "index"</note> of this hemisphere must represent the substance of the Sun; therefore, it should be attached at the end of the diameter of darkness, so that it can point out the degrees of the signs and the days of the months as if with a finger.

### CHAPTER IV.

#### Concerning the Hour-Wheel.

**L**et a small wheel be made, quite small, whose radius <note>original: *semidiameter*</note> has a width of 20 degrees, and let it be divided into as many parts as the hemisphere is divided by its meridians <term>meridians: longitudinal lines used here to mark the 24 hours of the day</term>, namely into 24. And through every sixth hour let a diameter be drawn, so that these two diameters intersect each other at right angles in the center. Let this wheel have its own pointer <note>original: *indicem*</note>, the edge of which must end at the extremity of one of the aforementioned diameters; the tip of this edge will denote the hour of noon for any given region. Therefore, it will signify the twelfth hour by counting according to the hours of the Astrologers <note>In the 17th century, astronomers and astrologers traditionally began their 24-hour day at noon</note>, who begin their day from the midday; and then the point opposite to this will be the thirteenth hour.
