### CHAPTER V.

->*Concerning the rule, both southern and northern.*<-

**L**et a small circle be made, whose radius <note>original: *Semidiameter*</note> is 10 degrees: Then through its center let a diameter be drawn, which ought to extend beyond the circumference of the circle, according to the distance from the center of the celestial hemisphere to its circumference or broad surface, and in that part it ought to hold a small arc of a circle, which arc indeed ought to have the width of a sphere equally dark and clear <note>This likely refers to a "shading" on the instrument to represent the division between day and night.</note>: In the middle of this arc, according to almost its entire width, directly opposite this extended diameter, let a small circle be made, whose area ought to be hollowed out, so that the dark and bright place of the orb placed beneath it may be seen through that circle, and this circle will represent the orb of the moon, beyond which the diameter, still drawn out, will form a pointer <note>original: *indicem*</note>, whose edge will be the diameter itself. Furthermore, it should be noted here that the inner part of this rule is to be divided by the parallels of the terrestrial hemisphere, and by the Arctic Circle and the Tropic of Cancer, on whose flat surface the parallels of the <term>Amphiscians</term> <note>People living in the tropics whose shadows fall north at one time of year and south at another.</note>, <term>Heteroscians</term> <note>People living in temperate zones whose shadows always fall in one direction (either north or south) at noon.</note>, and <term>Periscians</term> <note>People within the polar circles whose shadows turn in a full circle during the day.</note> ought to be explained, which are so named for a three-fold reason of shadows, and similarly the differences of hours for any part of this hemisphere: and in this way the northern part of the Cosmographic <note>The study of the general features of the universe, including geography and astronomy.</note> Hemisphere will be completed.

# CHAPTER VI.

## Concerning the Southern part of the Cosmographic instrument.

**T**he Southern part, or southern hemisphere, beginning from its center in all its circles—both meridians and parallels—will be arranged just as was described for the northern hemisphere. Similarly, two circles, namely the Antarctic and the Tropic of Capricorn, are to be drawn at the same distances as measured from the Equinoctial <note>The Equator.</note>.

*A description of the southern hemisphere should also be selected, and the regions depicted according to the description of Petrus Plancius <note>Petrus Plancius (1552–1622) was a prominent Dutch cartographer and astronomer who helped define several southern constellations.</note>. This hemisphere should have a similar margin, or another for the sake of variety. It should also have an hour-wheel of the same appearance, with a pointer similar to the aforementioned northern pointer in all respects; these are to be placed together as shall be described below.*

*In center A of each hemisphere, both southern and northern, let center B of the celestial machine <note>A 'celestial machine' in this context is a volvelle—a rotating paper wheel used as an analog computer.</note> be attached, upon which the semi-zodiac is situated. Place the hour-wheel at center C, and upon the center of all these, place the handle or ruler at its center D. Let arc E be a cutout representing the image of the moon; this must be made with the width of the arc matching the width of F. F. F. of each celestial machine. In this way, by turning the handle D. E., the arc—without passing the limits or margins of the orb F. F. F.—demonstrates the various phases and appearances of the moon for a given time.*

As for what pertains to the hemisphere or celestial machine, its construction should be proportioned in the manner of the preceding one, except that the surface of its circumference should not be as wide as the northern one. Its width from the center to its outer surface should be the distance between the center of the terrestrial hemisphere and the outer surface of the Equinoctial circle. In all other respects, let the Semi-zodiac <note>original: "Semisignifer"; the half-circle of the zodiac belt containing six signs.</note> be drawn as in the preceding northern section, and let it also be divided into six equal parts: the first part is held by Libra, the second by Scorpio, the third by Sagittarius, the fourth by Capricorn, the fifth by Aquarius, and the sixth by Pisces. The ruler of the southern hemisphere is also to be divided with the same dimensions designating the climates <note>A 'climate' in historical geography was a zone of latitude with specific daylight lengths.</note> as the northern one. At its extremity, an image of the sun ought to be painted, moving within an eccentric circle; this should be represented beneath the sun's orb on the celestial surface, so that the sun's highest point <note>original: "arx"; literally 'citadel' or 'fortress', used here to mean the apogee or the sun's furthest point in its orbit.</note> and its opposite can be very easily marked. On the outer part of the sun, an index or "finger" can be formed, the edge of which must pass through the center of the sun; this is to be adapted for explaining the contents of the outer orbs. For the outer part of the hemisphere is to be divided into six spheres or orbs: the outermost will denote the months with their days and the degrees of the sun in the celestial signs; the second will indicate the twilight <note>The light before sunrise.</note> of any day of the whole year in hours and minutes; the third, the sunrise; the fourth, the length of the day and night; the fifth, the sunset; and the sixth will demonstrate the evening <note>The light after sunset.</note>, just as appears from the preceding demonstration.

<header>TRACTATE II. PART IX. BOOK II.</header>

## CHAPTER VII.

### *Regarding the Horizon of this instrument,*

**W**e have not attached a visible horizon to this instrument of ours, lest its bulk or physical presence make this mirror <note>The author uses the term "speculum" (mirror) to refer to the polished face of the astronomical instrument, likely an astrolabe or a similar calculating plate.</note> of ours more difficult to see. However, if desired, a ruler of very narrow width may be added and attached to its assembly, provided that it is quite thin. But rather, to compensate for its absence, let the radius <note>original: "Semidiameter"</note> of the latitude ruler be placed over the location being investigated. Then, let a wooden ruler be placed crosswise over the mirror or instrument, specifically so that it passes through the center like a diameter, with the condition that the latitude ruler passing over the given location is raised, as it were, at a right angle <note>original: "orthogonaliter"</note> above the horizontal ruler. The latitude ruler will therefore denote the zenith <note>the point in the sky directly above an observer</note> or the meridian of the given town; the ruler added for this purpose will demonstrate the horizon of that specific place. In this way, we can very easily determine the rising and setting of the planets and stars for any given region, and similarly the motion of the Sun itself over the hemisphere at any hour, along with many other things to which experience will lead the practitioner <note>original: "Artistam", referring to a skilled user or navigator</note>.

---

# BOOK THREE.
## On the use of our Cosmographical Planisphere.

---

### CHAPTER I.
### *On the practice of this, our Cosmographical instrument, in general.*

We could indeed satisfy many questions with this instrument of ours, pertaining as much to <term>Astronomy</term> <note>The study of celestial objects</note> as to the description of the earth, so much so that their number could be multiplied almost to infinity. But truly, omitting the others, we will turn our discourse only to those which are commonly better known and more everyday. And first, beginning from higher things, we find the start of our speech in the lunar region, ascending all the way to the sphere of the fixed stars.

---

### CHAPTER II.
### *On the method of investigating for how long the Moon illuminates this Hemisphere of ours, and consequently, when it rises and when it sets.*

To know those hours in which the Moon presents itself to our sight and illuminates the earth, one must seek the day of the moon's age in the lunar circle, shown in the northern part of our instrument—specifically, the one found in the second-to-last <term>small disk</term> <note>original: "orbiculo"; likely a rotating paper or brass part of the instrument known as a volvelle</note> or circle of that machine or instrument, which we have called the "lunar mode." Having found that day there, the hours and minutes of the moon's appearance are shown under the same division in the outermost small disk. 

But it must be observed here that the progression and order of days begins from the <term>new moon</term> <note>original: "novilunio"</note>, proceeding toward the full moon according to the natural succession of the <term>celestial signs</term> <note>The twelve signs of the Zodiac</note>; the new moon begins its cycle in the lunar circle from the outer point of thicker blackness, and the <term>full moon</term> <note>original: "plenilunium"</note> exists in the place of broader whiteness, opposite to that point of blackness. For example, if the age of the moon is the tenth day, the number 10 occurs in the second-to-last disk, across from which we find in the extreme disk eight hours with 0 minutes. Likewise, if the moon has reached the twelfth day of its age, we find 9 hours with 36 minutes. And so for the rest.

Regarding the rising and setting of the moon, two hours must be assigned for its passage through any sign for the sun's motion. Once the sign through which the sun is passing is known, and the age of the moon itself is understood, it will be very easy—by the distance of one from the other, having observed the time of sunrise and sunset—to find the rising and setting of the moon as well.

# TREATISE II. PART IX. BOOK II.

## C H A P T E R  III.

### *On the method of determining what portion of itself the Moon displays to us on any day of its cycle.*

**P**lace the day or the Moon’s index over the degree of the zodiac sign in which the Sun is located on the day the question is asked. Next, turn the pointer of the latitude rule <term>latitude rule<note>original: "regulae latitudinis"; a movable arm or pointer on the instrument used to measure coordinates or degrees of latitude.</note></term> to the number representing the days of the Moon’s age <note>The "age of the moon" refers to the number of days elapsed since the last New Moon.</note>. Once this is done, you will see the form or phase of the moon for that requested day through the opening at the end of the latitude rule. For example, if the Sun is found at the 25th degree of Sagittarius, the index of the lunar volvelle <term>volvelle<note>original: "volvuli"; a rotating paper or parchment disc used in early scientific books to perform calculations.</note></term> should be turned to the 25th degree of that sign; then, if the age of the moon is seven days, you will find one half of the lunar body dark and its other half luminous.

---

## C H A P T E R  IV.

### *On the method of investigating which part of the terrestrial globe the Sun passes over at every hour of the natural day.*

**F**irst, one must seek the sign and the degree of the sign in which the Sun is found on the day the question is proposed. Once this is found, for the specific hour of the day—which is expressed on the small disc <note>original: "parvula rotula"; likely a smaller sub-dial on the instrument.</note> near the center of the instrument—the hemisphere is divided into as many hours as the sun establishes on that same day. When the latitude rule is placed under the hour in which the question is raised, and that sign with its degree is turned under that rule, the terrestrial region or the specific place on earth sought will appear under that degree arranged by this method.

---

## C H A P T E R  V.

### *On the method of finding over which region of the earth any of the other Planets moves at any given hour.*

**W**hen the location is known—specifically the sign and degree in which any of the said Planets remains—and the Sun is placed in its true position according to the teaching of the following chapter, you will find directly beneath that sign and the degree of the sign where the other planets exist that part of the earth standing perpendicularly, over which any of the Planets passes on the requested day and hour.

---

## C H A P T E R  VI.

### *On the length of the day in any part of the year.*

**F**or the clarification of this question, one must look at the outer part of the Southern Hemisphere; on the fourth small ring found on its margin, the length of every day of the entire year will be demonstrated. Therefore, when the pointer of the handle <note>original: "manubrii digito"; likely the index or "finger" on the main pointer arm.</note> is placed over the degree in which the sun is found at that time, the fourth ring will reveal the length of the day in hours beneath that degree. Once this is known, it will be very easy to also calculate the length of the night.

## CHAPTER VII.

->*On the rising and setting of the sun.*<-

The **S**un's rising on any day of the year is determined by means of the third small disk on the outer part of the Southern Hemisphere. This is done if the pointer of the sun's handle is turned over the degree of the <term>zodiac sign<note>The twelve divisions of the sky through which the sun appears to move throughout the year.</note></term> through which the sun is passing on the day in question. Beneath that pointer, on the third disk, the hour and minute at which the sun rises on the day of the inquiry will appear. Its setting, however, is very easily found once the length of the day is known.

---

## CHAPTER VIII.

->*On finding the twilight of each day.*<-

The **T**wilight of each day is investigated by means of the second small disk on the outer part of the aforementioned Hemisphere, by turning the pointer of the handle over the degree of the Sun. For under the diameter of the handle, on the second disk, the hour of twilight for that day will appear. The evening, or the twilight of the night, is found through the length of the days.

---

## CHAPTER IX.

->*How to investigate over which part of the terrestrial globe the fixed stars move at any hour of the day.*<-

**F**irst, the Sun must be brought to its proper position in the Hemisphere for the requested hour of the day. Once this is done, the other celestial signs will remain in their proper places over any particular region of the earth. The location of the remaining <term>fixed stars<note>Stars that appear to maintain a permanent position relative to each other, unlike the planets or "wandering stars."</note></term> positioned outside the zodiac will appear in their longitude in the table written below, always maintaining their references or relationship to the signs of the Zodiac.

### C H A P T E R X

->*Regarding the method of investigating which sign rises at any hour of the day.*<-

**P**lace the Sun, according to the aforementioned doctrine, in its proper position for the hour of the question proposed, and there will appear in the east the <term>sign<note>A sign of the Zodiac.</note></term> which rises at that same hour. Once this is known, all the fixed stars of the same longitude or latitude—whether Northern or Southern—that usually appear in the Hemisphere will rise with that sign, according to the teaching of the preceding table.

---

### C H A P T E R XI.

->*Regarding finding the parallel of any region, and whether it is among the Amphiscians, Heteroscians, or Periscians.*<-

**L**et the <term>Rule of Latitude<note>A movable arm or scale on a globe used to measure degrees north or south of the equator.</note></term> be rotated over the given part of the earth or nation. The distances measured on that rule will denote the position of the proposed place under the parallels of the <term>Amphiscians<note>People living between the tropics whose shadows fall both north and south at different times of the year.</note></term>, <term>Heteroscians<note>People in temperate zones whose shadows always fall in one direction (either north or south) at noon.</note></term>, and <term>Periscians<note>People in polar regions whose shadows move in a full circle during the day because the sun does not set.</note></term>.

---

### C H A P T E R XII.

->*Regarding finding the distances of places according to longitude and latitude.*<-

**F**irst, the distance of longitude between two places, whether cities or towns, is sought in this manner. The <term>Rule of Semidiameter<note>Likely the horizon ring or a measuring arm extending from the center of the globe.</note></term> must be placed over one location; in doing so, the part of the Semidiameter intersecting the <term>Equinoctial<note>The Celestial Equator, or the Equator on a globe.</note></term> will denote the true degree of longitude for that place. Next, turn the Rule of Semidiameter again so that it passes through the <term>zenith<note>The point directly above a specific location.</note></term> of the other city or given place, and observe the degree on the Equinoctial which its semidiameter intersects. Afterward, you shall count the distance in degrees from one intersection to the other, and you will have the distance between these two places in degrees of longitude. Here it must be noted how many miles and leagues constitute one degree of the Equinoctial, as follows:

<header>ON THE USE OF THE COSMOGRAPHIC PLANISPHERE</header>

To find the latitudes of two locations, the Latitude Rule <note>original: *Regula*; a pivoting measuring arm on the instrument</note> must be turned over one given location, and the degree of latitude of that place, which lies perpendicularly beneath the rule, must be observed. Then, let the same Rule be turned over the other location, and the degree above it should also be marked. Afterwards, the distance between the degree of the first and second locations should be observed; this will indicate the amount of distance between the two said locations in latitude. Furthermore, this latitude is properly called the "elevation of the pole" for the location where it is found.

---

## CHAPTER XIII.

*On the method of finding under which zone of the world any region may be situated.*

**O**ne must search on the terrestrial part of our instrument to see if a region is located between the polar circles and the poles themselves; if it is found there, it is situated in the frigid zone <term>frigid zone: the polar regions characterized by extreme cold</term>. If, however, it lies between the polar circles and the Tropics, it is placed in the temperate zone. But if it lies between the Tropics and the Equator <note>original: *Æquinoctialem*</note>, it is subject to the torrid zone <term>torrid zone: the region between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, thought by ancient geographers to be potentially too hot for habitation</term>.

---

# BOOK ONE
## On the Types of Astrology.

---

### CHAPTER I.

->On Astrology in general: what it is, and of how many kinds?<-

**A**STROLOGY, if it were rightly and perfectly known in its hidden nature (a thing which has certainly happened to very few, and only by the singular benefit and gift of God), would not be held in such great hatred by almost everyone, nor would it be considered so vile by the common sort of men. For the operation of this science is as certain, and deals as truly with its object, as it is indubitable that the stars themselves move constantly and complete their motions through infallible revolutions for a determined end ordained by the Creator himself. Therefore, the science itself is not to be condemned on its own account, but rather those ignorant men who, being occupied with it, through their own lack of skill, cause that just and harmless science (whose truth was known to few, but falsely claimed by many) to be hissed away <note>original: "sibilis explodatur" — literally to be driven off the stage by hissing.</note> and commonly held as lying and profane. Indeed, if we ever look deeply into the nature and definition of this astrological art, we will clearly perceive some degree of certainty in it, *since it is the science of divining from the consensus of the heavens and the underlying elements, or the doctrine of the effect of the stars upon the elements and those things which consist of the elements*: <note>The author defines astrology here as a physical science of cause and effect between the stars and the material world.</note> that is, its duty is to foretell from the motion of the stars future events in these lower regions, which is certainly verified not only in ourselves, but also in beasts and plants. Indeed, there is no one who does not know how to predict that the approach of the Sun brings us a warmer temperament of the air and renders the herbs green and alive, of which kind there are also many other things, which we shall discuss more at length below.

Furthermore, some divide this science into either *natural* or *superstitious*: **the former** they wish to be concerned with the temperaments <note>original: "complexionibus" — the physical and humoral makeup of a body.</note> of bodies, which vary according to the tempering of the stars, such as health, sickness, weather, sterility, etc.; **the latter**, however, they say concerns contingent matters and those things which are subject to human will, which the Metaphysicians <note>Philosophers who study the nature of reality and existence beyond the physical.</note> treat very sparingly.

However, it is not our purpose in this place to treat that latter part; for if any such thing lies hidden in the vitals of this science, we willingly leave all that to the Kabbalists <note>Mystics who study a form of Jewish esoteric wisdom, often associated here with more spiritual or magical applications of astrology.</note> and others much more sagacious than ourselves in this art. Our intention
<margin>←</margin> looks purely toward dealing with the Astrological matter Physically, and treating this science of ours according to the laws of nature—not
<margin>←</margin> differently than painters are accustomed to delineate one certain image by mixing various colors together. In the same way, I say, we also intend to describe a certain composite, whether concerning the breath of the body, or inanimate things, or the constitution of the air, from the various mixture of many elementary qualities according to the proportional position of the Planets, signs, and the rest of the stars.

# ON THE SPECIES OF ASTROLOGY.

## CHAPTER II.

### *On the parts of Astrology in particular.*

**S**ome astrologers divide this art into six parts, the first of which they call *introductory*, which is indeed concerned with its principles—namely, the signs of the zodiac, the other fixed stars, and the natures of the Planets, about which we speak more extensively in the second book of this work. The *second* part deals with great revolutions, which consider conjunctions and Eclipses. The *third* denotes the genitures <note>original: "genituras"; the casting of individual birth charts or horoscopes</note> of individuals. The *fourth* treats of interrogations <note>original: "interrogationes"; the practice of "horary astrology" where a chart is cast to answer a specific question</note>. The *fifth* is concerned with elections <note>original: "electiones"; choosing the most auspicious time to begin an undertaking</note>, and the *sixth* teaches the construction and operation of images <note>original: "imaginum fabricam"; the creation of astrological talismans or statues intended to capture celestial influence</note>. Others distinguish it into four parts, the *first* of which deals with the Crisis and the causes of diseases, which we discuss in *our second Volume*. The *second* is occupied with the questions of the Arabs. The *third* considers elections. The *last* denotes the changes of the elements. But we have collected all these aforementioned parts into the following distinction more correctly, as it indeed seems to us.

And this final branch, although it possesses wondrous effects—as historical accounts in both Byzantine and other records have handed down to us—is not out of envy, but rightly called "superstitious" by us above, following the opinion of other astrologers. They believe this specific type of astrology differs little from Magic or Idolatry, especially in those matters involving <term>Necromantic images</term> <note>original: *imagines Necromanticas*; here referring to the practice of carving astrological symbols into talismans to "trap" or "call down" spiritual powers</note> of angels, or rather of Demons, and the inscriptions of other unknown names and characters. Similarly, it includes those practices that require various fumigations and invocations for their operations; all of which are nothing other than manifest signs of a pact entered into with Demons. Consequently, the ignorant may fall into idolatry through this method and be miserably deceived. But we understand these things to belong to the more metaphysical part, which we have called *Necromantic*, and which must be entirely avoided. Yet, truly, those who do not distinguish the abuse of a thing from its proper use are unjust; for purely Astronomical characters and seals are very often in use even among the most excellent Physicians. This is evident in the writings left to us by those most distinguished Doctors, *Arnold of Villanova and Theophrastus Paracelsus* <note>Two of the most famous figures in medieval and Renaissance medicine; they combined chemistry, astrology, and traditional healing</note>, who wrote several books on the use and power of these seals in the healing of almost incurable diseases, as well as the method for constructing them. And concerning this part of Astrology, we shall also treat it in our *second volume*, where we intend to discuss the different methods of curing diseases.

However, as for the other parts of Astrology, dealing with *the public fortune of empires and governments*, we shall omit them, since it is not our purpose to present them in this place. Similarly, we shall also transfer *Genethlialogy* <note>original: *Genethlalogiam*; the branch of astrology dealing with birth charts and individual destinies</note> to our second volume dedicated to it, since it deals with the disposition and state of the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The "little world," a common Renaissance term for the human being as a reflection of the entire universe</note>. In the second book of this current volume, we will *first* consider the celestial signs and the fixed stars. Then, in the third book, we shall report on the dispositions and accidents of the Planets. *Thirdly*, we will mention the erection of the celestial figure <note>the casting of a horoscope</note> in the fourth book. In the *fourth* place, we shall denote the changes of the air (weather), dedicating the fifth book to these. In the *fifth* place, we shall arrange questions pertaining to theft and the thief, and adapt the sixth book to them. In the *last* book, we shall say something, albeit briefly, concerning <term>elections</term> <note>original: *electionibus*; the practice of choosing the most auspicious astrological time to begin an undertaking</note>.

### C H A P T E R III.

->*Whether the stars impose necessity.*<-

**A**ll who have written about Astrology have converged upon this opinion: that **GOD** acts upon these lower things according to His "ordering," while the stars act according to "execution." Since this is so, who—unless he is entirely like a brute animal—will deny that the human mind is also subject to divine ordering? However, I would not want it understood that the human mind is in any way subject *by its own nature* to the operations of the stars, since it is by nature far more excellent and divine than the nature of the stars. But that vehicle in which (to speak in the Platonic manner) the Empyrean mind <note>The highest, most spiritual part of the intellect</note> is transported into bodies—insofar as it is an ethereal spirit (as we shall declare more extensively in the *first treatise of our second volume*)—participates in the changes of heaven. Consequently, it cannot be hidden from anyone of sound mind that the master of that "chariot" <note>An image used by Plato to describe the soul's relationship to the body and spirit</note> is incited as much as possible by the actions of the heavens, according to the appetites arising from them, just as any part suffers the alterations of the whole. But to explain this more clearly, it must be known according to the *doctrine of Hermes Trismegistus* <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a vast body of mystical and scientific literature</note>, *that the ethereal Spirit is the receptacle of the mind, just as man or the sensitive soul is the receptacle of the Spirit*, so that the Spirit...

*...it is certain that it participates in both—namely, in the super-celestial nature and in that sublunary <note>The "sublunary" realm refers to the Earth and everything below the moon, subject to change and decay.</note> one—since it is of the nature of the middle heaven.*

If, therefore, the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato or Neoplatonic philosophy, who emphasized the hierarchy of the soul.</note> say, the Spirit clings to the mind and flees the pleasures of the flesh, it is made blessed and is exalted above the celestial nature from which it had its origin, receiving only the good actions of the stars and sagaciously avoiding the evil ones; in this way, that prepared Spirit by no means obeys all the actions of the heavens. But when that Spirit, by rejecting the rays of the mind, clings to the other extreme <note>i.e., the physical body and carnal desires.</note>, it suddenly turns from a good **Daemon** <note>original: "Dæmon"; here meaning a guiding spirit or intermediary entity rather than a purely "demonic" being in the modern sense.</note> into an evil **Daemon**, and then it becomes capable of all superior actions—especially the evil ones, due to the body's proneness to malice. This occurs because the body and its ruler (the sensitive soul, which depends on the elements as perpetual receptacles for celestial influences) exist in total opposition to the mind. They are naturally fit and disposed to choose and greedily seize upon the very worst gifts of the heavens: namely, influences that are voluptuous, wrathful, sad, mournful, cruel, drunken, sluggish, impudent, lascivious, and full of concupiscence, along with the rash affection of every other vice. Conversely, the good Spirit of a man chooses from the better influences of heaven, through which he renders himself eager for praise, and warlike or strenuous in honest and lawful matters (such as for the sake of religion), and it makes him just, pious, amiable, studious, liberal, and endowed from birth with the other virtues. We shall discuss these more fully in our *second Volume*, where we will treat **nativities** <term>Nativities: The practice of casting and interpreting astrological charts based on the moment of a person's birth.</term>. We say, therefore, that all these things happen according to God’s ordination and are necessarily carried into execution by the stars as His ministers, whom several philosophers have thereafter—not unsuitably—called the <margin>→</margin>**fingers of nature** <note>original: "naturæ digitos"</note>, as they are the means without which nature does nothing and works nothing in these lower realms. But because the human mind is like a living ray of God Himself, the celestial ministers can no more act upon it than they can upon the Ordainer Himself, namely God. Consequently, the mind must always be considered immune to every worldly influence or change, and subject to no passion; that is, it always acts toward goodness and never <margin>→</margin>suffers the invasions of the wicked. But its vehicle, the Spirit, is sometimes deceived by carnal and worldly <margin>→</margin>allurements, and along with the flesh, it sometimes receives the impressions of the heaven’s wicked affections together with the good—specifically when the <margin>→</margin>mind is either entirely absent or operates only a little. And it is from this that even the worst men sometimes produce good fruits against their own natures; they are made wealthy and are successful in war or other worldly affairs, even while the divine mind is scarcely, or not at all, assisting them. Similarly, an inconstant Spirit, clinging sometimes to this extreme and sometimes to the other, is occasionally good and pious (neglecting the flesh and the world) and at other times wicked and prone to all vices. From this also, the Spirits of certain men, being carnally affected and disobedient to the mind, love slaughter and are occupied with robberies; indeed, they are even readier and more eager to perpetrate such evils at one time than at another. For the Martial stars <note>Stars associated with the planet Mars, the god of war and violence.</note> being more powerful in the heaven arouse a thief who is more or less "Martial" from birth, according to his position and aspect with other stars. This is also provided by other celestial significators according to their agreement with the Lord of the seventh house at the hour of birth. In thefts, therefore, it is manifest that the stars impose a necessity, just as they do in other similar vices, because the divine mind is, as it were, absent in men occupied with such things, <margin>→</margin>and it allows their Spirit to operate according to the wicked imaginations of the flesh. Whence, <margin>←</margin>since the spirit possesses the second place after the mind in the body, and is of the substance of heaven, what prevents the celestial bodies from acting upon it just as they do upon their other similar parts? Similarly, since the actions of the heavens occur chiefly in elemental bodies, both simple and composite, what stands in the way of the celestial bodies acting upon...

<header>TREATISE II. PART IX. BOOK I.</header>

...the Spirit being vacant, since those [celestial bodies] act as much upon physical bodies as those bodies act upon the Spirit itself. From these things, therefore, it is beyond doubt that if a certain knowledge can be obtained regarding the powers <note>original: "virtutibus," referring to the inherent occult properties or influences of stars</note> of the stars, their mutual operations, and their qualities in any given conjunction or aspect, it would not be difficult to boldly pronounce—and infallibly indicate—the stature of a thief, the disposition of his body, and the inclination of his spirit. This is done according to the nature of the "signifying" star <term>Significator: The planet or house that represents a specific person or topic in an astrological chart.</term> combined with the nature of the place in which it is found and the "aspect" <term>Aspect: The specific angular relationship between two planets, thought to influence their combined power.</term> of other planets looking upon it. Such a judgment reveals what the stars impose upon a person by a "necessity of sinning" when the rational mind—which never consents to evil actions—ceases to govern.

<margin>-</margin>Furthermore, as it pertains to the forecasting of storms and the changing of the weather, it is beyond all controversy that all this "lower matter" <note>The "sublunary" world; everything below the moon made of the four elements.</note> and every part of it tends toward growth, decay, alteration, or any other change by the power of the inflowing "celestial soul," as we have clearly demonstrated in the *first treatise of this work*. It follows that if the stronger disposition of the heavens is prone to humidity, then these lower things receive that same nature; if toward heat, the physical elements are perceived to become hotter; if toward cold, colder; and if more inclined to the agitation of winds, then winds and gusts are stirred up in these lower regions. This happens by a certain natural necessity, according to the natural position, power, and dominance of the "celestial ministers" <note>The planets and stars acting as agents of the divine.</note>. Even the beasts, and indeed even inanimate things themselves, show us ocular testimony of this truth. Annual experience teaches us that the seasons of the year, the growth of plants, and all changes follow the motion of the sun; by its approach all things grow green and the air grows warm. Similarly, as the Moon increases, the waters swell, and all bodies, through an invisible succession, become more and more moist and filled with humors. And when Saturn reigns in his own "house"—namely in Capricorn—and invites the other planets to himself as if to a feast (which happened around the year 1608), the most intense frost and cold reign in these elementary regions, and so it is with the rest.

<margin>-</margin>We conclude, therefore, that the power and efficacy of the heavens upon these lower things is so great, and operates with such a certain effect, that it was not without reason that *Hermes Trismegistus, in the second chapter of his book* titled *Asclepius*, calls the heaven a *perceptible GOD*. By this, he means that the heaven performs through action and execution the same things that the Intellectual God performs *through arrangement and decree*. For this reason, he also names the heaven in that same place the *administrator of all bodies*—whose increases and decreases are allotted by the Sun and Moon—and *calls God himself the governor and effector of all things that exist in the world*.

To answer these people briefly, it must be understood that not...

<header>ON THE TYPES OF ASTROLOGY.</header>

# ON THE TYPES OF ASTROLOGY.

<margin>→</margin> ...not that there is any fault in the science itself, but much in the Professor, who, although he understands nothing or very little, nevertheless attempts anything. Indeed, this age of ours has seen very few, or perhaps none at all, who are exactly skilled in this science; meanwhile, quite a large number of *Spurious Professors* <note>original: "Professores Spurii"; referring to fraudulent or self-taught practitioners lacking deep traditional knowledge.</note> are found everywhere. These people are utterly ignorant of this art and far removed from its "marrow" or core; they promise much but perform little or nothing. The reason for this is that this art is 
<margin>—→</margin> cabalistic <note>In this context, "cabalistic" refers to a hidden, mystical tradition passed down through history, rather than strictly Jewish Kabbalah.</note>, first revealed to the ancient Jews and Egyptians, from which they drew wonders in the divination of the future and the revelation of the past. As is declared more extensively by Josephus <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century historian who claimed that the pillars of Seth preserved astronomical knowledge from before the Great Flood.</note> in his history of the Jews, he teaches that this science was first discovered by Adam himself and flowed down successively to others. Beyond doubt, if it is known correctly and perfectly, it is as certain in its operations as the movement of the heavens and the aspects of the Planets are certain, and their determined time even down to the minutes. However, the ancient sages hid the "marrow" of this science to blind the foolish and the unworthy, not unlike the Philosophers who were well-versed in "Lower Astronomy" <note>A common early modern term for Alchemy, viewing the transformation of metals as a terrestrial reflection of the stars.</note>—namely, those skilled in the preparation of the Physician’s Stone. For just as Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Hermeticism and alchemy.</note> and the other *Chemical Philosophers* treat the *Philosophical Stone* parabolically, allegorically, and with sophisticated trickery, one often seems to contradict the other—with one saying "Take <note>original: "R." or "Recipe."</note> this," and another strongly dissuading it and shouting "Take that"—and in this way they deceive students. So too does it stand in this present art, concerning whose secrets various Astrologers have written various things, so that one seems to entirely contradict another in this study. In this way, they deceive the curious with the uncertainty of the doctrine and force Artists to give mostly fallacious and lying responses. This, therefore, is the most certain reason for the uncertainty in that science: it is indeed uncertain, but only relatively—that is, in respect to the persons who do not conceive or handle it absolutely as it is in its nature, but badly. For beyond all doubt, the effects of the stars on these lower things are as certain as it is certain that G O D has ordained all things that happen in this lower world, not only in the simple elements but also in the "elementated" things <note>Things composed of the four elements, such as minerals, plants, and animals.</note>, both animate and inanimate. Nor should it be believed that the Devil himself knows the future and the past by any other knowledge (since, as Scripture testifies, he shares nothing of the secrets of the mind), except insofar as he has learned all events from the motion of the stars, as if he had seen them described in golden letters in the ethereal fields. Indeed, he is believed to be the most practiced among all the Astrologers of the whole world, as one who has long labored in this science and has observed the operations of the stars since the beginning of the world. Through these, he continually notices the will of G O D in natural things, no differently than a servant hearing the words and voice of his Master understands from their sound what he wants and what his intention is in any matter. But of the secret mysteries of G O D he understands no more, nor of His metaphysical operation, than a servant knows his Master’s private thoughts before he declares his intention in words.

<margin>§</margin> From these things, therefore, it is clear that the certainty of this science is supreme (for among all others it is the most sublime and closest to the Creator himself), but the truth among the Artists of this century is minimal, because the truth of this science is hidden under false veils and concealed in the darkness of contradictory words. I, however, leaving aside the diversities and various paths of the Egyptians, Jews, Arabs or Chaldeans, and Babylonians, have followed them only in that point where I perceived them to agree most. And although our path is far from a true and complete knowledge of the art, nevertheless, because we have experienced that true divinations have mostly come from this kind of operation, we shall treat it briefly, omitting the ambiguous curiosities of the ancient Sages.

<header>TREATISE II. PART IX. BOOK I.</header>

## CHAPTER V.

### Concerning those who forbid the practice of Astrology to men.

**V**ery many people are to be found—though they are quite unskilled in this science and submerged in the obscurity of darkness, conceiving nothing in their minds beyond what they can see and touch—who insist that this science should not be used. They argue that because it concerns the ministers of God himself, it is wicked to seek such high things or to search out the secrets of the Creator so anxiously and scrupulously. Others, however, as has already been mentioned, are found who assert that Astrology is either no science at all, or at least a frivolous one, being in no way certain. These latter critics were satisfied, I believe, in the preceding chapter. 

As for the former group, I would wish them, in their hesitation, to diligently read our epistle placed at the beginning of this volume, and thereafter to weigh within themselves whether it is more fitting for a beast or for a human adorned with the gift of mind to think such things. Is it right to judge a creature as noble as man so cheaply and despicably, as if his mind—infused into him by the Creator specifically so he might communicate with Him, and without which a man cannot be blessed—were unable to ascend into heaven? This mind contemplates and climbs the very same scales <note>The "scales" or ladder (Latin: *scalas*) refers to the Neoplatonic idea of the soul's ascent through the celestial spheres.</note> by which it originally descended from heaven into the human body.

Let us hear, I pray, the opinion of *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the beginning of alchemy, astrology, and magic.</note> on this matter, who speaks in the *first discourse of the Pymander* concerning the wisdom of man in understanding Astrology in these words: *Since man had power over all things in himself, he observed the handiwork of the seven governors. These governors, rejoicing in the meditation of the human mind, each made man a sharer of their own order; and after man had learned their essence and beheld his own nature, he then desired to penetrate and break through the boundary of the circles, and to comprehend the power of the governor presiding over fire.* <note>original: "septem gubernatorum... vimque gubernatoris præsidentis igni." The "seven governors" are the seven traditional planets; the "governor of fire" often refers to the Sun or the Demiurge.</note>

Truly divine are these words of *Trismegistus*, exalting the human mind to the height of excellence. By its nobility, he teaches that man may not only know the certain essences of the stars and consequently learn their effects in the science of Astrology, but may even contemplate metaphysical actions (and that by divine permission). Hence, in the same discourse, the same *Trismegistus* speaks thus:

> GOD, creating man in his own image and truly delighted by his own form, granted all his works to human use.

It is certain, therefore, that the human mind—since it is so noble and divine—naturally tends in every way toward high and sublime things, and even toward GOD himself, like a true ray and spark of the divine light. In these lower regions, to which it is committed during life and into which it is transported and delivered by the <term>Spirit-vehicle</term> <note>original: "Spiritu vehiculo." This refers to the "astral body" or "pneumatic vehicle" which, in ancient philosophy, served as the intermediary between the immaterial soul and the physical body.</note> as if into a dark prison, the mind is restricted and hemmed in from its natural liberty. Thus, it is held in a region entirely contrary to its own nature. For just as the mind and the body are two extremes in the order of nature, so too are their dispositions more contrary to one another than heat is to cold or moisture is to dryness.

Therefore, we think it not foolish to conclude that *it is not impossible for the human capacity to know the essences and dispositions of the stars and those governors*, nor is it done against the divine will. For it is granted to the human mind to penetrate more deeply and to speak with God himself through divine contemplation. However, the thickness and darkness of our bodies blinds the soul and takes away its judgment, much like a cloth drawn over the eyes takes away the certainty and shape of a visible object. Thus, the primary knowledge of the stars was declared to the human race through revelation, and thereafter continued by the <term>Cabalistic tradition</term> <note>original: "Cabalistica traditione." Here, it refers generally to the oral transmission of secret or sacred knowledge.</note>.

### Rule III.

Therefore, in every series of products, except for the lowest one, the difference Plus <note>The positive sign</note> towards the left must be expressed without the Minus, just as occurs in standard multiplication, as is demonstrated in the preceding example above.

### Rule IV.

Once the multiplication is complete, a Cossic addition of all products is always performed, as was stated in the abstract; and this is made clear in the preceding demonstration.
<note>'Cossic addition' refers to combining like terms, such as adding all the $x^2$ values together.</note>

### Rule V.

When the multiplier is larger than the multiplicand <note>meaning it contains more terms or higher powers</note>, then the multiplier should be moved into the place of the multiplicand, and the multiplicand into the place of the multiplier; then one must proceed as before, as in the following example.

->ON COSSIC ARITHMETIC.<-
<note>original: "DE ARITHMETICA COSSICA." The term "Cossic" comes from the Italian "cosa," meaning "the thing," which was the standard name for the unknown variable (x) in early algebra.</note>

# CHAPTER VI.

## On the division of Cossic numbers.

<margin>Four things are to be noted in this type of calculation</margin>

- **The Signs, which** <note>original: "Differentia," referring here to the mathematical polarity (positive or negative) of the terms.</note>
    - If { Unlike, are to be added / Alike, are to be subtracted } **First Rule.**
    - When multiplied by themselves, they are either:
        - Alike, such as multiplying { **Plus** by **Plus** / **Minus** by **Minus** } **Produces Plus.** } **Second Rule.**
        - Unlike, such as multiplying { **Plus** by **Minus** / **Minus** by **Plus** } **Produces Minus.** }
- **The Symbols** <note>original: "Characteres," the specific signs used to represent powers of the unknown variable, such as the root, square, or cube.</note>
    - The subtraction of one symbol from another } **Third and fourth rules.**
    - Finding the remainder, and its arrangement }
- **The Arrangement of numbers**
    - Where nothing remains at the beginning after subtraction is done, the fifth rule.
    - Where in the last place the divisor is larger than the dividend, the sixth rule.
    - Where a fractional number is left over after the partition is complete, the seventh rule.
- **The Proof, which is performed by**
    - Dividing the dividend by the quotient, the eighth rule.
    - Multiplying the quotient by the divisor, the ninth rule.

---

### Rule I.

> *Where unlike signs <note>original: "differentiæ"</note> occur together, there the numbers must be added, as is held in the rule for subtraction; conversely, numbers must be subtracted where the signs are alike.*

### Rule II.

> *The first number of the quotient toward the left claims for itself the sign **Plus** (as in the third rule of multiplication), which, when led into **Plus**, will give **Plus**. Similarly, **Minus** into **Minus** will give **Plus**. A second sign multiplied by its opposite will produce **Minus** by the second rule of the same. However, **Minus** by **Plus** or **Plus** by **Minus** is added. But **Plus** by **Plus** or **Minus** by **Minus** is subtracted, according to the fifth rule of subtraction.*

### Rule III.

> *In the subtraction of a lower number from an upper one, the value of the lower <term>symbol</term><note>character: here referring to the algebraic power or degree of the term.</note> must also be taken away from the upper one—namely, from the dividend—and the <term>symbol</term> of the remaining value must be expressed. However, it must always be understood as the first <term>symbol</term> toward the left of the number whose quotient is sought. For the <term>symbols</term> toward the right do not diminish the values of the upper ones. It should also be noted that the remainder of the value of the upper <term>symbol</term> must be placed in the quotient, with its sign arranged according to the second rule of this section.*

### Rule IV.

> ***Q.** <note>The "Quadratus," representing the square of the unknown ($x^2$).</note> is the smallest Cossic sign or Symbol that is divisible; for **R.** <note>The "Radix," representing the root or the unknown ($x$).</note> is just like unity, which cannot be divided. Moreover, the remainder of the value which the sign retains—*

## SPHERE OF THE RESIDUAL VALUE OF CHARACTERS
### *after subtraction has been made.*

---

### *The use of the preceding spheres, through which the value of the quotient's character number is perceived.*

Look for the dividing character under the "crown" or rim of the sphere (or wheel) described above, and with your finger or another pointer, follow the path of that sphere until you reach the point where the character to be divided is found in its outermost and highest sphere. The pointer will then indicate the resulting quotient character. For example: a "Square-cube" (<note>original: "Q. c.", representing $x^5$</note>) divided by a "Square" (<note>original: "₵", the Census symbol representing $x^2$</note>) leaves a "Cube" (<note>original: "C", representing $x^3$</note>) in the quotient; and a "Square-square-square" (<note>original: "Q. Q. Q.", representing $x^6$</note>) divided by a "Square" (<note>original: "Q", $x^2$</note>) will give a "Square-square" (<note>original: "Q. c.", which in this context likely represents the fourth power, $x^4$</note>) in the quotient; and so it continues for the others.

<note>The original text uses abbreviations for "Cossic" powers: q. for quadratum (square), R. for radix (root/variable), and D. for drachma (unit/constant). The symbol ⊕ represents addition.</note>

The divisor 3 is found twice in the dividend 6. Therefore, 2 is to be noted in the quotient, just as is done in the division of abstract numbers. Then, according to the 4th rule of this species: when a Root is subtracted from a Square, a Root remains, which must be set out in the quotient after the 2. Afterward, because by the second rule the difference of the first number toward the left—both of the divisor and the quotient—is a Unit <note>original: "D" for Drachma</note>: multiply therefore, as in abstract numbers, saying: twice 2 are 4, and a Unit times a Unit makes a Unit by the aforementioned proposition. And the Unit is subtracted from the Unit by the second rule of subtraction: therefore, when 4 is subtracted from 19, the residue will be 15, which must be written above with the Unit designation.

Finally, let the divisor be moved by a single step toward the right, proceeding as in the previous steps. For 3 is found in 15 five times; therefore the number 5 is to be noted toward the right in the quotient, and a Root from a Root leaves [nothing]. From these, therefore, 5 times 2 becomes 10, and five times 3 are 15, which when subtracted from the numbers above leave nothing.

### EPILOGUE

Regarding the reduction of Cossic fractions and their various types—namely addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division—as well as the "rule of three" <note>Also known as the Golden Rule, this is a method for finding a fourth value when three are known based on proportions.</note> (which practitioners call "Golden" because of its unique excellence), the extraction of roots, and the Algebraic rule known as the Rule of Equation: I believe you should be referred to Stifel, <note>Michael Stifel (1487–1567), a German monk and mathematician who popularized the use of "+" and "−" signs.</note> Record, <note>Robert Recorde (c. 1510–1558), the Welsh scholar who invented the equals sign (=).</note> and countless other authors who have written most brilliantly on these matters. I am content to have written something openly and clearly only about these principles or primary "species" <note>In early mathematics, "species" referred to the basic operations of arithmetic.</note> of the art. Other writers—as if envying the world this so exalted and hidden science, and fearing it might someday become common knowledge—have treated these principles too briefly and obscurely. Indeed, when the principles of any science remain unknown, that science itself is rendered entirely hidden and concealed in every way. It is for this reason that this art, so distinguished and noble, is discovered only with great difficulty and by so few. But now that these four operations have been sufficiently and clearly explained to the world, it will be very easy to investigate the rest of the subject through sharpness of mind and for any willing student to master the entire science.

<summary>In this closing statement, the author explains that he has focused on clearly teaching the basic principles of algebra (Cossic arithmetic) because previous authors kept them intentionally obscure. He directs advanced students to the works of famous mathematicians like Stifel and Recorde for complex operations and equations.</summary>
<keywords>algebra, Cossic arithmetic, Michael Stifel, Robert Recorde, mathematical education, rule of three, equation rules</keywords>

**A** linear number is one which, beginning from two and always adding a unit, forms a line; one must therefore begin from two, because just as a line is composed of points, so a number is composed of units.

A superficial number <note>original: "Numerus superficialis"</note> is one contained by two sides, namely length and width, or it is a number beginning from three; because no surface is enclosed by fewer than three lines.

## ON GEOMETRIC ARITHMETIC.

*A triangular number <term>triangular number: a number that can be represented in the shape of an equilateral triangle (e.g., 3, 6, 10, 15)</term> is one which, when plotted in width according to units, is bounded by three angles and sides arranged with equal measurement.*

->15.<- ->21.<- ->28.<-

*A square number <term>square number: the product of a number multiplied by itself, which can be arranged in a square grid (e.g., 4, 9, 16, 25)</term> is one plotted in width according to units, with four angles and sides arranged with equal measurement.*

*A pentagonal number <term>pentagonal number: a figurate number that extends the concept of triangular and square numbers to a five-sided polygon</term> is one which, when plotted in width according to units, is bounded by five angles, with sides arranged with equal measurement.*

*A corporal <term>corporal: from the Latin 'corporalis', meaning pertaining to a 'body' or three-dimensional solid</term> or solid number is one contained by three dimensions—namely, length, width, and depth. Alternatively, it is a number which, when its units are arranged in length and depth, represents the shape of some solid body.*

*A <term>pyramidal number</term> <note>original: numerus pyramidalis; these were early modern ways of visualizing numbers as physical stacks of spheres or blocks</note> is arranged in its units in the manner of a physical pyramid, namely that it begins from a wide base and always decreases in its ascent until it reaches a single unit, which is its <term>apex</term> <note>original: conus</note>.*

*A <term>columnar number</term> <note>original: numerus columnalis</note> is arranged in its units in the manner of a physical column, such that it rises from a wide base to the top with equal width, neither decreasing nor increasing.*

*The body of a round column <note>A cylinder.</note> of the same size is measured by multiplying its circumference by its length.*

### Rule IV.

*If you take the base of a round pyramid <note>original: "pyramidis rotundae"; in this context, the author refers to what we now call a cone</note> and multiply it by a third part of its height, the resulting product will be its measurement.*

### Rule VII.

*To find the dimensions of regular solids <note>original: "corpora regularia"; here referring to three-dimensional shapes like rectangular prisms</note> where the three surfaces are clearly different, one side must be multiplied by another that is unequal to it, then let the product be multiplied by the third side which differs from them; for the final product will be the measure of the body.*

### Rule VI.

*With the diameter divided into 14 equal parts, if a perpendicular line is raised above the eleventh part to the circumference, and from that point of contact on the circumference a straight line is drawn to the beginning of the first part, that straight line will be the side of a square whose area will be the same as the area of the circle.*

<note>This rule provides a geometric construction for "squaring the circle"—an ancient mathematical challenge to find a square with the same area as a given circle. While we now know this cannot be done perfectly with only a compass and straightedge, Fludd’s 14-part division method was a common historical approximation.</note>

# CHAPTER V.

## On Transformation. <note>original: "De Reductione." In this context, "reduction" refers to the geometric process of converting one shape into another of equal area.</note>

### Rule I.

*A triangle is transformed into a rectangle <term>quadrangulum: a four-sided figure, here specifically a rectangle</term> of the same area, where the base is contained six times within its perpendicular height, if a line equal to the base is raised at right angles at the end of the third part; then, by the common method, a parallelogram is formed with the other side, the area of which is the same as that of the triangle.*

#### Examination. <note>original: "Examen." This section acts as a proof or a step-by-step walkthrough of the geometric construction.</note>

<note>Translator's note: The following section contains references to points on the accompanying diagram. An ink stain on the original manuscript has partially obscured this text, but the logic remains discernible.</note>

Because a. b. e. f. is part of the triangle a. b. d. f., and because the part of the rectangle a. b. e. f.—namely, a. b. c.—is equal to b. d. e.; therefore, the rectangle a. c. e. f. is of the same size as the <insert>triangle a. d. f.</insert> and is transformed into the parallelogram a. c. e. f.

---

### Rule II.

*A triangle of the aforementioned size is transformed into a circle if its base, or a sixth part of its height, serves as the circle's radius <term>semidiameter: the distance from the center of a circle to its perimeter.</term>*

### Rule III.

*Two unequal squares are combined into one if the sides of both are placed at a right angle, and a straight line is extended from the end of one to the end of the other, forming a triangle. For that hypotenuse <term>hypotenuse: the longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle</term> will measure the sides that must form the square containing the two aforementioned squares.*

<note>This is a practical application of the Pythagorean theorem: the sum of the areas of two squares built on the legs of a right triangle equals the area of the square built on the hypotenuse.</note>

### Rule IV.

*The area of a square is transformed into a parallelogram <term>parallelogram: a four-sided figure with opposite sides parallel; here used to mean a rectangle of equal area</term> if the base of the square is extended to any desired length; let the top side of the same square also be extended to the same dimension, and let two parallel lines be fixed to form a quadrangle, labeled a. c. d. e. Then, let a straight line be drawn from angle c. to angle e., and where this diagonal line intersects the side of the square b. f., mark it as point g. The length of the line g. f. will then be the width of a parallelogram equal in area to the given square.*

---

The parallelogram i. l. d. e. is therefore of the same capacity <note>original: "capacitatis"; meaning area or volume in this context</note> as the square a. b. f. e.

# CHAPTER IV.

## Concerning addition with subtraction.

### Rule I.

*When semicircles of unequal circles that differ proportionally are added together in the same proportion, they form a spiral line.*

### Rule II.

*By adding parts subtracted from four circles of two different sizes—where the radius <note>original: semidiameter</note> of one is equal to the diameter of the other—an oval shape is created.* Therefore, let **a, b, c, & d** be two circles of a smaller proportion drawn around the centers marked **e**; and let those of the larger proportion be **f, g, h, i**, whose centers are the intersections of the smaller circles, specifically marked as **l**.

## Rule IV.

*The <term>area of a polygon</term><note>original Latin: *superficies polygonalis*. In this context, "superficies" refers to the two-dimensional space within the shape.</note> is measured by multiplying the sum of all its sides (or the bases of the triangles that compose it) by the length of one side <note>The diagram shows this means multiplying the length of one side by the total number of sides to find the perimeter.</note>, and then multiplying that product by half of the <term>perpendicular line</term><note>In modern geometry, this is called the "apothem"—the distance from the center to the midpoint of a side.</note> drawn from the center angle to the midpoint of the base.*

---

## Rule V.

*A <term>trapezoidal area</term><note>original Latin: *superficies Trapezea*.</note>, in cases where there are no right angles but two sides are equal while the ends are unequal <note>This describes an isosceles trapezoid.</note>, is measured by averaging the two unequal ends (adding them together and dividing by two) and then multiplying that average by the length of one side.*

---

For if that trapezoid is reduced into a <term>parallelogram</term><note>A four-sided figure with opposite sides parallel and equal.</note>, and that shape is measured according to the second proposition of multiplication, the resulting capacity will be the same as was demonstrated previously.

## Rule VI.

*Regarding a trapezoid <note>original: "Trapezeam"; a four-sided shape with at least one pair of parallel sides</note> that contains two right angles: if half of that portion of the line by which the longer side exceeds the side opposite to it is added to that opposite side, and the surface area is reduced into a parallelogram, you will measure it very easily through multiplication. This is because triangle a. b. c. is equal to triangle d. e. c.*

---

->E X A M I N A T I O N.<-

When this is multiplied by the other side—namely, 8—it produces 112, just as demonstrated above.

### Rule II.

In exactly the same way, the height of an object is perceived in a mirror by approaching the mirror until the summit of the tower appears in the center of the mirror; then, by multiplying the interval from the center of the mirror to the foot of the tower by the height of the eye, and dividing the product by the distance from the man's foot to the center of the mirror. See the following figure, Number 1.

### Rule III.

By a similar progression, the height of an accessible tower is also calculated using a square <note>The "square" refers to a surveying instrument, often found on the back of an astrolabe, used to measure angles and heights</note>: Because, if you multiply the distance from yourself to the base of the tower by the intercepted points of the <term>reversed shadow<note>original: umbrae versae</note>|A technical term used in surveying for the vertical scale on a shadow square, used when the object is taller than the distance to its base</term>, and divide the result by 12, the quotient will be the height of the tower. Let the distance be 18 feet, and the intersected points be 4, as in Number 2.

->### Rule IV.<-

**The height of an inaccessible tower is found** by dividing 12 by the number of <term>points marked off</term> <note>original: "punctorum abscisorum"; these are the units of measurement on the scale of a geometric square or quadrant</note>—for instance 3—and saving the quotient, which is 4. Then, having marked the location of your station, move backward to take a second station, and divide 12 by the points marked off there—namely 6—the quotient will be 2. This is to be subtracted from the first quotient, if the second quotient is smaller than the first, and the remainder is saved (whereas if the second quotient is larger than the first, the first must be subtracted from the second). For example, when 2 is taken from 4, 2 remains. Finally, let the space between the first and second station be measured—suppose it is 40 feet—which is then divided by the two <note>the remainder from the previous subtraction</note>. To this quotient, the height of the observer's stature <note>the height from the ground to the observer's eye</note> must be added—let it be 5 feet—and the total sum will be the height of the object.

## Rule III.

You may divide a right-angled triangle into as many equal parts as you wish if you construct a quadrilateral <note>original: "quadrangulum," here implying a square or rectangle used as a reference area</note> based on its orthogonal <note>perpendicular</note> line. You then divide the area of this square by 4 and extract the square root of the resulting number; this value, when measured from the cone <note>the vertex or apex</note> of the triangle toward the base, will mark the first fourth part of the triangle's area. The second fourth part is found by taking half of the square's area and extracting its root; this root, descending from the vertex toward the base, will indicate the point for the second quarter, equal in area to the first. Finally, the third fourth will reveal itself by extracting the root of three-quarters of the square's area, always descending from the vertex toward the base, and so on for any further divisions.

->For example.<-

## Rule IV.

In this same manner, we are also able to partition non-right-angled triangles into equal parts by treating the side that falls most closely to the perpendicular as the side of the square.

->*On progression or proportion.*<-

### Rule I.

**T**he doubling of the measurements correctly found from two stations <note>The specific locations where a surveyor stands to take a reading</note> of a three-foot staff (the slider of which shall be half a foot) will be the measure of the height of the object; for twice the distance between a. and b. will be the height of the tower, c. d. For the ratio of a. b. to c. d. is the same as 2 to 4, and 3 to 6.

->*For example.*<-

### Rule II.

*The length of an object is also gathered by the proportion of its width: for as the triangle A. B. C. relates, so also is the triangle of the instrument, c. d. e., proportioned. Therefore, the side of triangle A. B. C., namely B. C., is similar to the side c. d. e. of the instrument. Side C. B. therefore differs from side A. B. by a ratio of five to four <term>sesquiquartal proportion: a ratio where the greater number contains the lesser once, plus one-fourth part of the lesser (5:4)</term>; therefore, divide side A. B. into 5 equal parts, take away one, and the remainder will be the length, B. C. We have demonstrated this extensively in the third book of our Geometry, where we made ample mention of the Jacob’s Staff <note>original: "baculo Jacobi"; a cross-staff used to measure angles and distances</note> in every kind of measurement. ### Rule VI.

->For spheres or globes where the ratio of their diameters is double, the ratio of their weights will be eightfold. Thus, if a larger sphere weighs 50 pounds, a smaller one [with half the diameter] will be composed of 6 1/4 pounds.<-
<note>This rule describes the "square-cube law": if you double the diameter of a sphere, you increase its volume—and therefore its weight—by eight times (2 to the power of 3).</note>

---

### Rule VII.

->Once the weight of a cannonball <term>cannonball<gloss>Latin: "globi bombardalis"</gloss></term> is known, its measurements and diameter can be determined by a progressive proportion along a line or a flat surface. To begin, prepare a globe weighing one pound made of the metal you wish to use for casting your artillery <term>artillery piece<gloss>Latin: "tormentarium"</gloss></term>. It must be perfectly round, with a diameter marked A-B, the circumference of which you shall draw upon a flat surface.<-

The progression is therefore as follows: the fourth part of the circumference of the one-pound globe, namely A-C, will be the radius <term>radius<gloss>Latin: "semidiameter"</gloss></term> of a globe that should weigh two pounds. In turn, the fourth part of that globe's circumference will be the radius of a three-pound globe, and the fourth part of the three-pound globe will establish the radius of a four-pound globe, and so on, progressing infinitely.
<note>This refers to a practical geometric construction used by early modern engineers to create "gunner's scales," allowing them to calculate the necessary size of a projectile based on its weight without complex cubic calculations.</note>

# CHAPTER III.

## *On the rule of three proportions.*

### Rule I.

**W**hen two proportional numbers are known, the third will also be known through this rule. For if five parts of the parallel line A. B. correspond to 14 parts on the line C. D., then 40 parts of line A. B. will give 112 parts of line C. D. <note>This is a classic "Rule of Three" calculation: 5 is to 14 as 40 is to 112. (14 × 40) / 5 = 112.</note> For triangle A. B. E. has similar angles to triangle C. D. E. <note>The original Latin includes an extra 'A' in the second triangle's label, likely indicating that vertex A is shared between the two similar triangles</note>. And the equally divided parts of the line or side A. B. are proportional to the divided parts of line C. D.

# CHAPTER XIV.
## On the extraction of the root. <term>root: specifically the square root, the base number which, when multiplied by itself, produces a square</term>
### Rule I.

A number of two digits has only a single figure for its root, because the greatest square number of two digits or figures is 81, whose root is 9. For example:

<note>The original text refers to the diagram here, which shows a 9x9 grid representing the square of 9.</note>

### Rule II.

The root of any square number composed of two figures is found by multiplying that digit by itself whose resulting product most closely approaches the square number. For that digit will be the root of the square; for instance, 6 is the root of the square 36. Similarly, 8 is the root of the square 64, because 6 led into itself <note>original: "in se ductus" — a standard early modern expression for squaring a number</note> will produce 36, which no other digit can produce. So also eight times 8 makes 64, which is its square number, and so on for the rest; regarding which, see the wheel below, whose outer sphere denotes the roots, and the inner denotes the squares.

## Rule IX. <note>original: "Regula IX."</note>

*If, after the extraction of a root, some remainder is left over (which always happens when a number is not a perfect square), the remainder shall be expressed in fractional numbers. For example, in the number 10, which contains 9 as its greatest square, the root of which is 3. One unit will remain, as is seen in the following demonstration.*

-> [Diagram of a 3x3 square grid representing the number 9, with a separate 10th unit excluded to show it is a remainder] <-

Therefore, the tenth part <note>The "tenth unit" in the number 10</note> is excluded from the square (because the number nine is a perfect square number). This remainder should be divided into 6 equal parts, which are to be attached to the 6 smaller squares <note>The outer faces of the 3x3 grid</note> of the two sides of the larger square. However, such a number cannot be squared exactly because of the corner, **A**, which is left empty. <note>This "empty corner" is a classic geometric proof of why the square root of a non-perfect square results in an infinite or irrational fraction; you can never perfectly "fill" the growing square without a tiny gap remaining at the vertex.</note>

-> [Diagram showing the division of the remainder unit into segments distributed along two sides of the 3x3 square, highlighting the missing corner piece labeled A] <-

### Rule II.

*The cube root is also found without the preceding wheel <note>original: "rota præcedente"; likely referring to the circular diagram shown in the detected images</note>, for the resulting number approaching closest to the value of the cube by multiplying a root by itself, the square which is produced, being again multiplied by the root, will be the cube of that square; or by multiplying any square number by the root, the product of which approaches closer to the value of the cube. Therefore, let the cube be 27. I multiply 3 by itself, and it produces 9, which is its square number; again I multiply 9 by 3, its root, and the product will be the cubic number, namely, 27.*

## Rule XI.

*In cubic numbers, where the divisor cannot be contained within the dividend, there a <term>cipher<gloss>A zero (0) used as a placeholder in a mathematical calculation.</gloss></term> is to be placed in the <term>quotient<gloss>The result obtained by dividing one quantity by another.</gloss></term> & the whole root is to be squared & the resulting number multiplied by 3 & what is produced will be the second divisor, as in the following demonstration.*

->8 242 408 (202.<-

### *How the nearest root of a non-exact cubic number may be found?*

## Rule XII.

*Extract the nearest root from the cubic number, & what remains will be the numerator; Then multiply the root <term>squaredly<gloss>By itself; i.e., to square the number.</gloss></term> & again multiply the product by 3 & what arises from the last multiplication will be the denominator, as in the following number, which is not a cubic number.*

->694 582 951 (885.<-

The larger cubic number, however, which is found within it, is 693,154,125, whose root is 885. Therefore, 1,428,826 remains, which will be the numerator, whose denominator by the preceding rule will be 2,349,672. They are arranged in this way:

->1,428,826<-
->-------<-
->2,349,672<-
