### Rule III.

*To find the <term>total sum</term> <note>original: "aggregatum"</note> of a <term>pyramidal battle formation</term> <note>A triangular or wedge-shaped arrangement of soldiers where each successive row increases or decreases by a set number.</note> with an even number of ranks, consult the second rule of common Arithmetic progression, as follows:*

->12<-
->1<-
->---<-
->13<-
->6<-
->---<-
->78<-
<note>This calculation follows the formula for the sum of an arithmetic series: (first rank + last rank) multiplied by half the number of ranks. Here, (1+12) * 6 = 78.</note>

*If, however, the number of ranks is odd, let us seek guidance from the third rule of that same progression.*

### Rule IV.

*The number of soldiers in a <term>Rhomboidal battle formation</term> <note>A diamond-shaped formation consisting of two back-to-back triangles.</note> is determined by doubling the pyramid and subtracting the largest number or rank from the total, as follows:*

->78 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 156<-
->2 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 12<-
->--- &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; ---<-
->156 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 144<-
<note>To form a diamond from a triangle of 78 men, you double it (156) but must subtract the shared widest middle row (12) so it is not counted twice, resulting in 144 men.</note>

### *The Use of this Species of Battle Formations.*

Such an arrangement of soldiers, which the French call <term>Pointed Battalions</term> <note>original: "Bataillons en point"</note> or <term>Lozenge-shaped Battalions</term> <note>original: "en lozange"</note>, is little used in the present day, except where necessity compels it. This occurs specifically when the level ground of a location offers a path for <term>cohorts</term> <note>Units of infantry.</note> on the march, but the entrance or exit is very narrow—being hemmed in by rocks, mountains, woods, rivers, marshes, or lakes—through which the army must pass. Similarly, such a form is required when invading an enemy town, and especially where the streets are too narrow.

### Rule V.

*Cohorts are quickly arranged into a <term>square formation</term> if you extract the <term>square root</term> <note>original: "radicem quadratam"</note> of the number of men. The extracted root will denote the number of men in each rank or file. For example, if the number of soldiers is 625, the root is 25.*

->25<-

## Rule VI.

*Whoever wishes to arrange <term>cohorts</term><note>A cohort was a standard tactical unit of the Roman legion, usually composed of about 480 men, though used here as a general term for a body of troops.</note> in battle so that the <term>battle line</term><note>original: "acies"</note> has a length two, three, or four times greater than its width, should divide the number of cohorts into as many parts as the desired ratio of length to width. For example, if the length ought to contain the width three times, the number of soldiers must be divided by 3; the <term>square root</term><note>original: "radix"</note> of the resulting quotient will determine the number of men in each rank and file. If four times, let it be divided by 4, and so on. Suppose, therefore, the number of soldiers is 2,310. Divide this by 3, and the result is 770. The square root of this is 27, and 41 men remain, who can be employed for other duties. The demonstration follows below.*

## Rule IX.

*The circumference of a circle will be triple its diameter*, <note>The author is using a simplified value for Pi (π ≈ 3), which was a common practical approximation in early modern military engineering and drill manuals.</note> for where the diameter is seven, there the circumference will be 21, and so it is for other internal circles. But the best method of all in the formation of round battles will be first to find the diameter of your circle and arrange it in the first place, then to fill the entire circumference with triple that number of men; and it should also be observed that the smaller diameter will consist of 3, as follows:

---

*(The manuscript contains a diagram of concentric circular military formations. The outer circle shows a diameter of 7 and a circumference of 21. The middle circle shows a diameter of 5 and a circumference of 15. The inner circle shows a diameter of 3 and a circumference of 9.)*

---

This form of battle is necessary when the enemy is nearby, so that the first ranks may resist the adversaries while the interior ranks form themselves. The <term>Antesignanus</term> <note>original: "Antesignanus". Historically a Roman soldier standing before the standard, but here used to denote a commander or key officer who must remain protected in the heart of the formation.</note> must always be placed in the center. Let the smaller circle be composed of soldiers who carry short weapons—such as swords with bucklers, halberds, and the like. The Germans and Hollanders are accustomed to organizing this disposition of soldiers more by continuous practice than by an accurate method or written rules of the military art.

## Rule XI.

*A crescent-shaped formation <term>figura lunaris: literally "lunar figure," a tactical formation where troops are arranged in a curve</term> is created by removing a certain number of men from a circular formation. ## Rule XII.

*The ladder <term>scala: used here specifically for a scaling ladder in siege warfare</term> by which soldiers may scale the walls of a town protected by a moat is best adapted in this way: Let the exact length be measured from the edge of the moat to the base of the wall, and likewise the height of the wall. For the straight line crossing the moat will form a right angle <note>original: "angulum rectum"</note> at the base of the wall. Therefore, the length of the diagonal line—which determines the necessary length of the ladder—is calculated by the same method taught in the Geometric Arithmetic, in the chapter on multiplication with subtraction, under the first rule.* <note>This is a practical application of the Pythagorean theorem ($a^2 + b^2 = c^2$) to determine the hypotenuse, ensuring ladders were the correct length to reach the top of enemy fortifications.</note>

# CHAPTER I.
## On Musical Proportion.

**T**o add in proportions is to multiply. To subtract, however, is to divide. To *double* is to multiply a thing by itself. Therefore, multiplication and division [in the common sense] do not have a place in proportions, because proportions do not admit the unit <note>In the mathematical music theory of this period, "1" is not a ratio; ratios require two terms. The author is explaining that harmonic "addition" of intervals is performed by multiplying their ratios.</note>; for one does not descend beyond the double. The demonstration of this rule can be seen, as if with one's own eyes, in the division of the Monochord <note>A scientific and musical instrument consisting of a single string stretched over a soundboard with a movable bridge, used to demonstrate the mathematical relationships between musical pitches.</note>.

A multiple proportion is one in which a larger number is compared to a smaller quantity and measure.

How all the remaining proportions relate to one another is shown in the book on numeration and the chapter on proportions.

---

*The letter A and the first tone on the monochord are found if you divide the whole string into nine equal parts; for the first division from the head of the string will be the letter A, and the space between Γ <note>The Greek letter Gamma, representing the lowest pitch in the medieval "Gamut" or scale.</note> and A will be a tone. Therefore, by removing the part Γ-A from the string, a whole tone is taken away from the string sounding Γ-π.*

*...[firstly,] if the distance between F and Π <note>The Greek letter Pi (Π) here likely marks the end-point or bridge of the instrument's string.</note> is divided into 9 equal parts. For the end of the first part will be the location of the low G. And the distance of string Γ G <note>Γ (Gamma) represents the lowest note of the scale.</note> will be a double proportion: for as 2 is to 1, so the whole string is to Γ G, which is its half part; therefore it is called by the ancients the Mese, or middle. And in this proportion consists the Diapason <term>Diapason: the interval of an octave, defined by the mathematical ratio of 2:1</term>.*

---

### Rule VIII.

*The high letters are to be found in exactly the same way as the low ones: namely, by dividing the remainder of the string G Π into 9 parts to find the location of high A; then the distance A Π into another 9 to find the place of high B, and so on for the others.*

### Rule IX.

*By the same progression, we shall proceed to the discovery of the super-excellent <note>original: "superexcellentium" — referring to the highest register of the medieval/Renaissance scale</note> or super-high letters, as will appear more extensively in the following demonstration.*

### Rule X.

*The proportion of a tone is as 9 to 8. But the proportion of a semitone to a tone is a superpartient proportion <term>superpartient: a ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number plus several parts of it; here describing the complex Pythagorean "limma" ratio</term> of 256 to 243. For example, if the monochord is divided into 324, that number represents a tone; but the second tone is 288. The semitone is 256. The Diatessaron <term>Diatessaron: the interval of a perfect fourth, ratio 4:3</term> is as 4 to 3. The Diapente <term>Diapente: the interval of a perfect fifth, ratio 3:2</term> is as 3 to 2, and the Diapason is as 2 to 1, as is evident in the following example.*

### Rule XI.

*From an <term>Octave<note>original: "Diapason"</note></term> combined with a <term>Fifth<note>original: "Diapente"</note></term> arises a triple proportion (3:1) or a double-sesquialtera proportion: From a double octave arises a quadruple proportion (4:1), and from a triple octave arises an octuple proportion (8:1). The <term>Fourth<note>original: "Diatessaron"</note></term> consists of a <term>4:3 ratio<note>original: "sesquitertia proportion"</note></term>. However, the Fifth remains in a <term>3:2 ratio<note>original: "sesquialtera proportion"</note></term>, as is clearly shown to the eyes of the observer in the preceding demonstration.*

### TREATISE II. PART I. BOOK VI. ###

The numbers containing the musical consonances were discovered through the weights of hammers. <note>This refers to the legend of Pythagoras, who allegedly discovered the mathematical ratios of music by listening to the different pitches produced by hammers of varying weights in a blacksmith's forge.</note> Just as there were four hammers, so there are four numbers found from their weights—as has been stated—which contain almost all the power of music. These numbers are 6, 8, 9, and 12. In these four numbers, you will find just as many proportions, and through this, just as many perfect consonances. These proportions are, namely: *Double, Sesquialtera, Sesquitertia, and Sesquioctava*.

*The double proportion* <note>original: "Dupla proportio"</note> is when the larger number, compared to the smaller, contains it twice within itself, such as 12 to 6, 8 to 4, 4 to 2, and 2 to 1. Under this proportion falls the consonance called the <term>Diapason</term> <note>The interval of an octave.</note>, as is demonstrated below on the <term>monochord</term> <note>A single-stringed instrument used to measure musical intervals.</note>.

If you wish to prove this, whether on strings, pipes, small bells, or large bells, and all things that make sound, it is necessary that one thing be double the size of the other; thus, one being half of the whole will undoubtedly sound the <term>Diapason</term> for you.

*The sesquialtera proportion* <note>original: "Sesquialtera proportio"; a ratio of 3:2</note> is when the larger number, related to the smaller, contains the whole smaller number within itself and one-half part besides, such as 12 to 8, 9 to 6, 6 to 4, and 3 to 2. From this proportion arises that consonance which is called the <term>Diapente</term> <note>The interval of a perfect fifth.</note>. Wherever the <term>Diapente</term> is found, the lower voice will always contain the whole of the other part and half of it again.

*The sesquitertia proportion* <note>original: "Sesquitertia proportio"; a ratio of 4:3</note> is when the larger number, compared to the smaller, contains it whole and a third part besides, such as 12 to 9, 8 to 6, and 4 to 3. From this agreement of numbers consists the <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>The interval of a perfect fourth.</note> consonance, where the lower voice contains the whole of the other part and a third of it again.

*The sesquioctava proportion* <note>original: "Sesquioctava proportio"; a ratio of 9:8</note> is when the larger number, related to the smaller, contains the whole smaller number and an eighth part of it, such as 9 to 8 (where the remainder is one unit). In this proportion, the <term>tonus</term> <note>A whole tone or whole step.</note> is understood; do not doubt that the lower voice contains the whole of the other part and an eighth part of it.

*Note* that wherever the aforementioned consonances exist, you will undoubtedly find those proportional numbers by which alone (and not by others) we divided the monochord, as shown above. By these numbers all musical instruments are formed, such as pipes, cymbals, and small or large bells; through these, harps, lyres, and viols resonate. Finally, whatever in the world resonates musically will in no way deviate from these numerical proportions.

---

->CHAPT. IV.<-

->*Regarding temporal proportion.*<-

->Rule I.<-

**I**n double proportion, two small notes are equivalent to one note of the same name and quantity, such as two <term>minimae</term> <note>minims or half-notes</note> to one, and two <term>semibreves</term> <note>whole notes</note> to one. Similarly, in triple proportion, 3 notes are equivalent to one. In quadruple, 4 notes are equivalent to one in measure and quantity, and so on for the others.

->Rule II.<-

->*Quintuple proportion is represented by the semibreve.*<-

->Rule III.<-

->*Sextuple proportion, because of its speed, cannot easily be expressed by the fingers or the lips using the <term>minima</term>.*<-
->Therefore, this proportion must always be composed using the <term>semibreve</term>.<-

## CHAPTER V I.

### On finding the true hour of any day in which a Conjunction, Opposition, Square, Trine, or Sextile occurs between two Planets.

**B**ecause it is necessary to erect a celestial figure <note>A horoscope or birth chart.</note> for the hour of an aspect, either for indicating changes in the air <note>Weather forecasting via astrology.</note> or for preparing elections <note>Choosing the most auspicious time to begin an undertaking.</note>. It is therefore done in this manner: *One must inspect the Ephemerides <note>Tables providing the daily positions of the sun, moon, and planets.</note> of the given year, and the month of that year, where the closer Planets which must make the aspect are also to be observed—namely, whether both are direct, or both retrograde, or whether one is direct and the other retrograde.*

*Where indeed both are direct or retrograde, their daily motion is to be considered: which motion of theirs is either equal or unequal. If truly they are unequal, the smaller number is to be drawn out from the larger, and the remainder will be the first term of the rule of three proportions. If truly the motions of both are equal, then the daily motion will be the first term of that rule. For example, a conjunction of the Sun with the Moon in the year 1600 occurs on February 14. The daily motion of the Sun is 1 degree. Of the Moon, truly, 14 degrees and 27 minutes.*

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; ☾ <note>Moon</note>. &nbsp;&nbsp; 14 deg. &nbsp; 27 min.  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; ☉ <note>Sun</note>. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 1 deg. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 0 min. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 13 deg. 27 min. **Z**° <note>The 'Z' likely marks the resulting 'Zone' or difference used for the calculation.</note>  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 13 deg. &nbsp; 27 min.  

*The second term, however, will always be 24 <note>Representing the 24 hours in a day.</note>.*

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 13 deg. &nbsp; 27 min. **Z** 24.

*The last term, truly, is collected by subtracting the motion of one meridian from the motion of the other. Moreover, the motion at noon is taken for each of those days in which the Planets behold each other. Whatever remains from the larger number will be the third term. Therefore, the motion of the Moon at the noon hour was 21 degrees and 40 minutes. Of the Sun, truly, 24 degrees and 38 minutes.*

### CHAPTER VII.

->On finding the ALTITUDE OF THE SUN.<-

*The declination <note>The angular distance of a heavenly body north or south of the celestial equator.</note> of the Sun's degree, in which the sun is on that day the question is raised, must be considered. If it is northern, it must be subtracted from the latitude of the region; if indeed it is southern, the same must be added to the latitude, and that which has been collected must be subtracted from 90. What remains will be the sun's altitude for that same day.*

---

### CHAPTER VIII.

->On finding the NUMBER OF DEGREES FOR UNEQUAL HOURS.<-

*Divide the portion of the diurnal <note>daytime</note> circle by 12, and the quotient will reveal the number of parts for the hours of that same day. This same thing must also be done when the number of parts for the hours of the same night is desired, namely by dividing the nocturnal portion of the circle by 12.*
<note>Unequal hours, also called temporal hours, divide the period of daylight and the period of darkness each into 12 hours. Consequently, a "day hour" is longer in summer than in winter.</note>

## C H A P T E R  IX.

->*On the finding of* EQUAL HOURS *for any day.*<-

**L**et the portion of the day’s circle <note>This refers to the arc of the sun's path above the horizon, measured in degrees.</note> be divided by 15, and the result will be the number of equal hours of the day. The equal hours of the night are also found in this same way, if the nocturnal portion is divided by 15. <note>In this system, a full 360-degree circle corresponds to 24 hours, meaning 15 degrees equals one hour.</note>

---

## C H A P T E R  X.

->*On the conversion of equal hours into unequal hours.*<-

**M**ultiply the equal hours by 15, and divide the product by the degrees of the hours of that day; and you will have the unequal hours. <note>Unequal hours, also known as "temporal hours," were a traditional system where the periods of daylight and darkness were each divided into 12 hours, regardless of the season. This meant a "daylight hour" was longer in summer than in winter.</note>

---

## C H A P T E R  XI.

->*On the conversion of unequal hours into equal hours.*<-

**M**ultiply the unequal hours by the parts of the hours of that day, and divide what results by fifteen, and you will have the <insert>equal</insert> hours. <note>The original Latin had a strike-through correcting "unequal" to "equal."</note>

---

## C H A P T E R  XII.

->*On the finding of the* DAILY MOTION *of any* PLANET.<-

**O**ne must consider the motion of the Planet, specifically whether it be retrograde or direct. <note>Direct motion is the usual west-to-east movement against the stars; retrograde is the apparent backward motion.</note> For if it be retrograde, the minutes and seconds must be subtracted. But where the Planet is direct, there the minutes and seconds must be added; for example, Saturn <note>original: ♄</note> is retrograde on the fourth day of November. The difference of its motion from the 3rd to the 4th is between 39 and 34. Similarly, its direct motion on the 3rd of July is between 24 and 13.

| Saturn retrograde 39 | Saturn Direct 24. |
|----------------------|-------------------|
| 34                   | 13                |
| ---                  | ---               |
| 5 daily motion       | 37 daily motion.  |

---

## C H A P T E R  XIII.

->ON THE CALCULATION OF THE MOTION OF THE PLANETS AT ANY HOUR.<-

**T**he daily motion of any Planet and the hours elapsed since noon must be reduced into minutes. Then, multiply the minutes of the one by the minutes of the other, and divide the product by 24. Let the resulting number be divided again by 60, and the quotient will denote the true motion of that Planet. For example, let the daily motion of the Sun be 58 minutes, and let the hour of the question be 20 hours and 30 minutes after noon.

## CHAPTER III.

### On Duplication and Multiplication

**D**uplication occurs when any figure is found twice in the same chart—that is, in different houses of the same figure. Similarly, multiplication is when the same figure is found more frequently in the same chart.

### Rule I.

*The first figure found in the second house portends riches and profit; in the third, it signifies something good from parents, and so on for the others according to the nature of the houses in which they are found, as in Figure 4.*

### Rule II.

*If any figure is multiplied within the shield, it signifies the success or misfortune of the seeker <term>querent|The person asking the question in a divination</term>, according to the nature and disposition of the figures that are so frequent; for example:*

## CHAPTER IV.

### On Increase and Decrease.

**I**ncrease and decrease occur when the total number of points in the 16 figures of the Shield either exceeds the total number of all simple geometric points (which is 96) or is less than them.

### Rule.

<insert>Hand-drawn arrow in left margin pointing to this paragraph</insert>
*When the slowness or speed of a future event is required, first let it be asked whether the total number of all points in the geomantic chart, added together, is greater or less than the given number 96. For the smaller it is, the swifter the outcome of the question will be, and vice versa. For example, if a prognosis is to be made concerning the length or brevity of a certain disease, and such a chart occurs to us as in Figure 5.*

## CHAPTER V.

### *On projection.*

<margin>☞</margin>
**G**eomantic projection <note>The method of calculating a final result or "point of focus" in a divination chart</note> is performed by taking the odd points found in the "heads" and "feet" <note>The top and bottom rows of the four-line geomantic symbols</note> of the 16 figures, the total of which is to be distributed through the 12 houses of the scheme <note>The houses refer to the twelve sections of an astrological or geomantic chart, each representing a different area of life</note>. For the house and its figure to which the final number is assigned will be the "conjunction" or connection of the question. For example, if the last point falls in the first house, it indicates that the question pertains to the petitioner <note>The person asking the question</note> themselves; if in the second house, it signifies goods and possessions; if in the third, brothers and parents, and so on through the others. As shown in the following shield <note>A term for the triangular geomantic chart</note>, the projection falls in the second house, and therefore denotes fortunes and riches, of which the figure <term>o o</term> <note>original: "o o"; likely referring to a specific arrangement of points in a geomantic figure</note> is the signifier; see figure 6.

### C H A P T E R VIII.

**B**ut indeed *Apollonius* <note>Likely referring to Apollonius of Tyana, a famous Neopythagorean philosopher and mathematician of the 1st century AD.</note> described another method of divination according to Pythagorean doctrine. He says, specifically, that future things can be foretold by the power of a certain <term>Sphere</term> <note>A divinatory tool often called the "Sphere of Pythagoras" or "Wheel of Life and Death," used to calculate the outcome of illnesses or events based on the numerical value of a person's name.</note> invented by Pythagoras. Insofar as I have examined various constructions of this sphere in various authors, I have adhered most closely to those points where the majority of them agreed, and I have followed their opinions: we have depicted the spherical figure according to their doctrine in this way. <note>The actual diagram usually follows on the subsequent page.</note>

In the wheel described above, the uppermost circle denotes the number of the letters in names; the circle placed below that contains the elementary letters themselves; the third circle from the circumference indicates the number of the days of the week; and the circle designated beneath it indicates the names of the days. Finally, a line in the form of an axis passing through the middle of the entire sphere, dividing it into two equal parts, acts as its Horizon, distinguishing one hemisphere—namely the upper—from the lower. The numbers placed above that diameter promise prosperous fortune; the lower ones, however, promise misfortune. The prognostications <note>A forecast or prediction of a likely outcome.</note> derived from this wheel are of this sort:

-> *To know which of the combatants shall obtain the victory.* <-

Take the name of one and likewise the other who are to fight one another, and gather the numbers assigned to each letter; then gather the number of the day on which the battle is to occur; similarly, the number of the Moon <note>This refers to the "lunar day," or the age of the moon in its current cycle (e.g., the 1st day of the new moon, 2nd day, etc.).</note>—namely, if it be the first day of the Moon, take 1; if the second, 2; and so on. Let these numbers be added together and divided by 30; having done this, look for what remains over 30 in the hollow of the sphere. If it is found in the upper hemisphere, he will be the victor; if in the lower, the vanquished.

-> *Concerning a fugitive, whether he shall return or not, or if he may be found.* <-

Proceed with the name of the person just as you did in the preceding account with each of the combatants, and divide the total number gathered from the name of the fugitive, the day, and the Moon by 30, and seek the remainder. For if it is found in the upper hemisphere, he will return or be found; but if in the lower, the opposite is true.

# ON PYTHAGOREAN ARITHMETIC. <note>original: "De Arithmetica Pythagorica." This refers to arithmancy or onomancy—divination based on the numerical values of names—rather than pure mathematics.</note>
<page-num>151</page-num>

### *Whether a pregnant woman will give birth to a male or a female.*

Calculate the number of the woman’s name and of her younger son, or, if she does not have a son, calculate the name of her husband; add 15 to the total, and divide by 9. If the remaining number is even, a male will be born; if it is odd, a female.

### *Whether the husband or the wife is destined to die first?*

Calculate their names by the value of their letters, and divide by 9. If the remaining number is even, the husband will outlive the wife <note>literally: "the husband will lay the wife to rest"</note>; if it is odd, the wife will bury the husband.

### *Whether in a one-eyed man his right or left eye will fail?*

Calculate the number of his name by dividing by 9, and add one to the result. For if, after the division is made, an even number remains, it will be the right eye; if odd, the left.

For the upper part of the sphere will denote victory, whereas the lower part denotes the contrary.

## Rule II.

*The aforementioned <term>places</term> <note>In the "Method of Loci," these are mental "rooms" or "stations" where information is stored.</note> will also very easily retain a series of two numbers through a <term>concept</term> <note>A "conceptus" here is a vivid mental image used to anchor information in the mind.</note>, if a double action is performed in any place—namely, from its lower part to its upper part—in this manner: Imagine that in the first place, a man or a girl is positioned, waiting for apples, nuts, or some other fruit to fall from a tree. In the second place, however, let a mental image be formed so that some people are seen ringing bells hanging at the top of a very high tower. In the third, a wolf or a fox greedily watching men hanging on a gallows. You will think in that manner, as shown in the figure immediately following (1).*

## CHAPTER II.

->On addition.<-

### Rule I.

**Let** the numbers to be added, therefore, be 164 and 335. <note>The author is demonstrating how to add 164 and 335 to get 499 using visual symbols instead of digits.</note> Let the imagination conceive of a man covered with a <term>square cap</term> <note>original: "pileo quadrato"; this represents the number 5</note>, who, greedily desiring the fruit of a tree, has violently thrown his <term>horn</term> <note>original: "cornu"; this represents the number 4</note> against the fruit, and by the force of that blow broke it into small pieces, the broken parts of which tear his cap. In the second place, let it be imagined that a <term>snail</term> <note>original: "limacem"; represents the number 6</note> with its horns has wounded a man ringing a bell; seeing this, the bell, knocking a <term>tripod</term> <note>original: "tripodem"; represents the number 3</note> down upon him, killed the snail. In the third place, let it be impressed upon the intellect that a wolf tries with a <term>spear</term> <note>original: "hasta"; represents the number 1</note> and by other means to cut the halter of a hanged man; while he is about to do this, a tripod <note>The text here refers to the tripod or <term>gallows</term> (patibulum) representing the number 3</note> falls, frightening him away and putting him to flight.

### Rule II.

*The aforesaid figures are added by the conversion of two figures into a third.* For the cap and the horn of the first order <note>The units column: 5 + 4</note> are transformed into a <term>serpent</term> <note>original: "serpentem"; representing the number 9</note>; the snail and the tripod <note>The tens column: 6 + 3</note> into a <term>dog's tail</term> <note>original: "caudam canis"; also representing the number 9</note>, with which the serpent will do battle because of the liveliness of the action. Similarly, under the third series of places, the third metamorphosis—or transformation of the spear and the gallows <note>The hundreds column: 1 + 3</note>—into a <term>square book</term> <note>original: "librum quadratum"; representing the number 4</note> will be expressed, as seen below.

*IF there should be three people, of whom one has gold, another silver, and the third lead, it will be very easy to divine, by the following rule, which of them has the gold, which the silver, and finally which the lead.* Give, therefore, the name of "one" to the first of them, "two" to the second, and "three" to the third. Then, command that whoever holds the gold doubles his assigned number; let him who has the silver multiply his by 9; and let him who possesses the lead multiply his by ten. Next, the resulting product must be investigated, and it should be observed how far, or by how many units, it differs from 60. Afterwards, it must be noted how many times 8 is contained within that number; for however many times [it is contained] will infallibly demonstrate who has the gold. For if it contains 8 once, the first person holds it; if twice, the second; if three times, the third holds the gold. It must likewise be observed what remains after the division by 8; because from this, the knowledge of the silver’s possessor arises: for if one remains, the first has it; if two, the second; if three, the third. Once these are known, the possessor of the lead is very easily identified.

---

->CHAPTER II.<-

<margin>Large initial S</margin>
*IF a ring is held secretly on a certain finger and you wish to know on which finger it rests?* First, the number one is to be given to the thumb for its value; let two be given to the index, three to the middle, four to the ring finger <note>original: *medico*, literally "the doctor's finger," a common historical name for the ring finger</note>, and five to the little finger <note>original: *auriculari*, the "ear-finger," so named because its size is suited for cleaning the ear</note>. Afterward, command him to double the number of the finger on which the ring is, and to that doubled number, let the numbers of all the other fingers be added. Then, subtract 15 from the resulting total, and the remainder will show the finger upon which the ring is placed.

---

->CHAPTER III.<-

<margin>Large initial C</margin>
*It is also known, through the marvelous aid of this art, in which hand two coins—one of an even value, the other odd—are separately hidden.* For if a coin of three denarii and another of two are handed to someone to be hidden in their hands, the coin hiding in the right hand must always be tripled; but the one enclosed in the left hand must be doubled. Therefore, let the tripled number be added to the doubled one, and if the total number is even, then the coin of even value is in the left hand; if, however, it is odd, it will be found in the right hand.

->THE END.<-

## A MOST LVCID
# DESCRIPTION OF THE
### PREFIGURED TEMPLE.

**OF** the structure and site of this temple, poets would sing wonders—those whose intentions are usually busily engaged around fables and fictions. Indeed, they would pursue this subject much more eagerly since Music derives its name from their own Goddesses, namely the Muses, as is held in its etymology <note>The word "Music" comes from the Greek *Mousike*, meaning "art of the Muses."</note>. I therefore ask pardon from them if I allow myself to be led by the stimulus and invention of "poetic fury" <note>original: *poëtici furoris*; this refers to the Renaissance idea that poets and artists are inspired by a divine frenzy</note>, though not by their poetic meter, in the description of this temple. Let us therefore imagine this **Musical Temple** built upon the summit of **Mount Parnassus**, the seat of the Muses, decorated on every side with groves and fields flourishing with eternal greenness, and surrounded by crystalline springs flowing sweetly here and there. By the murmur of these waters—which often induces a peaceful sleep in those passing by—the little birds frequenting those parts and inhabiting the woods seem diligently to provide a "base" or foundation with their sharper songs (so that they might pour forth diverse <term>consonances</term> <note>Consonances are intervals or chords that sound stable and pleasant to the ear.</note> of sounds more symphonically). By this melody, the **Nymphs** themselves around the temple, the **Satyrs** led by **Sylvanus** <note>The Roman god of the woods.</note> through its groves, and the **Shepherds** (with **Pan** as their leader) across the fields are moved to lead their dances. Among these delights, therefore, that divine gift of **Apollo** is established, preserved, and indeed worshipped with the adoration of all souls. All its constituent parts, dedicated to peace and concord, are so bound to one another by the mysteries of <term>harmony</term> and <term>symphony</term> (which include the concordances of the heavens and the elements), that it would be necessary for the whole universe to perish and be reduced to nothing by the strifes of discord before its consonances either fail or are corrupted.

The President or GODDESS of this temple, therefore, is *Concordia* <note>original: "Concordia"; meaning Harmony or Agreement</note>, the ineffable and great offspring of the Being of Beings. By the adoration of her, small things grow; and through contempt of her, great things fall apart. <note>This is a reference to a famous line by the Roman historian Sallust: "Concordia parvae res crescunt, discordia maximae dilabuntur."</note> Her guardian or priest is *Thalia*, the sweetest of the nine Muses; by her teachings, the hidden mysteries of harmony are explained to travelers and to those who humbly seek her Oracles.

<margin>/</margin> Therefore, the man of science will observe every part of this structure with eager eyes, nor will he despise its smallest portion. This is because in every part, as much as in the whole, there moves that harmonic soul of Apollo and that spirit of Music. This spirit is accustomed to breathe through all the nerves of this structure like the West Wind <note>original: "Zephyri"</note>, sweetly soothing and gladdening the souls of living creatures. It carries away human desires and restrains the madness of malignant demons with its sweetness, imbuing them as if with a certain humanity.

<margin>/</margin> I say you should greedily gaze upon the spiral revolution of the tower of the greater temple, <margin>/</margin> which denotes the movement of the air after it is struck by a sound or voice. The two golden doors, the organs of hearing <note>The ears</note>, signify that without them, a sound produced cannot be perceived; nor is there any entry into this temple except through them.

<margin>/</margin> In the second place, you will observe its three smaller towers, representing the dispositions of the <term>musical notes</term> <note>Specifically the "soft b" ($b$ rotundum), "square natural" ($\natural$ quadratum), and natural notes.</note>. <margin>/</margin> Along with the observation of these, three parallelograms are to be keenly inspected (each built beneath its respective tower and naturally related to it), which demonstrate the various natures, names, and places of the aforementioned notes within the <term>system</term> <note>The "system" refers to the musical scale or gamut.</note>. Furthermore, the pipes or organs expressed at the summit of these parallelograms denote the differences of voices and sounds for each parallelogram.

Nor should the division of the column of this temple be despised, since it delineates the true proportions of the <term>monochord</term> <note>A one-stringed scientific instrument used to measure musical intervals.</note> and the various species of consonances. The clock <note>original: "horologium"</note> must also be carefully weighed, lest time slip away unexpectedly, or proceed with too slow a foot (that is, with no observed proportion or measure). This clock, therefore, is like a guardian of the regular time of the notes, and a most ample mirror of their simple value.

Why should one not also inspect the triangle of commensurable quantity? It examines the diversity of the proportion of times, both in diminution and augmentation, and clearly demonstrates the perfection and imperfection of the notes. <note>In Renaissance music, "perfection" and "imperfection" referred to triple versus duple meter.</note> The symphonic triangle of the system of intervals must also be inspected with no small care, as if it were the final mystery of all the rest; for through it, and from it, all musical consonances are drawn, without which no symphony is made. Over this triangle is depicted the history... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "ria," which completes the word "historia" (history) on the following page.</note>

...history, by which the reasoning behind the discovery of these harmonies is explained—namely, the observation of Pythagoras. By chance, he happened to be passing by a blacksmith’s shop and perceived a harmony of sounds coming from the strikes of four hammers. He ordered those hammers to be weighed, and from the differences in their weights, he discovered the three musical proportions or consonances: the <term>Fourth</term> <note>original: Diatessaron; the interval between the first and fourth notes of a scale</note>, the <term>Fifth</term> <note>original: Diapente; the interval between the first and fifth notes</note>, and the <term>Octave</term> <note>original: Diapason; the interval where the frequency of one note is double the other</note>. We have explained these more clearly through the letters of the three windows of the temple and the connections between those letters; these contribute just as much to the composition of symphonic harmony as that "symphonic triangle" <note>likely referring to a specific diagram used by the author to show harmonic ratios</note>. If you, eager Reader, inspect these parts of this temple wisely, you will share in all its mysteries and become a highly skilled master in this excellent science.

# BOOK ONE,
## On the Subject of Music.

---

### CHAPTER I.

->On the Definition, Etymology, and Inventors of Music.<-

<margin>In Music, first to be considered are its</margin>

<margin>Definition, which is taken</margin>
> **Generally defined**, it is a divine science by which all worldly things are joined together by an unbreakable bond, and in which, in every single thing, like is related to like in equal proportion. This definition applies to worldly, human, and instrumental music. <note>This refers to the "Three Musics" of Boethius: *musica mundana* (the harmony of the universe), *musica humana* (the harmony of the human body and soul), and *musica instrumentalis* (audible music).</note>
> **Specifically defined**, it is the science of singing well, the skill of playing stringed instruments, and the art of composing songs well and fittingly in low and high pitches; and it is the subject of this Music that we shall treat within this temple. <note>The author uses "temple" as a metaphor for the structural arrangement of his book.</note>

<margin>Etymology, for its name is derived either</margin>
> From *Moys*, which is "water" in Latin <note>original: "Moys". This refers to an old belief, cited by writers like Jerome, that the word comes from an Egyptian root for water</note>, as if it were a science discovered near water, because without the benefit of moisture no song or delight of the voice can exist.
> From the *Muses* according to the myths; and the Muses are named from *muso*, that is, "I seek," because, as the ancients hold, the power of poems and the melody of the voice were sought after. Socrates also confirms this in Plato’s *Alcibiades*, witnessing that the Muses were the first guardians of the musical art, from whom Music took its name. And it is for this reason that we have represented *Thalia* as the guardian of this temple, who far excels the other eight of her order in joyfulness.

<margin>Inventors. For according to</margin>
> **Moses**, *Tubal* of the lineage of Cain before the Great Flood was the inventor of this art. <note>Tubal-Cain is mentioned in Genesis 4:21 as the father of all who play the harp and flute.</note>
> **The Greeks**, *Pythagoras* discovered the beginnings of this art from the sounds of hammers and the striking of stretched strings. He labored over this science for a long time, yet could find nothing certain about it; while tossing in this uncertainty and endlessly revolving many ideas in his mind, he finally came to a certain blacksmith’s shop. There he saw men striking one anvil with five small hammers, and he perceived that they created a certain harmony with their strokes. Therefore, he ordered the hammers to be weighed. Having discarded one, which was dissonant with the others, he weighed the remaining hammers: the first weighed 12, the second 9, the third 8, and the fourth 6. From these numerical weights, the harmonies are born which constitute the whole art of Music—namely, the <term>Diapason</term> <note>The Octave (ratio 12:6 or 2:1)</note>, the <term>Diapente</term> <note>The Perfect Fifth (ratio 12:8 or 9:6, both 3:2)</note>, and the <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>The Perfect Fourth (ratio 12:9 or 8:6, both 4:3)</note>, as we have discussed more extensively in our *Musical Arithmetic*.

<summary>This page introduces the study of music by defining it as both a cosmic harmony and a practical art, tracing its name to the Muses or water, and attributing its invention to the biblical Tubal and the Greek philosopher Pythagoras.</summary>

->**ON THE SUBJECT OF MUSIC.**<-

# ON THE SUBJECT OF MUSIC.

> After *Pythagoras*, *Boethius* <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), whose "De institutione musica" was the standard music theory textbook for a millennium.</note> flourished and left behind wonders in this art. Then came *Guido the Monk* <note>Guido of Arezzo (c. 991–1033), credited with inventing the staff and solfège (do-re-mi).</note>, who was the inventor of the system. He was succeeded by *Franco* <note>Franco of Cologne (mid-13th century), a pioneer of "mensural" music, where the shape of a note indicates its rhythm.</note>, who established the alteration, perfection, and imperfection of figures in measurable song.

However, regarding the origin of Music and the invention of Musical instruments, a great controversy arises among writers. For *Pythagoras* himself asserts that this discipline was not invented by men, but by the craftsman of the world himself; who caused the celestial spheres to move with a certain harmony in their intervals and motions, from which he affirms that human Music flows. The Poets make *Apollo* the leader and moderator of this science; and certainly not without reason, since among them the Sun is the leader and prince of the spheres and the moderator of the other lights, the mind or soul of the world, and the heart of heaven itself. *Heraclides of Pontus* makes *Jupiter* the inventor of songs. *Amphion*, the son of *Jupiter* and *Antiope*, invented the lyre, and *Terpander* was the first to publish the rules of the lyre. *Apollo* invented the cithara <note>A professional version of the lyre, often associated with high art and order.</note> and the flute <note>original: "tibiam," literally an aulos or pipe.</note> according to *Macrobius*. *Pythagoras* was the first to discover Music, a view which we shall follow more closely. But according to *Pliny*, *Amphion* and *Cethione* first revealed it. According to some, *Lamisus Heroneus*, son of *Chabrinus* (who was numbered among the seven wise men of Greece in place of *Periander*), wrote the first book on Music. *Tyrrhenus* invented trumpets, the *Phrygians* invented flutes, the *Latins* the cithara, *Mercury* the lyre, and *Phanius* the pan-pipes.

---

## C H A P T E R  II.

### *On the different types of Music.*

Music is either:

*   **Worldly** <note>original: "Mundana," referring to the cosmic harmony of the universe.</note>; which pertains to:
    *   The etheric spheres.
    *   The elemental regions.
*   **Instrumental**, which is:
    *   **Harmonic**, consisting of:
        *   Human voice.
        *   Melody.
        *   Symphony.
    *   **Rhythmic**, which is created by:
        *   The number of syllables; in this way, the Lyric poet composes songs.
        *   Arithmetic proportion, distinguishing the intervals of a temple.
    *   **Metric**, which is created by:
        *   The measurement of syllables, which Poets use.
        *   The metric arrangement of feet, which dancers use.
        *   The measurement of intervals and small notes.

**T**hat worldly music is produced from the essential effect of the Planets and the elements; for their excellent order and proportional arrangement undoubtedly produces the greatest symphony in those parts, if we grant any faith to the opinions of *Plato* and *Cardanus* <note>Gerolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian polymath who wrote extensively on music and mathematics.</note>. They say that the finest harmony is generated from the gathering and rotation of the spheres, which cannot be perceived by our ears because of the great distance. Similarly, the elements themselves are bound by such a link that their enmity is made peaceful through the intervention of "friends" <note>An alchemical and philosophical concept where opposing elements (like fire and water) are reconciled by a shared quality.</note>, and chaos—once a formless mass—is now essentially and distinctly shaped by a sympathetic arrangement.

<vocab>Pythagoras: Ancient Greek philosopher who discovered the mathematical ratios of musical intervals. Boethius: Late Roman philosopher who classified music into "mundana," "humana," and "instrumentalis." Musica Mundana: The "Music of the Spheres," an unheard cosmic harmony. Cardanus: A Renaissance scholar interested in the intersection of mathematics and nature.</vocab>

<keywords>History of Music, Pythagoras, Music of the Spheres, Musica Mundana, Musical Instruments, Boethius, Guido of Arezzo, Harmony of the Elements</keywords>

TREATISE II. PART II. BOOK I.

In a very similar way, the soul is connected to the body of the **Microcosm** <term>The human being viewed as a miniature reflection of the vast universe or "macrocosm."</term>; from this connection, the wonderful actions of life proceed, along with a consensus of the humors <note>The four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) believed to govern health and temperament</note> both for providing life and for physical growth. For one function helps the other in a sweet and kindly manner. Indeed, that species of music called **instrumental** is concerned with discerning and understanding songs. It includes **Harmonic Music**, which is responsible for distinguishing sounds into high and low. This consists of numbers and figures. It is either *local*, according to the proportion of sounds and voices in continuous quantity, or *temporal*, according to the proportion of long and short figures in discrete quantity. From these facts, it is clear that *harmonic music* is the discernment of modulation, the science of singing truly, an easy path to perfection, and the knowledge and consonance of several dissimilar but proportional voices—or, the science of number related to sounds. From this, it is established that **Melody** and **Symphony** are contained under Harmony; of these, **Melody** is the harmony of sounds, bent into a certain system and mode according to the singer's emotion; **Symphony**, however, is the concordant harmony of distinct sounds and melodies. Universal harmony is produced into action either by the striking of a voice (called a **natural instrument**) or by the vibration of strings (as in the lute), or by the collision of air through the openings of a hollow body (such as a flute). These latter two types are **artificial instruments**. Under instrumental music, **Rhythmic** and **Metrical** music are also included. *Rhythmic* music is that part required for the scanning of poems created for songs—determining whether the words used in singing and reading cohere well or poorly. *Metrical* music, however, shows the measures of different meters with probable reason, as is seen in Heroic, Iambic, and Elegiac meter and the like.

---

### CHAPTER III.

->*On the operation of Music in the soul and body.*<-

**T**he operation of Music is certainly to be admired, and its power over the soul and body is wonderful; hence, according to the opinions of several philosophers, a knowledge of it is necessarily required for the arrangement of human life and character. For:

- It penetrates the inner reaches of the mind and strikes the soul most vehemently.
- It brings a certain graceful form, through which anyone who is rightly educated in Music is made graceful and beautiful.

<margin>Plato in the third book of the *Republic*.</margin>
For this reason, he concludes that Music:
- Should be taught to boys, so that they may be rendered gentler and more harmonious, and more prompt in acting and speaking.
- Should be employed in the state to produce more civilized and gentle character; but one must abstain from voluptuous music.

<margin>The harmony of Music, according to Marsilio <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), a famous Renaissance philosopher who wrote on the healing power of music.</note>, through:</margin>
- The movement of the subtle air, it penetrates vehemently.
- The body moves the "aerial nature" <note>The 'spiritus' or vital spirit, thought to be a thin vapor connecting the soul to the physical body.</note> which has been set in motion.
- The purified air excites the spirits, and the "aerial knot" of the soul and body.
- The emotion affects the senses.
- It conveys meaning to the mind.
- It sweetly soothes contemplation.
- With a certain wonderful pleasure, it bathes both the spiritual and material nature in a conforming quality, and at once seizes and claims the whole man for itself.

# CHAPTER IV.

## Concerning the Musician.

<margin>Boethius in <unclear>Bo</unclear>ok One, <unclear>c</unclear>hapter the last:</margin>
HE WHO only sings is not a Musician. For according <unclear>to...</unclear> a Musician is one who, with weighted reason, does not <unclear>labor</unclear> in <unclear>menial</unclear> service, but by the command of speculation <note>In this context, "speculation" refers to deep theoretical contemplation or scientific study.</note>, <unclear>possesses</unclear> the science of singing <unclear>...</unclear> as we have seen in the work of <unclear>...</unclear> and of wars. <margin>A Musician is either</margin>
<margin>Perfect, who does not merely compose parts of music, but can provide the true reasoning for them. Therefore, for his perfection, there are required:</margin>
- *Natural Philosophy*, so that he may best judge harmonic music and provide a perfect explanation of its subject.
- *Arithmetic*, so that he may well perceive the rhythmic nature of music.
- *Geometry*, so that he may explain the metrical essence of music and be able to determine the proportion of intervals.
- *Astronomy*, so that he may not be ignorant of the music of the spheres <note>original: "mundanam Musicam," the ancient concept that the movement of celestial bodies creates a form of divine harmony.</note>.
- *Metaphysics*, so that he may be able to judge human music <note>The internal harmony between the human soul and body.</note>.

## CHAPTER V.
### On the matter or subject of Music, and on the sense of hearing.

**T**he matter or subject of Music is *sound* <note>original: *sonus*</note>, which is the unbroken striking <note>original: *percussio*</note> of the air and its forceful vibration through low and high pitches. By its spiral and rolling motion in the air, tending upward in a diagonal ascent here and there (according to the disposition of the medium), it finally penetrates the ears through the forced revolution of that same medium and invades the interior senses. And it is for this reason that we have fashioned the twin doors of the temple in the likeness of the pair of ears at the summit of the system. For without the sense of hearing, the entrance to the *Temple of Concord* <note>A recurring allegorical structure in Fludd's work where the human anatomy is mapped onto classical architecture.</note> does not lie open. Similarly, we have represented the spiral revolution of the air after the emission of sound above both doors, so that the unbroken motion of the air can be better grasped by the mind; all of which we have described in this place.

In musical sound, two things are usually considered:
{
  **Difference**, which is either {
    **General**, which is considered either by {

        **Non-unisons**, of which one is lower and the other higher by a certain amount, and they are either {
          **Consonants**, which when joined produce mixed and pleasant sounds.

        }
      }
      **Quantity**, namely {
        **By Place**, from which there is also a twofold division {

          **High**, contained under the order of high and super-high <note>Latin: *superacutarum*; referring to the highest register in the hexachord system</note> keys.

        **By Time**.
      }
    }

        }

  }
  **Motion** in Music occurs either by {

# BOOK TWO

->On the Musical System.<-

### PREFACE TO BOOK II.

**W**e call that square section of the Temple of Music—which we have illustrated below as being composed of three parallelograms—the "musical system." This system is essentially the foundation formed by lines and clefs <note>original: *clavibus*, literally "keys"</note>, containing the proportions of sounds and the melody of song. Without understanding this square surface and its various steps, it is impossible to enter the gateway of this temple. For without understanding the governing and governed notes <note>This likely refers to the relationship between the primary notes of a scale and those that are dependent or accidental</note>, along with the syllables and clefs—both primary and secondary (the distinctions of which define the musical system)—no one can ever reach mastery in this science. 

The first parallelogram of this square, located on the left, denotes the clefs and voices of the song or the "soft B" system <note>original: *b. mollis*, referring to the hexachord containing B-flat</note>. Thus, it is depicted beneath a **round tower**, where soft sounds or deep-tolling bells are imagined to hang and ring, varying according to their syllables and instruments. 

The second or middle parallelogram distinguishes the **natural notes**. This is clearly illustrated beneath a tower shaped like a flame—that is, ascending sharply—for fire is often described by philosophers as having a naturally sharp or pointed nature. Within this tower, one might imagine bells or voices that sound between the low and high registers. We have depicted the top of this tower as more pointed, as if standing out between the two variations of the "round B" <term>B-flat</term> and the "square B" <term>B-natural</term>. 

We have placed the third parallelogram beneath a **square tower**, because this "hard" system <note>original: *systemate duro*, the hexachord containing B-natural</note> produces "square" sounds. Therefore, the bells found in this tower are those that ring with a hard and "square" quality. This section of the Temple of Music is illustrated here on its own, and we shall devote the entirety of this second book to its explanation.

### CHAPTER XI.

->*Concerning the materials of fortifications, their foundation and height, and their slope.*<-

**T**he material of fortifications <term>munimentorum</term> <note>defensive structures or works</note> is generally of four types: namely Earth, wood, bricks, and stones. In regular fortifications, earth is traditionally the internal material, sometimes mixed with timbers arranged transversely; however, these earth <term>Ramparts</term> <note>a defensive wall or bank of earth; original: "Ramparda"</note> should be faced <note>cladded or revetted</note> either with bricks (such as those of the city of **Arras**), or with small squares of grassy turf cut from meadows and mixed with <term>fascines</term> <note>bundles of sticks or brushwood used to reinforce earthworks; original: "fasciculis"</note> (like those of the town of **Calais in Picardy**), or with squared stones (as at **Peschiera in Lombardy**). As for what pertains to the foundation of the defense, it must first be observed whether the location is watery and marshy; in such a place, the foundation should be laid...

<summary>This page concludes the geometric layout of a six-bastion fortification and begins Chapter 11, which discusses the practical materials (earth, wood, brick, stone) used in building ramparts.</summary>

### ON FORTIFICATIONS AND BULWARKS

on top of piles with transverse timbers, which should also be long. The first layer will therefore consist of thick or small timbers, the length of which will be 12 or 15 feet. Over these, a layer of earth should be placed; afterwards, another layer of wood and fascines <note>original: "fasciculis"—bundles of brushwood used in civil engineering and military fortifications</note> is positioned on top of that. By following this order—placing layer upon layer until the required height is reached—the body of the rampart <note>original: "Rampardae"</note> will be completed. It will then not be difficult to face this with bricks, square-cut sods of turf, or stones. 

However, in the foundation of bastions <note>original: "Bastionum"</note> for a town or city on dry ground, the first layer or stratum—especially toward its front—should be made of stones two or three feet high. Once this is done, the engineer <note>original: "Ingeniator"</note> should have a good quantity of thick and small wood with fascines ready, arranged in such a way that their ends face the front of the bastion. Then, other timbers are placed transversely over the first layer of wood. Finally, another layer of well-prepared earth is placed over these, maintaining this order until the required elevation of the mound is achieved. In conclusion, if the work is necessary or if time permits, it will be essential to face these bulwarks with the materials described above.

In many places, and notably in the Italian city of *Genoa*, I have seen the construction of bastions and curtain walls <note>original: "Courtinarum"—the straight defensive walls between two bastions</note>. There, before they fill them with earth or raise them, they build many partitions out of bricks joined together with gypsum <note>original: "gypso"—plaster or mortar</note> in the form of small walls. These are arranged so that the ends of these partitions face the front of the points and the curtain wall, as shown below.

---

![Diagram showing the internal masonry partitions of a fortification, designed to hold the earth in place and provide structural integrity against artillery.]

---

Certainly, this invention by engineers is excellent where wood is not used. Were this not done, the curtain walls and bastions would be very quickly destroyed by the constant hits of siege engines <note>original: "tormentorum"—cannons or artillery</note> because the earth would easily scatter and shift.

Regarding the height of the bulwark <note>original: "Bulvardae"</note>, it is necessary that all its parts be of moderate height, depending on the terrain. If they are too deep <note>meaning high/steep from the base</note>—as we see in all ancient town walls—they bring great disadvantage to the besieged. For if the bastions are captured by the attackers, their height leaves the defenders no place to refortify themselves, as the bastions will then excessively dominate the besieged. Conversely, if the ramparts are too low, they can also cause irreparable damage to the besieged, because the attackers are accustomed to building a mound which they call a *cavalier* <note>original: "Cavalieram"—a high platform built to overlook and fire down upon enemy positions</note>, which can hold dominance and command over the ramparts. Similarly, if the parapets <note>original: "Parapettae"</note> are broken too much, the bulwark will be left open and exposed. 

A slope <note>original: "inclinatio"</note> must be observed on the external surface of the fortifications so that it may longer resist the battering of cannons. This slope should be greater or lesser depending on the material or substance from which it is built. For when positioning large square stones, a greater inclination is required than where the structure is made of bricks, or earth with wood.

The Citadel of **Antwerp** is also composed of five bastions, as well as <term>curtains</term><note>The straight part of a wall between two bastions.</note> and <term>cavaliers</term><note>Raised platforms within a fortification that allow cannons to fire over the main wall.</note>. I also saw a fortification of this kind in **Tuscany** <note>original Latin: "Hetruria"</note>, situated upon an elevated mountain between **Siena and Pisa**, which they called the *Apogeum* <note>Meaning 'high point' or 'summit'.</note>; it was, moreover, faced with stone. I also observed another fortification of this kind surrounded by the Rhine river, which is located in that place for the defense of the town called **Rheinberg**; it also holds dominion over that river, such that nothing can be transported up or down stream without its permission. The material of its construction was the same as that of **St. Andrew** <note>Referring to the 'Fort Sint-Andries' in the Netherlands.</note>.

### CHAPTER XVI.
#### *Regarding examples of simple irregular <term>bulwarks</term> <note>Latin: propugnaculum; a general term for a defensive fortification or rampart</note>.*

Chavarino or Ciavarino <note>Modern-day Győr, Hungary</note> is a very strong Hungarian town, which was seized from the Christians by the Turks and recaptured in the year 1603 under the leadership of Count **Schwartzenberg**. It is fortified by seven <term>bulwarks</term> <note>Latin: bulvardis; large defensive bastions, often made of earth and masonry</note> which are excellently positioned. Furthermore, it is rendered even stronger on all sides by the meeting of two great rivers, namely the *Raab* and the *Danube*. Therefore, following the layout of the terrain (especially because it is naturally fortified by water), it was given an irregular shape at its founding, the main body of which we have illustrated here.

There is also a certain <term>bulwark</term> in Holland called *Bommena*, protected on all sides by water, which is equipped with four <term>bastions</term> <note>Latin: bastionibus; projecting structures that allow defenders to fire along the face of the walls</note> according to its specific location. This is accurately depicted here at *Number 1*.

Crimpen <note>Krimpen aan de Lek</note> is another heavily fortified town, which was besieged and attacked by the Prince of Orange in the year 1576. We have described it in this place according to its position, along with its five <term>bastions</term> and its natural defenses, at *Number 2*.

### CHAPTER XVII.

### *Concerning examples of composite fortifications.*

We call those fortifications "composite" which contain other internal defenses within themselves, so that if the outer works should be seized by the enemy, a strong resistance can still be made from the inner ones. For example:

Near *Tunis*, the royal seat of Libya <note>The author uses 'Libya' here in the classical sense to refer to North Africa.</note>, there is a certain double fortification situated between the sea and a great lagoon called the *Goletta* <note>original: *Guleta*</note>. It was once besieged by Philip, King of Spain <note>This refers to the 1573-1574 siege of Tunis involving Philip II.</note>. Its inner fortification <term>propugnaculum: a bulwark or defensive structure</term> consists of four bastions <term>bastion: a projecting part of a fortification built at an angle to allow defensive fire in several directions</term>; the outer one, however, consists of six, with a blunt ravelin <term>ravelin: a triangular fortification located in front of the inner works</term>. Both are protected by moats filled with water from the sea and the lagoon. Its description follows.

The Castle of *Brescia* in Lombardy, situated on the peak of a rocky cliff, is defended by bastions and curtains <note>original: *courtinis*; the straight walls connecting two bastions</note> toward the east, south, and west; because from those directions it slopes down squarely toward the city, making it accessible. Nevertheless, this accessibility is filled with sharp stones, both to hinder the ascent of besiegers and so that cannonballs falling among these stones might bring greater ruin upon them <note>The stones would likely splinter upon impact, creating lethal shrapnel</note>. Every bastion has its own <term>cavalier</term> <note>original: *Cavaliera*; a raised interior platform that allows artillery to fire over the main defensive walls</note>, and within the curtain walls there are other defenses which serve as general cavaliers; for they are filled with earth up to the top, and they also possess certain old, round bastions. Furthermore, within these walls others are raised to a higher position, encircling the center of the citadel.

Toward the northern side, however, the cliff is very steep and deep, looking out over a vast valley, and that part is also fortified by a large and high curtain wall with two towers and round bastions constructed in the ancient style. The moats on the other sides are dry. There is only one entrance into this bulwark, and this is accessed by bridges; for every wall has its own bridge and gate bearing the insignia of Saint Mark <note>original: *Sancti Marci*; referring to the Lion of Saint Mark, the heraldic symbol of the Republic of Venice, which ruled Brescia at the time of this writing</note>; these are strongly guarded. All the cavaliers and bastions are excellently equipped with their own artillery <note>original: *tormentis*</note>. It is described in this manner.

### TREATISE II. PART VI. BOOK I.

I shall, however, describe the following design of a **composite <term>bastion</term>** <note>A bastion is a projecting part of a fortification built at an angle to the line of a wall, allowing defensive fire in several directions.</note>, the excellent invention of a certain German, along with its various parts; it will appear to be the strongest of all fortifications I have ever seen. 

And although that fortress and seat of **Livorno** <note>original: "Ligornæ"</note>, a maritime town of **Tuscany** <note>original: "Hetruriæ"</note>, is considered by everyone to be an impregnable bastion, we nonetheless judge that it should by no means be compared to this one. For many fortifications are included here within a larger whole, which correspond to the greater structure in all respects. Furthermore, all parts of the fortifications—both external and internal—are arranged in relation to one another in such a way that each internal bastion is successively positioned above the external one by virtue of its height and location. Consequently, if the exterior is captured, it can be very easily recovered by those in the interior positions. 

But it must be noted here that since this structure consists of six bastions, it is necessary for it to be drawn upon a flat surface or a level field.

## C H A P T E R XVIII.

### *On the reinforcement of the weak parts of a city.*

**W**e call those parts of a defense <term>weak</term> <note>original: "debiles"</note> which are commanded <note>meaning they are overlooked or threatened by higher ground</note> by some external point due to its height or elevation. These areas are nevertheless strengthened by skill—specifically by very deep moats, or by <term>ravelins</term> <note>triangular outworks located outside the main ditch</note> (also known as spurs), <term>bastions</term>, or <term>cavaliers</term> <note>elevated platforms within a fortification that allow cannons to fire over the main wall</note>, all perfectly proportioned through the expertise of the engineer. # BOOK TWO

## Concerning the siege of fortified places.

---

### CHAPTER I.

#### *Concerning the things necessary for the siege of a fortified place.*

Just as in the art of fortification, so also in the siege of a fortified place, there is primarily a requirement for the keen intellect of Engineers <term>Ingeniatorum; military architects and strategists</term> to foresee future dangers. By this skill, the power of the enemy—both within the fortification and outside the site of the besieged place—may be observed. One must consider whether the site is strong by nature or by art <note>original: "naturaliter vel arte"; referring to whether the defense relies on natural terrain or man-made walls</note>, and in which place it is most neglected by nature or art; whether it is surrounded by water or not; whether any error is found in the structure of the bulwark; and where its greatest weakness lies. Is it threatened from any high ground from the outside? Is its material stone, earth, or brick? Is the ditch filled with water or is it dry? In which part must the besiegers protect themselves with ditches and ramparts? Which places are most safe from danger? In which part is it best to establish a battery <term>batteria; the placement of heavy artillery</term>? How many engines of war <term>tormenta; general term for cannons and siege engines</term> are needed, and of what kind? In what span of time can a breach and weakening be achieved by the engines, and how large a hole is required?

Then, one must consider by what methods an invasion might be carried out—and indeed with less danger—once the breach or weakening has been made. How many soldiers are required in the ramparts to sustain and impede the enemy's excursions? Furthermore, scouts should be stationed in every part to perceive the enemy's intentions. If there is any river, pond, or lake near the fortification suitable for safely receiving troops (for this will be a great advantage to the besiegers, provided it is out of the reach of the artillery), it should be noted. The foot soldiers <note>original: "pedeftres"</note> should be organized into battle lines without the rest of the infantry and disposed at the front; the stronger regiments should be planted in that part where the invasions of the besiegers are most expected. The cavalry should be placed in the second rank with other great forces, so that they may appear more ready if the occasion requires; and each of them should understand his duty. Let the ramparts and ditches be completed with as much speed and force as possible, so that the spirits of the enemy may be more cast down and terrified. Other matters of this kind should also be investigated with the highest industry and observed with great diligence.

Furthermore, it is necessary that everything required for a siege be carefully prepared. These things include money—which has always been held to be the nerves of war <note>original: "belli nervis"; a classical idiom suggesting that money provides the essential strength and movement for a campaign</note>—about 2,000 pickaxes, 500 or 600 axes, and as many sickles or hooks for making fascines <term>fafces; bundles of brushwood used to fill ditches or reinforce walls</term> and gabions <term>gabiones; large wicker baskets filled with earth for protection</term>. Moreover, many pliers and small hammers are needed, and about 30 planks upon which the artillery may be moved. Let there also be a multitude of Pioneers <term>Pionnerorum; soldiers tasked with digging and engineering</term> by whose work the ditches and ramparts may be more quickly constructed. And where the fortress is defended by the best bastions, there at least 12 Cannons are required, and two or three Culverins <term>Culverini; long-range, slender cannons</term> with the balls and powder requisite for them. And lest food should fail, the greatest care must be taken so that all passages are kept open for its more abundant transportation to the camp.

### Rule I.

*The **siege** <term>obfessio; the act of surrounding and blockading a fortified place</term> of locations is conducted according to their site and according to the opportunity of the season: for in cold weather, access to **fortifications** <term>propugnacula; defensive outworks or bulwarks</term> situated in damp or marshy places becomes easier.* <note>The author refers to how frozen ground or ice allows heavy cannons and troops to cross marshes that would be impassable in summer.</note>

---

### CHAPTER II.

->*Concerning the explanation of certain technical terms.*<-

We call a **Battery** the place from which engines or **Cannons** fire their shot against the **bulwarks** <note>Bulvardas; the projecting parts of a fortification</note> of a defensive work; such a place is protected by **gabions**.
**Gabions** <term>gabiones; large wickerwork cylinders</term> are also like round fences, constructed from very strong stakes and smaller wood, woven in the manner of baskets upon flat ground, whose hollow centers are filled with well-prepared earth.
**Pioneers**, whom the French call *les Pionniers*, is the name given to those men who use mattocks to dig ditches and ramparts and to undermine the walls of fortifications.

---

...be placed; and let the <term>cannons</term><note>heavy artillery pieces used for battering walls</note> and <term>culverins</term><note>long-range, slender cannons known for their accuracy</note> be positioned among the <term>gabions</term><note>cylindrical wicker baskets filled with earth, used to shield gunners</note>, as close to the edge of the fortification's ditch as can reasonably be achieved. This is because the sheer vibration of the artillery shakes the fortress walls as much as the impact of a cannonball, especially if they are fired from even a short distance away. <term>Batteries</term><note>groups of artillery pieces positioned together for a coordinated attack</note> should be established in three locations: specifically, overlooking the two sides of the rampart. A battery on one side of the rampart destroys the <term>revetment</term><note>the stone or brick facing of a wall</note> on the opposite side of the <term>bastion</term><note>a projecting part of a fortification, typically shaped like a diamond, allowing defenders to fire along the face of the walls</note>. However, a battery placed in the middle will always displace the earth and demolish the wall at the bastion's point. This type of battery is also employed to crush and break open <term>casemates</term><note>vaulted rooms within the walls, often used as protected gun positions</note> and to knock out the guns within them. It also destroys the <term>parapets</term><note>low protective walls on top of the ramparts</note> of both the bastions and the <term>curtain walls</term><note>the straight sections of wall connecting two bastions</note>, so that the fortress may be more easily invaded and attacked.

### *Rule I.*

> *Experience has always taught that in every fortification, whether it be made of stone, brick, earth, or wood, breaches and collapses occur more easily at the point or acute angle of a bastion than in any other part, provided that material is removed first from one side, then the other, and finally from the middle of the bastion.*

# BOOK THREE

## On the Ordering of an Army in the Field.
