### C A P. I.

#### On the Military Disposition of Certain Nations.

<margin>The Spaniards possess in their military discipline both</margin>
<margin>Virtues,</margin>
They are faithful to their kings, for they are rarely traitors.
They are perceived to be obedient to their leaders and governors.
They are good infantry <note>original: "pedestres"</note>, and keep their arms polished and bright.
They do not desert their comrades in times of necessity.
They are peaceful among themselves.
They live soberly, and without drunkenness.
They observe good order while marching.
They are well-vigilant and keep good watch, and wherever they go, they fortify their position.
They know what must be done before they depart from their stations.
They maintain themselves excellently during reconnaissance and observation.
They do not rush headlong into unknown places.
They do not approach rashly, nor with great danger.
They well compensate and honor those who have conducted themselves well in war.
They are better in the execution of maneuvers than the Germans, but not as stable against direct invasions.

<margin>Vices, because</margin>
They are proud and boastful.
They scorn and mock other nations.
They are esteemed more for their military practice <note>technical skill or experience</note> than for their natural spirit and valor.
They are very often cruel toward the defeated and devoid of mercy.

<margin>The French also follow in war both</margin>
<margin>Virtues, because</margin>
They are very courageous and excellently disposed toward war.
Their cavalry <note>original: "equestres"</note> are superior to almost all the nations of Europe.
They have many high-spirited and noble leaders who are very expert in the military art.

<margin>Vices, for</margin>
They lack good discipline and industry.
They are very inconstant and changeable.
They are very often traitors to the King, and almost for nothing; which happens because of their inconstancy.
They are cruel, greedy, and desirous of revenge.
Among their infantry, there is the worst discipline and a wicked sense of order.
They cannot tolerate the labors of war.

<margin>The Germans also possess in military discipline</margin>
**Virtues, because**
- They are fairly well armed.
- They observe the ancient formation of infantry.
- They use the harquebus <term>harquebus: an early, heavy portable gun supported on a tripod or a forked rest</term> passably well.

- They preserve their ranks in war exceptionally well, so much so that they would rather allow themselves to be killed than break their formations and files.

- They are very obedient to their leaders.

**Virtues, because**

- Foreign wine is contrary to their nature because of their habit of drinking beer; it affects them with burning fevers and especially the "Calentura" <term>Calentura: a tropical fever or heat exhaustion common in sailors, often involving delirium where the sufferer imagines the sea is a green field</term> in hot regions overseas.

## CHAPTER II.

### *Concerning the different fighting methods of cavalry from various nations.*

**I**n the organization of *French* cavalry (whose formations I name here because of their great skill in this art), two methods are considered. The *first* is ancient and used almost to this day, in which the companies of horsemen are extended and usually arranged for battle in a long formation, much like a hedge. The *other* method is to arrange them in a square formation before they attack the enemy companies. However, those more skilled in war believe the latter of these methods should be followed. *First*, because in the former arrangement, everyone is seen to fight at the same time and they give only a single strike with their lances; once that initial fury is repelled, no other sudden response can be expected. Furthermore, significant danger can simultaneously fall upon both the leaders and the <term>vanguard</term> <note>original: "Antesignanis"; those who fought in front of the standards</note>, as well as the better soldiers; if they fall, the rest are terrified and, as if lifeless, very easily turned to flight. *Second*, because in the square formation, the charge is stronger and made with greater violence; and, if some in the front of the square are knocked to the ground, others are immediately supplied to take their places and fortify the position. For this reason, experience teaches that even if there are three or four equal companies arranged according to the first method arriving one after another, they can be destroyed by a single square formation. From this, it is clear that every battalion, whether of infantry or cavalry, ought to be composed of a suitable thickness.

Different nations, however, clash in different ways, embracing various methods and disciplines in their fighting, one being more excellent than another. And so it is that one method is to be preferred and is better in one type of conflict than in another.

As for the different ways of handling *cavalry lances*, we will deal with them briefly here. The *Hungarians* and *Turks* place and hold the handle of the lance firmly against the front part of the saddle when they must charge the enemy. The *French* guide the lance by the strength of their arms; their custom is far more secure than that of the *Turks*, because the lances are guided by the arms at will. The *cavalry of Lower Germany*—namely, the seventeen provinces <note>This refers to the Habsburg Netherlands, roughly modern-day Netherlands, Belgium, and Luxembourg</note>—use <term>harquebuses</term> <note>An early type of long-barreled firearm</note> instead of lances, with certain supports suitable for holding them lightly and firmly, so that in a single charge they sometimes load the gun with two bullets and fire them at the enemy. Today, the *French* (entirely neglecting lances) mostly follow their order.

Something must also be said about the use of *swords*. For the *French* cavalry, after discharging their firearms, swing their swords backward and with the back of the hand. This discipline is considered better than that of the *Poles*, *Turks*, and *Hungarians*, who, after they have done their business with their pistols, draw their swords and strike with the front of the hand. This execution is not done with as much vigor and agility as that of the *French*, who, while striking, simultaneously turn the horse to flee <note>A tactical retreat or maneuver to reset for another charge</note>; such agility and cunning is of great value in war.

The *Turks and Hungarians* wear their spurs over the soles of their boots or a wooden base, so that if by some chance their horses fall, they can nevertheless be freed from the spurs very easily, merely by moving and shaking their feet, so they can fight more dexterously while standing.

### C H A P T E R III.

->On the army and its parts.<-

**T**here are those who claim that an *Imperial army* cannot be built unless it is composed of many nations experienced in the discipline of war; they assert that a gathering of soldiers consisting of only one or two nations should not be called an imperial army, but rather a meeting of soldiers. Indeed, their opinions do not seem far from reason, because in such an army, warlike men highly experienced in all military matters must be chosen. Among these, some should be found more ready for invasion, more fit for scaling the walls of fortifications, and more ready for conducting a battery <note>The "battery" refers to the concentrated fire of artillery or the assault intended to breach a wall.</note>; others are by nature more suitable for maintaining the unity of the ranks in battle; and others should be found far more agile than the rest in equestrian discipline and the management of horses (in which all the virtue of the ancient Roman and Greek armies consisted). 

<margin>☞</margin> *For sudden invasions and the more dangerous occasions, one should rather choose Spaniards, Italians, and English, as these are perceived to be bold in the Battery; Germans and especially the Swiss are chosen for maintaining the order of the battle line, as they are known to face death rather than break their ranks or violate the form of the line.* 

The French are rather to be 
<margin>☞</margin> taken for the cavalry, because they cultivate and love the art of riding: in which they are no less engaged in our age than the *Parthians* <note>An ancient Iranian people famous for their light cavalry and skilled archers.</note> were in the times of the Romans, who, on account of their equestrian virtue and agility, kept themselves undefeated against the Roman Republic. 

The army, therefore, being forged from the said nations, is composed of many parts, of which the <term>Tuldum<note>A late Latin term for the baggage train or the logistical supplies of an army.</note></term>, or the baggage, is like the tail of the whole army; and indeed, 
<margin>☞</margin> *as the baggage train follows the army immediately*, so it is of the greatest importance within it. Therefore, industrious and most faithful men and a most noble leader are chosen *for the guarding of the baggage train*, 
<margin>☞</margin> who usually precede the *baggage* in a square formation. It is also customary to place one squadron of cavalry next to each of its sides, who not only defend the *baggage* from sudden invasions of the enemy, but also keep the rear of the phalanx safe and guarded from their ambushes. 

<margin>☞</margin> The *Body of the army*, consisting of infantrymen carrying pikes, is what we call its *phalanx and line*: This relates to the whole just as the human body—namely the belly and the thorax—relates to its other parts. For just as the chief virtue, vigor, and strength consist in the human body, so too must the greater hope of victory be placed in this part of the army. This body is fortified by arms, sleeves, or wings, which are usually 
<margin>☞</margin> composed of <term>Harquebusiers<note>Soldiers armed with the harquebus, an early type of long-barreled firearm.</note></term>. 

The body or the line is preceded by *squadrons of <term>pioneers<note>original: "vastatorum"; military laborers or engineers who clear the way, often called "pioneers" in a military context.</note></term>*, whom we have compared to human teeth; for just as teeth prepare food so that its passage to the stomach is not hindered, so also the pioneers prepare the way and remove all impediments by which the army 
<margin>☞</margin> could be disturbed on its journey. *Two squares of light horsemen* preceding the cohorts of pioneers we have likened to the image of a man, and to his reason and intellect, because they are accustomed to foresee future inconveniences. For the said squadrons of cavalry are always ready to defend the front of the line and the cohorts of pioneers, and to repel the injuries of the enemy. 

The <margin>☞</margin> *scouts, observers, or spies* <note>original: "Præcursores, speculatores, seu Catascopi"</note> (who are light cavalry), because it is their duty to observe the habits of the enemy and explore their intentions, we have compared to the eyes of animals, whose task is to direct the mass of the entire body well and to govern it rightly.

<summary>This page describes the ideal composition of an "Imperial Army" as a multi-national force and uses an anatomical metaphor to explain how different military units (scouts, baggage train, infantry) function like parts of a human body.</summary>

### C H A P T E R IV.

->*On the method used by the Italians for the arrangement of an army on the march.*<-

**W**hen the Italians pass through a suspicious place or a hostile region with an army—specifically where a sudden invasion by the enemy is feared—they arrange the parts of the army in the following manner: The first position is held by the <term>scouts</term> <note>original: *præcursores* or *speculatores*; these soldiers rode ahead to gather intelligence</note>; these are followed by two squadrons of <term>light cavalry</term>; one on the right side, the other on the left. The cavalry is followed by companies of <term>pioneers</term> <note>original: *vastatorum*; these were laborers and soldiers who cleared obstacles, leveled roads, or "devastated" enemy fortifications</note> arranged in a parallelogram shape with their leaders. Next come the <term>field pieces</term>, which they call <term>cannons</term>, raised upon wheels and drawn by horses. After these follows the main body of the army, or its <term>phalanx</term> and battle line, arranged in a square formation. The battle line is preceded by the <term>baggage train</term> <note>original: *Tuldum*; the collection of wagons, supplies, and non-combatants following an army</note>, and between the baggage and the battle line, a squadron of soldiers is stationed to guard the <term>baggage train</term>. Two squares of cavalry on either side of the <term>baggage train</term> protect its flanks from harm; one of these, specifically on the left, is armed with <term>harquebusiers</term> <note>soldiers armed with the harquebus, an early type of long-gun</note>, while the other is composed of cavalrymen. We have depicted the image of this entire arrangement on the following leaf under the letter A.

### C H A P T E R V.

->*How the Spaniards arrange an army on the march.*<-

**I**n the time of the Emperor Charles V, when there was war in Germany under Duke Barrabano, the <term>phalanx</term> of the army—or the <term>rear guard</term>—composed of the Spanish nation, was shaped in the form of an exact square. This phalanx had two <term>sleeves</term> or <term>wings</term> consisting of <term>harquebusiers</term>, one of which extended more toward the front of the phalanx, while the other faced its rear. Furthermore, at the head or front of the army, and at its tail, two <term>horns</term> of <term>harquebusiers</term> were established. Behind the tail of the phalanx followed a squadron of nobles, excellently armed, upon very robust and powerful horses. Finally, these were followed by light troops, distributed into two "sleeves" as it were, and with these the <term>baggage train</term> of the army and all other necessary supplies were conducted. In the forward part, they had scouts, pioneers, and field guns, not much differently from the Italians. We have depicted the demonstration of this army on the march in this manner under the letter B.

### C H A P T E R VII.

->*Concerning the arrangement of an army into a Crescent shape.*<-

**T**he arrangement of the main body of an army—including other officers and infantry, but excluding the Harquebusiers <note>original: *Harquebuzeos*; soldiers armed with a heavy portable matchlock gun</note>—into a crescent <note>original: *lunarem*</note> shape is very convenient and can be done quickly during the night. This can be achieved suddenly, either by the swinging of a rope or by using cloaks to mark the positions. And then in that first *rank*, that is, in the outer rank, the Sergeants or officers of each company are to be stationed in a crescent shape. *In the second rank*, toward the center, the armed infantry carrying pikes <note>original: *hastas*</note> shall stand. *In the third row, those not in armor, carrying pikes. In the fourth rank, those equipped with Halberds* <note>original: *Alabardis*; a polearm with an axe-blade and a spike</note>, and so on until the final rank, in which the drummers are to be placed. However, all these ranks should be arranged so that a large enough empty space is left near the center where the Captain General may reside with his cavalry. In the opening between the two horns of the crescent, a Major Sergeant <note>original: *Sergans major*</note> should be positioned to carefully watch the rank of Harquebusiers stationed outside the crescent formation. For in four parts, equally distant outside the crescent shape, four compact bodies of Harquebusiers are arranged; these are positioned as if at four corners to preserve the crescent shape from any unexpected danger from attackers. We have depicted the figure of this type of army arrangement in this place, marked with the letter D.

# BOOK FOUR

## *On several machines very necessary for war.*

### CHAPTER I.

#### *On the invention of a certain ladder, which can most easily be carried with any army or simple troop for climbing the walls and ramparts of any fortification.*

This kind of ladder is not only light in weight, but it can also be packed into a very small space. Therefore, let a pole of very strong composition, or some other wood of the same kind—which is usually ash—be divided into many equal parts of one and a half or two feet in length. At one end of each stick, a hole large enough should be made; at the other end, the wood should be shaped so that it can easily enter the hole of another stick. On the top end of only one of the sticks mentioned above, a large iron hook <note>original: *hamus ferreus*</note> should be fixed, and that quite firmly, so that it can be placed and held tenaciously and strongly upon the summit of a wall. Then, take two ropes of the same length and size. With one rope, bind all the ends of one side of the sticks together, in such a way, however, that the hole of one stick is joined with the end of another that is shaped to enter that hole; and let the distance between the sticks thus tied be about the measure of one foot. Afterward, from their opposite ends, a proportional binding should be made with the second rope. 

When, therefore, an army on the march wishes to carry such a ladder with it, all the sticks are to be bound together like a bundle <note>original: *fasciculi*</note>. But where this ladder must be applied to the top of some fortification, then the sharper end of each stick must be strongly pushed and fixed into the hole of the stick next to it; and in this way, the ladder will take the form of a very long pole. By using the summit of this pole, which carries the iron hook, it will not be difficult to reach a firm part of the top of a fortification. Once the hook is attached, with a slight force and a pull, each stick is separated from the one next to it, and it will take the true form of a ladder. The ends of the ropes hanging down toward the ground must be fixed with strong binding to wooden stakes driven deep enough into the earth.

The illustration of this ladder—both tied together in a bundle and prepared for raising to the top of the ramparts, and also in the form by which its sticks are to be separated and drawn out into the appearance of a ladder—we have depicted in this place clearly enough.

### Treatise II, Part VI, Book IV
->Page 414<-

<note>This page consists of a detailed technical engraving illustrating the specialized equipment required for scaling fortifications during a siege.</note>

**The Engineering of Scaling Apparatus**

The primary figure on the left illustrates a **rope ladder** <term>scala funis</term> <note>original: "scala," meaning ladder; "funis," meaning rope</note>. This device is constructed with flexible side-ropes and rigid, horizontal rungs to provide stability for a soldier's weight. At the very top, it is fitted with a large, four-pronged **grappling hook** designed to catch onto the stone masonry of a parapet or wall.

The figure on the right demonstrates an alternative design for a vertical ascent. This apparatus consists of a thick, central support—either a heavy **rope** <note>original: "funis"</note> or a slender pole—to which a series of **rope-loop steps** are attached. These loops served as individual foot-holds. Like the ladder, this device is crowned with a sturdy **grappling hook** to ensure a secure anchor at the summit. 

Such tools were essential components of <term>military engineering</term> in the early modern period, allowing infantry to bypass the primary defenses of a fortress.

<header>CONCERNING CERTAIN MILITARY MACHINES.</header>
<sig>Fff 2</sig>

### C H A P T E R  II.

->*Concerning a certain instrument which soldiers can sometimes carry with them, for tearing apart bars and opening gates, and destroying them, however strong they may be.*<-

**T**he construction of this instrument must be mostly of iron, so that it does not break, or at least its sides should be made of very strong wood covered in an iron skin, joined together with very sturdy joints. The rod <note>original: *radius*; here referring to a toothed rack or bar</note> passing through its middle must be made of iron, or rather the strongest steel, carved with very strong teeth along its forward half. These teeth must be fitted to the teeth of the wheel marked A; the construction of which must also be very strong. All the power and strength of this instrument consists in the multiplication of those mechanisms which are ultimately called "force." <note>The author is describing mechanical advantage through a gear train.</note> Therefore, the first moving axle must pass through the middle of both longer sides, extending through the iron rod at right angles; on its side near the handle of that axle, spiral teeth <note>original: *dentes spirales*; these are worm gears used to increase torque</note> are to be fashioned, so that they fit easily into the wheel of the adjacent axle. On the opposite side of that same adjacent axle, other spiral teeth similar to the first are to be carved, which must also turn the wheel of a third axle; and on the opposite part of the third axle, again other spiral teeth similar to the previous ones are to be made, which, entering the wheel of the fourth axle, also turn it. And in this way, you can multiply the force of this instrument infinitely, until you reach the final axle, whose wheel—driven by the teeth of the second-to-last axle—will also turn that strong wheel fitted to the teeth of the iron rod. By its rotation, the iron rod will be moved little by little and step by step against the gate. But here it must be carefully noted that at the front of this machine, very large and strong iron hooks are to be joined and connected; these must have a firm grip and adherence with hooks fixed to the gate, or with some other part of the gate's structure. Once these things are done, the central axle is to be turned with the handle by the strength of only one man; as it moves, the horns <note>original: *cornua*; the working ends or prongs of the device</note> of the iron rod itself will very easily penetrate the gate and will easily break and tear apart its planks, however much they are reinforced with iron.

Here indeed it must be noted that all the aforesaid axles with their wheels and spiral teeth must be made of steel or iron of the strongest composition. The illustration of this machine follows here.

<vocab>military machine, instrument, iron, wheel, spiral teeth (worm gears), gate, handle, steel, iron rod (rack)</vocab>

### C H A P T E R III.

->*Concerning the discovery by the besieged, through which they are accustomed to understand if the besiegers are digging any subterranean passages to overturn and remove the ramparts of the fortification with gunpowder.*<-

**T**here are several inventions used by the besieged <note>Those defending a fortress during a siege.</note> to recognize the mines <note>original: "fodinas"; tunnels dug under walls to collapse them, often using explosives.</note> of the besiegers. By these means, they not only perceive the efforts of the enemy but also the exact location of the fortification or rampart toward which those passages have been directed. Therefore, when the besieged fear such a stratagem (for most often during the time of digging, the besiegers are accustomed to fire their cannons and create a great noise with drums simply so the besieged are less able to hear or perceive their subterranean works), they place a drum upon that rampart which they hold most in suspicion. Having placed a needle upon its top surface, if that subterranean work is being carried out near that bastion or wall, the needle will be seen to jump for every stroke the diggers make underground. In that place where the needle is perceived to move more, higher, and more vigorously, the danger is to be more expected in that location. Once this is known, the besieged immediately build other counter-mines <note>original: "contrafodinas"; defensive tunnels intended to intercept or destroy the enemy's mines.</note> to impede and resist the efforts of the besiegers, by which they destroy the enemy’s works. Some also fix small bells to sticks, or by tying them to a string, they suspend that string between two sticks fixed in the ground; in this way, the bells will give a sound at every percussion made under the earth. Moreover, the manner of these operations is declared in the following two demonstrations.

### C H A P T E R  V.

->*On the method or invention by which cavalry can most easily break into an enemy phalanx.*<-

**L**et a machine be fashioned from steel plates of a sufficiently thick substance, having a single angle, and let that angle be as acute as can conveniently be made. Let the height of the angle be equal to the height of a man sitting upon a horse. In its lower part, let there be a wheel upon which this machine can be moved, and let a "tail" <note>original: "cauda"; likely a steering or hitching bar at the rear</note> be attached to the wheel, so that two or three horses can be harnessed to each of its sides; however, let it be done in such a way that both the riders and the horses are protected by the sides of this angular machine. Once this is done, let the horses, briskly urged on by spurs, be made to move rapidly toward the enemy <term>phalanx<note>A dense tactical formation of infantry, usually armed with long spears or pikes.</note></term>. Because of the sharpness of its angle, the machine will very easily penetrate through the spears, and by the force of the horses—who ought to be very strong and spirited—the footmen of that phalanx will be thrown into consternation and will grant entry to the cavalry following this machine. Once the order of the phalanx is broken and the line of the entire army is scattered, it will not be difficult to obtain victory. The design of this machine follows at the letter E. <note>Refers to an illustration labeled "E" in the original manuscript's figures.</note>

### C H A P T E R  VI.

->*On artificial fire combined with a small cannonball, which not only easily penetrates any iron breastplate, but also burns the human body wearing those arms by the violence of its flame.*<-

**I** saw this experiment with my own eyes in <term>Paris<note>original: "Lutetiæ", the Roman name for Paris.</note></term>, where it easily penetrated a breastplate set before it, and even after that penetration, the flame of the fire remained unextinguished. A certain friend of mine, who revealed that experiment to me at that time, handed down its composition to me under an oath of secrecy in this manner: Take powdered camphor as much as you wish, and dissolve it in the best <term>water of life<note>original: "aquâ vitæ"; high-proof distilled alcohol or brandy.</note></term>, and add to it linseed oil or pig fat, and a little wax or <term>Burgundy pitch<note>A highly flammable resin squeezed from spruce trees.</note></term> (take a little of each of them), and let a waxed cloth be made with these. This being done, let a small lead or iron ball or square-bolt be taken and first moistened in that water in which the aforementioned camphor was dissolved without any other substance; afterwards, let it be wrapped in a portion of the said cloth and thus placed into the <term>bombard<note>An early form of cannon.</note></term>, and everything that was promised above will be performed.

## CHAPTER VIII.

### On the use of the elevation or depression of cannons.

Since in military affairs the knowledge of the elevation or depression of the muzzle of a <term>cannon</term><note>original: *tormenti*. While this Latin word historically referred to catapults or siege engines, in this 17th-century context, it refers to gunpowder artillery.</note> is extremely useful and necessary, we believe it is worthwhile to discuss the variety and reasoning of this positioning here. Indeed, according to this positioning, the shot of the ball is made either farther or closer. But so that this may be understood more correctly, we will first set forth two propositions by which the logic of the motion of the balls will be explained; then, we will explain the construction of the instrument, or <term>Quadrant</term><note>An instrument shaped like a quarter-circle used to measure angles of elevation, essential for aiming artillery at distant targets.</note>, for the certain and determined knowledge of the elevation or depression of the cannons.

### Proposition I.

*All equally heavy bodies, at the end of some <term>violent motion</term><note>Aristotelian physics divided movement into "natural motion" (an object falling to its natural place, the Earth) and "violent motion" (movement caused by an outside force, like an explosion or a throw).</note> that is outside the perpendicular of the Horizon, will move with their natural motion, which will be continuous with the curved motion caused by the violence. For example: A ball violently shot into the air, finding no resistance at the end of its violent motion, will be moved by its natural motion in this manner.*

A. B. C. D. is the description of the entire line, both violent and natural, where A. B. C. will be the passage of violent motion, and C. D. the passage made by natural motion, which will be continuous and tangent with the curve B. C. at point C.

### Proposition II.

*The longest effect <note>In this context, "effect" refers to the range or distance traveled by the projectile.</note> which an equally heavy body can cause from its origin by violent motion upon a plane, or some straight line, is that which is precisely terminated in*

*...on the same plane or straight line, since the ejection is made with similar power and violence.* For example, if the **motive power** <term>motive power: the initial force applied to a projectile, such as the explosion of gunpowder</term> at point **A** violently emits a body **B** of equal weight into the air, whose passage follows the path **A. E. D. B.**, it must be concluded that point **D** is the instant dividing the <term>violent passage: movement driven by external force rather than gravity</term> **A. E. D.** from the <term>natural passage: the downward fall of an object toward its natural place, the Earth</term> **D. B.** and that from point **A** to that point **D**, the line **A. D. C.** should be drawn. Now we say that point **D** is the furthest effect from point **A** that body **B** can produce upon the line **A. D. C.** or upon the plane where the said line **A. D. C.** is situated. For if the said body **A** <note>The text likely means "the motive power at A"</note> were to eject body **B** higher above the horizon, it would then produce the effect of natural motion upon the said line **A. D. C.** as appears in the line or passage **A. F. G.** at point **G**; this effect at **G** will certainly be closer to point **A**, for its body **B** will not end its violent motion on the line **A. D. C.**, but rather above it at point **F**. Thus, the higher body **B** is emitted, the closer it approaches its starting point **A** upon the line **A. D. C.** The reason is that its violent motion is further removed from its limit or end—namely, the line **A. D. C.**

Similarly, if that body **B** is raised less from the line or passage **A. D. C.**, and the power at **A** ejects it so that its passage is along the line **A. I. H. K.**, then the effect of its violent motion will be upon the line **A. D. C.** at point **H**, which will also be closer to its origin than **D**, because the end of such violent motion will reach below the line **A. D. C.** at point **K**. And finally, the more downward and lowered the ejection of body **B** is, the closer its effect will be to its beginning at **A** upon the line **A. D. C.**, because its violent motion will end below the line **A. D. C.**

### On the Gunner's Quadrant.
<note original: "De Quadrante Tormentario">A 'tormentum' was an engine of war, hence 'tormentarius' refers to artillery or gunnery.</note>

However, **Geometers** divide their **Quadrant** into only twelve sections; those skilled in the **art of gunnery** <note original: "bombardica arte">The science of using 'bombards' or early cannons.</note> also follow this in the description of their quadrant, and they construct their instrument in the following manner.

Let a **gnomon** <term>gnomon: here referring to an L-shaped square used for measurement</term> be made of copper or very solid wood, in whose interior angle the quadrant must be included, along with its **plumb line**. But it should be noted here that one leg or limb of the gnomon must be longer than the other, so that it can, at will...

### *How should a piece of artillery be positioned to achieve its longest distance in firing?*

By natural geometric reason, it is established that a piece of artillery must be elevated 45 degrees above the horizon, which is half of the 90 degrees that constitute a quarter part of the world <note>The author uses "world" to refer to a full 360-degree circle</note>: Therefore, so that this may be done more aptly, let the previously described quadrant be taken, and let its longer leg, namely A. B., be placed into the mouth of the artillery piece; then let the weapon be elevated until the plumb line passes through the middle of the quadrant—that is, so that it divides the part of the quadrant E. G. F. into two equal parts, specifically at point G. For then it can be said that the weapon aims directly at the 45th degree above the horizon, or 6 parts on the quadrant: An example follows, *Number 1.*

Proof of this matter was established in the city of **Verona**, where a certain master, eminent in this art, named **Leonardo Justinianus**, was debating this aforementioned assertion with another **Master from Padua**. He strenuously defended the principle against the other, who wished to lower the weapon by two points out of the six given on the quadrant. Therefore, with silver and coins deposited as a wager for the victor’s prize, a <term>Culverin|a long, slender cannon designed for range</term> was brought out from *Santa Lucia*. That **Veronese** master fired the first ball according to his elevation, and the distance between the start and the end was 1,972 measures, each of which consisted of 7 feet according to the Veronese calculation. Afterward, that **Paduan** master, according to his own theory, lowered the weapon by two points and fired his load from the Culverin; only 1,872 of the aforementioned measures were counted between the beginning and the end of that flight. Consequently, the judges verified the aforementioned opinion, which they had previously doubted much; the example of the positioning of the weapon according to the **Paduan's** intention is shown here, *Number 2.*

434

TREATISE II. PART VII. BOOK I.

<meta>catchword: BOOK</meta>

-> ### CONTENTS OF PART VII. TREATISE II. <-

In the construction of machines that cause motion, two primary factors are considered:
- **Instruments**
    - Oblong [straight], such as the **Steelyard** <note>original: *Romana*; referring to the 'statera Romana' or steelyard balance, representing lever-based mechanics.</note>
        - <gloss>A. The Steelyard discovered by proportions.</gloss>
    - Circular, such as **Wheels**, of which there are two distinct types; for some are moved:
        - From the exterior and the circumference, of which there are 2 kinds:
            - One is moved by **combs** <term>pectines: gear teeth or comb-like strips used to drive a wheel</term>.
            - Another by force at the end [of the radius]: **Simple** or **Multiplied**.
        - From the interior and from the center, that is, by the **axle**, which is either **Minor** or **Major**.
- **The Agent and cause of motion**, of which there are two types, because it is either:
    - **Unstable and falling**, such as water or sand.
    - **Fixed**, localized, and not receding, such as a comb [gear tooth], force at the end, etc.
    - And it should be noted that force in machines is either:
        - **At the beginning**, that is, from the center.
        - **At the end**, namely from the surface [or perimeter].

# BOOK ONE
## Concerning long moving instruments.

---

### CHAPTER I.
### *Of the Steelyard, and of instruments invented from the Steelyard.*

The **S**teelyard <note>original: "Romana"; a type of balance with unequal arms</note> is an instrument commonly used in France, Italy, and Spain, by which the correct weights of sold goods are determined. It is described in this manner.

<note>A diagram showing a steelyard balance with a hook or pan at point A, a pivot (fulcrum) at B, and a sliding weight on a long beam marked with graduated letters from C through R.</note>

The overbalancing <term>praeponderatio: the act of one side weighing more than the other</term> with this *Steelyard* instrument consists in moving the weight away from its center. Therefore, two equal weights at an equal distance from the center of the instrument will stand in equilibrium; however, by as many degrees as one of them is moved further from the center than the other, by that many proportions it will infallibly outweigh the other that is less distant from the center.

->*Demonstration.*<-

Let there be, for example, two equal weights, A and C, specifically of one pound; because they are at an equal distance from the center of the instrument, B, they are balanced in equal poise. If, however, weight C is moved further away from the instrument's center—namely to the points marked D, E, F, G, and so on—it must necessarily outweigh the other weight that is less distant from the center, which is weight A.
The further the weight progresses from the center toward the end of the instrument (provided the movement is proportional), the greater its overbalance will be, yet it will remain proportional: from this, it is clear that the "multiplication" of weight is nothing other than the distancing of the weight from the center of the moved line.

->*Demonstration.*<-

The force of this proposition is clarified through three propositions of geometric and arithmetic progression or proportion previously described by us.

*Second Treatise of the Macrocosm.*

# ON OBLONG MOBILE INSTRUMENTS.

A, B, C, D are hooks, to which we can attach massive weights, so that the lifting of the load might become easier.

*E. is the load to be raised.*

*F. is a small wheel <note>original: "rotula"; likely a pulley or sheave.</note>, to which the cord G. L. is attached, and in whose hollow groove the cords M. and N. are accustomed to slide for the easier raising of the load.*

*I. is the center of the instrument.*

*K. H. is the cord to be pulled by a man, raising the entire load E.*

Since, therefore, the distances G. and P. are equal, and likewise the weights suspended at those points are in equilibrium, it follows from the first proposition of this work that point K. will multiply the force applied to weight P. or G. Consequently, a smaller weight <note>In this context, "weight" refers to the force or effort exerted by the person pulling.</note> at point K. acting through the cord K. H. will cause the larger load E. to ascend more easily, the more the beam <term>lancea <gloss>A horizontal lever or arm</gloss></term> K. G. has been extended in length.

### CHAPTER II.

->*Concerning wheels, the parts of wheels, and their proportion.*<-

**S**ince the wheel is the mother of all instruments, and its construction consists in the circle and the proportion of the circle, it seems necessary to explain briefly how the proportion and power of the circle are observed in building machines and how they are put into practice. Regarding the proof of this matter, we wrote something above when we mentioned the steelyard <note>original: "Romana," referring to the *statera Romana* or Roman balance scale, which uses a sliding weight on a lever arm.</note>, for indeed it should not be considered as anything other than the radius <term>Semidiameter</term> of a certain circle, as we shall explain in the following sections.

->*Rule I.*<-

->*Every wheel turning on its own axle is moved more easily the larger it is, whether it is touched upon its surface or when the force that acts upon it and causes motion is applied to it.*<-

From these principles, it is clear that wheel A. C. is moved more easily than wheel A. B., and wheel A. D. more easily than A. C., and so on for the others. We stated the reason for this in the first proposition of chapter 1. For a weight of one pound at A and another at B will stand in equilibrium <note>balanced equally</note>, but the same weight at C will outweigh...

### TREATISE II. PART VI. BOOK I.

...it will weigh twice as much as at A; however, the same weight at D will outweigh A three times over; and so it follows for the rest. From these facts, it is manifest that the further the radius <note>original: semidiameter</note> extends from its center, the more rapid its motion will be. We shall provide an example of this principle through a common experiment.

*A. will be the underlying center <note>the fulcrum</note>.*
*B. a load <note>onus</note> placed a short distance from the center.*
*C. a hand at a shorter distance from the center; thus it lifts more weakly.*
*D. a hand at a greater distance from the center, which therefore lifts with more force.*

This lever <term>vectis<gloss>a mechanical bar used with a pivot to move a heavy load</gloss></term>, when placed under a heavy weight, possesses greater efficiency for lifting the longer it is, provided that some support is placed beneath it to serve as the center.

->Rule II.<-

Since there are two types of driving force <note>ratio agentis</note>—namely that which is fluid and shifting like water, or that which is fixed, localized, and stationary like a gear tooth <note>original: pecten</note> and the force applied at the end—therefore, concerning the fluid or shifting force, this proportion must be observed: in any wheel whose outer surface is divided into many equal parts (for instance, into 24 or more or fewer parts), if a single weight is applied to each of these parts, this weight at the straight extremity A would exert its full weight; at the middle angle B, only half its weight; and at the direct point C, nothing at all. Thus, you will be able to measure the total weight of any wheels by the division of a straight line beginning from the center and moving toward the circumference, as was stated in the preceding proposition: For by this divided line, it is shown—

### Rule III.

*If the <term>axle</term><note>Latin: "axis"; the central shaft on which a wheel revolves.</note> of any wheel is large and thick, its wheel will turn with difficulty: on the contrary, if it is small and thin, its wheel will rotate easily.*
The reason is that the surface of an axle, when far distant from the internal point of its center, is easily hindered by the force acting upon the surface—that is, by the physical material placed against it, touching the surface upon which the axle rests or over which the axle turns.

### Rule IV.

*The larger <note>original: "altior", literally "higher" or "taller" in diameter.</note> the wheel is, and the smaller its axle, the more easily it is moved, provided the motion is applied to its outer edge—that is, if it is acted upon from its surface: But regarding wheels moved from the center, the opposite must be understood; which will be discussed in the following chapter.*

## Rule V.

*In all machines that exert force, wheels must be placed that are moved from the outside, and the load must be applied to the axle through some suitable means, such as a rope; and although the lifting proceeds slowly, it is nonetheless done more securely than by other methods, because the force of the entire wheel is always driven back into the axle. For just as every heavy object, no matter where it is placed, always naturally seeks its own center and freely falls toward it, so the forces of the entire wheel are gathered in the axle, as will appear clearly in the following sections.* <note>The author uses a gravitational analogy—where objects seek the center of the Earth—to explain how mechanical advantage concentrates force at the central spindle or axle of a machine.</note>

---

### CHAPTER III.

->Concerning the first distinction of wheels, that is, concerning wheels moved from the outside.<-

**T**here are two primary types of this distinction of wheels: one is moved by a <term>comb</term> <note>original: "pectinem"; in this context, it refers to a toothed gear or pinion that meshes with another wheel.</note>, and the other by <term>force at the end</term> <note>original: "vim in fine"; this refers to a worm gear or endless screw mechanism where the driving force is applied at the end of a threaded shaft.</note>. The first type is more common because it can operate either more quickly and lightly, or even more powerfully when necessary; it is suitable for any method of construction and is constantly employed in the structure of clocks and other machines used by cooks for roasting food. <note>These "roasting machines" were mechanical jacks that used weights and gears to automatically turn a spit over a fire.</note> The second type, using force at the end, acts more slowly but more powerfully, because *for any given period or revolution, the force at the end can only advance a single tooth.*

#### Rule I.

*A wheel placed below a worm gear can never act upon or move that gear in the same way a wheel moves a toothed pinion; rather, it would be broken.* <note>The author is describing the "self-locking" nature of worm gears: the screw can turn the wheel, but the wheel usually cannot turn the screw.</note>

#### Rule II.

*The worm gear must have at least three threads so that one can support the other, as is shown below.*

#### Rule III.

*The wheel to which the worm gear is connected can be made in two ways, both of which are good; however, the first is better than the second because it is stronger and more easily prepared: their appearance is shown here, Figure 1.*

#### Rule IV.

*The higher the wheel, the greater its force, according to the first and second rules of the second chapter: but then its motion is slower.* <note>A larger diameter wheel provides more leverage but requires more movement to complete a rotation.</note>

#### Rule V.

*The force of the wheels is doubled if another wheel is applied to the driving pinion or to the worm gear: for then the weight will not be so great that it cannot be lifted by the hand of a single man, which is demonstrated in the following figures, Figure 2.*

### Rule VI.

*If a third wheel is added to the preceding machine, it will be an instrument of enormous power; however, the wheels must be proportioned such that the first driving wheel is always larger in diameter <note>original: "altior," literally "higher" or "taller," referring here to the diameter or height of the gear wheel</note> than the second, and the second (or intermediate) wheel is larger than the third. Likewise, the first should be narrower and more delicate than the second, and the third must be stronger than the other two.*

The reason is that the first wheel undergoes the least stress <note>original: "patitur," meaning to suffer or endure force</note>, the second more, and the third the most. Nevertheless, it is not as critical to focus on the height of the wheels as it is to ensure that the final wheel is the strongest; see Diagram No. 1.

->### TREATISE II. PART VII. BOOK I.###<-

The principle of motion in this instrument is the same as in wheels of the first category—that is, those moved from the outside—where the force is broken down and spread out into smaller portions proportioned over time. Thus, to lift any load using instruments that are light to move from the start, time is multiplied along with the weight: that is, as much more time is consumed as the instrument is pulled more lightly at the beginning. <note>The author is describing the fundamental law of mechanics: what you gain in power, you lose in speed or time.</note>

Such instruments can therefore be called **weight dividers**, assigning to each of a man’s pulls only such a weight as can naturally be lifted without any mechanical aid. For example, a person who can lift one hundredweight <note>Latin: *Centenarium*; a unit of 100 pounds</note> from the ground to a height of one foot without an instrument, can—once he has the instrument—lift ten hundredweights just as easily and with no greater effort. However, it is necessary to perform the same motion ten times over ten feet, whether the path is a direct vertical, straight, curved, in a winding circle, or however else it may be configured. Therefore, in ten minutes, one man lifts by means of the instrument what ten men would lift in a single minute without it.

A similar principle is found in the instrument depicted above, because a single man can lift a maximum weight; but to lift it to the height of one foot, he must pull nine palms <note>Latin: *palmas*; a measurement roughly the width of a hand</note> of rope. This is because the rope is added in a sixfold arrangement, and the remainder is taken up by the width according to the size of the circular wheels.

The cause of this ease <note>Latin: *levitatis*; literally "lightness," referring to the reduction of effort</note> is that the rope is forced by these small wheels <note>Latin: *orbiculos*; likely pulleys or rollers</note> to deviate from its direct or taut line away from the center, and this occurs as many times as you place other small wheels beneath it.

One should note here a double progression or multiplication, from double to double; for as much strength as you acquire through the first small wheel, you have twice as much in the second; likewise in the third, double that of the second, and so proceeding consequently. The fact that such a diversion of the rope from its center—that is, from its taut line of pull (whether the pull is made in a straight or indirect line)—brings about ease, is established by logic: because the rope must be longer in such a curve or bend than in a straight or direct line; and when the rope is longer, the operation is slower, as is clear from the illustration.

## CHAPTER IV.

->*Concerning wheels of the second classification, that is, those moved from the center.*<-

**T**he use of wheels that are moved from their center is specifically for clocks and those machines which cooks use constantly for roasting meat <note>original: "cibos assandos." This refers to mechanical roasting spits used in large kitchens</note>. In such devices, force is not the primary requirement, but rather speed—meaning a high frequency of rotations. This is designed so that from the first fundamental wheel, which sometimes turns only once in 24 hours (more or less), the speed is multiplied until the uppermost small wheel may turn two hundred times. This is achieved through three or four wheels with an equal number of pinions <note>Latin: "pectinibus," literally "combs," referring here to the gear teeth or the small gears that mesh with larger ones</note>, and rarely with more, except in clocks with double weights which are designed to run for a longer duration.

### *Rule I.*

->*All clocks are either moved by a mainspring <note>Latin: "mola," literally a millstone, but used here to describe the coiled spring mechanism</note>—such as the small ones worn around the neck or placed upon a desk or table—or they operate by the heaviness of a weight, as is the case with all larger clocks built in houses, buildings, or church towers. However, the principle of the wheels is the same for all, regardless of their diverse construction.*<-

### *Rule II.*

->*All clock wheels are moved from the center, as has been said above.*<-

### Rule III.

*This horological motion is the release of forces inherent in the center, although it expands through the multiplication of wheels and revolutions <note>original: *peridiorum*; likely referring to the peripheral rotations of the gears</note> into imperceptible parts; whereas the previously discussed motion of machines is the restriction, or the gathering and union of many wheels and tangential or lightly moving parts into a single center.*

It is therefore evident that the power <term>vis</term> <note>Latin for "force" or "power," referring here to the mechanical energy driving the device</note> of clocks originates at the beginning, or from the center, and is dilated and expanded outwards: whereas the force of the aforementioned heavy machines is found at the end, and is collected in the axles, as has been previously stated.

The **p**ress used by printers for copper plates <note>original: "æneas tabulas"; these plates were used for high-detail engravings</note>, or for flattening metal sheets, when it features two rollers <note>original: "voluolos"; cylinders used to apply pressure</note> or shafts, it should be noted that the upper one ought to be of a smaller thickness, and the lower one of a larger thickness. The water wheel <term>rota aquaria</term> stands twelve feet in height—that is, its total diameter. The second wheel, labeled D, is five feet in diameter, while the height of the third wheel, A, is four feet. This second wheel (D) has 72 teeth, and the third wheel (A) has 50. The small pinion gear B is made with 12 teeth, and pinion C has 10. It is therefore calculated that the water wheel must rotate thirty times for every single revolution of the third wheel. <note>The gear ratio is calculated by dividing the teeth of the driven wheels by the teeth of the pinions: (72/12) × (50/10) = 6 × 5 = 30.</note> To the spindle or shaft <term>arbor</term> of this third wheel, the pumps or water-lifting machines <term>haustra</term> are attached. Their lead pistons <term>pistilla plumbea</term> are designed to be heavy enough that they fall back down by their own weight after they have drawn up the water.

However, if they are sufficiently heavy, it is actually better to attach the pistons to a crank <term>manubrium</term> on the third wheel; in this way, they can be both lifted and pushed back down by the mechanical action.

First, the outer surface of the large wheel is set in motion by the force of the flowing water. By its rotation, pinion B drives the second wheel D. The pinion of this second wheel then drives the third wheel in a circular motion. As this third wheel turns its axle, it simultaneously moves two wooden beams that pass through its center. As the ends of the first beam move successively away from the shaft’s rotation, they press down on one end (K) of the beam F-K. This depression causes the opposite end to rise, which pulls up the iron rod F-R. At the exact moment of this lift, the end of the other beam (S) is pushed down because of the weight of the lead piston and its valves <term>ventilibus</term>. Thus, these two beams act alternately with opposing motions. Through these actions, water at the bottom (T) is lifted upward through the pumps and is discharged into the channel V-V.

The crank of the third wheel will perform the same duty as the aforementioned axle or shaft. In that configuration, the curvature H would take the place of beam n-n, and the other curve I would replace beam G-P. In our opinion, this second method is the one that should be chosen.

<page-num>458</page-num>
# TREATISE II. PART VII. BOOK II.

**A.** The main wheel. **B. C.** Weights on one side. **D. E. F.** Weights on the other side. **G.** The carrying rod. **H.** Supporting the rod. **I.** The lifting roller. **K.** Its comb <term>comb<gloss>the teeth or cogs of a gear</gloss></term>. **L.** The crown wheel. **M.** The comb of the crown wheel. **N.** The interrupted wheel <term>interrupted wheel<gloss>a gear with teeth along only part of its circumference, allowing for intermittent motion or release</gloss></term>. **O.** The axle. **P.** The small pulley. **Q.** The cord. **R.** A weight of 4 pounds.

The main wheel is constructed in this way: it is divided into 12 equal parts on both sides, and 6 pins are fixed to each side, arranged at the same distance from one another. However, they are placed so that any given pin stands in the middle of two others on the opposite side of the wheel, and not directly next to each other. Once the 6 weights are hung (of which 3 are on the pins of one side, yet all 6 are on one side of the wheel relative to the center), this wheel is found to be burdened with a weight of 15 pounds. This is because weight **C** has a leverage of 4 pounds in a straight line, **D** and **E** are about 7 pounds, and **B** and **F** are 4 pounds; when added together, these equal 15 pounds, as is evident from the first rule of the first chapter and the first and second rules of the second chapter of the first book.

The wheel now moves so that the lowest weight approaches the pin of the carrying rod; being positioned near **B** and **F**, the rod receives this weight through its hook, where it is carried upward while clinging to it, and the wheel, emptied at the bottom, proceeds. Meanwhile, the next pin approaches, following **B**, and in the same place where **B** just was, it receives the weight placed upon it by the rod. In this way, the wheel is always loaded in the upper part and unloaded in the lower part. This is because it is necessary for the rod to ascend while one-twelfth of the wheel turns, and for the same rod to descend again while another twelfth part turns. The rod is elevated by the roller **L**; by turning three times, this roller reaches the full height of the rod, lifting it to the desired pin. Such a roller is turned by its comb **K** by the crown wheel **L**, which is itself turned once by the interrupted wheel **N** via its own comb **M**. The interrupted wheel **O** <note>original: "interfractæ O."</note> always has teeth in every other twelfth part of its circumference, with empty spaces of the same kind in between; this is to release the rod, which is forced to fall by its own weight, and by its fall, it forces the roller **Q** and the crown **M** to return. To prevent it from falling with too much force, it is suspended by the cord **Q** attached to another rod through the pulley **P**, because as much as one rod falls, the other ascends.

The interrupted wheel is fixed to the shaft or axle of the main wheel and is rotated by its power. The reason that similar instruments are placed on the other side of the main wheel is so that the work of loading and unloading the wheel is constant and continuous; when a weight is removed from one side, it is hung on the other. Thus, the rim always has 5 weights hanging, and one always on the ascending rod.

But, although this Swiss man’s theory is ingenious and plausible—that 5 weights attached to the wheel ought easily to pull and lift one weight—nevertheless, because the force is not proportioned to the time, nothing is achieved here. The ascending weight must travel through the weight of 5 <note>The author means the weight must move a distance equivalent to the displacement of the other five weights</note> or through the space of as many parts as the single weight moves; thus, the single ascending weight lasts as long as the other five by reason of the long transit. Therefore, it cannot overcome itself.

We have described this invention of the Swiss Engineer and his error in this place so that those curious about this science might be struck with a greater diligence in the knowledge of proportions, and might observe them carefully.

*A. A. is the water wheel, by whose motion the small wheel B., attached to the end of the shaft C. C. C., is moved; and by this action, the shaft or axle C. C. C. is also revolved. Along with it turns the channel or pipe D. D. D., constructed from quite hard and thick leather <term>leather (corium)</term>, which winds spirally <note>original: "spiritaliter," referring to the Archimedean screw principle</note> around the axle, as you can see.*

*E. is the valve <term>valve (ventile)</term> placed in the throat of the larger end of the pipe, submerged downward in the water; for the sake of easier understanding, we have depicted this valve separately with the letter F.*

The purpose of this is so that the water entering through the opening in the throat of the pipe does not flow back, until by another revolution of the axle, the mouth—filled with a greater weight of water—pushes the lesser weight through the upper sections by its own heavy load. A greater quantity of water is contained between the mouth of the leather pipe and its throat than between the throat (or valve) and the end G. Because of this, the continuous "preponderance" <note>the physical principle where the heavier volume of water in the lower coils forces the water in the upper coils to move upward</note> of water in the opening of the pipe causes a continuous discharge of water at the top.

<header>TREATISE II. PART VII. BOOK II.</header>

### *Explanation of the preceding diagram.*

Each <term>scoop-pump (haustrum)<note>A flexible, bucket-like vessel, often made of leather in this period, used to draw and lift water.</note></term> is weighted with a proportionate lead weight, marked as **I**. As these scoops are raised by the paddles (**n. n.**) on the spindle (**Q**), the leather is stretched out, expanding much like a folding lantern. Since "nature abhors a vacuum" <note>The author refers to the classical Aristotelian principle *horror vacui*, asserting that space must always be filled with matter.</note>, and because this lantern is sealed at the top so it has no "breath" (meaning it cannot draw in air), it draws in water in the manner of a siphon through a <term>valve (ventile)<note>A one-way flap or valve that allows fluid to move in only one direction.</note></term> located at the bottom of the scoop. Thus it is filled when it is at its highest point. 

As soon as the paddles pass by, the scoop falls and is compressed by the lead weight (**I**) which weighs down the scoop's cover. By this contraction, all the water is compressed and forced out through the valve opening (**E**) located on the side in the opposite wooden channel (**C**). At the same time, it passes through an opening (**m**) in the wooden base of the scoop (though placed higher than the other valve). This opening is outside the scoop but inside the side of the channel, where it is sealed with a lead plate. This must also be called a valve, because when the scoop is being filled, this plate is pulled shut by suction, but when the water is being expelled, it is pushed open by the force of the water. At the end of this channel, a pipe is attached to it along with another valve—which is not strictly necessary but is included for the sake of safety. The water is then forced through this pipe to ascend to whatever height is desired, provided that the proportion of the weight is correctly observed and all the instruments are well-sealed so they do not "breathe" <note>In this context, "breathing" refers to air leaks that would break the vacuum and cause the pump to fail.</note>.

### *The proportion of weight for the scoops and pumps.*

Weigh the water that can fit inside your scoop; then measure its height, and multiply these against the height of the discharge pipe, and you will have the exact proportion. 

For example: Your scoop contains 16 pounds of water and is 2 feet high. Your pipe, however, is 20 feet high. You see, then, that you have ten times the height of the scoop. Therefore, you shall multiply 16 (the weight of the water) by 10, which gives 160. This is the number of pounds of lead required to squeeze the water out as far as the mouth of the pipe. 

Now, add another 10 pounds, making a total of 170. These extra ten pounds (at the very least) are necessarily added for three reasons: 
1. First, because the machinery itself requires weight to overcome its own resistance. 
2. Second, because the water must exit the pipe with some force, rather than just reaching the opening. 
3. Third, because water compressed within a tall pipe becomes a more compact and heavier mass than if it were weighed out piece by piece. 

And these 170 pounds will be your lead weight, with which your scoop must be burdened to achieve an elevation of 20 feet. Otherwise, you will achieve nothing.

A. The <term>draw-pump</term> <note>original: 'haustrum seu pompa'</note> or lifting machine.

F. This is the wheel driven by the lower wheel G; the pinion E is moved in a circle by its teeth.
H. The pinion that drives wheel G.

## The Use of this Instrument.
This instrument is classified among wheels of the first order and is highly necessary for many purposes. There is no doubt that it can lift a great quantity of water with very little effort, thanks to the mechanical advantage provided by the arrangement of the wheels. 

The length of the pump A is 35 feet, while its width is 1 and 1/4 feet.

### Explanation of the preceding diagram.

The primary mover in the carriage turns the handle **K** <note>Latin: *manubrium*</note>. This handle, through its axis, moves the wheel **L** described on the side. Wheel **L**, by its gear-teeth <note>Latin: *pectine*, literally a "comb," referring here to a toothed gear</note>, turns the wheel **I**. The small wheel **I** turns the shaft **F.F.** <note>Latin: *arborem*, literally a "tree," used in mechanics to mean a main shaft or spindle</note>. That shaft, with its teeth, acts upon the teeth of the axis **E.E.**, forcing it to rotate as well. This axis moves the small wheels **H.H.**, which use their teeth to drive the teeth of the wheels attached to the sides; thus, those wheels are turned by the force of the aforementioned small wheels. These side wheels, moving forward or backward, also move the front wheel **A** either backward or toward the front.
